title: Excellent protection
text:

In fact, do not lose sight of the fact that this is an insert that is designed to go into another case. I am using mine to store a wireless microphone, received and power supply. Overall, this is a wonderful way to protect delicate equipment that is carried in unpadded (or lightly padded) bags. I am so impressed with it that I am considering ordering another for my second wireless microphone set up.

title: I Love This Keyboard, But...
text:
...if you don't have a wrist rest or pad already, I highly recommend that you get one at the same time you get this keyboard. I was introduced to the chiclet- or scissor-style keyboard because of using one at work (using an Apple wired keyboard with an Intel Mac), and I have to say that I prefer it in every way to the more traditional keyboards. It is much quieter, and, for me, the feedback is pleasant. One thing I did not take into account, though, is that I had a wrist rest at work. So when I got this keyboard for home use and started using it, I loved it immediately--until the day I used it for hours on end. Then--ouch! My wrists began to ache.

Overall, this is a great keyboard. It connected to my computer without a problem, and the only lag in keystrokes I have experienced has been when the computer had just been "awakened" from sleep mode. For reasons I will not go into here, I am using this keyboard with a laptop: the laptop keyboard's lights indicate whether or not I have Caps Lock or Num Lock engaged on the wireless keyboard. I understand that won't help people using this keyboard with a desktop computer, but thought I'd put it out there anyway.

My conclusion: if you're a fan of the scissor-style keyboard and you have or are willing to invest in a wrist rest, you will enjoy this keyboard.

title: If You Told Me A Black Briefcase Would Make A Teen Girl Squeal , I Would Not Have Believed You
text:
When I ordered this case, I expected it to be the usual. I would open it, use it, review it and then put it among my other storage bags which I find very handy for my growing collection of electronic devices and other gear that goes along with it. Then my daughter saw it. The squeal was confusing as she snapped it up and ran with it. Why?

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
I have to say, once I pried it out of her grabby hands after she returned from a weekend at a friend's house, I am really impressed by this bag. I think she thought I was going to take it back because she kept hiding it on me!

CONSTRUCTION
This is VERY well made. All edges have reinforcement of cording on them to avoid seams pulling out.

FABRIC
The fabric is very tough nylon. It is sturdy

COMPARTMENTS/POCKETS
There are pockets and storage galore in this thing.

FRONT
It has a flap on it that vecros shut with lining.

NEXT POCKET
Is a half sized compartment with room for pens and pencils and phone pocket.

CENTER
The center is divided by a padded divider. There are pockets for cords, mouse, and other things, as well as padding for laptop and tablet if you choose to put them in there.

FILE POCKET
This is perfect for filing paperwork and manuals, etc. There is a divided section which would be great for invoices and then paid ones, etc.

OUTSIDE POCKET
Another zipper pocket with lots of room for books or papers

HANDLES
The short handles are covered for easy holding so that the straps don't press into your hand.

LONG STRAP

text:
I've been wanting one of these since I first discovered them on a tech blog last year. I have a bad habit of being a grumpy morning person; part of it is going to sleep late, the other part is the way I wake up.
So I then discovered that some alarm clocks wake you by showing you artificial sunlight. Perfect, I thought.

I was excited to get this set up when it arrived. I found the box a bit light, but I got out the pieces and assembled everything straight away. The settings were very easy to get done, even though the buttons seemed confusing at first.

There are touch buttons on the light part, as well as alarm and volume buttons on the base. The lamp itself is a bit light, however. I mean weight-wise. It tips over my nightstand quite a bit.

And that brings me to the buttons. My daughter, two, loves to touch gadgets. This is no exception. If you plan on getting this, put it somewhere where kids can't reach. Even at her slightest touch the settings are constantly reset, so I have to put them back. As of right now I have to reset the settings again, but I do love the clock and I find myself in a better mood in the mornings.

But not when I see my daughter reaching for the clock as I get up.

The light glows after some time, and really gets a good light in my face. The days are getting warmer here in Chicago and so the sun is shining more and more through the windows. Still, I'm able to utilize this alarm to get the sunlight less offensive.
The speaker on it is really clear for the size; maybe I'm just surprised at how well speakers have gotten in alarm clocks.

Overall, great. The lowest brightness for the clock isn't too bad. You can't really see it when the bedroom light is on, but at night it does get a little brighter than it seems. On my nightstand I put a pillow there to block just above the digital clock so the numerals get blocked out but I still get the light from the actual wake-up light.

Overall I'm pleased with it. I could have some heft to keep it more stable, and I'd prefer harder-to-press buttons (both for my toddler and my snooze tendency). Still, it's a lot better than using my phone as my alarm clock, especially since I don't like bringing in phones into my bedroom, thus allowing me to get to sleep right away.

title: OK tablet, poor kindle!
text:
Kindle Fire is an adequate tablet (GREAT tablet for the price) but it remains a tablet with a marginal Kindle reader app. If you like the Kindle app on your iPhone, you will like the Fire. But it will never be a Kindle replacement until the app provides a way to organize books. There is no equivalent to Kindle shelves. You can view books by title, author, or most recent. You can filter them by books on the device, or all books including those in the cloud. That is it.

There is no way to mark a book as 'read'. There is no way to see only unread books. There is no way to view books by topic.

I can't express how annoying it becomes to download a book from the cloud to see if you have read it, find that you have (and that it was really not all that good) and have it automatically move to the top of the 'most recent' sort... which is really the only proxy you have to view unread books. This is probably OK to manage a few dozen books, but when you acquire hundreds, it is totally unmanageable. I have to use my Kindle to determine what I want to read next, and start reading it so it moves to the top of the 'most recent' sort; then I can use my Fire to read it.

The cynic in me says that Amazon wants to sell me both a Kindle and a Fire. But I don't really believe that is it. Some sage said to never assume a nefarious plan when events can be explained by simple incompetence. I think Amazon just needs to add some reasonable management facilities to an otherwise OK app and they will have an adequate tablet and a great Kindle, which I have to believe is the real plan.

title: Easy To Setup Using WPS--Surprisingly Good
text:
This review is for the TP-link AC750 Dual Band WiFi Range Extender

I am using this on a network that has a Mac Mini, a couple of iPhones and an iPad. None of these devices could print to both printers; it was one or the other and not both on every single Apple product. After trying everything I could think of, I bought this extender and tried to set it up using the Quick Setup instructions. Anyone EVER had the experience of those Quick Setups working? I haven't and I've been using this stuff for decades. After Quick Setup failed to do anything other than connect to my router and open my network up to anyone that could get signal, I tried a different approach.

The EASIEST WAY TO SET THIS UP is to use the WPS button on your router and on the device. Press the WPS button on the router, then, press the WPS button on the extender. After a minute or so, the router and extender are paired/connected and the result is a secure connection to the router (uses the router's password--you do have a password don't you) with a much stronger signal in what were dead zones. Placement of the extender is sort of an experiment and moving it from plug to plug will show you the best location. Moving the extender after pairing does NOT foul up the connection.

I have two printers, a Samsung M2070W laser and an Epson Eco Tank inkjet. Both have wireless capability and can use WPS setup. To setup other WPS capable devices, just press the WPS button on the ROUTER and then the WPS button on the next device you want to connect. The connection to the router goes through the connected extender with no problem and does not interfere with the router/extender pairing. Do each device one at a time.

This was the solution I needed and now all wireless devices work together. It's a neat solution to solving signal strength and connectivity that can be an enormous hassle when using multiple devices from different makers.

title: Mixed Bag
text:
I've had this lens for almost a year now. It's a mixed bag, but as long as you understand it's strengths and weaknesses, and use it accordingly, then it's a great general purpose walk around lens.

Here's the deal. It's sharp in the center at all apertures (except f22) and focal lengths, and between 30-60, it's sharp corner to corner and edge to edge, at all apertures (except f22) and focal lengths. So, when I'm shooting scenery, or people, and I know I want it sharp all across the frame, I try to keep it those middle focal lengths.

At 24mm, it's still a great lens, and I shoot at that focal length a LOT, but I know that corners will have a bit of softness. Same thing at 70mm, a bit of corner softness. But it's makes up for it by being able to focus fairly close at 70mm, giving me the ability to do some nice close up work.

I think the biggest problem that folks have with this lens is the price. Most feel that for $1200 it should be a bit better in the corners at 24mm and 70mm. I got mine used, so I feel like I got what I paid for. It's been an outstanding lens, and I much prefer it to using a bag full of prime lenses.

Happy shooting!~

text:
Definitely a neat experience with the horn. I am now considering how it would be to add a 3rd for a center. I also added my little DIY 8" 250 watt sub from Parts Express (Part # 300-7150). A lot of bass now. These little Klipsch could be on their own pretty happily but the added sub really gives it those dynamite explosions.

Update #3 4/20/2019 Maybe Steve Guttenberg is more honest than I originally thought. These are growing on me more all the time. I got in some stands (HA-BKSPKS) that work very well with these speakers. I like them high up where the woofer is with my ear. Higher than one would expect. It makes me suspect the floorstanding versions may not be high enough?

I have tonight lowered the treble to 10 o'clock and upped the bass to 2 o'clock on my Yamaha HTR-5250 receiver (an ancient receiver that was about $500 in 1999.) And now the bass is really thumping hard, no need for a subwoofer and the gritty graininess in the highs are much less bothersome. I thought the treble sounded a bit grainy and the mids a bit edgy but getting the bass up seems to take away any troublesome notes I was hearing. Perhaps a much more costly receiver / amp would make the sound better but I am satisfied with this until I can get out my big system (when I have more house space). Becoming a believer in the Klipsch's. I was a tough sell but they are hooking me.

Update #2 (I'm sorry I hope no one is frustrated with me yet): Rating changed from 1 to 3 and could be a 4 for movie watching or even a 5 in their own way but I have heard better, let me continue:

I have decided to keep these for fun and basically a lack of time and patience to return them - working 12 days straight and being lazy in my time off to deal with returning.

I still don't think these sound better than Elac UB5, those speakers are amazing Andrew Jones got it practically perfect to my ears. The Elac are so PERFECTO but may be a bit boring when compared to the Klipsch? The Klipsch are different; They are fun and some of the best tv speakers because they can produce lifelike "you are there" experience but they have a problem, IMO, of producing layers on layers of music. They become tumultuous on busy rock tracks.

I would classify the RP600M more as the sound you might get from speakers at a good restaurant with a pool table (if that makes any sense) that's just how I have come to think of them. Concert speakers? I don't know, I don't attend concerts regularly, I never really liked the sound at rock concerts (irony).

These are very attractive speakers but so are the Elac UB5. My recommendation get the Elac UB5 if you can only get one set. Get these if you have funds for a second set of fun lively speakers. If you can't afford either the UB5 or the RP600M, get the Fluance ai40 (but they all have their own strengths - the UB5 has no weaknesses that I am aware of, though). I really did originally think the RP600M was a HUGE FAIL and disappointment, but it's not a total one after all but it isn't nearly as clean sounding as the Elac UB5. It's not the ONE I would choose for critical listening but good for excitement and movies, IMO. I haven't tried the UB5 on movies...

Update: These speakers are hard to explain and understand. I want to add that these can play guitars nicely, they can play drums admirably, they can make cymbals and snares lifelike. Voices sound big and room filling. However, when you try to put them all together that is when it becomes a wreck. That is what other reviewers seem to be leaving out. It's not that they are lying, but they are seemingly to deceive.

Rock seems to shine out every flaw of these speakers - the tweeter's frequency emphasis, the woofers muddiness and the lack of focus of the mid-range. With other music, these have an enjoyable sound, even with some garage rock and oldies. It's when you play rock bands like Breaking Benjamin that I believe these speakers do not do those bands justice. Also, with other hard music to play smoothly like contemporary (Christian) or anything of the like. These can sound lacking, thin, and not able to separate instruments well. I think other speakers do those genres of music must more justice than these. And the other reviewers seem to promote them as "specialized" speakers for those genres. I believe that is where my impression so far differ from other reviewers. It's not that I hate these speakers, they just aren't what I expected them to be. For critical listening I would not want these to be my every day speakers.

These are marketed as a "concert" speaker but isn't it hard to replicate a concert with mixed studio edits? Keep that in mind and think about it what you will. If you think that would work or if you think it may work for certain music. Would you expect a bit of a wreck from speakers that try to put off a concert sound with mixed studio music? I mean, you kind of trying to fit a square peg into a round whole if you ask me, at least, for probably 90% of rock out there. Just want you to think about it. I wanted to love these speakers and I do find them interesting in a I want to understand why I am not enjoying like others but I believe what I have come to understand and describe to you is where the issues between me and my enjoyment of these speakers. I will say they could be rated up to 3 stars for rock, but I believe that is generous for the price and competition out there. I still think these are better for other genres than rock and the Fluance ai40 can be more enjoyable for rock but not for other genres because the bass is lacking.

Original Review:

I do not understand why so much critical acclaim has begotten these speakers. They probably deserve a 2-star but not for the price. For the price, they are abysmal disappointments.

These are absolute horror with rock music. They are unfocused, unable to separate instruments well, unclear, mid-range is lacking, highs are heavily concentrated in one frequency. The overall sound is edgy - mids are shouty in some ranges while being lacking in other ranges, imbalanced and unclear. I do not feel I am getting any sort of idea what the song really sounds like and are just getting a loud racket of bleeding together noise. Very underwhelming. I am not entertaining the idea that I need $6000 of high-end gear to make these sound "good". The fact they need gear of that price tells me they are not good on their own.

They look great. I strongly considered my disappointment just being me, thinking they will get better. After 3 weeks, though, and turning on another song and them being inconsistent as always, I have decided to return. I am much happier with my Elac UB5 and Fluance ai40. These sound good for other music like rap and dubstep but for rock they are a dreadful mess.

title: Big sound small package
text:
I needed a speaker for the kitchen because my wife insisted on playing music off of the laptop. While I am no audiophile, this drove me crazy. I also wanted some type of wireless system in order to optimize speaker placement without the hassle of running wires. I felt that bluetooth speakers would be more convenient than Airplay speakers, because finding IP addresses for speakers doesn't add to my listening enjoyment.

This speaker has a small footprint and is easy to pair with a bluetooth capable device. The sound is very good and fills the room. I tend to keep the speaker volume a bit short of maximum capacity because it will develop a "buzziness" if set too high. This solution is a far cry from laptop speakers and would probably sound spectacular if paired with multiple compatible speakers and a subwoofer. I have noticed we now play more music in general because of the ZiiSound.

Two caveats may be noted. First, pairing devices intially is easy, but I have found that when switching among devices, such as our iPhones, the speaker may have trouble picking up the second device. This happens more often after the speaker goes to "sleep" and sometimes necessitates restarting the bluetooth on the phone or hitting the power button on the speaker.

Second, I have found moving the speaker above arm's reach can be a hassle. Due to the somewhat regular need to hit the "connect" or power button on the unit I found that mounting the speaker lower is far more convenient. Mounting brackets are not an option for this unit, but a small shelf is more than adequate.

Despite these small concerns I am very happy with the sound and ease of use of the ZiiSound. The expandability of this system also suggests intriguing ways to enhance the sound of the room at a fairly reasonable cost.

When I got this laptop, the F keys were automatically preset to their functions instead of simply being F keys. Normally, you have to hold "Fn" and hit an F key to use the function, but it was reversed on this machine. Also, the keyboard backlight turned itself off after 20 seconds of inactivity whether or not it was plugged in. It kind of defeats the purpose of a backlit keyboard, in my opinion, when you can't see the keys before you start typing.

At any rate, both the F key and backlight issues were mostly fixed when I updated the BIOS directly from the Acer support site. I was then able to find settings for both in BIOS and disable automatic function key and backlight timeout. My only gripe is that there doesn't seem to be any way to keep the backlight on for more than 20 seconds when unplugged, no matter the power settings or BIOS configuration. Lots of Googling and worthless Acer chat support sessions later, I'm convinced there's no workaround.

That issue aside, I can't really say anything else negative about this machine. At this price point, this is about as good as it gets. If you plan on doing anything other than browsing the internet and using Office, I do recommend purchasing an additional 4GB RAM stick and installing it yourself. It took me maybe 5 minutes with a YouTube tutorial video. Between that extra RAM and the stock SSD, I can run low-end games with Chrome and Skype running in the background all at once with no slowdown whatsoever. It's lightweight, the screen is decently bright, and it'll go for hours without needing a charge.

If you're in the market for a light-to-medium spec laptop for everyday use, this should be your go-to.

title: Fantastic case
text:
I just put my Asus in it, so I'll update this review if my opinion of it changes with use, but the first impression is phenomenal.

tl;dr The pros vastly outweigh the few cons--which are either non-issues or to be expected with any case you choose.

Pros:
- Feels sturdy
- Looks really nice (I got the navy one)
- Doesn't inhibit button, port, or fingerprint scanner use at all
- **Can hold the computer upright at much shallower angles than the computer's built-in kickstand, which is much better for tablet/touchscreen use (it makes it actually comfortable to draw while it's upright).**
- You could still use the pen loop on the keyboard attachment if you want to. The pen actually moves around less using this because you can secure the other side of the pen with the elastic strap when closed.
- The elastic strap to hold it closed was a nice surprise (I didn't notice it when I was choosing the case)

Cons:
- Seemingly doubles the weight of the computer
- They keyboard isn't as strongly secured at an angle because of the straps (this doesn't hinder use, it just makes the keyboard more likely to be knocked flat. The case does NOT weaken the actual connection between the computer and the keyboard. The area where the keyboard is actually plugged in is completely unobstructed).
- You can't fold the keyboard behind the tablet anymore. You have to detach the keyboard if you want to use the computer like a regular tablet (I could see this being a deal-breaker for some, but I was detaching the keyboard most of the time anyway. I wish luck to anyone wanting to find a case that still allows them to do this. The ability to have the tablet upright at much shallower angles makes this a complete non-issue for me).

text:
I purchased this to compare to another case that I own - the [[ASIN:B00V6I7NBE TOUGH Cardioid Condenser Microphone Hard Case with Dense Foam for Audio-Technica AT2020 / AT2020USB / ATR2500-USB / AT2035 Studio and USB Microphones]]. This case is significantly better than the Tough case. For one thing the diced foam is easy to remove. For another, the three bottom layers of foam (described in the product description) make it more convenient to work with, as well as the extra depth and overall inside dimensions of this case. Bear in mind that this and the case to which I am comparing it are the same price.

I do wish there were more dividers included, and also that the long dividers would go across the entire width. However, for my purposes what came with this case is more than sufficient.

One final point of comparison - I believe that in the long run the Tough box will outlast this one because of design and materials. That one is all plastic, while this one is a combination of materials that over time are going to break if roughly handled. That said, I prefer this case and will probably order a few more for some other microphones that I own.

title: Solid performer as a TV or for mirroring from a small screen; some usability quirks
text:
Overall, this is a decent monitor provided you’re not looking for a high-res PC monitor. I’m using it mainly in its TV mode and have been very impressed with the picture quality. The built-in tuner works well (with one exception, as noted below) producing a rich image. It’s also very well suited as an extension for a small screen device, such as a tablet. I’m using it with my Kindle Fire (via HDMI), and it provides for an excellent viewing experience.

Although the native resolution is 1366x768 pixels, the screen size of 24 inches is small enough that the lack of full HD is not missed. What I did miss is the lack of adjustability of the stand. There’s no tilt or swivel – the stand just holds the screen in a fixed position. It really interferes with proper positioning if this is used as a PC monitor, and is also a problem when using it as a TV. While I don’t expect a lot of extras at this price point, the lack of any measure of adjustability is a big oversight.

If you’re familiar with Samsung TVs, the menu system and remote will be straightforward. If you’re not familiar with Samsung TVs, the menu system will take a bit of time to master with all the nested menus. There are a number of short cuts for various picture modes (such as “sports mode” and “movie”) which are simple to select. Once you get more familiar with the options you can delve deeper and make more specific tweaks.

The sound quality is not great – pretty tinny sounding and there’s little bass. An external speaker is highly recommended if you want to get any measure of impressive sound out of this.

The TV tuner is easy to program with channel favorites. I’m using it with an over-the-air antenna, and have been pleased with the number of channels and the signal strength. There is, however, an annoying long lag between pressing the channel up/down button and having the channel lock in.

The remote is typical Samsung – lots of buttons that are all the same size. Workable, but nothing special.

Considering the price point, I find this to be a 4-star product. It would be a 5-star one with the current feature set and limitations if the price were $50 or $60 less; it would be 3-stars should the price go past $225. A worthwhile choice for TV or small screen mirroring provided you can live with the limited adjustability.

title: Reliable long range with no false alarms!
text:
[[VIDEOID:686708847ade6f20c569ff007bf91f40]] The unit comes minimally packaged in a molded clear plastic tray in custom box, inside the shipping box, so no worries of damage. There’s the sensor (with the solar panel, battery, switches and PIR) in a single-piece molded coffee-colored housing, and the black base/receiver unit, now with an external antenna and all the red LEDs to tell you where there is sensor activity, low battery, etc. There is also a USB/micro plug on a long cord to either recharge the sensor battery or power the base unit (which also runs on 4AA batteries, handy for checking out transmission/reception range and locations or in case of power failure.) Also a comprehensive User Guide and Quick Start in perfect English ;) Oh, and they even pack it with a screwdriver so you need nothing else for installation.
After completing charging the sensor with the included plug (20 mins, comes almost fully charged), I put it near the gate to my 400ft long driveway. I have 2 large dogs (45# and 60#) and neither one of them alone will set it off. Both of them together will, and my body will, or a passing vehicle will – so quite sensitive against false alarms. There are 2 switches on the bottom of the sensor (for range and channel), and the plug should you need to boost the battery charge. These are behind a perfectly molded silicone flap on the bottom. We’ll see after one of our sluicing, days-long rains but it looks completely waterproof to me, on the bottom of the unit which shouldn’t really get wet anyway. I found this a convenient placement for changing the settings, too.
The sensor is at the front of my lot, which is enough clear, and the receiver in the house 400ft away picks up the sensor being tripped without flaw. For a real challenge, I took the receiver to the back of the lot, almost 900ft away from the sensor, up a hill with my house in the middle, and such dense jungle with trees and undergrowth 6-10ft high there is no way you can just walk through it. Using a cell phone to coordinate with a friend tripping the sensor at the gate, the receiver went off EVERY SINGLE TIME the sensor was tripped!! I have zero doubt these units would go a full quarter mile and more through less dense natural obstructions (I’m not sure about buildings, but my whole house is in the way for this test!) So I am very happy I didn’t shell out 2-3 times as much for the expensive driveway alarms – this one has a fantastic range!!

title: Unable to Reach Boot Menu and Advanced Recovery Options
text:
UPDATE 03-02-23: After unplugging the machine and letting it sit overnight, the Setup and Boot options became available again somehow. Very strange. I then really, really fought to get a Linux distribution on this machine. I have created dual boot (Windows/Linux) computers 5+ times before easily. This was a real battle. Some of the issue was this machine and weird bios settings, some conflicting Internet directions (not this machine's fault). In the end I finally managed to just wipe it entirely and install Mint. I had wanted to keep Windows 11 in order to be able to experiment with it. I may end up keeping this machine after all, but for gods' sakes, don't try to put Linux on here and please read original review below.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
I bought this machine to dual boot in Linux or at least re-image into a Linux machine. The first few times I entered Setup (by pressing Escape) it seemed to respond correctly. A few different Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Debian w/ Raspberry PI desktop) would not give me the correct disk options to be able to setup dual booting (might not be the fault of this machine?). When I went to try a 3rd time (Mint), the keys for Setup and Boot menu (Escape/Delete/F9/F11) would no longer respond -- the machine could only boot to Windows. I looked up how to access Advanced Startup Options from Windows 11 (there are many ways) as I should have been able to access Setup/Boot/Start-Up options that way. Instead -- BMAX does NOT display the standard Advanced Startup Options of Windows 11 -- it gives you a BMAX "Recovery" screen where your ONLY options are to restore to factory default settings or continue booting to Windows 11. Restoring to "Factory Default Settings" DOES NOT fix the problem -- which it would if the machine truly restored to factory settings.

Why does BMAX fail to be able to enter Setup and Boot Options?
Why does BMAX replace Windows 11 Advanced Startup Options with its own far less functional screen?

This PC is being returned if I can as I consider this malfunctional.

On another note, one of the other negative reviews seems to claim that the machine calls home to China resulting in multiple attempted hacker attacks. I found no evidence of this. I ran my Internet connection through Pihole -- a program that lets me monitor all outbound traffic from the machine to the Internet. I observed all the usual very extensive telemetry and outbound data that Windows 11 sends out about me/you, but NO Chinese websites or weird connections that could be hacks other than what Windows 11 normally spams the world with. So I don't think this machine does that (although you should watch YouTube videos about how to lock-down security in Windows 11 generally).

I have now wasted almost an entire workday trouble-shooting this machine for nothing.

title: I really wanted to love these, but ...
text:
There are some very nice features to these buds, and I do intend to keep them. (Another reviewer was about to return them.) But there are some things that just aren't as good as I had hoped. I'll try to be as detailed as possible.

First, the out-of-box experience is kinda nice, but not fabuous. The smallish box presents the much smaller charger box that the buds live in, and a tiny box that contains a charger cable. Wait -- are there really no instructions? And I thought there were interchangable ear thingies to accommodate ears of different sizes. Ok, so the very brief instruction book clings to the top of the box because it's too big not to fall out on its own. And the ear thingies are hiding in the box where the charging cable is. I seem to be ok with the default ear thingies that are already installed on the buds. (Note, you have to use your own charger with the charging cable. You probably already have too many of those.)

You'll need to download and install the Galaxy Wearable app (on Android, a different one is available for iOS). The app helps you connect to the buds, pretty easy, and is reasonably fully functional. There are numerous options you can play with.

The fit -- quite comfortable actually. Looking at the peculiar shape, I wondered whether these would stay in my ears, and whether they would be uncomfortable. Yes, they stay put, even when walking around, and no, not uncomfortable. This was a pleasant surprise; Samsung really got this part right. I feel as though I could wear these at the office all day and not get ear fatigue. Much, much better than a clumsy pair of headphones slipping off my head when I'm walking around. When wearing the buds, you can hear outside sounds/conversations very well, and perhaps that's the whole idea of these buds. I like this.

There's an equalizer section on the app's main screen. The equalizer options are sort of ok, but not wonderful. I don't know why there's no option for a 10-band graphic equalizer. I just settled on the default after not liking the other choices any better.

You can turn on and off the ANC (active noise cancellation). I have a pair of conventional headphones (not Bose) with ANC that works really well. You feel like you're in a cocoon. These buds have ANC that you can barely tell is working. It sounds a little different, maybe even a little bit of an improvement, but it doesn't seem like it's getting rid of any particular noise. So the ANC is sort of a bust.

Now let's talk about sound quality. As I say, I really wanted to love these little guys. The sound quality is good but not great. Maybe I'm expecting too much. My pair of $250 conventional headphones sound spectacular, and I can listen to music for hours with them. These buds aren't that impressive. The sound quality is ok -- just ok. It's not "bad" in any way at all, but it's not great. I listened to an entire CD that I know well and like. The experience was pleasant, but at the end I really wanted to listen to it on the stereo instead. As I say, maybe I'm expecting too much. The sound quality is probably good enough to listen to at work all day. I had the volume up a little too high, and when my test CD was finished and I took the buds out of my ears, I felt that my ears were ringing a little bit. Next time I'll set the volume lower.

As an interesting aside, I'll compare the sound quality to another wearable that I just got, the Bose Frames (audio sunglasses, a weirdly interesting product). The sound from the Bose Frames is "smooth" in a very wonderful way -- much better than the buds. However, the Bose Frames have absolutely no lower end -- no bass sounds at all. The sounds they do have are great. By contrast, these buds are full range, with pretty good bass. But the sound just isn't smooth.

I didn't try to take a phone call., so I don't know how seamless this works. Considering it's Samsung, and I have a Galaxy S9, I bet this works well enough. I'm not very fussy about sound quality on calls -- I just need to be able to understand what's being said. So "good enough" for me is probably not hard to achieve.

There's a "button" on the buds that you press to skip a track, answer a call, etc. It's not a real button, it's just a touch-sensitive area on the outside of the bud. I haven't been able to get this touch point to work reliably. I don't think there's necessarily anything wrong with the bud, probably just my fat fingers.

Bottom line? I think I'll have a use for these, most likely when I want to listen to my own music without disturbing others, and without the very wonderful but cumbersome conventional earphones. When I'm walking out and about, the smooth sound from the Bose Frames is better. So it's a toss-up with the Galaxy Buds Live. They're good enough, but unfortunately not better than that.

title: A very nice keyboard with many connection options.
text:
Typically I stick to higher end gaming keyboards. Mechanical and optical switches are generally my go to. I had never used a keyboard from this brand before so when I was given the chance to grab one, I figured I would see how it stacks up.

So far I'm fairly impressed. I've used some tournament edition keyboards with the smaller form factor from other brands so I knew what I was getting into when it came to the size of the keyboard. All in all, sizing is fine. They key placement and distance between keys works fine. I do run into issues at times where my fingers get lost on the right side of the keyboard. Getting used to that will come in time though. The key response is quick. They are mechanical switches but they do manage to deaden the sound a bit which is nice. The RGB features are basic at best. You have a few settings you can select from and all of it is done directly on the keyboard itself. It has your normal basic modes. It illuminates well though and you can increase/decrease the brightness. The build quality is nice. For being a 75% keyboard, it has some weight to it. I like the fact the keys are labeled for both Mac and PC. I primarily use it on my PC though. The place where it seems to shine is in the connectivity department. I can connect it by bluetooth to numerous devices or I can have it wired. I generally run wired to my main PC and if I need to use it on my MacBook or other devices, I just unplug it from the PC and connect by BT to the other device. It works out nicely.

From a gaming standpoint (which I do a lot of), I'm not certain that I like it as much yet. Emphasis on the "yet". I know it takes some time to become accustomed to a new keyboard. The response and feel. I'm going to continue gaming on it for a while to see if I become more adapted to it. It just feels different than what I'm used to. It most likely has to do with the key spacing more so than anything else.

This is definitely a nice keyboard and I recommend it. I will most likely continue to use it as my daily keyboard for a while longer to see how it holds up over time.

title: Super Comfortable & Good Sound Quality
text:
What to appreciate about these headphones and other thoughts on these:

Sound quality is pretty good - the only thing that doesn't register very well to my ears is bass.

Headphones are super comfortable - I wear them for an hour at a time and my ears still feel great.

Packaging is well done - box can be saved and used as a stand for holding headphones when you are charging them or not wearing them

Headphones seem to last a long time before needing recharging - I can go a week or so between recharges. The manual says they will last 8-12 hours of use which sounds about right to me.

Setup is pretty standard - very easy if you have experience connecting other bluetooth devices.

Comes with two cables - one for charging and the other for connecting to your phones if you prefer a wire connection. Audio cable is sufficiently long - seems like the standard headphone length. It has one of those little control units on the cord that allow you pause, change music tracks forward or backward, or take/end calls.

When plugged in using the audio cable the headphones can still play back music - no additional wiring required. This is nice in case they run out of juice - I keep the audio cable on me so I can plug in if they run out.

I find their controls for volume and song skipping a little finicky - you have to swipe on the side of the headphones which is convenient but the headphones don't always register your swipe.

A little weird when I plug in an audio cable - I would assume it would know to stop playing over bluetooth and start playing whatever's coming through the cable - it will keep using bluetooth. When I disabled bluetooth on my phone to switch to cable I found I had to unplug and replug the headphones before they switched over to using the cable for playback.

Took me awhile to figure out color changing mode - the manual documents this feature incorrectly. It tells you to hit the power button twice once instead of twice, and doesn't tell you how to switch between color options (swipe on the headphone face left or right, which as I described before is a little finicky). Still once you start playing around with it, it's pretty easy to get right. Personally my preferred color setting is off but you can choose from a ton of standard colors or have the color of the light ring respond to your music.

Has a neat wireless audio sharing feature that you can use with other headphones by this manufacturer - I haven't tried that.

title: Takes pixelated pictures but the printing part is fun
text:
No, I will not be reviewing camera specs, aperture, sensor size, etc. This is purely a toy camera that happens to print on thermal receipt paper.

As such, this camera does what it says. It takes pictures and can immediately print them out in black and white on receipt paper or stickers. For this purpose, the pixel count on this camera is enough. But what if you wanted to download the picture because it is actually worth keeping? That's when you'll discover that even pictures from the cheapest smartphone looks better.

Should one expect that the camera would be any good? No but you are expected to spend $100 for this device. The pictures really should be useable outside of printing on to receipt paper, right?

So the problem is with the price charged vs what you get. Camera technology has gotten much cheaper (the raspberry pi camera unit costs $20 and takes MUCH better pictures than this) and a thermal printer is not going to justify the price of this device.

With that said, if you can get over this aspect, this camera is a neat little toy that kids can have fun with around the house or with friends. As I said, just don't expect to be able to use the pictures for much else. What a shame it would be if the kid takes a very interesting picture but the resulting file is just unusable.

text:
Summary: This is an excellent projector for basic needs. It projects well even in lit rooms, is easy to set up, and takes up little space. Not the best in terms of color matching, but just fine for standard business presentations.

I'm very pleased with this projector. I'm using it in the office for run-of-the-mill PowerPoint presentations, and it works very well for those. No more having to have people huddle over a screen - everyone can see the images at the same time!

Setup is straightforward, as is hooking it up to a PC (a Windows 7 laptop). The projector is compact and lightweight, which is good, but I would be concerned about traveling with this. If you're a regular traveler at the least you'll want to get a very good case.

The picture quality was pretty good. Images are very bright and easy to see even in a lit room, despite the fact that I'm projecting it just on the wall, rather than on an actual screen. Quiet when running, and it has an "eco" mode that uses less electricity (and supposedly also extends the lamp life).

My only quibble is that the colors are a bit off. Not way off, but enough to be noticeable on images such as logos where I had a point of comparison. A bit of fiddling made it better, but it still was not perfect.

This is not a significant issue for my needs since I'm only projecting PPT charts and graphs where spot-on color matching is irrelevant. But, if you have more precise color rendering needs, this may be too basic of a projector for you.

Excellent choice if you need a basic projector for the office that works well, is easy to use, and won't break the bank. Highly recommend.

title: nice ruggedized Google Chrome tablet that runs Android apps
text:
I've been using Chromebook laptops and Android phones and tablets for years, but until I saw this product, I didn't know that Chrome tablets were a thing. This Chrome tablet appears to be targeted at the classroom environment, where the teacher wants all the kids running the same Chrome web apps at the same time. That is different from the typical Android environment, where there is little built-in support for synchronizing multiple tablets.

If you are using these tablets in a classroom, they work great. The screen is is brighter and sharper than the Amazon Fire tablets (which are admittedly much cheaper). The pop-out stylus works well and does not need a battery. This is a smart Wacom stylus that is much more accurate than a cheap rubber-tipped stylus or using your finger. Unlike most Android phones these days, this tablet supports micro-SD cards for expandable memory and it has a headphone jack. The tablet has stereo speakers, but they are on the sides, so aren't as loud or clear as tablet with front-facing speakers. The tablet is a little thicker than an iPad, but it is also sturdier with a rubberized shell for easier gripping and drop resistance. The tablet is lightweight for the 10 inch screen size at barely 1 pound. The camera is mediocre, but I am always carrying my phone with its much better camera, so I just use that.

Speed is really good, especially startup speed, which only takes a few seconds (much better than Android tablets). The Chrome operating system gets regular system updates for security patches and new features, unlike the Android operating system on most tablets that often gets obsolete quickly.

If you're using this tablet stand-alone (not in a classroom), it is still pretty good. The Chrome operating system runs both Chrome apps and Android apps, so it is a little more confusing than a pure Android operating system. The application launcher shows both types of apps and figuring out which is which is a hassle. Also, sharing data between Chrome apps and Android apps is a lot more complicated than sharing data between 2 different Android apps. A casual user should think hard about buying an Amazon Fire 10 inch tablet instead of one of these, mostly because the Amazon tablet offers much of the same functionality of this tablet for 1/3 the price. The Amazon tablet is much slower and doesn't have as nice a screen and doesn't have the pop-out stylus and doesn't have access to the full Google Play Android app store, so you do get what you pay for.

There is no manual in the box with this tablet. I suggest that you go to the Asus website and download the manual for this product. The manual tells you where all the buttons and ports are and how to use the stylus.

The tablet comes with a bulky high-power USB-C charger, but if you already use USB-C for your smartphone or laptop, that will probably work with this tablet as well (as long as it is not too wimpy).

4 stars because the $330 price seems high for what you get. If the price was close to $200 or even $250, I would have given it 5 stars.

title: Not as good as the old one
text:
I own this new bluetooth version and the previous non-bluetooth version and compared them side by side and inside out. They are both excellent radios, but the old one has some advantages I think are worthy of mention.

(1) The old one has two-way power, It comes with an AC plug and can also accept an external DC supply. The new BT model no longer has an AC plug and consequently no longer has an internal transformer. The new one includes a stack of steel plates inside to make it feel as heavy as the old one. Why do this? I guess they didn't want it to feel "less substantial". Getting rid of the internal transformer should have the advantage of less hum, but neither of mine hum at all to my ears. There is definitely less AC interference on AM with the new version, but there is also a little less AM sensitivity it seems. Not sure if I prefer the silent background or the weak station reach better.

(2) The new one is a completely redesigned radio circuit. Other than just not having an internal power supply, it uses a variable resistor for tuning rather than a variable capacitor fwiw. The old version appears a little more substantial in build throughout, probably because more components were needed "back then"? The internal antennas FM and AM are larger hand-wound wires. Both have excellent attention to detail like wire routing and gluing and support of components. They have the appearance of hand-made craftsmanship. Whether they are or not I do not know, but in my opinion this is a lot of radio for the money and it's even more evident inside than out.

(3) To my ears, the new BT version does not sound as good. There is a noticeable shrill to the treble that is not present in my old non-BT AC version. Also the old one seems to have a bit more "oomph" before distorting, but this may be a side effect of the treble spike. I prefer the original voicing. Perhaps the speaker is different?

(4) They both tune well and have excellent receive sensitivity, but the new version comes with a telescoping FM antenna whereas the old one came with an external wire. Both work fine but the metal telescoping version looks nice and is easier to adjust for me.

title: Good charger performance; lots of useful features
text:
I’ve been using XTAR chargers for many years and have always been pleased with their performance and durability. This is no exception – it’s easy to use, but also has a number of very useful features that other chargers lack. Chief among them is the storage charge feature. It will charge the cell to 3.7v, which is ideal for storage. If the cell is above 3.7v when inserting it into the charger, it will discharge the cell to 3.7. It’s a very handy feature, but it is limited to the first 4 bays.

The overall build quality is decent, with smooth moving tension bars and a decent heft (for an all-plastic charger). The screen is clear and easily viewed. I do wish the fonts were a bit larger, but it makes the best of the space available given that there are 8 bays.

I also like the ease of changing the input. While having it auto set is a nice feature, I prefer to charge my cells at 0.5A to minimize the stress on the cell. There’s good feedback provided on screen as to the charge status and operating mode.

I also like the compact size. I also have the Gyrfalcon ALL-88 8 bay charger, and this Xtar 8 bay charger has a notably smaller footprint and takes up less bench space.

For the price, it’s hard to beat this for quality (see the flashlight forums for detailed reviews about the charging profile of this), ease of use, and features. Very pleased!

title: Slow, corrupt, poor Customer service
text:
This disk is not reliable.
The first issue I noted with this disk is that the download speed was exponentially slower than it should have been for what it was advertised as being. I typically use SanDisk of this same type, but with half the bites, So I am familiar with speed and function.
The second thing I noted was that upon the completion of a download of any file - MP3, .doc, .pdf - I would get a dowload error message. Sometimes, if I went to the download folder, which I designated on this disk, I could find the downloaded file. Other times, the file was there, but I was unable to open it.
The third problem I noted was that files were corrupted. In the photos accompanying this review, there are titles of pre-released audio books. I am given a "one use only code" to be used on a special web page, and I get to download the audiobook files for free. In return, I write a comprehensive review of the narrator's performance. The files come in as a zip file. I unzip, rename, and move the file of MP3 chapters to an allocated folder so that a special app will play these MP3 files that are not formatted into an audiobook yet. After several days with this disk, I was listening to a book, and chapters were missing, and another book had corrupt files. I let the audiobook company know, and they checked their end. Their files were clean, and so it was on my end. At this point I went in digging looking at my folder on this disk and discovered that many of the batch of books designated for this new Microdisk had folders that were empty; these folders were not empty several days previous. One book I had already listened too and left my review, but the MP3 files were missing.
Because these are pre-release files with copyright, and the disk still contains some intact files, I could not return the disk. I also did not want to erase the disk. I was going to have to ask for 20 of the audiobooks I had been assigned, to have a new "one use only" code sent to me(embarrassing). I did not want to erase the rest of the books and and have to request these also.
Another problem is that once the files have been unzipped and moved to the designated folder for the player, I cannot move the file again, or I will be unable to play the audiobook. The reason for this is for copyright infringement rules. I can't share or send these books to family and friends, or sell them for a proffit.

Unfortunately, the company of this disk could not comprehend any of this. The Customer Service Representative had no idea what I was talking about, and refused to understand any of these basic ideas. This company clearly did not want to take responsibility for a defective disk.
The second unfortunate situation is that I tried to explain this dilemma to Amazon, and they did not understand the dilemma either. I cannot return the disk with books on it, and I will not be further embarrassed by this product by having to ask for all of my assigned books a second time.

Conclusion: The company was not investigated for merchandise that is defective, and I did not get my money back.

If what you are using this disk for is important, do not buy this product. Buy a known brand that stands behind their product.

title: The ULTIMATE Business or School Computer Case
text:
Wow. That is the only word that came out of my mouth when I first saw this case.

I have several older electronic devices as well as smaller new ones and the problem I run into is that most cases are either way too big or way too small to accommodate more than one or two devices without crowding too much. This case, however is AMAZING!

-REAL leather on corners will make this last a lot longer than most cases

-great color inside allows me to see what is in there but not prone to show dirt
-outer compartment allows me to slip in notebook etc if I need constant quick access

-inner velcro strap allows laptop and tablet to be protected while accessing other pockets and compartments
-key strap is bright red so it is easy to locate quickly

WHAT I DON'T LIKE (very few things)
-no outer pocket for easy access to cell phone to make it quick to answer when ringing while carrying case
-outer fabric does show dust and dirt easily but I can live with that
-magnetic closures barely attract at all (but weight of flap helps to stay closed anyway)

WHO MIGHT FIND THIS CASE USEFUL
-graphic artists (even room for graphic pads if necessary)
-business people who travel a lot
-women who want to combine purse and carry bag
-students, especially those who have to travel to different buildings and classes
-business owners who need all of their necessities and electronic devices in one place for easy access in stores or offices
-sales people and product reps

title: Wasn't that great the first night, much better now.
text:
The first night I opened it, I was not at all impressed, I wish I had just kept my SD4000 IS PowerShot and asked for something else for Christmas. I took pictures side by side and it wasn't that impressed. Not sure what the problem was then (condensation? The box sat outside for hours before I brought it in and opened it) but it has gotten better.

1) There are lots of improvements over my older Canons but this is definitely bulkier and bigger
2) The wireless feature works great with my home wifi and my Android. Took no time at all to setup either.
3) Low light pictures do seem a lot more bright, as if there is a hidden flash, but are grainy.
4) Camera is solid, feels great in your hand
5) The "ring" isn't a smooth turning one, it "clicks" quite awkwardly between each setting, so you go clicking through options and not in a way you can run through them, one at a time, and not smooth at all, I find myself using the menu items instead.
6) The touchscreen is awesome!
7) Touchscreen picture taking is useless, you'd be taking pictures all the time, there is no way to hold the camera really without touching the screen

In the end, I was quite happy to get a new and fairly cheap camera, but it simply isn't THAT much better than my SD4000, except in low light, and then not super low light, just low light.

I have since ordered and received the Sony RX100. Which is why I waited to return this camera, wanted to compare them side by side. After a couple of days of "playing" (yes I'm clearly not a professional, but I'd guess nor are most consumers), here are my thoughts:

1) The picture quality of the RX100 is better, but not always, and not that much more, sure it has a lot more pixels, but over all, not a huge difference. For just pictures, for ordinary consumer, I'd say get the S110, for being almost half the price, the pictures aren't THAT much different.

2) The RX100's menus are awesome for those who aren't well versed in photography, it actually explains what each setting does and is for, even with a sample picture, and then within each has sub menus explaining what they do, with yet more pictures, and finally has a help button. FANTASTIC!

3) S110's wifi is great, RX100 has none. Sending pictures to your phone and then posting or emailing them on the fly is really great.

4) As great as the S110's low light "brightness" is, the RX100 is a good 10 times better on really low lights. When there is enough light for you to see fairly clearly, they seem close, but when it's dark enough where you can't make out too clearly what you are looking at, and you can no longer see the colors, the RX100 can still take pictures that look like a cheap camera WITH a flash took (with a flash of course they both look great), where as the S110 takes pictures similar to what your eyes see when it's that dark. The RX100 really shines with no flash in pretty darn dark settings.

5) There are lots of other things the RX100 does, but might not be of interest to you, but they are there, like take pictures while recording video (but only in interlaced video, when I put it on p it doesn't let me take pictures), but those pictures aren't as great as doing so without video recording in room conditions. The function ring is much better as well.

6) S110's touchscreen awesomeness is missing

7) You can still put an S110 in your back pocket, though it would be like a thick heavy wallet. The RX100 however is almost a centimeter thicker and most of that is the lens sticking out further so I wouldn't call it a pocket camera. The S110 feels better (grainy, square metal feel, but the Sony has a smooth more rounded metal finish) and looks better.

text:
I installed the Hard drive in my desktop computer and have had it installed for two weeks.

So far, everything is working well. Easy installation and no problems using it. Keep in mind this will only work on desktop computers, not laptop computers.

Because I already have a SSD drive and regular hard disk on my computer, I am using it to store games, movies and music.

Overall, I am extremely happy with the performance of this device, and how simple it is to utilize effectively.

This is a hybrid drive which means that it contains a big storage disk (in this case 2TB) that automatically notices which files you use the most and load them onto a smaller but faster drive. The files that have been moved to the faster drive will load noticeably faster, it will take you less time to load up the programs, games, or files that you use most often.

Because it does this automatically, you don't have to manage which files you want to load quickly, and it will stay up to date as you change your usage patterns (say, you start playing a new game or start working with a large document regularly).

This means you get the best of both worlds: a hard drive that is good at loading the information that you use most often quickly, and a hard drive that can store a lot of information (this bigger drive is still 7200 RPM, which is. On top of that, it comes at about $50 less than buying separate drives, so you're saving money and benefiting from the convenience as well.

Because I am using this drive as a secondary drive (when I built my computer I put an SSD drive and a regular HDD in it), my OS is stored on the SSD drive and so this did not reduce the time it takes for my computer to turn on. However, I did install a few games on the drive and noticed that the game I loaded the most (Citied Skylines) seems to load quite a bit faster than it did before.

I would definitely recommend this drive, particularly if you are building a new desktop computer and will make this your primary disk drive. If I were building a new computer today, I would strongly consider putting this drive in it.

title: I can hear!
text:
This is a great pair of headphones - if you need them. These are not a regular set, but you could use them as such if you wanted.

I use to have a similar pair of headphones years ago that I got with the purchase of a big screen television. And I used them a lot, but someone left the headphones on the couch and they were broken when they got sat on. These Sennheiser HDR 195 TV/HIFI headphones are way beyond the pair I use to have both in quality and features.

These headphones are geared more toward someone with hearing issues - for instance myself. I'm in my mid-50's and have problems hearing certain frequencies clearly and a touch of tinnitus in my right ear. Most times when I watch television I have the Closed Captioning turned on as I at times have difficulty understanding what is being said. I also have that problem doing other things - especially with understanding speech when there is a lot ambient noise.

You have two options of providing audio to the base unit - regular analog using a standard 1/8" stereo audio cable or digital using a To-slink optical cable. Both of which are provided in the box. The base unit is also powered with a wall transformer (which comes with a selection of adapters for different power outlets). The power cord is a pretty decent length - about 6'. I tested out the headphones with both inputs. For the analog, I hooked the base unit up to my iPod touch and spent the day listening to both music and an audiobook. The headphones performed adequately with both.

The best feature of this headphone system is that you have a number of audio presets that you can switch between to enhance your listening. Basically there is a six-position (A-F) selector knob on the front of the base unit which acts like an equalizer. Position 'A' emphasizes the low-end (bass) and sort of mutes the high-end. Position 'F' is pretty much the opposite - emphasizes the high-end and mutes the low-end. Position "D" seems to be right in the middle - no enhancement. The other settings are somewhere in-between the two extremes. I found myself using 'C' for music and 'E' when listening to the audiobook. You also have the ability to adjust the left/right balance if needed. There is also a 'Mode' setting - which is goes from speech, regular listening, and music. Haven't really experimented with it enough to describe how works.

The base unit also acts as the charging stand for the headphones. It doesn't matter which direction you put the headphones (front or back) they will charge.

Before you use the headphones, you have to install the two rechargeable AAA batteries. One goes in each earpiece. To do that you have to gently twist off the individual cushions pieces. And then they need to be charged. I left the headphones on the base unit over night to charge. The battery life seems decent enough - I probably used the headphones for over six hours with no problems.

The headphones are a bit clunky in my opinion - in a bulky sort of way. Not uncomfortable, but I did find myself removing them a number of times just to give my ears a rest. I will say that while you're wearing them outside noise is greatly minimized (but not completely eliminated).

There are some controls on the outside of the right side earpiece. You can cycle through the modes and adjust the volume up & down. That's pretty much all you can do from the headphones. Controlling the sound source is strictly from whatever remote / control that device provides.

I had some logistic issues with connecting these headphones to my main television. I would have liked to use the digital input, but I have a sound-bar using that output. So I had to make use of the headphone jack. The headphones work well with the television audio - I found that I could hear dialog much clearer. But I ended up installing these on my smaller television in my bedroom - where I was able to use the digital audio output. Using the headphones for that set gives me two benefits. One, the CC on that smaller set was too small to read at the distance - so being able to hear better made it where I didn't need to. And two, now I can watch TV late at night and not worry about disturbing anyone else in the house with the sound.

I'm very happy with these headphones and recommend them to anyone with similar hearing issues.

title: She's an Amazing cooler, but you better like big Girls.....
text:
I have had this CPU fan now going on 5 months. I love this fan. I hadn't upgraded for nearly 10 years and decided on an AMD FM2 Black Edition 6300 6-core CPU with an MSI 970A-G43 Plus economy Micro Board and 16GB of Corsair Memory 4GBx4 in the 4 slots. I use my computer for gaming and all around use. I wanted a CPU cooler that would be quiet and still keep my cpu cool when I cranked it up for high-performance gaming. I found it with this AND it didn't break the bank. With the Turbo Clock OC setting it will idle down and bolt up to 4300mhz seamlessly while the fan moves from it's WHISPER silent 36c idle and general use, to it's 42c full bore o'clocked gaming use. The fan keeps it cool, and never does the fan become obtrusive or loud.

This fan is BIG. Don't even consider it if you have a micro or small mid-tower case. Your case must be generous in it's width to accommodate this cooler. Be sure to check the dimensions of your case with the unit. I have an older Antec 900 case it fit snugly into. I did have to remove the optional side window cooler intake fan I had installed with the prev board, cpu and cooler to allow it's fit. Also be sure your motherboard design placement of Memory slots is such that your Memory will clear it. My board's Corsair Vengence Memory JUST cleared it by a couple mm's laterally, and the top of the memory overtakes the bottom edge of cooler by about a quarter inch. If you are in the process of building your system a choice with low profile memory that doesn't have the tall heat spreaders would be a wise choice and safe bet if you are unsure about clearance with a board design that puts the memory slots very close to the CPU and cooler position. In the first photo attached I REVERSED the fan position to PULL the air thru on Left for best clearance instead of PUSHING the air through on the right if you just don't have the room, that flexibility is very handy. I wasn't satisfied with the cooling level and re-positioned the fan on right to PUSH it through later on and it sent the temps down a few more degrees. As you can see though in the second photo, it is much more snug.

Bottom line, a great cooler IF your case and build offers the room to fit it in. I would recommend it for those wanting great overclocking cooling performance and very quiet operation. I think most overclock enthusiasts would be well served to try this value priced solution before expensive and complicated water cooled solutions.

title: Stores Your Laptop and Dozens of Related Accessories
text:
Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case is a storage and organizational device that is very useful for storage of both laptops and related accessories. I use this case when going on vacation and making other short trips. My laptop almost always accompanies me, and having a safe place to keep my computer is important.

This laptop computer bag looks much like other computer bags from the outside. Its black color and Case Logic metal badge with logo make it look like a briefcase when viewed from a distance. This gives the bag a more professional, serious look that makes it a good choice for businessmen and businesswomen. At the same time, the bag looks casual enough that others can use it as well. It could even double as a storage bag for other items and many students could use this case for hauling around a few books, folders, notebooks, and papers.

Opening up the Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case reveals an obvious fact: This is no ordinary briefcase/laptop carrying bag. There are separate sections and zippers galore. There are four main sections and these are subdivided into other storage sections with variations in each section that help users find the perfect place to store their notebooks, cell phones, calculators, pens, etc. One of the end sections is designed exclusively for your laptop and includes pillow- like walls to keep your laptop computer safe from damage. The other sections have a combination of pockets without zippers, pockets with zippers, deep pockets, shallow pockets, and even a nylon mesh pocket. With so many pockets and storage areas, one can quickly find the perfect place to store everything from cell phones, to calculators, to CD's, and more.

Carrying the Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case is made easy through the two available options: The briefcase- like handles and the optional shoulder strap. I usually use the handles, but if my bag is overloaded, I have found that the shoulder strap is the best way to go. Not only can this strap be used to carry the bag hands- free, it can also be used to strap the bag to a piece of rolling luggage, for even more freedom of movement. The strap is long enough to fit around most any piece of luggage, making a quick run through the airport fast and simple.

One other nice feature of the Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case is that it is designed with airport security in mind. This is one of the main appeals of this laptop bag because more often than not, when I am packing my laptop into a bag, it is for taking it on a trip and more than half of my trips involve flights. Case Logic designed this laptop case in compliance with TSA government guidelines so that you don't have to remove the laptop from the case in order to pass it through airport security. This is great for those who don't have time to waste and need to get to their gate as quickly as possible.

Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case has many great things to offer, so are there any cons? I can think of only a few. One is the lack of padding in the majority of the compartments. The laptop compartment is protected by padding, but the rest of the case is not. Thus, you have to be careful not to place anything delicate in one of these non- padded sections- particularly the one on the outside. These more delicate items will have to be placed toward the center of the bag instead of at the ends. Another possible con is that this bag is not expandable. Granted, it has enough storage space and is large enough that most anyone can find a place to store what they have. But the lack of expansion means you cannot place a large object inside this storage bag and it also means that some of the larger laptop computers may not fit.

Still, in spite of these minor inconveniences, the Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case is a very nice computer case with many great things to offer. It can be used to store your laptop computer and related accessories in many different ways, with a design that is both practical and imaginative.

title: The cord holder works great, the glow int he dark not so much
text:
We got this CordBrick™ Weighted Cord Holder to hold some cords my wife keeps on her desk in our home office. She actually switches between two spaces since moving into remote work, so there are a few cords that’ll get left on the desk and she’s tired of having to crawl underneath every time to get them again. Different methods (like putting them under a book or something) usually resulted in them falling before she could grab them or some such thing, and she gave up. Then I spotted this CordBrick™ Weighted Cord Holder in a glow in the dark green and we gave it a try. She (we) love the CordBrick™ Weighted Cord Holder, but are underwhelmed by the glow in the dark element.

As you can see in the picture, this is about the brightest it got to be. We got it because we thought it might be cool, but more so, that we’d take it when we travel and the brighter color would help us see it in the dark and remind us it’s there in an unfamiliar setting. At home we thought it would stand out in the darker corner where her desk is set up. I’ve used glow in the dark tape before during my theatre days that had better glow. We have tried under two different types of lights and in a window. Nothing seems to get it as strong as we’d hoped.

But it’s not truly a dealbreaker for us. If you’re going to offer it as an option it should work and we did consider dropping a rating star for it, but in the end went with the 5 stars because what we have it for actually works - it holds the cords in place. She uses this one on a desk, with various sized cords and in some cases the cords are in this CordBrick™ Weighted Cord Holder while the item they are plugged into are on another level - so they stay in place even that way. The CordBrick™ Weighted Cord Holder itself is weighted by the silver thing on the inside - you can see one end of it - giving it a feeling that it’s substantial, but not heavy, nor light. You can stick it in a purse or pocket and be comfortable. You can plug in a few cords (we maxed at three - and it stays in place. It looks like the cords might pop out, but we tested in a few ways (dropping pulling, pushing it around) and they don’t move. We no longer have to pull cords from the floor or behind the desk - saving a lot of frustration. in the end we are happy with the CordBrick™ Weighted Cord Holder, and though the lack of glowing green is a disappointment, the bright white of the non-glowing color means we can see it easily.

title: Amazing for the price
text:
I have a ton of portable keyboards. Pictured are the two nicest, the iClever BK05 and this one, the Logitech K380.

The iClever is definitely more portable. And the square keys are more traditional and feel a bit better. And it has a backlight, but... don't let that influence you. That backlight isn't bright enough to be worthwhile.

Both (and the MX Keys) are clearly membrane keyboards. They're better than an on-screen keyboard, but cannot compare to a Keychron K8 with decent switches. But that's not so portable. Choose your poison.

Both easily pair with three devices. (The iClever also can work in USB mode; the K380 cannot.)

The K380 feels far more solid. If your goal is an iPhone (e.g.) keyboard for home, this is a great keyboard; you don't need it to be portable. If you want to bring it with you, use the iClever BK05; it feels a bit better and costs almost twice as much, but is lighter and folds smaller.

Where the K380 wins is that it is 60% the price of the iClever and seems far less fragile. I have the K380 for use at home with my iPhone, an MX Keys for my work and home PC when my (Siberian)

Is your goal a solid keyboard for sporadic use at home? K380. Is it a keyboard you can take with you, even if more expensive? BK05. Both are great, just slightly different use cases.

The nylon braiding over the cable is durable and hasn’t frayed at all like I’ve seen in similar cords. This is a big deal for me because I have a cat that loves to chew phone cords but this one is so well protected it has withstood a few attempts from her. That alone makes this a winner in my book. The main selling point of this cable is the smart factor, aka an led light that changes color to let you know your phone is charging and when it’s done. Is it useful? Yes. Is it something I would seek out or pay extra to have? I doubt it. I have gotten so used to tapping my phone screen to see the charging status that it’s a hard habit to break but I’m trying. I waited a little to write this review because I wanted to be certain of how this cable would hold up. Nearly every charger I’ve bought has worked great at first but after a couple weeks I’d end up having to have it angled just right or it wouldn’t charge. Now that I’ve given this cable a through test, I can happily say it’s the best one I’ve ever owned.

text:
[[VIDEOID:43080b865b752bd653af5dfe533a6667]] I have very mixed feeling with this smart watch. I have Galaxy Watch 5 and I HAD Apple Watch series 6 previously. Since this was on Vine recommendation list and I just gave it a try. Apps are not stable, problems are here and there but still it's only $30. So I really don't know how to give ratings for this product. So here is what I think.

Build Quality & Design:
It has old Galaxy watch, round shape body with assumably tempered glass. The body is made with aluminum. They give 2 silicone straps gracefully. (Are you seeing this, Samsung & Apple?) For build quality, it's amazingly good for $30, and even without considering the price, it has pretty good quality.

Screen:
They say it's IPS HD resolution but well, it's nothing like major smart watches. Dots are quite visible, probably we are all get used to UHD or QHD level of high resolution screen too much. It's not specifically bothering though, but definitely it's nothing like mainstream watches. It doesn't work as smooth as mainstream watches, then again it's $30.

Comfortableness:
It is pretty comfortable, just like others. I specially like the soft silicone texture of this watch.

Apps:
So, this is the problem. So practically, even with full permission to most of the apps, something works and something doesn't. This watch has connection app and you can manage all your setting there. With full permission, call works pretty good both for dialing and receiving calls. But even with the accessibility permission for messaging, it doesn't show any incoming message nor I can send any, nor does Whatsapp. I'm not sure I'm setting this right or not, but it's true that it's not so convenient. So if someone succeed, please let me know and I will fix rating. The step tracking is somewhat unstable, so it works on and off. The health monitor works pretty well in INCREDABLY SHORT TIME (BUT shows very different number from Galaxy Watch, lol) but blood pressure measure is somewhat unstable, it fluctuates like crazy. I guess it's immature technology since Galaxy Watch 5 didn't open this function for US market yet. So I won't believe whatever number comes up from this watch.

Charger:
It comes with one light plastic charger. Again, it's $30.

Buy it if you need: budget random smart watch for your kids. I mean, it's "working" smart watch for $30.
Don't if you need: you need a real smart watch for messaging and health management. It's just not so credible and reliable.
