title: Corrections to Some False Statements
text:
Corrections to published details are in order. First some sellers state these are 5 watt output power. When you get your radio and read the manual, look at the manufacturer's label under the battery or go to any of the web sites (Baoffeng bf888s, Retevis h777, Pofung 888s, all the same radios) you will find that the transmit power specification is ≤ 5W which literally means "less than or equal to 5 watts," NOT 5 watts!. That is a totally non-committal specification. It could be 500mw, 1w, 2w or anything they want at or below 5 watts, to be within spec. One could say that these are ≤ 100,000 Watts and be just as accurate. It's like "On Sale for UP TO 50% off. That simply means anything less than 50%. 0% is "up to 50% off." Actual output power on High is measurable at 2 watts at best, more closely 1.8 watts measured at the antenna connector with the factory antenna. This is about what you get out of a standard GMRS blister pack GMRS/FRS radio. So I tested the range of this radio compared to 2 blister pack (Midland and Motorola 2 watt and 1 watt) GMRS/FRS radios in a rural area of single story buildings. All three yielded about 3/4 mile. The only difference was that the BF888s/H777 had much clearer voice until it was lost and batteries last MUCH longer. Batteries are Li-ion which means they lose almost no power (1.5% - 2% per month) just sitting there unused for months compared to the ni-cads in most radios which lose 10% = 20% per month without being used.

The next absolutely false statement by some is that these are legal to use in the US right out of the box. NOT!!!. Most of the channels are programed for Licensed Business use and GMRS frequencies all of which require a license to transmit on at this power. Just look it up on FCC.gov. In addition channels 10 and 11 are programmed for Medical Use only frequencies. Channel 10 is programmed for the base station of Medflight in my local area. Channel 15 is programmed for a Police ONLY frequency, the exact same frequency my local police department uses for dispatch. If you want to verify any frequency conflicts in your area go to radioreference dot com and look them up for your county.

I don't think you want to be caught jamming your police radio frequencies or medical emergency channels either. DO YOUR OWN HOMEWORK AND HAVE A CONSCIENCE!!!!!

Low power setting is greater than 500mw so these cannot be programmed in any way to be used without a FCC license even on FRS channels. Even GMRS requires a $90 (for a family for 5 years) for a license.

Just be aware of what you buy and what can happen if you go by the old adage "Ignorance is Bliss." Especially if you get hit with a 5 digit fine by the FCC or are responsible for someone not getting emergency services. Don't think that the police will not trace down someone interfering with their dispatch channels!!!

Other details are pretty much covered in other reviews. These are pretty good solid radios which are NOT FCC Type accepted.

text:
I had my doubts, not realizing how simple this little thing works. I attached it to my Sony ICD-UX71 digital recorder, stuck the earpiece in my ear and then made a phone call. I tested it while on the road in my car using my Palm Treo680 cell phone. It picked up the call from both ends remarkably well. I also got all the sounds from the car, but that may be a function of my Sony recorder, I don't know for sure. Either way, the microphone on this device is sensitive and works very well!

The earpiece felt a little awkward at first, but I soon got used to it and it did not cause discomfort. For those wondering how this ingenious little device works, the other side of the earpiece, the part that goes against the phone when you have it to your ear, is a microphone and picks up the sound from your phone receiver.

when listening to the playback of my recordings, I did NOT notice the caller's voice lower than mine, as another reviewer pointed out. However, you can tell it is a phone call and not a face to face discussion. Altough that could be a function of the phone equipment I was using as well (both from my end and the 2 people I called - both of them were talking to me from an iPhone3G).

I mention the recorder make/model and the cell phone make/models as the recording quality may have a lot to do with these factors.

title: Battery Issues
text:
This is my third update. I started at 5-stars. . . went to 2-stars. . . and now I'm at 3-stars. . .

B&O sent me a replacement speaker. . . but. . . I'm still having the same "issues" with the length of battery time. It's kind of all over the place, though the "conditions" are about the same. By "conditions" I'm talking about the type of music I'm playing. . . the volume. . . and the location of my phone to the speaker. All of these things are supposed to effect the length of the battery. I have yet to find a "reason" that I get less battery time sometimes. . . and more at others. . . But I've yet to get 24-hours of time, after the very first time of using it. I can say that I think having it plugged-in and listening to it can certainly cause shorter battery time when you unplug it.

I really wish there was a battery level on the speaker. There is not. There is a tiny light that will be red (and the speaker beeps) when the battery is low. . . When you plug it in the light will be orange and flash when it is charging. It will be green when it's supposed to be fully charged. . . but. . . you can't simply press something and find out what's left on the battery.

All of my "issues" are with the battery. The sound from the speaker is great. I've never had a complaint about the sound from the speaker. That part is really great.. . . and if the battery gave 24-hours of playback most of the time, then it would be 5-stars.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

My original review is below. I started out with 5-stars. . . but now I'm down to no more than 2. The reason is that the battery will not hold a charge. I charge the speaker overnight, but can get only an hour or two of play time, at best. I contacted B&O and they responded with the "generic" "it depends on how loud you play". . . blah. . blah. . . blah. Sorry, but no matter how loud I play. . . it should last longer than an hour or two. For this amount of Made-in-China $$, it should last longer than a couple of hours. Also. . . There should be a battery level indicator. . . and there's not. It will "beep" when the battery is low, and there is a tiny (size of a pin) light which will turn red, but that's all.

Again. . . The sound is fantastic. . . but if it will only play an hour or so. . . that's not good. So I've returned it.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

I just received this portable speaker. Granted, I'm not so happy about the fact that it's made in China. . . . but what isn't these days.

Please Note: There is one BIG "issue" about this speaker. To charge it you must plug it into the wall with the included AC adapter. You can NOT charge it through the USB port. Having said that, there is a USB port, which is used solely to charge a cell phone (or other such device), should you need to do so. . . but. . . by doing so it will greatly reduce the speaker battery charge. Of course you can plug your phone into the speaker. . . then the speaker into the wall. . . and charge both at the same time. Nonetheless, having to use an AC adapter to charge the speaker might be considered a "negative" by some. B&O should have made this VERY clear in the included information. . . and they don't. Heaven knows what would happen if someone tried to charge it using the USB port.

FYI. . . The speaker comes with the "short" leather strap. A longer strap is supposed to be offered, but it does not come with the speaker, and I've yet to find it anywhere. . . Other than on the set-up video.

Speaking of set-up. . . It's a breeze. It works right out of the box.

The sound quality is wonderful. . . as it should be. At almost two-pounds six-ounces, it's certainly not light. . . buy in this case, that's not necessarily a bad thing. It's study enough to produce great sound.

The issue of not picking up motion other than right in front of the doorbell was never really addressed or resolved. The random car passing being picked up was supposedly due to the wheels … they said sometimes the wheels are mistaken for human movement … hard to believe, but that was their response. Even after reducing the detection zone per their suggestion I would still get random notifications from a car passing.

In ideal surroundings, this device may work as depicted in the YouTube videos, but it just did not work for me.

title: Large, nice GPS with LIFETIME MAPS!
text:
Electronics such as a GPS always have some good features. . . and then there are some which you wish it had. But unlike other electronics, with a GPS, the main thing is whether or not it can get you from point A to point B without a problem. I'm happy to report that the Magellan RoadMate 5175T-LM does that well. Some might say "duh. . . it's a GPS. . .of course it can". But that's not necessarily so. I've had four different GPS systems, and one, the Garmin Nuvi could not find its way out of a wet paper bag. From constantly telling me to drive the wrong-way down a one-way street. . . to taking forever to "recalculate" the route if you pass a turn. (You literally have to pull-over and stop and wait for it to recalculate. So far, the Magellan RoadMate 5175T-LM has not sent me the wrong-way down a one-way street. . . and it's very quick to "recalculate". Having said that, here is my take on some of the features of this unit:

Pros:
* Lifetime map updates. What a GREAT feature.
* Street names are spoken
* A bell rings when you're about to turn left or right (but you can change it in the options)
* You can both plug-in the unit via USB to update, or use WiFi to update
* You can operate in "portrait" or "landscape" mode. Though . . . quite honestly. . I don't know why you would want to operate it in "portrait" mode, but you can if you like.
* It's a very flat (skinny) device.
* Large 5" screen. Though the screen is 5" diagonally, the unit measures 5.5" X 3.5". There is a stainless steel "frame" around the screen, which looks good, and feels good also.
* Bright, crisp screen. . . though, like with many such devices, it's not all that easy to see in bright sunlight.
* When entering an address, you can start with the zip-code.
* Mini SD card slot. This is especially nice when using larger maps and when your unit becomes "full" due to lots of addresses and extras that you've added. My TomTom has a VERY small hard drive, and updates and such are "challenging" because there's no way to add additional storage, so I can really appreciate this feature on the Magellan.
* Attaches to any weighted dashboard mount. (Amazon has some nice, inexpensive ones)
* The booklet shows that it has a 2-hour battery life.
* QWERTY or ABC Keyboard

Cons:
* It doesn't come with a complete user's manual, but you can download it from the Magellan website.
* Your position on the map is shown as a little triangle, and there are no options to change that.
* You can't change the voice. On the one hand, that's not a big deal, because I've found that with other GPS systems, even if you can change the voice (and purchase additional voices) most of them cannot speak the street names.
* Web browser is really useless. I'm not sure what they were thinking on this. If you have another web-enabled device, such as a smartphone, iPod Touch, iPad/Tablet, etc. . .you'll a lot better-off using that. WiFi is nice to be able to update the unit, but it's really impossible to browse the web. It's very slow, you can't read it, most things you cannot tap, etc. It's just awful.
* Not as much information on the screen while driving as I would like. My TomTom has at least double the amount of info.
* I'm accustomed to tapping the screen to get to the menu on other GPS devices. Not so on this one. You tap the "Menu" button on the right.
* When you get into the menu, I haven't been able to find an easy way to get back to the "main" part of the menu or the map itself. You either have to keep going back. . back. . back. . back. . . or. . . just wait and eventually the map will pop back up.
* I haven't had a lot of experience with the traffic part, but I don't think it's as good as what I have on my TomTom. . .but. . you have to pay for traffic on TomTom (it's a bundled monthly subscription which also includes Google search, and fuel prices) and it's not offered on all TomTom devices. . .just the ones which offer "Live".
* There's no way (that I have found) to enter "map corrections", which is a great feature of TomTom.
* When you plug the unit into your computer, there's no "home page" like there is with other GPS devices such as TomTom and Garmin. I miss the "home page" because there are lots of things you can do from there to add things to your device and such.
* You can't "lock" the device.
* It doesn't warn you when you're going through a traffic camera intersection, as TomTom does.

FYI in the information with the unit it shows that there are two ways to charge the unit. Either by the "optional" AC adapter. . . or . . . when you plug it into your car. But, like with other devices, it will also charge when you plug it into your computer via UBS.

This is a good, nice, somewhat "generic" large GPS that will fit most traveler's needs. For the most part, it's easy to use. With "lifetime maps", it should keep you happy for years to come. If they would do a software update to make the WiFi browser work better, then I could give it 5-stars.

My one concern is the long-term reliability of the little plastic flash lock lever. It seems to me that this should have been made of metal, but I guess time will tell how well that works. In any case, I'll report back in 6 months and let you know how it's doing.

Yes, the 50r (with almost twice the power) would be nice to have, and I may end up getting one for an extended flash setup some day, but for general purpose use, this is a great portable flash for an Olympus m43 system.

title: Secure, positive connection, flexible options
text:
This mount arrived with my Lilliput 7" HDMI monitor. Sony L series lithium ion batteries fit it perfectly.

Pros:
- pushbutton locks the battery into the plate securely
- reliable battery contacts
- power-out coaxial socket; no wiring required (5.5mm x 2.5mm)
- included power out cable
- multiple mounting options

Cons:
- shipping from China costs more than the unit

UPDATE:
There is a second "Con:" When the battery is mounted, a green LED lights up to indicate charge state, I believe. If the battery goes dead, it turns red, I think. Haven't really let the battery go dead but it does briefly flash red.

To power this LED, there is a rather complex circuit board inside the unit that seems to do nothing but make the LED function.

In other words, if you leave the battery on the adapter, the LED stays lit, draining the battery over time.

I wanted to build a 14.4VDC power supply for my GH4 YAGH unit.

I mounted two of these adapters onto an aluminum plate and wired them in series to do so. I wanted more reliable contact than the coaxial power connectors (which can be pulled out by accident) so I pried open the cases (which isn't easy), unsoldered the wires inside and removed the circuit boards and coax connectors. Then I directly soldered a wire to the contacts so one battery's positive contact flowed into the next battery's negative contact. I then soldered the positive wire to my camera's power cable to the unused positive contact of one battery and the unused negative contact of the other, providing double the voltage of a single L-type 970 battery.

Now the two batteries together provide the 14.4VDC I need in a compact, high amp-hour, inexpensive unit.

I like using L-Type Lith-Ion batteries because they power other devices I use -- small monitors, my mixer and external recorders. They are widely available, lightweight, inexpensive, charge quickly and reliably, do not have memory effect and hold a charge on the shelf for much longer than Ni-Cads. I'm told they actually work better if you leave them on the charger, too.

title: One of the easiest-to-use and install dashcams I have come across
text:
I received this as a free review sample. M.Erb's extremely detailed and helpful video review of May 14, 2016 covers this in a great deal of depth. I'll add my thoughts and reasons why I also rated this five solid stars.

First, I have tested and used at least a dozen dashcams, many of which were excellent in their own right. However, the shortfall in each was the screen and a complicated array of controls. With this one your screen is your smartphone or tablet, and your controls are those that are provided with the app you need to download (for free) to control the camera and settings. There is a separate remote control, which is really just a clicker that does one thing: triggers a short video and a snapshot.

Another thing I personally love is the mounting kit. This one, properly used, will run your power cable in an unobtrisive manner (well, as unobtrusive as possible), and the cable is sufficiently long to run the cable from close to my rear view mirror to my dashboard lighter socket in my 2016 Outlander. Other dashcams either forced you to put up with dangling cable or - in one case - have the power and video feed cables professionally installed. Plus this uses a standard USB cable with USB A on one end and micro USB on the other. Some dashcams require a proprietary cable with a barrel connector that makes it difficult to replace if necessary.

Video quality is not award winning (indeed, the camera lens is a fisheye), but is still more than sufficient to capture accidents and even scenic drives. You can also use this for other than a dashcam. I discovered that will fit in a standard microphone clip that fits a Shure SM58 (i.e., a very common size.)

You can use up to a 64GB micro SD card, which will store almost eleven hours of video. Most dashcams are limited to 32GB. The instruction manual is adequate, but not comprehensive, and it also does not cover the software and its capabilities. I hope the company rectifies that, which will make this dashcam even more user friendly, especially for novices. However, most folks do not want to wade through a manual anyway, and the one that comes with this will get you going.

Bottom line: as far as dashcams go, this one is probably the easiest one to use that I have come across. My FAVORITE feature is simplicity that allows my phone or tablet to be the screen and controls.

title: Excellent Continuous LED Light with Good Feature Set
text:
I selected this light after doing some research on continuous LED lights. I had a situation where I had only a strobing light available to me and it made getting even a still exposure without banding very difficult. My requirements for a continuous LED were that it had to be compact, bright and have variable color output. This light met those requirements, and in addition I found some favorable write-ups of this light online. Though on the pricey side, I took the plunge and so far I have no regrets.

I will state right up front that this is not marketed as a general purpose light and it is not a proper substitute for such. There are less expensive and more practical lights available if you need general lighting. Yes, it will work as a general purpose light source, even as a flashlight in a pinch, but that’s akin to using a blowtorch to light candles when a simple match will do.

This is a very small light, about the side of a king-sized candy bar. Even after reading the description and reviews, I was surprised at just how small this light is. That’s good for me because it fits perfectly in my camera bag and can go with me without taking up extra room or requiring space in the car or luggage. When stored in the case it takes up about as much room as a small jar of peanut butter.

The light has ten brightness settings as well as a boost mode which makes it almost blinding. The lowest setting is quite dim but usable, and the brightest outside of boost mode is bright enough to illuminate a 10’x10’ space reasonably well. The light color is constant unless using the color “gels” (more on that in a moment). When using boost mode, it remains in that mode for a period of roughly a minute before switching back to one of the normal settings. It takes some time before boost mode can be used again, likely a safety measure due to increased heat output.

Included are several color “gels” that are more like hard plastic plates that fit in front of the light array. These allow for some adjustment in color. The colors tweak the color range to be warmer or colder. I used the darkest orange to give a scene a warmer, golden glow that worked remarkably well. These plates are held in place against the array with a clip-on harness that fits over the front of the unit.

Also included is a silicone diffuser that reduces the harshness of the array. When the clip-on harness is in place it is difficult at best to attach the diffuser.

There are several effects modes to emulate different lighting situations, including a flickering light, lightning strike, glow from a television and more. While these are interesting and some will find these modes useful, particularly for video, they do not serve my purposes.

What I did not realize is that this light has a mounting hole on the bottom that allows for attaching it to any standard tripod or even a monopod/selfie stick. I attached it to a higher-quality telescoping monopod with a swivel base and was able to get the exact lighting angle I needed. With a tripod it becomes hands-free.

Though it is waterproof I have no intention of using this in water.

It includes a couple of patches that allow it to be semi-permanently attached to a surface. I am contemplating building a large light box and attaching this light inside.

This is a really excellent and versatile continuous LED light. It is as bright or dim as you need it, it includes some color plates for adjusting the color output, it includes some special effect modes and it is small enough to fit in my bag without any trouble at all. This is a very easy light to recommend if you need a continuous LED light.

text:
Basically, this is an excellent home computer for one person or a whole family. The Bang & Olufsen speakers provide a soundbar look below the screen and a pretty impressive sound for PC speakers. Although I find this to boot a little slow (my last desktop computer booted in a fraction of the time and it was a much less powerful system), it’s still pretty quick.

The touchscreen works beautifully for both general navigating, and also for graphics work both with finger or stylus. I replaced the keyboard and mouse with more robust wireless once since I can be pretty hard on them. The ones included are pretty basic quality.

The display is beautiful! I use a screen calibrator to adjust the colors for accuracy, and I hardly needed any tweaking at all.

As a graphic/web designer, I’ve used a lot of computers over the years. I need the power to process the things I put my computers through. I’m also good at crashing them. This computer has been my work and crafting computer for a week now.

First, let’s start with a tip: Get an external CD drive to attach while installing software if you have any on CD. Most of mine were downloadable, but there were a few that I had to install from a CD drive.

Setup was a breeze. Cortana is great at helping you get started. Once I was all set up, I began removing the stuff I didn’t want before adding my software and apps. There’s a lot of trial stuff on there that I never need, so removing is easy enough. OneDrive is not too hard to remove or disable if you don’t need it. I like to have more control of backing up my files on a local backup drive, so I always disable OneDrive first. I remove McAfee and use Windows Defender, so make sure that’s active.

I added three printers easily, all working together smoothly. Bluetooth devices connect well, but I had trouble connecting to a Klipsch Bluetooth soundbar across the room. Not sure if the trouble was this computer or the soundbar. Everything else in the room connects to it easily, so who knows.

Next, I added all my crafting apps and connected the devices. A Silhouette Cameo connected via USB and works perfectly. A Cricut Explore Air2 works wonderfully via Bluetooth, and the Brother ScanNCut works beautifully both via USB or Bluetooth. All three software/web apps work beautifully on here.

All my graphics/video editing software works beautifully and smoothly. I mainly use CorelDraw now (I no longer use Creative Suite since it’s web only), and this runs it really well. I haven’t done extremely graphic intensive work, and don’t really do that much anymore, but if that’s what you need, you really do want a more powerful computer than this.

Where did I trip this machine up? I must confess, I’m a font nerd. So in organizing my many fonts, I’ve managed to crash Corel Font Manager repeatedly. Once I have them organized, I’m hoping it won’t crash as often, but I think I’ve worked out that I need to slow down to let the system catch up. So, unless you’re moving and organizing thousands of fonts at a time, you probably won’t see screen freezing or crashing much at all! Normally, I have to CTRL+ALT+Delete & dump stuff via task manager at least once a day on ANY computer. This time, It’s only been twice in a week, both times very much my fault with the font addiction.

So have I mentioned how much my dog loves his new space on the floor by my feet? It’s so nice not to have a big bulky PC under my desk. Now a little pup is very happy to have a blanket to lay on in that spot!

title: Worked great, order more than two if you are new to soldering MMCX
text:
This was my first MMCX work (converting a pair of grado SR80x's into some custom planar magnetics with drivers from the goldplanar GL400's) I ruined my first one accidentally getting solder on the threads (my fault) but the second one went together nice and easily. Just make sure you're using very Fine gauge solder (0.022 was what I used) and appropriate gauge wire (28 AWG is perfect for these) along with flux paste. For security, I got a pack of fine heat shrink too. A set of helping hands (cheap ones will do, but cheap ones with a magnifying glass are better)

Here's how to actually solder these things

Firstly, tin the wires (critical) by dipping the ends in flux and then adding some solder to them. This will make the connection way faster and cleaner.

Then tin the mmcx itself. flux the very ends and add a TINY amount of solder to the very end of the outer rim and the center pin (that's the signal pin, where your positive wire goes) Then carefully solder the ground wire first, and the signal wire second. Make sure that you can get the nut over the wire, secure the connector where you want it (if you're doing MMCX grados, you need to use your soldering iron or a drill bit to make a new hole next to the original one since these are smaller than that) and then slip some heat shrink around the ground wire to separate it from the signal, some shrink around the signal wire, and then a piece over both.

I would honestly order two of these for one job if it's your first time, or get a 5 pack. These are quite small, so make sure you have all the right stuff. Small gauge wire, small gauge solder, flux, some helping hands.

title: Decent low-cost copper-compatible 360mm radiator with few limitations
text:
TLDR: This is a decent, low-cost, high-density copper-compatible 360mm radiator with a few minor limitations that do little to detract from it.

The best feature of this radiator is probably its 20 fins per inch. While it's hardly unique in that regard, many popular alternatives, such as the EKWB CoolStream Classic SE 360, are 16 FPI at a higher price point.

It is also a copper/brass radiator, meaning that it must only be used with other copper components. Using it with any aluminum water cooling components will result in galvanic corrosion. (Aluminum components are cheaper and don't perform as well, so copper is the best choice for maximum performance and efficiency. Sadly, it costs accordingly.)

Due to the 20FPI, you'll want three 120mm fans with good static pressure. I used three Noctua NF-F12 4-Pin 120mm PWM fans ( https://www.amazon.com/Noctua-NF-F12-PWM-4-Pin-Premium/dp/B00650P2ZC ). The F12 fans are optimized for high static pressure, making them an excellent match for this radiator.

I tested this radiator using an Nvidia RTX 3090 (w/front & rear active plates) running a 420W BIOS and an AMD 5950X rated at 105W. I mined Ethereum on the GPU and ran a 32-thread sysbench on the CPU to generate load. The observed power draw of the two components combined was just over 500W. I let this run for two hours to get to a steady state and took temperature differences between the loop reservoir and room air at 90 minutes.

I tested both push and pull fan configurations. Both kept the reservoir temperature about 12 degrees C below room temperature while the loop dissipated over 500 watts. There appeared to be a slight variance in observed temperatures on the GPU; the memory temperature went to 68 in the pull config and 70 with push. So although I suspect that the pull configuration might be slightly more efficient (it usually is), you can use whichever configuration your case demands without concern about losing much cooling capacity.

For comparison purposes, I performed the same tests with the closest alternative I have on hand: a (now discontinued) EKWB CoolStream SE 280mm, which is the same thickness and has about 95% of the surface area, and a pair of Noctua NF-A14 140mm fans. Air moved for both configurations is about the same at 165cfm, but the NF-F12s have 2.61 mmHg static pressure, slightly better than the NF-A14s at 2.06 mmHg.

In both configurations, the Shott equaled or outperformed the EKWB, which produced reservoir and CPU/GPU temperatures ranging from the same up to 3 degrees higher than the Shott. That's most likely due primarily to the Shott radiator's higher fin density, aided by the higher static pressure from the smaller fans.

But there's still room for improvement.

As at least one other reviewer experienced, my kit arrived missing one screw. All twelve of the long screws (fan side) were present. Only eleven of the short screws (case side) made it. That's a minor problem as 4-8 mounting screws are more than enough under almost all circumstances. I tested the radiator threading with other M3 screws and found that they were a perfect fit. So if you do need different screws, that should be no problem. But as multiple people have experienced missing screws, it's something for the seller to look into.

The other issue that has come up in other reviews is the concern about fins under the screws. This is a bit of a misnomer, as the real issue is that the tubes are under the screw holes. If you bend a fin by screwing in too far, you reduce your cooling performance by 0.0001%. If you pop a tube by screwing in too far, you've got a leak on your hands and potentially a ruined radiator or future system short. However, this design is, as others have observed, pretty standard. Avoiding that risk entirely would require making the radiator wider or reducing the cooling area. Neither are good choices compared to exercising appropriate caution during installation.

To test this concern, I screwed in one of the fan screws to the limits of its threading. Even after doing so, I found more than enough room to pass an index card between the end of the screw and the fins. So this shouldn't be an issue for most people. It should be darn near impossible with the provided screws, it would require a fair amount of force, and it would probably involve bending something.

Bottom line: Amazon doesn't allow half-stars, but I'd give the Shott Tech RAD360C 4.5 out of 5 stars.
* It's on the less expensive side for copper custom loop radiators.
* It delivers capable cooling for a CPU & GPU, provided its 360mm form factor fits and it's paired with appropriate fans.
* The minor issues don't seem like they will detract from the product for most customers.

I received this product for free through the Amazon Vine program in exchange for this review. I have attempted to be as honest, objective, and thorough as possible. My goal is to provide you with enough information to form your own opinion rather than asking you to rely on mine. If this review is helpful for you, please hit the "Helpful" button so I can continue creating detailed reviews of niche tech (and other) products!

title: Sharp, fun, well-built Nikon-mount lens
text:
One of my favorite Nikon lenses is an old 16mm fisheye from about 1977, I think. It has two problems: it is a fisheye and curves straight lines at the edges and it's a non-CPU lens, like many of my aged old Nikon lenses. Non-CPU means I have to remember to select it from my list of non-CPU lenses using that menu feature of the D800, and that there is no focus assist. It's full frame, however, and now that we're back to shooting full FX 24x36 sensor, the old lenses are making a comeback.

That 16mm fisheye costs a pretty penny today and the 14-24mm Nikon f/2.8 zoom is even more. And I'm sure they are both fine lenses.

So I bought a Samyang/Rokinon 800mm f/8 mirror lens for two bills and said, "that ought to be fun, even if it's not that great a lens for such little money." Funny thing: it's a pretty good lens.

That good purchase experience allowed me to select this 14mm Rokinon f/2.8. It is surprisingly good considering it's one third the cost of its Nikon equivalent. Even wide open at 1.5 feet, it is tack sharp.

The main difference between this and the Nikon is that this Rokinon is a fully manual focus lens while the 14mm Nikon is auto focus, although I'm not sure how accurately a 14mm lens can focus automatically. I've often simply estimated the distance and set the lens to that distance using the barrel markings. The focus ring is a pleasant long throw, with the ring rotating about 270 degrees around the lens from infinity to .28 meters (less than 1 foot). Focus drag feels silky smooth. Focus happens internally -- the front element does not rotate.

This Rokinon has a clickstop f/stop diaphragm. It also has a chip in it, giving it enough smarts to qualify as an AI-S lens. To use it on a D800, you have to set it to minimum aperture (f/22) or you get the flashing "fee" in the viewfinder. Ah, takes me back....

Setting it to f/22 (marked in orange) tells the camera what f/stop the lens is working at and allows control of the f/stop from the front selector wheel on the D800. The focus indicator in the eyepiece also works -- you see the left/right arrows and the little ball that verifies it's in focus. It also automatically records f/stop and focal length data in the metadata with the shot. In other words, it's a real lens, just without auto focus, for one third the cost. Old Nikon AI-S lenses have a little lock that holds the f/stop ring at minimum aperture that's not present on this lens, but the click stops are secure and the f/stop ring stays where you set it.

The front element is radically curved and is protected somewhat by the flower petal shaped built-in lens shade. Be careful: that front element is really exposed to the weather.

The front lens cap is terrific and very well designed. It's a durable hard plastic unit that slips over the flower petal lens shade and snaps securely in place against detents in the the lens shade. You have to squeeze both plastic flush-mount buttons on the front edge of the cap to release it. It won't fall off by accident under any circumstances. Only drawback it that it's about 1-3/8" deep and 3-5/8" diameter, so it doesn't exactly slip into a back pocket when it's off the lens.

The cosmetics of the lens are appealing. Even has a brass/gold colored band around the front that mimics real Nikon lenses. The focus ring rubber grip is good and the the body of the lens, minus the front element, is about the size of a 50mm f/1.4 lens. Focus distances in feet and meters are clearly engraved. One nice thing it has that I wish all lenses had is the focal length clearly and largely printed on the side of the lens so you can tell at a glance what it is. Nice. The mount is precision machined and fits the camera like it should. There are five little electrical contacts that interface with the camera body to communicate exposure info. For transport, it comes with an unpadded velour drawstring pouch. May want something a bit more padded if it's bouncing around inside a camera bag against other gear. But the bag's adequate, folds flat when not in use and is compact.

As for performance, I'm not going to go into lines/per millimeter sharpness. What I can say is that it's great for architectural interiors and wide, WIDE rectilinear shots. And in analyzing a snap of my dog I pushed in on his eye as far as I could looking at the D800's rear screen and could see the finest of eyelashes, showing off both the resolution of the lens and the remarkable resolution of the D800's 36 megapixel sensor. The lens distinguishes itself from all the wide/medium wide 24mm/35mm lenses out there. Do I really need to have a heavy, giant, hyper-expensive zoom lens that zooms 10 whole millimeters from 14mm all the way to 24mm? Not hardly. If I need serious wide angle this 14mm will fill the bill nicely, even wide open.

No filters for it, of course, because the front element is so deeply curved.

I'm particularly interested in using the 14mm for video shoots, which I use the D800 for more than for still photography. I'll be able to see the whole world with this lens, even in the most cramped of situations.

This will be a fun lens. Highly recommended.

title: Charges batteries more fully than basic chargers
text:
When this EBL charger arrived I put in a battery that was "fully" charged with an AmazonBasics charger. Sure enough, the charger indicated that it required further charging. Other reviews complain about how long it takes to charge batteries, but that happens when you're charging your batteries past 80%. The "fast charge" portion is as fast as the AmazonBasics charger, but the final trickle charge takes its time so as not to damage your cells. I'm not seeing any overnight charge times, but I don't run my batteries completely dead.

This unit charges batteries individually! Many chargers at this price require you to charge in pairs, and turn off when the most fully charged battery is done. When a cell is done charging in this unit, the current to the battery stops. You can tell because the battery that finishes first is cooler to the touch than the others.

The batteries do get quite warm in the charger. Not warm enough to burn your hand, but warm enough that you can't use them right away. Ten minutes and they're at room temperature in a 70F room.

The charger has a three segment indicator. From what I can figure, if the battery shows empty with one bar flashing, it's at 25% or less. One bar solid and one flashing, 50%. Two bars solid and one flashing, 75% or above and doing the final trickle charge.

Pros:
- Individual battery charging.
- Doesn't shut off the whole unit when the first battery is done
- Individual charge level display
- Long trickle charge to charge batteries fully
- Inexpensive

Cons:
- Batteries hard to remove. You have to turn it upside down and whack it against your palm to pop the batteries out.
- Batteries get very warm, which means longer cool down time before you can use them.

Other:
Power plug is offset to the left, which may be a blessing or a curse. If you're plugging into the last outlet on a power strip, it keeps the body of the charger out of the way. If you've got switch or any other plugs to the right, you wont be able to plug it in.

title: Excellent Range, Looks Great
text:
Growing up I always had a radio in my room. Times are a little different now and I tend to get my music from the Internet, but there are still times when local radio stations are a better choice - particularly during power outages or when getting local news. I have had very good fortune with Sony electronics and computers in the past so I was eager to try this AM/FM tuner and had high expectations. It did not disappoint me.

Let me very clear about this unit - it is for AM/FM receiving only. It does not play MP3’s, it doesn’t play CDs and it doesn’t stream from the Internet. It’s just an AM/FM tuner. It does this quite well, though - better than most other tuners I have used in the last several years.

Right out of the box, this unit looks nostalgic. It has a classic AM/FM radio look and feel, very similar to a radio my father used to have in his workshop when I was a kid. This is a big plus for me, just for the fact that it takes me back to my childhood.

I plugged it in and turned it on, and I immediately tuned to one of the [relatively] local stations. It picked it up and played it very clearly, better than most other tuners I have used in the last 4-5 years. It is definitely better than the car’s radio. I “surfed” the dial and found other stations that I have listened to in the past but thought were out of range and this little radio did a good job of picking them up and playing with minimal static. That’s really all I could ask. It’s not a miracle radio though and it cannot pick up FM stations hundreds of miles away, but it has better range than most I have used recently.

I like that it can be used on AC power or on batteries. That will be handy during weather events.

I can’t find any real reason to complain about this tuner. It works great and looks great too. It is a little on the pricey side which is par for the course for Sony electronics, but it is a fine tuner that is worth its asking price.

Bass is kind of weak, though that is a common problem in this price range. 3 hour battery life is about average for this price range. Comparing $50 headphones to $100 headphones is not really fair, but if you do want to spend more money, most headphones will give you much better bass and richer overall sound quality. More expensive headphones also give me better battery life (usually at least 4 hours without any recharging). On the other hand, if I'm out running or riding on the subway, I'd rather use these $50 headphones instead of risk losing much more expensive headphones.

I am impressed by the build quality of these Soundcore headphones. They headphones feel solid. They are comfortable in my ears. The case is sleek and the recharging system works well. The buttons that control the headphones work easily and reliably. I do wish they used a modern USB-C charging system instead of the old-fashioned micro-USB.

Purchased this 4 year plan in November 2016 on a Dell Laser Printer. Thus the printer was a little over 2 years when it started doing weird things and I made a claim.

Basically ... the printer stopped printing black ... it just got lighter and lighter. I attempted to clean the heads and change the cartridges to no avail. The printer would also keep running and not stop after done doing a printer job.

I printed my receipt / invoice off Amazon to PDF. I then went to SquareTrade's website attached the receipt. I then made a claim. The claim process was pretty easy and they actually approved me for a full refund. I just needed to fill out an affidavit. I did this but a week later I still had no refund. Somehow my affidavit didn't get logged even though I got a confirmation email. I called them on the telephone and they fixed everything and were kind about it. Within 24 hours they emailed me an Amazon gift certificate (my choice) which gave me an additional 5% back. I this received a $121 refund on an $118 printer that died in its 3rd year.

I have no complaints and would purchase a square trade warranty again.

Bits of interest as I read other people's low reviews:

1) You purchase a 4 year warranty, but really, for example, it is just 3 extra years beyond the purchase's original 1 year warranty (or however long applies). If your item dies in a year, you have to go to the manufacturer for help.

2) You need to have your receipt. No biggie. Amazon is super amazing that way. I can see all my order back to when Amazon just sold books. Print the invoice / receipt to PDF and there you go. Receipt. Proof of purchase.

3) There is no paper copy of this plan. This is great. It saves trees. You would probably lose it anyway. But Amazon also kept a copy of the fact that I purchased this along with the printer. It was in my order history. There is your proof and all the telephone numbers are there. It is so easy. You don't need a stack of papers.

4) If you file a claim and get 100% of your purchase price back, you cannot file a claim for the same item again. No brainer.

5) This isn't accident insurance. If you do a dumb thing like leave your camera on top of your husband's big rig fender and it ends up in a million pieces 1/2 mile from your house ... it is NOT covered. If you think it should be ... well then ... Take out an insurance policy ... not a warranty. Those are two different things.

6) If you got a deal and paid $65 for your item, but the item now sells for $400 ... you still only paid $65 and $65 is all you are getting back. You don't make money off warranties.

title: Very happy with this
text: My house is 1800 ft.², so I got the package with one satellite instead of two. Did a great job boosting the signal, I don’t get any delay on my phone in the master bedroom. Set up took longer than I would have liked. The nighthawk app walks you through it very nicely, but it could not find my Internet on the first try and I had to reset the modem. Don’t get nervous if you have to try again because it does work eventually. Set up is a lot less technical than I expected. It’s not like setting up a modem. You do not need your IP address. You will have to set up a Netgear account, it is free but another password you have to remember. My friend has one of these and he was able to set his up in 20 minutes. Mine probably took 40. I have a lot of smart devices and most of them automatically reconnected to the “new” wi-Fi. During the set up process, you will have to rename your Wi-Fi. It’s helpful to remember exactly how your old Wi-Fi was spelled. That will help your smart devices reconnect automatically. My iPhone, iPad, Alexa and Samsung smart TVs all reconnected automatically. I had to manually reconnect an Amazon Wi-Fi plug, the MyQ garage door opener, nest thermostats and Dyson air purifier manually. The only smart device that would not reconnect was the Dyson. I was glad the nest thermostat reconnected because it supposedly only works on a 2G network. On my old spectrum router, I had the option of 2G and 5G. Nighthawk only has one option to connect to. Be advised that you do not need a new modem for this system. I have been a little confused about the difference between a modem and a router. The router is basically just a antenna the transmits a Wi-Fi signal. Every Internet provider needs to give you a modem since it is required for any Internet service. Most of them charge you a monthly fee for the router. That’s why a lot of people buy their own. I did have to purchase an additional Netgear ethernet cable splitter, since several of my smart devices need a hub that you have to plug-in to the router. The night hawk does not have enough ports for all my smart devices. Hope this helps.

title: Huge Upgrade from Point-and-Shoot - This is the Camera I Always Wished I Had
text:
I did a good deal of research to find the right camera. I wanted a solid camera with a generous feature set but I didn't want to spend a huge sum either - my budget was roughly $500. At Christmastime the NX300 went on sale, enough of a sale to put it in my price range. After doing a little more research to make sure I had found the camera I wanted, I committed. So far I have been very pleased with it.

Every digital camera I have used before this one has been a point-and-shoot camera, the best of which was actually another Samsung. These types of cameras are great for casual use like a day at the amusement park or making memories on a day trip, but for making really exceptional photographs these cameras are usually ill-suited. Either the focus is flat (meaning everything is one-dimensional), the zoom isn't granular enough, the color is wrong or something else is off just enough to make the picture not quite perfect.

The Samsung NX300 is a "prosumer" camera, meaning it's a high-end consumer and low-end professional camera. Unlike point-and-shoot cameras it has an interchangeable lens system and can be manually focused. It has a good number of features I have not seen on less capable cameras too, such as Wifi connectivity, the ability to add color filters to the lens and much more. I'll hit the highlights.

Without the lens in place, this camera is about the same size and weight as a point-and-shoot camera, maybe slightly larger but not appreciably heavier. Adding the lens adds some bulk and heft to it but it's not as large as something like a Canon Rebel or a high end Nikon. To me this makes this camera a lot easier to carry around than some other models with which it competes, and that can be important when traveling. That said, if not used to working with a camera that has interchangeable lenses there's more to carry (particularly if you use more than just a single lens). A good camera case is a good investment.

This camera has several modes of operation, each optimized for specific shot types and accessible through the spin dial on the top of the camera. The one I use most when experimenting is Auto, which does most of the adjustment for the user and tries to calculate the best settings given the lighting and conditions. It's a good, general purpose mode for most situations. Smart mode is a good choice too, which has presets for a good number of predefined situations like optimized face shots, panorama views, night shots, light traces, silhouettes and several more. Of those smart settings, "Beauty Face" makes adjustments to portraits to compensate for imperfections and this is a great feature. There is a mode for giving the lens the highest priority when it comes to adjustment and that's the mode that gives the user the maximum control over zoom and focus. Manual mode gives the user good control over what to focus on automatically but the camera maintains most of the control. Shutter priority mode allows the user to adjust the shutter speed which is great for when a faster shutter is needed (like an action shot). Aperture priority mode adjusts the aperture width and thus the amount of light allowed in. Program mode seems to be roughly equivalent to Auto mode; I am still learning about that one.

The menu system on this camera is accessible through a nice touch-screen interface, providing access to all manner of settings. I will not go into great detail on the menu system as to do so would make this more of a novel instead of a review. I will say this, though - it is very easy to accidentally make changes when using the menu system if handling the camera in any but the most careful of ways. Just picking up the camera when it is turned on must be done with care as it is almost too easy to touch the screen and make changes without intending to do so. It's fantastic that the screen is sensitive and can be so easily manipulated but it's so sensitive that care is required.

One of the greatest things about this camera is that it can take pictures that have a 3-dimensional quality to them. The main subject of the picture in the foreground is clearly in focus and the surroundings at different depths are in varying levels of being out of focus, and this gives the photo a depth that usually is very difficult to achieve with a point-and-shoot camera. I spent an afternoon playing with the camera just experimenting with this and was thrilled at how natural and easy this camera makes it to take this kind of picture.

Built into the camera is the ability to connect to a Wifi network for uploading images to a smartphone or to share online. This is a nice-to-have but it is not a feature I personally need.

The lens system on this camera is what makes it shine. I bought the 18mm-55mm OIS lens with the camera and this is my first exposure to smart lenses. The lens assembly itself has smarts built into it and when the camera mode it set to give the lens the most control the lens controls the digital zoom and the focus. The focus ring on the lens allows the user to determine what specifically in the picture is in focus which allows for overriding the camera's idea of what should be the main subject of the picture. Sometimes the camera gets it wrong and by using the lens to override it's possible to get the focus just perfect, even on very distant shots or shots that are very busy.

Samsung occasionally updates the firmware for this camera - and the lenses - and updating is relatively simple. With a PC connection the firmware download to the camera is quick and the update is applied through the menu system.

Though this camera is more than capable of taking high-quality video I do not use it for such. I prefer using a dedicated video camera. That said, video recording is easy with the touch of a single button on the back of the camera, to the right and just above the touch screen. What little recording I have done with it has turned out excellent of course, but I will not use this function most of the time.

For all of the positive things I can say about this camera, I do have a couple of minor gripes. First, though it's convenient to have a removable flash I would have preferred to have the flash built-in to the camera body. It's a minor issue but it's worthy of mention. A printed manual would have been nice too, but at 200+ pages it is understandable why one is not included. At least it's on the CD in the package. It is common knowledge that the battery life is not great on this camera and that the only way to charge the battery (without buying a separate charger) is to plug in the camera, either with a USB charger or into the computer itself.

I have found the camera I really wanted. It is a highly capable camera with a really generous feature set and it takes amazing shots (with some practice). There's a learning curve with it if all you have used prior is a point-and-shoot, but the effort is worth it.

title: Works with Ring Doorbell 2!
text:
I hate to change the battery for the Ring Doorbell. It's one of the reasons that I didn't purchase those "stick up" cameras to put up around the house. I am not interested in having to change batteries every month. With that in mind, I set out to find a solar panel that works with my Ring Doorbell 2.

Looking at other listings, I saw that the ones that claim to work with Ring generate 5v, 3amps. I confirmed that this board also generates 5v, 3a (check my pictures) and took the chance to cut off the microusb connector that it came with.

What was exposed were two wires; red and black so there was no guess work necessary to figure out which wires would be positive and ground (usb usually has 4 wires). After stripping the wires, I screwed the wires to the back of the doorbell and crossed my fingers.

From my pictures, you'll see that the Ring app recognized the solar panel and also charged from 46% to 55% after one day in the sun.

Note: The wire is a little bit short so it may not reach your roof. I was able to get around this by soldering a longer wire from an old cell phone car charger.

title: the TV was tilting pretty dramatically to one side
text:
This is my first large TV and first TV stand. So not much experience with either. I have a 55inch Hisense, on sale from Walmart for 300 bucks. After debating about wall mounting it I decided to try a stand first.

The directions indicate using a level to make sure the brackets on the back of the TV are level. I don't know how you are supposed to do that. Its a rigid bracket, with symmetrical, with pre-defined holes. Assuming the TV holes are machined correctly and the bracket, I don't see how it could be anything but level. In any case, when I first put it on, the TV was tilting pretty dramatically to one side. I didn't know how to fix it. After slightly manipulating the TV for a bit, it seems to have gone into place and looks fine now.

The directions are extremely clear with everything labeled, with a little humorous flavor added to it. They come with many different size screws. They had the correct screws for my TV, and I have many screws unused, so I would bet they have the screws needed for any major TV brand.

In case you are like me who is not experienced with this, this is how the stand works....

You screw the pole to the base, then the horizontal long piece to the top of the pole. In the product picture, you see the 2 long thin brackets mounted vertically, 1 on each side of the horizontal part. These actually screw on to the back of the TV.

When you get the brackets screwed to the back of the TV, you then tilt the TV and hang it on the vertical part. When you get the "hook" part of the bracket in place you start tilting the TV back down and then its fairly secured there. There are screws on the bottom of the main mounting place that screw up to secure it in place. It might sound like an unstable way of doing things but it actually seems to be pretty tight and solid. I did this all by myself. I am an adult male. It wasn't too difficult or anything but it was awkward handling a 55inch tv by yourself. If that .00001% thing happened it could have been a dropped TV. I would probably just ask someone for 5 seconds of help to be safe.

So far enjoying movies and tv shows on it and couldn't be happier.

text:
Ok. I'm a 66 year old woman who is tired of being screwed by my cable company who is now requiring Digital Transport Adapters of all of my TV's. And the picture quality has suffered greatly using the DTA's. Add that I'm going to be charged for their rental and cannot purchase my own. WTF! I'm paying more to get a whole lot less. Time to cut the cord

So I found that video that was mentioned in other reviews (binder clip antenna), on making your own antenna. Holy COW! I had all the parts except for this transformer. So for a one time purchase of $4.00, I thought why not give it a whirl? Guess what...it totally works. Took about 10 minutes to assemble the whole thing, attached it to my TV and I'm getting a far better picture than I ever got with the cable even before the DTA conversion.

I'm getting 28 channels so far (perfect HD picture quality) and while they are only the local broadcast channels, including PBS, ION, MeTV and a bunch of others, I'm perfectly content with those. I can stream all the other programs I love (like the Vikings) through the Internet features on my TV and Blu-Ray.

To TWC...just because the FCC says you can, doesn't mean you should. And a one time $4.00 investment as opposed to $800.00 per year, ad infinitum means I'm saying "snip,snip, bye bye". I can rent A LOT of movies for that cost or get them free through my Amazon Prime (which I LOVE!)

This review is about what I think >90% of users will care about. The detail specs are a step further, higher and faster and advertised and advertised. The Asus ZenBook 13 has been my go-to everyday toting computer for some 7-8 years.

I have last year’s i5 gen7 ZenBook 13 to directly compare the two.

P.S. This Zen-book has been so good that I had it modified to incorpoarte medical practice compliant HIPA secured software. It's a step function increase in my nightly homework replacing my 7-year old Dell. This laptop is ubiquitously practical with 180 screen twist for descirbing patient procedures. With the med-system handshacks, its like 3x faster than the Dell.

First, this new i5 gen8 ZenBook 13 has a quarter inch all-around smaller footprint. The 1/4" is immediately noticeable from last year’s edition. The 1/4" bezel is noticeably better. As small a footprint as the two have, Asus has reduced the size with no compromise in keyboard utility.

This year's ZenBook is noticeably thinner. Recharge and headphone jack are reversed. This year's hinge is slightly more robust to account for the reduced thickness. The hinge has been a 'should improve' on ZenBooks since inception. This years may solve the issue for good.

The plug-outs are changed. Make sure the output ports are what you want. For my purposes, the addition of a standard HDMI vice last year’s mini-HDMI is an improvement requiring no adapter. Last year’s SD input has been correctly reduced to the increasingly popular/common micro-SD. Plug-out needs are easily resolved with a USB-C adapter hub.

The discrete Nvidia graphics will be an interesting exploration.

The Asus fingerprint reader has never failed. This edition looks identical to last years and has been creatively moved right and off the touchpad. The ZenBook has been the very best reader compared to my HP Envy (dang good) and Dell XPS (50:50 chance).

This year's battery is new tech. The lithium-polymer battery promises up to 14 hours and includes fast-charge technology that takes "just 49 minutes" to recharge to 60% capacity. I get 11 hours out of last year’s battery every day. I can't recall running out of battery on last years on battery save mode on trans-con flights.

Wish it came with Windows Pro instead of Home, but oh well.

Finally, both last years and this year are so fast you'd have to instrument to tell a speed difference. The ZenBooks 1-2-3 second boot to Windows is 'instant' for practical purposes.

Love it. Exceeds expectations. There's no purchase mistake to be made with the UX331.

title: Good Hardware, Not-So-Good Setup
text:
I work a lot with smart watches but this is the first health monitor/GPS watch I have used. I was excited to have the
opportunity to work with it, and I was hopeful that it would be a good unit. Epson is a brand I know well from their printers, so out of the gate I had some expectations. This watch has proven to be a mixed bag.

I will start with what I believe are the strongest features. This watch has a much better-than-average charger. Many watches I have used have a magnetic charger that is either poorly constructed or will not stay on the device it'’s charging. This one, however, is a clamp-based charger that does a good job of holding the watch even under its own weight without letting it slip or shift. I would have liked to see other manufacturers adopt this kind of charging clamp.

The battery lasts for a very long time. I charged it up completely and after taking it from the charger I deliberately left it on the shelf to drain. It's rated for 20 hours, and I assume that is for active use. Letting it sit idle, it lasted two weeks for me. It of course drains much faster when it is actively being used so once I started using it I had to charge it again. This is a handy data point if you're traveling - if you're going for a weekend, it holds enough charge to get through in most cases, and if you are an infrequent user it will retain a charge for a while.

The display is very clear and easy to read. I have had no issues at all with the display and I am very pleased with how easy on the eyes it is.

One of the issues I have with most wrist-wear of any kind is getting it to fit properly. I have large hands and wrists, and I found this watch to be a bit snug on even the loosest setting. This is par for the course for me. I was hopeful it would fit a bit better, but it wasn't to be.

The aggravation started when I set up the software and paired the watch to my phone. The Bluetooth pairing did not go smoothly and I tried several times to get it straight. I finally switched over to setting it up through the watch instead of through the phone, and I was able to get it working and connected. While this is an acceptable work-around for someone with patience, it is an aggravation for someone who prefers things to just work the way they're supposed to.

I will say I am not especially impressed with the software app. I think it is a little too overly complex and counter-intuitive, but it does work and it has a lot of features. It does a good job of tracking progress.

So, aside from setup and fit, how does it work? It seems to work well. I am very familiar with sport GPS units so I assumed this one would work about the same, and it does. It acquires the satellites and uses those to report position back to the phone app so you can track yourself. This is useful when you want to see where you went and how far. The speed of acquisition of the satellites seems to be roughly the same as with my hand-held units. The heart rate monitor seems to be good and in measuring manually for comparison it appears to be accurate. The step feature is a good quick measurement and is sufficient to replace a dedicated pedometer.

Overall this is a decent health watch, but there's some room for improvement. It looks great, it works well and it's easy to read. It is hampered by less-than-idea setup and software, and it would be nice if it fit a little better.

title: Bluetooth has many options
text:
This item comes with a huge array of options for ear gels (plugs) and cushions along with 3 over the head and behind the neck headbands and 2 clear ear hooks for when you don't want to use a headband. BlueParrott claims the wireless range is up to 300 feet and has 10 hours of talk time and 13 days of standby.

The very first thing I did was to make sure the device was fully charged using the USB cable that was provided. The center square light will turn from red to blue when charged and will go out once you remove the USB cable. Setting up the BlueParrot is quick. You have to press the square button to make it light up red, and then hold it for 3-4 seconds until it flashes. Once paired the light will turn blue and on my phone Bluetooth preferences it shows up as C300-XT. When I click on the C300-XT the setting has on/off for phone and audio. I turned both on and left it there.

The round voice button above the square button is for voice commands and it has several. It seems that every time I ask a command I have to include the word Command. For instance when wanting to call a phone contact I would say Phone Command, then the device would pause, open Google assistant on my phone, and wait for me to name a contact. Within 5 seconds it would begin calling that person. Other voice commands are to check if Bluetooth is connected, battery life a nice feature and others like. You can answer a call or ignore a call by just saying so. The sound quality is very good and it does block out background noise. The bottom 2 switches + and - are for volume up and down. However, I wouldn't use this device in a loud construction area as the volume may not be strong enough. Otherwise for people that have very good hearing it may be okay or by just selecting the right ear cup may help.

The C300-XT feels to be of strong construction and weighs 1.6 ounces with a headband attached. I did like using it with the cushioned ear pad for comfort. As mentioned above there are so many different accessories for ear set ups, one should find comfort.

One thing I’d like to point out is that the manual is very lame with regard to details. All voice commands and how to set this item up are assuming the person has an extended knowledge on Bluetooth headsets. The manual has only once small page for each How to Pair, How to Wear, How to use, and Voice Control. These are all very basic. I can see where some folks would have issues getting all the voice commands to work and understanding what they do. I also believe the manual should explain more to help people with set up using Google assistant.

Overall the C300-XT is an advanced piece of technology but large in size and I think you will like it. You can also stream music or use to get GPS directions. You can connect to 2 devices with multipoint and there is a free app for android/iOS to configure the parrott button for more advanced communication features. Be patient and take your time with this item as you should enjoy the features. Good luck.

title: Positives & Negatives
text:
I bought my pair of Bluez 2S directly from AfterShokz company, and not via Amazon. Just like with so many things there are aspects to like and aspects to not like.

I will start with the negatives. If you are in a noisy environment, such as working out in an exercise room, the volume just is not loud enough or satisfactory at all. You need earplugs in the ears to get the satisfactory volume. Yes, earplugs. Of course, that defeats the whole purpose of buying headphones that do not go inside or cover your ears.

You can test this out by simply putting a finger in each ear and then you'll hear the remarkable level of volume change.

Because of the lack of loudness one can achieve in a noisy environment, I cannot recommend these (unless you want to buy earplugs and wear them at the same time).

The only other negative for me personally is the lack of a way to go back to a previous song, or repeat the currently playing song. (You can skip forward to the next song, but you cannot go back.)

The positives: These are comfortable to wear and very lightweight. The Bluez 2S offers the ability for decent call quality when using them to make calls. Microphones seem good (I have only tried this indoors, and not outdoors, so I cannot comment further on this particular subject.)

title: Get your own, cut your Comcast bill
text:
Comcast has repeatedly lied to me, sending me letters and alerts telling me that I need a new cable modem or my service will be seriously degraded. One time they went so far as to set a date when my service would NO longer work at all! Of course, I would never believe them without double-checking for myself, and I found out it was indeed an outright lie. Even the oldest DOCSIS versions can handle more than my 30Mbps connection. I suppose the lie was because they want me to rent their modem for $10 or more a month and relinquish control of my own network to them.

That said, it makes sense to upgrade when convenient to be sure you're future proofed. Eventually even the cheapest Internet plans will be upgraded to higher speeds. When I heard that I could register this on Comcast's network online without having to call them (and have them speak extremely condescendingly to me even though I'm a Systems Engineer), I was sold. Worth doing.

Note that just because DOCSIS 3.0 can reach speeds of 10Gbps with maxed out number of channels, this modem is 680Mbps, which will be out of date eventually, when we finally get Gigabit Ethernet to residences.

Another (of a million) thing(s) I hate about Comcast is that they by default use your AP (that they rent to you as part of a router/AP/modem combo) to create a public (virtual) wireless AP for their other customers. They say this will not affect your bandwidth, but it can affect your throughput. And it uses your electricity. And why would you want to help Comcast, when they take advantage of you any chance they can.

Point of all this is me encouraging you to get your own modem, get your own router and AP (or combo unit, although I prefer them separate) and pare down your ISP bill as much as you can. Stop giving them money.

Note that apparently if you get voice service through Comcast, you'll still need their combo modem unit of some sort. Well, cut that service from your monthly budget too. If we just had some competition, I'd cut Comcast out of my life completely.

Another thing is that if you have their modem and you need help with it, they may call it your responsibility and charge you for any "help" they provide. At least if you own your own stuff, you'll know if it's your problem or theirs.

Modem is straightforward and easy to use as any. If you ever download at high rates for days on end, it'll need cycled, but that's not the modem's fault; it just happens.

F2 has |<<, which did nothing when pressed

The action on the keyboard is nice and a lot quieter than the Logitech keyboard I am replacing. The mouse action is good and also quiet.

title: It's one of the better projectors in this price range
text:
This is a decent entry level projector for every day use and a very good unit for specialized purposes like outdoor viewing on a large screen.

Its picture quality is better than most I have seen in this range and is brighter as well. The native 1080p image is sufficient for what you are buying, but one would never compare it to a higher end model. Of course, most of those start by adding another zero to the price, just for starters. I have had a couple of projectors in this price range and none of them really have a "great" picture, and that's honestly to be expected.

With this projector, you get a watchable image in daylight hours, but really improves if you black-out the room with darkening curtains or are watching after dark. The image will clearly show on a light color wall, but will improve drastically if you use an actual screen.

The fan noise is a little more intrusive than I would like, so it does interfere a bit if you are just using the included speakers. My suggestion is to connect it to a stand-alone external speaker setup. This is especially recommended if you are setting up an outdoor viewing screen.

It does tout 4D±50° Keystone correction, but it's not really as good as all that, in my opinion. I could never get the picture shape quite right at these angles. Connectivity is adequate, with several input options, so that's really a plus. I had it hooked up to an external hard drive as well as my Amazon Fire Stick and it handled each of them nicely. The WiFi connection is adequate and I had no issues connecting to my network. 5G connection is definitely a plus here as long as you are relatively close to your router.

Overall, I would say that this projector is a good value for the money spent. Try it out to see if Projection Television is for you. It's a whole new world, that's for sure. text:
I have had a need for an additional storage solution for my laptop which will enable me to back up files, and transfer between desktop (my workstation) and my laptop when necessary. My goal is to have it as an alternative mini hard drive, so to speak. Let's take a Look.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This is a tiny Jumpdrive, for those who have never used one, it is similar in appearance to a dongle that you use for wireless keyboard or mouse in the USB port. It does not have a case and the packaging is rather difficult to open.

WHAT IS THIS FOR?
This is designed not to carry with you all of the time like some of the flash drives, but to use almost as a mini hard drive and keep it in your laptop or even desktop if desired. It will keep your files handy, has a pretty fast transfer rate, and has a decent amount of storage, depending on what kind of files you plan to store on it.

WHAT ELSE CAN YOU USE THESE FOR?
This can also be theoretically used to keep in the car as a way to play music on your sound system via USB port. I have not been able to do that yet as I have had some issues setting up the right format. I am not sure how security will interact with that..

DOES THIS HAVE SECURITY ON IT?
This drive has a program called ENCDataVault Lite. That will allow you to encrypt your files and have them accessed with a password you set up in case you lose your drive at least your files will be somewhat protected unless it is a hacker who finds it.

HOW IS TRANSFER RATE?
I have used this in a USB3.0 as well as USB2.0 port and both worked well.

DOES THIS FIT TYPE C CONNECTION?
You can not use this in a type C port so please check your laptop or desktop prior to purchase to be sure you have an actual USB port to use this in that is not already being used.

WHAT I DON'T LIKE ABOUT THIS
This drive should come with a tiny case on a keychain or with at least a loop handle on it so that you can put it somewhere safe and not lose it. It does not come with that. Something this small needs to have a colorful case to make it harder to lose. I know that the idea is to have it stay in the unit you use it on mostly, but sometimes you have to take it out and it needs a case.

THE BOTTOM LINE

title: plastic construction is not durable enough for outdoors use, 3 foot cable limits placement options anyway, no VHF support
text:
Before you buy, check the Monoprice website for this item. The price may be much cheaper over there.

This is a very inexpensive, relatively low quality TV antenna. You get what you pay for. They advertise this for both indoor and outdoor use, but the mostly plastic construction will not last long outdoors in areas that get a lot of wind, ice, or bright sunlight. The attached 3 foot cable really tells you what their intended use case is. If your TV is near a window, hang the antenna in the window, plug it in, and you're done.

The advertised 50 mile range is for ideal conditions, mounting the antenna outdoors in an area where there are absolutely no obstructions between your home and the TV broadcast tower (no trees, no buildings, etc). Expect much worse range for an indoor mounting and if there are any obstructions. If you live in an area with trees etc, you should get a more sturdy antenna that can be mounted on a pole on top of your roof so it can receive a signal over the trees.

This antenna is advertised for UHF frequencies only. Most TV stations use UHF these days, but in my area there are a couple that use VHF and this antenna is not usable for those channels. If you really want VHF, I suggest getting a different antenna from this one.

1080p and 720p content looks OK. From normal distances things look very good, but any closer you see a rather soft picture with the basic upscaling. 4k content lacks this issue, and it's nothing unexpected. I'm sure there are better upscalers, but not in my price range.
