text:
Probably the best speakers I have ever listened to. I own or have owned Definitive Technology BP8020 (pretty good but a bit unexciting - definitely prefer the BP8060), Klipsch RP600M (which are grave disappointments of the year), Fluance ai40 (a very good imaging and enjoyable sounding speaker), Infinity Beta 50, Optimus Pro LX 10, some Bose box Bose speakers from my younger days, Aiwa Exos-9, Doss Soundbox XL, a pair of Sony floorstanders and a variety of headphones including my faves the Sennheiser HD600 and to a lesser extent the Monoprice M1060. Elac UB5 are every bit as enjoyable as my sennheiser HD600.

The treble is a bit laid back but usually it is very clear and clean. The mids are slightly imperfect but are usually outstandingly detailed. Bass - these guys can push really low. I don't need a sub in my room. I have a DIY kit sub from Parts Express the 8" 250 DSP sub, which is great, but even it takes away from the sound, being slightly not blended and calling attention to itself. I feel no need for it anyway. I mostly listen to Rock. If I listened to more bass heavy music I could probably readjust the DSP settings of the sub to get some reinforced bottom end, but I never felt these were lacking bass - or tonal quality.

They say these need a lot of power and beside the Klipsch RP600M they do need more but my 50W Emotiva A100 drives them perfectly well. They do shine, the bass is substantial. Emotiva seems to make solid gear for an affordable price. I picked these up when they were $280 and I am very impressed.

I expected these to look rather boring and ugly. However, getting them in my room they look quite modern and delightful. I appreciate the type of material they have used on the box - it is something like a gritty textured machined material. I am sure it is wood but the finish has some sort of metal type of look reminding me of a metal amplifier with the machine lines - so it doesn't quite look like a simple paint job but something modern andd decorative. I like the bigger box of the old design. They look really cool in my room and the sound is highly pleasurable and smoothly soothing.

I have spent a lot of money in audio over 25 years. These $280 speakers are true to source and I endorse them 100%. If you are comparing these with the Klipsch RP600M, I say those were a huge disappointment and Joe'NTell was correct that these Elac UB5 are my favorites, too. If you need a good speaker and can equalize it and need to save money the Fluance ai40 are highly enjoyable speakers and a huge value.

Thank you Joe from Joe'NTell, Andrew Jones, Elac and Amazon!

I purchased the My Book Live 2 TB drive in the hopes of centralizing my media across multiple computers (mostly Mac's) in my home. The initial set up worked fine, took a bit of time to set it up across the multiple computers in my house. The Mio setup for remote access took forever (about 30 minutes), and was very slow and cumbersome to use. I was expecting something like a DropBox experience, but the interface and speed of remote access are very slow and crude.

About 2 hours into backing up my media files, a message popped up from the hard drive strongly recommending me to download the latest firmware update - which I promptly agreed to, and asked it to download and install. The hard drive started downloading the update - did it for almost 30 minutes, and then sent an error message about how there was some communications problem. I was on the internet on another computer at that same instant - so I knew we had internet access (high speed FiOS). I tried to ask it to redownload which it started doing, but then gave me the same error message. Shortly after the second error message - I couldn't see the drive on my network. Within minutes, the green light on the drive turned red. I looked up their manual, it asked me to restart the drive or reset it. I did both - but the hard drive kept giving me the red light, and it wouldn't boot up. I gave up on the process after spending about 45 minutes on trying to revive it.

I am very disappointed with the product. I am sending it back. I am a Toshiba external hard drive user - was very excited about this one due to the remote access functionality, and could have been a convert. But, I guess I will be going back to Toshiba and its reliable performance.

What my wife is a bit afraid of is that I had managed to copy our iPhoto library on this hard drive before it went down. She is afraid of sending it back to WD without scrubbing it clean, and is not confident of whether Western Digital will scrub it after repairing it and shipping it to some other customer. But I can't scrub it because it won't boot up. So hopefully WD does the sane, ethical thing and scrubs it after it repairs it, before sending it to someone else.

title: A basic projector with great brightness and full HD resolution
text:
The WEWATCH Video Projector with WiFi and Bluetooth is a basic projector that has all of the necessary features that one needs.

The description of this product may lead you to think otherwise, but this projector is not really a "smart" projector. It does not run on Android and the built-in user interface is quite basic. Yes, it will play videos and show photos from USB drives and it has WIFI... for whatever reason (I didn't really look into it because I simply plugged in a FireTV). The bluetooth, on the other hand, does have a function. I'll get into that in a bit.

So for video input, you have two full sized HDMI ports, a VGA (for those ancient laptops that your office may have lying around?) and a USB port which outputs enough amperage to run a fireTV, so no additional power adapter necessary.

There is no automatic keystone adjustment, but what is there works well. You can adjust the four corners up and down, although I found that it still seems to have some bloating in the middle no matter how I adjust it (could be a problem with my projection screen and projector positioning). A tip for doing the adjustment: If you aren't able to move the corners in the direction that you need, try adjusting the zoom first. By zooming out, it allows the corners to be pulled up or down more.

Audio is as expected in that it is not winning any awards. It can get pretty loud, but it still sounds empty. This is where bluetooth or the 3.5 mm headphone jack comes in. For wireless audio, you can either pair a bluetooth speaker/soundbar to the projector itself or you can pair the speakers directly to the FireTV or whatever dongle you're using. The advantage of pairing the speakers to the projector is that they will work for both HDMI inputs. If you really wanted to get full surround, you'll have to extract the audio out of the HDMI wire. Basically plug the HDMI into an audio receiver, then the audio receiver to the projector. The receiver can take care of decoding the surround depending on your setup.

For the brightness, the 1100LM beats out many other projectors of this price and resolution. You can really tell that the picture just pops. It will work well enough in a dimly lit room, but you can only truly appreciate it when the lights are completely off.

Overall, this is a low-priced projector that will work well for outdoor, temporary use, or even a permanent setup inside the home.

text:
I tried my M10+ tablet for a day without a case, I only use it in my bedroom and it's stored in a pocket on my bed rail. I don't plan on traveling period, so this case does enough. It's easier to grip though it takes an extremely thin and sexy modern tablet and bulks it up to look like something from years ago. Small price to pay. I don't like that the slightest movement causes the magnets to disengage and I can see the tablet come on while closed and in my bed rail. I've adjusted the self-timer on the screen to shut off sooner than I normally have my tablets set just to save battery life. The inner lining is a soft either felt like or microfiber material so the screen won't get scratched. The case has enough texture to make gripping it while laying in bed (adjustable bed) much easier than the aluminum table alone. That's what I needed, that's what I got. Better magnets would really have helped. I really haven't used the foldable cover to make a stand, I don't sit or use a tablet where that would be useful. Again, I bought this because:

title: "Will You Still Need Me, Will You Still Feed Me, When I'm 64?"
text:
OK, I admit it. They say that 60 is the new 40. Unfortunately that doesn't work with technology. I've tried to keep up but I find myself becoming a little more like my wife. She just wanted a cellphone to take and make calls on. I preferred and appreciated the extra features and apps and was willing to learn them. Now I find myself just wanting a great TV picture (and sound) without all the bells and whistles like 3D, video streaming, and everything else that requires extensive research and understanding to use.

So, based upon my willingness to 'own up' to being behind on the current TV magic, knowing that a few problems have cropped up for customers buying direct from Amazon (and the problem of repacking and return shipping), and knowing my propensity for seeing Murphy's Law in action, I decided to buy this TV locally. When I did, they matched Amazon's $2,199 price. So I paid the extra $250 to have them deliver the set and integrate it into my home theater unit. That way they would take care of the unit's return if it was faulty, jostled in shipping, or dropped by one of the techs when he was stung by a wasp while bringing it up the front steps.

It turned out that there was nothing faulty with the TV, but watching the two guys setting up and calibrating the set saved me a tremendous amount of time and frustration. Since it took two of them about three hours to set it up, it probably would have taken me weeks. Until recently I never understood why my father always wanted to keep things simple and easy. It seems like everything we buy (cars, phones, computers, appliances, etc.) come with a 400 page manual--or require you to go online and read the information there. I'm pretty much burned out on that, so much so that I MIGHT stop buying certain things because of the college courses I need to take to use them.

Sorry. Another result of aging is the meandering thoughts encountered when trying to explain myself. Back to the TV. I had a Samsung LED unit for the last four years that had a great picture but also a propensity for burned out pixels. A $500 repair solved that problem and relegated the set to a junior level in the basement. (See, there I go again.) I love the picture on this TV. I have been watching the Tour de France at night and thoroughly enjoy the spaciousness and clarity of the picture. Blu Ray movies 'pop' on this set. Switching back and forth from an HD channel to the same analog feed shows the tremendous difference between the two. My home theater unit supplies a wonderful listening environment so I haven't used the TV speakers. Most people probably don't.

So I'm very happy with this Sharp TV. I have owned Sony, Mitsubishi, Hitachi, and Samsung units but of course the picture quality has come a long way since I bought my 70" rear projection set in 1981. If you are not completely comfortable with setting this TV up, STRONGLY consider hiring an expert to do it for you. Younger people will laugh at this suggestion, but you know what I mean.

I'll admit, I've bought into the Amazon/Kindle crack. I own three now, the old e-ink, the old Fire and now the Fire HD. I'm sure if there's a new version that comes out, I'll probably find an excuse to buy it at some point as I keep finding uses for the older ones. That said, it took me a while to warm up to the Fire HD. Perhaps because I expected so much from it, it being the first real tablet Kindle to come out, even though I'm not going to rave about Apple or the others.

At first I mainly stuck to the reading and video capabilities - of course it's easy to download, manage and read material on the Fire HD. Videos look great on the screen as well, and as someone who streams their Prime account as well as Hulu and Netflix all of the time, I haven't noticed any issues with the video quality or capability. Some days I watch more on my Fire HD than I do my tv.

Music streams and plays well, also (though have a complaint with the playlists on Kindles and how they can time out. Why no loop feature, Amazon?).

I'm not the biggest app person out there - I've been able to eventually track down what I need and notice that there's more out there all of the time, but again, it's not like I hit the app store that often. I've never had an issue with the apps I have downloaded.

It took me a while to get used to the Silk/internet feature. I'm not the biggest fan of this aspect of the Fire HD - if there was something to detract stars from,t his wold be it. Maybe because on a regular pc I'd have a couple of dozen tabs open and tons of bookmarks, and I don't think the bookmark nature of Silk is very intuitive and I have to remember to keep the tabs to a minimum for it to function well. Here's hoping to improvements in future upgrades.

All in all, the Fire HD is a great tablet/multi-media/entertainment device. It's something I use pretty much every day and can take anywhere, and it's easy to figure out and set up. It also comes with fantastic customer service.

title: A truly great mirror less with few compromises
text:
I've always yearned for a quality mirror less camera with interchangeable lenses (before they even existed), though early examples fell short in execution in one or more key areas. Fuji came a little late to the mirrorless party, and they got much right, but when I tried earlier examples, the autofocus was subpar and it just felt too slow for a $1000 setup.

This addresses those concerns and gets just about everything right. Some of the pros:

Compact, but not overly so to diminish "holdability"
Lens selection (already among the best for mirror less)
Great "kit" lens (phenomenal build, better than average light gathering, and quality images)
Built in flash that can be bounced (by holding it up)
Speedy AF (no longer an issue)
Excellent image quality
Great high ISO performance
Solid intuitive controls (the menus do have quirks)

and the cons:

Not pocketable (not necessarily a con, but do know it's too big for most pockets, even with a "pancake" lens)
Quirky menus (no real con, but it could still use work)
Poor battery life (somehow it needs to be bigger) for rigorous use with the built in flash (using an external flash helps tremendously)
Limited video usability indoors with kit lens (doesn't get enough light)
You'll fall in love with the ecosystem and buy lots of lenses, flashes, etc... (really a pro, but your pocketbook sees it as a con)

Simply put I love this camera. It's speedy, delivers great results, offers great lenses, and other than battery life, I don't see any notable negatives. It has it's quirks, and if your used to Canon or Nikon, it's just different (not really a con). The one quirk that does annoy me (not a show stopper), is the film simulations. It's great for someone who has used Fuji's professional films, but for anyone who never used film, only shot other brands, shot Fuji's consumer film, or simply forgot what things looked like, it's would be nice to also offer a more traditional way to adjust color profiles (some is offered via menus). One mitigating factor is that the menus offer a preview of each simulation along with a quick description of each. These minor issues aside, everything else is done right, especially speed, AF accuracy, image quality, and ergonomics. Simply put, everything looks great, and it's a joy to use.

5 stars for an avid photographer coming from an advanced compact, a rangefinder, or a SLR
I would be reluctant to recommend this to a novice (the similar and cheaper Fujifilm X-M1 would be a better choice), unless they're looking to learn more about exposure (then I'd wholeheartedly recommend this).

I updated my review to clarify my concerns about battery life, which does improve dramatically when used with an external flash. I continue to marvel at how well this camera works at high ISOs. I regularly use it at ISO 800 with limited artifacts beyond my expectations for ISO 200. This greatly enhances the usability of the kit lens with or without the built in flash. Surprisingly, I use the excellent EVF sparingly, preferring to use the screen on back. This likely won't be the case in bright daylight, but for indoor use, you may be satisfied with the X-M1 (same sensor, different lens, lower price).

text:
Mesh networking and this particular setup shows a lot of promise, but like any promise, it has to be fulfilled. Today I cannot say whether or not it has, but I like what I see. For starters, a three pack really starts to hit the potential of mesh networking. There are better and cheaper single device routers, and to be honest, a router and some form of repeater/access point makes for a better two device solution. For folks living in a sprawling ranch, two story, or home with an occupied basement, three devices starts to become the norm, and a dedicated mesh can better handle three or more devices.

This particular setup is packaged in a smart and compact box, and it certainly looks less like a typical D-Link, Linksys, etc... device and more like something different. Setup continues this by being something you do on your phone or iPad as opposed to a computer. Web browser setup doesn't appear to even be supported. Had I not previously used a Google OnHub setup, this would have been more off putting, but I'm. warming to teh approach. Likewise some of the fine grained manual control is missing. It simply works and uses the know how of Luma to make it easier. Of course most people would prefer this, and all in all it does the basics (and I don't mean that to be disparaging in any way--most people really only need the basics) rather well. I really appreciated the help setting up ad placing the devices, and it made mid level tasks like parental controls and security a breeze. Guest access was particularly well managed.

Fine grained control is there in places, and I wouldn't say a grizzled router veteran would be too frustrated with this. Wired access is a bit limited, and that's a bit of a chore, but I have a couple 24+ port switches, so I can work with them to make the magic happen. My old wired leanings die hard, but I'm very impressed with coverage and speed. Some is inherent with any modern AC router, but the seamless coverage is new.

As far as what needs to come, fine grained controls for advanced routing/firewall aren't really there, and I'd love to see some support for powerline or wire based back haul. Both are fringe use cases, but they matter to me. I also see to see some odd channel choices using my scanning tools. It's hard to say for sure the hardware is making the wrong choices, but it appears so.

Given whats right and ongoing development, I'm comfortably giving this a strong recommendation, albeit one I may update down the line as the system grows.

title: Home Made Might Be Better
text:
So it’s 2014 and I finally entered the world of touch screen computing and like a good sucker, I dished out $28 for the Kensington Virtuoso Pro Pen 39526 WW (Stylus and Pen combo). It arrived before the computer, but I decided to examine it nonetheless to see what makes a stylus a stylus. First of all, I didn’t like the feel and weight of this item and the pen leaked on my finger. The pen’s tip is a heavy weight metal, which makes it good for writing, but when it’s flipped for screen use, the heaviness is on the top of the stylus (where the pen is) instead of at the bottom. I don’t like that type of imbalance for drawing. I discovered that this item is an overpriced do-hickey that anyone can make at home from practically anything that you have lying around the house. For the how-to video instructions on how to make your own stylus to suit your personal taste and/or needs you can check out the websites that I’ve listed below and/or read the summary that follows.
Our smartphone, computer, or tablet’s touch screen senses touch because our fingers produce electrons, hence sending an electrical message to the screen that allows us to write or draw. Therefore to make a stylus, we need something that will behave as a conductor between our finger and the screen. Metal is a conductor. Inexpensive good metal conductors include aluminum, a metal rod (such as an antenna barrel or metal pen), a paper clip, a naked copper wire, or the metal spring that’s inside an old pen. A wet sponge or Q-Tip can also conduct electricity and neither of them scratches the screen.

To design a scratch-free stylus, insert a strip of sponge or Q-Tip into a metal casing (such as an old pen or a slender antenna tube that you’ve cut to size). Each should fit tightly into the barrel in order to make a good contact and connection with your finger and the metal casing. Wet the tip of that sponge or Q-Tip and use it on your touch screen.

If you don’t have a metal barrel available, you can use a cheap plastic pen. Drill two holes, one on either side of the plastic barrel. If you don’t have a small drill handy, you can burn the holes through the pen using a heated ice pick or paper clip. Insert the sponge (make sure it protrudes through the pen’s tip and that it also makes contact with the holes that you drilled). The final step is to insert a paper clip or a stripped copper wire through the holes and the sponge that you packed into the pen’s barrel. Next, wrap the wire tightly around the pen’s barrel. When you write, make sure your finger(s) touch the wire, which will transmit your electronic touch to the sponge and your tablet’s screen. title: The best that I've used
text:
Since getting my Yoga 10" tablet, I've purchased and tried (much to my financial dismay) three different screen protectors. The first two came from ebay. The first product was the SuperShieldz HD Clear protector. I got it positioned onto the screen well, with minimal bubbles. But the transparency quality was badly compromised by a weird purplish streakiness that was very noticeable when angling the tablet so that any light source was bouncing off of the protector. In case you're wondering, the tablet screen was pristine clean before putting on that particular brand of screen shield. There were three protectors that came with the purchase, and all three showed that streakiness even before I put them on the screen. Plus, they seemed to attract smudges and fingerprints. Just a bad product, and waste of money.

The second ebay screen protector was part of a purchase I made that included a case for the tablet. I'm not too thrilled with the case. After waiting 2+ weeks for it to arrive, I'm disappointed by the quality. It's rather cheap. And the screen protector that came with it was even worse. Extreme bubbles and no amount of effort could get them out. So, another waste of money.

Then I held my breath and bought these iLLumiShields from Amazon. They arrived earlier than expected (although no speed records were set). But the bottom line is this: They are by far the best screen protectors of the ones I tried. Crystal clear. Not the finger-smudge magnet that the SuperShieldz were. Fairly easy to put on. Decent instructions. And I like the lifetime warranty. My only regret is that I didn't choose these first. I would have saved myself some grief, and money.

If I like a product that I buy on Amazon, I usually give it 4 stars initially and then, if the product continues to perform well over time, I'll upgrade my original review to 5 stars. But I will give iLLumiShield 5 stars right out of the gate because, comparing it to the others I bought, it is far superior.

One more thing...and you would be wise to heed this advice: If you want a satisfactory outcome installing your screen protector, then the devil is in the details. (A) Thoroughly clean your tablet's screen before putting on the protector. Don't cut corners here. (B) Wash your hands before handling the protector. (C) I suggest working on a clean table top. (D) If you do notice an ill-placed bubble caused by a speck of dust or lint that managed to get on the screen, carefully peel back the screen protector to where the bubble is, locate the small dust or lint particle, and use the adhesive side of a post-it note to remove it.

Hope this summary helps you in making your purchase decision.

title: Note: These Aren't Psychic Headphones
text:
Overall, I'm happy with these headphones, but they are sometimes completely useless.

These headphones are enticing because I work in two different environments, depending on the day and time: some times I'm in the office, other times I'm out in the shop. In both of these environments, being able to hear other people around you is really important (especially when operating machinery like the forklift).

I did a good bit of research before buying a pair and every gave the same explanation for these things: these headphone work by bypassing your Outer/Middle Ear and Eardrum and going straight to the Inner Ear/Cochlea. Something that's rather important that EVERYONE leaves out- and, parenthetically, I really should have thought to ask- is what happens when sound comes from both directions.

The answer, as you might imagine, is that the louder noise wins some degree depending on the difference between the two: your Inner Ear is still a bottleneck going to your brain and therefore outside sounds may significantly impact your ability to hear the headphones (ergo- not Psychic Headphones).

Here are some concrete examples so that you can get an idea of whether or not these will work for you:
Office vs Headphones @ low volume: (Ideal scenario)
Once your ears adapt to the volume of the headphones,they sound perfect and I don't even notice the ambient office noises (computer under my desk, printer down the hall, other people talking casually in other offices). When someone walks in to talk to me, they're loud enough that I can hear them perfectly well

Car vs Headphones @ low volume:
Car/traffic ambient noises are perceivable, but the headphones are still perfectly easy to hear. I imagine you should still be able to hear honking/sirens perfectly well.

Office vs Headphones @ mid+ volume:
You can only hear the headphones; you might barely hear someone else come in, but you definitely need to pause your music/podcast in order to hear what they are saying.

Weedwacker vs Headphones @ max :
Weedwacker wins for the most part (could make out some of the music, but none of the lyrics)

Lawnmower vs Headphones @ max:
Barely hear the headphones at all: you can catch snippets here and there, but basically worthless

Chopsaw (on metal):
Chopsaw only: I absolutely cannot hear anything from the headphones

Forklift vs Headphones @ mid:
I put this out of order because it's actually a surprising result. Because the forklift is pretty loud, I would have assumed that it would drown out the headphones like the lawnmower did, but for whatever reason this isn't the case. I actually can hear the headphones decently well (words/lyrics on podcasts/songs do not get lost) and can still hear when other people are around me (at least, as well as you normally can while on the forklift).

The other thing to note is that these headphones actually come with earplugs: I assume this is to encourage you to confirm that they are not simply little speakers near your your ears; that they are in fact conducting the noise into your skull. This is interesting because it does point out that you can make the headphones work in loud environments using earplugs (and, in fact, I know people who work in environments that *require* the use of earplugs for safety reasons, so these would actually be great for them). However, for many people who are buying these for the "Open Ear" prospect, this seems highly ironic.

So, overall, I have in fact been getting use out of them, but depending where I'm at and what I'm doing I have to swap out to an in-ear headphones, which can be a bit tedious.

title: A swing and a miss from Bose
text:
These headphones are a disappointment. I purchased these to for the most part use indoors on a treadmill. This headset seemed a good way to avoid dangerous dangling wires that can accidentally get hit with the hands.

The most positive thing I can say about these is that the noise canceling is quite good. It is almost as good as my two pairs of QC20 but not so good as the QC35 (the QC35 is around the ear so this is no surprise.) My treadmill is a noisy beast so the NC is very nice to have. The adjustable noise cancellation actually had to be set near the middle to effectively squelch the drone of my treadmill. Advancing it more "higher" actually made the noise more audible again. I assume this is some effect caused by the nature of the sound being canceled. I only mention this to notify others that it should not be assumed that maximum is the most effective setting against noise. You may have to experiment a bit.

The headband and earbuds are ridiculous. Not only in appearance but in function. The rubbery band is unexpectedly heavy and becomes sweaty against the skin. During exercise I have to keep a cloth under it to keep it from chafing my neck. Sometimes I even put the band over the top of my head to get it off my neck because it is THAT annoying to me. The power/pairing button is very hard to press and it's hard to tell when it is properly activated as it does not click. The voice feature is annoying since the female voice is always at low volume and the enunciation and clarity of the words are not optimal.

The so-called instruction manual is a leaflet in tiny print and a dozen languages that is not at all helpful. One sentence per function on a few pages. It is insulting to receive such a manual for an item so expensive. I had to go online to Bose to download the real manual. I did not know it was there, I just got lucky to find one.

The tiny little controller is too small. It should be larger and the indicator lights and power button should be on it as well. I have large hands so finding and pushing the correct button is more frustrating than productive.

The Bluetooth did not want to pair at all with a Pixel C. After struggling with this for many minutes I finally got it to pair. The Bose app was not helpful at all in pairing. I believe it is not able to work with the latest Android Nougat. Even when I was paired, and the headphones were working, the app showed I was not connected. Very disappointing. It did work OK with a Samsung 7.

The Bluetooth connection cuts out often. And when reaching to press the hard-to-find power button to ensure the connection is live but then be unable to see the invisible lights it is not the best experience.

The package is a tour-de-force in excessive and wasteful use of materials. First, there is a slip sleeve. In that is a fancy black box with foldout full color sections for the box cover. These panels extol the virtues of the product. When unfolded, the array is about 3 feet wide. Inside the box is a plastic tray holding the product and below the tray is the miscellaneous items. The box alone weighs one-and-a-half pounds. In contrast, the headset weighs 2 ounces.What a ridiculous amount of packaging.

The more I used this headset, the more I disliked it because of all its annoyances. I'm going back to my simpler, non-noise cancelling Bluetooth Plantronics or most likely the QC20 and take extra effort to keep the wires out of the way.

I feel like I am beta testing this Bose QC30 headphone product. In my opinion, this is a dud from Bose and it needs work. It offers nothing over the rest of the Bose headphones except there are no dangling wires.

text:
I purchased these for cleaning electronics contacts and circuit boards, using IPA and contact cleaner. They can perform this task better than q-tips, due to having a pointed foam tip - they leave no cotton threads behind when they are done - and they are quite useful for getting into small spaces (though not quite small enough to clean a micro-USB jack).

Better than q-tips, but otherwise deficient. The foam is very thin and doesn't hold up well to cleaning activities - every time I've used one, the foam has ended up torn and frayed within 30s. I always have to use two or three swabs to finish the job. It is possible that I'm not using them for their intended purpose - I often have to clean up small leads, solder pads, and chips which have sharp edges - but I'd like to see a little better durability from them.

I'll keep a few in my kit, and use them for cleaning smooth, delicate connectors, but I doubt I'd order them again.

title: Plug & Play WiFi With Good Coverage, But Not A Fan Of "App Only" Devices
text:
This is a very good product from Google. Easy to set up, great WiFi coverage (up to 4500 feet when using 3 nodes utilizing mesh infrastructure), aesthetically pleasing (little white pucks are very unassuming) & effectively hands off (if you want that).

However, I'm kinda old school when it comes to being hands on with most stuff. And so many products on the market today rely SOLELY on an Android or IOS app to interface, configure & troubleshoot the device. Therefore distancing the user further from the device.

For example, I have a "smart" kitchen faucet that's like this. However, without the app, it's pretty much rendered a "dumb" faucet. As NOTHING can be controlled, updated, adjusted or tested without the proprietary app being functional. And guess what, it's never worked from the day of install. So I use it just like a regular, stinky old faucet :-\

Personally, I think it's a flaky control unit. But again, there's no alternative way to interface with this thing to diagnose. And contacting the manufacturer has led nowhere. As their still trying to figure it out too.

So, there's that.

Google WiFi is the same way.

Google wants this product to be so easy to set up, that it's almost plug & play. And if that's your goal, then you will probably be very happy with this system.

However, without the app, you're reduced to a cool looking coaster if something goes south.

And if you get rebellious, & try to access the IP of the router thru a web browser, a page comes up telling you if the router is online or offline, then directs you to download the Google WiFi app :-/

Now, there are definitely some advanced functions that can be controlled once you're in the app. Setting up things like alternate DNS, changing the IP scope on your LAN, port forwarding, etc.. are all doable. On the other hand, there are just some things you may not want to share with Google. Your WiFi network is probably one of them.

So, between that privacy concern & the app-only control issue, it's a pass for me.

However, I'm just a weird dude like that. Most people have no issue using apps to control everything or opening up their homes to various cloud or smart devices like doorbells, thermostats, garage door openers, security cams, home lighting, & now Google WiFi.

And if that's you, then you will probably love this product. If it's not you, then possibly consider alternate mesh systems out there that give you the granular control you desire & privacy considerations that you deserve.

title: Good, basic machine with a discreet graphics card and plenty of ports
text:
This HP Pavilion desktop is a solid, but basic PC that, while it can be considered a gaming PC with its discreet Radeon RX 5500 card, that isn't going to raise too many eyebrows with its specs. What's out of the realm of this machine would be 4K gaming and VR, but it can run most modern games at medium settings at 1080p.

That's not why I needed this machine, though. As a Plex server, this serves well. It is quiet and can transcode videos using hardware transcoding. Unfortunately, it only has a single slot for an additional hdd. As a video editing machine, it can handle 1080p videos, but will struggle with 4K. As a photo editing machine, it can edit pretty much anything from the devices you have, but if you work in print, you'll find this machine lacking. For emulation, this machine will work quite well for all classic systems and even some more modern ones. Of course, for everyday web browsing and watching videos, this thing will be more than enough.

Overall, this is a fairly priced machine that is a step up from the basic computers that one may find and the discreet GPU will help to make this machine last longer than those with embedded graphics.

title: Great WIRED headset!
text:
It's so good to find more wired TRRS headsets hitting the market. For a while it seemed like only wireless ones were selling and the wired models were all low-end earbud styles or the kind that have the mic embedded by your ears instead of your mouth.
This is a good over-the-ear style set, with decent bass response and sound quality, as well as a mic on the wire. I really like the placement of a microphone on the wire, it is second only to the telescoping mic style you see receptionists and gamers using. It keeps the mic relatively close to your mouth (rather than headsets that put the mic by your ears) so you pick up your voice more than ambient noise in the room. Just keep in mind, it is a TRRS set which means it has the extra pin on the plug for a mic. It may not work properly in standard TRS headphone plugs (stereo only, designed for use with headsets without a mic), although some can work with both.
Most modern laptops support TRRS, as well as tablets and phones (if you're lucky enough to still have a 3.5mm headset jack!).

title: Like everyone else, these are great headphones, but it has its issues.
text:
I was ecstatic to receive these headphones because, while I like to do some gaming before I go to bed, my wife gets shuteye earlier as her workday begins at the "buttcrack of dawn" (her expression); but while the TV is located next to the bedroom, the volume has to be kept at a reasonable volume so as not to disturb her beauty rest, which leaves me, then, with little to no volume.
Therefore, these headphones seemed like a lifesaver for the PS3, but when I first received them, I could not for the life of me get them properly connected. Like everyone else, it took me a while (days, unfortunately) to realize that I would need to use the RCA cables from the PS3 to use these to their fullest potential.

To start off, and due to the fact that I couldn't get them hooked up the PS3 first, I'll explain testing them on the Mac. They work terrifically. I tested out a bunch of music and some videos, and the sound was supreme. The software is a digital download from their site, and necessary to fully utilize the headphones' capabilities. At times it sounds a little overwhelming, but tweaking it to your standards with the software helps to alleviate that. It even lets you save profiles in case someone wants to set the settings to their own preferences.

After one charge, I've yet to recharge the headphones and been using them for days. Once I was able to wrap my head around the fact that I'd have to dig for my RCA cables from the PS3 box, I plugged them in, followed the slightly confusing instructions that came with the headset, and played away. True, the sound isn't the greatest in terms of clarity, but it suits basically nonetheless. For the price, you're probably better off getting other headphones that are specific to consoles. While these headphones advertise as being cross-platform, the Mac/PC audio leaves much to be desired from console hearing.

With that, the customer service is marvelous. I placed a comment on another's review before posting mine about the console frustration I was having, and I received an email a few hours later from a customer service rep from the company, asking me to get in touch with them about the issues I was having. With some patience and instruction, I finally realized that the HDMI cable just isn't enough to use these.

If you want some good cross-platform headphones and don't mind sacrificing quality for consoles, these are excellent; if you do more computer gaming than console, then go ahead. However, if you want some headphones that are superb for PS3 and/or 360, I'd suggest other ones. I didn't get to test these on the Xbox 360 as I don't have one, but from what I've heard don't even bother.

title: Surprisingly good earbuds
text:
I have never been a big fan of earbuds but I do use active noise canceling (ANC) headphones on a daily basis. I have a pair of Bose QC 15s and a pair of Sennheiser PXC-450s (both over-the-ear types of headphones) that I use every day in a noisy lab and they have been a blessing at cutting out the noise. I was interested in comparing these earbuds with both of these. Considering the cost, Creative's earbuds are great. I found only minor shortcomings with them.

One of the most important considerations when using earbuds is comfort. Typically they either "hook" to the ear (like Apple's earbuds) or stick into the ear canal a little bit. Creative's earbuds are the latter and I usually find these types of earbuds to be very uncomfortable. THat said, these are the most comfortable earbuds I have ever used, mainly because of the very soft rubber pads that fit into the opening of the ear canal. I was very pleased that these were actually not uncomfortable to me, a big plus right out of the gate.

With the battery in I turned on the power. In a very quiet room, there is a very faint hiss when the noise canceling engages, and I have heard others say that this is unacceptable. Personally, it is so soft that I don't regard it as an issue. In a noisy computer lab, however, the noise canceling takes on a new dimension. In my tests, it is every bit as good as the Sennheiser set and definitely knocks out a very large majority of ambient noise. For the most rigorous test I stood between two large air handlers and swapped back and forth between the Creative earbuds and the Sennheiser headset, and the differences were small.

I loaded up some music and gave the earbuds a sound test, using some club tracks. Very unusual for earbuds, these have great bass. The highs are also strong, which is normal for earbuds. The weak spot is the midrange which is slightly flat but not to the point of being hollow and lifeless. These earbuds outperform other earbuds I have tried in the past and actually compete strongly with good over-the-ear phones.

A couple of miscellaneous points: These buds work like normal earbuds when there is no power, so the battery is not a requirement unless you want ANC. Also, they come with a "Monitor" button which is a temporary mute button so there's no need to take them out when carrying on a conversation. The mute button alone is a great feature and I wish more earphone makers implemented this (the Sennheiser set has something similar, but that's the only other place I have seen this feature).

One thing I wish Creative had added to these was volume control. There is certainly room for a volume slider but it's not there. Instead, volume is controlled from the source. This is a disappointing design choice.

Overall, these are great earbuds. The price is high for earbuds but then again getting ANC in the deal with much better than average sound quality is well worth that expense. If you like earbuds, and if you want active noise canceling too, these need to be on the short list of options.

title: Tremendous Value
text:
I'm regularly amazed and the kind of sound quality that's available at a low cost these days. I've developed a bit of a habit for cheap IEMs, but in the past I've always associated earbuds (that don't seal with the ear canal) with tinny, middling sound. I got these on a lark, given the cost, and I've been very pleasantly surprised. These are good-- not just "for the price," but on their own, and they've found their way into regular usage for me, even compared to much more expensive headphones and earbuds.

Comfort is a big reason for that: the earbud form factor is light and convenient, making them great for around the house wear. They don't block out external noise, which can be good or bad depending on your use. In terms of sound, I don't want to oversell them--they're $10 headphones--but they're undeniably solid, and for listening to music in the background they provide a nice, balanced sound. They remind me a bit of the Koss KSC75s, another famous value headphone: a little bright and light on bass, but otherwise a better tone than you'll find in significantly more expensive headphones.

The build feels a little cheap, which is understandable since they *are* cheap. Still, I'd be a little concerned about durability if I were lugging them around everywhere. And a caveat: earbuds like these can be very sensitive to positioning; if they sit in your ear a little differently, that can have a significant impact on the sound. For me, though, I've got no complaints. These have punched well above their weight.

title: Note the difference between PCB and Perfboard/Breadboard
text:
The pattern of the pins on these isn't mentioned, but they're designed for PCB's: i.e.- boards specifically printed and milled to receive Ethernet jacks. This pattern has the pins offset into two rows so that they have extra space around them for soldering and connecting. Having looked at my salvage pile, I can confirm that this is the standard layout for on-board Ethernet ports.

This means that they will not seat on Perfboards or Breadboards where the holes are uniformly spaced. In my case, I ended buying a set of breakout boards off of Ebay, which raised the price above what I would have wanted to spend, but at least let me finish my project.

For my tablet I have divided my extensive music library into genres and have them backed up to these cards. A 32GB card will hold about 150 CDs, so the space savings along over the physical media is significant. In fact one of these cards cost about the same as a rack for 150 CDs.

These are also excellent for saving practice sessions that I sometimes record using my phone or tablet. I pop my primary SD card out of the device and swap one of these in to video record. Since this card will hold about six hours of video it's perfect for that use.

Overall, these are reliable cards that have worked in a number of devices I own. I can assure anyone wanting to use them in a newer Samsung Note 2 or 3 phone or Tab 3 tablet that this card will work, and it is also excellent for HD video recording. At the price point it's an absolute bargain.

title: Such a cool backpack
text:
This is mostly cool because of the battery pack in this backpack, but it's also a high quality backpack. I liked that you can't tell from the outside that it's a "Powerbag"

I wish that I had something like this in high school, because I would have been the coolest geeky kid around. It has a micro USB, mini USB, and iPhone jack. It also has a USB port, so you can bring your own cable, so it can charge practically anything. It delivered for me of being able to do two full device charges.

This is a must for camping, or any other activity where you might be without power, or stuck with a bunch of electronic devices that you forgot your power cables for. For me, I always forget to bring a mini USB connector, so my older devices lose power after the first day. But, bringing this bag along is a great insurance policy.

You have to press a power button to start charging, and you have to long press it for about three seconds. And, there are no lights to remind you that the device is on, so getting used to it can be a little confusing. For a simple device like this, I didn't think I needed to read the instructions, but I did.

It comes with the 3000mAh Battery, which is very light, and charges two devices, and is easily replaceable, and Powerbag sells replacement batteries that are up to 9000mAh, or 6 device charges, so you really could get a bag full of these batteries, so that you could live without power for a month.

Pros:
+Very high quality backpack, looks very nice
+Does two complete device charges (at least for my smaller devices)
+Charges anything
+Power cables are completely hidden
+There's a little pocket that exposes the power cables
+The battery is easily replaceable

Cons:
-It would be very difficult to remove the battery from the backpack, and it would be even more difficult to get the battery back in
-The charging lights are confusing, until you get the hang of them

title: A miracle product, but did not work with one computer
text:
I gave this a four because it did not work on one out of three devices I tried it with (and I know each to work with a short HDMI cable). I'm not sure why this had a lot of flickering when used with my Alienware computer, but it worked perfectly with another computer and my QNAP NAS (worth noting is the NAS puts out a very weak signal and does not work with my in-place 25-ft. traditional HDMI cable).

I had almost written this off because usually HDMI is a crapshoot when it comes to any sort of distance and I didn't even realize such a product existed until I read about fiber optic cable inside. I thought that was a generic brand typo type of situation until I looked this up and realized this is a real thing. I didn't study it, but I gather/assume that there is a chip inside that changes electrical signals to low power lasers to send the signals this way. Interesting, though, because there are not 19 fibers inside (a traditional HDMI cable has 19 pins, I think).

I probably need to research this further just because it's totally cool, but I love this thing because I can now watch my NAS directly on my TV even though it is down in the basement (and there is a great app to act as a remote since I now do not have line of sight for the IR remote). I only took off a star because it apparently has some issues with my one computer - not sure why but if you need a couple of these, you might want to buy one at a time to be sure what it does and does not work with. I love it, but had to remove a star for that reason.

title: lightweight and useful pc
text:
The laptop arrived in a cardboard box that was a bit mangled, but the LG box is designed to protect the laptop. There's also plastic covers on the brushed metal casing. Set-up is easy as you plug it in and power it on, and the MS assistant 'talks' you through things, allowing you to use voice or keyboard control. It's Windows 10 on the laptop, but no MicroSoft Suite (you have to pay extra for that).
With a SSD and 8 RAM memory, everything is very fast and responsive - I can have multiple tabs open on my internet browser, be playing music and have an app or Windows up and nothing is slow at all. It wakes up out of sleep mode quickly, too, and there's a fingerprint sensor for log-in or I can use a pin or 'drawing picture' function (there's lots of security options available).
Music/sound - the speakers are on the back/around the hinge, so if you're on a flat surface, the sound is good (it's not a high quality 'music/entertainment' laptop). But if it's on your lap, it may be muffled a little, fair warning.
Image/screen - it has good resolution and images are clear/crisp, but due to the fact that it's so lightweight, it's not a glass surface and has a little 'give'. When touching it, it leaves a faint 'trail' behind, but that does fade away quickly.
Keyboard - keyboard has some nice 'give' to it and I had to use Fn+F8 to make the backlight work. It didn't light up automatically, but you can turn it on/off and adjust the brightness.
There's three USB ports, an HDMI port, one for headphones and a micro SD card and others, split between both sides. That's a nice amount for a new laptop.
This is indeed a lightweight computer. It's lighter than my older generation Surface. The touchpad is responsive and the battery does have a good charge (at least for now), depending on what you're using (how many apps, backlight, etc.). All in all, this is a great laptop for work, writing, some entertainment and anything you would need to take on the go due to its light weight and thinness.

title: OK Budget Phone, no NFC, bad sound
text:
This phone A10s is basically the worse version of the old Galaxy S7 Edge from seven years ago. Slightly higher battery capacity - 4000 instead of 3600, same screen size, but the quality of the screen is not as good. S7 screen glass is much better quality, it's smoother and it's scratch resistant. A10 touch screen response time is worse than S7. There is some kind of a split second lag which feels strange after using S7.

Unlike S7, A10 doesn't have wireless charging :(

Blue light functionality doesn't work when I flip the blue light button. Button is there but functionality is not. No physical home button anymore.

NFC is not supported, can't pay in the store using this phone. Item specs here says "Connectivity NFC" which is misleading. Old S7 supports NFC.

Sound is HORRIBLE for single built in speaker. Comparing to old S7 playing the same song this phone is missing low frequencies, sound is flat and unimpressive, no Dolby. S7 sound has lots of volume, low and high frequencies and it feels like surround sound, like movie theater experience.

Dolby Atmos is disabled on A10 for built in speaker. Adaptive sound functionality is completely missing, nada. When I plug in earphones, Dolby Atmos gets enabled but doesn't make any difference and left ear piece is much more quiet than the right one. The phone doesn't distribute sound equally between the left and right ear pieces.

Not possible to opt out from sending Samsung all your phone logs info. All preinstalled apps had rights to mess up phones operation system and access everything on the phone and send your private info everywhere. I had to go through every setting to change that. New icons look ugly.

Good features are dual sim and a radio tuner so one can listen to the local FM radio without wi-fi or cell service. It still has a jack for wired ear phones, the wire is used as an antenna for the radio tuner. Fresh battery holds charge better than a seven years old Galaxy S7 Edge. It was easy to set up and install applications from Google Play. Phone is unlocked and can be used overseas.

It's an OK unlocked budget phone for everyday use that works with certain carriers only. But lack of NFC, no wireless charging, and bad sound is a big No.

title: Not professional, but one of the better ones this price bracket
text:
[[VIDEOID:91ed971de75e2a1d366c0694560e3ad4]] Let's get this metric straight: Those who are saying a projector under $300 looks good, are probably comparing it to other cheap off-brand projectors. I've tried a few of these to use as throwaround backyard movie night things, when I don't want to get my expensive prosumer home theater ones dirty or burn out the bulb, and they all suffer from things like flat colors, lack of brightness (fudging the lumens numbers) and the worst: Inconsistent focus. Nothing makes me crazier than trying to nail the focus and finding the center focuses while the borders are out of focus, but adjusting for the edges makes the center out of focus. Usually this is because the lens is cheap and lacks proper rectilinear support, and it is MADDENING once you notice it. In short, sometimes you might find it looks better on a smaller TV than a bigger washed out and fuzzy projector.
But... usually, you should expect to pay somewhere towards DOUBLE this for a brand name projector that looks decent, so I'm trying to keep my expectations realistic for the price range. And I have to say, this is the first one that actually seems to have proper focus across the projected image! I mean, you do get some chromatic aberration in the corners (see image and video attached), but this is nothing compared to others in the sub-300 dollar range. I love that this also has built in features like miracast (which I tried and works great!) as well as an Office Suite so you can technically show a presentation without a laptop or casting device- just plug in a USB stick with your content and go!
These are not necessary in my opinion, I'd rather have better colors and sharpness than gimmicks, but honestly I think this might be the best of the lower end projectors I've tried yet! If you care about how your movies and presentations look, I'd still recommend a brand name like Viewsonic at the bare minimum. But this is fun for the kids, backyard movie nights, or impromptu presentations when a bigger and more expensive projector wouldn't be cost justifiable.

title: Cat 8 is overkill for home users
text:
Cat 8 is overkill for home users, since home users lack the equipment needed to take advantage of the extra speed. No home user can come close to the 40 Gbps theoretical speeds. US home fiber optic networking caps is 1 Gbps and most people have Internet speeds from 25 Mbps to 100 Mbps.

Cat 8 cables, at this point in time, benefit data centers, not home users. The marketing for this product targets home users by mentioning things like Xbox, Smart TVs, Alexa, and Siri. The marketing is misleading and the vendor is stuffing in search keywords. These cables are not faster than cheaper Cat 6 cables, unless you are in a data center with high-speed switches. The marketing says that users will see faster speeds from this cable over Cat 6 and Cat 7, but real-world tests will show that the speeds are identical. I did this test with this cable and the speeds were identical. I got 100 Mbps on a file copy test, where the bottleneck is the hard drive.

This cable is waterproof and weatherproof, which might benefit users trying to connect one room to another by running it outside or through soffits. The flat flexible cord will also be appealing to many users, since other Cat 8 cables are thick and stiff.

25 ft is the smallest length they sell, and longer than most people need.

Cat 8 will do nothing to speed up your home internet or make video games faster or improve video quality. The bottleneck is elsewhere. You are unlikely to come close to maxing out a Cat 5e cable. If you already have working Cat 6 cables, and you are not running a data center, there is little reason to buy a Cat 8 cable.

Cables do go bad over time as they get bent, and they can be slowed by interference, so you might notice a speed bump from a fresh undamaged cable, or a better-shielded cable.

title: Good tablet at a good price
text:
I got the 8-inch T290. If you are aware of what you are getting for your money, this tablet is worthy of five stars. No it doesn't have the top processor speed or display resolution. It's a budget tablet at a really good price (especially if you catch it on sale), and you get a lot of bang for your buck.

The display is 1200 X 800 pixels which qualifies as HD, but not ultra HD. What counts the most when it comes to font legibility on screens is pixel density. A 1200 X 800 8-inch display has a pixel density of right at 180 pixels per inch (PPI), and that's not too shabby. My 6th generation Kindle Paperwhite has a pixel density of just over 210 ppi, so this tablet isn't too far from that. If small fonts are hard to read, you can scale up the fonts and size of things in the settings.

The display also has good color and contrast, and is plenty bright. The blue light filter app included doesn't offer as many options as I like, so I add one from the Google Play store.

And speaking of that, with an Android tablet (and this one comes installed with Android Pie) you do have full access to Google Play store.

The sound is a lot better than I expected, and that can be enhanced even more with a third party volume booster.

And I find an 8-inch tablet is just the right size. A 10.1-inch tablet is too cumbersome in my opinion, and a smart phone is too small. And an 8-inch tablet like this one will fit in the back pocket of men's pants. (But not so much if you have it in a case.) And at just 12 and a half ounces, it's a lot lighter than a 10.1-inch tablet.

So understand what you're getting, don't expect top of the line, but you get a good tablet for the price.

The imuto 65W charger has two ports, USB-C and USB-A. When using both ports simultaneously, the USB-C port can deliver 45W while the USB-A port can still deliver its maximum of 18W. title: An OK Household Router
text:
I read some of the one star ratings and they made me a bit skeptical about getting this router. It is a good-looking design (it sits on my kitchen counter next to my phone so it has to look decent) and I've heard good things about Belkin but I didn't want to have the same problems I had with my previous one. At home I connect my iMac, my Blu-ray player and my work PC as well as the odd iPad and Android phone. I had been having problems with a different brand router where the Blu-ray wouldn't connect or the Mac would have to have the Airport turned off and back on. Those one star ratings were for these kinds of problems.

The Belkin N300 has yet to do any of that goofiness. It just works. I like that there is an option to schedule reboots which is probably part of the secret to this router's stability. I used to have to periodically restart my old one. Setup was not bad. It ships with a default SSID and password so you can pretty much plug and play. I didn't want to have to go around and change the settings on all my devices so I did the set up manually. Also, there is a setup utility you can run on your PC to handle this stuff but I didn't want it messing with my wifi settings so I didn't use it.

So far so good!

UPDATE: I've had this router for a year now and I am replacing it. I set up two laptops with Ubuntu Linux and they chronically have problems accessing popular websites like Facebook and YouTube. Also, my iMac will stall when accessing a website. It will start loading and then hang for a while. Most of the time it completes. I bought an Epson wifi printer and that constantly shows off line. I'm not positive the problem is with the router but I suspect it.

The reason I decided to replace it was because of the problems I'm chronically having an also I think it is going bad. Ping times to Google were around 4,000 msec via wireless. When I plugged my laptop into the router, ping times dropped to about 1,500 msec but when I plugged directly into the DSL modem, they were constantly about 53 msec. I checked for a firmware update and there were none. Unplugging it for a few minutes got the time down to the 500 msec range.

I wanted to try to flash it with DD-WRT or Tomato but you can't. Even though it is a year old, I still have the box (I hope!) and will try to return it.

title: Much better than my much more expensive InnoView!!!
text:
[[VIDEOID:eff5c8a1b7462cbcd7e12b21147f753c]] I put up a seven-minute video comparison, so feel free to watch that.

This Ounshli monitor has many of the same traits other portable monitors have. It's 1080p, fairly lightweight, takes the same types of inputs, comes with a selection of cables. If the only output you have is mini-DP, you'll need an adapter, which again is perfectly common. (You can see me using a miniDP to HDMI for both the Ounshli and the InnoView in the video.)

The video quality is good. Again, watch my video. Sound is good, better (gets louder) than my InnoView portable monitor.

And the Ounshli can play content the InnoView goes into a reboot loop on. Both can handle most things you might throw at them, but the InnoView can't handle high-motion high-depth video from YouTube. I have no idea why - it should be telling the computer what it can't handle, or just ignore it. The Ounshli does everything it should.

I also love love love that that Ounshli has the integrated case, because I had to purchase a separate case for the InnoView (which bumped it up to being about twice as expensive, 18 months ago, as the Ounshli is now.)

So highs are:
- Much less expensive than my other monitor
- Equal picture, might be a bit larger
- Better sound
- Integrated screen-protecting case
- Works with video content that my other monitor goes into a reboot loop on

The only gripe I have is that the integrated case is how the tilt of the monitor is set, and isn't removable. It IS the stand. And it only has two positions. You could use a separate stand or use binder clips to create any angle you want, and the two options are decent, so that's a very minor gripe.

title: Sound quality is fine but connectivity comes and goes
text: Have bought two of these in about 30 months after my first one broke about 9 months ago.  Had some issues with the first one where it would require me to connect about 3-4 times to my ipad or iphone before the connection would work.  It would show the headphone and battery bar icon on my phone but when I played music the music would come out of my phone or ipad and not the headphones.  Occasionally I would even have to restart the apple product and reengage the bluetooth again to get it to work.  It was rare that it connected perfectly on the first try but 2 tries was most common.  The first set eventually broke when it wouldn't connect to my phone at all anymore.  It kept saying searching and my phone would not see it come up.  I tried the headphones on 4 different devices to make sure it wasn't the connecting device that was the problem, but it failed to connect on any so I threw it away.  I bought another pair because for $25, lasting nearly 2 years was good enough for me.  I would absolutely recommend these over wireless beats as I went through three pairs of wireless beats (2 for me and one for my wife) in 2 years.  For the ripoff price beats charges they had better last 5 years not just under 1 year.  Sound quality for these phones and beats were even to me and neither really do much noise cancellation at all, which is fine because I wouldn't expect much out of this type of design.  Of important note, my second pair of these headphones does not have any issues with bluetooth connectivity and I honestly don't think it has EVER failed to connect on the first try, so perhaps just got a bad pair for my first go round (or an unusually lucky pair this time!).  One issue I see with all three pairs (both of mine and the pair for my wife) is that they all fail to show the battery strength accurately on the phone.  The battery bar on the device starts at 100% and then goes down to 75% or 66% or so immediately on the icon on the phone, but never goes below that ever.  Thus I have had many a workout where my headphones died 15 minutes in to my 60 min workout which is very annoying!  For that, I try to keep rough track of my workouts and try and charge the headphones after each 3rd or 4th workout to be sure they don't die on me, but occasionally i still forget.  Have a pair of Bose noise cancelling headphones (that are amazing!) that always tell me battery strength remaining when I turn them on and that notification is always accurate.  Wish these headphones did the same.

There are no instructions. You have to figure out which set of outlets are controlled by which top switch. The switches feel cheap and engage/disengage roughly. There is no separate power button for the USB plugs (my other tower has one) and the red system power light is blindingly bright. I'm going to see if I have any black electrical tape to partially cover it. It's truly annoying.
The plugs don't want to hold two prong cords, grounded cords hold a little better (not much) but my devices that use just two prong cords barely stay plugged in! Tap it, move something that brushes the cord, the slightest pressure and the plug pops out.
It works and the ten foot cord is nice. I was able to plug this in half way across the room and get it onto my desk but. . . I don't like it. Thin cheap plastic. Klunky switches. Tips over too easily. It doesn't instill confidence in the product. I like the idea of a desktop power tower and have one I rely on. I don't recommend this one.

title: A pretty darn good space saving, high performance machine
text:
I picked up this little beauty to replace both an ancient and cranky 5-disc CD Player and a single disc DVD player. I now have breathing room in the old entertainment center, so even my antique turntable can take a creaky spin every now and again.

Seeing that I can't connect a toaster without help, I called on my trusty better half to unravel the mystery of setting it up. In non-technical language, a.k.a. plain English, this is what you need to know about this mighty machine:

1. The manual needs a lot of work. It's neither user-friendly nor idiot-proof. Ditto for the boxy silver remote.

2. It is easy to set up if you already know how to do that sort of thing. (We have component video connections to the TV and digital coaxial connections to the receiver.)

3. It gives excellent sound from both CDs and DVDs. With the benefit of 5.1 surround, movies like Master and Commander can literally move you, and CDs have never sounded better.

4. It is as convenient as a 5-disc CD changer as it is a 5-disc DVD player, except that when you're playing more than one CD you'll need to put it in "CD Mode" first.

5. It can easily play different types of media, such as audio Cds, MP3s, DVDs and those other mysterious formats - just put in the discs and play away.

6. The video quality is very good on a regular TV. You can set up different pre-defined picture quality modes, or customize to suit your own taste if you're a techie or a buff. If you have difficulty making up your mind, ignore this option.

7. The player is chock full of options, but you have to explore for yourself, which can be a bit confusing until you get the hang of it. Read the manual, you say? See Item 1 above.

8. There's on-screen information for MP3s and photo CDs, with different views available for the contents. (Groups/folders or entire playlists)

9. I can't comment on the progressive scan feature, since I don't have an HD or HD-ready TV - yet. (Still waiting for that lottery win)

10. It is supposed to play DVD-Audio discs, but you need 6.1 channel inputs on your receiver to play them. Unfortunately, our receiver is lacking these inputs, but then again, I am also lacking any DVD-Audio discs.

Electronics buffs will probably say that it needs a bit of "tweaking" to get it to look and sound just right, but it looks and sounds great to me. All in all a very good player, perhaps excellent when you factor in the price.

Amanda Richards, October 1, 2004

title: Absolutely PERFECT For Our Business Files, DEFINITELY Worth It For Us
text:
My daughter and I decided to start a small jewelry business. We have a lot of files that we need to keep stored in a place that is easy to get to, easy to use, stands up on its own, yet is not too big. When I saw this satchel bag, I was hoping it would be perfect. Let's take a look..

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This satchel is just like the photo. It is very stiff which means that it stand up on its own. The leather is VERY thick. There are two handles.

HANDLES
The top handle is thick and easy to carry. It is strong and sturdy. It is put on in such a way that the weight of the contents won't pull the handle off the satchel easily. The strap that comes with this has an interesting hook system which allows you to put it quickly on the loops on the sides. That allows for shoulder, or cross body carrying.

CLASP
The clasp is a strong metal clasp which stays shut nicely. There is a piece of leather to help pull the clasp apart when opening.

LINING
The lining is a very sturdy twill fabric. It seems to be extremely sturdy and looks like it will last a long time. The lining is done perfectly. The construction is HIGH QUALITY

POCKETS AND SECTIONS
There is a zipper pocket on the back wall of the satchel. The pocket goes to the bottom of the back piece so it is deep. There are three sections which have a lot of room in there for a laptop, files, and other storage necessary.

CREDIT CARD HOLDER
The front section has four sections which are sewn perfectly for credit cards and other plastic cards. It is sewn so that the cards are all visible in each pocket- very nicely done. Each pocket can hold two or three cards if necessary.

PEN AND PHONE HOLDER
There are two loops for pens and they can hold a pen that is fairly large so they are not too small. They are leather and do not stretch. there is also a phone pocket out of leather which is large enough for a small smart phone, but a larger phone might have to be put into the back pocket.

EASE OF USE
This is a great satchel. We can put all of our bank folders in there, paperwork, laptop to work on the website, our cards we need, as well as paperwork for at least a year or two of business. If it takes off, we will get a larger container. When you put this down, it stands up and does not slouch down or fall down. I LOVE THAT FEATURE.

WIDTH OF BOTTOM PIECE
The bottom piece allows for this satchel to expand at least 3 inches or a bit more.

CARE?
I plan to keep this well oiled with neatsfoot oil- the same stuff they use for baseball mitts.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For a very sturdy HEAVY DUTY satchel that stands up, has great storage space and is beautifully made, this is fantastic. I have to say we are both very impressed with it and it will serve us well as we start our fledgling business. The is great for any business person who is hard on items. It will stand up well.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. I really love this and am very glad to have it.

title: Inconsistent and innacurate GPS
text:
I really wanted to like this watch. I trail run ultra marathon distances and have been looking for an inexpensive GPS watch to track my workouts and races. Comparisons were tested against Apple Watch Series 2, iPhone 7, and Garmin 935.

Pros:
- Battery life is legitimately great.
- Integration with iOS seemed great.
- Heart rate tracking seemed accurate, by comparison.
- Screen was always easy for me to read.

Cons:
- Inconsistent GPS tracking: Over several runs of the same 4 mile trail route my distance would be anywhere from .5 mile short to an entire mile too long.
-- On a 20 mile trail run my distance was .5 mile short, but elevation recorded was 2k ft more than reality.
- Inconsistent activity information synced between watch and iPhone app: On that same run my watch activity read 19.5 miles, but the MiFit app read 19 miles. ??!! When I tried to export to AmazTools the .gpx file only shows 12.7 miles. :/

Conclusion: if you are running in a straight line, slowly, and with no tree cover this watch MIGHT record accurately for you. I've really tried to test this watch -- I think it's a budget watch that gives you budget quality information. If that works for you - go for it. If it doesn't - this isn't the holy grail of ultra running watches.

Overall, an excellent case that is well worth the price. Highly recommended.

The reason for the 4/5 stars is that these filters are resin (plastic), and are prone to scratch easier than a glass filter would. text:
What has happened to us???

Why would we --pay money-- for Big Brothe- I mean Amazon- to see into our homes 24/7? After all the smart appliance eavesdropping/conspiracy fiascos last year, and all the privacy rights and issues going on? The 'internet of things' is absolutely hackable. Do you want your home life to be observed and hacked (or deliberately watched!) any more than you want your SSN and credit card numbers being spraypainted in big, clear writing, on the side of a City Bus?

Why would YOU personally, yes you, reading these words, right now, why would YOU want cameras in your home watching you all the time?

What is it you believe about the rest of humanity that makes eternally viewing your possessions or monitoring people in your home, or being in your own home, worth PAYING for?

Seeing something doesn't make you more secure. It might help a lawyer prosecute a criminal. But it won't fix the problems that lead to crime. And it won't prevent a bad thing from happenning. It'll just provide you with a tool to witness it. In detail. Repeatedly. Remember when we all watched those towers go down, over and over for weeks, every day? Yeah. Like that. But YOUR home. Or kids. Or whatever you value enough to feel scared of losing and then feel soothed about that fear by pointing a camera at it.

Knowing your kids are home safe? Can a phone call not verify that? If they are doing somwthing you feel the need to surreptitiously watch, what does that say about your/their abilities to form healthy trust and boundaires and respect in your relationships? And if you catch them doing wrong, could you somehow prevent it from a screen? Like, what's the result of having that evidence of wrongdoing in hand? Is it actually going to be a positive to evoke the changes you seek underneath it all? Is there somethig else that could work better?

Because pointing a security camera just says "I don't trust 'x'." It's not like a baby monitor, and you're in the next room and can respond right away if the need arises. There is a LOT of far LESS INAVSIVE technologies that can accomplish most goals this system is being pitched to solve.

Do you really want to watch whatever events unfold that you might falsely feel you are 'protecting' whatever you think will be protected from, by being able to observe it from afar?

These are PRODUCTS. Designed to make profit for manufacturers. Full stop. How do they sell security? By giving the fear of insecurity to us, and then providing a 'solution.' And at such a great price! Because it's 'introduced'. They literally have introduced us to a fear you maybe we didn't even know we had.

Sure, some of us have been victims of domestic crimes, or have pets or parents or offspring to care for. But products like this only give the illusion that we're actually DOING those things.
