title: Outstanding value and performance for the price
text:
While this flash doesn’t outperform the Canon Speedlite, it comes the closest of any of the Speedlite “clones” I’ve tried so far, and does so with impressive build quality.

I was impressed with this right out of the box mainly due to the care taken with packaging. No, packaging doesn’t impact the performance of the flash, but it does take the worry out of getting one that is damaged due to UPS handling. The flash is packed in a carry case (which is very well-made and has cushioning) and, in turn, packed inside of an air-filled tube case. Together they provide more than ample protection against transit-born bruises short of being run over by the UPS truck.

The flash feels very solid. The head articulates up/down/left/right and has indents at the most commonly used angles. The head is a bit stiff to move, but I consider that as a positive since I don’t want the head getting bumped out of place when I have it positioned the way I want it.

The hotshoe frame is plastic but feels very solid. There’s a rotating locking ring to keep it in place while on the camera. It made contact and worked just fine on a 5D Mark II, a 4D and a Rebel.

The battery compartment door has a spring-loaded hinge so it pops up when unlatched. Again, good build quality on that (which is a common point of failure on other low-cost flashes I’ve used). It uses 4 AA batteries. It ran fine on rechargeables.

The control panel and LCD screen are both easy to use and see for the most part. The buttons beep when pressed, but that can be turned off if you want a silent operation. Some of the icons on the screen are very small – I needed to squint a bit to make some of them out. Then again, my aging eyes could be a contributing factor.

Most of the commands are executed by pressing a button and then selecting options using a rotating wheel. The wheel is the only part that didn’t work all that well at times. Sometimes a single twist moved it through the menu; other times I needed to twist it a couple of times to get it to register.

The capabilities of this flash are very impressive given the price point. It offers synch flash, manual flash, curtain synch, up to 1/8000 second synch, master/slave mode, AF assist beam, TTL flash, zoom settings and an LED lamp. It also has a nice amount of convenience features such as auto off (with various timed settings ranging from 5 minutes to 2 hours), a lock mode, screen on/off and test mode. It even has a USB port that can be used to update the firmware should updates be available (at this writing I am not aware of any updates).

The manual is not great. It offers a decent listing of the capabilities, but is often sparse in pointing out the details. But, if you have some measure of experience with a flash, it’s not hard to figure out (with a bit of experimenting) how to use it.

Given the price, this is an excellent value. It probably won’t suit the needs of a professional photographer but for an amateur (even a very avid one) it’s an excellent alternative to Canon gear at a much nicer price.

title: 3.5 stars; heart rate consistently inaccurate; notification setting issues
text:
Mixed review here. This was easy to pair and has ok integration with the iPhone health app, and has an ok app it its own right, though it is not very easy to access individual days and sections of days to really understand the data in a useful way. It also offers notifications via vibration on the wrist to let you know what’s happening on your phone…sort of. The thing is, it’s not very customizable. Below are short breakdowns of features:

iPhone notifications: it doesn’t exactly let you pick which notifications and when, so you end up with something of an all or none situation. Example: I do NOT have facebook messenger notifications on my phone or laptop. I don’t want them, so I turned them off. For some reason, I get them on this watch and have no way to remove it. Very annoying. Also, there’s no “do not disturb” feature, so I get buzzes at night and in the morning sometimes, disturbing my sleep.

Heart rate: consistently off. It’s too low by approximately 10 BPM, which is a HUGE margin for error. This data becomes useless when it is that far off so consistently

Sleep: nice feature that lets you know roughly how much deep and light sleep you are getting. This is pretty helpful for me, since I have sleep issues and like to know how it’s going. However, you don’t get a breakdown by time, which you also sort of see with fitness tracking…

Fitness/steps: this feature works ok, but the app doesn’t really break this down in a way that’s easy to track, analyze, or understand. They need to work on the interface to make the data useful. Right now, this is on the low end compared to about a dozen fitness trackers I’ve reviewed.

Battery life: superior to many comparable smart watches. Lasts several days without charging, which is good

Display: ok but somewhat clunky and unattractive. Not many options, but enough to have legible and mostly useful info.

Connection to iPhone: meh. Some good things, some not so good, and a LOT of questions about security. You can also start and stop music/podcasts/etc through your phone, which is nice when you are using bluetooth headphones and working out—less need to be close to the phone.

Overall, this is ok+, 3.5 stars rounded up to 4. Seen better, seen worse, but not something I particularly recommend.

title: Getting harder to find, especially MFi ones
text:
This cable bears the MFi (Made for iPod/iPad/iPhone) logo on the packaging and looks nearly identical to the real thing. The only things different are there is no Apple logo on the cable and it does not carry the Apple price tag.

I tested it both as a charging cable and a synching cable with an iPad 2 and it performed flawlessly.

The thing that is the same is this is manufactured to Apple's specs and did earn the MFI certification. Why this is important to me is most third party manufacturers have dropped this legacy cable and are now licensing Apple's Lightning cable (if they are even MFi certified). Decent 30 pin cables are becoming scarce, and the ones from Apple are pricy. That leaves a lot of fly-by-night cables that have a high failure rate, and I am frankly tiring of replacing cables on a monthly basis (I had been purchasing them from a well known big box store as well as a nationwide electronics chain.) When I was offered this one as a review sample I could not resist.

I've been using this as my sole cable for over a week and am not disappointed. The construction is identical to Apple's, and the performance is too. If you are in the same quandary as I - experiencing high failure rates on 30 pin cables - check this one out.

title: Excellent low end as claimed with a qualification
text:
The qualification I mentioned in the title is as long as this is used as a close, personal speaker the superior bass frequency response is there. Since M. Erb thoroughly covered most of the characteristics in his excellent July 24, 2014 review I am going to focus on the sound quality and a few observations.

As stated, this speaker provides high quality sound in the lower frequency spectrum as long as it's within one to three feet. Even at twenty feet the sound is excellent, but the effect of the bass diminishes. The woofer is in the bottom part of the casing and do emphasize that part of the frequency spectrum.

Although this is marketed as a 'bass machine' the high and mid range response is actually better than the bass (to my ears anyway), and the overall sound quality makes this one of the best personal speakers that I have tested. In fact, while I normally use Miles Davis' [[ASIN:B00IS4187Y Kind Of Blue]] to test speakers because it does exercise the full spectrum, for this one I used two other albums. First was Scott Lafaro's [[ASIN:B007CSETZU The Complete Live At The Village Vanguard 1961]] because Scott LaFaro's bass is prominent. That is how I arrived at my assessment of the bass response that I described above. I also tested this with a Chico Hamilton Trio album titled [[ASIN:B0089PCUT2 Jazz Essentials]] that contained a fuller range of instruments, including cello and flute. The reproduction of frequencies across the full spectrum was so spectacular that I had to give this speaker five stars.

For features and characteristics read (and watch) M. Erb's review. If you are picky about sound quality, as far as I am concerned this should be on your short list of personal speakers. It will not fill a room with sound, but you'll be able to hear every nuance if you have it near by.

title: Takes some configuring, but then it's perfect
text:
For the image quality, I give it a 5. You can have it dim in a dim room, which I find easier on the eyes. It shows a crystal clear picture, and glorious 3D. It's easily movie theater quality.

For gaming, it supports dual screen with separate glasses [[ASIN:B007VQLJ60 LG Electronics AG-F310DP Cinema 3D Dual Play Gaming Glasses (2 Pair)]]. With this both players see their game full screen, in full HD. I highly recommend this accessory for the gamer.

The sound system is worth 5 stars if you set it up exactly right. You can set the sound for wall mount or stand. You can normalize the audio levels for extra clarity on the dialog. There is an option to automatically sync the video to the audio. The last two are turned off by default and you'll have a superior experience if you turn them on. There are a lot of options, and it's worth the trouble to spend a little while playing with them until you get the configuration that works best for the acoustics of your room. The TV is capable of excellent sound out of the box, but truly amazing audio once you have it turned just right.

The TV is exceptionally clever at points. ESPN 3D broadcasts on a top bottom split, so if the TV isn't in the correct mode, you see two images one above the other. HBO on Demand 3D does it left and right. With other TVs I've seen, you need to use the remote to tell the TV that it is supposed to be 3D and which mode it is being broadcast in. This one initially shows the split screen, but figures it out and makes the switch itself in less than a minute.

The remote is the weakest element. You can use the pointer (think wii mote), and it has a nifty "shake to center" feature. You can use the up and down arrows to point to your selection. You can give it voice commands. "Show Netflix" and "CBS". You don't need to be precise so "Hulu" works the same as "Show Hulu". When you use the voice command and say "watch TV" the screen shows the phrase "live TV". You do not want to say the phrase "live TV". Just trust me on that one. You can use the voice command to pull up the HDMI selection screen, but then you need to point and click to the one you want. If it can't figure it out, say if you ask for "SyFy" for which there are multiple stations, it will show a list of best guesses. If you ask for HBO, it will always bring you to HBO Go.

On the plus side, the keyboard is convenient for searching, and the buttons are similar to those on a phone. Integrating with other systems is done via IR blaster. You sit an IR device over the IR receiver on the device you want to control and the TV pretends to be that device's remote. It is good at pulling up the guide for your local programming provider, and changing channels, even without IR blaster.

Overall, this TV falls somewhere between "Wow" and "Belongs on the Starship Enterprise".

title: Review from professional driver
text:
I am a limo driver and depend on this thing all day. I am very satisfied with it except for a few issues.

The good:
-Map graphics are great and shows direction of streets. In regards to information - I prefer the map format and image scheme/theme over Garmin any day. In fact bought and returned a popular Garmin model.
-Graphics for real-time moving travel graphics is also superior to Garmin.
-Size is just right as it does not block too much on my windshield.
-Display is configurable.

The bad (minor issues):
-May lose satellite reception in extremely bad weather, or extremely tall and dense buildings (like in the Wall St. area of NYC). However this was the same case for the Garmin models.
-Traffic is a joke. Rarely does it show accurate information in NYC. In fact, I just use it without the TMC cable, since it speeds up the processing. (Also note - Lifetime traffic only means that you get the RDS-TMC receiver cable. You can just buy this cable on Ebay for $15 or so for the "lifetime" service. Lifetime maps on the other hand is very valuable.)
-Screen calibration (if needed) is very involved.
-Suction requires really clean windows and may be difficult to twist on in some situations.
-Does some inexplicably bad/strange routing in a few cases. Maybe due to some errors in the mapping.
-Gives too much weight to certain major streets and avenues in regards to how fast you can travel through them, when in fact they can be very slow to travel through; again, just due to bad data.
-Occasionally has wrong address issues; again, data.

title: The Best Value For Your Money in Photography
text:
First of all, I would like to start with highly recommending this camera to ANYONE who wants premium image quality with expandability, power and flexibility.

Pentax is one of the only companies out there that is driven entirely by photography and NOT by a marketing department that makes outrageous claims. To this end, even this, their lowest-end camera, is PACKED with premium features. Let's take a look at them:

1. Dust Reduction: Dust WILL get into your camera! This keeps it off of the sensor and increases the time inbetween cleanings.

2. Shake Reduction: It's good for a couple of stops of shooting leeway and you get it with every lens you use. Other companies build their systems into the lenses, meaning ONE lens can cost as much or more than the camera, itself! Lens-based anti-shake systems are more effective at long zoom than body-based systems, but unless you're rich, you won't be able to afford a suite of good lenses! With this camera, you can use ANY Pentax lens and get anti-shake.

3. AA batteries: Proprietary battery packs are NO GOOD. Hmmm, if you're on a shoot and your pack dies, you're not taking ANY photos unless you get a spare, right? With this camera, pick up some 2500mAh Ni-MH AA's and you can afford to get three sets. However, the power drain is so small, you might not need more than one set.

4. 6 MP sensor: Don't EVER get trapped in the megapixel hype. Megapixels mean nothing in the DSLR game, except for noise issues. Let me explain. The sensor sizes on almost all DSLRs (except for $5000 full-frame pro cameras) are APS-sized, meaning the sensor size on this camera and the Nikon D300 are very nearly the same dimensions. This means that photosensors on the chip have to be made smaller to get more pixels...meaning that the closer together/smaller sites are LESS light sensitive and they will also interfere with each other. 6 MP is a perfect sweet spot for noise and image sharpness. You get a base ISO of 200, meaning your camera is TWICE as sensitive to light as one with a base ISO of 100! This camera records color accurately and makes prints up to 8.5"x11" with no problem.

This camera has huge features and, even with the release of the K20D and K200D cameras, still maintains a good feature/image quality set with a proven CCD sensor and a suite of easy-to-learn features and settings. I LOVE this camera and even though I have a K200D for the weather sealing and larger burst capacity, the K100D super is the camera I ALWAYS take with me in trips. You're better off getting this camera plus a really nice lens and a 360FZ flash than a more expensive camera with a base kit lens and no external flash.

Believe me, this camera's quality will not fail to impress you and it will grow with you. It can use ANY lens its bigger brothers can and it uses them effortlessly.

A superb camera and one for the record books!

If you are planning to make this a primary boot drive I recommend that you carefully read some of the critical reviews and take them into consideration because there are reported latency issues that make make it untenable in that role. title: APC BR1000G Back-UPS Pro 1000
text:
I got this for Christmas and have only been using it for a few days now. I did have a problem with the set-up since there were no step by step instructions and you are left to figure out what goes where. I had omitted attaching the USB/phone jack between my old Windows XP computer and the UPS. I've used UPS's in years past, but they did not require a USB connection to a computer. I found out I had a problem when I was trying to install the software and it stopped loading and gave me a problem message, but no solution. I called the 1-888 number and without any fuss or waiting I got to speak to someone in the tech department who spoke very good English and solved my problem quickly.

I was tempted to deduct one star for the lousy (or total lack of) any instructions on how to connect this to your computer but didn't since the tech help was so good. There was a picture drawing instructing the user to remove the battery and turn it over so the green tape is on top which I managed to do alright. I don't hear any fan noise whatsoever as some others were complaining of. In fact, it's so quiet I can't even tell it's on unless I go and see the 3 LED lights on the top panel.

I tested it out a few minutes ago by turning off the power to the room that my computer is in. I was downstairs in the garage at the fuse box so I don't know if any beep occurred upstairs, but when I got there the computer was running off the UPS. Every 30 seconds I heard 4 beeps from the UPS telling me that it was being used as the power source. I only have my computer, monitor and modem connected to the UPS. I figure I don't need the extra peripheral equipment to stay powered up since it only sucks more energy from my UPS. I didn't wait to see how long the UPS would power my PC but I did sit there for about 3 minutes before I went downstairs and turned the power back on. My computer had a message on the screen saying that it was now being powered by regular current again (or something to that effect).

So far I like this UPS a LOT. There's nothing more frustrating then losing your work if the power goes off for only a couple of seconds. I edit a lot of music and it's not always easy or convenient to save it while I edit it just because of the nature of the program I use. So, I really like the idea of hearing my 4 beeps to let me know I might need to close out and shut down and not lose any work. I don't always have lights on so there may be nothing to tell me there's been a power outage except for the beeps on this UPS. There is a mute mode, but I need to hear the beeps.

title: Versatility is key.
text:
Let's do the pro/con thing.

Pros:

+ Sound is definitely amazing coming from 1 amp @ 5 volts. I wouldn't have guessed that was quite possible. And the stereo effect works well, especially if you're positioned indirectly to the speaker (i.e., not right beside it). That said, it's not an amazing amount better than the SBX8, so I wonder if the (untested by me) SBX10 would be the sweet spot in terms of size to sound ratio.

+ Integrated microphone features work well, although I'm still not sold on voice commands.

+ Bluetooth combined with direct AC power option makes it truly versatile.

+ This would be awesome to have as the communications centerpiece in a temporary apartment while on the road, to use in any room that doesn't have speakers, or even as a centerpiece in a smaller apartment. That said, it's a bit large to want to travel on planes with, but I would do it for a long trip.

+ As long as you're getting your power via an electrical outlet (and NOT a computer, although as an "ejected" (from the computer) device, it should work as well), you are able to communicate to the speaker with bluetooth and with the line in jack, which allows this to be a more permanent fixture. You can have it work with your phone and still be hooked up to a more permanent sound source. In fact, the speaker will play two sources at once in that case, but a full USB connection to a computer shuts it off to the rest of the world (i.e., in that case, it will ignore the line in and the bluetooth connections.

+ Cool capacitive touch controls.

Cons:

- No way to shut it off short of unplugging. This makes a more permanent setup less attractive. Not that it's eating much power just sitting there, but still...

- Included (thankfully) AC adapter could be smaller and shaped more efficiently. It comes with plugs for US, Continental Europe, UK, and Australia (which covers most of the world since most countries use one of those), but the latter two hang off the front of the unit awkwardly. You couldn't plug it in beside most AC adapters. Anyway, most people have some other ones sitting around if this one is not adequate.

- My BB - although it recognizes the device as a SoundBlaster SBX20, not generically - cannot control the volume like a bluetooth headset I use. This must be done from the integrated controls.

- I have to reinitiate bluetooth connection from my phone (thankfully not from the unit) after each power down. Actually not sure if this is a pro or a con...depends on your thinking.

In summary, this is a really cool, versatile device with a lot of interesting features. It is a niche, however. I'd call it just about perfect for someone on a long term assignment away from home and perfect for some people as an in-house permanent setup, although the lack of a power switch bothers me for those uses. It's a bit large for short term travel unless by personal vehicle. Hopefully this helps you decide if this is right for you.

text:
You'd have to accept this for what it is. It is a serviceable low cost monitor that doesn't look so cheaply built as most of the other low cost monitors I've seen out there. I really don't use a desktop anymore but decided to make use of a dormant desktop for hosting a home media network. My 17' CRT monitor just didn't have the size to display current media so I needed to get something cheap. No, this is not a monitor that will compare to your flat screen tv (unless you have a low cost one), it doesn't even look as vibrant as the 17" Mag crt it replaced. It does, however, show a lot of screen space to display today's content packed web pages, or media resolutions - the old 17" just wasn't showing enough to be useful. It also takes up a lot less desk space and makes my desk area less cluttered. The viewing angle is small, as some have said, so it will wash out if you move your head too much (usually, you wouldn't move much when working on a desktop anyway right?). I'm not a gamer, but I definitely wouldn't recommend this for that - the video quality just isn't that great to give you that "immersed feeling". It did have a matte finish and that might have something to do with the lacking color vibrancy.

I got mine on sale for $70 bucks and that is about my limit for what I would spend for something like this again. Any higher and I'd rather pay a little more and get a really good one. I did replace the video card at the same time to get the most out of this. Overall, great bang for under $100 bucks (heck, my Mag Innovision 17" was $350 in the mid-90's), but definitely no Apple quality level monitor.

title: An excellent center speaker that hits the mark on all counts
text:
I'm very pleased with all aspects of this center speaker. The sound quality is excellent. This replaces an old KEF center speaker and the difference can be clearly heard. The Polk has a crisp, clean sound that clarifies and enhances dialog but not at the expense of a nice solid bass (although I also have a subwoofer in the setup).

It's about as unobtrusive you can get with a center speaker without compromising sound quality and performance. Polk did an excellent job with the design.

I looked at the new version of this (the ES35) and, while there are some small incremental improvements, I didn't consider them to be worth the extra $100 it costs. Plus, this was on a price dip for the differential between the two was $150, making this the clear choice.

While I have been partial to KEF in the past for speakers, the performance of this Polk has really wow'd me. At present I'm using this center speaker with KEF left and right front speakers, and KEF for surround. I've been so impressed with the ES35 that I'll be changing to Polk for my L/R soon, and keep the KEF only for surround (5.1.2 setup).

An excellent center speaker that hits the mark on all counts. Five stars.

title: Truly Couldn't Be Happier {Updated 04-04-2017}
text:
I knew, due to my disability, that I was going to need to find a professional installer to install this Boss Audio Systems B9351WRC head unit and wireless reverse camera along with two replacement door speakers I decided needed replacement (and wow, they really needed replacing). The installation took approximately three hours or so. The only problem which may not be a problem but I'm a worrier. The bracket for the wireless reverse camera somewhat, but not entirely, covers the plate expiration stickers somewhat. Other than that the head unit fit as good if not better than the stock radio fit. in the dashboard.
This radio plays AM/FM stations though there's very few decent radio stations around here. The unit also plays from USB thumb drives which plugs into a port under a panel under the volume/pause/power button. I put 600+ songs on a USB 2.0 16 GB driver and it played everything as far as I could tell. There might be a couple VBR or odd format MP3 files it may not play but I haven't gotten to them yes. Nothing's refused to play and even a couple that had imbedded album artwork actually showed up but so small it was almost impossible to see and I had no idea how to make it better. The instructions in the manual were basically "Play with things and see what happens!" more than specific directions how different functions work.
What I went with, is a 32 gig micro-SD card that had the same 600+ songs the thumb drive has. But with the micro-SD card you can close the hatch under the volume and control knob which you couldn't with the thumb drive. There's also an AUX input jack for old style MP3 players and phones.
The six inch screen is sharp and crisp. The backup camera, even with a streetlight thirty feet away had more than enough light to back out of my garage. I even backed down the street a ways in almost complete darkness and could see just fine with just the reverse lights on the car. Now as long as no cops have a problem with it I'm golden.
I tried home burned CDs and while it took a few seconds longer to recognize it played them fine. I tried store bought CDs and they played right off the bat. OH! and it plays DVD discs jut fine in case my passenger wants to watch a movie as we drive. I promise I'm no dumb enough to watch a movie while I drive.
According to the installer I can leave the micro SD card in the unit all the time. So, 600+ songs anytime I want which I can shuffle or randomly pick and play songs anytime I want. I couldn't be happier. With the stock deck I'd sometimes get to my destination just as the deck decided to recognize the CD so this deck is a godsend when I really needed a new one. Now with as many songs as I can cram into a 32 gig drive. Right now I've got 687 songs and tons of free space. I may have to start buying more music and ripping some more albums from my collection to add to my micro-SD card.
So I can play hundreds, thousands of MP3 songs on a micro-SD card. I can play CDs both homemade and store bought. I can watch DVDs on a pretty sharp (all settings can be changed in the system) the dimmer is a bit bright until it goes off completely but it's not too bad or too bright. There's a user setting EQ option as well as several other preset settings to choose from. There are options to add sound effects such as large hall, church, cavern, etc. I avoided them entirely and set my own EQ settings with the loudness off. The new speakers sound great for high end and midrange. The stock back speakers add some needed bass.
All in all? This is an affordable head unit with all the features and functions one could ask for. It comes with a remote that I'm not sure I'm even going to keep anywhere in the car. Anything you need to do can be done on the deck and no one's sitting in the back seat of a '07 Hyundai Accent, seriously. So the remote is useless but amusing.
I love this unit, the backup cam is awesome, The many ways to play music. The fit and finish, it's close to perfect.
This a little long and meandering review but I really like this radio and I'm glad I replaced the door speakers and went with a professional installer who's basically given me a lifetime warranty on his labor. I couldn't be happier.

Update 04-04-2017: It's been nearly six months since I had this head unit and backup camera installed. Radio reception is still bad, I still despise listening to radio so that's no big deal. Have kept a micro SD card loaded with hundreds of songs installed. Turn the unit on it automatically defaults to that. Everything is still working fine. Professional installation was worth the money.

title: All the right holes, a bit thin
text:
Imagine my dismay when I found that my VESA-compatible display would not fit on my VESA-compatible wall mount! There are too many VESAs! (I remember when it was a hacky high-speed standard for video cards back when ISA wouldn't cut it.) But that's on me; I should have double-checked!

This product bailed me out. It is the right size and has all the Vesa holes a person could want, from 75 x 75 right on up to 400 x 200.

The big advantage of this plate over the slightly-cheaper 4-piece "X" options is the time you save not having to fumble with angles trying to get things lined up and level. The breezy and level-on-the-first-try install was well worth a few extra dollars!

The only serious drawback I found is that I had wanted to mount my 25lb, 100x100 display to the wall mount's 400x200 option. When I did that, this plate visibly flexed under the weight of the display.

I expect almost all applications of plates like this are to adapt the "big ones" (200x200 and up) to the "small ones" (100x100 and down). So this use was foreseeable. This type of plate must carefully balance thickness and weight; this one seems very slightly too thin.

Nonetheless, using the 200x200 holes instead of 400x200 worked perfectly; it did not flex at all in that configuration.

It would also be a nice upgrade if they included nuts in the hardware kit. Sure, the display side is going to screw directly into the back of the display. And you'll probably have to use the display's specific bolts to do it. But in almost every situation, attaching this on the mount side will require nuts. It seems like nobody ever includes those. (The mount didn't either.)

Related to that, I wouldn't have turned up my nose at some spacers either, though that may have more to do with the mount than this plate, so I don't hold the lack of them against it.

So in my case, I ended up using my own nuts and bolts, nylon washers, and some scavenged spacers. That worked out fine. M8 is the perfect size bolt to use with this plate.

So although I give this only four stars for not being quite sturdy enough to live up to its full promise, that doesn't stop me from recommending it for any case where 400x200-to-100x100 isn't a hard requirement. Just be prepared to bring your own fasteners to the table on the mount side.

title: Acceptable for portable storage, will probably not cut it for PS5.
text:
The Centon Premium SSD at 1TB is priced higher than even the WD_Black while claiming faster speeds. Before I get into my conclusions, I need to say that I'm only testing this drive through a USB enclosure so the conditions aren't optimal, but my conclusion about this drive is in comparison to another drive that I test through the same enclosure, meaning all conditions are the same between the three drives.

I had two other drives that I was able to performance test against this Centon drive. The first is a [[ASIN:B09575SWX5 Pioneer NVMe]] drive at 256GB and the second is a [[ASIN:‎B08695D3VW Klevv NVMe]] drive at 512GB. All three drives were placed inside a USB drive enclosure and connected via a Type-C cable capable of video transfer (meaning it's made for data transfer, not just charging).

Because I'm only testing through USB 3.1, I'm not expecting to reach advertised speeds but using the relative performance between the three drives under the same conditions, I can make some conclusions. The Pioneer drive is advertised at speeds of up to 2,100/1,600 MB/s and in my setup, I was able to reach 1,041/937 MB/s which is quite impressive. On to the Klevv drive: it is advertised at speeds of up to 2,050/1,650 MB/s and my results for this drive was 915/922 MB/s. Both drives are quite affordable and for use as a fast, portable storage, they work well.

Now, the Centon makes big claims. It is advertised at 5,500/1,800 MB/s. That's faster than WD_Black's advertised speed of 3,600 MB/s read! This is obviously aimed at those who are looking to upgrade a PS5 with more storage, but my results can be see in the screenshot. Under the same conditions, it only meets the performance of the Klevv and is slower than the Pioneer. I don't have high confidence for this actually being great for a PS5.

In addition, just as a previous review stated: I received this drive in an electrostatic bag inside an Amazon Prime envelope. I was lucky that the drive was still functional when it got to me.

Not impressed.

title: Amazing
text:
I recently purchased this to go along with a new TV purchase I made. I listened to the system at a Sears store, and it sounded okay, but it didn't seem to be outputting the kind of sound I would expect from it (just be the look of it). I knew it was capable of more. I have heard great things about Onkyo, and I was set on purchasing an Onkyo system for myself.
I looked through a lot of systems, and this one seemed to have the best balance of features and price. Plus, it was on sale! I was a bit worried about ordering a system with the smaller type of subwoofer (compared to the 290w versions), but I needn't have been.
And I was quite correct. After hooking this system up myself and adjusting some settings, I was very impressed by the sound quality. Listening to a Blu Ray movie with the volume set to a moderate-high level was reminiscent of being in a movie theater: rumbling bass, clear voices, and sharp high-end sounds.
The initial setup was easy, and I had virtually no issues setting it up. All those nice A/V connections in the back are empty and lonely, watching the full HDMI section with envy. I hooked up my TV, my Blu Ray player, my Roku, my HD DVR cable box, a media streamer, and even my PC (using an HDMI switch, since that's one too many connections). Everything works flawlessly.
The receiver has nice on-screen menus for things like setup and volume, and it was easy to set up most things. I have it set to pass through the HDMI, so even if I turn off the receiver, I can still watch other devices on my TV using the TV speakers. Awesome!
This thing has a ridiculous amount of listening options, and I haven't tried them all out yet, but the PLIIx Movie and Music, the DTS, and the DTS Master Audio all sound great.
I was a bit worried that 7.1 wouldn't work great in my room, so I was going to set this up as a 5.1. However, I ended up trying the 7.1, using the wall mounts shown as an oft-purchased product with this system. It set up very nicely, and I am very glad I chose to use the full surround setup. I am still surprised sometimes, thinking there are odd noises coming from behind me, before I realize it's just the surround speakers!
This subwoofer kicks some ass! It may not be their biggest woofer, but it is pretty big, and it can output some major bass. Low ends sound crisp and clean, and this thing can make my whole room rumble like an earthquake if I crank it up. I will probably be evicted before long, so I'll have to find somewhere in the street to hook this baby up!
The auto setup was a little wonky, and I ended up changing the settings manually. It may work better in a larger room, but where I have it set up, it came up with some very odd numbers for the speaker distance, and it set everything to negative volume levels, so that there was very little bass, and I had to turn the volume way up to get loud sound. After changing these settings myself, it sounds superb.
I was also very pleasantly surprised to see that the USB storage function offers a nice on-screen menu! I plugged in a 32 GB flash drive full of music, and had no issues playing them back. Nice!
This may not be the most high-end sound system on the planet, but it is more than sufficient for my needs, and I am very happy with my purchase. It is very well priced, it is easy to set up, and it sounds amazing. I would recommend this to anyone looking for a great entry-level theater setup.
Edit: the speaker wire that ships with this unit is a joke. Make sure you order some higher gauge wire. I used 16 for the rear speakers, and 18 for the front.

title: ABSOLUTELY INCREDIBLE BLUETOOTH SPEAKER
text:
I have tested and reviewed literally hundreds of Bluetooth speakers and while I am not a fan of music that is particularly bass heavy I found this speaker produces rich, vibrant sounds from all wave lengths. It produces more than ample volume for most any setting and has several connection methods.

While I have tested and reviewed Bluetooth speakers costing far more than what this does, the sound quality from this speaker rivals them. In relation to the sound quality this speaker is simply incredible.

In regards to charging time and battery life, both are outstanding. In my tests charging takes about approximately 2 hours to charge the built in whopping 10,400 mAh battery and the speaker lasts a solid 6.5 hours at max volume - 10 hour with volume midway (of course this will vary a bit due to exact settings).

There are multiple ways to connect to this speaker including Bluetooth 5.0, which can reach much further than previous versions, through an AUX cable, a 3.5mm jack, TF/SD card and you can even connect via NFC (Near Field Communication).

I have taken this speaker with me to the pool for the last couple of months and have been thoroughly impressed with its performance. The battery, being 10,400 mAh, it’s much longer lasting than most allowing for all day listening and the sound quality has been outstanding. The battery is so awesome this can even be used as a power bank to charge your phone - most speakers can’t make that claim.

This speaker is rated IPX5 meaning it is tested and proven safe for splashes - technically, a device with a level 5 water resistance rating can survive small water jets projected by a 6.3mm nozzle at any angle. The testing lasts for 15 min and the volume of water is 12.5 l/min.

If you have 2 of these speakers they pair for true surround sound producing a full, rich, encompassing sound environment that is hard to believe can come from a pair of small Bluetooth speakers.

All of this battery and speaker comes with weight - 5.28 pounds to be exact. That is definitely the downside to this speaker.

This is an all around great Bluetooth speaker that I certainly recommend.

Packaging

Directions

I found the app "Da Fit App" from the product description, though the directions only show a QR code. The App
-Very well laid out and some details were provided earlier but you can adjust the notifications you receive and it all pairs through Bluetooth so as long as they are on (and you accept push notifications on the phone) you'll receive the notifications on the phone. You can make a lot of the adjustments you want through the watch, but the app can allow for a faster level to set all at once.

The Modes
Phone calls, sleep (need to leave on during sleep), heart rate test, steps, training (stopwatch), blood pressure, SpO2 Test, Weather, Reminders, Shutter (photos/video), start/stop songs, Alarms, Timer, Stopwatch, Theater Mode (turns off vibrating and brightness), Move reminders, Drink reminders (stay healthy), Health reminders (menstrual, pregnancy, gender health).

The watch will sync to your timezone once the app is set and you can also get weather notifications which I set inside the app.

I am really thrilled to use the watch and was able to even deny a call earlier without having to grab my phone (unwanted caller). Excellent product and totally worth it!

title: Outstanding Sound and Solid ANC Function
text:
I have used active noise canceling (ANC) headphones for many years and I have come to expect - and look for - the subtle differences between them. I have worked with ANC phones from Bose, Sennheiser, Monster, Noontec and quite a few more. All of them have their strengths and weaknesses. This is my first experience with Sony ANC phones, and I anticipated good ANC functionality and a solid sound profile. At the price point ($300 as I write this) they need to be excellent to be worth any kind of consideration. These were a huge shock to me: the ANC is nearly on par with Bose and the sound profile is solid, giving better results than I imagined.

I will address the ANC function first, then the sound profile, and afterward I will discuss design and features. I apologize ahead of time for being long-winded, but I’d rather give too much feedback than not enough.

The ANC function is, in a single word, outstanding. Bose is the standard by which I compare others and very, very few headphones get anywhere near the same level of noise cancellation as my Bose sets (QC-15 and QC-20i, by the way). Those that get close usually have the same weird pressure sensation for which Bose is known. My primary test is a loud fan that I use for generating white noise when I want to drown out everything around me at night. I turned the fan on high speed, plugged the Sony’s buds into my ears and turned them on. I put them in ANC mode and the fan all but disappeared. All that remained of the noise was a faint, higher-frequency hiss (distinct from the ANC hiss which I will explain later). Of all the phones I have used, this set and the Bose are the only ones to wipe out that much noise. I also went into the bathroom and turned on the ventilation fan to test, and these phones again wiped out a large majority of the fan noise. For this fan, the Bose sets have a very slight edge but you have to be looking for it to notice.

The main difference between the Bose sets and these is the utter lack of that weird pressure sensation with these. If you don’t like that sensation but you want very high ANC, these are simply excellent. Like a lot of ANC phones, these generate a faint hiss that you really won’t notice unless you’re not feeding any sound at all to them and you’re listening for it.

The sound profile is also quite solid. Usually with ANC phones, because of the cancellation of certain bandwidths the phones compensate by twiddling the sound profile to fill in what was dropped, and usually this means overcompensation in the bass range (if you use Dre Beats, you know exactly what I mean). Heavy bass gives me headaches so I avoid headphones where the bass has been given too much boost. With these, Sony did not overdrive the bass at all but it’s still very solid and full - love it. The midrange is very warm and rich and music has the right depth. The highs are very bright and clear but not piercing. Overall, I am very pleased with the sound profile - not audiophile quality but closer than most.

In terms of design, these are a wireless earbud product with a neck harness. So, these are neither on-ear or over-ear phones. The harness and slack but adjustable wiring to the actual earbuds ensures that they can be set up so they won’t tug or pull when you’re working out, running or otherwise doing physical activity. Being wireless, there’s no cord to tangle up either. And, one size really does fit all which is a problem with some regular phones. The neck assembly has a leatherette padding that is soft and will not chafe.

The Bluetooth functionality works great. I paired these to my phone and they paired and connected in less than 5 seconds which is really all I could ask. After a full power-off, I turned them back on and they immediately connected to my phone again. I have no complaints there.

One of the really interesting features of these is the ability to turn off the ANC and use them without any cancellation, but they have another unusual mode that I have only seen in one other pair of phones - they have an “ambient sound” mode that you can turn on that dampens the feed in the buds and slightly increases the surrounding noise without turning off the ANC. Assuming the volume is not turned up too loud, this allows for carrying on a conversation without turning off the feed. I will say, though, that listening to my own voice coming through in this mode is disconcerting.

I do not know yet how long the battery in these lasts. So far I have not run them all the way down.

Included in the box are the phones themselves, a conversion cable so that they can be used with an audio jack (handy when Bluetooth is not an option), a cable for charging, an in-flight audio adapter, several silicone tips fo the buds so you can get the size right, and a protective carry bag.

The carry bag is the only complaint I have with the whole package - it offers little protection from drops and crushes. If you only are concerned about keeping everything together and keeping the set very clean, the bag is acceptable, but if you need better protection that consider getting a third-party hard case or use the original packaging box.

Sony got these right and even at the price tag these are easy to recommend. They’re comfortable (more comfortable than I expected for ear buds), they have excellent sound and the ANC function is outstanding. I prefer these to my Bose phones and will be using these instead.

title: Bad outside shooting results
text:
When I looked at "The best ultra compacts" list of the SnapSort web site, I found out this camera as #1 within this category.
I was excited that this small size camera is very popular and has a very good characteristics. So I've bought it.
Within 1st week I made about 450 shots and was very disappointed.

Pros:
Small, handy camera, easy to operate, good price.
Not bad low light image quality.
Good videos.
Good quality of construction.
Looks like a good toy.

Cons:
BAD image quality for the following situations:
1. Flat and discolored people faces for outdoor shooting.
2. The glare is very strong in high noon sun.
3. Softness and discoloring on trees and grass images.

So, this is good camera when using indoor, but, on my opinion is not good for outdoor shooting or when using the Portrait mode.
I lost my 5 years old Olympus C7000 2 months ago. It did not have any new functions such as image stabilization, wide-angle lenses, high ISO settings, etc, but had a SUPER image quality and broad range of manual settings. (Unfortunately the Olympus don't have now any new cameras to replace my beloved C7000).
I returned the SD1400 back and bought the Panasonic Lumix DMC-LX3. It's more expensive but image quality is just INCREADIBLE for both outdoor and indoor shooting.
I don't recommend to buy the SD1400 camera, unless you don't care of REAL image quality for outdoor shooting

title: Do yourself a favor and get the one with a pass through
text:
I wanted to doubt the speed of my AV600 kit. It doesn't. It's hard to say what the issue is, and I get that turning electrical wiring into ethernet is magic in itself. I did get 25-40% bump in speed, and if I were buying one, I'd get the Power Line 1200 with the pass through. This works, but you'll need a separate power strip, and it will need a particular kind of plug (most will do, but some angled ones will cause issues). As with all of the TP-LINK gear, it's easy to setup, as well as secure (optional but recommended). The connection is stable, and all in all I'm rather satisfied, but I'm left wanting a bit more of a bump in speed.

Another thing to consider is whether or not one device is all that needs ether. This (and all of the other Power Line gear) works well enough as a bridge, but you may still need a switch or an access point to serve more devices. Of course you can add a switch or access point, but when you combine that with the possibility of needing a power strip (which may need room to plug the access point and or switch into), all of a sudden you got a lot going on. None of this is a negative as much as an item to consider. They make ones with a switch, but those are slower; likewise there are Power Line equipped access points, but they are older.

Anyway, this works, and it works well. It could be faster, but it handles high bit rate 1080p fine, and I'd get the 1200--just the version with the pass through.

I wanted to build a relatively inexpensive computer to replace my 7-year old machine (also custom built), and after looking at various options I opted for this MSI mobo. title: If you want someone sturdy and high quality this is it
text:
The original image doesn't do it enough justice.

I even have mine mounted without the plastic cap add on that is meant to hide the metal wall mount. If you have a heavy speaker above 30 pounds or more, this item will be perfect and sturdy to hold 100 pounds as advertised. It installs like a regular flat screen wall mount. Metal bar that sits across the wall (and semi adjustable before tightening the screws).

I needed something sturdy that could hold my Klipsch reference center speaker that is 30.4lbs and with a measurement of 8" Height (20.3cm) ,WIDTH: 23.5" (59.7cm) and DEPTH:12.8" (32.4cm) with grille. Pretty massive and decently heavy. After looking around I only found mounts that could hold 30 pounds maximum and they looked fragile but limited length. Until I saw this unit. Payed more but well worth the price.

I installed it in the center under my LED, but floating above my subwoofer which is also under the LED, but on the floor.

The item has 3 parts (I will upload a few pictures later). The wall unit, and two metal hook arms that can extend, but fit perfectly for my speaker which is massive already and had room to spare in the front without extending the arms. Under the two arms is a metal slider with a latch connecting it to the top part of the hook arm. This is how you adjust it to extend the length. I didn't even need it since it had room to spare in it's default configuration.

It also came with a plastic cap which is what you see in the original manufacture photo. Never added mind since it made the wall mount stand out. If you're using this for a big speaker, it should hide the wallount so I would recommend not using the plastic cap. Two screws, two anchors and directions. Its pretty straight forward and mounts the same as flat screen wall mount but instead of 4 screws only uses 2.

PROS: Solid, sturdy and feels strong and easy to mount. (Two holes)

CONS: None other than including a shiny plastic cap to hide the wallmount. This is really trivial and not really a negative since you're not forced to use it. It's optional. I found the wallmount blended better without the plastic cap. The cap makes the wall mount bigger and stands out due to the reflect nature of the plastic. It's already tiny and adding any speaker should instantly hide it.

NOTE. AFter installing the hook arms right under it has a screw which you can screw in to lift the arm if needed.

I'm pleased with this purchase.

This seems to be a high-quality cable at a cheapy-cable price. It's thicker than any other USB cable I've ever used (and I've been using them since USB became a thing), and it has a ferrite core (that little barrel thing near the mini-USB end), the purpose of which is to reduce or eliminate EMI (electromagnetic interference) and RFI (radio frequency interference). I've only used this cable to say "check check, testing" into my Blue Yeti a few times so far, but the sound is beautifully clear with no hint of buzz or any other undesirable noise, and for a ten-foot-long USB cable that's snaking amongst a whole lot of other cables including AC cords, that's impressive. I think I'm going to buy a couple more before these cables get "discovered" and possibly go up in price and/or down in quality, as seems the fate of so very many products in our shamelessly (and often unethically) capitalist society.

I still haven't even found the right space to set it up because it is enormous and my laptop's desk is the armrest of my couch. The ViewSonic VX3276-2K-MHD 32 Inch Frameless Widescreen IPS 1440p Monitor even delivered a surprise. When I plugged the HDMI cable into my laptop, I heard audio coming from the monitor. I didn't know it had built-in speakers. I'll be using my higher end speakers, but It's was a nice bonus. I've been streaming videos for the last hour so now have a 32" 1440P TV in here too. All I can say is Yipppeee!

The display is big, bright and crisp from corner to corner. I am a graphic artist so having such a large screen is a welcome relief to my tired eyes.

I've wanted a 32" frameless monitor for as long as I could remember and was suffering from analysis paralysis when trying to decide which one to choose. When this became available through the Vine program, I jumped on it. It almost seemed too good to be true, so I kept my expectations low.

I am not a gamer, but I am a professional web developer and graphic artist and work in Photoshop. I had to rely solely on my 15" laptop screen when working from home so having this much screen real estate is fantastic. It has made all the difference in my work, and I am no longer suffering from massive eye strain. I really should have gotten one of these sooner.

If you are looking for a good quality large screen monitor with excellent features on a budget, you cannot go wrong with this choice.

---Update----

After almost a week I have been noticing more and more backlight bleed. First, it was at the lefthand corner and now some near the top right towards the corner. Only noticeable when streaming video with a black background, but it hasn't become super bothersome yet. My desktop image is predominantly black and it is only marginally noticeable, but nonetheless, it is noticeable. I have reduced my rating by 1 star. title: Keystone componant for my home theater.
text:
The following details may allow someone to cobble together a budget home theater just like I did, which relies on this BT transmitter for it's audio. My setup consists of either screencasting streamed media over wifi from a tablet or using a DVD player, connected to my projector which has a built-in speaker. This worked fine in a very small location, but I moved to a larger location. Since I had to set everything up again anyway I wanted the sound to come from the direction of the screen, and I didn't want to run speaker wire all over the room or spend a lot of money. The Avantree Audikast aptX plugs into my projector and allows me to connect to an affordable tv soundbar. No extra wires and I have a remote I can use to adjust volume now. As the aptX can sync 2 devices I am tempted to get a second soundbar and mount one on each side of the screen. That way I have better audio and can control both with the same remote. Could I have done a more efficient setup? Of course. But I couldn't have done it at such a low price point.

If you follow in my footsteps and rely on all this wireless action to stream from a tablet or phone on to a 92" screen be mindful that you are introducing multiple points of coding, broadcasting, and decoding and you may experience desynchronization of your video and audio.

Cellular/Wi-fi -> Phone/Tablet -> Projector -> BT Transmitter -> Soundbar

That is a lot of work going on behind the scenes before it even gets to your Avantree Audikast aptX, and is NOT necessarily its fault. Keeping that in mind, the most delay I've seen, if any, while doing things the hard way was maybe a couple of ms sound delay and it didn't bother me and seem to come more from my tablet lagging.

text:
This headset is very very good. Bass is really sounding as in theaters, Only listening to it on first out of two levels.
It can get loud, Surround is ehhh, I cant compare to other True surround headset since this is my first ever, though virtual surround headset that I used to have Icemat 7.1 Virtual Surround to which I still keep the USB adapter worked imho better. Or maybe not even. Thing Is when I try to play with the surround sound source positioning, its very hard to tell the sound comes from back or side drivers, fronts are somewhat faded and unified on both sides so theres obvious front position, perhaps distance of the front is further from the rear and sides which definitely gotta be really really close. Hard to tell but even to use it as a regular headset, the sound is very good. Bass is superb. I really like the power of it makes the eardrums shake even :P and! Playing horror games are more surreal than on the non-vibrating headset. It kinda thumps hard so for the price this is definitely a go with headset.
Now I had heard about people having static noise, it happened to me too, it got ridiculously loud HOWEVER, that is a software issue of a real time playback of the microphone, even unplugged. You need to mute the microphone playback !not the recording! and you should not hear weird static noises. Hope this helps if anyone experience the neverending strange sounds that are rather annoying to an extent you want to throw these excellent headphones in the garbage.
UPDATE: 2 Years Later, they still work as I remember from day 1. While there was an issue with win10, firstly not having drivers, rosewill did upgrade and made win10 compatible drivers probably within 3 months? Can tell the company keeps thinking of their products and mainly customers with older peripherals. There was temporary workaround but it was complicated and didnt work as official win10 driver.
As stated earlier though, the positioning is more like a guess, you can hear theres something running behind you, but its unclear and you may think its front. Vice versa. Though the sound is phenomenal with tweaking the EQ and setting the surround, clarity and other settings within the drivers software to this headset including microphone morphing called Magic Voice with 4 presets. Wish there were more though.
I just took one of the earcups out of curiosity if these are even true 5.1, yes they are. Its just shame that the drivers arent positioned differently and maybe in an elevated center plastic piece. I may try to mod them myself. And I spotted green and white wire just sitting there with no use. No, I didnt snap them out, theyre just there, one was dangerously exposing few strands of actual wire so I did trim then off, though Im guessing this couple of wires could be for additional driver, thus providing you an option for 7.2 surround sound. Not sure though.
Overall I'm satisfied with these as theyre good not only for games but music and movies as well and would highly recommend them for the price.

title: Properly identifies TRS vs TRRS!
text:
Rather than the pigtail style adapters I've used in the past to bring my much lamented headphone jack back, this plugs in with a very sturdy connection and simply extends the phone in a way that I find much more aesthetically pleasing and easy to wear in a jacket
But what impressed me most: It can detect the extra ring for headphones with a mic vs not! This is something the last few 3.5mm adapters I tried could not do! In other words, if you plug in headphones with an in-line mic, it can be used for calls instead of the phone's mic (great for keeping your phone in your pocket on a call). I confirmed this by tapping on the headphone mic vs the phone during a test call. But if you have standard stereo TRS headphones (the kind with one less ring since it lacks a mic), it will automatically use your phone's mic instead. Just like a real headphone on a phone would do!
The one thing I'm disappointed about, since it says it in the description, is the lack of fast charge capability. This says it supports PD charging, but I tried it on my OnePlus with the OEM charger and it did not work. That's ok, I figured the "Warp Charge" VOOC that OnePlus uses isn't compatible, so I tried a standard PD charger. That didn't work either. Odd, because it specifically says it should. So removing one star for that, but I'm loving the TRS/TRRS detection! It's about time I found one that did that correctly!

text:
I purchased this T260HD 26-Inch LCD HDTV from J&R through Amazon and it arrived all the way from New York to CA within just 7 days via ground UPS! I hooked it up to my Windows Vista PC as a second monitor and it took only a few minutes to figure out the proper configuration. This puppy has a 1920 x 1080p resolution!
My primary monitor is a Samsung 22" SyncMaster 216BW, but I could just as easily switch the two around. However, I like to watch TV while I am on the computer so most of the time I use the T260 as a TV monitor.
This monitor has built in speakers and the sound is very acceptable for day to day listening. It has an optical output if you'd like to hook it up to an amplifier.

title: Great budget device for streamers!
text:
This is a great little capture device for streaming and recording content from HDMI sources! I've been asked to stream a lot of live events (graduations, benefit concerts, etc) since Covid19 started. With this, I can take the feed out of my camera directly into the box, and stream or record using something like OBS software on my laptop. The input is considered like a USB webcam to the system, so really anything, including Zoom or Skype, can utilize the content coming from a camera or other HDMI source.
I have a Magewell HDMI to USB box that I was using before this one, and while the quality of the stream was professional (excellent color and stream clarity), it actually would often overheat and drop frames. I actually had to put a cooling fan on it to prevent that from happening on a long event outdoors. But so far, this adapter seems to be better at handling heat- likely because the overall box is bigger so the heat can dissipate. Crazy because the Magewell cost a lot more than this. Also this one has an HDMI pass through, which the magewell did not! That means you can split this with another ouput, for example run it out to a TV, a camera monitor, projector, or external recorder like a Atmos Ninja. The magewell couldn't do any of that without a separate splitter sitting before it to copy the signal to multiple outputs.
Yes, there are cheaper capture card adapters out there, but in my experience they are a mixed bag of mostly unreliable performance and subpar coloring, and lack the features this offers. The Magewell might still be the most pro version of this I've used as far as color and clarity, but it is more expensive and only offers a single input with no passthrough, not to mention overheats easily. I'd definitely recommend giving this one a try!

There's a volume control button on the cord, and the USB cord is about 8 feet long, which is plenty generous for connecting to my computer and doing speech recognition.

The only problem with this headset is that I want to use it for hours on end while narrating articles. I'm a freelance writer, and sometimes I either just don't feel like typing, have a sore wrist or fingers, or feel like I can narrate my thoughts faster than I can type them. After about two hours of using this headset, my ears start to ache. I haven't figured out any way of changing the tension on this headset so it doesn't press so hard on my ears.

While I would definitely recommend this headset as a low-budget alternative to higher end products, and for people who would like to use a headset for just an hour or so at a time, I would not recommend it for people who want to use the headset for any kind of professional or serious hobby endeavor. I can see from other reviews that I'm not alone in having my ears hurt, and since I have a small size head, and ears that do not stick out very far, I can only think the problem would be worse for most people than it is for me.

title: Fast, Reliable Performance Even When Configured for Second Home Network
text:
This triple-band LINKSYS AC3200 (EA9200) SMART WI-FI ROUTER represents another significant advancement in home networking power. It has one standard 2.4 GHz band, and two 5 GHz bands that it can automatically "steer" between, to balance the traffic between your connected, in-use devices and maximize their performance. To make use of this feature, you must set up your devices to use the 5 GHz bands (and not all wireless devices are 5 GHz-capable).

A feature that I love about this particular router, is the built-in stand that holds it in a vertical position. This not only reduces the router's footprint, but also ensures that the router gets adequate ventilation. (My horizontal Linksys AC1900 router got so warm, I had to place it on a ceramic tile to protect the tabletop.)

This Linksys AC3200 broadcasts signals (all bands) that are as strong as, or even stronger than, the signals broadcast by my rock-solid [[ASIN:B00F0DD0I6 Netgear Nighthawk Router]]. The signals reach every corner of my two-bedroom, two-story townhouse. OOKLA speed tests show that I'm getting the full benefit of Comcast's high-speed cable Internet (download 68.12 Mbps, upload 12.15 Mbps in mid-morning; even faster speeds at night). This is true despite my unusual current configuration--the Linksys router is connected to the Netgear router as a wired device, by Ethernet cable between an Ethernet port and the Linksys router's Internet port.

The unusual configuration gives me two independent home networks. (You can have one network for yourself, and one for your spouse or kids; or one network for home and one for work.) All of my wireless devices are able to connect normally to the Linksys network, using the network and router passwords, though my wireless printers cannot be shared across the two networks. Settings for either router can be accessed and adjusted from a computer or tablet that is connected to the router's network.

The Netgear and Linksys routers are peacefully co-existing on a small table near my coaxial cable connection for Comcast's high-speed Internet. Neither interferes with the other, even though they are literally inches apart.

This router is extremely easy to set up. You just connect it, and follow the prompts from the built-in software. When you access the router to adjust the settings, you can click on "Help" at the top of the display, to get good, concise explanations of each the router's main features. title: Adorable, no nonsense, no frills quirky little thing w/ analogue dial tuning
text:
I now own two emergency types of radios, this one, and another. This means I can compare this to something directly. The following are the reasons why I like this radio more than the other:

1). It’s TINY. It can fit in the front pocket of your shirt or jacket.

2). It’s analogue. This old fashioned tuning style happens to be my preference for radios. It is simple, and you have more control in tuning into the exact radio station that you want without hassle.

3). This radio comes equipped with an antenna extension that includes what appears to be a copper coil. So if you can’t get good reception with this radio’s built in antenna, out comes this Tesla-esque looking attachment!

4). It is yellow jacket yellow. It won’t get so easily lost in the clutter, if you choose not to use it unless hazardous weather conditions are reported.

Now: things that I like less about this radio:

1). It isn’t water resistant/ waterproof

2). For the money, I think that an extra feature or two could be added. For the same price, I also have an emergency radio that has solar panels, reading lamp, compass, an SOS alarm, flashlight, a hand crank, and provides a powered docking station for my devices in case of a power outage.

But to each their own. Perhaps those reading this review aren’t interested in owning an emergency radio that is a transformer. Maybe you want to keep things simple, and are not as enamored of gadgets as I. Regardless of which radio you ultimately go with, and this one is great for size and analogue tuning, you should always keep it charged up and use it frequently enough during non emergency times that you will fully understand how it functions and not be taken by surprise by a random power outage.

title: Disturbing Blindingly Bright Blue Indicator Lights On This Modem
text:
I am shaking my head wondering why Arris would think putting in blinding blue indicator lights on this modem was a good idea! The blue upstream and downstream indicator lights on the SB6121 and SB6141 are not nearly as blinding. Why?

I am not exaggerating at all. The blue lights are blindingly bright. Do not stare into them.

Of course, I could turn the modem around, but why should I have to do that on a $130 modem?

I could put tape over the lights...but that defeats the purpose of having the indicator lights in the first place.

If your shelf or cabinet setup is such where the modem is hidden from view, this modem is fine. But if you are in a situation where your room is small and the modem has to be in sight, by all means you should avoid this modem.

Do the people at Arris not actually look at the lights after designing?

This modem is listed as compatible with Cox Communications...and I was able to get it to work with Cox at full speed. However, due to the blindingly bight blue indicator lights, I either have to hunt down a different modem, or place something in front of it to block the lights. (Or tape a piece of paper or cloth on the front, which I'd have to lift up if I want to check the lights.) I paid $130 for this modem, and I have to do that? Mind-boggling.

title: First impressions...
text:
Photos:
*The very top pocket looks like it'd be tiny from the outside, but it's actually pretty deep. A Dish remote can go about halfway or so down into it. I can fit my Galaxy S9+ with an OtterBox case in it.
*However, the other front pocket is too small for much other than a map, a phone, or a very small book. For example, I cannot fit my paperback version of the Buffalo Creek Disaster. It's just a hair too big. This pocket also contains the lanyard, so maybe it is better suited to keys, cards and wallets anyway.
*The two laptops I used to test fit in the bag and how they compare to each other: A 15" Acer gaming laptop and a 15" Lenovo ThinkPad. The Acer is about 3 years old and hefty. You can see it's dimensionally bigger, but the thickness is literally double of the Thinkpad as well. They both fit well. The Thinkpad didn't jiggle around, and the Acer is proof that just about any 15" should fit this bag.

Review:
I just got this backpack, so this will be first impressions. I hope to update later with performance.

I bought this to use for college classes, so I plan on packing a 15" Thinkpad laptop, books and materials needed for classes.

The construction looks solid, but it's not a heavy bag at all. The padding is very thick on the straps, the top handle, and along the back. It's really nice. I could see this being weighed down and the straps not digging into my shoulders, and with as thick as the back is, there's no way a book or errant pencil would jab into my back. Granted, the back is also the laptop compartment, so this padding is two-fold. The back has much thinner padding along the spine, and I think that might help a little with airflow. At the very least, the bag shouldn't suction itself onto my back on a hot day due to this design.

The laptop compartment is well padded. It doesn't open very wide (the zipper pretty much just runs the top curve of the bag), but it's plenty to get a laptop in and out. But I wouldn't put little things inside of it, because they would be lost. At the very bottom is a "sling" of strong material, so if you had this backpack full and dropped this on the floor, in theory, it should help keep the laptop from smacking the floor on its edge. Nice touch. The sling is only up maybe 1/2 to 3/4 of an inch from the very bottom, so you don't lose much room for the feature. However, if you were to drop some change or something in there, I could see it potentially winding up under the sling and disappearing forever.
As for the size of the laptop compartment, I tested it with my ThinkPad and an older Acer gaming rig (15" Aspire VX). There should be a photo of the two on this review. The Acer is larger and literally twice as thick as the ThinkPad (it's a beast), and while it's a snugger fit, it does fit just fine. Would a 17" laptop fit? *Maybe*. It would be really tight. The Acer fits nicely in that there's a little room on either side and an inch or so to the zipper at the top. If it was much larger, I'd be concerned about the laptop being difficult to get in and out, and that the edges would be at and touching the side walls of the backpack, making dings to the laptop much more possible. So.. if you have a 17", tread carefully (hold onto your receipt or buy one that can be returned easily). Just about any 15" should fit fine, though, and be properly protected and easy to get in and out of the bag. I am very glad I opted for this model and not its little brother, the Division, however. If this bag were much smaller, I'd have my doubts about that Acer fitting.
I saw a review where someone complained that the stitching might eventually rub on their laptop, and I could see that happening. The stitching is heavy duty stuff inside, and several lines of stitching run along the inside of that compartment in rows. Easiest fix? Make a cheap sleeve out of some fleece fabric. You don't need padding, as that is ample in this bag. But if you are worried about little scuffs from the thick stitching, a piece of fleece would do you fine. Definitely not a deal breaker to me. That is an easy fix. The padding is the important need from the backpack that I needed, and this bag provides it well. But, I do wish they would have thought of that and just fleece lined it. For as much Timbuk2 wants for them, that shouldn't have been a problem for them to do that.

The front compartments are nice. I can see pens and chargers and all that fitting well in the large, divided, inside compartments. This section of the bag does not unzip all the way (the zipper goes almost 1/2 of the way down the bag), but I found it very easy to access the pockets and interior. I kind of like the interior material at the sides that keep that section of the bag from flopping open, considering that's where my loose pens and chargers will be held. No more spilling everything all over the floor!
There is a main area that is a blank slate. It contains one very thin padded area towards the back (the other side of the laptop compartment), big enough for a thin tablet of just about any size or folders. The main area looks like it would hold a couple of text books (2 at least) and maybe a bag lunch on top of that. I will try and update how much I can cram in there when school starts.

The very, very front has a small pocket towards the top for what I think might be for sunglasses or a wallet. I was surprised that it fit my Samsung Galaxy 9+ in an OtterBox Defender case! The case makes my phone super thick, and while it was a bit tight getting it in there, it did fit! Impressive. You might be able to fit glasses in their case in this pocket. Again, a minor complaint in that this pocket is not fleece lined, either. If it's meant for glasses or whatever, fleece lining would have been a nice touch, and would have helped justify the price point.
There is another front pocket that would be good for something flat: a map, a guide, or maybe a phone. It looks like it'd fit a sodoku book well, but not anything much thicker. A small paperback novel, tops, depending on how full the other compartments are. It's not tall or wide enough for a standard sized notebook, but possibly a really small planner or one of those little notebooks? A parking tag or the likes. Not sure what I'll use this for. Inside of this pocket is a sewn in lanyard with a metal clip at the end. It's not very long, though, but might be fine to hold an access card or keys if you need them to be secure in your bag. But the lanyard is not really long enough to make good use of traditional door keys without unclipping them every time. I'm not sure they thought that out.

The one water bottle holder on this backpack is indeed slender. I was able to fit an insulated 16oz bottle that was given to me as a gift, and it was tight. I kind of like that the neoprene holds so snug. I don't see my bottles tipping out very easily at all. I would not expect this to hold anything much bigger than a 24oz water bottle unless it's designed to be taller and skinnier. That works fine for me, but it's something to be aware of.

Overall, I like the backpack. It seems sturdy and padded and isn't too huge on me (I'm just over 5'). I like that the chest straps are removable, and that the very bottom clasps (the ones that will hit the ground most often) are metal. The layout is good and I think it will work well for me.

But would I pay $120? No. I paid about half that and I feel that was a fair price. If you can get it for ~$70 or less, I'd say go for it. But do not pay $100+.

title: EXCELLENT NEW OUTDOOR CAMERA BY VIMTAG
text:
I have been using Vimtag cameras for over four years and absolutely LOVE them.

This new outdoor camera by Vimtag is absolutely outstanding.

Installation was as easy as all their other cameras have been. Simply follow the instructions and you won’t have any problems whatsoever. You’ll download the Vimtag app, plug the camera into your router via the included Ethernet cable, log in to your network and establish the connection. Once added into the Vimtag app it’s just a matter of mounting the camera.

This new B4 Outdoor Camera by Vimtag has several advanced features the previous Vimtag Outdoor cameras did not have - it has both a speaker and a microphone, allowing for two way communication, a super bright motion activated LED light and superior lenses allowing for crystal clear viewing and recording.

There are so many things I love about the Vimtag camera system. Firstly, each camera holds its own micro SD card so you don’t have to pay for monitoring or video storage, unless you want too. The only downside to this is if the camera was stolen you’ll lose the footage. Another option you have is to utilize Vimtag’s S1 Storage Box which will store the data from up to 6 cameras. In addition you can subscribe to cloud storage.

While other reviewers have commented on their cameras being hacked, I have never had this be an issue but I understand internet security and utilize firewalls that prevent access. While the first versions of the Vimtag cameras had vulnerabilities I have found those to be secured now.

This camera has worked flawlessly. Motion sets it to record whatever is going on or send an alert to my phone. If the motion takes place at night the bright LED Light comes on and I receive crystal clear images. The two way communication is incredibly clear on both ends.

This is another outstanding product by Vimtag that I don’t hesitate to recommend.
