title: 4-PIN, not 3-PIN like V1.  Noticeable hum.  No mention of controller needed
text:
Firstly, if you see any comments stating its 3-PIN, this is false. The 3-PIN was the old version. This version is 4-PIN. While this is fine for new setups that can plan around this, I was purchasing this to replace a loud V1 thinking I could just swap them out without issue. Nope. Thankfully, despite being older, my mobo had a single 4-PIN fan header listed as "Optional CPU Fan" that I was able to use.

However, there's an issue here: No controller. If you had to use a 3-to-4 pin adapter, you'll have no control over your fan and it will just run at max speed. If you were able to actually plug it into a 4-pin port like I was, you'll still end up having to fiddle with your BIOS to set up its speed settings. Without a controller (which the listing doesn't mention will be needed), this is your only real solution to fan speed control.

Why would you need to bother fiddling with the speed? Because, at least in my setup, when set to Standard mode, the lowest speed is about 50-60%. Even at this speed, the fan gives off a very noticeable low-droning hum. It's at just the right low tone that I could even hear it in the other room while my PC simply idled on the desktop. I had to adjust it to Silent to keep it from humming just when idle or web browsing. I'll likely have to manually tweak the graph myself to avoid the humming when playing games as well. Thankfully I'm using this as my top exhaust fan, so its not super vital and doesn't require running at high speeds, but I can't imagine even attempting to use this as a primary intake or exhaust fan. The sound would be grating.

Honestly super disappointing as the V1's did a solid job for several years without any major sound issues.

title: Perfect for extending a network via coax
text:
It's important to understand what this is and is not. Considering the low price, I got it hoping that maybe I could use it to ditch my VZ Fios router. No dice---the coax light didn't come on when I disabled my VZ router. However, I found that the VZ router produces a MoCA signal over the coax line. So, with the VZ router connected, you can connect this to any coax in the house (assuming all your coax lines are connected) to yield a wifi or ethernet access point. This is similar to powerline adapters, but better because the speeds are higher.

Update: I'm now using two of these devices to extend my network via coax (to somewhere that would be difficult to wire via ethernet). My computer is connected to #1 via ethernet. #1 is connected to #2 via coax. #2 is connected to my router via ethernet. Now I understand that these are essentially repeaters which convert to/from MoCA. I'm about to have my Fios updated and converted from coax to ethernet. I'll be able to ditch the VZ router and connect my mesh wifi router to the main Fios cable. But, my computer isn't close to the Fios box, so I'll use these two devices and existing coax wiring to connect my computer (and other devices that need regular cables). Since the coax I'll be using is all internal (and my ethernet will be protected by my mesh router firewall), I won't need a coax filter.

Speed test screenshot is for a 75/75 Fios so the two devices don't seem to slow the speed at all---I get about the same with a direct ethernet connection.

Edit: This was the perfect solution for a room that only had coax wiring (where it wasn't worth running ethernet). Speeds max out around 150/200 (I now have a 400/400 Fios connect).

title: CONTINUOUSLY VARIABLE PLAYBACK SPEED from 1/8 speed to 8 x times speed playback
text:
Update: I previously complained that this device does not offer variable playback speeds. I received this information from no less a source than the AGPtEK product engineer, Leo Zheng. His email, and I quote, read: "Sorry. Our product can fast-forward, but does not support the 2 times faster speed playback function." Poor Leo needs to learn more about his product, specifically the AGPTek Longevity 1.6 Software V1.101.10 Music Player. And, I admit, I have a master's degree in electrical engineering from the California Institute of Technology. So, don't feel bad, Leo. Here is how to do it:

From the Play Music screen which displays album art (not the histogram screen), push M. Then select Sound Settings. Then select variable speed playback. The playback speed can be set at any speed between normal (1 x times speed) to 8 x times playback speed, to 1/8 (one eighth) the normal playback speed, with continuous variability!

If the above instructions sound too easy to be true, they are. The software for this unit has a bug. Depending on the history of how you got to the Play Music screen, selecting Sound Settings will or will not offer "variable speed playback" as an option. What seems to work fairly predictably is to let the unit play a song until the screen goes dark. Then briefly press the center button to wake it up. You will then be at the Play Music screen, in a historical state which puts playback speed variability into the pick list under Sound Settings.

title: Charged my Lenovo right up!
text:
I have a discarded 7th generation Intel Lenovo I was given from an office to scrub and give to someone who's working from home during the coronavirus shutdown here in NY. Problem is, they gave it to me without the charger and I can't go back to the office and get it until they reopen the doors. Thankfully, it uses a standard USB-C shaped plug to charge. I have plenty of phones and tablets that use that, but apparently laptops need the more robust Power Delivery standard, and not the lower power of USB phone chargers.
Amazon to the rescue, with this excellent replacement PD adapter. I love that modern computers and devices are starting to embrace a standard like this going forward- Macbooks and PC laptops both use this now, and it's even backwards compatible with USB devices like phones and tablets (the reverse isn't true- I couldn't use my phone charger on this laptop, but this laptop's PD charger can charge my phone).
This device worked great for getting that Lenovo back up and running, very appreciative for a future full of standards!

title: Pleasantly Surprised On How Well This Stand Is Made
text:
I'm always on the hunt for a solid & affordable tablet/cell phone stand.

Unfortunately, my endless quest has left me with my share of duds.

Many are constructed of cheap plastic & easily break. Or don't have a sturdy base & topple over. Or are just not thoughtfully designed for their intended purpose.

So when this stand by FCXJTU (terrible name, BTW) arrived in its nameless (other than "Lifting Folding Desktop Bracket"), generic white box, I had no expectations that this guy would be any different than his predecessors.

Man, was I glad to be wrong!

This compact stand is very well designed & executed.

It's constructed from combination of plastic & metal elements with silicone grips in all the right places (on the device cradle & on the bottom of the base).

Although, I would like to see the bottom grips a littler more aggressively "grippy."

They allowed the stand to slip across the desk when applying somewhat decent pressure.

However, this was not a deal breaker as I was purposely pushing fairly hard. Under normal use this won't be an issue.

The base of the stand is well weighted to keep your device safely in place. It doesn't slip or slide while typing, swiping, using a stylus or while adjusting angles, heights, etc...

The cradle (where your device sits) has folding feet that automatically pop out to support your phone or tablet.

The top of the cradle adjusts in size so you can customize to the height to your electronics.

One HUGE plus of this stand is the actual mounting arm.

It's made (at least the outer shell) of a metal or alloy. There are real screws that hold it together! (not rivets or plastic clips).

The arm extends out to twice the length of its normal size. It ratchets up or down precisely allowing your to make "micro" adjustments to the arm height. Very nice!

The joints (where the arm attaches to the base & where the arm attaches to the cradle) are VERY tight.

This is a big deal!

If you've dealt with crappy stands, the you know that if the joints are all sloppy & loosey goosey, then your device sinks over time.

This little guy is hanging in there even when holding a Surface Go in a Kensignton Blackebelt case with keyboard attached.

That's OVER 2 lbs of weight & the stand doesn't budge.

The last thing I will say about this little gem is its size.

He folds up to 4.4"L x 2.6W". That's smaller in height than an iPhone SE (2016) (see pic).

And it weighs in at just under 7 ounces.

In comparison, a Samsung Galaxy S9+ with a polycarbonate hard shell case weighs around 9 ounces.

So this stand is definitely very portable.

To sum things up, I have to say this guy is a for sure winner.

The price point ($16.99 w/ Prime at the date of this review) is right on. It's compact & portable so can easily be slipped in to your pocket, bag or backpack. And has a sturdy build that allows adjustment into dozens of positions to support a variety of electronics without slipping, sagging or sliding.

An all around sweet deal!

title: Worked Great in Windows 8 - Not So Much in Windows 7 or OSX
text:
Voice quality is superb on these speakers, better than my expensive computer speakers. I could listen to all five hours of Windows Essential Training at lynda dot com with relative auditory ease (counting the three hours of sleep). Audibooks while traveling would be a great use of these headphones.

Music quality varied based on the connected device. On the iMac, music quality was good at best. My computer's Harman Kardon speakers were obviously the best but even the built in speakers on my iMac were as good as the music quality when I had the headphones direct wired to the computer. Music played via bluetooth connections were more rounded than using ear buds but sounded less full. Not only did the volume drop when compared with wired connections, but the base faded out. The quality of the recording makes a lot of difference when testing speakers. I tried dozens of different artists (Hendrix, ZZ Top, Etta James, Alison Krauss) but Eric Clapton playing JJ Cale best displayed the range of the headphones.

On the Yoga Pad 2 Pro, bluetooth music quality was great once I changed the bluetooth driver. I switched from the default driver to the IBM integrated bluetooth IV. The headphones connected, and I had two Koss devices to choose from. I chose the stereo version, put on Clapton and was amazed at the difference in quality. The base and treble were perfect. I'm taking these to work tomorrow to try out on more mac and windows machines.

Connection Issues - Bluetooth pairing on the iMac was a pain because it kept disconnecting. The iMac couldn't find the headphones in bluetooth mode unless the power cable was plugged in. Once it connected, I could unplug it and maintain connection. Use was straightforward in Windows 8 on the Yoga once I switched drivers. Strangely, I was able to keep connection for a longer distance when connected to the iMac. I could maintain full connection with as many as four walls between the headphones and the computer but it started breaking up as I headed downstairs. With the better Yoga connection, it started losing quality after the third wall and at 21 feet.

Buttons - On the iMac in bluetooth mode, pressing the pause button caused me to lose connection. I'd attach the power cord, reconnect, select the headphones again, close and restart my media player, and begin playing again. In wired mode, none of the three buttons worked for playing songs via iTunes. In Windows on the Yoga, everything worked perfectly.

Instructions - lacking. What they had were decipherable but I would have liked more explanation, particularly about the power. The last comic panel shows you that the power button turns blue when fully charged. Mine turned blue after less than an hour connected but may not have been fully charged. It's supposed to flash red when it gets low and it wasn't flashing but that's as much as I know. You need to know ahead of time how to set up bluetooth for your device because, unlike some other bluetooth headphones (Jabra Revo), it includes no instructions.

Carrying Case - Well designed hard carrying case. Pockets for cables, molded form holds headphones tightly in place.

Construction - Well constructed with quality materials. Although lightweight, they still seem durable. I prefer headphones that aren't collapsible because it reduces the chance of breakage.

Comfort - Everyone who tried them on commented on how comfortable they are. Because I use headsets for recording, I look for padding that keeps it comfortable for two hours or more. Not sure that these would be comfortable that long. I walked around the house with them on and they were barely perceptible except for the music. The headphones sit well on my head - no slippage. I could even do laundry (front loaders) with these on. I see no evidence that it was designed with a left-right orientation.

Because I got these for review before they went on the market, I don't know how they will be priced. If they cost more than $143, do a physical comparison with the high rated Jabra Revo.

I am rating these based on their Windows 8/Yoga 2 performance, assuming they have the potential to work as well on other devices if I set them up right. I'll test this assumption over the next week and report back.

Addendum: Couldn't get it to connect via bluetooth on one new iMac, one new Windows 7 computer, and one old Windows 7 computer at work. Wired worked fine on all.

It's a good router. In many ways it's a very good router. Might not be the choice for a large family with a lot of bandwidth consumption but it does do a good job for our small family usage. I've had multiple devices online at the same time the living room T.V. was streaming an HD movie. That and good coverage is all I really need. With our previous router the Echo Dot at literally the other end of the house had problems maintaining a streaming signal. Since installing the AC900 it's streamed music all night, every night for the two plus weeks it's been up and running. Signal strength was dramatically increased everywhere in the house. Speeds are a little better but not by too much. I had more of a consistency issue than a speed problem with the old router. The router sits low and doesn't seem to have great cooling so I have it sitting on a brace that I made so it's now couple inches off the shelf it's on. Better and more efficient cooling and less chance for dust build up.
I was happy to see that using a web browser you weren't required to install any software to get into the router's management although there is an Android app to manage the router. I've found the web browser access have be as easy if not easier to use though rarely I have to reload the main page a time or two but I think that's my choice of browser and not a problem with the device itself.
The router is great, for the novice, intermediate or even expert user. Unpack it follow the easy set up guide (pick a decent password) then connect your devices and you're done if you want to be or you can dig deeper and have fine control over the router's many features. It may not be the perfect choice for every installation but if you don't need a lot there's no reason to spend a lot.
In the end the AC900 delivers a lot of bang for the buck.

title: Nice Ring, Decent Lighting For Various Style Photos
text:
WARNING- SOMEWHAT IN DEPTH REVIEW- If you prefer a short summary, see section marked THE BOTTOM LINE
------------------------------
I have been working with photos for a business situation, so I have managed to acquire some equipment for different uses for products. When I saw this, my partner wanted to put this to good use, so we decided to try it out. This review will be somewhat in depth.

RING SIZE
The ring itself is large sized which makes it nice for doing personal videos like makeup, and even just discussions and research, but it also is nice for doing larger product photos.

RING ROCKER SWITCH
The controls are a bit finicky. The on off rocker switch is kind of temperamental which is why it took me so long to get this review out. When turning on the rocker switch, the light sometimes will turn on and then off quickly. It takes a few times to get it to stay on which is frustrating.

PLUG
The plug insert is just under the switch. It goes in pretty solid.

CORD
The cord is about 10 ft long- I measured it. The plug is 2 prong. It has a pretty good fit into an outlet and is not loose.

DIALS
The two dials determine the brightness of the light and also the temperature. They are infinite settings so you can fine tune them pretty well.

LIGHT QUALITY
The light quality of this ring is solid. It does provide a lot of light and it does help to get a nice atmosphere for photos or video. The brightness can go pretty high and you can get it lower but one problem is that it will flicker as you get it on the lower settings.

CAMERA
The other issue I have with this is the camera. There is a screw that you can supposedly put a camera on, but that will not allow me to screw on the camera tightly so that it faces the same direction as the light. Then there is the issue of the camera holder. So, when I screw the camera onto that- it is a ball joint holder- I can screw it into the ring, but for some reason, once the attachment is in place, the ball won't tighten completely and the camera has some play in it.

I can tighten it and it stays put off the tripod,, but when the weight of the camera is on the ball joint, it does not like to lock tight for some reason.

WHAT TYPE OF CAMERA DO I HAVE?
I have a Canon G12 camera which is not that heavy or large, so this issue is not due to me trying to use a camera that is way too big.

PHONE
There is a phone holder so you can use your phone on this ring as well.

TRIPOD
The quality of the tripod seems solid. It can be set up to compensate for uneven ground and does seem to perform reasonably well when I have used it. I think it is fair to say that I do most of my photos indoors on even floors, so I have not put it to tough testing in that department. I love how it folds away to fit in the case.

CAN YOU USE THIS RING WITH OTHER TRIPODS?
I was able to screw this into a taller tripod that I have to use it if I wanted to, which I don't.

CASE
The case is part of the charm of this light. It is padded and fits the ring nicely. The tripod folds up perfectly compact into the back holder and pocket, and the front pocket with a zipper holds the attachments. It is fabulously designed.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This light ring is nice. It has great light, nice temperature settings, and is easy to use once you get it set up. Problems with attaching the camera and getting it stable, and occasional blinking of the light make this four instead of five stars, but I still work with it until I can figure out a solution.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. I like this set. It is perfect for taking on location filming or shooting photos, and it works well when I work past the frustrations.

MY PHOTOS
I took 3 photos for you of the exact same thing at the same time so you can see the difference in lighting and color perception. They are labeled for ease of understanding which is which.

title: Absolutely Outstanding
text:
I work with a lot of headphones, headsets and earbuds. I am very partial to one very special set of headphones that I own, a pair of Monster Inspiration phones that includes active noise cancelling (ANC) and this is the pair of headphones against which I compare all others. Although I have worked with many sets of very excellent headphones it takes a lot for me to really rave about a specific set. To be that awesome, the headphones have to be very, very comfortable, have brilliant sound, be made well and have at least good passive noise cancelling if not ANC. These phones by Geega are nothing short of outstanding and actually complete very well with my Monster phones.

These are some of the more comfortable phones I have used. They are completely over the ear phones and cover my entire ears so there is no pinch. The earphones themselves are padded with a soft leatherette that is almost buttery soft and the headband is covered in the same material. These are very easy to adjust to get the fit just right. I can wear them for long periods of time and they do not pinch or get uncomfortable though they do get warm after about an hour. Because they are over-the-ear they provide some measure of passive noise cancelling.

The sound profile is excellent. The bass is at about the right level - not weak and not too forward so the bass response is very good. When the bass drops, you know it but not because it causes a headache. The midrange is very rich and full and the music has amazing depth, better than many others I have used. The highs are absolutely brilliant, bright and crisp. I would stop short of calling these audiophile headphones, but the sound profile is every bit as good as a pair of $350 Sennheiser headphones I own - better, actually, and it makes me sad to know I spent that much on those phones when I could have spent a lot less for these. I intend to connect these to a Bluetooth transmitter and connect them to a professional sound mixing board to see how detailed the sound is - I will update this review when I have done so.

I have these paired to my tablet from which I stream Pandora to them. They paired and connected without issue on all of the devices I have tried - my laptop, my phone and finally my tablet. They identify themselves as “GEEGA S204” and on all three devices I tried to connect I had no issues at all maintaining the connection.

These phones come in a nice, hard protective case that provides good protection from crush damage. There is a mesh pocket inside for keeping the included USB cable for charging and the AUX cable for alternate input.

The range on these phones is 20' - 30' which is very much in line with most phones I have used. Interestingly, they did not stutter and cut out, they just completely cut off when I passed that threshold. I am not sure if this is just a function of my environment or if they really are that sensitive at the threshold.

Overall, these are simply outstanding. I have not found any other set of Bluetooth headphones with the same level of comfort or sound quality. These are the best wireless phones, of any type, that I have ever used. These are my new reference point for wireless/Bluetooth headphones and are the standard by which I will judge any others. I will still use the Monster phones, for the ANC function and for comparison against other wired phones, but these phones by Geega will be used for listening in my home office where I enjoy listening to music most.

Disclaimer: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at no cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

title: Quality Budget Friendly Optical Zoom Blue Iris Camera
text:
I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

As with all security systems my advice is never use cloud based recording - this opens your entire network to not only the company who you are giving blanket access too but also to hackers. The same is true for WiFi. Obviously WiFi is more convenient but if your privacy is a concern this really needs to be taken into account. Hackers have become quite adept at hacking into WiFi cameras and being able to not only watch your feed but control your cameras and access your entire network. If you choose to utilize WiFi cameras take the time to understand your router and employ proper VPN protocols.

Due to my security concerns with WiFi cameras my current security system is completely run through a dedicated computer utilizing the Blue Iris software. While this may seem intimidating to some, it is well worth learning and utilizing for the huge advantages in privacy and security.

I’ve noticed many people have asked if this camera works with a Blue Iris and it does without any issue. Just update to the latest firmware. The remainder of setup within Blue Iris is straightforward. The RLC-522 supports PoE 802.3af and will work with 48V active adapters which are more expensive, but you can also rely on a PoE switch, which in my opinion is a much easier, straightforward option. Something to note, if you plan on powering via a DC cable this is not included.

The varifocal lens is a major feature that sets this camera apart from others. With an adjustable lens size of 2.8-8mm the optical zoom is excellent in comparison to digital zoom where pixels are simply enlarged. This will allow for this camera to be hung higher giving a better over view shot of an area while still being able to zoom in. The 1/2.7” CMOS image sensor is decent in low light, certainly not as good as 1/1.8” but I’ve found the low light capabilities strong in comparison to many similar cameras. The 18 IR LEDs do a decent job of illuminating objects in the fore and mid ground areas.

The camera has a built in microphone that allows for sound recording, though no speaker so two way communication will not be possible with this unit.

Unlike many similar cameras a mount is not required to be purchased separately. Mounting is fairly simple although care must be taken to mount so your lens is ultimately pointed in the direction you want as this camera does not pan nor tilt.

The varifocal zoom is not particularly fast so if you were trying to zoom in on action, such as a moving vehicle as it passed, you will likely miss it. Although if you have an area you want to focus on for a period of time it works fine.

In terms of storage, the RCL-522 utilizes H.264 rather than H.265 which will require more space to record the same data. Storage options include a MicroSD card slot with support up to 64GB - which I find lacking, cloud storage via FTP, the propriety Reolink NVR systems, or as I use set ups utilizing software such as Blue Iris.

When all things are taken into account this is a very solidly build varifocal camera, suited to outdoor environments, decent daytime / nighttime resolution, fairly easily mounted, and setup in Blue Iris was easy and straightforward. While I would prefer to have pan and tilt capabilities at this price point that is unrealistic. Overall I have been quite impressed with this camera and would recommend it for many security situations.

title: Grow Your Network without Running CAT Cable or Wireless Annoyance
text:
Many of us would like to use our computer in a certain room or area of the house, but it really is too expensive, or too difficult, or not practical to run Cat5/6 Cable to the location (drilling holes, going through walls, floors, ceilings, etc.). There are also those situations, because of building structure and/or materials that wireless tends to drop internet connections or is unable to supply a desired or required amount of bandwidth.

In my own case, a few years ago, I needed a solution to bring the Internet to the 3rd floor of a 140 year-old building, which had wiring (only two-prong) more than just a few decades old. From previous experience, I knew wireless would not work (at least work well). There was also little or no hope, in the near future, of running a CAT5/6 line for a hardwired connection.

A fair amount of research first led me to find the [[ASIN:B001J2ZSL4 Cisco-Linksys PLK300 PowerLine AV Ethernet Adapter Kit]] (made up of two Cisco-Linksys devices: PLE300 & PLS300 network adapters). I was a skeptic, but the reviews on Amazon.com and other sites convinced me to give it a try. Because of this product, I had Internet service the same day the product was delivered. The PLE300 plugs into your router or switch and an electrical receptacle. The PLS300 plugs in a wall receptacle where you want to use the network/Internet. The PLS300 is a four-port adapter (having 4 RJ-45 connectors), acting like a normal switch, giving Network/Internet access to 4 computers or any other network devices.

Since then, I have updated (actually added) several components to the network including this [[ASIN:B007ILFFS6 Netgear XAVB5101 Powerline Nano500 Set(XAVB5101)]]. One of the units in the set replaces the above Cisco-Linksys PLE300 router connection. The other unit is now connected to my computer, replacing the PLS300 (now used elsewhere). The network connection appears as 1.0Gbps, but I am sure that these units go nowhere near this speed. While the Cisco had boasted of up to 200Mbps data rates, these claim speeds up to 500 Mbps. There is a very noticeable difference in how quickly the monitor displays a screen. I find them impressive! Plus, it's all Plug and Play!

Besides these Powerline adapters, I know of no other solution that provides Internet access to any part of a home or office so quickly and efficiently. The network is easily expandable by plugging additional single-port adapters into electrical outlets anywhere in the building controlled by the same electrical service. A network switch like [[ASIN:B0000BVYT3 NETGEAR GS105 ProSafe 5-Port Gigabit Ethernet Desktop Switch - 10/100/1000 Mbps]] can then be plugged into the adapter, as I am doing, to allow several devices access to the network/Internet. From a user's standpoint, you should experience Internet speeds comparable to what any cable or DSL service provides. These are fast enough to watch streaming HD video from Netflix or other services on internet-ready HD TVs. It's cleaner and easier than most other solutions.

Since initially buying my first Powerline adapters, there have been many companies that have have gotten into the "powerline" market. Cisco/Linksys, Netgear, and Monster are just a few. A little research and reviews can point to many accessories that are compatible and backwards compatible with the Homeplug AV technology standard used in these products. This also competes with products like the [[ASIN:B003VWY0VY Western Digital WD Livewire Powerline AV Network Kit]].

title: A useful flash for Sony mirrorless cameras
text:
I've had this flash for a year-and-a-half. In A (Auto) mode this flash does the job with the Sony mirrorless. I am not a prolific flash user but there are times it has come in very handy. I have no problem using it as a bounce flash with the diffuser attachment. Overheating does not seem to be a problem with this flash. I fired off about 60 full power test shots in a row and the overheat cutout never kicked in. Recycle time was only a couple of seconds so it seems the battery life is respectable for light use. The flash did get warm, though, and the NiMH batteries were just shy of what I'd call hot when I removed them.

There's no way to connect external power so if its to be used all day better have spare batteries handy.

I have a lot of experience with Nikon speedlights and they are very smooth and solid units so far as construction is concerned. The Nissin, to me, seems brittle and not so refined in comparison. It is almost toy-like in the crudeness of some moving parts. Edges tend to be sharp and some parts feel loose and others are tight. The mounting foot is the worst so far as inspiring confidence. It is plastic with sharp edges. It fits so tightly in the camera's shoe that it seems like something will break when mounting it. Dismounting it is an exercise in keeping the release button pressed while carefully wiggling the unit just a bit while pulling it back. The large wheel is only slight raised from the back of the unit and it has weak detents for each position. I defy you not to move it while mounting/dismounting the flash. It needs to be thicker and click positively instead of nearly freewheeling from one setting to the next.

The tilt and swivel mechanism does the job but it does seem to be a bit noisy and loose in operation. However, it does repeatedly click into the proper position when adjusted. The battery door always feels like it is about to break. It has an exposed mechanism that extends and slides the battery door. Once again, it does not inspire confidence.

The pop out card for eye catchlights is good. The slide out beam diffuser works fine. I had no trouble with the zoom mechanism and it automatically motors back and forth to follow the lens. To me, this is a silly feature but everybody's doing it now. I like that there are no silly latches to press to unlock the tilt and swivel adjustment. The detents are strong enough to hold the head in position.

For all the faults I've pointed out I can't deny that this flash is still working OK for me. It's small, light, but would be easier to tote if it could fold flat.

The holder for the S-Pen holds the pen in the position for charging. Mine charges as long as I'm sure to have the pen rotated so that the flat of the pen is facing the tablet. If Samsung can make an S-Pen small enough to fit inside my Note 8 phone, then why can't they make an S-Pen fit into a storage slot inside a tablet??? I don't need a club-sized S-Pen that I have to worry about losing. Sorry for the rant, but I've never understood Samsung's laziness here. Thankfully the Thankscase comes through for this.

My only complaint with Thankscase is the selection of colors/patterns. title: Good choice for a first tablet
text:
Although I've been mucking around on a computer for many years now, this was my first venture into the tablet venue. I wasn't really sure what to buy. Do I go all out, buy a larger one with all the bells & whistles for the price of a base model laptop? Or do I stick with something simple & inexpensive?

I decided to go with the Samsung Galaxy Tab 2. The price was a definite consideration, I liked that it was under $200. I preferred to stick with name brand, as I've had too many friends who went with an inexpensive brand that broke within a few months. The size seemed sufficient for me to play some of the fun apps & keep notes for school.

It's been around 6 months since I first bought the tablet, and I'm overall pleased with it. I do wish it had two things. More storage, because the OS takes up a great deal of space. In hindsight, I would have paid more to have 16GB rather than 8. Also, I wish the charging port was a micro USB instead of 30 pin data port. My husband's Samsung Note has the micro USB and so does my daughter's Nexus 7. It would be really nice to be able to use other charging cords like they do (my husband can use his phone charger) than having to make sure I don't EVER misplace this one.

But for a simple tablet from a trusted brand, I do think the Samsung Galaxy Tab 2 is a good choice.

It may not be an issue for someone else, but it caused me to ding it a star. I haven't yet tried these on an airplane, which is where I normally use noise cancelling. But base on how it worked with the A/C, I expect these will do a great job. Just don't expect it to wipe out outside noise. I could still hear the TV going and my husband talking. Just no A/C loud rumbling noise. Now if only I could sleep in these to kill the sound of my husband's fan.

title: Quick and responsive - premium grade laptop
text:
This Surface Laptop 4 model from Microsoft is an excellent premium grade laptop. My prior laptop is an older 17" Lenovo. This one is smaller (obviously), but much, much quicker.

The aluminum chassis is thin, lightweight and solid. The display is looks great- colors are detailed rich and vibrant, and the touchscreen is effective and appropriately responsive. I find myself simply reaching for the button on a given sites screen, rather than maneuvering the cursor and tapping. (Although, the TouchPad is certainly responsive, too). The keyboard is comfortable and responsive - the surface around the keys and track pad has a texture that makes it seem sort of "soft" (even though it's not). Sound is rich and full. Very nice!

Very few ports - only what you need and not much else. A USB Type-A and Type-C, a headphone jack, and the chargers connector. (Or you can charge using the USB Type-C port).

Set up is straightforward, I loaded in some software (Wordperfect suite) and everything just fell right in place and all worked as it should without issue)

5.) The keyboard is good. It’s not the best, a little spongier than the MacBook Pro 16’s, with a slower rebound, but still among the “good” keyboards on the market, - reasonably tactile. It has physical F-keys, something I wish I had on the MacBook Pro 16. I think the TouchBar is one of the worst things to happen to MacBooks (inadvertent touches are the worst!), so I hope Apple reverts to physical keys this coming year on their flagship system. Rumor has it they will.

6.) Ergonomics are decent, though it’s actually a bit tricky to open the laptop as there’s no indent where you’re meant to flip the screen up, - a peculiar oversight. Bezels are a little large for 2021, but far from offensive.

7.) Sound quality is not bad, but a far cry from the bass that the MacBook Pro 16 is able to generate. You could certainly listen to music here, but headphones would be preferred.

8.) Battery life and thermals are absolutely fantastic, decimating the MacBook Pro for general usage, which is just a portable toaster. The laptop just runs remarkably cool with this AMD setup. That said, when the fans kick in, they kick in with a WHOOSH, which can be a bit disconcerting. Battery life is superb, easily giving me 8-11 hours for general web usage, a good 40% longer than my MacBook Pro doing the exact same things at a comparable brightness.

  9.) The SSD is nothing too special. While yes, any SSD is faster than not-an-SSD, this is on the lower end of the spectrum in terms of NVMe performance.

Overall, I really enjoy the Surface Laptop 4, but it’s not hard to see where Microsoft could make some massive improvements and solidify the Surface line as THE Windows 10 systems to buy.

4 out of 5. A worthy alternative to high-end laptops, but not yet at the top of its game.

title: Buggy But Fast
text:
UPDATE: After a few months, I'm still fairly okay with the performance of the Orbi when it is working. However, there are a few things I wish I'd known ahead of time. For one, you won't get all the features if you have FIOS. You have to run the Orbi in bridge mode, which means no Circle. For another, the router does a poor-to-mediocre job of saving the names it lets you give your devices. I spent a day running down which MAC address went to which device. Next day, poof. Gone. A third issue is that the router needs to be reset every so often when it inexplicably slows down to dial-up speeds. Wouldn't be such a big deal if - IF - everything would just connect back up, but the Orbi doesn't play well with some devices. It HATES my Ecobee thermostat, which I have to assign a new static IP to with each reset, because the Orbi refuses to let it on dynamically and always gives the old static IP to another device. I wasn't looking for something so high maintenance when I forked over the money to buy these things.

Basically, this is a fast wifi network system that really does cover my whole house and is working well with a nighthawk EX7500 as an extender. It has some bugs and some limitations. It comes into a mostly Apple ecosystem and works fine with the computers and airport express extenders as well (but not airport extreme routers, because they will only bridge another airport extreme). The bugs are bad enough to knock it to three stars, but I like the speed so much that if the network stays up a week in a row, I will add a star.

I do not hate this at all. I bought the system because I was spending too much time on the phone with my ISP over an end-of-life router situation. There is no brand replacement coming for that router, at least not anytime soon, which is a bummer. I scoured the internet and settled on this.

I have set it up a couple of times now. The first time, it took all day to convince it to stay connected to its own satellite, worked a couple of days, and then would not connect to the internet. I called my ISP and got them to look at it through my modem (I don't know what it is they do or how they are able to "see" what router is connected to my modem). It went back up at screaming speed. This time it worked for about 24 hours before booting half of my smart devices. So, I set them up again, which took a while, since I now needed static IP addresses for some of them in order for Orbi to let them online. I do not know why.

I also tried to add a NetGear Nighthawk EX7000 extender so that I could have a remote disk via USB. So much nope. Even though it was in bridge mode, with no reason to exist except to make an external hard drive accessible on my network, the extender and Orbi were doubling IP addresses, so every so often people would get the "another computer is using your IP address" message. Pulled the extender and no more issues since then. It has only been about three days without an incident.

The good is great. I get coverage everywhere in my condo in an Edwardian building that has been added onto in strange and wonderful ways that make good wifi impossible upstairs. It works with an EX7500 extender (which is boss). I get well over 200Mpbs near the main router, and the lowest I get is 175 anywhere else. I am only paying for 200. As noted above, it also works with my Apple Airport Expresses, so I can have remote USB disks and printers.

I enabled Circle to stop my teenager from going on the internet in the middle of school nights without having to keep my husband, who works nights, from being able to check his email when he gets home. So far, that is rudimentary but okay. I am trying to figure out where QOS settings are. I think I found them on one of the router login places (there's the Orbi app, the Netgear Genie, the Orbi login page, and I think one other). So far, I think the only thing that works with Alexa are some very basic commands like pause the internet and when is my bedtime. I need to be able to tell it to pause the kid's internet. EDIT TO ADD: I can pause the kid's internet through IFTTT.

Bottom line: I'm okay with this, but I expected a smoother set up process for the money. If I'd known what it was going to entail, I probably would have waited to buy.

title: Fits the bill, avoiding shortcuts
text:
This cable has everything I want in video surveillance cable: it is slick and easy to pull without lubricant, but remains flexible and robust without kinking easily. It is pure copper; some other cables are copper clad aluminum.

Also, the power cable is 18AWG, which is good for power transmission up to 2 amps (for this reason, I suggest using this for all your CCTV runs, even if you have some free (probably 22 AWG - good for up to 0.92 amp) cables that came with your security package - this will allow you to be uniform and ready for any potential upgrades. (If you really want to be ready for the future, run some Cat6 at the same time, which you can use for PTZ, audio, and upgrades to IP cameras). BTW, the free cables that come with the packages share the ground conductor, which can make installation messier and annoy you if you are a perfectionist.

It pulls apart easily, but only when you need it to. The cable is marked by the foot and the box has a place to write how much is left. It was also easy to connectorize with the RG-59 BNC compression connectors I bought here on Amazon.

My only install tip is when you cut the end with your coax tool, ensure that the stranded ground cable (outside the dielectric) remains to make a ground with the connector, but that none of the strands remain long enough that they can come in contact with the 20AWG signal conductor when connectorizing.

title: GREAT video quality (even in low/no light), easy installation and great customer service.
text:
I bought two different brands of drive recorders for my vehicles. I bought this one, and I bought the Apeman C420D. Granted it costs a couple more dollars, I am blown away by how vastly superior the Kingslim D2 is compared to the Apeman.

Firstly, the video/picture quality is outstanding on the Kingslim. It’s crystal clear on both the front and rear cameras. Even when moving at high speeds, there is no blur or bounce to the recording. At night, the Kingslim is still amazingly clear compared to the Apeman. The Apeman records terrible footage in low/no light. I have angled my rear camera upwards rather than facing the ground (as a back-up camera would be angled) so that I can record license plates/road ragers of vehicles behind me, and I am able to read the license plates/see the driver almost as clearly as I am able to see from the front camera.

Secondly, the setup was fairly easy, and I think anyone could do it themselves. All you have to do is run the wires through your trim to the lighter socket and back of your vehicle, and depending on if internal or external mounting your rear camera, through the back of your vehicle. You can also splice the wire to your reverse light wire, which will turn the camera system into a back-up camera. I decided not to do this because you can just instead change the front camera’s screen to the rear camera’s feed and use it that way temporarily.

Lastly, and most importantly, the customer service. I had an issue with the parking sensor and headlight sensor on my Apeman C420D and contacted support about it. All they could tell me was that those features were made that way and were functioning properly, and that if I didn’t like it to just turn them off.

I’ve had zero issues with my Kingslim so far, so the only interaction with their customer service was a letter that they sent me (I was surprised by that, as it’s usually just an email), thanking me for my purchase. This shows me the difference between how Apeman sees their customers and how Kingslim appreciates us.

All in all, you will not be disappointed in this camera. It is exactly as advertised!

title: The Cable/Satellite Terminator that Performs Updates during NFL Playoff Games
text:
Overall it works well. And I love the no-monthly fee part of this unit. Though the unit runs slowly, as if it runs on a 1990-circa CPU.

The setup was super easy and straight forward. Picked up about 70 channels in the Denver market. (Didn't know there were that many.) Though half of them didn't actually broadcast anything. Then I had to narrow it down to about 10 channels that broadcast meaningful contents. It took a long time to download and apply updates during the initial setup. Took about 2 hours.

The menu navigates slowly. Each action took about 3-5 seconds for the unit to finish. The OnePass makes recording a series far more complicated than necessary. I have to jump through many hoops to make it happen. On my cable remote, I can simply press the record button twice to setup a series recording.

I really like how seamlessly TiVo integrates with my Netflix, Amazon Prime and Youtube accounts and leads me directly to the episodes. It is very convenient to use and it's quite a pleasant surprise.

My only gripe is when I view a recorded program and navigate the menu, I cannot exit the menu to go back to full screen viewing of my recorded program. The "back" button only backs out to the main menu. So I have to select the recorded program and resume viewing. For live TV, I can simply click on the "Live TV" button to go back to full screen viewing.

Despite its imperfection, the TiVo with no monthly fee is an outstanding value. For those who are looking to cut the cable or ditch the dish, this is the way to go.

[Update 2017.01.24] Downgrading from 5 to 3 stars. TiVo is supposed to do periodic updates only overnight, but two Sundays in a row, the unit attempted to perform updates during the day. The first update froze the unit so we missed 3 quarters of a NFL playoff game. The second time we caught it in time, so only missed a few minutes of another playoff game.

title: No performance advantage to the upright position and likely performance detractors for most people.
text:
I like the idea of an attractive upright very much, especially since the mohu leaf knockoff Amazon Basics Extreme Performance I have been trying this week has needed to be retaped in various awkward positions at the furthest end of its cord extension just to get a fraction of the channels I am "supposed" to be able to get at my address.

I had hoped that going with the original brand and the newest design would mean a step up from the Amazon Basics extreme. But the reality is that the upright position limits where it can be put enough that I get far fewer channels on it--only two networks and several junk channels you would never want. I really got creative with trying to put it in more places too. For instance I threaded it in loops through the books on my bookshelves in order to try to get it to sit on various bookshelves (despite the hefty cord wanting to pull it off). It just couldn't get the channels. It couldn't even get as many as the Amazon leaf did in spots near the tv b/c the ability to tape to the wall there was a substantial advantage.

ETA: I tried both the Mohu leaf 50 and the Mohu curve in the end, and no matter where I put them, the Amazon Ultimate outperformed them. I do really need the leaf design in my house b/c of how few the antenna hot spots are, but even the Mohu leaf grabbed fewer networks in the optimal positions. I still cannot get PBS off of the AmazonBasics Extreme, although the station is less than 35 miles away. That is my biggest disappointment. But none of the antennae could grab it.

The good is that the tactile response is close to the orig MS board, I like it. Works. Overall, the keyboard works fine.

Cons? Well, the ALT/Ctrl/Windows keys on the bottom are WAY too tall. The MS board had sloped keys there so you didn't accidentally hit them while typing. The keys on this board are squared and HIGH! I'm getting used to holding my wrist up while I type, but then that defeats the purpose of an "ergonomic" keyboard in the first place, right?

The only other "con" is that bios sometimes doesn't recognize it. So if you need a keystroke in response to a boot issue (like to acknowledge booting from a CD or something), you can't, it just sits there until whatever timeout is reached. Once Windows loads, you can enter a password and all works as it should, but something about this USB keyboard isn't seen until Windows starts. Weird. I've loaded defaults in BIOS, set legacy USB's active, all USB ports, blah, blah, no change.

If you're like me and tear a board up whipping a book out, then get this. Just put a pad under your wrists so you don't hit the keys on the bottom. The feel is good and positive and they seem to last OK. The MS boards now are crap, so this is about your only choice for a natural.

EDIT: This has almost hit the wall a few times now. I like the tactile feel, but the annoyance of losing your writing or going to some place you didn't intend in an instant from hitting the Alt/Windoze, etc., keys that stick up at the bottom like trees is getting to be too much.

Find a NOS MS Natural or maybe wait for another mfg or this one to figure out that people don't want to hold their arms in the air to type to avoid hitting the keys at the bottom...

------------------

EDIT #2: A few months into using this board and it started to smell like burning electronic components. That unmistakable smell. No smoke, but the smell was strong and coming from the keyboard. Now my system randomly reboots. When I plug back in the very worn-out MS natural, no reboots. Plug THIS back in and a few minutes (5-20) later, system reboots. Like bad clockwork, but it's consistent. I'm not reducing my rating on it, but I will give a hazard warning for this board. Prob should find another option.

------------------

EDIT #3: Board has been fine for over six-months and a few renditions of the guy smashing his keyboard, then tossing the monitor out his cubie. Maybe not that far, but it's had (I'm not telling how many) "spirited" bangings and came through like an MMA fighter. It's almost abusing it whipped it's problems into shape or something. Been rock solid after some good poundings that would have sent a Logitech to the morgue. So I've actually upped my rating on this board. Still hate the ungodly high special keys at the bottom, but I've gotten used to them. And the tactile feel to the keys is lasting longer than I had expected.

title: Super simple installation; some usage frustrations
text:
IP cameras have always been a total pain for me to get up and running. There’s always something that goes wrong, and I end up spending hours getting it to work. This model, however, was a dream to install. The installation quick-start guide is very clear, and offers two options: installing it if you have a D-Link router; or installation with a non-Dlink router. I used the non-Dlink router approach. You download an install program from the Dlink site that walks you through the installation in a clear, easy step-by-step fashion. I had it running in a couple of minutes in hard wired mode, and a couple minutes more to get it to run wirelessly. Very impressed with how easy it was.

The build quality of the camera itself is pretty good. It’s very lightweight but still feels sturdy, and comes with a stand that has a ball and socket joint so you can rotate and position the camera pretty much any way you would need it. The only hardware issue that I didn’t care for was the power cord. It’s rather short (about 4 foot), which limits where I can position the camera. A longer cord – at least 6 foot – would have been a lot nicer.

Using the camera is both easy and frustrating. There is a mobile app, but it’s really only to view the live feed and take snapshots on demand as you watch the live feed. For finer controls and adjustments you need to use a PC and the My D-Link site. That’s where things can be frustrating.

For example, on the settings page there is a clear section dedicated to email notifications with a checkbox. It is strongly implied that checking the checkbox will allow you to receive email notifications after you have set parameters for either motion detection or sound detection. However, after I set parameters for motion detection and then checked the box for email notifications, I did not receive any emails. After doing some searching via Google I found out that I needed to access the "advanced settings" and set up email there too. This was a far more complicated process and required more online research, but after a little bit of trial and error, I got the email notification working. You’ll need info such as the SMTP server address for your email client, the SMTP server port number, and two email addresses for yourself (one for the sender email; the other for the receiver email).

Why a product with such an easy install process has such a complicated usage setup (with much of the info needed not present on the D-Link site) is frustrating.

Once I got the email notification working, I could choose to have it send me an image at the moment of detection, or a set of 6 images (3 images just before detection and 3 images just after detection, at ½ or full second intervals). I can have it always on, or set it to detect only at certain periods of each day. So far I tried the 6 images option and have it always on, and that's worked out reasonably well.

Night vision and day vision seem to work well, with an acceptably clear picture. I have noticed that some times the view remains in night vision mode even when the room is sunny. Not sure why that is happening. Regardless, the picture remains clear.

It cannot record video captured since the camera does not have an SD card option.

You may need to play with the motion sensitivity adjustment and area of sensitivity to get something that works to your preference. I've found that sensitivity definitely needs to be adjusted higher for reliable night views, which means fiddling with the settings each day. While d-link allows you to adjust motion sensors on a day/night basis, it doesn't let you automatically set sensitivity for different times of the day, so that still has to be a manual task.

Although getting some features working is frustrating due to the lack of info on the D-link site, the overall ease of hardware installation, decent build quality, and good picture quality earn this 4 stars. If the D-Link site was improved this would be a five-star camera at this price point.

title: Bluetooth 4.2 and no true ANC
text:
I am reviewing the ‘TruSound TruWireless Noise Cancelling Earbuds | True Wireless Earbuds with Charging Case for Buds and Phone | Comfortable, Secure Fit | Immersive Stereo Sound, Deep Bass | Easy Touch Control Operation’.
Based on my experience thus far I would like to share my thoughts.

Pros:
1- The sound is decent but compared to other Wireless Earbuds that I have tried, these are pretty average.
2- The case is rechargeable via the included 18650 battery. This allows you to have extra 18650 batteries on hand which is an interesting feature.
3- It comes with extra ear tips.
4- It comes with a mini USB cable and even a USB type A to Mini USB adapter.
5- Aesthetically the earbuds look nice, feel comfortable and don’t protrude much when wearing them.
6- They stay in place quite well and do not randomly fall out.
7- Earbuds are held in place magnetically when in the case charging.
8- They pair up real fast and very easy. I have had no issues at all with pairing.

Cons:
1- I ordered these based on the description stating “active noise reduction is also a standout feature of TruSound ear buds, ensuring a distraction-free audio experience”. I took this as they had ANC or Active Noise Control. This is not the case. These “isolate” the outside sounds via the ear tip inserted into the ear canal. If you get the right tip fit, they do “isolate” the outside sounds but just not as expected.
2- No USB type C. In my opinion all new devices should have USB C charging.
3- The case is a bit bulky due to the fact that it uses the 18650 battery.
4- The case is plastic and uses two plastic tabs to snap the lid closed. The design makes it really hard to open the case once it’s snapped shut. I am worried that I will break the plastic tabs at which point I would need to use a rubber band to keep the lid closed.
5- The Stand-By time is not the greatest. I fully charged the 18650 battery with my own charger when I first got the Earbuds. I used the Earbuds briefly while initially testing them and when I went back a couple of weeks later to try them again, the battery was already dead. I have other earbuds that have this same issue. I should be able to fully charge my earbuds, keep them in my backpack for a few weeks and have them ready to go when I want to use them.
6- No IPX rating? Pretty much all of the newer Earbuds these days have some kind of waterproof rating. It’s not advertised so I am not really sure if they are.
7- No Bluetooth 5.0? These have Bluetooth 4.2+EDR which isn’t bad, but there are sync issues when watching YouTube, Netflix ect. It’s not bad, but it’s noticeable and I could not use these to watch videos for too long.

Overall these TruSound Earbuds are average, and I feel that compared to the flooded market of True Wireless Earbuds these are a bit overpriced. With that said, I do like these but, I do feel there could be some improvements made that would ultimately increase the value.

title: Fours stars only for such a high price point
text: Okay, I'm not saying these are bad at all - I tested these against two other "smart" earbud sets by name brand makers.  All have apps that you can go onto and change the equalizer and turn the anc on/off and a few other things.  These Devialet Gemini feel good in my ears after I changed out the pads to the XS size.  I have that problem with pretty much every pair I've every owned/tried - guess I have very narrow ear canals and I believe that is the biggest reason the "stem" style of earbuds just do NOT work in my ears at all.  Anyway, getting these set up with their app was easy enough and I still have fun messing with the equalizer when listening to different songs/artists, but the main reason to wear these is the listening experience so I did my test with these and my other two pairs by trying different music:  classical with Mozart, Beethoven and Vivaldi, hard rock with AC/DC, Quiet Riot and Metallica, traditional country with Patsy Cline, Marty Robbins and Hank Williams and last, some alternative music that I love, Tangerine Dream, Patrick O'Hearn and Vangelis.  These Gemini earbuds performed well with all kinds of music, but the question is, did they perform so much better than the other two name-brand earbuds that were around half the price?  No, in all good conscious, I can't say they were that much better - more like just on a par with the other two pairs.  That does not mean they are bad.  The sound they produce is high-quality for sure, but in my own opinion, the price point is far too high.  Bring them down to be comparable to some of the other high-end name brand earbuds and I'd be happy with the cost and how they sound.  Other than the price, I can't fault these earbuds in any way.

Tina's New Stars Scale: 3 = as expected. 4 = better than expected. 5 = much better than expected. Conversely: 1 = much worse than expected. 2 = worse than expected. This New Stars Scale thus allows a negative rating as some have complained that they "Can't give negative 5 stars." Well now you can as 1 and 2 are in effect negative ratings, being lower than 3 which is essentially "OK. It works as expected, no better, no worse."

Well this mouse gets a New Stars Scale rating of only 2 because there is no way by glancing at it to tell if it is on or off. Rather one has to either 1) wiggle the mouse and see on the computer screen - if it is up and running - what the cursor does, or even if it is there or 2) pick up the mouse and look at the tiny black on/off switch on the bottom. Whereas my Amazon Basics mouse has a red jewel on top that lights up when it is on. Good idea! And it has a solid feel and better click. It is better then expected (or normal) so it gets a 4.

title: Decent dashcam for the price, a pain to configure, not the image quality I expected
text:
For the price this is hard to beat. It has lots of great features, including a Wifi app, but resolution/quality even on the highest settings are slightly disappointing. I have everything configured to provide the sharpest possible image (highest resolution and bit rate, etc.), and if a car is more than 30' away, zooming in on a screenshot of a license plate is iffy at best, even if the footage was taken in bright daylight (screencaps taken in VLC). Something seems off to me. Yes, I removed the protective films, and yes, my window is reasonably clean (normal conditions). I have attached two photos: one of the unit in a fantastic little case I found for it (see below), and a screencap showing the problem I described. The van in front of me is semi-readable, and was about 25 feet away. The car 15-20 feet further away on the left is unreadable, as is the plate close to me on the left. And yes, I have the CPL filter installed on the lens.

Configuring this was a bit of a hassle. The Wi-Fi app is not intuitive, and some quick googling led me to discover you have to temporarily disable your cellular data the first time you use it to get the camera to connect. Once configured, the camera itself acts as the network your phone connects to. This means your phone cannot be connected to any other Wi-Fi network while you are connected to the camera. I have no idea why they don't just allow you to use Bluetooth for this--it would be simpler to set up, that's for sure. Honestly, having integrated security video will be a factor in the next car I purchase. This is all way too much work.

Many PCs will not play the default file format this records in as they lack the correct video codec (H.265) or enough processing power. I think there must be a way to change the format it records in, but I was unable to find the configuration setting to change in either the app or the camera itself. To get this to play files on your PC, I suggest using VLC Player. It is free, and if you are running the latest version (check for updates in the application), it will run them just fine if your PC has the juice for HD at this level. If you experience dropped frames or choppy video when playing back on your computer, this is probably because your computer is not equipped with a GPU to support this high resolution of video (many aren't; if you don't have a dedicated video card in your PC, you may experience this). My office desktop does not have a dedicated video card and the video is a bit choppy if other things are running--expected.

If you are interested, the case is the "Mchoi Hard EVA Travel Case for Garmin inReach Mini GPS", (ASIN: B08F9QV1BQ), which is very sturdy and cost me $13.49 in Feb 2021. I looked for EVER for a case for this, and this was the best fit I found.

title: Works pretty well on a 3rd generation Flip Ultra HD
text:
This does a good job without vignetting. You get a much wider field of view with a Flip, and the lenses are pretty good quality.

The lens comes with peel-and-stick metal rings that you attach to the camera. The lens then sticks magnetically to the metal ring. It doesn't stick all that firmly -- you could shake the lens off if you're shooting video while running or something. But for most uses it sticks well enough.

I was concerned the mount would not work on a 3rd generation Flip Ultra HD because the ring around the lens on the Flip is tapered, and the metal mounting rings that come with the lens are flat and won't bend to shape. (It comes with two mounting rings, not three as shown in the picture.) I followed the instructions and allowed the ring to sit for fifteen minutes after applying it so the adhesive could set, and the adhesive turned out to be aggressive enough to hold the ring to the Flip. If it loosens later I may reinforce it with some CA glue.

You actually get two lenses that screw together. When you unscrew and remove the wide angle outer lens, the inner one functions as a fixed-length macro that focuses well at around 2 to 4 inches from the subject.

It also comes with a pouch (not a lanyard) and a couple of lens caps that fit rather loosely.

For the price, it's a good buy and really adds some versatility to a Flip Ultra HD. A better fitting mounting ring would be nice, but that might require machining and that might run the price up. It still works well, it's priced reasonably, and I think that makes it a good deal.

title: Not quite as flexible as advertised
text:
So... based on the product description, one can assume that any laptop that runs about 13"-14" should fit neatly into this sleeve. Well, not so much, really. When it arrives you'll see that the tag clearly states that it is for the Macbook Pro/Air 13. Nothing else. No Inspirons, no Yogas, and really not my Alienware 13. Oh, I can squeeze it into the sleeve if I work at it, and if I take the plastic insert out, but it's a lot like trying to fit into your skinny jeans after a weekend of Netflix and ice cream. You can do it, but it's not going to be pretty. And unfortunately getting my laptop back out of the sleeve was even harder. I checked the seams after two insertions and removals, and while they look fine now, I fear that repeated use might be hard on them.

So does it protect my laptop? Well, yes and no. It's in there pretty tightly, so the protective layer is stretched thin. And the end sticks out. I simply can't get it all the way into the sleeve. There's maybe a quarter to half an inch that protrudes. Now if I was tossing this into a briefcase or backpack, I wouldn't worry, but as it is, it's still vulnerable to being dropped along that edge or to being rained on or spilled on.

So overall what I would tell you is this: If you don't have a Macbook Pro/Air 13, then compare the measurements of your laptop to those of that model. If you're not close, look elsewhere.

title: Nice managed switch with basic PoE and without any cloud hassles
text:
While this is a PoE switch, don't get your hopes up. Being fanless, it rocks a modest 55w power budget, but it's still nice to have for a device or two. That's really a bonus on top of a rather capable switch at a ffair price, and best yet, there's no cloud features or subscriptions.

There a lot to take in if you've come from unmanaged switches or basic routers, but it's all quite familiar if you've used another managed switch. I used the web UI for all configurations, and it's quite similar to Linksys switches and not too far removed from my older Netgear managed switch. I was able to create LAGs, join VLANs, and join a spanning tree easily enough. I tend to connect my switches with a LAG and then go with single ports for these small 8 port switches, and I did that here. It connected to a master 26 port switch and was a peer to another 8 port switch and a 2 26 port switches. The rest are all currently Linksys switches (post Cisco breakup). All play nice.

Even if you don't need to do any managed switch functions, you still get a solid metal build, fast switching performance, and better overall support than lower end solutions. title: New improved design for the 504PLong
text:
The 504PLong plate that arrived is a genuine Manfrotto in Manfrotto packaging. It came with a newly designed plate that does not have the brass anti-rotation pin as before. This is fine by me. The permanently installed brass pin was mostly in the way. I like this new design.

What you get with the plate is a little ziplock bag with two 1/4-20 screws, two 3/8-16 screws, a rubber plug that stops the screws from falling out of the plate after they're installed and two black plastic anti-rotation pins. See the pictures. If you want to use them, press them into a newly-designed hole where they snap in and hold securely.

None of my cameras except perhaps my Canon camcorder even have the anti-rotation socket, so I prefer not to have them permanently installed like the original plate. They just get in the way. Now, if I want them, I can install them, which I won't.

I give the plate four stars because Manfrotto cannot standardize on a single plate design. They drive me crazy. This 504PLong plate works on my 504HD head and my [[ASIN:B006TZE0UQ Manfrotto 502 Video Head MVH502AH]], but is just different enough that it doesn't fit the [[ASIN:B00009XV3M Manfrotto 3433PL 577 Rapid Connect Adapter with Sliding Mounting Plate]] and Manfrotto does not make a QR adapter that does take the 504PLong plate. What gives, Manfrotto? Why do you have so many different plates for very similar applications?

Secondly, there is no part number on any of their plates, so if you have several from different Manfrotto devices, you better label them or you will get them all mixed up.

Otherwise, it's a good plate.

title: An amazing camera that DSLR owners and first timers can both use.
text:
I've been shooting with a SLR for years. First with a 35mm film SLR and then with a DSLR. I generally find point and shoots overly simple and can't match the ability of SLRs to capture great shots.

The Fuji FinePix, however, does an amazing job in bridging the gap between a DSLR and a all in one.

First, let me say this is a fairly large camera. It looks very much like an SLR and handles like one. For its size, though, it is very light. It is comfortable in the hand, and the build quality is very nice. The only part of the camera that feels a little flimsy is the battery door.

The controls feel secure and well thought out. Perhaps for people used to digital zooms on smaller cameras, who may accidentally shut off the camera when intending to zoom, as the on and off switch is in a place common to zoom controls on lower end cameras.

There is a large LCD screen for viewing your shot, and reviewing your images and movies. For SLR users like me, who perfer to use a eyepiece, you can use that by shutting off the LCD screen. The only drawback to that is, unlike a SLR where you are actually looking through the lens, the eyepiece is, instead a small camera so image quality through that option is a little less than I would have liked.

The lens has focal lengths of 24 to 1,000. I need to have two lenses for my DSLR to match that, and this has it in an all enclosed package. For people not familiar with focal lengths that amounts to a 42X manual zoom. Manual zoom is important to take quality long distance shots as it doesn't diminish quality of the shot the way that digital zooms do. As a digital zoom is basically just a software thing that cuts and resizes the image as you zoom. There is an optional digital zoom, but I don't suggest that.

The camera has a wealth of options that would make for an overly long review to go over here. I will say that there are options for the serious and expert photographer. You can choose manual mode; you choose aperture and shutter speed. There is a shutter priority where you choose the shutter speed and the camera chooses the aperture, and aperture priority where you choose the aperture and the camera compensates and chooses the shutter speed.

There is also an purely automatic mode for quick point and shooting, as well as pre-programmed advanced modes as well as the EXR option which can pre-set options for tilt shift, low light, depth of perception, and on. You name it, between the EXR option and the Advanced presets, the camera can compensate for you.

You can choose ISO speeds from 100-3200. You can also set it to automatically adjust the ISO with a maximum setting you prefer, so if you want a maximum ISO of 800, but want to also shoot outdoors without changing settings the camera will do that for you and perhaps change to 200 or 400 as needed.

Picture quality is wonderful. The camera shoots and automatically focuses quickly. Boot time for the camera is also on par with high end DSLRs. From the time you turn on the camera until you can shoot is very fast. No missing shots here.

Video quality is very good, as long as you have a fast SD card. I would suggest a class 10 at lest. The camera has a mini HDMI output so you can view your images and movies on your television.

To connect to your computer you unfortunately have to use their proprietary USB cord, which is included. It would have been nice to use standard MICRO USB.

This is a great camera. Good for seasoned shooters, newbies, and everywhere in between. Well constructed, and easy to learn. I will probably be finding myself using this camera more and more, and using my CANON DSLR less and less.

I have found, read, and enjoyed books I normally would not have tried because of the ability to sample a fair amount of text before purchasing them. I am reading more e-books than I did paper books.

Cons: It is frustrating not to be able to share a good book with a friend. I am spending much more money on e-books than I spent on paper books because I am buying/reading more.

text:
Maybe it's just the set I received, but on a few levels I can advise against these. For starters, the price.
I do not feel these are worth what they're charging. Although the filters look nice with the colorful trim, etc, that's about as far as I'd go with them. The case is okay. It's plastic and has a snap style latch to keep it closed. However, the filters just sit in foam. When I received mine and pulled them out of the box, all of the filters were out of their foam slots and just floating around in the case. After pushing them back into their foam spots, they seemed to hold in place. There's a lot more case than needed for the 6 filters so if you're trying to consolidate space, you may want to put them in something else.

The huge issue I have with all of them is how loose they fit the Mini 3 camera. Each one of mine can practically fall off. I'd understand if maybe one of them was super loose, but for all of them to behave the same it seems like a design flaw to me. I've used other brand filters that hold in place equal to that of the stock attachment but I'm afraid these are going to fall off too easily. Maybe not necessarily in flight since it's on a gimbal that accounts for turbulent air but I almost guarantee they'll fall off when fiddling around with the drone in your hands. A suggestion to the manufacturer would be to create a little more tension where they lock onto the camera like DJI and other brand filters do to prevent them from spinning back the very slight distance it takes for them to come off.

We recently upgraded our 10/100 Mbps wired network to 100/1000 Mbps and that was a impressive upgrade but we kind of expected a gigabit network to be really fast. We have wanted to put an XBMC media center nettop in our bedroom (similar to the one we run in the living room) but the bedroom is in an awkward location upstairs at the back of the house. We tried to stream movies and music over our wireless network but it was just not fast enough to stream HD MKV/MP4 files or blue ray rips. The thought of running cat5e cable all the way up there was not an enticing proposition to us.

However, after having upgraded to the Netgear N600 router there are no problems what so ever streaming HD content up there!

The router itself does what its supposed to and the speeds alone make me a very satisfied customer! a bit expensive but an awesome investment none-the-less.
