title: Decent Slider, but Room for Improvement
text:
I am primarily a stills shooter. That said, I do have an excellent camera that is very capable of shooting video and I do need it for such on occasion. I was interested in this camera slider as a way to get smooth shots and to reduce reliance on lens-based stabilization which is not included in my camera body. This has been a learning experience and while I like this slider there is definitely room for improvement.

I will start with the basics. This is a large and fairly heavy animal, which is to be expected. It is roughly 3' long and in it’s most basic configuration rests on a flat surface with no issues. It does have some adjustments that can be made to the individual feet on the frame so it can be adjusted slightly for uneven but mostly level surfaces without using any other equipment. To get much more versatility out of it, though, it can be mounted on tripods on either end to raise it higher or to set up angular shots.

The motor on the frame is controlled by a remote which comes with a battery pack. The remote is not wireless and has to be connected to the motor via the provided cabling. This is all right, but wireless functionality would make it much more versatile. It should be noted that the remote controls the slider, not the camera. I had some concern about this in the very beginning, thinking that the remote would be incompatible with my camera and that this unit would not work for me.

I encountered some issues that bother me. First, when powered on and running the motor runs the slider down the track until it is either stopped or a stop point is set. If one is not set, it bumps into the end and keeps trying to go beyond, making an awful noise that will surely mess up any video that requires sound. In my mind, the motor should detect when it hits the end and stop, even if start and stop points are not set.

When the motor is running and it is not near a stop point, it runs at constant speed and it is very smooth. When manually paused, it stops quickly but it doesn’t jerk to an abrupt stop like it hit something. But, if one of the end points are set and is reached, the motor slows down, then jerks to a stop, enough to notice in video footage. This is most obvious when the remote is set up to film in a loop as the issue can be observed repeatedly.

The motor is not silent, though it is quiet. It is not loud enough to ruin a shot unless absolute quiet is needed, and the motor produces a low-volume, low-frequency hum that slightly resembles the sound of an electric trolling motor on a bass boat, but quieter. The point is that it is by no means silent, but it should be good enough in the majority of cases. This is out the window if the motor is allowed to reach the end of the track before it is stopped, in which case the noise is likely to be a serious issue.

This is a decent slider and if used with some thought will serve nicely. There are definitely some places where it could be improved, particularly in the way it fails to handle reaching the end of tracks.

title: Nice feel - easily integrated with my windows 10 system and software
text:
I had been looking at these types of drawing tablets and wanted to give this one a try. I'm not a professional, and I know that things like "lag" are sometimes a concern, but I personally didnt find excessive lag (not that I could notice, anyway). In fact, I found this to be very impressive in that regard for this price.

Installation was a breeze, simply download the apps and away you go. (I'm using a windows 10 system). I was able to immediately use the Penwalker thing on my main screen with nothing open (scribbling notes right across my screen, etc). Then I pulled open photos hoping and tried some simple scribbling- that's when I noticed that the touch sensitive nature of this system is really effective - pressure effects line weight, etc. The pens are lightweight, yet the pressure sensitivity gives them a certain "feel". I think I could get used to this.

Then I opened Clip Studio Paint Pro and just doodled for a moment. Alternating between brushes, fades, erasers, etc. Again, the "feel" is what impressed me most (in spite of the lightweight pens). There's function buttons identified right on the tablet, (everything appears to work as it should), and when you bring the pens tip within an inch or so of the tablets screen, you can use to pen like a mouse to position the cursor- then touch the screen to do your work. Same with the eraser end - turn the pen around and point the eraser end to the screen and position your cursor with it - then touch down to erase.

As an amateur, I've barely scratched the surface of this tablets capabilities, but I can already tell that it's going to be fun learning some new skills as I spend more time with this. For me, this one's a winner!

title: fine performance for a budget-priced SSD

Modern computers are a lot more reliable than computers from 10 or 20 years ago. Computers are not getting a lot faster every year like they used to. I no longer replace my computer every couple of years. If your computer is getting a little sluggish, instead of replacing the whole thing, you can usually give it a huge performance boost by upgrading just key components. In particular, upgrade your memory and upgrade your hard drive. This SSD does not add a lot of capacity, but it gives you a lot of speed so that programs or databases that you use a lot will load much more quickly.

This drive installed and formatted easily on my Windows 10 desktop computer. It's been running flawlessly since then and the performance is great for me. Performance is great for general-purpose home or business use.

There are a lot of different SSDs on the market these days. Check your computer manufacturer's website to see what is compatible with your motherboard. This SSD has an entry-level design and a budget price to match. High-performance SSDs designed for hard-core gaming or video editing can be twice as fast but also cost twice as much or more for the same capacity.

title: Reasonably Priced Security Kit for Your Home - Wish It Had More Than One Window Alarm
text:
With crime rates going up in NYC, this is an ideal kit for anyone living in an apartment, especially if they're alone and elderly. It covers two areas most vulnerable to thieves: your window and the door, while the key chain is best for when you're coming home late at night on a dark, lonely street. Just pull the pin and the alarm screams.

Of the three items, I would say the window alarm rates highest in terms of usefulness. In fact, I wish this set came with three of them. We travel a lot, and the biggest fear we have is intruders breaking in through our high-rise window, as we have a fire escape near one of them.

The door stop is the least useful to me as a thief would have to break through one of our windows first before going through a door. My front door is already secured by locks and the other doors in our place generally remain open. I suppose we could reinforce the front door with the doorstop, but it seems like overkill. If you lived in a dorm and wanted a particular room to be off-limits, I suppose it would be useful in that case. This item reminds me of the alarm that would be set off if you used an emergency exit. As if in acknowledgement that this item won't be used as much as the others, no battery was supplied for it, unlike the others.

As for the key chain, this is one of those devices that will lay dormant for long periods (knock on wood). You'll have to remember to check and test the batteries occasionally because it will be rarely used.

Overall, for the price this set can't be beat. It feels more like a "sampler" pack, though, as it has only one of each product when multiples of each one would have been more helpful.

title: works great with my Google Pixel 2 Android phone and Open Camera video recorder
text:
This microphone has a lot of options, so figuring out what modes worked best (or at all) with my smartphone took a while. I have a Google Pixel 2 Android smartphone, which is not well documented in the product literature. If you have an iPhone, you may find that setup is somewhat easier.

Here are the basic steps that I had to take to get this working with my Google Pixel 2 phone:
1. Charge the receiver unit using the included mini-USB cable (not the micro-USB cable). I am disappointed that they are still using mini-USB which is obsolete these days. Why aren't they using USB-C for charging, which is the international standard these days?
2. The receiver unit has built-in clamps to attach to a smartphone. You can also mount it to SLR camera's flash shoe or a tripod.
3. Install 2 AA batteries in the microphone.
4. Turn both the microphone and receiver unit on.
5. The microphone is pre-paired with the receiver. If you want to pair a second microphone (not included), you can do that at this point.
6. Use the screwdriver inside the microphone to set the gain level (so that the light on the receiver unit doesn't flash red for the highest volumes that you plan to use with the microphone). I set mine to about 75% of maximum.
7. Connect the receiver unit to the phone using the included micro-USB to USB-C cable (my phone has a USB-C port, but no 1/8 inch audio port).
8. The default Google Pixel camera app unfortunately does not support external microphones. I installed the "Open Camera" app which has a setting to use an external microphone. This is a very popular and powerful 3rd party apps. I'm sure there are others that will also work.
9. Start the camera and now you have a video camera with a wireless microphone. Range and sound quality are pretty good as long as I stay in the same room (and you generally will want the microphone and camera to be in the same room when recording).
10. I set the output volume in the Samson receiver unit to 4/5 since higher volumes were distorting. You have to experiment with this for the types of sounds you are recording.
11. Unfortunately, I could not find an audio-only recorder app that supported the USB-C digital signal coming from the Samson receiver unit. I can use the analog audio signal with the 1/8 inch audio cable connected to the Google Pixel audio dongle that came with the phone. I presume this is a problem with the audio recorder apps, not with Samson hardware.

I've only played the audio and video back on my phone and it sounds fine. If you're recording professional-quality music videos, you may want something better than this.

I'm generally pleased with this microphone. Some negatives: the microphone is big and heavy and the mostly plastic construction looks and feels a lot cheaper than it costs. The product has lots of different parts and no carrying case to store them in, except for the original and not durable retail package. I could not find any way to determine the remaining battery level of either the microphone of the receiver unit, so your batteries could easily die in the middle of a recording session. Replacing the microphone batteries is easy since they are AA, but charging the receiver unit is very slow. I have not compared the audio quality of the large microphone with the lavalier microphone, but the latter is a lot smaller and less bulky and may be a better choice for people recording voices and not music.

text:
There's not much to say about the strap as a strap. I mean, it's perfectly nice, and the fabric has a nice slippery silky feel to it, and it's easy to adjust. That's all great but there are lots (and lots and lots) of straps in this world.

The thing that makes it awesome is the "clip" technology. I cannot overstate how much I love how easy it is to unclip and reclip the strap to the camera. Here's the Holy Grail that's long eluded me: I like shoulder-held camera bags (like, over-the-head to the right shoulder with the bag hanging on my left). It's the way I've carried a bag for decades. But carrying a camera on a strap — especially a side-hanging strap as I've been doing for a few years now — is a pain. What I'd really like is to have the camera strap on my neck first, then a jacket (if it's cold, and then the bag on over that (with the camera and bag on opposite sides of me). However with a conventional strap that doesn't work; the camera strap ends up trapped by the bag strap, and the whole arrangement doesn't work.

With this thing, I put on the camera, put on the jacket or hoodie (although I've decided that hoodies and bag straps were never meant to be worn at the same time), and then put on the bag. Then, ~*click*~ ! I unclick one of the camera attachments, flip the strap to the outside of the bag strap, and reclip. It takes like 2 seconds once you've done it a couple times. Yaay! Bag is happy, camera is happy, I'm warm, and all is right with the world.

I need to investigate other products from these smarty people but I can only take so much awesome in a given amount of time.

title: Excellent Quality Camera at a GREAT Price
text:
I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

If you are new to home security camera systems, I recommend going with wired (non-WiFi), NVR or computer based recorders run with systems such as Blue Iris. This type of system is infinitely more secure and stable. While initial setup costs are a bit more the security it affords is worth every penny. It always pays to research the products, discuss them with those in the field, understand vulnerabilities and PLAN YOUR SYSTEM PRIOR TO PURCHASING ANYTHING. If you are at all tech savvy at all you can do it. While there is a bit of a learning curve it is not awful and in the end you will be thankful for the time you spent in the beginning as it will save you time, money and endless frustration.

I have set up, tested and reviewed more security systems and individual products than I can possibly remember. Without question my go to solution for home security solutions is a computer based, Blue Iris system with PoE cameras run off of quality PoE switches. This type of system is not only easy to operate but is highly secure.

While this camera is not natively a PoE camera I’m happy to share the 5 Pairs Passive PoE Injector and PoE Splitter Kit with 5.5x2.1 mm DC Connector RJ45 Power Over Ethernet by Exgoofit ( https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07F82YK6P/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o03_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1 ) allow for this camera to operate almost identical to a PoE camera. The power adapter must be plugged in where the Ethernet cable is plugged in with the first pigtail adapter while the second adapter plugs onto the cameras power port and Ethernet jack. By utilizing this you can avoid the security concerns associated with WiFi cameras and still only have minimal wires run to the camera.

As with any component there are a host of factors to consider. In terms of cameras more megapixels is not always better. For instance 2MP cameras often perform better in low light while 5MP will allow for more detail when lighting is good. One disadvantage of higher megapixel cameras is the recordings will take up more hard drive space. Depending on the number of cameras, this can become a larger concern.

Highlights of this camera include:

Awesome Pan Tilt Zoom - Utilizing a 110° wide-angle lens and the head rotating 330° horizontally and 90° vertically, a 360° view is easily obtained. This makes this camera an outstanding choice to be placed on a corner of an eave where it can constantly monitor the largest possible area.

Jide Tech lens 5MP - in my tests over the last couple of months I have been impressed with the performance of this lens coupled with the CMOS image sensor SONY IMX335 and the HiS3516 chipset. Obviously this will not allow for the zoom capabilities of a varifocal lens but in comparison to many other cameras in the marketplace the performance of this camera is very good.

Low Light Capability - Images are excellent at even low light, far better than most similar cameras in this price range. IR lighting is dependable and nighttime / low light images are better than expected. My tests showed accurate images within 25’ of the IR lighting.

ONVIF compatibility - critical for using with software such as Blue Iris. Interestingly, I noticed another reviewer mentioned this camera did not work with Blue Iris, that was absolutely not my experience. I have only used it with Blue Iris and it has worked flawlessly. I have set it up with advanced features such as Watchdog and utilized multiple detection zones.

2 Way Audio - I have had no issues utilizing the 2 way audio through Blue Iris - sound is accurate, clear and minimal lag.

Great build quality - this camera is well built and will hold up outside in all conditions

I’d like to thank Joanna who works support at YoLuke who did her best to always provide the highest level of customer service as I researched this camera and worked on this review. Knowing there is a quality customer service team behind the scenes of security camera products is always important and in my experience, I feel that has been the case.

Over the course of my testing this product for a couple of months I’ve been thoroughly impressed. It loads into Blue Iris without any issue and advanced features work without any problems. By using the PoE splitter kit I referenced above you can easily make this a secure camera by avoiding the use of WiFi. Build quality is excellent - this is made to last and hold up even in severe conditions.

This is a product I would definitely recommend. While this is the first YoLuke camera I have reviewed I look forward to seeing other cameras they create. All indications point to this being a manufacturer that makes high quality security cameras that are dependable and made to last.

title: So-so. Getting better.
text:
This is a bit of a strange duck. I was initially very unsatisfied with this monitor, but it is going better.

When turning it on there is a flicker that looks like a collapsing power supply. I though the thing will bite the dust soon. However, it did not and the flicker reliably disappears, always. Using it for 18 months now. Pressing thumbs it doesn't die.

Some idiot decided that the DisplayPort input is configured for DP 1.1 by default, and you need to go into the OSD to change it to DP 1.2. If you do not do that then you are limited to 30 Hz. WTF? HDMI is always limited to 30 Hz, BTW. There is an excellent review by a person name Adam Simmons out there that tells you all these things. Google it if you have or consider to have this monitor.

The default color temperature and other color-related settings are also so far off that even with a color calibration device I couldn't beat this thing into looking halfway natural, at least before reading Adam's findings (see above).

At the time when I bought this monitor was very cost-effective, and now that I found out that it can, in fact, do 60 Hz at full resolution we are getting along pretty well. The resolution is around 105 dpi, which means you don't have to change all the fonts in all your software when going 4k. That's good.

The menu is accessed via a single wiggle button on the back of the monitor. That is a total pain in a multi-monitor setup where you might not be able to reach around the right or the bottom of the monitor.

USB port looks pretty decent and is 3.0. Didn't use it, though. Good input options except that as mentioned there is only one input that supports 4k @ 60 Hz, and that only when using the OSD to switch to Displayport 1.2.

The stand is useless, no adjustments.

I live in a standard development with 50 feet or so between houses, and according to Sonos, there is too much wireless interference. Mind you, no neighbor's signal is strong enough to be useful to me (wifi analyzers show all nearby signals to be very weak, and there are not nearly as many neighboring signals than when I've lived in apartments or in more compact neighborhoods), but apparently few and far away wifi networks are too much for Sonos. I can't imagine how it would be in a much busier neighborhood or apt complex where neighbors' signals are much much much stronger and in greater numbers.

Either way, I am constantly having connection issues and Sonos customer support is constantly blaming other wifi signals. I thought the purpose of a private "Mesh network" was to operate separately from other wifi signals. I've also been told I can't use Sonos if I have a cordless phone (I have not had a land line in many years, but it's worth noting).

The system constantly disconnects and just stops playing, or half the units in my setup (5 total units) suddenly ungroup and don't see each other. Every month I have a 30 minute to 2 hour time of frustration trying to make things work again.

In addition, for the over 5 years I have had Sonos, there have been seemingly hundreds of required updates to the units' software. Updates for a 5 unit system are slow - often nearly 30 minutes in length (each unit downloads software and updates, one at a time). This is just embarrassing... People come over and I go to turn on music, and we have to sit there for a half an hour looking at a progress bar - not to mention a few recent updates have removed features I actually liked. If I were to have the money to start over with another system, I would start over with another system.

August 2015 update. With the newest software update that was forced upon me, dropouts and disappearing units are even more common. I even bought a new 5 Ghz router and turned off the 2.4 so there would be NO similar band interference, and that has not helped.

title: Wrong instructions and wobbly, but still fun to use.
text:
Before ordering this telescope, I researched the difference between reflector and refractor telescopes. The last telescope I had was a hand-me-down (I forget which brand) refractor telescopes. I've developed a strong passion for everything beyond earth, so I looked forward to using this telescope--my first reflector telescope.

Because the telescope requires assembly, I pulled out the instructions...and became very confused. While some of the parts looked similar to what was in the box, I quickly realized the instructions were for a completely different model. Even if these were the right instructions, the photographs provided were taken by a camera and not the clearest quality; good assembly instructions usually have computer-generated images or diagrams, not photographs taken by a camera. The rest of the instruction manual was a general guide on using telescopes, though a much better quick-start guide can be found easily online.

So, with some trial and error, and a lot more time than I anticipated building the telescope, I finally got it assembled. And just in time too, because the moon had just crossed the window of the room I build the telescope in, and the moon was in great view. The opportunity also let me play around with the features of the telescope. It's not very easy to use because the stand is *very* wobbly. The counterweights are too much for the tripod, and the tripod should have used a better, more sturdy material. The dials and weights are easy to use, but the tripod makes everything longer to set up because the view won't always stay while moving.

Despite all that, it's super fun to use. It comes with decent eyepieces to play around with; I didn't know how much of a difference eyepieces can make. With this telescope, I was able to view details of the moon for the first time. It really is just a big ball of rock spinning around.

title: Works Great in an MX ERGO
text:
I bought this replacement ball for my Logitech MX ERGO, which worked well for me before I accidentally dropped it and subsequently put a pock mark on the original ball. The ERGO still worked but would occasionally get stuck when the support pegs would catch the pock and cause the ball to resist - not enough to really hurt anything but just enough to make digital drawing difficult and just enough to annoy me. This replacement ball has taken care of that for me and has proven to be a worthwhile expense for me.

The ERGO and the M570 have the same size ball, so this ball can be used in either (I was using the ball from my old M570 in the ERGO while I waited for this ball to arrive). Replacement is a 30-second procedure and requires no special tools, though a pencil does make getting the old ball out a lot easier.

There are two different finish types available, glossy and matte. I chose the glossy in red. Operation has been absolutely smooth with no resistance at all and no catches. I haven’t noticed any operational differences between it and the original gray ball that came in my ERGO. And, in my opinion, the dark red of this ball actually looks a little nicer than the original silver ball as well as the blue M570 ball.

This wasn’t an expensive replacement and so far it has worked out very well for me. It has restored operation of my trackball to what it was before I damaged the original ball, which is really all I needed. Based on my experience with it, this is an easy replacement ball to recommend if you need to replace the ball in either a Logitech M570 or an MX ERGO.

text:
To be honest, I really like my x52 and plan to keep using it. However it could be so much better because of a few problems.

Problem #1, can't recalibrate. You'ld think some program that came with the 52 would be able to recalibrate the joystick, but no, it requires editing registry settings in regedit. Fine for a guy that knows computers but a bit advanced for others.

Problem #2, a lot of people are experiancing a huge dead-zone that is apparantly a hardware, not a software issue. Please read the forums at saitek for this issue at
saitekforum.com/showthread.php?t=6176

Problem #3, the mouse wheel does not work. See this thread at the saitek forums for more info.
saitekforum.com/showthread.php?t=6264

Possible problem #1, the stick is HUGE, and this size gets some getting used to. It feels like you have to throw the stick back and forth because it is so tall

Possible problem #2, the response curve for the joystick is different than for other joysticks. I've heard that the curve is linear instead of logarithmic. I don't know if this is true, but you have to adjust your in-game settings in order to get this stick to feel like others (In Pacific-Fighters, which is what I play, this means sliding all the sliders for the joystick responses way up). Furthermore, there is no Saitek utility to edit this response curve, if there isn't an in-game joystick response option page in your favorite game, you're stuck with what you're given here.

There are other problems posted by users at the Saitek forums, but I have not experianced them personally. My recomendation is to read through the forums and see if you can handle the risk involved in getting the stick.

My subjective conclusion: great idea and design, but it lacks quality assurance.

title: Yet another great Fuji prime
text:
I've owned a Fujifilm X100 (sold for X100s), X100s, X-E2, 18-55mm OIS, 35mm f/1.4, 56mm f/1.2, Zeiss 12mm f/2.8 and a couple flashes. I'm biased towards my positive experiences in the system and the "look" I get from the jpegs (which are amazing btw) and RAW. With that in mind ...

I love this lens. This and the 56mm were the two I most looked forward to. I do a lot of candid shots of people and more shots of my pets than I want to admit. I used to think the 56mm is the ultimate portrait lens, but in many ways this eclipses it (both have great merits).

For starters 90mm is a great portrait focal length. ~85mm-95mm is probably the most common one for DSLR users these days, and it's much more flattering than ~50mm. Cropping helps with some things, but good ole fashioned focal lengths help with conveying depth, or in this case slightly compressing it. 90mm will start to make features more subtle (the extreme opposite effect can be seen in ultra wides which can fill a frame with a nose), and most of us look better with subtle features. That model in a magazine or catalog was probably photoshopped, but pick up old magazines. They still looked great. Yeah there were some darkroom tricks, but it's not uncommon to see 135mm-300mm used in studios to compress features. Fuji didn't invent this effect, but it's one huge leg up this lens has on the already stellar 56mm f/1.2. 90mm generally is better than 56mm for portraits (1.5x focal length crops really don't matter here, but even if you think they do, 135mm is better than 85mm).

Onto this particular lens. It's really your only option for the X system outside of adapters and manually focusing with a lens from another system, but even if you could magically put a Nikon or Canon 85mm lens on with AF and everything, this lens has them beat. It's amazingly sharp edge to edge. You will get a noticeable bump in sharpness stopping down to 2.8, but honestly it's good to go wide open. Sharpness is just one aspect, and while easy to see/measure, it's probably less important than contrast (my opinion at least). This lens excels there as well. Pictures really shine with a very crisp clear yet flattering look. It's not quite up to the best Zeiss glass (sadly neither does the Zeiss glass available for the X system), but it's quite remarkable, and better than my Nikon primes.

It is heavy, but it handles surprisingly well on my X-E2. I'd prefer a X-T1 and a grip, but It's not too bad, nor do I worry about my strap lugs pulling out. The generously sized MF barrel (no surprise, as there's no need for a zoom) is well damped, but I'm not generally a fan of MF feel on the X system. The aperture ring is a nice step up from earlier ones on the 35mm f/1.4 that seemed to lose their place a bit too easily. In both cases, my old Nikon glass does still leave me wanting here (direct manual focus and an aperture lock), but that old glass has nothing on this. Autofocus isn't a strength here again, but it's no worse than other X system glass. Plenty for portraits. Not ideal for moving subjects (unless they are parallel to focal plane).

The rest is all good. Modest but generally low distortion, flare, and CA (distortion and CA should be fixed automatically), and ghosting is all but a non issue. Compared to the 56mm f/1.2, I'd say this is a better portrait lens, and it's a bit better all around (YMMV and sometimes 56mm fits the bill better than 90mm no matter the lens). The basis for this is the overall sharpness wide open (though stop down the 56mm to f/2 and it's comparable), more flattering focal length, and better close focusing. The 56mm f/1.2 has a greater minimum focal length. It's a real tour de force and statement with the f/1.2 max aperture, but this lens is a bit more practical. Then again, I enjoy owning both. Plus the same grads, polarizers, NDs, etc... work on both.

Do I recommend this lens? For some, absolutely. If you're already using the system and and you're comfortable using primes, it's highly recommended. I'm quite delighted!

title: This vendor (Selens) delivered what they promised -- a 59x78.7inches Pop Up Green/Blue Screen
text:
My order was delivered on time within 2 days. It is the correct material (thick woven material that I cannot see through, and slightly shiny), chromacolor green and blue color, and correct size. It was in its carrying case and the case was sealed in plastic. I knew other seller products were supposedly hard to fold back down and so I tried folding mine right away. It folded down for the most part easily (took me two tries to get the hang of it), but then it popped closed easily. It opens flat. There are a few small wrinkles that should shake themselves out if I hang up the screen, but I think they are fine to use the screen with anyway. And there are straps to hang the screen in portrait or landscape layout, which I like very much.

I really searched for a vendor I could trust. Some of the other sellers had customer reviews saying their screens were nylon and not muslin, had dark colors, wouldn't lay flat, and couldn't be closed. I didn't want to buy from any of those vendors and waited a long time for a seller who might deliver a product that matched their ad. I took a chance on this seller (Selens) even though they had no reviews mainly because they were so very accurate in listing the size of the screen as 59x78.7 inches. I thought that this was a seller who wanted to do a good job for their customer. Thank you for delivering what you promised, Selens.

One comment -- there is a small (oil?) stain/streak about 2 inches on the green side, but you can't see it when looking directly at the background so the manufacturer probably didn't see it. But if you look at the screen from a high angle it is noticeable. I'll have to shoot some video/photos to see if it is a problem. I don't think it will be. I didn't see it on the blue side which is darker, but I just glanced. I'll look to see if it is on both sides later. Again, I don't think there is a problem as on the green side you can't see it if looking directly at the screen. But otherwise I liked what was delivered so far. :-)

title: A little noisy and not exactly a micro-sized projector, but versatile and a cheap way to get a big screen
text:
I received this as a free review sample. I subtracted a star because in small quarters the fan can get irritating, and also the picture area is a little skewed. The latter is not enough to ruin a video, but combined with the fan noise I felt that this falls into the four star category. To be fair, this is about on par with other portable projectors in this price range and sharing the general form factor.

On the plus side, this is an inexpensive way to get a large screen TV (assuming that your wall is the screen), that does a credible job of projecting movies, TV and presentations. I tested it using a Chromecast and streaming video from YouTube to my phone, then casting from my phone to the Chromecast dongle connected to one of the HDMI ports in the rear. No issues and it was actually a treat. I also tested it with an old Roku in an HDMI port streaming a movie from Netflix. To be sure, neither experience compares to my HD TV screen and surround sound system, but this does not come close to the price tags of those. Bang for the buck this is excellent if you are in a budget.

Frankly, I did not test the other ports, but do want to point out that the 'SD' card port is really USB A that will take a flash drive or an SD card using an adapter. Actually, I think that is a plus as well because flash drives are cheap and a 32GB one can hold a respectable amount of movies, home videos or presentations.

Sound quality is not spectacular, but is definitely adequate. Overall, this is as good as any projector among the four that I have either owned or tested, and is better than some. It would easily be a five star projector if it had a quieter fan. If you can live with that you will probably love it.

title: Fine Black Diffusion Filter
text:
I have worked with K&F Concept filters in the past and generally had good experiences with them. They're good, mid-range quality filters at (usually) a budget price. I haven't worked with any black diffusion filters prior to this one so I have no basis against which to compare, but so far it seems to work as designed and seems to be made very well.

In a nutshell, this type of filter softens light a bit, causing some gentle halos around light sources, without impacting image sharpness or detail. Where I have seen the most noticeable impact is in images where there otherwise would be a lot of shadows and contrast; instead of stark contrast and strong shadows, the filter has the effect of brightening up the shadows somewhat and creating smoother color gradients. Sure, this can be done in software after the fact, but it is a lot easier to do this at the time the image is taken and it certainly is a lot less work.

The filter is very easy to install. This is my first magnetic filter and it is as easy to attach to my camera as I could have hoped. The threaded ring attaches to the lens in the same manner as a step ring or another filter, and the filter itself just snaps securely into place due to the magnetics. Removing the filter is just as simple, especially if you choose to leave the magnetic ring in place on the lens.

The assembly seems to be well made. I have had filters in the past that have been poorly constructed and rattle in the frames when shaken, or have been mildly blemished, or just felt cheap. This filter has none of those issues and appears to be well made.

This is a nice black diffusion filter. It's easy to install and use, and it just works. I will be using it more in the coming weeks.

I bought what ended up being a smaller version and returned it because it didn't fit my daily gear (13" Mac & cord, Nikon body with attached 18-55 lens, zoom, and a macro lens).

I received an email from the company suggesting this larger version, which fit beautifully and is equally as gorgeous.

The bag comes with a removable padded camera insert and four removable dividers. There are two slots--I can fit my laptop in one and files in the other. There's a zipper pouch on the side closest to the body which I'll use for my wallet and/or camera, and a buckled compartment that fits my cords, batteries, and SD cards.

The quality of the padding and leather are beautiful. I haven't used the bag a lot yet, but the hardware feels sturdy and the stitching is really nice .

I was hoping it would serve as a cross-body messenger, but it's a little stiff for that...more like a briefcase. So, it won't be the only bag I keep, but I will enjoy it as a great upscale grab-and-go bag at a quarter of the price of the name brand camera bag I was going to get.

The one adjustment I'll make is to punch a hole in the strap to make the strap fit me a little bit better, as I'm not that tall and I like the bag to fall higher on my hip, but I'm pretty handy and will do that myself. So far, I am very happy with this bag and the customer service.

I'll give it a 5 for beauty, fit, and customer service, and a 4.5 for the adjustments I'll make.

title: Fantastic
text:
Immediately, I realized I love these headphones. I'm not in love with the color, and I'm perplexed why companies always say something is for iPad, etc., although I suspect it is just the "cool" thing to do. I have no apple devices, but this worked immediately and perfectly for my Blackberry 9700, Xoom, and Win7 Laptop.

The first device pairs by itself, and devices 2-8 pair by holding 2 buttons for 5 seconds. After that, if multiple devices are turned on when you turn the headphones on, it seems to want to pick the first one you paired it with.

The BB picks it up as a Logitech Wireless Headset (not something generic), and you can then control the volume with the BB or with the headset itself (Did I mention the controls are all well positioned on the right headphone? - just two volume buttons, mic mute, micro USB charging port, and LED indicator), and you can also toggle between BB speaker phone and headset - they are obviously fully compatible - not generically. Pressing the mute button give you an audible cue, but does not change the BB display.

You'll never catch me in public with a normal bluetooth earpiece on anyway, so this is also great for calls at home - it will cancel out more background noise (because of the foam on both ears) so you can comfortably concentrate on your call. My tests show it working well more than the claimed 10m away (of course that partly depends on the other device's radio as well).

As another reviewer said, these sound good (and are capable of getting louder than I'll ever need), but are probably not as great as the full over-the-ear headsets. BUT, the wireless capability is really great to keep you fully uninhibited when exercising, cooking, or whatever you're doing when talking on the phone or listening to your music. For the record, I am 100% opposed to wireless shelf/tower speakers in a real home system, but this is a great solution for a headset.

Also, the mic backing out of the way is a must, so thankfully that is included. It not only pivots, but flexes toward or away from the mouth as well - very good design. Finally, the folding feature is great; any space saved is important. And the connecting wire connecting the two sides is accessible, if all that bending ever has it in need of a replacement.

Past helmet use has me thinking my skull is about as large as they come, and these are comfortable on me with the sides fully extended.

title: Very poor Bluetooth performance in otherwise very good product
text: Been in audio for 40 years, first as a performer, then in pro recording. Tried lots of gear, heard tons of hype, and know a great deal about audio. Bought this product as a means to listen to audio while exercising and operating a riding mower. Corded products are not optimal for either purpose, so Bluetooth was a key feature for me. This product comes from a well-known company, though its history is predominantly one of instrument and amplifier manufacture. PureSonic earbuds are not in the same class as in-ear monitors, but as earbuds' specs go they're pretty good. Good frequency response over the practical spectrum - as long as you keep the fit tight. Fairly lightweight. Ergonomically sound design both in the earbuds and the controls. Spent a few days trying these out and am very disappointed to report that their Bluetooth capability is extremely limited; it's not an over-statement to call it "hobbled." Using the same iPhone 7 Plus I can provide signals to eight other Bluetooth products out to 15+ feet with no problems. The PureSonic earbuds cut-out and fail at less than three feet. title: Review from a long-time Apple user
text:
3.5 stars

NOTE: This review is not meant to be one of those juvenile Mac vs PC things. Everyone has preferences, and people generally like to stick to what's familiar. I grew up with PC (the 90's through 2005) and have used Mac since then (2005). This review is mostly written for people who, like me, have been using a Mac for a while and are considering switching. Anyone taking it personally...well...that's a little silly and pretty sad. It's just a computer, not your identity.
And now, ladies and gents, the infinitely down-voted review as I wrote it:

The last time I owned a PC was in 2005, and while the transition took several months (getting used to differences, understanding the layout, etc.), I clearly chose Mac over PC. I never had the blue screen, everything was user-friendly, and the whole feel of using my computers was smooth and simple. Lately, I had been curious about PC again after some frustrations with Mac (pricing, difficulty in finding some types of software mostly). I gave this computer a try, and while I still need to give it more time to fairly assess it, I still prefer Mac.

The first thing I noticed was that it didn't come with Microsoft Office, which was very disappointing. I remembered always having that software with my new PC's pre-2005. I am not sure when they stopped offering this, but it was a key selling point. Macs come with their own software that is somewhat comparable, but Microsoft Office will always be my favorite, which means Microsoft has still been getting money from me all these years. My point here, however, is this: at least my Mac came with counterparts to Word, Excel, and Powerpoint with the computer. This one did not, which means you need to add about $200 to the price tag of this laptop.

Thankfully, this computer does come with some other very nice features, like a large, beautiful, touch-screen display that lets you interact with the software in several ways. It would probably make more sense to allow the keyboard to detach, however, because you are always at an awkward angle with your fingers if using it as a touch-screen, especially if you have longer fingernails. Likewise, it is very thin and lightweight! The days of PC being a clunky and awkward counterpart to Mac are over. This is a very sleek piece of technology!

The main issues as a Mac-user trying to get back into PC were these:
-Not very user-friendly in terms of finding things on the home screen with multiple tiles of applications. It feels cluttered. Very Cluttered. On the plus side, with some time, it is customizable.
-The track-pad/mouse pad is very awkward and cannot (as far as I could tell) be customized. It does not work intuitively at all, which means having to scroll and switch screens in a time-consuming and annoying fashion.
-I have to find anti-virus software. (Yes, I am aware Macs can also get viruses, but there are other protections that make it a little easier to avoid. Knock on wood...)
-It is not plug-and-play ready to work with my phone. I will have to do some research and post updates, but I am not sure how well it will work in terms of synchronizing music, calendars, etc.

I am sure this is an excellent laptop for those already using PC, but for a long-time Mac-user, the transition is a little rocky. I look forward to working out the kinks, however, so I can be fluent in both! This thing has potential, and I want to learn how to use it.

text:
I was extremely skeptical upon receiving this speaker because I mean after all, it is a tiger head with the speakers located in the eye sockets. Okay. Then I plugged in my Iphone 4 - and played Evanescense, Ennio Morricone, and John Barry. Totally blown away.

I have owned portable speakers by Logitech, JBL, and Ihome - all very good, some a little better. My biggest complaint with them was that they were too large to drag in and out of the house and just not portable enough for my needs. But since I wanted good sound, I'd put up with the inconvenience. Till now.

I know you won't believe me because I can't even believe it myself, but this little speaker packs quite a wallop in the sound department. No need to adjust knobs for bass and treble (there aren't any), because the balance is excellent. Put in 3 triple A batteries, adjust your smart phone to the highest volume setting, plug it in the already attached adapter cord, and flip the little switch at the bottom of the tiger's head. There is a sliding volume control on the side of the head which you can then proceed to raise or lower according to your needs. That's it. The sound is rich and deep without the tinny trebble or heavy bass you get from other models. It even sounds terrific when I switch to my Pandora app.

The only drawback is that there is no where to plug in an adaptor for charging my smart phone. But big deal - now I can use my more expensive, bigger speakers to do that. Cause this little guy can be held in one hand along with my Iphone and I can go from room to room playing my music and setting it down anywhere I want.

Please give this little guy or one of the other animal heads a try. You'll be as surprised and thrilled as I was to discover such a cool, useful and perfect little speaker buddy.

UPDATE (4/2/13):

I've been using this speaker every single day since I got it. The sound is still amazing for such a small, clever design and the batteries seem to last longer than I'd originally believed. In fact, I'm so happy with this item, I've decided to place an order for the Panda version so I can have one of each in different parts of my home. I will review the Panda once I receive it, but I'm pretty confident it will be just as terrific as the tiger's been.

title: IMPRESSIVE ROOM MONITORING CAMERA LAMP
text:
This new video camera lamp by Panasonic is really a quality product - outstanding camera, nice lamp, and great features seen in few other systems.

Set up was very easy requiring minimal effort - I just followed the enclosed directions and what the app said and breezed through putting it together and setting it up.

The HomeHawk App is easy to use and overall quite intuitive. I’ve had no problem figuring it out as I’ve worked my way around within it. Once you get into the more complex settings it takes going to multiple areas of the app which is unnecessary.

The lamp has many settings to choose from - the preset modes are Home, Away and Basic, each with different predetermined settings or you can create your own.

The camera holds up to a 256 GB microSDXC card (Class 10, or UHS Speed Class 1 or higher) so you won’t have to worry about monthly cloud storage fees. Once the card is full it will automatically write over the oldest data. It records both audio and video data and can be set to record in a multitude of ways.

The camera records at up to 1920 x 1080 pixels, 2.0 megapixel, and 140 degrees - providing an ultra clear image of the entire room. While the lens is discreet it is visible if anyone looks at the front of the lamp. This is certainly not a hidden camera.

The lamp has three different sensors that detect presence - it detects motion, sound and temperature. In my tests I found this system to be incredibly accurate at detecting when there was a presence in the room and recording.

The base of the lamp holds eight AA batteries that act as a backup power source in the case of a power outage and will power the lamp for 1 hour.

One thing to note, while the listing says that it provides color night vision - what really happens is when the lamp detects presence it turns the lamp on in order to record in color. True night vision - in the dark - is monochrome.

While the listing states that the device or app can be connected to Dropbox for free cloud based video storage I have yet to find where it’s possible to do that and the online guides do not refer to it.

As someone who has used, reviewed and written about SmartHome products for many years I can say this is a quality product. I can see a few areas where it can be improved on. While the LED lamp provides a nice ambient light source it would be far better if colored light could be selected to match other SmartHome lighting. More shielding should be in place to prevent interference from other electronics - I assume that is the cause of the issues other reviewers have experienced. The app can use a bit of work in order to make it more straightforward in regards to the settings.

This is an extremely high quality camera system built into a nice modern lamp. It has sleek lines and will compliment most any room’s decor. The lamp provides a very pleasant ambient light while also providing video and audio surveillance and security.

This is a product that I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend.

⭐️As with all Drew’s Reviews, if I discover something new about this product - good or bad - I will UPDATE my review. I believe in creating detailed, complete reviews because, like you, I depend on them when I am shopping. If you found my review HELPFUL - please click ⬇️ below!⭐️

title: Disapointed...Updated from 2 to 5 stars
text:
I bought this screen protector for my Kindle Touch earlier this year and love it. I just bought a Kindle Paperwhite and I had one left over from the first order. It fit perfectly, except the small gap ended up on the top and I did not realize that the line cut through the top of the menu until I turned it on to read. I'd rather have the gap at the bottom where it's not noticeable so I ordered another pack. I just got my order today and after two screens, I realized that they were too wide for the Paperwhite screen. I had to cut the last screen to get it to fit. I was bummed since it fit great before and I thought I'd get it perfect on the first try. I'm not completely happy with the final result but I don't want to pay for another pack not knowing which size I'm going to get. Also the edges used to be rounded and they aren't anymore so I can't get the edges to stick flat to the screen which makes the screen protector more noticeable, whereas on my Kindle Touch, I actually have to look carefully to see where the edges are. I just don't understand why these things changed. I don't know if I got a bad batch but if this is the size they are selling now, they shouldn't advertise that it fits the Paperwhite.
As far as applying, I give that four stars. I can normally get a bubble-free application. If anything goes wrong it's usually a speck of dust. I use compressed air and a credit card to get the best results. A credit card is more solid than the smoothing card it comes with so it works a lot better.

UPDATE 11/18/2012: The GreatShield company responded to my review and they sent me a replacement order right away. Awesome customer service from those guys. After getting my replacement, I can safely say that the order I had before was defective. The new order fit the screen perfectly and the edges are rounded. It is installed on my Kindle Paperwhite and I'm a happy customer. In light of this, I have changed my rating from 2 stars to 5 stars.

title: Beautiful sound quality and tons of features
text: I’m super impressed with these earbuds and I love everything about them. I’ve tried a lot of different pairs but none offered the combination of sound quality, comfort and features that I wanted. The Razer Hammerhead buds have it all so my search for the perfect pair has finally come to an end. They arrived in a nice box with plenty of ear tip options and useful instructions for setup.  I chose the Comply foam tips and wow are they nice. They take a few extra seconds to get situated but the difference is amazing.  The app is well designed and easy to navigate. There’s a fit test that is well worth your time. It helps you adjust the buds so you get the best sound. It’s amazing how much of a difference a little adjustment can make. You can change the equalizer and tap settings through the app and see how much battery life is left. I really like being able to customize them to my liking. This pair excels in its sound quality and options. I have a toddler at home so even though I’m often listing to something through the day, I still need to be able to hear what’s going on around me. I’ve tried other pairs with ambient noise but they just weren’t great and whatever I was listing to was usually washed out. That isn’t the case here. The ambient noise doesn’t overpower the podcast episode. The ANC is also superb. On the flip side of needing to hear my toddler is the times when my husband is home and I just want to enjoy some peace. When I turn on the ANC, all that noise around me just disappears and it’s heavenly. This is a feature that’s become pretty common with earbuds but none that I’ve tried do it as well as this pair. The sound quality is excellent. The default equalizer setting is THX, which sounds wonderful. The custom option lets you tweak it however you like. Gaming mode is perfect for games, obviously, but also for watching videos or movies. The low latency wipes out any lag. Battery life is great. I’ve used these for hours and the light just turned orange to indicate it was low. The only thing that isn’t great about this pair is the microphone. I tried a couple phone call with them and they didn’t go all that well. I could hear them perfectly but they had trouble hearing me. That’s not a deal breaker. I have a nice headset I prefer to use for calls but for someone that intends to use these as their sole pair it’s something to consider. Razer is a brand known for making excellent gaming accessories and I think these earbuds live up to that reputation. This pair offers a wonderful combination of quality and features that put them at the top of my favorites list.

title: Solid and Inexpensive All-Manual Lens
text:
This is my second TTartisan lens for my Fuji X-T3. I have been deeply impressed with my other lens, especially considering the price point, so I had high expectations for this one and it does not disappoint. It's a solid all-manual lens that performs well.

Right out of the box, I can't help but notice that this little lens has some serious heft to it. It's a very small and compact lens but it is made of metal and glass, not plastic, so the materials make it more hefty than expected. I like this; I have an expectation that if I fumble this lens it has some chance of surviving a moderate drop.

This is a fixed focal length lens with a fast F/2 aperture. It's an all manual lens that does not share data with the camera body, so if you are looking for a lens that autofocuses or sends exposure data to the camera, this is not the lens you want. If you like working with all manual lenses, or if you want to learn more about working with them, this is actually a good choice.

Exposures with this lens are dependent on the skill of the photographer, of course, but with the lens set properly exposures come out sharp, bright and with nice bokeh. There is a small bit of vignetting at the corners which is not completely unexpected, and in my case it is actually welcomes as I happen to like mild vignetting in many cases. At the widest aperture setting images are not quite as crisp and sharp as when this lens is stopped down a little, which isn't completely unexpected either. For me, F/2.8 works better, though my "default" setting is F/5.6 (true on all of my manual lenses).

The focus ring is tight and smooth and the aperture ring has a solid feel to it as well. It's an easy lens to work with and to "fine tune" when shooting.

The focal length makes this a very good choice for portraits.

I like this little lens and I will be working with it more in the coming weeks and months. For the price I have no complaints. It's not perfect, but it is better than the price suggests and it seems to be very well made.

This has literally at just three months has doubled the average lifespan of my USB cables. This device which is plugged in 24/7 (unless I need to charge my eReader) gets used numerous times a day, it just doesn't sit there. I'm extremely happy with the durability of this cable.

Update August 10th 2017 - I am amazed. No other cable has ever lasted as long as this Anker. I've had cables fail the same day, the same week and as I've mentioned it has developed a distinct bend from the way it hangs from my tablet, kept in the pocket of the grab bar on my bed, the cable shows almost imperceptible whitening just above the connector from strain but no cracks, splits or crumbling. title: The sound on these are first class - really great highs, mids, but ANC has slight hiss.
text:
I wanted to find a cheaper alternative to my wife's wireless Bose headset, something with decent noise cancelling for flights and work. So far I've used Bose, the MPOW H5, Treblab, and Woltix with ANC.

The sound on these are first class - really great highs, mids, and lows - tons of clarity (when active noise cancel is on...otherwise it sounds a bit muggy). Very comfortable and light. BUT - I got these because they are wireless with active noise cancellation, and although the ANC is effective, if you are in a quiet room you'll hear a slight hiss when the ANC is on - many people report the same thing in reviews, and it's true - you'll hear it. You won't notice this when music is on or during a flight. I often use these at coffee shops just to zone out and focus on work, and I could notice the slight hiss in quieter environments.

I've also used Bose, the MPOW H5, and Woltix with ANC. I didn't want to buy another Bose headset when my wife and I travel together. Nothing will compare to Bose noise cancellation, but the MPOW H5 and Woltix are actually really nice for the money. The MPOW H5 don't have as good audio clarity as the Treblab, but at the end of the day I got noise cancelling headphones for the noise canceling. I ended up returning the Treblab and the MPOW H5 and I kept the Woltix because they are more comfortable than the MPOW and had the best low-price ANC. The MPOW also had some sound interference issues randomly when the ANC was on.

So:

Bose: Best noise cancellation, good audio, comfortable, but definitely expensive!
Treblab: Best audio, worst noise cancellation (you can hear a slight hiss when turned on), comfortable, but large and they don't fold down too small.
MPOW: Good audio, good noise cancellation, but was getting some weird sound interference with the ANC on sometimes. Tight on ears.
Woltix: Good audio, good noise cancellation, most comfortable (way lighter and less tight on the ears than the MPOW), and fold down the smallest.

title: I am very pleased with this device
text: Let me start by saying I am just a layman so I can’t go into technical issues about this router, if there are any. But I can tell you, as an average person, I love this router. I am using this in lieu of the FIOS router they tried to force on me. it also replaces a pricier TP Link router that failed miserably after 2 weeks. I wanted to be able to cover as much of my house as possible and IF possible eliminate the WiFi extender. This router does that. When I had FIOS installed the line was put in my living room downstairs on the furthest away spot. Great for my entertainment area terrible for my upstairs office on the other side of the house. Which is why I needed an extender for my computer. Now my computer gets almost full signal strength and phenomenal speed. Since my computer only works on 2.4 band speed sucked. With this router I am very close to my 100/100 FIOS speed on the computer! Very happy. Another thing I’ve noticed: when i tried to play 4K content on my TV it constantly buffered. No more. I have been watching 4K with NO issues not even a stutter. Not only do I find the signal strong it is robust enough to handle all my devices (smart electric plugs, blink cameras, computer, phone my Echo and Ech Dot, etc) and it wants more. There’s nothing weak about this router. As for the cons: setup was time consuming. Not impossible but it wasn’t intuitive. I got it done in less than 1/2 an hour but it could have been quicker. The user interface is decent. There are a lot of options. Heck you can even choose the signal strength for each band, and you can set up a VPN. Previously I had to use DD-WRT to do that. Not now. What makes me even happier? The price! Under $60 and I got one heck of a router. I think the material is what I would expect. So no disappointment there. As you see by my pictures my 5.0 band is what I have always gotten: the speed I pay for. BUT my 2.4 signal is much much better (close to the 100 mb I buy) than it had been using “name brand”’routers. I am very pleased I bit the bullet and bought this. I almost didn’t because it’s not a name I know and some reviews were less than glowing. For me this works great and I hope if you buy it you too are pleased.

title: Watch for the sales - and be prepared
text:
First and foremost, in deciding what you are willing to pay for this bargain tv, you should include the costs of buying a decent stand and some speakers or a sound bar. The stand that came with my TV broke within a couple of months (the panel is too heavy for the cheap plastic - we made do by drilling extra holes crossways and adding screws, but that it certainly not a living room friendly solution). The speakers built into the TV are abysmal and won't do in a room that has any other noise.

This is my second Seiki. I also have a 40 inch Seiki [[ASIN:B004NF1KES Seiki LC40G81 40" 1080p 120Hz LCD HDTV] ]and I like that one a lot. I like this one, too, but not as much.

This is a budget television, no doubt about it. The frame is made of plastic that neither looks nor feels expensive. When installing the stand, you want to be very careful to get those screws in all the way (without stripping them), or else the television will not be steady on the stand. The rest of the set up process was very easy. Probably my favorite thing about this television is that it has component and composite inputs, meaning that I can still use my older dvd player and dish network dvr with it. One thing to be aware of, though, is that it has only one analog audio input, so you can use a component video source and a composite video source, but you can only get audio from one of those devices.

The size difference between 40 and 42 inches is more noticeable than what I thought it would be. If bigger is better for you, or if you are replacing a tv that's 42 inches or larger, I think you might like this one - the SE421TT - better. The picture is not quite as good, and there is some fade out at the edges, but the blacks are nice and deep, and the colors are vibrant. The first thing I watched was a PBS HD documentary on elephants, and the picture was quite stunning. The television sits on a high boy dresser in my bedroom, and the viewing angle is still excellent from down low.

Using input from a standard definition dish network dvr, the picture was considerably less stellar, with blurring and occasional lag. My 40 inch tv does a noticeably better job of rendering from the satellite dish. Both televisions are excellent for over the air HD content, and the 42 inch tv, surprisingly, did a better job of connecting with my Mac Mini over a dvi-to-hdmi cable. Unlike the 40 inch, which is a newer model, the 42 inch gives full 1080p with no over-scaling.

The sound is where the 42 inch falls apart. Tinny, weak, and truly awful out of the box. I was able to get an acceptable sound for a bedroom tv (which is what I am using this for) by playing with the equalizer and presets (I set it to jazz and dynamic). I do not think it would work in a busier, louder room. For now, the picture and sound are enough better on the 40 inch that I have decided to keep that one as my living room tv (my living room is tiny), but the 42 inch is great in the bedroom.

I shopped around a long time before I bought the 40 inch tv, because I've got serious budget constraints, and I needed something I could afford AND that I wouldn't regret buying every time I tried to watch it. Now that I have both of these, I have to say that I still think the 40 inch is the better bargain with two "unlesses" - 1. Get the 42 inch if size really matters to you, and 2. Get the 42 inch if your primary video source is going to be 1080p dvi-to-hdmi (i.e. you have cut your cable and are using a computer as your main source of entertainment). If that's the case, you'll probably want to get a decent set of speakers to go along with this.

title: Not Your Local Walmart's Surge Protector
text:
Pay attention to the measurements of this thing. I didn't, and I was shocked by how long it is. Most of us think of a surge protector as a compact set of outlets that can easily fit behind a computer or home entertainment center. Not this one. It's more than four feet long with the outlets in a single line running down that entire length. It's what you might see in a store's electronics department where they have a line of television sets all turned on at the same time so you can readily compare their pictures.

The instructions specify that it is for home not commercial use though. I have trouble visualizing a home set up that would require a row of outlets set in a four foot straight line. Perhaps a home workshop with power equipment? Or a more elaborate computer set up, one with components on a rack of shelves? The surge protector can be wall mounted so it could work well with a rack of components.

Despite my own bafflement I am still giving this surge protector a 5 star rating for a reason. If you have a place where you can use something along these lines, this could be an excellent product for you. It is solidly built with a durable heft to it. The rating for 600 Joules of protection is significant. A quick google search about Joules turned up a site saying that most surge protectors bought for home usage are rated at 200-300 Joules and as such are essentially worthless. The minimum suggested was 400 Joules and this surge protector is comfortably above that. That won't help in case of a lightning strike but should be good for more normal occurrences. I'm looking forward to reading the other reviews of this item to see how people would use it in a home.

P.S. I dunno if they would actually have something like this in a Walmart as I've never shopped there, or anywhere else, for a four foot surge protector. :)

title: Well done!
text:
I'm using a Logitech Harmony Companion remote with the Harmony hub on my home theater setup. My setup consists of a 51" Samsung plasma TV, Vizio Soundbar, Roku and a Windows 7 HTPC with two OTA tuners running Windows Media Center. The Companion works great controlling everything, but because it works with the HTPC over bluetooth, it can't wake it from sleep.

I ordered the FLIRC hoping to figure a way to get it to work with the Harmony to add the wake from sleep to my power on sequence. It turned out to be super simple and is working perfectly.

I downloaded the software and driver from the FLIRC website and installed on my HTPC. I plugged in the FLIRC to a front USB port and Windows loaded the driver. There was a firmware update available and the FLIRC software prompted me to update which I did. I then selected the WMC MCE remote profile in the FLIRC software and selected the "Start" button that displayed on the image of that remote and then pressed the power on sequence button on my Harmony Companion remote. The software recorded that key press and saved it. That's it, done.

One button press on my Harmony companion will now turn on my TV, set it to HDMI 1, turn on my sound bar and wake my HTPC from sleep. This is how well designed technology works; simple and straight forward.

title: Sticking with Plantronics... thanks.
text:
I bought this headset thinking to replace my aging (yet still functional) Plantronics that I've used every day of the week for 5+ years.

Well, I'm still with my old Plantronics, and after using this, I'll probably replace it with a similar model from them!

The good:

1) The ear pad is comfortable and largish, which works for me. I like a headset that feels comfortable against my ear for long periods of time (as in many hours).

2) The price here is a third of what I paid... can't believe I didn't research this, but I fell for the old "if it's expensive, it has to be good" marketing ploy at an Office ***-***** style store.

The bad:

1) The bumped out hard rubber piece that sits on your non-listening ear was both uncomfortable and shaped the opposite of how it will fit your head

2) The "mute" button only works while you hold it in. How does that help me on a 2 hour conference call? My Plantronics has a switch.

3) No Voice volume boost? Come on!

4) The "noise cancelling" is also "voice cancelling" to some degree. I had to increase my volume just to be heard. This was the main reason I ditched it after two days of testing with a newer phone system. It turns out that my Panasonic 2-line 5GHz cordless units also lower the output of my voice, but this thing does too. Going back to my old headset made it more reasonable for others to hear me. I don't have to shout as often (the problem with my new phone system made me question if I was being objectionable about the headset at first)

5) The fold out style of the headband is pretty inflexible and seems sort of pointless. I found that it dug into my head a little.

I've always been one to try new technology, and this looked on par with my original headset. I was (and still am) firmly in the Plantronics camp, but I thought I'd give it a try. Sorry to say that I did. After this, I may never try another brand. (No, Plantronics didn't solicit this review, but they sure could send me some money if they feel like it!) ;-)

Don't buy it. You'll probably return it just like I did.

title: Poor Construction
text:
I selected the Meade 20225 TerrStar telescope as my youngest son is often asking me where to find certain constellations in the sky and has always been interested in celestial events. I thought this telescope might be a good entry level scope with which to foster his interest. While it does work, I would hesitate to recommend it, mainly on the basis of its build quality but also for its usability.

My son decided to assemble it himself and it was done by the time I got home from work. He had no issues putting it together and he managed to get it assembled correctly without any assistance. In short, it's easy to put together. However, his very first comment to me was that it was very cheaply made, and it did not take long to determine what he meant. The whole assembled unit is slightly wobbly and a little unstable though it does not feel like it will tip over without a little help - I would be more concerned about it breaking outright. There is much more lightweight plastic than metal and there are numerous opportunities to break components which all feel cheaply made.

One of the packing decisions made was to put the lenses in the carry bag which is folded up in the box. So, until we realized this we thought the lenses were not included in the package. While this is not a major problem - all the parts are there - it does show a lack of understanding of the consumer who is likely to call the support line first before searching the carry bag.

We took the telescope outside and started looking for objects in the sky, and we discovered a serious issue. Once we find something to view, the scope's positional setting is so loose that even the very slightest bump either knocks the object from view or causes the scope to shake which makes viewing impossible. At a minimum the scope itself should be mounted tightly and should move only with deliberate effort. I have found no way to tighten this up which is very unfortunate.

I have trouble recommending this telescope. It's very cheaply made and this shows all through the product from assembly to use. Research other options before selecting this telescope.

title: Tiny but mighty
text:
I'm pretty much a long-term tech nerd with quite a few sadly deceased laptops over the past 25 years. Other than my first (which is always exciting!), this is by far my favorite. Its sheer elegance from the packaging to performance is unsurpassed. The sleek lines, ultra-thin form, visual elegance are so gorgeous, I love just looking at it. And that's without even turning it on. The keys are so easy to read, even before turning on the backlight (which every laptop should have!). It's not much bigger than my tablet.

And yet, for a machine so compact and lightweight, this is a major performer! I am blown away every time at the boot speed. Boom. On. The fingerprint reader is a breeze to set up and use, and with just a touch it lets you right in. Or not, if you're not in the system. Oh so quiet. This little powerhouse doesn't make noise. There are automatic adjustments happening when you switch from browsing the web to say, a high graphics game that will switch the quiet fan setting off. But guess what? It's still virtually silent! I've put this thing to the test quite a bit. As a business owner, I run Quickbooks Pro but as a nerd, I play video games for unwinding. I can seriously alt-tab from one tot he other with no slow down or crashes. This has been my litmus test for the past 10 or so years since QB & high graphic video games have rarely played nicely together. My solution has been to keep them separate most of the time. Now I don't have to! This baby does both fine with nary a crash or sputter.

Aesthetically, this machine is gorgeous. Does it get fingerprints? I haven't had a laptop that doesn't with a sleek surface yet. I'm a bit of an electronic clean freak, so my desk drawer contains a stack of screen wipes. I use them on my phone, tablet, and laptop almost daily. For the outer surface, there's a little included cloth. A 5-second wipedown makes the fingerprints go away. For all the amazing features this has, the fingerprints aren't even a concern! I mean, what do athletes look like before, then after a power session?! Right?

Charging. This keeps a charge for much longer than any laptop I've ever owned. I have to check every couple hours but most of the time don't need to plug in. If I'm using a lot of graphics intensive stuff, it'll drain the battery faster, but still has amazing battery life. Charging is really fast, too. I do a lot of graphic design work and this runs CorelDRAW and several video editing tools easily. The touchscreen is amazingly responsive, too. So much better than my last HP laptop.

You will not regret purchasing this machine. I have been working with it for a few weeks and have yet to trip it up despite the workouts I'm putting it through. Updates and installs are smooth, even printers. We have several printers that have given us trouble with various PCs and laptops, but this set up quickly and works great with our Canon, Epson and HP printers

The last point, although I could go on for ages, this is the most portable laptop I've ever owned. It's like carrying a tablet, it's so compact. And yet, the keyboard is perfectly comfortable to use, with huge easily readable keys. Seriously as light as a feather.

title: Good mouse, bad ergonomics
text:
I've owned a lot of "high-end" logitech mice like the mx700 and the mx1000. Both were great mice. They had drawbacks, but I always felt they were well thought out.

I had high expectations for the Performance Mx, but I'm disappointed with it.

First the good:
The mouse tracks well and delivers on its DarkField technology promise. I also really like the button on the scroll wheel that allows you to control the scroll rate (if it's clicked in the wheel functions like a regular scroll wheel, if released, the wheel has a lot less resistance letting you move through documents quickly). The task button is handy, but I hardly use it.

The Bad:
What I don't get about the mouse is the location of the forward and back buttons. I have large hands and have never struggled with being able to reach buttons on a mouse, but I do on the performance mx. The buttons are located near the top. And, while you can reach the back button easily, the forward button is very cumbersome to operate.

I don't think I've ever used the zoom button for zooming. I just reprogrammed to go back and used the back button to go forward. It's nice that I can do that, but it's annoying to have a button I can't use on the device (I.e. the forward button).

All in all:
It's a decent mouse that looks great, but the ergonomics need to be rethought.
