title: Good durable storage, albeit USB2.0 read speeds
text:
This is exactly what it claims to be. It says very clearly that this is USB2.0 speed, so keep your expectations realistic. It seems like some people rated this poorly because it wasn't as fast as other USB devices, and that's not really fair if comparing to modern USB3 or Thunderbolt speed device made for data transferring regularly. This is more like a write-once-read-many distribution device.
I'm attaching speed benchmarks here, and this honestly seems pretty average for a USB2 connected device. I have many old USB2 sticks that are slower. A USB3 SSD connected to my USB2 port faired a little bit better. To be clear and give this a sense of scale:
An old 4GB USB stick connected to my USB2 port clocked in at 15-20MB/s.
An ultra fast USB3.1 SSD connected to the same USB2 port: 42.24MB/s (so one shouldn't be expecting to a USB2 to be faster than this or even reach this maximum on an average setup).
This device, at 30.59MB/s, seems pretty on par.
Where you will feel the sting, however, is in the slow 5.87MB/s write speed. That's also not uncommon for sticks like these- they are designed for durability and fast read times, to read data off quickly and conveniently. This is great for distributing finished media for a client to play on a projector, or have your resume / photo portfolio on your keychain. Reading more often than writing. A friend of mine who does wedding video would use a stick like this to distribute the finished event production to the client. It's perfect that for what it claims to be and do, a solid 5 stars.

title: charging ports break after exposed to weather for a while
text:
So I owned two of these cameras (argus eco). They work okay - miss a lot of events but that was not the biggest problem. I had both charging continuously with a solar panel. For some reason I had to take them in at some point because they were not charging. Reolink support recommended charging them indoors with the usb. Each of the two times I did that, the charging port sunk so far into the camera that I could not connect it. After dealing with this for a while with Reolink support, the bottom line was that since it was out of warranty, there was nothing they could do. By the way, one of these was a replacement camera they sent (for a different issued) that was only 6 months old but they do not count the warranty from that, they count it from the original purchase date. So this happened on a camera that was only 6 months old as well as one that was a little over two years old.

Since I could not charge the camera, it was not usable so I decided to take it apart to see what the issue was. The pictures show that the connection port is thinly attached to a computer board. The computer board is held in place (pushing the port up through the connection hole), simply with tape. So the tape dried out and now slides down (see pictures), taking the port with it when you try to plug in. This is a ridiculously simple problem to solve by the company. They should simply screw in the board to the part that holds it in place. So now I have two cameras that should work (well, one I destroyed by opening it up) but don't because there is no way to charge it. Also, the soldering that connects the port to the board is also very weak. It super easily broke off when trying to fish it out with tweezers.

So, I might be stupid in that I ordered two more reolink outdoor cameras (a different type this time). If the charging ports are built the same, I expect to have the same problem in the future. title: A Solid Performer for the Price - 4 Stars for Value
text:
It is important to thoroughly read the manual for any camera and test it out fully before making a decision on keeping it. For example, the "it picks some random focus point" issue can be solved by choosing P mode and telling the camera that the focus point should always be in the center. A lot of this camera's hidden beauty lies in its ability to be fully manually operated, from zoom (albeit awkwardly with buttons) to exposure. Unfortunately, this camera falls slightly short of being a great camera due to excessive noise and no optical image stabilization.

Let's hit the bad points first and then balance them out with the good ones. The Olympus has no manual zoom control or manual ring focus control. This hurts because the motorized zoom is a lot slower than a manual can be and it is very noisy. Next, CCD imaging chips have a lot of pixels on them. Each pixel is sensitive to one color, so you'll have some of the pixels dedicated to blue, some to red and some to green. If a red pixel is placed on the sensor, only red will be sensed at that location. This is OK, because the camera's processor is able to guess the value of the missing colors and output it to the file. The ability of a camera to accurately guess colors (unless it's a 3 CCD camera with one imaging chip for each color) is what makes its photos look good or bad. Additionally, pixels are a certain size. As manufacturers put more pixels on the same-sized chip, these pixels must necessarily be smaller and are therefore more subject to electrically interfering with each other when the chip is exposed to light. This interference is called "noise" and is usually heavily processed out so that it doesn't mess up the photo's resolution. ISO ratings are an old film standard that defined the size of the individual film grains (100 being larger grains than 200, 400 or 800), with larger grains being able to capture more light and smaller grains being quicker at exposure, but shorter on detail. Digital cameras use this same terminology for their light sensitivity settings, with 100 being a bright daylight setting and 3200 being almost pitch dark. This camera is good to about ISO 200, after which, unacceptable amounts of noise creep in, preventing the use of the full 7.1 MP resolution print sizes. It'll make good 4x6s or 8x10s to ISO 800 and, after that, the camera will limit its own resolution to 3MP around 1600 and 3200. I would say that if you were shooting a lot of low light scenes without the flash, you'd be better off getting a DSLR and high quality lenses. This problem with ISO ties into the picture stabilization. The camera will adjust the shutter speed and flash and bump up the ISO to counteract camera shake, but, if you're using the stabilization and the light's not bright sunlight, you'll get a higher ISO and therefore more noise in the photo. This concept makes the higher end of the zoom unusable without a tripod or at least a monopod. The last real downside that is glaring is Olympus's refusal to allow CD cards in their cameras. They want you to buy their special media which is only available up to 2GB and has a higher per-byte cost than any other card. An SD or even a CF slot would have been welcome here! By the way, the flash is not automatic. It's got a little pop up button and you have to manually push it to get the flash up. Not a big deal, but might put people off. Another Olympus blunder is the LCD screen. It's big, but only slightly more than 100,000 pixels...meaning that it will NOT show the photos you take in their full quality. The electronic viewfinder is equally bad. You'll take a bunch of blah photos that will look great once you get them off of the camera...Olympus isn't the only guilty party-other big name manufacturers use a similar trick so they can advertise a 'HUGE SCREEN" and save money on the build cost. Check for this before you buy!

Now for the good things. I know the ISO noise thing sounds like a killer, but the noise level is pretty much on par with other cameras in this class. Most long zoom cameras are basically point and shoots that try to squeeze too much out of their lenses and imaging chips and ISO ratings suffer for it. As long as you learn how to use the camera and learn how to take photos (for which this FULL MANUAL capable camera is ably suited), you'll be able to adjust. The lens is good and doesn't soften too much or distort more than any other camera in its class. This camera features a RAW shooting mode, where you can get the image straight off of the CCD without processing and then tweak it yourself...this is HUGE for this class of camera because even though the files are a LOT bigger, you can basically "take the photo" all over again in processing by adjussting levels and color saturation. This is well worth the effort, but realize that the JPEG color saturation is pretty good already. I would recommend shooting at the next-lowest level of resolution if you're shooting JPEG. This will help the noise problem a little bit by increasing the size of the pixels because they're grouping together. You sacrifice some resolution, but save noise. This camera is light and comfortable to hold and the battery life is outstanding. The camera is responsive and you can save custom settings easily. I also liked the lock on the bottom battery door; it's a small issue, but having a door pop open and batteries raining out of the camera prevents phototaking! The tripod mount is close to center, but the memory card slot is on the back/side of the camera, meaning that you can change cards without removing the tripod! Very nice. The movie mode is great, with the big lens catching a lot of detail and the 640x480 resolution at 30fps making things smooth. The videos don't look too bad on a TV, although they're not in the MPEG format. The software is good and offers a complete solution for not only viewing/editing (especially RAW files) and phot stitching, but also for updating the camera's firmware. Also note that using an Olympus-branded card will unlock a special panorama mode for your camera.

This camera is a good, basic camera that tries to get a little too ambitious and falls slightly short of great. Some of it is due to Olympus's reliance on xD and noisy imaging processor and some of it is due to cutting corners to save the retail price, but overall, the camera is a good buy for the money. People that are disappointed with this camera will be people who might not want to do manual control but just want a camera for point-and-shoot and want quick snapshots to be perfect and fast. Other people want $2000 worth of quality and features in a sub-$400 camera and get upset when it can't match a DSLR with a full-sized imaging chip. Believe me when I say that, if you're wanting a commuter car that will get you there, save power and do it well, this is the camera for you...if you want a sports car, go spend the money and get one. Don't think this is an adequate substitute.

A definite recommend for amateurs who want more control, but can't afford the $150-$200 more that other cameras cost.

title: Says it's a good gaming monitor, but really not made for all games, just the casual ones.
text:
This is a pretty good monitor. It's a 2K and not a 4K -- sometimes the terms QHD and UHD get tossed around and it can be confusing. The resolution is 2560x1440 which is sometimes referred to as 2K or Quad High Definition (QHD) because it's almost four times the pixels as regular 1080HD.

Nothing stands out in the design -- it's simple and not flashy like some of the newer monitor case designs. It's lighter than prior generations of the same resolution and it's got a good set of controls for getting the picture correct.

The most noticeable issue is that this monitor has no speakers -- it's just a monitor with no sound. It differs from much of its competition in that way, and at the current price of about $300, I would expect some kind of speakers, even if they weren't superb quality since a lot of computers deliver the sound over the same HDMI cable.

It's mentioned that it's good for gaming and I'd argue that's subjective according to the level of gaming that you're going to be expecting. At 75Hz refresh rate, it's better than some older monitors, but for most games 120Hz is going to be the standard. AMD Freesync is good if your graphics card is made by AMD, but the Freesync functions won't work if you have and nVidia card. You can still use this with an nVidia graphics card, but you're not going to get the adaptive frame rate and will probably notice the tearing when your game's graphics start to slow down during a graphic-intensive game. Which basically means, you're going to notice it on games with a lot of action and motion, but on simpler games without a lot of higher-end graphics settings, you won't notice much of a difference. If you have AMD graphics, then you're good to go.

I didn't test the Display Port input, but the HDMI gives a good picture with a nice range of colors. The backlight is noticeable around the edges in a darker room, but it's not that bad in a well lit room.

As for whether or not this monitor is a good value depends on your purposes. I'd almost definitely rule out gaming of any type simply due to the lack of speakers which means you'll need to buy something additional (extra $) for the sound, whether it's a headset or a set of PC speakers.

The monitor's physical size and its resolution makes it a fair choice for an office computer because you'll have a larger workspace and can get more windows on the screen.

I can't recommend this monitor whole-heartedly simply because there are better choices out there at this price-point. It's a bit too expensive for using with recent computers where even the cheapest ones can easily output a higher resolution. And the picture quality is good, but doesn't justify the lack of sound and the cost.

Overall, this is a fair quality monitor at a rather high price, especially when it lacks sound output, making it a a poor choice for most gaming. It's maybe suited for watching HD movies and doing non-graphics-intensive office work with a larger desktop, but still, there are better monitors for the price. At the current $300 price-tag, I'd give this one a pass unless you found it on sale.

I've tried a few of these devices, and all work ok with the right cable (I use shielded factory terminated Cat7/Cat8 cables spaced apart and away from power lines). I assume many use the same guts inside the boxes, and for me the biggest deciding factors are: HDMI passthrough, USB, resolutions/color depth support, and power.

This device lacks 4k support and no claims of 4:4:4 color (my upstairs TV lacks it anyway), and it also lacks a HDMI pass through. Not looking great so far, but the 1080p picture looks great (my TV only is 1080p anyway), there's USB, and if I keep it very simple, I don't need to have power upstairs. The mounting tabs are a nice touch. Now things are looking great!

Well the USB and using POE sounds great, but using a couple devices (a keyboard and Xbox One wireless controller adapter) leads to sadness. title: Good keyboard case that makes typing on an iPad much faster
text:
I really like this case. This case with an 11” iPad Pro 2021 attached weighs 2.8 pounds, which is the same weight as a MacBook Air. The case by itself is 1.7 pounds, from what I measured, which is more than the iPad. If you are going to use the keyboard nearly all the time, you are better off with a MacBook Air. This device is good if you often use the iPad without a keyboard, for watching movies and playing games, but occasionally want to type. When it comes to typing, this keyboard makes it much faster than using the on-screen keyboard. The keyboard is small, so it takes some getting used to. I could not figure out how to trigger a tap on the screen using this keyboard and trackpad, and it might not be possible, which is an unusual limitation because you have to still use the touch screen on the iPad if you need to tap. The case is top-heavy and unstable when in the keyboard configuration on your lap, and it is prone to tip over. If you do not need the keyboard then you can twist the screen around so the keyboard is behind the iPad, which makes it stable.

The iPad needs to go without a separate protective case for the magnet feature to work. Putting an iPad into a case prevents it from sticking to the magnets on this one.

It is not a five-star product because it is heavy relative to the iPad, it is a bit too top-heavy and unstable, and I cannot seem to trigger a screen tap using the keyboard and trackpad. A simple on/off switch would be better than a long button press. I would still recommend this case unless there is a better keyboard case without these limitations.

title: Well made, quality, but doesn't fit many phones especially with cases
text:
I got this as Az Warehouse for a great price. It's a nice, looks like high quality, phone holder. I was thinking about mounting this on my bicycle and using an old smart phone to play music, show a GPS speedometer, etc but unfortunately it doesn't fit well on most of my old phones I tried, both with and without cases. First off, this won't fit any of my phones with cases because the cases are a too bulky and the arms on the sides of the phone holder don't stick up high enough. Perhaps a simple PU cover might be slim enough if your phone is flat enough... but no luck here. Phones without cases may sit low enough but it still depends on how old and thick the phone is. If the phone is taller than 3/8 of an inch laying flat on it's back on a table then I don't think it will work. Also, if any phone buttons are in the bottom 3 inches of the phone then the holding arms will likely interfere and you won't be able to mount it properly in the holder.

I fully understand the issue some are having with the phone rotating. The rotation mechanism "clicks" into portrait or landscape orientation and can swivel all the way around... nice if you're making changes but I see how this could flip around when not desired. Tightening the middle security screw does not change how it easily swivels. The handlebar clamp bolt also has a security hex head.

It came with a security hex key, rubber spacers for handlebar mounting, and rubber pads for inside the arms. Instructions are decipherable

Overall I really like this holder, I just wish the arms to hold the phone were taller so I could use this on a phone with a case. I'm a bit limited in terms of fit on my old phones.

title: Great sound and microphone for the price!
text:
If I had bought these headphones solely for listening to music for $130, I'd be happy with my purchase. But they also come with a great microphone.

Sound:
Bass has good sense of pace and impact without being too overly hyped like certain trendy music listening headphones. With a proper headphone amp, bass is fuller and better defined. Treble is extended enough but not terribly airy. Good sound staging for a headphone in this price range. Through the front panel jacks on a PC, the sound as A OK as these drivers are plenty efficient. These don't sound like a high-end Sennheiser headphone, but they also don't sound like crap without a headphone amp and they're much more affordable.

Looks:
Most gaming headsets look ridiculous. No neon green or flashing lights on these. Understated black with red trim.

Volume Control:
The volume control rolls off the treble just a tad. Not an issue for gaming but for music listening you'll want the volume on the headphones full up, using the volume on the device instead.

Background Noise:
These are open back, so they hardly block out any background noise, but you have the added advantage of being able to hear your voice when you speak. Fully closed headphones make me a bit claustrophobic but that's a personal preference. For noisy environments you'd be better off with the Game Zero as those are closed back.

Microphone:
The mic is excellent. It is neither boomy nor shrill. The noise reduction isn't overly aggressive. Voice sounds very natural. Mic shuts off when the arm is in the up position.

Comfort:
These aren't so comfy you forget you're wearing them like the Sennheiser HD-600. The velour pads are stiffer, as is the clamping force. The big takeaway is these things stay on your head. With careful adjustment they can be comfortable enough. They do not make my ears sweaty. I wore these the week my A/C broke down in 90F heat. They aren't swampy like some headphones.

Cables:
I refuse to buy headphones that don't have replaceable cables as the cable is usually the first thing to fail. These come with a cable for PC and a cable for phone/tablet/controller. Single entry into the left side cup. Snug connection but easy to pull out to swap if tugged on directly.

I would recommend these to a friend.

title: I like this tablet
text:
Wow - nice update. I've owned a number of the older 7" Fire tablets (and a couple of the 10" Fire HDs) and never consider getting one of these 8" tablets. Buying this one was sort of a spur of the moment purchase when I saw them on sale about a week ago. Like I said - I have two of the older model 7" tablets, but neither one of those had the option of adding extra storage space and to be honest they seemed to be a bit slow in their operation. The two 10" tablets are still great - but a bit too large to carry around with me during the day. So this 8" one seemed to be a viable solution.

One of the reasons I never really consider getting one of the 8" Fire tablets is I sort of figured why bother 8" isn't that much bigger than 7" - I was wrong. The bigger screen size makes reading books with lot of images and text easier. I have a bunch of technical books in my Kindle collection, as well as books like the Bloom County comic strip books and the Calvin and Hobbes books. On the 7" screen those are barely readable (one of the big reasons I bought the first 10" Fire tablet). What's surprised me - is that while the screen is bigger, the case of the 8" tablet is nearly the same size as the 7" tablets. I can even use the same sleeve case that I have been using.

This new tablet is fast (course, all new tablets seem fast - till something faster comes along). I really like the new operating system and the way the menus and control screens work. Vast improvement over the older models. The one and only comment (complaint?) I have is about the screen itself. All of the previous Amazon tablets I've bought the screens have been glass - slick glass. This new tablet's screen feels a little different - it has a bit of friction to it where my finger tip doesn't slide across it like the previous tablets. Almost like there is a screen protector on it - but it doesn't appear to be. I'm sure I'll get use to it eventually - but for now it is a bit annoying.

I added a 128GB memory card to the tablet (Samsung EVO select), and the tablet had to format it before it could be used. Formatting took a few minutes. The tablet comes with a power charger and a charging cable.

All-in-all I'm happy with my purchase and think this is the best tablet yet.

title: Not very powerful.
text:
This has some stellar features and ease-of-use options that go above and beyond other gimbals. The problem lies in the motors. I tried this with a Canon 200D and a Sony A6400, both with kit lens and no external mic. Both are well below the weight limit for this gimbal. Both were too heavy for the motors.

Pros:
The app - This app goes above and beyond what any other gimbal offers. You can control EVERYTHING the gimbal can do. Fast and responsive. LOVE IT.
Features - There are many different software locks for the motors to keep your gimbal pointed at whatever you want or steady along the axis you want. They work extremely well and movement was fluid....until it wasn't. Has a nice Inception mode that works very well. Selfie mode worked great. Lots of things can be micro adjusted, too...Just so many great things going on with the software.
Build - lightweight and easy to handle. Buttons were smooth and responded immediately. Everything feels great in the hand, and the gimbal is light enough to carry comfortably for long shoots. The tripod is wide and very stable, even under load and while moving the camera on the different axis.

Con:
Motors - Too weak for my cameras. At many angles there was juttering because the motors couldn't handle the weight. Even sitting on a tripod and using tracking....sometimes the motors would give out and the camera would stall in place jerking around. Not acceptable. This does extremely well with a phone in a cage, though.

So...Here's my final verdict: I think this is an amazing gimbal overall...but not for an actual camera. If you've got a phone in one of those mountable cage rigs (a BeastGrip), this might be something to think about. At the right weight, this could easily be used for some amazing shots. The features are leaps and bounds over other gimbals...but the motors are just too weak for a DSLR.

It's tough to give this a bad review because there was so much to like about this as a whole. With an extremely light set up this would be the absolute perfect gimbal. Honestly, if you've got a Beastgrip, you're obviously willing to spend money for phone videography....This will be the best gimbal for you. It just didn't work for me....I sent mine back.

title: Dell XPS is universally well reviewed, but still has its issues
text:
Super thin, huge 17" touch screen with colors that just POP, large touchpad mouse, and silent chiclet keyboard. These are just the initial impressions one would see at first blush when approaching this high-quality laptop. Look a little deeper and one would find that this Dell XPS 17 sports a powerful 11th generation I7-11800H cpu with a dedicated RTX 3050 graphics card with Nvidia's real-time ray tracing and 16gb of ram. A 512GB ssd rounds out the entire package.

The Dell XPS 17 is simply elegant and high-quality. I was able to upgrade this laptop to Windows 11 painlessly and the new UI just looks great on this screen. It runs silently during normal web browsing and video watching. When playing games, the fan kicks in and the cooling seems adequate, but I still have an external laptop cooler helping it along.

Speaking of games, this laptop will run the latest games, but being at the bottom of the RTX line of graphics cards, the screen's 3840x2400 resolution simply is too much for the 3050 to run at the highest quality. It means that one would either run at a lower resolution or lower quality. The resolution issue can be alleviated if one turns on DLSS for resolution scaling.

So that is one of the first problems I would point out with the specs that I have in this laptop. The RTX3050 paired with the super high resolution means one must compromise in some way. In addition, performance in VR is somewhat poor. Half Life: Alyx runs well at low quality settings but any higher and the screen stutters and can cause nausea -- this was tested through wired and wireless configurations.

The second complaint that I have for this laptop is that the only included ports are 4 usb Type-C ports, headphone jack and an SD card reader. It is great that the ports support up to Thunderbolt 3, but the fact that no Type-A ports are available, dongles will be a part of life. It's nice that Dell includes a dongle that sports an HDMI and a Type-A port, there is no ethernet or display port support out of the box.

A good 9-in-1 dongle will cost you at least $60 and even then, the quality could be questionable. I happened to have a 9-in-1 dongle, but the ethernet port seems to lose connection constantly. This means that either you take a chance with a $60 no-name dongle or you spend over $100 for a proven one.

This then brings me to the last problem that I want to point out. A gaming PC has very high power requirements. Currently, there is no Type-C product that will provide (or pass through) the 130W that the Dell XPS 17 will require. It means that the nifty dock that you bought to get the additional ports that you need? It won't be able to power the laptop. You can connect a 100W charger to the laptop, but you will get a warning from the operating system. So perhaps on travel, one can get away with trickle charging the laptop, but at home, you will always be stuck with taking up two ports, one for power and one for your monitor.

Overall, this is a GREAT laptop with high quality build, but at the current specs, some things just cause awkward situations that one needs to work around.

title: If you're in doubt, doubt no more.
text:
I was researching televisions for MONTHS and could not figure out which one to buy. My boyfriend is better at this stuff, so after I spent countless hours comparing TVs in Target, Wal-Mart and PC Richards, (and even securing a pre-order for a Coby, [which I quickly cancelled after hearing bad things]), I told him to see what he could find on Amazon. He found this TV and after sorting out what could be "insider reviews" from genuine ones, we decided that it sounded like a great deal for the money, and though the name is not exactly a household one yet, it was worth a shot, as another buyer said the same thing happened with Vizio a couple of years back.

So, we bought it for each other as a joint Christmas gift, figuring what the hey. If it wasn't as advertised, we'd send it back. And it had a lot to live up to, considering this was essentially our only gift to each other this year. It has been over a month now, and we LOVE this television.

Pros:

- No side glare - you can see the picture well, even if you are sitting on the side of the television.
- It is lightweight and super thin, so it is easy to transport.
- Very clear picture.
- Decent enough sound - you don't really need a sound bar if you don't have one, especially since there are options to change the sound (i.e. "music", "film", "surround sound", etc.)
-Provided you are not signed in to a game system (which you can change the video input from your remote), there is a setting where the TV will automatically shut itself off after 10 minutes of lack of use. This is very helpful if you have a roommate who tends to fall asleep in front of the television.
- There are plenty of settings to customize the picture and sound, as well as "label" your game systems with the pre-loaded options so you know which video input to select for your X-Box or PS3 (for example, I have the PS3 set to "Blue Ray", whereas the X-Box is set to "Game").

Cons:

-It is not a "smart TV", if you are in the market for one of those. It's a simple design, which was perfect for us.
-There are no buttons on the TV itself, so if the remote ever breaks, I have no idea how we are going to turn it on and off, aside from buying a new remote.
-There are a shortage of plugs in the back for cables. For example, I can hook up the cable box, X-Box and PS3, but there is no room now for the sound bar. Not a huge deal, but I could see where some people might find that to be annoying.

This television lived up to all of the positive reviews it received here on Amazon, and I am so thoroughly satisfied that we decided to go with this one that I kept reminding myself to write this review so I could help others who were as in the dark as we were about which TV to buy. I didn't get the dreaded "green screen" upon turning it on, as some people have experienced, and the packaging didn't overly give it away that it was a TV, (though we got the 48" one, so I'm sure people could figure it out).

Bottom line: If you are in as much doubt as we were about which TV to buy, trust us on this one - TCL rocks!

text:

I also had the ability to do videos, but for some reason it will only do formats no longer supported in most places. So, I got this to do videos.

HOW DOES THIS COME?
This comes in a box that has foam insert. The parts are in boxes and wrapped lightly.

PERFORMANCE OF VIDEO
I used this for both photos and video. For basic overall video taking for reviews, it is okay. For close up macro videos to get any kind of detail, this is disappointing. The camera has a hard time focusing on items I want to get detail on even if I really work with it.

PHOTOS
The photos are not bad. They are adequate for doing some basic photos. They don't compare with my G12 though. The detail is pretty good and the color capture is good too. With some photo editing, it can be altered to get an okay photo.

MACRO LENS
The lens I thought would make close ups easier, but it really didn't seem to help as much as I would like.

TRANSFER PHOTOS
You can either plug in the camera with the micro SD card in it, or take the card out and put it into an adapter to use it in the computer or laptop right from the card. Either way works.

SAMPLES
The first post I put up for you is a video with the macro lens to capture the details of Moissanite earrings. As you can see, it is not the greatest video and it is hard to capture the details of the earrings. This was the best of all of the videos that I have to show you.

The next few photos are as follows. The first photo is without the macro lens and the last 2 are with the macro lens. They are okay, but not as good as I had hoped for.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For basic photos and videos of larger objects without fine detail this is a great camera for basic videos. For detail high quality photos, this is not the best but it will get acceptable photos and some videos with some detail.

MY RATING
THREE STARS. This camera is okay, and I am glad to be able to take video for reviews, but as for high quality and something worth raving about, it is not as nice as I had hoped it would be. I can not use my phone for a lot of video work, so this is acceptable for what I wanted it for.

title: It works, but not so well...
text:
I'm keeping this unit only because it fits the space that I wanted it in very well - I'm not at all happy with the performance of it.

I purchased this TV to mount on a very large desk that I have. The mounting is pretty straight-forward (they supply a cardboard drilling template and a few different spacer options). One thing to keep in mind on the mounting - make sure to allow for extra space for the speakers when drilling your mounting holes (the template does not have this space added).

Electronically, this is just a very average to below-average unit. I'm using cable as my video source. The TV that was in this location previously had an excellent picture. This unit has a snowy picture, and very poor color balance (I have tried adjusting it many times - it never does get a "good" picture).

The sound is awful. You have to create a balance between two different volume sources - one on the front of the main unit, the other on the TV itself (controlled by buttons on the TV, or by the remote). Between the two, if you turn it up to the point of what I would consider normal volume, you hear a faint but noticeable high-pitched whine (my Jack Russell Terrier hears it too...). The quality of the sound is pretty bad too - very thin and tinny. They should have added an Audio Out Jack, so that you could hook up a decent set of amplified speakers to it.

The Power button on the front of the unit is a cheap, spring-loaded design; I can tell that it will create problems in the long run (it has already stuck a few times).

The clock display is a bit annoying also - most digital displays will display the single-digit time without a zero in front nowadays - 3:00, for example. This clock displays it as 03:00.

The remote must use very unique frequencies - I was not able to program my regular Tivo remote to it (not even when cycling through the hundreds of preset codes that the Tivo remote has). I then purchased a "learning" Tivo remote - even that remote wouldn't accept the "power" or "volume down" functions ("volume up" was the only button that would accept the programming).

text:
I bought a refurbished version of this product. It had a couple little scuffs, but otherwise was perfectly fine. Except, it didn't come with a usb-c cable. No biggie. Usb-c cables are pretty universal, right? WRONG.
In order to use this docking station and get video, you're going to need a hefty usb-c that can handle video and power. I saw another reviewer here recommend a Lenovo brand cable, but damn... that's over $50 right now. Instead, I got an Anker Power Line 2 (usb-c 3.1) cable, and it worked great, but was significantly less expensive (still not cheap tho). Once that happened, my monitor was working. I did have a little bit of an issue with the hdmi, but instead of fiddling with that (old cable maybe?) I just used the display port. Worked beautifully.
I previously had an Amazon docking station, and it worked, but the damn thing crapped out only a couple months after the warranty, in the middle of a very important exam. Lesson learned: spend the money on a good docking station. I'm hoping this will do better, especially given the longevity of my Lenovo laptop (it's been great!).

Anyway, the TL;DR is, the doc works, it works good, but you may or may not get a good enough usb-c cable that you'll need to really make it work. Order a really good usb-c 3.1 cable or better if you buy this. Worst case, you get lucky and just return the cable. I knocked the product one star specifically because of this. It's not a cable you can just go to Walmart and find, ya know? It should be included, always.

title: OK but the speaker plug is out of date and this causes problems
text:
The unit itself sounds ok - not great - but ok. It gets pretty good volume and some people would like the blue light across the front (which you can turn off).

The big issue is the old fashioned 3.5 mm plug - it only has 3 contacts - what is called a TRS plug. Most all modern phones and laptops use a 4 contact plug - TRRS. If you plug this into a modern phone or laptop, it's hit or miss whether it will work or give you lots of buzz and a poor sound. You need an adapter cable - something like a 3.5mm TRRS Male to Dual 3.5mm TRS Female for this to work reliably with newer equipment. They should be including that adapter or having a big note about the need for one with new gear.

title: Sadly, I agree with all the naysayers
text:
I had reviewed the Sennheisers and a Sony pair other sports headphones before I found the Koss KSC75s. My review of the Koss is below, and below that my original reviews of the others for comparison. I was skeptical that $20 headphones could compete with the much more expensive ones. Delighted to find I was totally wrong!!

Koss KSC75 Portable Stereophone Headphones
The good:
a) The best sound overall for working out. Great bass, nice integration, very serviceable middle and treble ranges. Better on all counts than the Sennheisers. While not as elegant and smooth as the Sonys, they more than make up for this with their bass and overall drive and punch. And at this price point (less than half of the Sennheisers and less than 1/4 of the Sonys), they are an absolute steal!
b) Ear clips look like they would be difficult to put on, but are surprisingly easy. It took me just two tries to get the hang of them.
c) Cord length is appropriate.
The less good:
a) Clips come off a bit more easily than ideal--not a problem when they're on your head--more when you're pulling them out of your bag if they get a little stuck. However, they go back on very easily so not a deal breaker by any means.
b) Would be nice to have a sliding clip that puts the earpieces together for storage to minimize tangling. On the other hand, these tangle less easily than in-ear buds, thanks to their larger size.
c) When you lie on your back, as for crunches or bench pressing, the earpieces can feel like they are going to come off your ear--they don't actually, and I found it just takes a minor adjustment to correct this.

Overall, these are by far the best pair of sports headphones I've tried and a fantastic buy!

I compared these to the Sennheiser-Adidas CX680i and the Sony XBA-S65, running with each for a long time after I broke a sweat. Here are my impressions:

1. Sennheiser CX-680i:
The good:
a) Ear fin design works reasonably well and is particularly fast to insert. I tried the various sizes, selecting the ones that fit my ear best. Nevertheless, after I broke a sweat, the left earbud slipped a bit every now and then, requiring me to push it back in. It never fell out entirely as many others do, but still this was a bit annoying.
b) Volume control on the cord works well. The Sony doesn't come with one, which is a pain and just plain thoughtless for a "sports" model
c) Bass comes through with that satisfying "boom-boom" sensation you want when you're working out. This is the best feature, in my view.
d) Sweat doesn't seem to bother the sound at all!
e) Very little sound leaks in from the outside--a plus or a minus depending on whether you'd prefer to hear oncoming traffic(!)
The bad:
a) Overall sound quality doesn't compare to the Sony, other than the superior bass "boom." Mid and upper registers are too bright and muddy, all at the same time. As other have mentioned, I had to set the iPod equalizer to reduced treble to make it reasonable, but that then removes a lot of the subtlety and sound distinction you'd like to hear. Also, the balance between the right and left seems a bit off--hard to explain, as it's not a matter of timing, but rather integration of some kind that is beautifully done on the Sony but not here.
b) As many others have written, the cable situation is bleak. I had expected that the complainers were just not trying hard enough to accommodate the design. Well, my apologies--I tried for 45 minutes during my run,and I couldn't figure it out either! The primary cable is indeed too short for anything other than an arm band. When I connected the longer cable with the volume control I found that the clip on the (somewhat bulky) volume control was cheap and close to useless. It's kind of like a cheap plastic version of the long clip on a pen, and as such seems designed to hook over the waistband of your shorts, or the outside edge of the pocket, rather than your shirt. But it doesn't hold at all because it's cheap and not tight, so it repeatedly slipped off my waistband, even though I had the upper part clipped to my shirt with the other provided clip. Clipping it to my pocket was better, but the upper cord is not quite long enough to accommodate that (i'm 6 feet tall, and I'm guessing this would be true for many at, say, 5'10" and above). Eventually, I found a configuration that seemed to hold for at least several minutes at a time, in which I jerrry-rigged the volume clip to my shirt also, but that was it. Very disappointing design. And don't even think about just letting the thing dangle--as everyone else has noted, the noise this creates, and the pulling, are not acceptable.
c) No controls other than volume. If you want to fast forward, rewind, skip ahead, etc. you're on your own, fishing the MP3 out of your pocket or reaching over to your armband.

2. Sony XBA-S65
The good:
a) Sound quality is superb overall. Crisp low mid and high range, beautifully integrated. You'll hear new things in your favorite songs. HOWEVER, as other have noted, the bass register is "flat" to the other registers. There's no possibility of boosting it (the equalizer doesn't help here) to get that extra "oomph" in the bass that I like when working out. It's kind of like the difference between a well-tended Camry and a Porsche in need of a tuneup. The ride of the former is smooth, elegant, well-integrated and, well, not terribly exciting; that of the Porsche is throaty and exciting, but rough and possibly annoying over time. I sense that my disappointment with the Sony bass may fade over time, because the truth is that these earphones are calibrated to deliver a well-integrated, "true" sound that is unlikely to cause listening fatigue. But boy I wish Sony had just provided an option somehow to open the bass up just a smidge more!
b) The "loop" earpieces keep the earbuds in place very well and there's virtually no noise leakaage (see above). However, they are fussy and take some time to get used to putting on properly, whereas the Sennheisers go on with no muss or fuss at all.
c) Cord is long enough and has a clip for your shirt that works fine.
The bad:
a) Not clear to me yet if these are as water resistant as the Sennheisers. I had one moment where the sound in one ear cut out due to sweat in my ear, but a quick flick was all it took to rectify this.
b) The bass register, as above. It's not that it's not there. It's there perfectly accurately. But there are times when you want more than accurate in the bass when you're working out!
c) No volume or any other controls. This is a thoughtless omission for an expensive "sports" model.

When I first tried these, I was sure I was going to go with the Sennheiser, just to get the bass I crave. But the more I compare the two, the more I'm leaning toward the Sony. I'm already experiencing some fatigue with the Sennheiser due to the screechy, muddy mid- and upper registers, and the lack of integration of the two sides. And the more I listen to the Sonys, the more I love the music! Come on Sony! You're most of the way there. Let's open up that bass just a bit, get a less fussy anchoring system for the earbuds and add some volume and other music controls!

title: Spring gimmick will likely cause ear damage.
text:
So these headphones have a great battery life, and feel decent for consumer headphones. The main gimmick is the "haptic bass"... the haptic bass is just two springy metal pieces that resonate at specific frequencies making the sound much worse and likely hitting decibel levels of ear damage!
If that isn't bad enough just taking a step or moving or tapping near the headphones causes the metal to resonate in a weird way.
I opened them up, and cut out the spring part of the headphones, and now they're decent isolating consumer headphones.
Beware, the slider haptic bass gimmick sounds bad and is likely harmful to your hearing so I'd go with another pair without that!

6. A built-in microphone allows you to use the Bluetooth function to place and received calls on your cell phone.

7. These headphones are lightweight, durable, and flexible.

CONS

text:
I got this for my iPad Mini because I thought the ability to rotate the iPad would be quite often useful. Turns out I don't use this functionality at all as every app I use works well in landscape. No big deal--here's why: the case is well made and it does not look or feel as though corners were cut. It is a package deal that combines a decent screen protector, the case itself, a static-free cleaning pad for cleaning the iPads screen before laying on the protection film layer AND adheres lightly to the back of the iPad for occasional use to clean the screen. The cleaning pad stays put yet it does not feel sticky, doesn't stick to me (I would have paid a buck more to not be stickified. It's a bonus). Better yet whatever makes the cleaning stick to the back of the iPad leaves NO residue behind. Even more... one reviewer noted this case lacks a magnetic screen shutoff feature (just a small magnet under the outer covering) IT DOES SHUTOFF the screen when you close the top cover. You simply have to make certain the over flap is snug against the iPad's face. To ensure proper contact and accidental case openings, a wide elastic band slips from the covering flap around the top of the to keep it closed snugly. Yes, it does also turn the screen back on when opened again. AND FINALLY OR TWO there is an elastic loop for taking along a soft-tio pen for tapping screen and menu items. YOU'LL PROBABLY THINK THIS ITEM is just part of the packaging to be discarded. It is a thin rectangle of thinnish blue plastic--about four times the thickness of plastic wrap. DO THIS WITH THE MYSTERY PLASTIC: Position it evenly lengthwise over the Apple logo on the back of the iPad and let its static cling adhere it over the logo. This plastic prevents a circular scratching around the Apple that will develop should you not cover the logo AND rotate the iPad a lot.

This package is complete, well thought out and decently constructed using good grade materials. I do see it as a steal for the price. One thing I would do if buying another one is select a brighter color. I chose the faux loepard skin style because I thought it would be easy to spot among the clutter of my desk. It's not; the brownish-orange background and the black leopard markings let it blend right into my clutter. So, buy yellow, pink, or maybe red. Hey, I'm retired and if I want a pink iPad case, by God I shall have one! Didn't Churchill say those same words in the early 1940s?

Nothing lasts forever and I suppose this case will eventually need replacing. I do reasonably expect this item to have a long useful period and I will buy another, just a pink one.

title: Cool Concept - Poor Quality, Short Battery Life and Connection Issues
text:
I have had the opportunity to review many headsets and headphones over the years and without question the recent technological advancements have aided this area by leaps and bounds.

I can not recommend buying Bluetooth 5.0 enough over previous technologies if your devices support it. Nearly all devices that are Bluetooth 5.0 capable, including this one, will be backwards compatible with earlier technologies as well.

While the listing boasts of incredible battery life my testing has proven that simply is not the case. Battery life is lacking with these headsets lasting on average under 3 hours each in my tests. It is easily charged using the included charging case which will allow the earbuds to be recharged a many times from its one full charge. Since the earbuds can be used together for stereo sound or individually you can potentially double play time by using one at a time. Even with this, 3 hours of playtime from wireless earbuds is way below average. Even having the case which allows charging on the go, this doesn’t mitigate the frustration of having to charge after a few hours of listening.

The charging case is cool. It allows for Qi charging of devices and will act as a portable power supply. The downside to this is the size and weight. Sometimes I want to travel light and this set does not allow for that.

After receiving, I made sure the case was fully charged then confirmed each earbud had a full charge. After verifying full power within each earbud I followed the simple pairing instructions and had no problems whatsoever. Once the earbuds are removed from the case they first pair with each other then you simply pair with your Bluetooth device.

These earbuds will require testing which of the 4 sizes of ear bud caps work best for the individual user. I typically use the medium size which with this set the medium small ones worked better for me. I purchase sets of replacement memory foam ear bud pads which I ended up replacing them with as they are more comfortable and simply work better. Even with having better pads these buds tend to fall out.

The sound from these headphones is mediocre - from the bass notes to the midtones to the treble - not terrible but also not great. I tested these headphones with a wide range of audio - from audiobooks to jazz, heavy metal, country, classical and blues - everything just sounded ok.

I have listened to both music and audiobooks through these as I moved throughout my home and interestingly while these claim to be Bluetooth 5.0 they do not have near the range of other Bluetooth 5.0 sets I’ve tested. I estimate the effective range at around 20 feet.

While these are ok for listening to music, how are they for calling? The sound through these headphones is again mediocre- on both ends.

Controls are overly complicated and the buds do not always respond to the commands given which is especially frustrating when listening to an audiobook as I often skip ahead or back not intending too.

After fully reviewing these headphones over the last couple of months I have to recommend passing on this set. They are simply overpriced for the quality.

Thanks for reading my review. I enjoy writing them as I value reading other’s reviews when I’m making a buying decision. I regularly update my reviews to reflect any changes I may discover and to include helpful tips you may need if you purchase the product. I will always make every effort to answer any questions I can as it is my pleasure to help.

title: A nice addition for lovers of blur
text:
I'm a huge Lensbaby fan. I've been using them with my Canon SLRs almost since they first came out, and have assembled a pretty extensive collection of them over the past few years. Yes, I am a lover of blur. It's one of those creative effects that you either love or don't (although I certainly will admit it can be overused with some horrible results). I've recently been playing around with Micro Four Thirds cameras and was thrilled to see that Lensbaby came out with a model specifically designed for the MFT format.

Quick primer for those not familiar with a Lensbaby: it's a very simple device that allows you to tilt the focal plane of the lens to shift focus to any area of the frame and produce a smooth blur effect. It can be in a small or large part of your photo depending on which of the several aperture rings you choose from (all supplied with this Lensbaby) and how much tilt you apply.

This particular version of the lens, called the "Composer" is part of Lensbaby's new Optic Swap System, which allows you to use any one of several optics (plastic, glass, double glass, pinhole/zoneplate) that you can easily swap out of the main body. This comes with the double glass optic - the other optics have to be purchased separately.

The new Composer design allows you to lock the tilt into place for some level of repeatability in your shots. A lot more convenient than earlier versions of Lensbabies, which required you hold the tilt with your fingers. Now it's just pick your aperture and your optic, tilt, and snap away!

This lens comes with an extra you can't get with other Lensbabies for other camera formats - the "tilt transformer." This is an attachment that will allow you to use any Nikon-mount lens as a close approximation of a tilt/shift lens (only close, since you really only get the benefit of tilt and not shift). With this attachment and a "regular" lens, you get a movable sliver, a line of focus, as opposed to the movable point of focus you get with a Lensbaby Optic. Same basic principle, but it produces a slightly different look.

Build quality is good. There's a lot of plastic in it, but my other Lensbabies have performed very well over the years with zero problems. The product comes nicely packaged, but only has minimal instructions. That's not really a problem since the company website has a lot of resources on how to use Lensbabies, plus has photo galleries, forums, instructional videos, and a lot more. Very nice resource if you own one. If you're not sure if a Lensbaby is for you, that should be your first stop to see what type of effects their products can produce. I've spent a lot of time there, and it has been time well spent. The company itself is excellent when it comes to customer service. I've contacted them a couple of times with questions, and they answer emails promptly.

This lens is versatile, and is more convenient to carry (both the Lensbaby as well as a MFT camera itself). I've found with all my gear that convenience of toting it means I'll carry it more often, and thus have more opportunity for taking great shots. The tilt transformer is a wonderful addition - you can play around with a tilt lens at a fraction it would cost you to buy a real tilt/shift lens.

While pricy for a Lensbaby, when you add up all the features it brings to the table, I find it to be a real winner. Highly recommend if you have a MFT camera.

I like the cloth covered cord, which feels a whole lot tougher than regular cords; and also the anti-tangle slider which works fine for me, but can be reduced in seconds to a tangled mess in the pocket of my ten year old son.

The big fat bass tends to overpower the higher frequencies a bit, but is still an improvement on other similarly priced models, especially as I prefer heavier bass over tinny trebly sound.

One minor improvement would have been if it had shipped with a case to store the extra buds which tend to get misplaced, and help with my son's tangling issues.

title: It Took Away My Wrist Pain
text:
My wrist was becoming quite sore from overuse on a traditional mouse. I knew that they were making new types of mouses, so I checked out the ergonomic ones. The reason I picked this one was mainly chance. There are a number of mice of this general configuration, and since this is not a store where you can handle the wares, I had to just go ahead and pick one. I am glad that I picked the one that I did. It is perfect for me. I would say I have a medium-sized hand, perhaps a bit large for a female and quite small for a male. When I grip the mouse, my fingers find the appropriate buttons instantly.

Not only that, but for the first time I am using the thumb buttons since they are easy to use. Within a few days of using this mouse, my wrist pain had all but disappeared. Now that I have had it for a while I have no wrist pain.

There is a learning curve for using this mouse. You move it around with your elbow and shoulder more than your wrist and this takes a while to get used to. At first, I was dragging my pinky finger beside the mouse so that it would not overshoot its destination. Now, I do not notice myself doing that anymore.

This mouse will not work with a neoprene mouse pad. I had to switch out to a metal mouse pad, and let the mouse travel on the "leather" side of the mouse pad. It squeals when deployed on the aluminum side of the mouse pad. It glides very smoothly and the piece of plastic to rest the side of your palm on is a great help.

I had to give this mouse a rating as far as its gaming capability. Unfortunately, I am not a gamer, so I just put in five stars because it is a nice mouse. Once you get control of it, it does glide around very fast with little friction. Also, I had to rate it as far as battery performance goes. This is a wired mouse with no batteries. This is a good thing for the environment; batteries in landfills create heavy metal pollution in groundwater, so I try to avoid accessories with batteries when I can, and use accessories with removable batteries which I can recycle if I must have batteries. I have always preferred wired mice.

I just examined the bottom of the mouse, and discovered an on-off switch. this controls whether the lines around the top of the mouse glow or not. There is also a button you can depress that I suppose adjusts the DPI. A visit to the manufacturers website reveals that you can download software and customize the buttons. I tried downloading the software, and found that a wide variety of functions can be assigned to the buttons on the mouse, including three types of wheel clicks that don't do anything by default. I set mine so that a simple click on the scroll wheel will double click what I am pointing at.

Cool.

title: Too High Maintence For Me To Bother With
text:
The need for an uninterruptible power source is obvious to anyone with a computer or other expensive electronic equipment. The very day this product arrived, before I even opened the box, a severe thunderstorm knocked out power in my neighborhood. My two computers immediately went down and the screen on one kept flashing on and off even after all the power was dead. So yes, a UPS seems like an important piece of equipment these days. Sadly, this one is not for me. To be fair to the manufacturer though I need to give you a bit of context to help you evaluate if my reaction and this review would be applicable to you or not.

At age 70 I have a pretty low tolerance for muss and fuss. If it requires special handling, if it is a hassle to use, I don't want it. If it's not plug and play, I won't bother with it. For example, I do all my laundry in one load throwing everything in together without any sorting of any kind. It all gets washed and dried on the hot cycle. Anything that can't handle that gets tossed out. I treat everything like that. This UPS looks like an industrial strength product but acts like a delicate little snowflake. Coming out of the box it has 20 pages of instructions they want you to read before using. I didn't bother, just plugged it in, turned it on, and starting using the USB charger to juice up a battery run children's night light. A little while later I noticed a burnt plastic smell and saw the warping on the case that you can see in the attached photos. So this thing is not for me. More detail oriented and careful folks might have better luck with it. Thus I'm giving it a neutral 3 star rating and suggest you read through all the reviews here before deciding whether you want to try it yourself or not.

Having a cover of some sort on your computer is always a good idea. I didn’t always think so until I turned over my MacBook Pro and saw all the scratches. Yikes! So I was stoked to receive this cool hard case (plus matching keyboard cover) to review!

I would recommend the Ruban® MacBook Pro 15″ 2 in 1 Soft-Touch Hard Case + Keyboard Cover to anyone with a MacBook (they sell covers for all sizes of laptops) who wants to protect their Mac from scratches and dirt.

I received a discount on this case so I could give my honest review. All opinions are my own.

title: Poor quality compared to my CM Storm Ultimate keyboards.
text: I have several Cooler Master keyboards with Cherry Brown keys.  This one is very different.  The others have a quick, snappy action.  This one feels like mush.  I'm not sure if the quality of the Cherry keys has dropped or if it's something about the way the keyboard is set up, but it's much less positive and well controlled than the others, not a whole lot better than a membrane keyboard and not worth paying the extra cost for.  I don't care about bells and whistles - the fancier the electronics, the sooner the thing dies, in my experience.  I want a keyboard I can type on fast and accurately (with backlighting :D), and preferably that lasts a long time.  I don't have much confidence in this one's durability, and I can't type as accurately on it as on the earlier ones.  Mediocre at best.  One other thing to note - while the earlier keyboards have the same layout for the USB cord, with channels to guide the cord out the back, the grooves on this keyboard are much too shallow to hold the cord in place and it won't stay in without being duct taped.  Come on, CM, does it cost that much more to make the groove deep enough to hold the cord?  I'm really disgusted with the drop in quality on these keyboards, especially as there hasn't been any noticeable drop in price.  It's so hard to find a good keyboard now.  Looks like I'm going to have to start looking all over again - which is infuriating.

title: Almost Right...
text:
I have been using a Wacom Intuos5 for a while now and I have been pleased with it. In the past I used a Bamboo Pen and Touch and while it was an amazing drawing tablet it did not suit my needs. I was interested in trying the Bamboo Pad, in hopes that it would be a better fit than its larger sibling the Pen and Touch. I have had mostly good results with it but I found one issue that detracts from an otherwise decent product.

The Bamboo Pad is a small and attractive little device, with a usable surface about the size of a 3"x5" index card. The touch portion works very much like a mouse touch pad as one would expect, except that it is bigger and can be moved away from the computer. What makes this pad stand out from a typical touch pad though is the addition of the pen which can be used as a pointing device (on the pad) instead of just relying on the touch portion.

For the uninitiated, this pad may be a little frustrating in use, specifically when using the pen. When the pen is used, the position of the pen on the pad is relative to the screen coordinates. That is, if you touch the upper left of the pad with the pen the mouse will jump to that place on the screen immediately, and if the pen is then moved to the lower right the pointer jumps accordingly. While this might be a bit unexpected, this is the default behavior for all of Wacom's writing tablets so those that are familiar with Wacom products will not be surprised.

I dislike the pen. For me, the pen is too small for my hands. People with smaller hands might like it but for me it is about the same as using a pencil that is just a little too short to be comfortable.

I loaded up Corel Painter and tried to use the pen for drawing and found a different issue (but not a flaw). With the Pen and Touch and with the Intuos5, the writing tablets have multiple pressure levels so that when drawing the amount of pressure used on the pad with the pen is evident in the drawing. With the Bamboo Pad, there is just one pressure level - on. So, there is no pressure variation in the drawing with this pad. Also, the angle of the pen is not considered either. A serious artist would not use this pad for artwork anyway but it's important to note.

I did try to use my Intuos5's pen with the Bamboo Pad and it didn't work. I was hopeful it would, though it's ok that it does not. It was worth a shot.

I have a different issue with the Bamboo Pad that is a more serious concern and represents the one real problem I have with it. It works well most of the time but sometimes it decides to just stop responding to touch for a few seconds. It acts as if it has gone to sleep and needs to wake up after a moment. This seems to happen at random and there doesn't seem to be any way to adjust for it.

The Bamboo Pad is a nice little gizmo and will please the user who likes working with touch pads. People with smaller hands will also like the pen, once they get used to how Wacom's products track with a pen. This is not an artist's tool but can be used for quick scribblings. The fact that the pad seems to "doze off" on occasion represents the one real issue I have found with it. If you like touch pads and prefer them to mice, or if you would like an interesting gift idea, this is not a bad device.

UPDATE 12/27/2013: I was informed that the Bamboo Pad is in fact capable of recognizing pressure levels with the stylus. After digging in a bit deeper to see why I could not get it to work I found a post online that explains that pressure sensitivity does not work under Windows 7, just Windows 8 and OS X, and even then it requires some set-up within certain applications for it to work. Being on a Windows 7 machine, it did not work for me. I do have access to a Windows 8 machine but I am not motivated enough to go get the software for it to test this out. This is unfortunate but not really a big deal for me. The unfortunate part is that support for pressure levels is very poorly documented. I hope Wacom addresses that soon.

title: Cool solidly built notebook; amazing graphics; nimble to the touch; a bit heavy
text:
See BUYER BEWARE NOTICE at the bottom of this review.

This is one impressive, sleekly designed, well-built notebook with a bit of a "cool" factor. The resolution and color vibrancy is amazing for gaming, movies, pictures, etc. The 15.6 inch (viewing region of 17 inch screen) touch screen is responsive. The red backlighting on the keyboard and speakers is cool. At almost 5 pounds (4 lbs. 11.9 ounces), this notebook is heavy.

After the system is set up, startup is practically instantaneous. Setup takes a little bit because the system has to be personalized (although some of the personalization can be skipped) and a Microsoft account has to be created. I had to temporarily turn off the MAC address filtering on my router because the MAC address of the wireless NIC is not supplied on the setup card that comes with the notebook. I could have used the supplied USB Ethernet Adapter but then I would have been tethered to my router and its location.

During setup, I had to check email on another device to verify my email account and get a security code. I'm not sure how this would be accomplished without having a second device (such as a Smartphone) with which to check email, authenticate your account, and retrieve the security code needed to finish setup.

After creating a Microsoft account, I was ready to use this notebook. One month's free subscription to McAffee "Virusware" is included. Additional setup is recommended for OneDrive and some personalization settings for McAffee.

OneDrive is your cloud storage for pictures, PC settings, and new documents. These items are backed up to the cloud (to OneDrive) by default so that they can be retrieved from any device if something happens to the laptop. However, that only works if those features were set up and the documents library was added during setup. Apparently, there's a way to turn off cloud backup if one so chooses after setup, but I haven't figured out how to do that yet.

The game graphics are stunning and the keyboard responsive. I was amazed at the vibrant colors shown in my flower photographs which were never visible on any other devices I viewed them on previously. The quality of the sound is pretty good; although I wish it were louder when watching movies. I did try to pair my [[ASIN:B00MPMK3GW Goal Zero 94014 Rock Out 2 Green Solar Rechargeable Speaker]] with this notebook using Bluetooth and it paired but no sound would emanate at all from that speaker. I believe this is a problem with the Rock Out speaker and not the notebook.

These are the few negatives that I discovered when using this Omen notebook.
- The function keys not easily seen. The Fx notations are so small but it really does not matter much because I am familiar with where all function keys are located.
- All four UBS ports are in the back of the unit. The power cord interferes with one of the USB ports. When I plugged in a mouse to the port next to the power cord, I had to swivel the cord until I could get the mouse cable to seat correctly.
- The audio is pretty good but not great.
- A fully charged battery lasts less than 2 hours on the HP recommended setting (not the Power Saver mode). For me it lasted 1 hour 35 minutes and then I got a warning that it was very low. I had about 10 more minutes left on my battery when I checked it.
- The screen only has 15.6" of viewing capacity
- The notebook is heavy at almost 5 pounds (4 lbs. 11.9 ounces)

Based on the setup information, the notepad I received came with:
- 462GB (only 426 GB are free at delivery)
- 16.0 GB RAM
- Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-4710HQ CPU @ 2.50GHz 2.50 GHz Processor
64-bit OS x64-based processor
- Full Windows Touch Support with 10 Touch Points
-Windows 8.1
- Generic PnP Monitor (Intel (R) HD Graphics 4600 (GeForce 333.55 Driver)
- Resolution 1920x1080 recommended
- It also has a Webcam, SD memory card reader, and HP Omen programmable gaming keys.

Despite its heft, limited battery power, good but not great audio, and the location of the USB ports in the back, I still feel this notebook is a great contender for gaming, movies, pictures, etc. It also comes with a one-year limited warranty.

BUYER BEWARE: The specifications on Amazon do not match the notebook I received although the model number was the same on the box (#15-5010nr). HP has several options available for the OMEN. Unfortunately, I've been unable to find a comparison chart on the differences on their website. For windows peeps, just go into your command prompt and find your IP (ipconfig). Punch that into your browser engine and hit enter. title: Polar M460 with OH1 is a great setup.
text:
I bought two M460s with OH1 heart rate units to use with my wife on bicycle rides at home and on vacation. We also use one of the OH1 units for indoor bicycle exercise with an iPod Touch mounted on a RAM Tough-Claw mount. As far as we can tell the OH1 units work every bit as well as the more bothersome chest strap units.

The Flow readout on the M460 is very visible, in simple black and white, for outdoor riding. We have our units set up to show speed, distance, elapsed time, and heart rate. After each ride you can scroll down on the M460 to see all of your ride data, including calories burned and percent of time in each heart rate zone. The Beat readout on the iPod Touch (or any iOS or Android device) is very sharp and colorful, showing calories burned, elapsed time, and heart rate, with a continuous timeline graph of your heart rate in each zone. The heart rate zones for either readout are easy to customize, so you can set your zone boundaries wherever you want.

We previously used Garmin bicycle units that did not include heart rate readouts or web site graphing - we like the Polar units much better.

One note - the straps on the OH1 unit are very fiddly. I would prefer a single stretchy band that pulls tight through the plastic guides and secures with a Velcro tab. I modified our units by cutting the strap loose on one side of the mount to create a single long strap that can be loosened to put the OH1 over your hand, then pulled tight to create a good skin contact on your wrist, forearm or upper arm. It turns out the plastic strap guides are tight enough so a Velcro tab is really not needed to keep the strap secure, although a Velcro tab would still be useful to secure the loose end of the strap. Polar does not mention wrist mounting, but if you are wearing a long sleeve jersey or a cycling jacket the OH1 is easier to wear on the back or inside of your wrist. It works fine in either location.

title: Wow! Absolutely love, love, love it!!!
text:
This is the most amazingly satisfying electronics product I have ever bought. The features are many and easy to learn. I especially enjoy some of the audio and video adjustment features:
Audio: DRC setting helps bring up quieter sounds while controlling loud peaks. Great for taming those annoying audio surges in 'background' music or battle scenes, etc. The Dialog feature lets you adjust the dialog perception so that you can hear the voices better over the background sounds in the soundtracks.
Video: You can adjust the Sharpness, Brightness, Contrast, Gamma, Hue, Chroma Level and BNR (block noise reduction). Each one has several levels to choose from and you get to sample it as it adjusts, so you can skip back and forth and compare the difference before you decide what to settle on.
The USB mode has great, easy to navigate menus. You can also record to your thumb drive from a CD that you are playing. There is a choice of different bit rates to do this and you can record individual tracks or all tracks. Very user-friendly menus for all these choices.
This unit has too many features to list, especially for someone like me, who is not quite fluent in tech terminology. Suffice it to say that it performs all the functions beautifully, the manual is very user-friendly and not only tells you how to adjust/change the various settings, but also explains the technical terminology in real English, so you know what those settings actually do when activated.
I do love the region-free feature too. But for me, this is more ho-hum, since I already owned one - a far inferior quality Philips one.
About the only thing I can think of to improve the user-friendliness of this product would be to have an alphabetized index in the manual. But, since it's only a 61 page manual, it's not such a big issue overall.
Another suggestion I would have would be to allow it to record audio from DVDs also. So often, the audio track on a DVD sounds so much better than the soundtrack that is published on CD (i.e.: Brassed Off, Eyes Wide Shut), although I recognize there may be some copyright issues with that concept.

I have wanted a soft-release button for my Fuji X-T3 for a while and finally decided to treat myself. I chose this one as it specifically names my camera as one model it supports. It seems to work well so far.

As a soft release button it works well. What makes it a worthwhile accessory though is the reduction in camera shake it offers when pressing down versus the effort needed without it. The reduced camera shake is what I think is meant in the description by “no wobbling”. The button itself exaggerates the play in the shutter button on the camera which is fairly loose (not firmly restrained from slight jiggling).

There are two of these little buttons in the pack. Properly installed, I suspect the second will never be needed. Both come in individual pouches and include a rubber gasket. Because if the size of the gasket, I’d recommend using a pair of tweezers to put it on the post - if you drop it there’s a fair chance you’ll lose it.

From the product listing’s photos this button looks convex. It is not - it is concave.

So far I am not unhappy with this soft release button. It fits my camera properly and it looks nice. It speeds shooting and reduces camera shake when pressing the button which for me is a win.

title: Really PREMIUM sound!
text:
I've heard a lot of wonderful things about the Sony noise cancelling sets like these, and let me tell you: it isn't just hype. The sound quality is excellent, and the noise cancelling is eerily amazing. I put it on my wife and kids with the noise cancelling off and then turned it on to demonstrate, and you can see each them suddenly smile like "whoa". Like my Sony studio headphones I use professionally for work, the actual fidelity of the sound it reproduces is excellent, and the microphone for calls is excellent despite being up by my ears and so far from my mouth (other bluetooth headphones I've tried were good for music only, the mic being up by my ears wasn't good enough to isolate my voice from ambient sound, but this definitely does a great job).
The app gives a ton of control beyond what I expected to really customize the experience. For example, I have mine set to auto-pause if the headphones are removed, and to turn off noise cancelling when it detects me speaking to someone, and then resume playback when the headphones are removed/replaced. These features are all customizable, as well as many more. But you need the app. And this is where the cons come in:
1) You really need the app to get the most out of this. I was thinking about pairing this with my desktop and/or TV, but without the app you have far less control, and to be honest I couldn't even get it to pair with my phone using just Bluetooth alone. There seems to be a way according to the instructions, but I couldn't figure it out without using the app installed.
2) For a set that costs this much, I'm surprised at how scuffed up it got after one fall from about 3 feet next to my car. Including pictures. This happened the day I got it. I'm not sure if there's anything that can be done about that, pavement is hard to recover from if anything is dropped, but it's something to keep in mind if you're spending this much money on a gadget. My studio headphones have been roughed around for years and held up fine.

All in all, I'd give it 5 stars if it weren't so reliant on the app to get the features going and/or more resilient to being dropped. Feels like I should deduct one for that. But as far as features and sound quality go, this is a solid 5 out of 5.
