title: Two-Thirds of what you need.  Not a switch.
text:
I bought the ERL3 to replace a [[ASIN:B019Z8T9J0 Qotom Q190G4 Intel Celeron Processor 3215U Dual Core Processor Barebone Mini PC]] which I'd loaded pfSense onto, when the latter died. (They replaced the broken bits, but it took over a month.) My goal was to improve my network security over my [[ASIN:B00FB45SI4 ASUS AC1900 Wi-Fi Router [RT-AC68U]]], which was fantastic but doesn't block outgoing IoT (internet of things) calls from marginally-trusted devices such as IP cameras or security systems.
The ERL3 can do a LOT. Of course, so can a box of semiconductors. The trick is in, how easily. And with the ERL3, the answer is, well, not very.
And how quickly? Again, not very.
You see those four Ethernet ports? You're thinking, one WAN and three LAN switched together via rules.
Nah, not the case. What you have is a monitoring port - it really does nothing a mere mortal cares about - and three assignable ports. Those three can be WAN, DMZ, subnet 1, etc, but there's a wrinkle... there's no switching hardware in the ERL3.
Switching hardware? Well, this means that if you want packets coming in on eth1 to be copied to eth2... in other words, you want devices on the middle port to be able to talk to the far right... well, that slows this puppy WAY down. I get around 700Mbps with really simple rules. A [[ASIN:B00N0OHEMA TP-Link 5-Port Gigabit Ethernet Web Managed Easy Smart Switch (TL-SG105E v2.0)]] will bridge subnets (and VLANs) far better, easily handling over 1Gbps.
So really this is a powerful router for connecting your LAN to the WAN (internet) with lots of control and power, a good Web UI, naming and additional services, but you'll still want a good (cheap) managed switch for a full solution at high speed.

text:
I rarely give a 5 star rating but this aperture control deserves no less. It functions exactly as described. It is well made from quality materials. It does not appear that the manufacture tried to pinch pennies to get the cost down, no plastic.

It has the heft you would expect from a solid build.

It attached easily to my Nikor 18-55 lens and gave me total manual control of the aperture.

What this device does do:
-Allows you to manually control the aperture on any Nikon F mount lens that is installed in a backwards orientation on any make of camera using a reversing ring - this is just the control. This will not connect your lens to the camera body. You need to purchase a reversing ring specific to your camera body for that.
-Allows you to add filters to the lens that is mounted backwards on your camera.
-Allows you to use a standard (52mm) lens cap on the lens that is mounted backwards on you camera.

What this device does not do:
-There are no optic elements to this device - no glass or lens.
-With this device installed on your lens none of the automatic features of the lens will function. You will need to focus manually.
-This device does not connect a lens to a camera. You need a reversing ring for that that is specific to your camera's mounting base.

If you are just starting out with this type of macro set up you would need to purchase:
-A reversing ring that is specific to the mount of your camera and sized for any brand lens (52mm, 58mm, etc). A reversing ring allows you to attach any brand lens to your specific brand of camera in a reverse, or backwards, position. You can use a Nikon lens on a Canon body or what ever. Just select the correct body mount for the reversing ring along with the correct lens threads for the lens that you want to use.
-A lens, one you have or any other lens....... If you use a lens that has a manual aperture control then you don't necessarily need the device that this review is about, but it does allow you to add a lens filter and lens cap to the lens that is mounted backwards.
-A lens filter to protect the optics on the lens.
-A lens cap.

Would I recommend this reversing ring? Absolutely!

title: Smooth, efficient--a great upgrade over a standard mouse!
text:
I bought this mouse for my husband as a Christmas gift. For the most part, he and I are not into technical gadgets, but I thought that a cordless mouse would be more convenient for our home computer setup, and after doing a lot of online research, I decided to go with the Logitech MX. This product looks/feels unlike any mouse I've ever used before. Although it may seem a bit unwieldy at first, however, it actually fits very comfortably into the hand and feels very natural. As other reviewers have mentioned, the mouse glides smoothly over any surface, no mouse pad needed, and the scrolling ability is amazing--there are actually two scrolling modes, one with zero resistance, the other the more traditional click-type scrolling for those who prefer moving more slowly. The mouse has some great features, too, some of which I have yet to fully explore. My favorite is the little search button that lets you highlight text to be searched and then access your favorite search engine automatically. I also like the thumb buttons which allow you to switch back and forth amongst windows and applications, although I have found these to be a bit less intuitive, thereby taking a little longer to get the hang of. Finally, I've been impressed by the battery life--we've had the mouse set up for weeks now and haven't had to change it yet (granted, we average only 2-3 hours computer time per day at home).

The only thing that stopped me from giving this mouse five stars was that we experienced problems during setup. Although everything seemed fine at first and the mouse began working immediately, the SetPoint software that came with the mouse wrecked havoc with our computer, causing a major crash. Someone more computer-savvy might have been able to resolve this issue immediately, but DH and I lost two days to trying to figure out how to correct the problem. Eventually, however, we were able to start the computer in safe mode, delete the SetPoint software, and reload the newest version of the software from the Logitech web site, and we have experienced no further problems since that time. So, as long as you are willing to accept the possibility of some initial installation difficulties, I highly recommend this cool little mouse.

You don't need one for this. You sync the device with your computer. There's no subscription or any charge outside of the price of the band. It lets you know how many steps you have walked, how many miles you have gone, and how many calories you have burned, as well as the date and time. title: Vendor of excellence!
text:
This is a compact radio about as tall and wide but only half as thick as a pack of cigarettes. The case is solid and sturdy. It's a good looking radio.

It won't bring in the weak signal distant AM stations (See Addendum below), like, say, a car radio sometimes will, but it's fine for local reception within a reasonable distance on both AM and FM. (FM reception is as good as any other radio.) (At least that was my experience the morning I used it when I put it through its paces.) Comes with an earphone jack or use the built in speaker. It has a collapsible antenna for FM and an internal antenna for AM. Sound quality is excellent on speaker and earphone. It's digital all the way so you won't spend eternity thumbing around with drifting stations.

The unit comes with instructions...which IF followed will let you program the little booger to your heart's content. I had NO problem and it was actually fun. All sorts of dandy features. As many and more as you'll find on a good car radio. In short, it's great for its purpose. Because of the design I would expect that if you take care of it, it will outlast you. I would suggest that if you plan on storing it for any length of time to remove the batteries and put them and the radio in a sandwich bag.

Now to the best part. Here's what the seller promises above.... "We are committed to providing you excellence and satisfaction.
If you are not happy with our product, we will refund 100% of your money..."

My radio came in missing a battery spring (I got mine to work for a test spin by robbing a spring from an old TV remote). So I contacted the seller the day it arrived which just happened to be Christmas eve. On Christmas day I found a reply in my inbox from Carrie Vondior.

Said she, "I am so sorry that your order of our AM/FM Radio arrived with a missing spring part on the battery compartment. You must have been sent a "lemon."
I have facilitated a new delivery for you for free! There will be no need to return the product that has an issue. We do not want to inconvenience you in sending back the said product."

We exchanged a couple of more emails and I can't begin to tell you how impressed that I was with Carrie and their whole enterprise. As refreshing as a snow cone in the desert. If you have ever been left high and dry or kinda mad because of lousy customer service before you'll understand my delight with my good experience.

I don't know their situation, but I expect that they are a small time vendor. They have GREAT heart and a business model that can not fail. They actually CARE about their customers.

As we all know the product is only as good as the warranty. As I write, my shiny new replacement is on my desk between me and you. It came in today as promised. And, the bonus was that I got to meet with THE seller herself through the email. What a wonderful person and company ethic.

Long story short, order with confidence and use with confidence. Thanks Carrie Vondior. You did good! Good product. Great customer service! Five stars for Carrie! (The radio too!)

Addendum: I'm going to leave the part in there about the "distant" stations because it was true the other day. However...I couldn't resist! When I stopped writing I plugged batteries into my new radio and guess what? I'm listening to WSM, home of The Grand Ole Opry. That AM powerhouse rascal is like 300 miles distant from here and the best test for AM reception in my situation. So this night it's pulling in the "distant" stations!! Well now! Looks like I just found myself a GREAT camping radio! A campfire and The Grand Ole Opry in my shirt pocket. Money well spent!

title: Excellent quality and functionality
text:
[[VIDEOID:93362313a270b063085f7e3a8762f80d]] I tried to think of anything that I would change to improve this sports duffle bag, and the only thing I would suggest would be to add a mesh water bottle holder into the fixed end compartment. That's the only thing I would change because with the exception of no water bottle holder, this gym duffle is the most well thought out and best made sports bag I've ever seen.

The bag is roomy enough to handle everything you'd need to carry to a game, to the gym, or for a weekend getaway, and it's also sized just right to work as an airline carry on bag and it fits into an overhead compartment. It's made of water repellant polyester and the material is thick enough to protect your clothing or gear as well as to keep everything dry regardless of weather conditions.

While most of the storage capacity is inside the roomy main compartment, the bag does offer several storage compartments on the exterior as well. There's a zippered compartment on the front that measures approximately 7.25" x 7.25" where you could easily fit sunglasses, boarding passes or other travel documents, and there are zippered storage compartments on each end of the bag as well.

One end compartment is fixed, and the other one has extra fabric lining that allows it to expand inwards towards the main compartment, so you can use this one to stash smelly or dirty clothes and shoes away. Putting dirty smelly shoes, clothes, and towels in the expandable compartment keeps grime and odors away from clean clothes or gear in the main compartment, and there are two air vents on the outside to let the dirty or wet things get ventilation.

Inside the main compartment there's a zippered compartment that measures approximately 6" x 3.5 that would work well to store keys, lip balm, wallet, cell phone, or other small items while you work out, and the main compartment has plenty of room for clothes or other gear as I hope my video shows. You can carry the bag by the carry handles which Velcro together and are comfortable to carry, or by the adjustable shoulder strap which has a thick adjustable shoulder pad. The straps are all heavy duty webbing and the attachments are heavy duty plastic with metal clips that won't slip off so the bag can handle some weight in it and still be comfortable to carry.

All stitching is even, tight, and well reinforced at pressure points throughout the bag. Zippers function well and all pulls have plastic handles to make them easy to operate. The bag will keep your clothes are gear dry as well as keep dirty shoes and clothes away from the clean ones and has an interior that's easy to wipe clean. I'm very impressed and pleased with the design, materials, construction and functionality of this sports bag, and frankly I am surprised that it doesn't cost more than it does.

This sports duffle bag was provided at no cost by the manufacturer for evaluation and review.

(i HAVE TO SAY WITH OVER 15 INTERNET / SMART DEVICES THE LITTLE CM820 Aaris 8x4 Surfboard held up for over 2 years that's what i bought from Amazon as it was the exact same as what Time Warner provided us when we still were being charged for modem rentals . Now Spectrum does not charge but I wanted better coverage during peak hours and i hope this will do the trick the Internet provider was very sure i would see a big difference )

Now on wireless I get 71 and 6 on Spectrum's own speed test site so I am happy , plus a lot less congestion at peak hour times I hope as I have owned it less than 1 hour . But i listened to another reviewer on Amazon and he broke it down like this on how to set it up and get the fastest install through your cable company/ or internet provider
1. Do not unplug your old modem yet (I found this helped as they want to see your old connection 1rst)
2. Take a picture of the MAC and Serial # (I only needed the MAC # which is on a sticker on the underside of the modem ) The only reason i say take a pic is so you can enlarge the #s as they are small . I am 41 and still have good vision but bigger still helps and you want to get it correct the 1rst time !!!
3. Call your provider mine was Spectrum / Time Warner , I had choices and went to internet , then a prompt said i do not see an outage in your area , next was chose another ... Replacing a modem ... Getting support with installing a new modem . I chose that one
4. Once I gave the Provider Rep my MAC# i asked if he needed the serial # he said no and by then it was working , Well as he was waiting to get a signal i switched out the modems , plugged the new 1 into my surge protector , then hooked up the cable wire and the cat 5 from the Router i have and when I finished i had internet . I told him its all lit up and i checked to see if amazon or other web pages would open and yes , Then he said let me verify it is working fully on my end and 1 minute later completed . title: Earbuds were DOA, but Jaybird made it right (and then some)!
text:
Ok, the basics:
- They arrived promptly.
- They were packaged well enough to protect the item well; yet not require me to be a wrestler or an origami grand master to get at them. Also, I didn't feel like I was killing every tree on the planet, nor creating so much plastic trash with packing materials to become an environmental nightmare (that's always a nice detail).
- The product looked great. Just like the photos, sleek black with grey buttons and connector covers that were simple to spot and use.

The details:
I purchased these when they were on sale, and didn't open the box and use the ear-buds for several weeks. When I finally did, the setup was simple and very easy to manage. Unfortunately, they began to malfunction. I contacted tech support at Jaybird, which was ALSO easy. I didn't have to manage an endless maze of voice menus constantly telling you "did you know you can find help on our website?".

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

On that note, I have to digress for a moment. Dealing with a call management system that's set up as a means of insulating the client from the vendor is a pet peeve for a few reasons:

1) It's completely obvious that the translation for "Did you know we have a website?" is, "We'd really rather brush off this call, and not waste our support technicians' time doing, um, support. Please hang up, and go play with your browser." It makes the customer service department seem like they're either cowardly, understaffed, or just lazy.

2) It is nearly always a waste of time to do so. I think most of us are bright enough to search through an FAQ page to look up an issue which was common enough to solve ourselves. I don't want to wait on hold before just seeing if my device is plugged in, or assembled as the instructions describe.

3) Lastly, even if the previous two reasons didn't exist, I'm the client. I gave you my money and purchased your product. If I want to speak to a human being versus arguing with a voice recognition system or dredging through your online documentation… I should be able to do so. Expecting you to stand behind your product is not unreasonable.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Now, all of that said - I had NONE of those concerns with Jaybird. I reached a pleasant, professional human voice almost immediately. They said, "Hello, my name is Mikey. What can I do to help you today?". Even better, it was a person here in the United States. I didn't have to wrangle with any language issues, cultural confusion, or regretting doing business with a company who sends jobs overseas!

Mikey was on top of the problem as soon as I explained my symptoms. He asked me to provide my proof of purchase (easy enough with Amazon). Then he arranged an RMA, emailed me all the details I needed to send the defective product back, and sent me an email documenting everything we discussed in case I needed to look it up. Further, since my buds were now discontinued, they replaced them with the next model UP at their expense (they didn't even grumble).

My first item may have been defective, but they stood behind it 100%. They replaced it very promptly, and with a newer, better product to boot. I could not be happier. Sometimes it takes something going wrong to show you whether or not you chose the right product and vendor to spend your money on. I would certainly do so with Jaybird again without reservation, and would recommend them wholeheartedly. Oh, and if you read this, thanks again Mikey!!

title: My first Chromebook
text:
I'm probably being stingy only giving this four stars: the truth is I just hate that you don't really own something that you pay $300 for. They won't let you even use this thing if you're not signed on to a WiFi AP connected to the Internet. And then you need a Google account. Yeah, I can fake yet another one, but I shouldn't have to. So I sort of have a grudge against the OS that won't allow me to give this five stars.

But the truth is, the latest iteration of Windows is so bad now that I can't say it's really any better. Microsoft has jumped on the Google/Apple bandwagon with their own app store, misleading apps that are free until you go to use them, wanting to track your every move, restarting your machine and installing updates without your consent, etc.

Truthfully, though, I like this a lot better than I expected, including the OS. It is surprisingly much like Windows (I guess MS had most of those basic UI things already figured out). And it mostly works. I mean, this is like a secondary machine just for browsing the Internet when the real computer is in use. I'm not trying to go this lightweight...I mean, you could with a good NAS, but it's not super smooth to get network shares working as well as they do with Windows.

But browsing is snappy and quick. But you're stuck with Chrome, I guess, which mostly is fine, but why can't I really get it to take me seriously that I never want notifications from any website? Ever.

Enough about the OS. Everyone is talking about the screen. Honestly, I went into this with a bias because so many people were complaining about it, but I just don't see the problem. In fact, I forgot all about it until my third session or so. I wonder if the complainers are trying to watch movies on it from across the room while laying in bed or something. Call me old fashioned, but I have a TV for that. Yes, if this was a TV, it would be super annoying whenever you're not looking at it square on, but when I'm just sitting like a normal person with this on my lap or on a table in front of me, it's just fine. If I'm constantly adjusting my position height, then it might start getting annoying, because it does lose a lot at an angle.

Oh yeah, if you want to watch movies with this, there is an HDMI port. Use a TV...

What is great? The touchpad. This is the fist computer in years - maybe ever - that I haven't turned off the tap to click feature. Even being this big, I haven't really had any false positives with tapping. It does have a "button" built in (you can physically push down on the lower left corner), but no right button, so you have to do the two-finger tap for a right click. I mean, I guess that's not really my preferred method, either, but I'm not complaining because the touchpad is super smooth.

It almost seems like for such a thin computer, it would feel smoother if it was smaller length- and width-wise, but then of course the monitor would have to be smaller. Regardless, as is, it's still a fantastic browsing computer. There are still some issues with it wanting to act like a phone (an example being that Teamviewer won't let me access the lower portion of my remote computer (the taskbar), presumably because it thinks the Chromebook is a phone. Another thing is that Plex wants money for its app to work because it thinks it's a phone...not that I want to watch movies on it, but that was part of my test).

Anyway, my only qualms with this thing are related to the OS and the software, privacy, and ownership issues because of the OS. And even I am more okay with all that stuff than I thought I would be. The hardware is very good and the monitor doesn't bother me at all for normal computer use. I am actually impressed.

There was a sub-rating feature here to rate the touch screen. There is no touch screen. Who is QAing these product listings?

I have several similar (typically larger) metal power strips in my garage and basement, which greatly simplify whatever I have going on. I mount (often with zip ties) securely and there's always an outlet handy. I never need to "rob Peter to pay Paul" or guess what plug is no longer needed. From time to time I reorganize, but before long I'm out of available outlets, and it's hard to tell which ones are battery backed up and which ones can be used for high current devices (that would kill battery life). I got a couple of these, mounted to my desks metal legs, and marked one for being on the battery (I actually use colored electrical tape with red being my code for battery backed up and yellow for not--good luck with neither!).

All of the above speaks more to the usefulness of this type of power strip. In use this one gets everything right:

1) there are ample outlets (anything less than 8 is useless to me)
2) the outlets are spaced/pivoted to allow for various "wall warts"

title: Logitech Eliminates Strain and Improves Precision
text:
Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse is one of the better computer accessories I have used and it offers a noticeable improvement compared to traditional computer mice. Its unique shape makes it much more comfortable and a no- sliding- necessary design eliminates the need to drag your mouse across a flat surface to move the computer pointer on your screen. To move the pointer, all you do is move the large, red marble trackball. There is less strain on the fingers and wrist, making for a more comfortable experience.

Besides the added comfort, another advantage of the Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse is that it requires less space than a traditional mouse. Because this mouse is stationary and doesn't need to be dragged across a desk or other surface, it can fit into many small spaces. You don't need to make room to drag it, so it can be placed in tight quarters. This is great for those who work in offices with limited desk space.

The Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse offers four buttons to use for clicking. The large tabs on each side of the mouse are used for the usual right and left click functions and then there are two smaller tabs right above each of the larger tabs that are used for various functions. These two small tabs can be programmed to perform several things, and many will likely program them to scroll since this Logitech mouse doesn't have a scroll wheel. But the tabs can be programmed for other things, too. Since I don't necessarily need to scroll, my small tabs have been programmed as browser back and forward buttons. This makes life a little easier because I no longer need to move my mouse to the top of my screen and click the forward and backward arrows in the upper left corner. I just click my small left tab to go back and my small right tab to go forward.

The Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse is a marked improvement compared to the standard mouse, but I admit that it does take some getting used to. Having used a traditional mouse for most of my computer- using years, I had grown accustomed to sliding my mouse across the desk surface. Thus, when I started to use the Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse, I kept sliding it around on my desk also, even though I knew this mouse didn't need to be dragged. It took some time to break this habit. It also took time to get used to the sensitivity of the trackball. The slightest movement sends your pointer flying and when I first started to use this mouse, I would continually underestimate the precision of the Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse. My movements of the trackball were far too extreme. The pointer would soar across my computer screen, even though I would swear I wasn't moving the trackball very much. It is a very sensitive device that almost seems too loose at first because it moves so freely and with such little effort.

Compared to a traditional mouse, the Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse has many great things to offer and it is a mouse I am happy I took the time to try. It is superior to the traditional model in most areas, reducing pain and strain and offering greater accuracy and an easy grip. It does take time to get used to, but it is worth it in the long run and even those who initially resist the change will be happy, in due time, that they made the switch to Logitech.

title: Slow Initial Charge; Odd Setup; Wildly Inaccurate Initial Location
text:
This SAMSUNG SMARTTHINGS TRACKER [SM-V110AZWAATT] is designed for wide-area GPS tracking. That is, you set a home location, and then when you travel away from home, the SmartThings app can show you on a street map where the device is currently located. I wanted something for in-home tracking of an oft-misplaced set of keys, and this is the wrong device for that purpose.

Since I was already using the SmartThings app to control my TV with Alexa, it was fairly simple to add the Tracker to the app, and to register it. I was surprised to learn that the Tracker came with one year of free tracking service (provided by something called ziptracker, I think), which presumably means that one has to pay for the service after that.

My experience with the SmartThings app is that it is quirky, and it proved so again during setup. Even though I began the Tracker device setup on my iPad, the setup process switched on its own to my Samsung Galaxy cellphone. Go figure.

SmartThings registered my Tracker with the service, but when I sent a signal to record the Tracker’s current location, the location was far, far off. The map showed the Tracker to be in a wholly different neighborhood from my actual home!

Probably the wildly inaccurate initial location was caused by the signal’s reporting from a Comcast or Verizon broadcast tower located in that spot--I’ve had trouble using other locator services (e.g., Find My iPhone) for this reason. However, the inaccurate location makes me wonder how useful the device would be for tracking children or pets.

One final complaint about the device is that it took a couple of hours for the initial charge. I don’t know how often it requires recharging. (My Tracker went straight into the hazardous waste recycle bin.)

NOTE: I’ve had some success at finding the oft-misplaced keys with [[ASIN:B0732P113R TrackR Pixel]]. It has a reasonably loud location signal, and a battery that lasts fairly well, so that the battery isn’t always dead when I need to locate the keys.

title: This camera is awesome!
text: This camera is awesome!  There are very, very few things I can say bad about this camera, so I'll concentrate on the good:  First, I love the battery compartment and operating voltage.  While some camera use 2 or 3 batteries, this camera uses 4 AA batteries.  Also, the voltage it runs on is 4.3.  I am a firm believer in NiMH batteries compared to alkaline or lithium IF AND ONLY IF your device can operate well using them.  I use NiMH batteries almost exclusively now.  Each battery is about 1.2V, so with 4 fully-charged batteries, I'm pushing 4.8 volts.  I have left my batteries in this thing for a month at room temperature with no problems whatsoever.  You have to really try to drain this camera, but it can be done, especially if you use the flash a lot.  I use this camera for my job regularly, and it's never let me down.  Next, the memory capability is great, too.  I am running a 16GB Class 6 Transcend card, and I can record over 1.5 hours of HD video!  I can take over 10,000 photos, too.  It's awesome with the Zoombrowser software.  Just hook up the cable and dowload your photos.  I like Picasa software from Google to edit my photos, too.  Picasa does slow your computer down, so be prepared if you use it.  Forget about the shooting modes--I don't even know how to use them all even tho I have read the manual cover to cover.  I just set it to "auto" usually and go.  The manual is really well-written, in my opinion.  I bought the underwater housing for this camera, and it's great, too.  I priced a new one of these cameras the other day on Amazon, and they wanted almost $1000 for this camera.  I couldn't believe it, because I paid about $300 for mine new.  There are several used ones on here for about $400.  It's a good deal for sure at $400, but there may be better values out there for $1000. title: We Love To Rub A Dub In This Tub
text:
We purchased this product before we were expecting, knowing that it was neutral gendered and would be perfect for a boy or a girl. When we had our first child, a 9 lb, 11 oz baby girl, I was SO nervous! I didn't know a thing about babies. My eldest sister helped me give her her first bath and complimented our whale tub. She said it was so nice that the green padding in the base would help prevent baby from slipping. By the third bath, I had it down.

As the weeks have gone on, our little one has really loved her tub. She began holding her head up at 4 days old and was doing so independently within a month of her birth. She loved kicking and splashing in her tub. She has never cried in the bath. We use a turtlemeter thermometer and she thinks of it like a little toy with which to play.

I would recommend this tub with the seat in it for a newborn baby up to about 12 lbs. Once our daughter was 13 lbs, she has trouble staying warm in the tub with the seat attached. It simply wasn't deep enough for her while she was lying down and she only got her bottom half wet unless I poured water over her, and the chilly air would then make her cold.

With the seat out, she needs to be sitting on her own so there was a two month gap where we did not use her tub, and instead bathed her with me in the big tub.

Once she was a successful sitter, we returned her to this tub for warmer nights, so she could sit and play in the water. She loves it!

After a bath, I would recommend not only using the drain in the tub, but turning this whale tub upside-down and and then turning it from side-to-side to drain it, as the water tends to get trapped beneath the green padded area. You can also remove the seat to clean under it. Using dish soap and a scrub daddy sponge, I am able to quickly clean the tub in-between uses.

The weakness of this mount is that the mounting bars that are screwed into the wall, and to which the bracket is attached, are too short (18"). title: LOVE!!!!  After 3 years, love it so much I bought the 2TB for more storage!
text:
Firstly, let me say that, being a closet tech-geek. I have owned countless hard drives over the last two decades. I own stock in Seagate, so I purchased [[ASIN:B000ND75C0 Seagate FreeAgent 500 GB 3.5-Inch USB 2.0 Hard Drive ST305004FDA1E1-RK]], (only the 1TB version) from them and, to my dismay, it just stopped responding to power after a couple of months (I got it working, but it was a let-down for sure with the stock thing and all). Then, I ordered this really, really expensive, crappy paperweight here: [[ASIN:B006Y5UV4A WD My Passport 1TB Portable External Hard Drive Storage USB 3.0 Black]] (same basic drive, just an earlier model no longer offered, I think), and was ready to use it for skeet practice in no time. I hated that I needed to use their software to access the data on the drive. As for the actual software, it was a total PITA. But it didn't matter because, within weeks, the damned thing crashed for good--and I wasn't even doing anything weird with it. :|

So, about three years ago, I stumbled upon the Fantom Greendrive and was, at first, kind of put-off by the apparent size (it's actually not as big as the Seagate, it turns out). I really wanted something small and portable. But, after all those issues with other drives, I really, REALLY wanted something RELIABLE. I first did some research, took a chance and ordered this drive.

DEAR GOD. IT IS MARVELOUS.

That was, as I've said, three years ago. Three years of constant use: heavy data transfer, being knocked around (even dropped on the ground a couple of times), never defragged (I got lazy cos' it's so reliable), never disk-checked, numerous power-loss and disconnection incidents....nothing can kill it! It hums along nicely no matter what you throw its way.

You don't have to ever worry about unmounting it before you turn off the power--you just unplug it and go. It's never failed me and, to be honest, that makes it better than one particular husband, in my book (the second is doing quite nicely, thank you).

The "Green" is for:

---Firstly, it doesn't take a lot of power. Nice.

---Secondly, despite being dropped a few times, it hums nicely and quietly. No loud grinding at all. I always have to check to see if it's on (which is easy because a green light shines through the grate of the front to let you know the power is on).

---Thirdly, if you have it plugged in but haven't accessed it in a while (like fifteen minutes), it will initiate a semi-hibernation, then go into a bit of a deeper hibernation after like a half hour or so (never timed it, but it's cool when it does it). So if you hear a click and a sound like the motor is clicking off, that's what you're hearing. Cooler still, the minute you click to access the drive it's ready to go--little to no wait.

It's also very fast. As drives go, mine is almost full and THREE YEARS OLD and, like I said, never defragged, yet it still runs faster for data transfer than my brand new laptop...which makes me wonder about my laptop. ;/

I actually love this drive so much, I figured with my bad luck, one day it's finally going to give up on me and quit for good. So, about a year ago I purchased the newer 2TB drive[[ASIN:B002XITVCA Micronet Technology Fantom GreenDrive 2 TB USB 2.0/eSATA Desktop External Hard Drive GD2000EUS]]for more space and extra backup. I love having the two of them because, unlike many products, Fantom keeps the peripherals consistent, so the power supplies (though upgraded to a one-piece rather than two-piece on the newer model) are interchangeable, as are the USB cables (though the 2TB, being newer, is obviously a 3.0 rather than a 2.0). Still, transferring data between the two is easy-cheesy and fast.

So, all in all, I have to tell you that, despite being an incurable tech-geek, this drive is honestly the best, most reliable, and durable piece of electronics equipment I've EVER owned.

title: Tomato Compatible and Cheaper Alternative to ASUS RT-AC66U
text:
I picked this router up at another online retailer as soon as I spotted it was on sale. I had my eye on the Tenda 1800/1801 routers for a while before that though, as these seem to be the only decent Gigabit / AC routers that are directly compatible with Tomato right out of the box, that don't break the bank!

My router is essentially the same thing as the much more expensive ASUS RT-AC66U, but with less memory. Having less memory on a router is not really the same thing as less memory on a computer. In other words, most people (including myself) will not notice the difference.

Hardware Look and Feel:
This Tenda sports the basic router design, and includes wall mounting screw holes that are 6” apart, and 3 movable antennas that are easy to install. There is lots of good ventilation on the sides and bottom, and a glossy white top. Altogether, the router seems will made, and doesn't feel cheap at all. Glad to say that it doesn't have a gimmicky cylindrical shape, or a stupid upright design, with an even more stupid non-adjustable plastic stand. I don’t mind at all that I can't take selfies next to my neat looking stylish black router to post on Facebook; Boring routers are just plain under-rated!

Stock Firmware:
I spent about 5-minutes poking around in the stock firmware before flashing to Tomato. To me the stock firmware seemed like an unpolished version of Asus firmware. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but why settle for stock when there is a specific version of the very stable, configurable, and admired Tomato USB written just for routers just like this! Enter Shibby K26RT-AC...

Tomato Flashing Process:
No feverish searching the internet for firmware “that will work” with your router, simply go to the Shibby download page, find the latest version for your router, download the compressed file, and unzip it.
Then unplug your WAN cable, open your routers firmware page, go to tools, upgrade, navigate to the folder your just unzipped, select the .TRX file, click upgrade, and wait about 10 minutes. Once it is done, you might want to do a factory reset in Tomato to clear the RAM.

That’s it people, no messing around with cumbersome flash utilities, no 30/30/30 resets in restore mode while holding your nose and saying the alphabet backwards in Pig Latin while crossing your fingers that you won’t brick your router. This one is as simple as it gets!

title: Perfectly ruggedized tablet!
text:
If you have read any of my other reviews, you know that I always tell you why I ordered the product. I also sometimes give a backstory. This one deserves both.

First, how I consider myself to be an authority on ruggedized computers. I have spent several years in the telecommunications industry. We always used ruggedized laptops and tablets in the field. And, as a police officer and paramedic, we also used these tools. Finally, I spent 13 years of my professional life as an information technology manager for the federal government. I supported all the branches that used this type of equipment in the field. So, I know this type of equipment from the user's standpoint, AND the support side.

This tablet from HOTWAV is exactly the type of equipment I would send out to the field with any operation, with confidence.

It should be noted that this device is heavy. It must be to endure all the abuse it takes. Anything less will wind up being repaired or trashed within a week of being deployed. I know. I have repaired or rebuilt countless machines that were not well suited for work in the field. The metal body (with heavy rubber guard) and Corning Gorilla Glass face make this device extremely durable. You'd have to intentionally abuse it to damage it. It's also highly water resistant. All ports are well sealed. Even the speakers are waterproof. The hand strap ensures that you won't accidentally drop your tablet when used.

I wanted a tablet like this to use in the field for my drone operations. I'm always outdoors, in all kinds of weather and often in very austere conditions. I needed a tablet that could stand up to the harshest of environments. This is the one.

Now, about the I.T. side of things. The RAM and ROM are excellent as is. And the ROM can be expanded up to 1TB by simply inserting a micro-SD card with the capacity you need. The octo-core processor is incredibly fast. It handles multitasking with ease. You can install the SIM card for any carrier you want, and the device is then service ready as a comms unit. The drone piloting business has gotten very complicated with the new legal requirements. Having cellular comms has become particularly important in that respect.

The Android 12 OS is very intuitive and full of features. Syncing this tablet to another Android device and duplicating all your apps and other features is effortless.

The display is bright and crystal clear, even in the brightest daylight. The front and rear 16MP cameras are good enough to serve most utilitarian needs. Granted, they don't match the quality images of most cell phones. But, this is not the sole purpose of this tablet. I've included a couple of shots with the camera to illustrate the clarity of the images. they're good enough for my purposes.

I am very pleased with this HOTWAV ruggedized tablet. I'm more than happy that I am adding it to my 'Drone Operations Go Kit'. In fact, my BIL is a crane operator and spends a lot of time sitting on his butt in the crane, waiting for his turn at the task at hand. He spends a lot of that time online. title: Good enough for my needs
text:
I don't have a lot of use for a laptop bag; I don't often take my computer out of the house. But when I do, the laptop-designed backpack I got as a perk with one of my computers has been fine for my needs. Nevertheless, having a messenger/briefcase style bag is probably a good idea, too. It's more professional-looking, and (probably) has more options for organizing whatever else I'd be needing in a business situation. So I ordered the Case Logic Laptop Messenger Bag, and I'm fairly well pleased with it.

The critical issue, to my way of thinking is: Will my laptop be well padded? The padding in the Case Logic bag seems sufficient to protect my computer from the normal range of bumps and jiggles, though I don't think I'd like to drop it. But then, how many soft cases -- ones that aren't encased in a foot or more of foam, that is -- could prevent damage under those circumstances? Laptops are like kids, you can't protect them from everything.

The next most important issue for me is: does the case have sufficient space, sufficiently well-organized, for me to carry the other items I need? In my case, an external hard drive, power cord, papers, a notebook, pens and pencils, a digital camera, flash memory, and yeah, my iPod if I want to listen to some tunes. Yes, the Case Logic provides all this and more, with a great many compartments. The only quibble I have with the design is that the compartment that holds a lot of these things only opens from the top. It would be far more useful if it unzipped around three sides so that the user would have easier access to things, particularly when the laptop is in place and the case is more rigid.

I'm not crazy about the neon green trim, but honestly, no matter what trim color is used, someone will hate it, so it's fine, it won't kill me. And the front flap really should be held down with a piece of velcro. As it is, it flaps around as you walk. It's not a security problem since most everything is zipped into the case, but it's annoying.

The real turd in the punchbowl is the strap. Man, this is the worst strap I've ever been forced to wrestle with. I still haven't figured it out, and am about halfway to wanting to just cut it off the case.

title: The best bang for you buck - bar none
text:
Let me start off by saying that I have used many, many different earbuds and headphones over the years, and these are by FAR the best bang for my buck in terms of quality, durability, and comfort. I've always managed to land jobs where I'm able to listen to audio content throughout my workday, and have consequently spent most of my working hours with at least one earbud tucked into my ears.

I thread these down to my pocket where they are plugged into my iPod full time. No matter how much running, walking, lifting, jumping or moving around I do (and I work as a package delivery guy, which means hundreds of movements and ten miles of walking a day), these things take ages to wear out. Under normal use, I'm sure they'd never need replacing unless you managed to blow out the speaker somehow, or cause blatant damage to them. They don't cut in and out from wear on the jack end or on the headphone ends like some other earbuds, which will give way after being cranked around a bit.

Next, I have to address the comfort of the ergonomically shaped buds themselves. They are formed to fit into ear, with the speaker being offset from the center of the housing. On others, such as the classic white Apple earbuds, the round shape causes me some discomfort and soreness after hours of wear. But these are just fantastic. I wear them for up to 11 hours at a time with no discomfort whatsoever.

Finally, the sound quality. While an audiophile purist will say that they probably don't meet the highest standards in the land, they do a pretty good job. They stand up to much more expensive earbuds, and if you use the proper sized adapter for your ear (three sizes included), the speaker isolates sound very well, so you don't even need any noise-canceling feature. I wear them while driving a diesel truck with the doors open driving down the freeway, and I can hear every word of the audiobook I'm listening to. The treble is good. The bass is excellent for such an inexpensive earbud. And the overall sound quality is going to put other in-ear buds to shame.

For less than ten bucks, there is no better ear bud out there. I've owned three pairs over the last two years, and I would only have needed one if I didn't abuse them so much with daily use and extreme wear. If you want to try these, but would like to keep a microphone feature for hands-free calls, you can get some identical to these with in-line microphone in the Panasonic RPTCM125K model.

title: For the home cabling system
text:
Contrary to the picture, mine came with two removable label holders for the front of the device and 8 labels; 6 ports are notated on one label, giving you four sets of blank labels.

The bracket is made of strong, rigid plastic, and has the fairly convenient push/pull pins that connect it to the main box (much like American-style commercial fiber optic patch panels).

For a home telecom system, this is a compact and fairly easy to use option: terminating twisted pair cables one at a time is easier and less stressful than doing a commercial style patch panel, not to mention allowing more room for common homeowner mistakes, like not leaving a service loop. And if you get the right connectors, you can even do it without a punch-down tool. And, if you don't need all 12 ports for twisted pair, you could save some space by terminating other cables here as well.

For a full blown telecom closet with plenty of room and 12 or more cable runs of each type, I'd probably be looking at commercial components, but for a homeowner who wants a small, manageable system she can take pride in, this is a good choice.

title: Not bad, but ANNOYING pairing and audio interface
text:
I've had a number of Bluetooth headphones and the overwhelming majority of them have an "audio interface" that makes sense - some bare bones, some quite pleasant. This interface is in the form of sounds the relate to each of the functions - power on/off, paring, etc. These headphones have a TERRIBLE interface. When you power them on an annoyingly loud series of tones blares in your ear. The tones rise in pitch. When you continue to hold the power button, to access the paring mode, all you hear is an extremely brief, muffled tone. Apparently, the makers thought this was enough of a signal to indicate you're in paring mode. Believe me, it is NOT obvious at all. When you power off the headphones, you hear the same annoying loud series of tones. In this case, the tones do not decrease in pitch, which one might expect.

By comparison, the audio interface of my other Bluetooth headphones are a joy - unfortunately, they do not have volume controls or skip and rewind. When powering them on, a pleasant female voice says, "Hello", and when you enter pairing mode, the same voice says, "Ready to pair." When pairing is established, the voice says, You're connected", then tells me how much charge I have - either full, medium or low. These Cootree headphones do none of that. You'll be lucky if you're able to tell if they've been turned off properly.

In terms of sound quality, they're okay - nothing exceptional. In terms of fit, they're okay as well. Again, nothing exceptional. To my knowledge, they do not have an active noise cancelling function, other than what little noise they may happen to muffle by covering your ears. I mention this only because the rating form asks about it.

text:
This SR-C20A is an entry-level Yamaha soundbar made for the smaller room and bedroom. The attraction to this model was the 3rd speaker, a powered subwoofer.

Most compact soundbars create bass through passive radiators integral with the bar … i.e. 2 powered speakers separated in width by a baffled tube radiating through holes. So, there is no controllable bass other than passive baffle sound effects.

The SR-C20A has a controllable powered subwoofer and a dual baffle radiator combined to deliver controllable high, medium, and low tones. There are five modes: standard, stereo, game, movie, and a virtual surround mode. I just picked the one that sounds best. The virtual surround provides a sense of depth and separation to my hearing.

The SR-C20A soundbar replaced a no-name 2-speaker with baffles. The difference is sizable sound improvement.

title: Problematic For Me
text:
I needed something bigger than my external hard drive to back up my files on my home computer which runs on Windows XP. I'm just about of space and all I want to do is to move stuff from my computer to the Black Armor NAS data server. Looks like it just ain't gonna happen.

After finally getting the program to install I get to where I'm ready to transfer data. Everything is correctly hooked up hardware speaking. After clicking on the "Black Armor Backup" icon on my desktop I get to this point:

It asks: "What would you like to do?" I click on "Backup".
It says: "Data to backup selection" I click on "My Computer"

I click on the teeny tiny box in upper left hand corner that says "Disk 1". It automatically checks NTFS and FAT32.
I click on "next".

It gives me 2 options: to "Create New Backup Archive" or "Add to Existing Backup Archive". It has automatically selected "Create New Backup Archive" which is what I want since this is the first time I'm backing up my computer.

In the "Backup Location Box" I see a few numbers and letters plus the "browse" box. The "next" button is greyed out so I have to do something here...hhmmmm...
So I click on "Browse" and Click on "Download on Seagate Black Armor NAS".
Then apparently I'm supposed to generate a name though it already has one in the box.
I click on "Generate a Name" and the name in the box changes by adding "\Download\My Backup.tib
I click "O.K."

Then: The file name, location or format"\\blah\Download \MyBackup.tib" is not valid.
Please type the file name or location in the correct format.
(I've gotten several different error messages at this point, but somehow it later lets me go the blue box.)

It goes to a small blue box asking user name and password.
I type in the username and password that the paper sheet in the box which came with the NAS told me to use.
And then I get an error message saying exactly the following:

"\\generated name| Download is not accessible. You might not have permission to use this network resource. Contact the administrator of this server to find out if you have access permissions.

Multiple connections to a server or shared resource by the same user, using more than one user name, are not allowed. Disconnect all previous connections to the server or shared resource and try again.

O.K."

So, I'm not anywhere near being a technical expert at this stuff. All I want to do is move some data from box A to box B so that Box A has a lot more room to work with. I've wasted a lot of time messing with this and nowhere in the PDF manual can I find the solution. I got this for free from Vine so it's going back in the box and in the closet. I'm reconnecting my other external hard drive which never gives me problems.

July 28th - I had to uninstall BlackArmor software. It made it very difficult to boot my computer. I got a fuzzy gray/blue screen with BLACKARMOR plastered all over it. My mouse would not work properly. I could only go up and down if I moved my mouse back and forth horizontally. This was just too unnerving.

title: Aftermarket HUD's have come a long way since the first models
text:
I've have quite a few aftermarket heads up display devices in the past and I'm pretty happy with this device. The walls on the sides of the display do an excellent job of keeping the sun off the screen providing a good picture. This is something that all of my previous devices had a major draw back on. The price is great as well as this is one of the cheaper HUD devices that I've owned. I do not agree with the other posts saying that the instructions were non-existant as I found them very easy to follow and 1 page was more than enough to explain how to use the product. It does have a few downfalls. I will lay out the pro's and the cons below:

Pro's:
- walls on the side of the HUD make visibility even in sunlight
- cheap price
- tons of functionality
- Pretty accurate after "tweaking"
- Customizable

Con's:
- it's auto-brightness needs some updates as around dusk it will get super bright then dim and go back and forth which can be distracting
- the clock function is military only
- it has a proprietary plug (most have a micro-usb plug that goes into the OBDII port)
- Where the plug is located makes it hard to place on the dash
- the double sided tape is useless, (buy some 3m tape when ordering)

All in all, I really like it, just make sure to have a "window tint install kit" in order to install the film. You want to have that installed as smoothly as possible. The trick that I found for the best install is, power up the HUD, and put a piece of tape on your windshield at the top if the display so you know where you need to get your film installed at. Then turn everything off and place a towel over your dash. soak the area where your film will be installed. place the film on the windshield and then squeegee out all the liquid and bubbles. This will take some time, but it's super important to do it right. This will be the difference between having a good HUD install and a crappy one that you will not be happy with.

Samsung is NOT falsely advertising. The drive DOES in fact come with the advertised space it’s just that in order for it to work properly and perform optimally it requires approximately 10% of the capacity to be overprovisioned free space.

This is a really great SATA SSD for the price. It's perfect for storing games that have long load times without paying a fortune for an NVMe SSD of equal capacity. I highly recommend it for people like me who need more space for games, projects, and other things like that who want them to load quickly. You can get an HDD like a WD Black for cheaper but the loading times will be much longer and for those who dont like to wait for long load screens this is a perfect choice.

Also don't forget to enable RAPID mode. It uses RAM to speed up the programs & applications that you have been using recently. My CrystalDisk benchmark shows how fast it is with RAPID mode enabled.

title: No keystone, 720p native, bright.
text:
The Salange 7500 LUX Mini Home Projector is a barebones projector that provides good brightness, good focus, full-sized HDMI input, but not much else. Connect a FireTV or AndroidTV device to this projector and you have all of the "smart" features that you'll need.

So the good of this projector is that it is somewhat compact, not as small as the pico projectors, but small enough... it's about the size of a bread box (as the saying goes). The focus ring is fairly tight, meaning that once you find your focus, it won't move. The USB outputs enough amps to power a FireTV and overall, it is very straightforward to use.

The bad is that there is no keystone adjustment, not even the analogue kind that tilts the lens. The resolution is only 720p and I found that projecting at a shorter range of around 9 feet, I'm able to see every pixel on the projected image. At a longer distance, the pixels may meld together better.

In summary, this is a low-priced projector that will project an image through an HDMI input. If that's all you're looking for, this will work, but if you're looking for something that you may set up more permanently, this isn't it.

title: A 5-star product
text:
From the manual:

Intel Core i5-4210U (1.7GHz)
15.6" touchscreen (up to 1920x1080 resolution)
1TB HD
8GB Ram
1x Headphone, 1xLAN, 1xHDMI, 2xUSB 2.0, 1x USB 3.0, 1x SD Card
Weight: 5lbs

Overall, it's a very nice PC. Here's an overview of my thoughts:

Pros:
- Tech specs are exceptional for the price.
- Screen flips over 360 degrees to become a feasible tablet. It's fairly heavy in this mode, but it works. It's also possible to set it up on an angle, like you would do with a tablet case while watching movies. You won't need a case with this, however.
- Recovers from hibernation in a blink. Boots up quickly.
- Buttons are nicely recessed in the keyboard, so they don't trigger in alternate modes.
- Minimal amount of bloatware. Much nicer than most of the HPs I typically purchase, where it takes me a few hours to remove all of the trials and useless stuff. It comes with a program called "Asus Install" which can quickly remove (or add) some unwanted programs.
- Touchscreen and mouse are responsive.
- 16 GB of online storage is provided for free.
- Case is metalic, seems incredibly sturdy.

Cons:
- Windows 8.1 (don't get me started on this one...but I guess we don't really have too much choice in modern laptops)
- The tablet mode is significantly heavier than what you'll get with models with detachable screens.
- Number pad on the keyboard off-sets the mouse pad (which I find very annoying)
- No CD drive (I'm still old school in wanting this on any laptop)
- Sound quality is good, but buttons are awkwardly placed when using the computer in a different mode (i.e. as a tablet or movie screen).

All of the cons can easily be worked around, and are mostly personal quirks more than significant downsides. A 5-star laptop for sure.

title: Jewelry for the Ears
text:
[[VIDEOID:98df0cfb6b0daad3ff2eecda806c4550]] Without a doubt, these are the most beautiful headphones made today, and I suspect that while others may follow, I doubt they will come even slightly close to this stunning set.
A few years ago, HP introduced the Vivienne Tam Mini, a red floral netbook with a matching scarf and bag. The following year was a gold butterfly version, seen in the Sex in the City film.
These machines were ridiculously expensive for the specs, but you paid for the designer and design, not printed on the case, but using a process known as in-mold labeling.
They were beyond gorgeous.

When I saw these, I knew right away that it was in-mold labeling, and someone finally embraced what the 'big guys' have been slow to catch up on.
There are those of us that want a DESIGN, not just a color, that speaks to us when we choose things that are personal to us, like headphones. We don't always want it to be the version selected by the celeb du jour, either.

I also knew I HAD to have a set! It was a tough call between the clean throwback lines of the Tron-esque 'Orion' and the opposite celestial dreaming of 'Skyline', the later being the winner by a nose (ear?).

WOW! Visually, you simply can not get better. You'll want to wear them everywhere, and here is the best part, you CAN. Unlike noise-cancelling headphones, you can still hear a bit of what's going on around you. I can finally get great sound and not worry that I'm missing the doorbell/dog bark/police siren or whatever.

They are light, in a comfortable way, not a cheap way. They fit over the ear as opposed to surrounding it, so you will not get a strong bass unless you fit the band slide perfectly. Since it adjusts smoothly, no problem.
You also don't wind up looking like you're wearing a Princess Leia wig...the big donuts over each ear.

Not many of us can carry that off, right?

But back to the sound...after all, it's what's UNDER the hood that counts.
Be it my iPhone, iPad, Galaxy (phone & tablet), PC, or Mac (tech household, what can I say), the sound is consistently true. Unlike some headphones tuned to over-accentuate bass, these nail it perfectly. That means classical comes through as beautifully as techno. And speedcore/splittercore comes through as.....well, speedcore/splittercore!

Buy for the looks, keep them for your ears and brain.

title: Not exactly what I was looking for
text:
I'll start with the good. The frame is nice looking and has a good feel as far as construction. It has some weight to it, so I don't feel like it's a flimsy product. The display is nice. Crisp images and large viewing area. The price was good for a frame of this size.

The bad. First of all, I hate the adapter. I specifically wanted something I could mount on the wall, knowing full well I would have to find a way to hide the cord. Unfortunately, this is not the kind of frame that has the bulky part of the adapter at the plug. Nope. It has a 2-part cord with the brick at the midway point. Naturally, this means if you are hanging this on the wall, you either had to hang it low enough that the brick is at outlet level or hang it over a piece of furniture that can hide the brick. Hopefully, you can figure out a way to hold the brick up so that it isn't pulling on the cord by hanging loose. This frame does NOT have the same back construction as shown in some of the older photos. Do not be fooled!

Second, I'm glad the frame has an internal 1GB of memory. Too bad that for whatever reason, half of my files were scrambled into some sort of gibberish and when I attempted to delete them from the frame and start over, I got error messages and couldn't do it. Instead, I uploaded my images to an SD card and inserted that into the frame. That worked flawlessly. If you get this frame, use the SD card slot. Fewer problems and that way you don't have to worry about not being able to return a product that is partially loaded with personal images you are unable to delete.

The stand on the back of the frame is the only flimsy part. It's nice that it's adjustable, but if you move the frame it can sometimes slide into another position. I haven't mounted the frame on the wall yet because I'm trying to find a spot where I can do it and not have to worry about the adapter looking like junk.

One more thing this frame does NOT do that is mentioned in other reviews. It does not have a random selection mode in slide show. When you select 'Random', you are selecting a random swipe from image to image. The images are displayed in the order they are stored in memory. Soooo not what I was looking for. I'm debating whether I'll return it or not. If I can get everything deleted from the internal memory, I probably will.

text:
Original review is below. This is an update after we bought an Echo Dot:

We recently bought an Echo Dot to use with the cherry Model One in our kitchen. It works great, allowing us to select our favorite FM channel (usually NPR news) when we come down for breakfast each morning and then throughout the day (usually NPR talk, classical, jazz, or blues). We like the kitchen Alexa setup so much we bought a second Echo Dot for my bedroom nightstand to use with the black Model One I bought a few years ago to use as a computer speaker. That setup also works great, so today I ordered a second black Model One for the nightstand on my wife's side on the bed. As a result, the Echo Dot and two Model One radios will replace the pair of Grace Audio Mondo ratios we have previously been using for bedtime music and wake-up news.

Original Review

We have had this radio in our kitchen for years and we love it. Since we live on a hillside where we get very poor radio reception we use it as an internet radio with an iPod Touch and the Tunein Radio app. Last week I bought another Tivoli Model One, along with a set of Bose Companion 2 Series III computer speakers, to see which would sound better as a speaker for our desktop computer.

Based on a direct comparison in our home, the Tivoli Model One had similar bass to the Bose speakers, even though it only has one speaker vs. the Bose' two separate bass speakers. The determining factor was that the Tivoli's higher frequency sounds were much sharper and clearer than the Bose speakers. I returned the Bose computer speakers and we now have an excellent monaural speaker for our desktop computer.

Because of my lack of an iPhone (oddly, I just got one two days ago, so I may give this another try and then update the review if I like the camera more) I had to use the included link to the executable Windows program. By documentation, I mean there are minimal instructions and no built in help files. I was able to get it to work by running the software with a lot of finagling and figuring it out by means of hunting around through my past experiences hooking up cameras.

All in all, a bit of a disappointment, I was hoping to catch the wankers who keep spraypainting my carport.

Update - Still using this with the PC, just a note, you have to leave the PC software running to report. This camera works through an extension cord but not a surge protector. Not sure of what the range is and at least in our house, it needed to be on the same circuit breaker as the base, but this could just be weird wiring in our house.

A nice feature of the camera is a motion detection feature, so you don't end up with hours of blank unmoving street view for example. For the recording, pretty much continuously, it takes about 2GB per night (this is with camera on from about 9pm to 8am). There is a way to look at the recorded footage in super fast motion, so it takes about five minutes to watch the entire night's events (use VLC);'oh, hello again, curious kitty who keeps hanging out on my porch.'

This is not an outdoor camera, but we are using it outdoors anyways (tried placing it near a window, but glare of light on the window blinded the camera). There are a lot of strange characters in our neighborhood and there have been a few incidents; nothing major, a crazy woman tried to break in while we were eating dinner, a man with dementia was wandering around our bridge, kids stealing wood from our woodpile, you know, ordinary disturbances, so this person was exactly what we wanted to see while we weren't home.

title: Absolutely No Unsightly Cords Or Annoying Vibrations!
text:
This is my 4th desk mounted monitor arm. Until I tried this arm, the best one I had was an Ergotron. Ergotron makes a superb arm with only two problems- the cords shift and look messy whenever you move the arm and the worst problem is the arm vibrates on any little movement. If I moved in my chair, the joints on the arm would vibrate. If I move my mouse too much or the keyboard, the arm vibrates. When I use my printer, it feels like a minor earthquake shaking the desk.

Now for the first time ever, 3M has made a sleek, heavy duty monitor arm that not only keeps the cords tucked away perfectly when moving the arm, but due to this superior design, no matter what movement I make, there are no vibrations ever! I've owned two higher priced Ergotrons and another less known name arm, and as good as they are, they don't even compare to the sturdiness, design and high quality of this 3M model.

I love the capability of having more room on my desktop by having the monitor above the desk with full adjustability, so the adjustable monitor arm is a must have on my desk. This 3M monitor arm comes in 3 heavy duty mostly metal pieces, with an adjustable plate for the back of your monitor and all the parts and tools you will need except for one- you will need a phillips screwdriver. You have the option of clamping it to the edge of your desk or drilling a hole for grommet mounting it. I clamped it on and it only took 5 minutes of my time. I then adjusted the tension screws in the arm with my screwdriver, as well as adjusting the arm with the allen wrench and allen key to support the weight of my monitor and that was it.

The arm supports monitors up to 20 lbs., and you can move it up or down, towards or away from you, and it swivels sideways 180 degrees in either direction. It's height has a 13 inch range which gives you the ability to view your monitor sitting or standing. We have also found this arm is outstanding in supporting a portable tv on any table in our home, giving the wonderful 180 degree adjustment and up and down and forward and backward movements for viewing at any angle!

It is so wonderful to never see cords coming out every time you move this monitor arm and especially to be able to never have those irritating vibrations whenever I use my keyboard, my mouse, move in my chair, bump the table and especially when using my printer! 3M has made a better adjustable monitor arm and it blows both my expensive Ergotrons away and for this reason alone, this arm gets 5 full stars! There is a 5 year warranty on this arm as well, but when you see the heavy duty structure of this arm without any loose or jiggly joints, you can see it will last decades, not just 5 years!

text:
To be honest, I'm really tired of these mice failing.

They work great at first, then eventually quit scrolling or, worse, get stuck in scroll mode and drive the cursor to the bottom of the page for no reason. Two have failed on me. The first was purchased in 2011 for $36, the second in 2014 for $30. Both failed to scroll reliably and made using them impossible. Other, cheaper, wireless mice work better, or at least longer.

This mouse has nice features like left/right scrolling by tilting the scroll wheel and they work on many different surfaces, but those features fall by the wayside if the thing doesn't work at all after some time.

I've tried blowing it out with compressed air to clear debris, but it didn't fix it. Haven't come to taking it apart and cleaning it, as some proffer, because it's simply not worth the time.

For how much these mice cost -- $66 for the two -- they should be bulletproof. Better to buy cheaper wireless mice and throw them away when the fail.

I'm trying the $11 [[ASIN:B074DV98R7 VicTsing 2.4G Wireless Mouse Wireless Optical Laptop Mouse with USB Nano Receiver, 6 Buttons,5 Adjustable DPI Levels,15 Months Battery Life]] next. I could have purchased six of them for what I've put into Logitech MX Anywhere mice, both of which become landfill fodder.

Logitech has lost my Anywhere MX mouse business.

title: Banna plugs are different than reuseable than RCA connectors.
text: Banana connectors fit much tighter than a RCA connector and for a person unaware of the difference; it would be easy to cause damage on ether end of the speaker wire to the female connected components. Therefore, I would recommend studying the literature or talking to the manufacture (for both connected ends if necessary). For instance,: in most cases if unaware, it would be easy to cause physical damage simply installing a banana male into a female component just by the tightness, (no clearance between M/FM parts that can fool you into thinking this is as it should be because the male banana is designed to squeeze into the female end and, probably remain as such even after someone trips over an AV receiver  speaker wire, and the A/V falls on the floor because the banana connector was so tight you could lift the A/V by the speaker wire. A banana male connector is designed to expand during installation. If you are in need of banana connectors, these connectors are extremely well made and are a very good bang for the buck.  They are also reusable and do not need any special tools other than basic wire strippers.

title: Feature rich, but comes with quirks
text:
I got this clock about a month ago for my birthday, and overall I do like it.
1. Sound quality is excellent. We live in a radio "shadow" and this radio gets the best reception of any in the house. Very clear sound, which is very important to me.
2. 3 options for backlight of display. Bright/dim/off. I have gotten to where I sleep with it off, but if I wake up I click it to dim as a nightlite if I have to get up, etc.
3. VERY complex programming. So many options to just set the alarm (which don't get me wrong, is nice) but really, you have to input the time, days of the week, select the sound to wake to (buzzer, radio, nature sound) and then the volume of that sound. I am not an electronics person (my hubby who gave me this clock is). It's probably MUCH easier for him to program.
4. Buttons are TINY and all the same, which adds to the difficulty programming, above. There are no dials on this clock, all very tiny buttons.
5. Very small footprint - if you have a tiny bedside table as I do, this is a great clock. It's long, but super skinny and doesn't take up much room at all.
The one feature that I find completely odd, and most difficult to cope with: The Snooze button also controls the dimmer on the display. So, if the alarm goes off, and you have the backlight completely off, there is NO WAY to see what time it is without turning the alarm OFF, and then the backlight ON. Normally you just click the Snooze button to toggle between brightness modes, but if you do that while the alarm is ringing and/or in the snooze/alarm cycle, it just adds an extra 10 minutes to your snooze, and you still can't see what time it is. That is a recipe for disaster, considering that this product is designed to help you get up on time.
I probably just need to spend some more quality time with the instruction manual.... but seriously, this is an alarm clock. Like I said, though, overall I'm happy with it as I learn more about it's functionality.

title: You're Going to LOVE it!
text: This projector comes packed in a very substantial, very sturdy box with a carrying handle and packing that should last for a long time. I would be using it as a carrying case for portable use. Out of the box this unit has a very appealing and very high-quality appearance. It appears to be extremely well-made. The connections at the back of the unit, as well as the controls on top of the unit and controls on the remote, appeared to be pretty straight-forward and fairly intuitive for anyone accustomed to connecting audio/video equipment such as VCR, DVR, stereo, etc. I did go to the Quick Start Guide and setup to get an HD picture on the screen from my cable box was quite easy. Power cord, remote control, serial cable, and DVD with manual were included.  The PDF manual on the DVD is quite detailed and easy to understand. While I really have no present intention of setting this projector up as a ceiling mount, it does have a very nice setup for that, with screw holes on what would normally be the bottom. The configuration from ceiling front or rear and table front or rear are very easy to change in the settings. When I set this projector up, I was about 6 feet away from the screen and had a 120 inch diagonal picture. And wow, what a picture it is! Immediately, the colors and sharpness just pop! And, as is mentioned in the information, it easily adjusts to lightness or darkness of a room. I opened and closed the blinds in the room on a sunny day and the picture was outstanding in both settings. Sound through the integrated speaker was very good, and the fan is, as described in materials, extremely quiet. The “keystone”, where the picture is originally in a trapezoid due to projection angle, was extremely easy to adjust, and upon adjustment compensation, the picture was perfect. I was able to connect my iPad to the projector via the MHL/HDMI port with an adapter that I have for a mini-projector that I use for work. It seemed to work quite well, although MHL is something I’m just getting acquainted with. In summary there’s no way I’d give this projector anything but five stars! I’m so looking forward to using it this summer out on the patio for “movie night” with neighbors. It must be noted that, while this particular projector has been promoted especially for gaming, I don’t really do video games, but it works wonderfully for everything else. From the YouTube reviews I’ve seen, it seems to work wonderfully for gaming, with exceptionally good performance, especially when it comes to lack of lag.  Made in China.

title: Clever design for a headrest mounted case
text:
The review sample that I received had a sturdy elastic band that did not break on me. I do not doubt the earlier reviewer who claimed that theirs did, but my experience was different.

When I claimed in the title that this is a clever design I am comparing this one to other headrest mounted tablet holders. I have tested literally dozens of other models and all required that either you remove your tablet from any case you may be using, or you endure less than optimum grips of the mount will accommodate a case. This one is a case plus headrest mount.

There are some trade-offs in this one's design. First, you can only mount your tablet in landscape mode. Since that is the mode I always use this is perfect for me. If you need a mount that will accommodate portrait mode, or you need to switch between the two, this is NOT the mount for you.

Some physical details that I do like include the heavily padded case when you are using outside of vehicle back seats. While the holder into which you insert your iPad is not the hard plastic, snap in design that affords optimum protection, it does dampen and absorb some shock. The covers are thick and provide a great deal of protection. In fact, that feature is better than ninety-five percent of every case I have ever tried. The organizer is handy, and all of the cutouts and accesses are perfectly aligned to an iPad's camera and various buttons and ports.

If you need a case that will function as both a case and headrest mount this one is worth considering - as long as you understand the limitations that I have cited.
