I like a smaller screen and keyboard, so this is perfect for me, and it's lightweight and has a slim profile, so it's easy to take along when I'm out and about. I love the way it converts to a tablet when you fold the screen back. Even the fingerprint recognition is dramatically better than anything I've had before. One thing I was skeptical about was the placement of the power button on the side. I was sure I'd be turning the laptop on or off accidentally, but I've discovered that it's not that simple, which is a load off my mind.

I could wish for a couple more USB ports particularly as I use both a wireless mouse and because there's no disk drive, so I have to attach an external one when I want to access files on disk. Eh, I'll survive it. There are always work-arounds.

Bottom line is that this laptop is a perfect match for me. I'm a writer (not a gamer) and this runs all the software I need, runs it fast and efficiently, and has tremendous storage capacity for all my files. I really couldn't have asked for more. Nicely done, HP.

title: Terrible as headphones, but my dog loves the case...
text:
When these first arrived and I put them on I was disappointed that I was unable to find ANY way to wear them without causing pain inside my right ear. I couldn't understand but assumed that as the right side is the control side it must be slightly different. I understand that I'm incredibly sensitive, but unfortunately that means that a piece of hard plastic pushing into the cartilige inside of my ear ends up being incredibly painful. Still, I tried to ignore this.

I was happy when I was able to quickly pair the earbuds with my Samsung Galaxy S7 (shows how cheap I am, but I'm happy for the upgrade from my S5.) I was also happy when I was able to actually answer a call. The sound coming through was unbearably loud, but that's no surprise for me, again Ms. overly sensitive. The frustrating thing was that although I was supposed to be able to adjust the sensitivity so that the next time I answer and make a call it would be quieter, I found that every single time I answered and made calls I had to adjust the volume down once the call was connected. Not very fun since I pretty much have to have the earbuds in my ears to do this. If I don't, I end up disconnecting the call with the overly sensitive buttons. I was on my way to blowing out my eardrums.

Along with my being overly sensitive I am unfortunately extremely quiet. Not so fun for anyone else whom I'm trying to talk to. No matter how high I turned up my phone AND the earbuds, and not to mention put all the energy I had into trying to use my diaphram to control my oxygen and voice level, the person on the other end was always telling me they couldn't hear me. What people WERE able to hear however were any sounds that were around me, such as birds chirping, a slight breeze blowing or water running.

These Bluetooth headphones were supposed to allow me to use my phone since I'm unable to hold it up to my head for more than a minute or two due to chronic illness related disability. It's been so difficult searching for a replacement Bluetooth for my previous Plantronic that I got at Costco many years ago. I especially miss the ones which were able to properly do voice-to-text.

People don't understand how hard it is for the disabled to be able to acquire products and technology necessary to assist them in their lives while meanwhile people who don't need such things are much more apt to come by these products and technologies. Sorry for the gripe, it was more a reflection that I used to have this on my $30 bluetooth for my Palm phone, but once that sort of thing became mainstream it's all of the sudden $300 and requires a $1,000 phone. Ridiculous what some people will pay money for instead of deciding that's ridiculous.

Oh well. I almost forgot the about the case. This headset comes in a semi-hard rounded zippered case. And my dog thinks it's the perfect size to grab and try to get me to chase her around the house for. So at least she likes the case. :) That's all that really matters anyways.

title: Promising Future
text:
When comparing streaming devices, you'll find that each has its unique features and the goal is to find the right one for you. The Fire TV Stick is slow with poor wifi connectivity. The interface is also a mess, but at least they have improved the remote to add volume buttons. It was for these reasons that I chose the Roku Ultra, which I believe is the best device for the intended purpose.

If you want more out of your streaming device, however, a Roku may not be your preferred choice. Many like the Fire TV Stick because of its seamless integration with Amazon Prime Video and/or Alexa. I couldn't care less about either, but I do like that the Fire TV Stick works with the Ring Doorbell (another Amazon product), while the others do not. I also like that the Fire TV Stick is more of an open platform, meaning that it's more customizable than others, like the Roku, which is essentially an appliance made to do one thing, but do it well.

For example, the Fire TV Stick has web browsers. If you own a wireless keyboard, you can easily surf the web on your TV (nice for looking up programming information). And if you don't own a keyboard, it has an onscreen keyboard that works with the remote, which is mostly all I use, anyhow. In comparison, the web browser for the Roku simply streams your mobile web browser screen to your TV, which is sort of pointless, imo, since every device can do that and they don't even need a web browser app to do it.

But what I really like most about the Fire TV Stick is the outlook for the future. Amazon recently introduced a "Live TV" menu, which for now is mostly meant for the Fire TV Recast DVR. It also works with Pluto TV now, and it's easy to imagine Amazon adding other apps in the future, so users will have a customized electronic programming guide. This is a feature that many cord-cutters argue is outdated and unneeded, but that depends on how you watch TV. And for those who spend time watching live TV, like I do, a built-in EPG is a huge asset.

In summary, I have high hopes for the future of the Fire TV Stick, but it's just not there, yet. The developers seem headed in the right direction, but first it needs work on making the menu more navigable.

But back to Fitness. Of course, it acts as a pedometer. But it also measures your heartbeat, every 5 minutes. This thing keeps track of everything! It even knows what kind of exercise you're doing. It maps out progress so that it's easier to keep an eye on where your goals are and how to meet them.
It's synced to my Samsung Galaxy phone, and it plays all of the music that I've got on my phone.

While it is not waterproof, it is water resistant. I'm one of those people that washes my hands a lot, and I haven't had any problem with water sprinkling on it.

Dislikes.

Overall.

The bluetooth connection.
I set the radio to bluetooth, then went to bluetooth settings on my IPhone. The IPhone immediately recognized the radio, and paired. I played both songs and the Audible books, using this connection. I ordered the radio in order to listen to hours of Audible books at night. I usually fall asleep while listening, and it played throughout the night. That way, I wouldn’t be exhausting my IPhone battery constantly, as it uses a lot less battery life, when it doesn’t need to pump out volume. title: Decent upgrade!  Some nitpicks though.
text:
I upgraded from a year-old, previous-generation Paperwhite, mostly to gain the new inverted white-on-black screen mode that Amazon insists requires new hardware and to have built-in Audible playback over Bluetooth.

This unit ticks most of boxes, and after some debate I've decided to give it five stars, but there are some imperfections worth knowing about. It's mostly good, though, and often great.

Battery life
No complaints. In several long international flights, I've yet to run it down more than about 30%, either in long reading sessions with the front-light or in lengthy Audible playback sessions over Bluetooth.

Audible content
The Audible player works brilliantly. Excellent sound, simple controls (including playback-speed adjustment). It does work best if you don't have a screen password enabled, though-- that will get in the way if you just want to rewind a few seconds to catch something you missed. Playback proceeds even if you have a case closed, which shuts off the front-light and saves battery charge.

There's no headphone jack-- this is for Bluetooth only. Fine with me. I have Bluetooth-enabled hearing aids (cochlear implants, actually) and it's a true joy to be able to listen to books on this device. Thanks, Amazon.

Screen
The screen is pretty much the same as my previous-generation Paperwhite's, meaning not bad but could use more contrast when reading in a dark room using the front-light. Outdoors or in well-lit areas, it's fantastic and mostly glare-free.

More seriously, the lack of contrast mars the new Paperwhite's valuable ability to invert text to white-on-black. This is a marvelous accessibility feature for those with "floaters", vitreous separation and other vision issues. Unfortunately, when used with the front-light in a darkened room, such as when reading at night or in a darkened airplane, the black background is more of a medium gray. So this new feature is less helpful than it could be. In fairness, poor contrast is characteristic of today's e-ink displays, which provide perhaps 8:1 contrast. If Amazon can significantly improve the contrast, I'd upgrade again in a flash.

The screen is plastic and will scratch. Keep it clean and use a case. Even with a case (I prefer one of the various "origami" cases available here, which allow the Kindle to prop itself upright) it will fit nicely into a pocket.

The touch-screen user interface is the same as the previous-gen Paperwhite's. I'm not a huge fan of it; too easy to touch it when you don't mean to, and end up on the wrong page. But, the earlier button-driven Kindles had sort of the same problem, so whatever. I recommend a simple fix, perhaps as a Settings option: require a double-tap rather than a single-tap. How about it, Amazon?

Connectivity
The 4G/LTE capability is a nice speed upgrade from the previous 3G connectivity. Downloading Audible content requires a WiFi connection as before.

Unfortunately I'm finding that global connectivity with the new 4G hardware is inferior to the previous-gen's 3G radio. For example, my year-old 3G Paperwhite connected without issue in Saigon, but the new one won't.

The user interface for turning Airplane Mode on and off could be improved. As it is, engaging Airplane Mode cuts all connectivity including Bluetooth. So if you're in the middle of listening to a book when the time comes to put your gizmos in Airplane Mode, it will cut your connection. Better to do what the latest iPhones do, and have the device learn if your usage prefers that Bluetooth remain active.

Browser
It's high time for Amazon to replace the minimally-functional "Experimental Browser" with something more useful. I get it that Kindles are all about battery life and browsers can be major energy hogs, but c'mon, it's 2019, and this browser feels like a relic from 1996. Probably is.

title: ABSOLUTELY AWESOME iPhone CABLE!!!
text:
I have had the opportunity to review more iPhone cables than I can possibly remember and over the years I have found there are certain characteristics that I look for in a cable that will increase its chances of being a high quality, long lasting cable. I knew as soon as I saw these cables by Maxrock they had those characteristics and after using it for the last 6 weeks I have been nothing but impressed.

I’ve found long, over 6.6’ or 2m, cables have to have increased shielding in order to not lose speed in data transfer and be especially well made to resist unraveling and the stresses from being that length. This cable suffers no noticeable loss in speed from its length during either charging or data transfer.

The primary failure point of any cable is where the cable meets the plug. Due to the strains constantly put at those junctions this is where electrical shorts are most likely to occur and thus cause eventual failure. As is clear with this cable this area is protected by the manufacturer utilizing reinforced plugs making it so the cable can not put the same strain at that weak point.

One additional feature added to this wire is a way to keep it coiled when not in use. This is definitely a nice feature especially for an extra long cable.

This is among the best cables I’ve had the opportunity to review and I definitely recommend it.

title: I figured the best thing to do was to return it and ask ...
text:
The first one that Amazon sent me was black, not titanium as I had ordered. I wanted a slightly different color than the black one I already have so I could differentiate the two. The box it came in said it was a WD My Passport Ultra but printed on the drive was only "WD My Passport" and it was also printed in the other direction, readable from "portrait" (or vertical) orientation rather than "landscape" (or horizontal) orientation. I thought that was little odd, but decided that it would help me to differentiate the two after all. So, I hooked it up to my windows 7 install and windows attmpted to load drivers for it but after a minute or so it failed.

No problem, I thought, I'll just plug it in to my Mac and format/partitition it there as I had done with my other My Passport Ultra drive. Nope. That didn't work either. Mac OS X Yosemite couldn't do it either and I couldn't even erase it to start fresh. It simply didn't work. I googled the error, thinking I could fix it with some command line process and found instructions on running FSCK to resolve it. I decided not to bother with that additional pain, because what if it still didn't work? Having ordered it from Amazon, I figured the best thing to do was to return it and ask for a new one.

So I returned the first one, explained that it was "dead out of the box." And Amazon promptly sent me a replacement. (Another reason I LOVE shopping from Amazon - aside from Prime - is that it is always fairly painless to return things).

The replacement arrived 2 days after I submitted my return claim and one day after I actually put the dead drive in the mail to send it back. The replacement was exactly what I had ordered - it came in the correct color - Titanium - and it has the printing on the drive just as shown in the picture (horizontal orientation). I plugged it in to my Mac and had absolutely no problem partitioning and formatting the drive to my specifications. it works perfectly so far and will be used as the backup for my other My Passport Ultra.

I am only taking off one star because of the first dead drive that I got, but really if the rating is for the drive that I have now, it's definitely a 5star.

title: A niche product, but the one I've been looking for!
text:
I have very average sized/shaped ears that fit medium eartips in any IEM. I am also ridiculously sensitive to stuff that causes any odd pressure points in my ear. I haven't had them long, so more testing is required, but superficially, the fit and size is perfect. I don't need audio for more than the ~3 hour battery life, and any more battery would negatively impact the size. These are kind of miraculously tiny for being full Bluetooth IEM's. After thet shut off, they work as pretty fair earplugs. Not gonna completely isolate a snoring partner, but again, they opted to not include any ANC software because that chews battery. Also ANC has a habit of making pillow rustle obnoxious.

The main reason I got them is because I'm a paramedic with insomnia. I always need some gentle podcast or something playing to fall asleep. The Bose sleep buds seem great, but I prefer my own audio, generic sleep sounds always wind up driving me INSANE because no matter how long or varied they are, my brain will laser in on any repetition and it just keeps me awake. So I need to be able to play my own audio and this is genuinely one of the only options. Again. That uses battery. So short of maybe releasing a version with Bluetooth 5.2, this is about as good as you can expect before making the earbud bulkier

The included sleep sounds are very limited, but they have the party piece of letting you use your own. So I can happily pick my own audio stream from headspace, YouTube, tidal, etc.

The earbuds have two EQ presets, "music" and "soothing". Soothing mode is a noticeable mid-bass bump, I'm guessing to help drown out environmental sounds. But they do have a relatively v shaped curve, and are surprisingly punchy. They genuinely sound pretty decent. I just went through my favorite tidal playlist for headphone tests and these are absolutely serviceable. Not hifi, but not bad at all. They'd also work well under a motorcycle helmet since they're INSANELY unobtrusive.

I can also confirm that they do have some SUPERB electronic noise isolation. Down to 1-3% volume, which is where I sleep, they have not even a hint of hiss. Not even my Galaxy bud pros manage that. They get really quiet and still sound very good at ultra low volume.

Honestly I really freaking like the design and attention to detail. I think a modernized version with the newest, most efficient Bluetooth revision would up the battery life, and if they wanted to invest in a broader library of basic sleep sounds, it wouldn't be unwelcome.

I wouldn't use these as my only headphones, since they do lack a microphone and touch controls (features I am glad they didn't include) and they have the obviously limited battery life, but these are going to happily accompany me to work, at home, and while traveling or camping.

Fingers crossed the build quality holds up because these are the ONLY real option in this space with this exact feature set I need.

title: Good enough for FPV
text:
I'm using this for FPV, mounted on my r/c transmitter (Turnigy 9xr). Certainly nicer than the 4.5" monitor it replaced (from the cheap HobbyKing goggles). The bottom 1/4-20 screw hole really helps with mounting (I'm using the carbon fiber mounting brackets with some creativity, but there are other options). Screen visibility is decent in daylight, you definitely need a sunshade (I made one out of some black-painted blister packaging and velcro)

The bad:
- It blue-screens, and does so instantly as soon as signal goes to all-fuzz.

The good:
- It un-bluescreens instantly as soon as signal is restored (no delay).
- It remembers its on/off state through power loss, so an external master on switch is convenient to use.
- It is fairly bright (adjustable from OSD)

The confusing: It comes with a dual-RCA jack cable, one male, one female, suggesting that one is input and the other is output to downstream video equipment. This is not the case, both are inputs (it has an input selector).

It comes with a cable with a PS/2 jack for quick disconnect, but I eliminated it altogether by shortening and soldering the wires inside the casing (so I just have 2" pigtails sticking out through the back (not the bottom)). As I did that, I also shorted both video jacks together so now one is input (from my RX) and one is output (to goggles).

I didn't use the base. Also, don't freak out if the image is upside down or sideways, it has a button dedicated to rotation.

title: Great computer for entertainment applications
text:
Being a Mac user for decades, it has been some time since I've had the opportunity to use a Windows based computer, so I was eager to try the Windows 10 operating system on this convertible notebook computer, also a first for me. The Acer Aspire R 14 R5-471T-79YN has far exceeded my expectations in form and function, despite the learning curve I'm experiencing. I won't get into the Windows 10 system, but will say that I can definitely see the influence of the Mac operating systems on its development and I am impressed. Perhaps I like it more than many users might simply because I can't even remember the last Windows system I used being that even my remote work situations tend to not use these computers now.

The Acer is not as lightweight as a tablet, of course, but it's also not the weightiest notebook of this size, and the brushed metal texture of the case is appealing. It looks sleek and feels good when the computer is used. I find the keyboard to be very comfortable, the touchpad is positioned well and the silver edging surrounding it is a nice contrast. I do not like the position of the power button which is directly beneath the power plug, as I find that if plugged in, I have to fiddle with it to turn on the computer. The USB ports, HDMI port, SD card reader and volume control are all easily accessible and have functioned well so far in every case I've used them this week. The speakers are a little odd, but that makes sense since the convertible form of this means that when used as a tablet ,the rear speakers will face the area between the folded computer. To my surprise, I find that the sound improves in tablet form, better than when used in laptop or tented configurations. I have mine set to ask if I want to switch to tablet layout because I found that it did not always respond appropriately when set to automatic conversion. The true HD makes this a very nice system on which to watch videos and with external headphones or speaker, either cabled or Bluetooth, it becomes a great system. I would actually consider this one to be best suited for entertainment, and would imagine that it is excellent for games although I have not used it for that purpose at all. The touch screen is very responsive, but it does take some time to get accustomed to the responsiveness. The computer is very fast, very quiet, very cool (temperature), and it starts quickly. I rather like the lack of an optical drive because that keeps it quieter and lighter, yet allows me to add a peripheral drive if I want or when it is needed. I rather enjoyed streaming a movie from my Amazon Prime directly to a non-smart TV. I've used this in the kitchen in both the tablet and tent configurations using the Kindle app and much appreciated having a larger screen than when using my Kindle Fire for recipe following.

For the price, I think this is a great convertible computer which comes with a single year warranty. I intend to give this Aspire a workout and hope that I never need to discover how the Acer warranty service performs.

title: Very disappointing, deeply flawed product
text:
I expected great things from the Kindle Paperwhite. What I received was perhaps the most frustrating electronic device I ever have purchased.

Two things made this unusable for me. First was the touch screen. While it usually would respond to a tap or solid touch, there always, always was a delay in response. And sometimes it seemed that nothing would get a reaction, not a light tap, not a solid touch, not placing my finger on the screen and holding it for many seconds, not a firm press on the screen, not a slow nor swift swipe of my finger across the screen. Was there something wrong with my touch? My wife tried it, and also found the response of the screen to be intermittent. Perhaps the one I received was defective. I have never laid hands on any Kindle other than this paperwhite that I purchased, so I cannot say whether my experience was typical.

Second, the 'experimental browser.' I have used other 'experimental browsers' including on a half-wit phone (I call it that because it is really not much of a smart phone) from Tracfone. While I have found other browsers to be limited, they have functioned. With the paperwhite, when I could get responses from the screen sufficient to test the browser I found it repeatedly would freeze if it encountered a site that confused it. Sites that my half-wit experimental browser handles with no problem would crash the paperwhite's browser. Using the pre-loaded bookmark for amazon.com took me to a page the browser could not handle. Restarting the browser would immediately take it back to the offending site, causing it to crash again. Clearing the browser history made no difference -- possibly because it would not clear the history before returning to the previously visited site. The only way I could find to un-freeze the browser was to reset the paperwhite to the factory settings, causing the loss of all personalized settings. I had not planned to use this to surf the internet, but I did want to be able to download kindle books directly from web sites, and this browser just could not manage that.

The display was readable, although it was annoying to have the flash to black as it refreshed each time I turned a page -- something it did regardless how I set the refresh setting. I would have liked a larger screen to reduce how frequently the page needed to be turned, but perhaps the size would be acceptable if it avoided the flash to black and responded more reliably to the touch to change pages. While the other flaws might have justified a rating of 1, I thought the paperwhite screen concept had enough merit to bump the rating up a notch.

I considered requesting a replacement to see if the problems I experienced were just the result of defects in the one I received. Perhaps a different one would have a screen that responded reliably and swiftly. But the browser issue seemed certainly to be software, and not something that will change from one to the next. The 'experimental browser' is so very, very wrong that I have to consider it to be a cruel hoax. If Amazon offered these with an Opera Mini browser, I might consider trying the next generation paperwhite.

For now, I have to say to avoid the Kindle Paperwhite unless you are willing never to download a book from a web site other than Amazon.

title: Thank goodness for the Fire
text:
My husband and I just purchased a Fire yesterday and I'm absolutely in love with it. We've been drooling over it for quite some time, going to "visit" it everytime we went to Target. At first when we found out that it didn't have the e-ink technology it dampened our feelings towards it for a second or two but then we found out all the other cool stuff it can do - videos, magazines and kid books IN COLOR and suddenly we realized that maybe this could be our answer to our computer problems. We own a serious lemon of a laptop and can't afford a new one at the moment but the Kindle Fire is perfect for what we need - checking e-mail, netflix, browsing, etc... so that is the primary purpose we bought it for. Here is a quick list of the good and bad I've noticed:

Bad:
-Even though I knew it was a 7" screen and I've seen the floor models it still kind of shocked me when we took it out of the box. but, so far it hasn't really been an issue - but if you have been looking at i-pads and and considering the Fire instead just realize that it is smaller.

Good:
-No Set up process - the most I did to start using the Fire was enter my amazon user name and password so it could link the device to my account
-Beautiful display. The color is crisp and there is no fuzziness - I am noticing now how fuzzy my work devices are now!
-Quick! Amazon Silk and the Dual Core Processor in the Fire result in an incredibly quick browsing experience, you flash from one screen to another with no loading time
-Cloud Storage - I love that I can store all of my amazon purchased material FREE on the cloud - no more running out of memory on a device. I purchase all of my ebooks and such from Amazon, but if someone else gets it from another source they can still purchase additional storage
-Easy to navigate. We aren't what you could call tech savy people, and this was the first Kindle my husband has ever touched but neither of us has had trouble navigating it.
-full color magazines and kid books - not that I'm going to completely drop my glossies but it will be nice to have some on the Fire when I'm on the go, I like to travel lite. We're especially excited about the children's books our two young daughters (both under 5) like to have me read from my other Kindle to them but they still need pictures and unfortunately on my other device the layout for these books wasn't great. The layout on the fire however, is gorgeous and I can't wait to show the girls

title: No one seems to make good-quality earbuds any more.
text:
My wife got these for me for Christmas because my old, $16 (like 25 year old) Sony ear hook buds finally fell apart. I've been writing a book and using Speechify for editing, using these earbuds. Initially, I liked that there were different sized silicone pieces to fit different size ear-holes. The sound quality seemed fine, and they were a bit bulky, a bit loose, but seemed not bad for $20. So now (1/10/21, or 17 days later) the charging port broke loose from the solder joints which affixed it to the little printed circuit board inside. Anyone who knows anything about wiring and electronics can tell you that a solder joint on a circuit board is inadequate to secure something that is going to have pressure put on it repeatedly due to plugging and unplugging. Obviously no one at Senso thought of this, or cared enough to put it into practice.

This is all part of a larger problem which is what is known as 'planned obsolescence' or put simply 'making things cheap so they break quickly (usually just after warranty expires) and you have to buy another one'. It's happened to phones (buy a new iPhone every 2 years), audio equipment, cars, televisions, and computers (don't get me started on the crap Dell sells, and forget getting any support from them).

AMAZON, if you're LISTENING, stop selling CRAP from SHADY SELLERS! Stop allowing companies to bribe customers for 5-star reviews. It makes reviews worthless and untrustworthy. Also, your buyers are obviously getting kickbacks, or if not they are terrible at judging quality. Either way, I cannot find good Bluetooth earbuds anywhere on the site. Even the Beats audio ones you sell for $110 are lousy with quality issues.

Disappointed, AMAZON. You own the internet but you can't sell quality electronics to save your lives.

I really like how the cable looks, the silver shine is the perfect complement to the rainbow backlighting and underlighting. The coiled part especially looks awesome.

The straight cable knocks it down a star for me. Both cables are braided, and when I see “braided” as a description, I expect a soft, pliable cable. This braid is stiff, so the straight cable is harder to manipulate. The included velcro cable ties help a bit because you can make a wide circle of cable (as pictured) but they have an odd design. I can’t get the cable ties snugged down small enough to hold the straight cable the way I’d like, so the aesthetics aren’t as nice as they could be.

title: FM Reception depends on installation; base features strong
text:
I was prepared to give this a poor rating. As other reviewers stated there is an issue with the fm transmitter strength leading to static.

I found there is stronger FM signal if the device is installed away from electrical components. Since most people, including myself, installed it initially on the dash, the radio and other electrical system components caused interference. I moved the device to be on the corner of the rear view mirror and had noticeably stronger FM reception.

The device plugs into the cars cigarette lighter. There is a port on the plug to insert an additional USB charger, so you can continue to use your phone's charger while this is plugged in.

Synching is fairly straight forward. Press the button the back of the device, search USB devices on your phone, and it will pair. The readout is red when not connected, blue when connected.

FM transmitter will transmit on most every frequency from 88.1 to 107.9fm. There is a button on the top to search for the best signal, but I found it was unreliable. It also has two presets so you can set two signals you know to work.

The button on the front lets you switch between playing music from your phone to working phone controls. It also allows you to pause music playback and end calls by pressing the music or phone button respectively.

Since it plays through your car stereo, music and calls play through your car speakers. When you are connected to a clear channel, the sound is clear and distortion free. Phone calls sound clear. There is a small microphone on the front that picks up your voice and I was pleased at the quality of my voice. Every person I called with the device were surprised to hear I was on a hands free speakerphone. They said it sounded better than my USB headset, and almost as good as using the phone's internal microphone.

Overall the base features were very good; music playback and phone features worked very well. There was an issue with the FM signal; there was often static, but found that it was improved by placing it where there was less electrical interference. Once I found the correct place, it was acceptable in that regard. Though I am only giving 3 1/2-4 starts as I am not fully comfortable with recommending it based on that alone.

title: Don't let age and megapixels fool you
text:
I picked up a refurbished version of this classic recently (06/07), and to be honest, there is nothing else that even comes near its performance for the price. Yes the heart of this camera is 2004 technology, and yes it is only 6 megapixels, but let's be honest, 6 megapixels is more than enough and great 2004 technology beats mediocre tech from any era.

I was a Canon admirer, and I even owned a Rebel Ti setup (a film SLR), but when I could finally afford to take the DSLR plunge, I couldn't help but admire the virtuosity of Nikon's white balance and metering. Even humble the D40 blew away anything Canon had for less than the price of a used car. What makes the D70 (and D70s) even more remarkable is that they both have the same tech as high end Nikons (ie D200, D2X series): 1/500 flash synch, 1/8000 max shutter, and 1004 point matrix metering (plus it hasn't been dumbed down like the D40, D40x, and D80 sadly have). It also supports all of Nikon's modern lenses with AF on any that offer it (unlike the otherwise stellar D40 and D40x which require AFS). Additionally, unlike the D100 and other previous Nikon DSLRs, the D70(s) models both support I-TTL, Nikon's most advanced lighting system. Additionally the D70(s) can serve as a master in wireless flash situations.

The camera, like almost all of Nikons, is built incredibly well, more tank than toy (I wish I could say the same for the Rebels), and it exudes confidence. It also features a solid grip that suits my oversized hands, but I firmly believe it could accommodate more modest sized hands just as well. Confidence is further enhanced by an uncanny responsiveness, incredible burst mode, and lightning quick focus (on my 18-135mm AF-S lens). You really feel like a pro, even if you are just taking pictures of your cat.

Compared to the D70, the D70s adds a better AF system (which can be added to the D70 with a firmware upgrade), wider flash coverage, faster transfer of pcis from the burst cache to the memory card, and a larger screen. It likely also has a bunch of subtle refinements throughout, but nothing else of note. The 18-70mm lens offered as part of a kit is excellent, though Nikon has a huge assortment of lenses to choose from.

title: Fantastic AV
text:
First part of review, 2nd day after install. It was lots of research along with REVIEWS that helped me decide on the Sony over Denon.
It took me about two months to gather all the equipment for my system, so I was a little nervous unpacking this open box deal. This AV replaces my Sony STR-DN1000 which was only five years old and lost a surround channel. The old unit was a bit clunky switching and lacked key features. This baby is really nice. The sound blows the doors off my old Sony. It is much more attractive, quieter and the features are fantastic. I was stunned by the difference in performance, including better preset sound phases to switch when you're between music and movies. My biggest surprise was the music which is no comparison. To be fair, I did add a new sub and center channel speaker so I expected better sound. And by the way, if you are debating whether to get a center channel, don't hesitate. This baby calibrated the speakers beautifully and the center channel is amazing.
It is driving a 5.2 speaker system which includes TWO EPI M250 bidirectional floor speakers from 1979. (I'd never part with them) main fronts. Two Polk audio in ceiling rear speakers for surround. Dayton subwoofer and Yamaha center channel. All paired beautifully with the auto calibration.
I have two reasons for the 4 star rating which I will speak more about when I update this review.
The first is the AirPlay. The manual has it compatible with only up to the 4S iPhone and the IPad2 which would mean the directions are old and obsolete. The AirPlay directions do NOT help and I am still perplexed as to how I get the unit to see the iPad Air I have.
The networking is confusin and difficult. I have this hooked directly to my router via Ethernet and cannot get it to see the network, so I am in for some troubleshooting. Setup for the sound was a breeze but this might be a challenge. So as for now, I cannot review the wired or wireless aspects which is a major added reason for buying this unit.
The other issue is the lack of an ipod/iPhone dock. My old Sony had an optional dock for my ipod that was powered, fit all units with the adapters, and worked the ipod from the remote. Every ipod function was easily accessed from the Sony remote which was amazing. I think that feature is no longer available with Sony. You just pop the ipod in the cradle and it charged as well as played by the remote. Now you can hook up your ipod to the sub, but you cannot control it and it lays flat on the table. The remote no longer applies so you cannot control the ipod unless you pick it up and use it the old fashioned way. Since the streaming wifi is now in place I assume Sony doesn't think it was needed, but it will be sorely missed, even with networking. The convenience factor for that was so nice. But certainly not worth not buying this unit.
All in all, I'm so far very impressed with this unit, but the jury is out on the all important wifi section. Will re-review when that is sorted out.

title: Consider the Whole
text:
Plenty of good points down further. First the gripes:

I highly encourage you to read the software application reviews for the Sonos2 app that you will need to download use this thing and also do some serious contemplation on what you want out of the whole of your audio system. A lot of those app reviews complain that older Sonos products have been essentially bricked (rendered unusable) with the rollout of the new software. This is a serious concern. Although I hope and want to believe that consumer protection laws prevent actual physical bricking without the owner's consent, there is nothing that I know of stopping the company from effectively bricking the device simply by declining to support it into the future. A few examples:

- New system software for Android or Apple comes out. You are essentially forced to update by Google or Apple or else you just buy a new phone that comes with newer software. Sonos declines to make a new app (perhaps they even pretend they cannot).

- You want to try out a new phone with a new OS. No app available.

I am not being paranoid. This is careful planning on the part of product manufacturers. I expected a lot of this nonsense, but the thing that bothers me most about this is that I tried to hook the speaker up with both ARC-enabled HDMI and with optical audio cables before downloading the software and it simply wouldn't work. Any other stereo equipment is simply plug-and-play. I am convinced they simply locked it down so you can't use the hardware you paid for without their permission and under their terms and conditions. BTW, you have to make an account and sign in before you can use the software, and thus before you can use the speaker.

The silver lining here is that at least once you get it working with optical cable (and hopefully with HDMI-ARC), when you turn it on, it continues to work with your TV if you don't have the app open. So now it at least functions like I expect a sound bar to. And although the company could conceivably wipe out my ability to use it for music, I suppose that it should continue to function as a TV soundbar assuming the internal battery doesn't go dead and that I left it on "TV" vice "playing music" last time I used it.

The second most bothersome thing is that any IP-capable device should have a webpage. This could easily be controlled via a simple webpage, effectively future-proofing it, but it was not. I have Heos speakers that have a webpage, but only show the IP address and allow no configuration. This speaker simply can't be reached at its IP.

And although I like some parts of the app and its music options, I am forever at their mercy as to what streaming services I can use. I don't stream anyway outside of my own network, but something to be aware of.

I have a HEOS (direct competitor) speaker that I use on rare occasion and thus leave unplugged (Wake-on-LAN devices suck down a lot of power and I already have a ton of computers running; would take even more on WiFi vice Ethernet). The other day I turned it on for my exercise hour. In addition to the 30 seconds I have to wait for it to boot up and get an IP address, it now decided it would not let me use *MY* hardware without a firmware update, so I had to wait for that to happen, and then it forced me to do an app update on my phone, again, before I could use !MY! device. By the time I could listen to music, I was halfway through my exercise hour. Infuriating. Relevant because you can be sure that this will act in a similar fashion. These are the problems with allowing companies to own your devices.

BTW, I am not afraid of technology - I am a Senior Systems Engineer, in fact, which I hope will also help convince you I am not stupid. I love good technology that works well, is proven, and that I control. But this type of thing bothers me a lot, and it really, truly irks me that consumers don't seem to push back about this. Is it just ignorance? Or do I just think different than everyone else? Because it's much more frustrating for me to play with my phone all the time trying to make something work than to just plug up some cables and make it work via hardware.

---On to other details now---

Despite the fact that I had to write a lot to express myself above, I realize the vast majority of consumers just don't care. So I weighted that lightly and didn't give it a poor review score. Here are the details most of you want to hear:

* Be advised that Dolby Digital+/Atmos/TrueHD do not work over optical, but only over HDMI with ARC. So if your TV doesn't have it, this cannot be used to its full potential.

BTW, I have had control for HDMI or audio working with my downstairs (Sony ~900F...please let us know if you got it working with this item) TV in the past, but I hated it because I can't use my stereo independent of the TV (although would work great with a soundbar). I never got it working with this (even using the change setting in the app) after I had originally set it up with optical. I don't care because the Sonos is going up to the guest bedroom with an older Sony TV that does not have ARC. But it does concern me that there may be some issues getting this to work right with some TVs. And by the way, the downstairs TV did see that an audio system was attached and said BraviaLink/Control for HDMI was on, but I could not get sound. May have driven me mad if I intended to use it on that TV.

* No optical input or aux input of any sort. It actually comes with an optical to HDMI pigtail I've never seen before, and I can only guess it uses power supplied by the device to the HDMI cable to change the electrical signal to optical somewhere along the line, much like the very long "optical HDMI" cables that have hit the market recently. Very interesting.

* As with Heos, Sonos' app allows you to see DLNA media servers on your home network. I don't even set up media servers to do music, though, because it just takes forever to index hundreds of thousands of files. And the thing that sucks about music is the metadata - you know how it'll show ten different albums for one because the album is spelled slightly different each time?

The additional functionality in the Sonos is that you can point it directly to your files and play music that way. BUT...it gave up pretty quickly trying to index all that music. There is definitely a limit and I'm guessing it's fairly low. I can overcome this by typing in the sub directories, which in my case is by band/artist, but this is super tedious and very much limits what you can do with your home network (see below**). In this case, you still have the metadata problem because you cannot see the folders and files, but it just reads the tags. But you can just make a playlist, which is also cumbersome, but no more so than any other mobile app for music that I've seen.

**Side note about music and stereos: I put in a whole-house audio system, which was quite challenging in my old home with plaster and lathe walls, but I totally love it. I have receivers with full functionality - no app required - but which are improved by their associated app, allowing you to change zone, volume, power, etc. And I have a Windows server reading music off a NAS, but I keep the Windows server to have Music Bee, which has an auto-DJ feature and allows for much, much easier playlist creation. I can get into that server on my phone if I need to via Teamviewer, but usually prefer to Teamviewer in via another PC. That is the only part that seems imperfect - if only I could use a phone app to easier control MusicBee on my PC (but I don't want to have to rely on the phone app to play anything via WiFi, airplay, etc. - none of that ever works as well, and also, a phone app could never index all that music)

I'm telling you this so you can recommend a solution if you know one, but I also want you to know what truths I hold dear and true:

- Wired is always better assuming you can't see the wires (do you own your home and can you run speaker wires? network cables?)
- Big speakers are always capable of more bass (do you want to reach down to 20Hz?)
- Too many things are cumbersome on a phone (do you want a system that allows availability and full functionality of all your local music?)

** Side note finished**

* It looks great. It may overlap your TV in some cases (thinking about those ultra-low sitting Sony OLED TVs), so take into consideration that point. I think it has an IR repeater in it (although I haven't seen that confirmed) so that it will not block your remote's access to the TV.

* It sounds great. Yeah. It really does, but it depends what you're looking for and the last thing you listened to. For most of my music, I just love to have tower speakers and a big, powerful sub). And for movies, I would of course like to have towers all around me and a giant sub. But for my spare bedroom, this is totally killer. Would like to try the surrounds and the associated sub, although I do wonder if sync issues would drive me insane.

For many people, this will be more than enough for their entire house setup, particularly if you have a smaller place and/or very close neighbors. No one will try to pretend it doesn't sound great. It's crystal clear and it does an excellent job with voices, even without the "voice mode" enabled on the app. The many speakers at all these different angles are not a gimmick - it really creates a full and fantastic sound. And it even sounds quite full frequency-wise...I'd like to know what frequency it gets down to...for the most part you won't miss the bass if you aren't accustomed to much bass...but considering today's consumers use these little battery-powered bluetooth speakers half the time, I think most people will get on fine with these frequency levels.

* Packaging is also amazing. It makes you feel like you got something truly awesome. (I mean, you did, honestly, but this accentuates that fact). Now you got a giant box and a specialized cloth sleeve you won't want to throw away - at least for a while.

**Conclusion**

Awesome product. Great technology, materials, design. Includes a processor, volatile and non-volatile RAM (much more than a speaker!). Aside from my above reservations, I'm still impressed. I'm now convinced this will run pretty much flawlessly as a (super high-end) sound bar, but it also incorporates a way to add a lot of additional musical functionality without wires or a lot of thought on the part of the consumer. I guess it's this functionality that falls a little short in my opinion, but the truth is it's a lot of great functionality if you don't have all the extra equipment running that I have (and I guess most people don't).

Yes, this was too long...

title: THE BEST HDTV
text:
I bought this TV at Best Buy and paid quite a bit more for it than what you see here. I am thrilled with this TV and is quite a bargain on Amazon. I have cable and a DVD with HDMI and it was a snap to connect and start watching from the get-go.
It is a beautiful TV, and now I am addicted to the larger size widescreen HDTV's. The 800 series of this TV is excellent, and has the best sound ever. No need for a home theatre, DVD and Blu Ray plays BEAUTIFULLY. I bought the expensive calibration service which I think was a waste of money, as the TV is easy to adjust right out of the box. I have my own perferences, and after it was calibrated, I never even used the Custom setting (that is where they put the "calibrated" settings) and went back to my own "Standard" settings after the calibration. I turned off the NR setting, put the black level to "light" and turned off the C.A.T.S. settings on the "Picture" menu. Keeping the black level to "light" and turning off C.A.T.S setting makes a big difference in the clarity of the picture, and makes the adjustment of brightness and contrast more accurate. It takes a bit of fussing, but you can get a perfect picture, all by yourself. I love this TV, and plan to buy a 800 series in the 50 inch, also. Both these series are pretty future proof, and will probably be the last TV's I buy.
I have read that keeping the Contrast and Brightness down to 50 for about 30 days before revving it up any higher will "prime" the TV and actually make it last longer. The 800 series of the Panasonic Plasma has my highest recommendation.
P.S. Be aware that there is some reflection issues with the larger TV, just because they are able to reflect things like lamps over a broader space. This is the nature of big screen TV's I am afraid. However, I have a Sony LCD (the best) and I still prefer the Plasma..far better picture.

Just wanted to give an (May 28, 2009)update on my opinion of this TV. It has stayed the same. I still love it. I have changed my mind about getting a calibration done, and I think it is worth the extra bucks to get a professional calibration. I was wrong about that, the TV does play better after a calibration. I bought a second Panasonic Plasma the TH 50PZ800U through Amazon, which was a great buy, and excellent white glove delivery. I wanted the 800U in the 50 inch for my living room and the reviews for the 800U (with THX) was higher than the 850U. However, I prefer the 850U model over the "certified THX" 800U, and I also prefer the 46" over the 50" size. The 850U has special professional adjustment features, and I think the picture is sharper on the 46". So if you think bigger is better, that is not always so, but it always comes down to your own personal needs and preferences. I also bought a Panasonic BMP BD50 model of Blu Ray disk players. Blu Ray is excellent on both Panasonic models. The Panasonic Blu Ray player is very good, but I plan to replace it with a Oppo Blu Ray player when it is released. The Panasonic Blu Ray 1080p upscaling for standard DVD's could be better, so I plan to replace with an Oppo brand.

title: TERRIBLE instructions.....
text:
The lack of instructions for this product is horrible. They even include a QR scan code to take you to an online instruction video. Which I watched twice just to make sure I didn't miss anything before reviewing this product.....

I am a former graphics installer. I also built/installed signage. I've run vinyl graphics and worked around this sort of stuff for a good deal of time. So there was really only ONE (1) thing I was looking for in the instructions and they failed!

If you are not familiar with the process of applying films like this, there are a number of steps that are missing that are imperative to keep you from making a mess out of your purchase.

The pros:

The film does appear to filter blue light.

Cons:

- Terrible instructions. Missing many key steps to ensure a quality install. They need to improve on this.
- Alcohol wipes are awdful. You better open and wipe the screen quickly before they dry out. You have about 5 seconds. And.... GO!
- The squeege they supply is a piece of cardboard.
- The "Dust Sticker" they supply doesn't work the greatest and can leave marks on your screen.
- Even with the 50/50 guess on which side to install toward the screen, I guessed wrong the first time and had to redo my work. Because of the lack of detail in the instructions, this caused some scratching, etc. when applying. However, since I typically work in a reduced light setting, they aren't noticeable most of the time. It still was a waste of money to have made this mistake.

Overall.... I'm not sure if I would buy this again or not. It does filter blue light and that was my only reason for purchasing. However, I'm less than satisfied with everything else they fell short on. I would hope that there is a company out there that would take the time to provide some decent instructions so their customers don't end up unhappy.

title: As Good As TV Gets
text:
I'm in awe. This TV is, by far, not only the best TV I've owned, but better than I've ever seen. The truth be told: I'm not testing. I'm all-in. I love this. This is like asking me to test Kobe beef or ask my opinion about flying first class. I apologize ahead of time this review of the "Sony XBR55A9F 55-Inch 4K Ultra HD Smart BRAVIA OLED TV (2018 Model)" will be filled with drooling.

My Testing
I'm a week into it. I've watched Thor: Ragnarok (you know which scene I went straight to: the fight scene on the bridge); The Good, the Bad and the Ugly; Kung Fu (TV series), some BBC nature shows, Death in Paradise -- all to get a sense of the range. I've watched on Netflix and Amazon Prime Video, as well as YouTube. 4K as well as old stuff. In other words, I can see it is able to show everything from UHD to older movies, the things we all watch in real life.

Through the pre-installed Google Chromecast, I've watched my own videos and looked at photos from my phone. My LG G5 pics of the box turtle which wandered into my yard looks vibrant.

I've also listened to Spotify. I'm a paid subscriber which, in part, means the audio is better than the free version.

Set-up took two people. I watched a unboxing video on YouTube to walk me through it. With something this high-end, I wanted to get it right. It isn't hard, but it is 80 lbs. I didn't want my review to begin, "Well, I'm sure it is good, but I dropped it."

It is set on a desk in my library. It leans slightly back but that's of no consequence. It faces a window. The blinds are closed but light still reflects on the glass screen. As such, it works best at night with the lights off.

It is almost all screen. There is minimal frame. Thin as it gets. All the brains and speakers are in the stand.

It is plugged into a standard outlet, and it is fed through my home's wireless system.

While it can do Surround Sound, I'm not using it. One: I don't have the right speakers; and Two: the sound is amazing for this room.

The default video settings do have a soap opera effect. As people move, it looks like they are in front of a green screen. You can adjust that. You can also adjust to default settings for games, cinema and more, depending on how you are using the TV.

I can see the image from any angle. While the screen isn't curved, I don't care. It is perfect as it is.

A bunch of useful apps are pre-installed, like Netflix and Prime Video. Others are available via Google Play. Just login and have at it.

Your home screen remembers where you've been. That helps.

The remote has all the usual buttons. One is wasted with a Google Play default. One I like: turn the pic off. When I listen to music, I don't really need to see the image.

OK Google or the press of a button on the remote allows voice commands like playing a Netflix video. Prime Video isn't ready for voice commands yet. It turns on/off via voice too.

While buying a TV involves a serious analysis of the video aspects, the sound is important. Here, it shines. The bass, the highs, all of it sounds amazing. As I write, Bruce Springsteen’s “Born to Run” album is playing. While it isn’t a top notch as my stereo speakers are, it is so impressive that I forgot that this is a TV playing music.

I haven’t cranked it higher than 30. I presume it goes to 100, but any louder than 30 is beyond my taste.

I cannot effuse enough. All my friends want to come by and watch with me. I'm pleased.

End of drooling. Planet Hulk is starting. Gotta watch.

Anthony Trendl
americanspeechwriter.com

title: Love this mouse!
text:
When my trusty Microsoft Intellimouse died, I had a hard time finding a replacement. I wanted to stay with a corded mouse, and needed a minimum of five buttons. I also wanted the ability to scroll horizontially, a feature not on the Intellimouse that I had. Not many to choose from.

But, found the M500 and gave it a shot. Very pleased with it. The overall ergonomics are excellent - I have large hands, and most mice are too small for comfort. This fits perfectly.

The button placement is excellent, although I wish the page up and page down buttons were a wee bit larger. The best feature is the free-wheeling scroll wheel. You can unlock it so it spins freely and cruse through many pages with just a single spin. It also can be used as a conventional scroll wheel when the lock button is re-engaged.

The software allows you to re-map pretty much any of the keys to do what you want them to do. My mouse did not have the CD - had to download the software from the Logitech site. Without the software you only have basic functionality. Zero problems loading and running it on XP with SP3.

Very pleased, and highly recommend.

UPDATE Sept 2018: After many years of use, my M500 started to fail. The mouse tracking worked fine, as did all the buttons. However, the scroll wheel would not work well most of the time. I expect it's due to getting gunked up over the years. Took a look at the options out there and the M500 is still the best choice for my needs, so I got another one. Still very pleased with the performance and features.

I am not happy about this and will not buy another one of these. I will format it and try again. Maybe there are hidden files that aren't showing up on it. But this is really annoying.

Update: I decided to format the drive and found that the bit size for exFAT is very small. As in less than my file size small. I changed it to NTSF, as it will only be used in a computer, and it is now working properly as regards to being able to actually fill it with 116 GBs. But it still took about 4 hours to copy 8 GBs of data to it. My USB 3.0 drive would have done it in less than 30 minutes.

title: Works well as a way to get analog out of your HDMI
text:
I'm running a 1080p projector for our home entertainment system, and have a high quality decades-old analog stereo system for sound. Without this Audio Extractor device, I used to be limited to source devices that let me separate the video from the audio (Fire TV box and other devices that offer both analog stereo and HDMI video simultaneously) since the sound has to go one way and the video feed another.
This device opens up possibilities such as more modern equipment that does away with analog connections entirely. A Fire TV Stick 4k for example, or Raspberry Pi board (yes, technically the Pi has analog outputs, but they are subpar and not recommended for high quality audio). I'm very happy with this device and the opportunities it opens for me. It works well for me with the 2ch setting and my equipment. text:
My mount simply popped off the dash. I still had one of the adhesive things left so I prepped the dash again with alcohol and a clean microfiber cloth. The alcohol was 70% off-the-shelf antiseptic isopropyl alcohol (As opposed to rubbing alcohol which contains fragrance and oils.) I let the dash dry completely.

This time I made doubly sure that I pressed the assembly down tightly and held it until my muscles cramped. I let it sit overnight. The next day I gave it another press downward and let it sit for an additional day. The following day I gingerly snapped the gps onto the mount. The first time I tried to adjust the angle of the screen the silly mount popped off again.

No one adhesive bonds to all materials with equal strength. Perhaps the slight fake leather texture of the dash covering in my car does not like this adhesive. Perhaps it grips tenaciously to some dashes and poorly on another regardless of how closely the instructions are followed.

Having said all that I am simply going to use my own strips of 3M VHB tape and fasten this to my friction mount instead of using the suction cup mount. (Suction cups always give way sooner or later and the GPS falls.)

I'm not happy with this mount. It should have stuck to the dash. I have previously used a Garmin disk on this dash with a suction cup mount. That disk stayed stuck just fine for at least 3 years until I removed it to attach this new mount. All told, I should have stayed the old arrangement and just been more vigilant in keeping the suction cup properly cleaned and latched down before each trip.

I thought cpus were better than that nowadays? I guess not. For the last 10 years I've been AMD all the way. But now I guess I'm going to be an intel fanboy. Background: I spec and integrate the highest resolution LCD’s produced in aerospace defense applications. LCD image performance is measured in hundreds of dimensions and environments. Sony is not a player in that space.

For home, I’ve been SID show and showroom shopping LCD, OLEDs, etc image quality for years. This year, I’m replacing a comparably sized exercise room 1080p LCD set. Sony has always been, to my eye, a superb comparative model and a $100 or so more than other competitors. Is the premium worth it?

This Sony X800H is an eye grabber across the showroom and on close inspection. It’s a phenomenal picture. Sony’s proprietary LCD foundries are unique in the industry. The Sony LCD foundry produces a distinctive LCD that is worth the premium price to the discerning.

Performance-wise, Sony reduced the native refresh rate to 60hz from 120hz last year. That’s quite practical as it will be some years before >60fps cameras are widely available at native 120fps. No matter, the 60hz to 120hz refresh is not discernible to the eye. The X800H imaging software can be seen to take care of latency artifacts at factory default settings … no viewing distance ghosting, inverse ghosting, blur or pulse-width modulation.

There is a comment regarding darkness, edge lighting, and illumination issues. The X800H is both edge and background light as best as I can discern without tearing it apart. It's uniform lighting no matter. Sony has always been the master of the best 'optical black' pixel to enrich the color pixel perception. The X800H is loaded with image quality controls. Image software quality defaults arrived set at factory default. It was perfect out of the box. Don't adjust anything. I rarely futz with default settings. No one should have to. The vast majority of image problems are video source input. Change the channel first and compare the image.

An old school key attribute is viewing angles … how many degrees left/right and horizontal/vertical are necessary to degrade the image. The viewing angles here are excellent. Viewing angles are a peek into the remarkable quality of Sony’s proprietary LCD foundry.

Sony’s software, firmware, Smart integration, and image processors are likewise Sony proprietary. Sony names these features like everyone else. Feature comparisons are mostly apparent in year over year Sony tech evolution.

Of course, the real story is in the final image quality. The X800H is one excellent viewing experience.

title: Dell 27" Monitor
text:
I’m using this Dell 27” monitor with a MacBook Pro. While the monitor offers VGA and HDMI connections, only a VGA cable is included. The product description left out that detail.

The main product picture currently being used shows a silver stand; the stand is actually black as shown in other product photos. I can’t really say if the design of the stand frees up more desk space or not since that’s never been a problem for me, but I do like that it’s a flat base. The viewing angle is adjustable but not the height of the monitor.

I also like the slim power cord! No huge brick adaptor for this monitor.

The main complaint I have with this monitor is how it bounces on my desk. I use a mechanical keyboard, and the monitor bobbles with every keystroke. I have a larger monitor that doesn’t have this problem, so I imagine it’s due to the small stand on the Dell.

Image quality seems to be pretty good. There’s not a ton of options on the monitor, but you can adjust contrast/brightness, and there are presets for “ComfortView” (blue light blocking), Movie, Game, Warm, Cool, and the ability to set a custom color.

When I use it with my laptop, I do my main work on the Dell screen instead of the Mac’s, which is the opposite of what I usually do. And not because of the increased screen size, but because I prefer the image quality.

title: Great for Mac users
text:
I have a 2017 MacBook Pro with 4 Thunderbolt/USB C ports. Of course almost every peripheral I use is USB 2.0/3.0, so I have adapters everywhere and can never find one when I need it, or don’t have enough ports to plug in everything I want to use.

So this USB C Hub from Flagtop is super handy to have around. I use it to connect a second monitor (HDMI port), an external mouse/keyboard (USB 2.0 ports), and the power cable (USB C port).

I like that the USB 2.0/USB 3.0 ports have a little space between each one. This makes them usable even if you have a thick thumb drive or cable plugged in.

I had to have the ports on my laptop replaced because they loosened up over time, so I like that I can reduce wear on the new ports by unplugging the hub to disconnect everything.

The port runs warm. It’s hot to the touch; my desk feels warm underneath it.

I do wish the cable for the hub was longer. If I have my laptop on a stand, the hub dangles from one of the ports. The cable is about 5.5 inches, and if I have several things plugged into it, I feel like that’s a lot of weight to have hanging off a single port on the side of my laptop.

title: Decent combo unit
text:
I recently upgraded my AV setup and one of the goals was to cut down on the mess of cables connecting everything. While I don't watch tapes very much, I didn't want to eliminate having a VCR since I occasionally will tape shows.

Looked at a variety of VHS/DVD combo units and they all seemed to have their problems. Took a chance on the JVC, and so far (been using it for about 2 months), have been pleased.

The best feature is that it will send both DVD and VHS signals through an HDMI cable. Just one cable connects this to my receiver -- no more tangle of cords! It also will upscale the VHS image but don't expect much. Yes, it's better, but not high def (or even DVD) quality.

The built-in tuner works well for me, but I do live in a fairly strong signal area, so pretty much every tuner works well. The recording feature is pretty easy to use, and the tape-to-DVD dubbing feature is a snap to set up. I've been able to play the disks that I've recorded on other DVD players without any problem.

The remote is not great. Lots of small buttons, and the layout is pretty poor. Load times for DVDs is pretty good. It does make more noise than my other DVD players. Not objectionable, but you can hear the disk spin up. It lags a bit when you hit the eject button. Upscaling for DVDs is decent. Clearly not on a par with an Oppo, but a solid performer.

While there are better choices out there for just a DVD player, just a DVD recorder, or just a VHS player, this is a good choice if you're looking for a single player that does all the above, plus offers a built-in tuner and single-cable connectivity.

Lastly, this is also sold at Sam's Club. You may want to check them out for pricing. Amazon also offers a pretty good price as well.

UPDATE: There's a firmware update available that fixes the problem with the recording shutting down in mid-program. According to JVC, it seems that some commercials trigger the copy-protection system, and it stops recording. It happens very infrequently, but the firmware update solves the problem. Easy to install -- just download the file from the JVC site, burn it to a CD, and pop it in. Full instructions come with the firmware file. Not essential to do unless you're having the problem of shutdowns mid-program.

title: I am really liking this headset, surprised by the quality of sound, noise cancelling, and comfort
text:
In my work I need long periods of quiet. I’ve done what I can to deal with a lack of quiet these last two years, between my wife working at home and the neighborhood seeing far more people at home. I’ve tried a few things, but in many ways had to sacrifice and learn to deal with the sound. For several months I was working from midnight till 3 or 4 am to get some of my work done. So I started to think about going back to headphones. I’ve previously owned a set of a well known, expensive brand that was good - well, great sound, but they were big and got to be far too hot on my head, especially over time. So I ended up getting rid of those. I still wear a set of those that sit on the outside of my ears for sound - which is outstanding - but they don’t always cover enough noise as they were designed to allow the athletes who wear them to actually hear sound around them. So....

I was thinking what I might do again. I had the chance to get these Ankbit Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Headphones, but went in knowing they too might be too hot on my head after awhile. I figured I’d at least get some work done in a few hours each day.... but would they be enough?

I should also mention, I have a lifelong issue with my ears that causes me to feel the pressure (think airplanes and storms) in such a way it can bother my head. The other reason I got rid of those expensive well know headphones was that they sat so securely on my head, the pressure was too much for my head. I again, could only wear them for so long before I had to take them off.

So, these Ankbit Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Headphones?
So far I really like them - a lot!
I’ve been wearing them every day for at least a few hours and getting work done. It has taken a bit of time to adjust, but what I am experiencing has been helpful and I am glad to have them.

The box they come in includes the headset, a bag, and needed cords.

The cords are easy to use, but I would say, it would be nice if the cord for charging were longer. I mean, this thing is SHORT! Where I could normally set an item off to the side with the cord reaching, I now have to set these headsets directly in front of the plug, meaning plugging in other things is difficult. So that would be one improved this set could use.

The bag is great. It is black, nice material, and holds the headset well. Glad to have it.

The Ankbit Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Headphones themselves are surprisingly great. I don’t know why it surprises me, other than I had that expensive pair in the past - which was outstanding - and I like these as much - in some ways, more (think ear discomfort and overheating).

1. The set is comfortable with the ear covers nice and soft on my ears. They are enough to sit well, hold in the sound (my wife has not complained about any sound bleed), and work as far as noise canceling. ** I'll come back to this in a minute. But I find the Ankbit Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Headphones to be very comfortable. If I had one “complaint” it’s that they are slightly large. I have a large head on which I wear large hats. However, even I find the top of this to be a bit larger than my head - which tells me someone with a smaller head than mine might have an issue with the size of these. They do fit, and the ears sit directly on my ears, but I can tell it’s just on my ears. It is comfortable, but something I take note of.

2. There is no (noticeable) pressure build up. Where my previous set caused such pressure that I’d have to take them off at least twice an hour, I’ve never had to take these off and have worn them up to 3 hours at a time - and could go longer.

3. ** The noise reduction works. We tested this the first day - including matching to another work style head set I got to also try and block the noise - the kind used on construction sites and the like - and this Ankbit Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Headphones worked as well or perhaps better than that set. While that set has no music or sound to it and this does, both blocked my wife’s talking and yelling within 2 - 3 feet of me to the point that I could barely hear her. This Ankbit Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Headphones offers the music as a way to add to the options - and I use an app to help if need be, with sounds such as white noise and thunderstorms. But in general, I prefer to be able to have no noise at all at times. With both the app sounds and no sound at all, I am able to block out MOST noise. I do add the app when my wife is working in the kitchen, which is behind my back where I’m working now she’s home. And the app takes care of the rest of the sound. But without it, I have great sound reduction and elimination.

You can also turn this feature off and have “transparency” which allows you to hear background noise, incase you need to listen for the kids or a phone. It still. blocks the sound, gives you good internal sound with music, but you can hear outside sound better. It is like my other, outside the ear set when in this mode, so I do not use it - I have those for that type of sound. But it is available.

4. The sound itself is excellent. I have listened to music and movies playing on these and both are outstanding. I truly love the sound and find it is full, rich, and well done. It’s a pleasant experience.

5. The buttons for on/off, volume up/down, and transparency are at the side of the ear phone on the right side and 1. EASY to the point of frustration that I keep hitting them - usually turning it off - when trying to remove the headset, and needing to learn how to not hit them and 2. easy to use overall. The four buttons are easy to adjust - I’m still getting use to which is which and not second guessing. The on/off is easy, but I’m really impressed with the volume up/down, which is in nice levels of degrees - not too much either way - and gives a great sound.

I also discovered - the hard way - when you close the computer it’ll go off, but open and it’s back up and running. There are so many little things like that. I don’t know, maybe they are far more common than I know - I have not been a headset user for some time - but these are details that impress.

Overall I really like this Ankbit Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Headphones for my work and the quiet it provides, but for the sound I get when I’m listening to sounds to help me work, or even better, the music and movies that help keep me going throughout the day. I’m impressed and if this set lasts for a few years... it’ll be an outstanding find!

title: Well-designed, easy to use, but no wired network
text:
The Roku Premiere player is easy to set up and has a well-designed user interface that requires no reference to a user manual. I connected it to the tv (using an HDMI cable), plugged it in, turned on the tv and selected the appropriate source. I was disappointed that there was no option to plug in a network cable for a wired connection (like there is for the Fire TV box; you have to go up to the Premiere+ to get that port). This might be a concern for anyone with a weak or problematic wifi signal.

The initialization was fairly simple: language selection, wifi connection (it supports AC as well as N), automatic detection of the tv display type, automatic software update, then a separate session on the computer to register the device and create a Roku account. I had another disappointment here: the account creation requires the entry of payment info, either credit card or Paypal. If I want to use the box just to watch my subscribed services, such as Netflix and Amazon, there's no reason for me to give Roku any payment information at all, it just increases the risk of malicious use. (If you really don't like this, you can sign up using a Paypal account, then go back into your Paypal account and rescind the Roku permissions.)

After that it was all plain sailing, and I had no complaints: streaming video was clear and glitch-free, the sound was good. All in all, a very nice streaming box for a reasonable price. For my money, however, I would consider upgrading to the Premiere+. Or, the Fire TV box, which is what I normally use at home.

text: I frequently travel ultra-low cost airlines, which means no in-flight entertainment, and all my stuff needs to fit in a personal item sized bag if I want to avoid baggage fees. I ordered a Fire HD for movies and videos while traveling without needing to lug a laptop and heavy charging brick. I've found with a keyboard, I can perform about 90% of my basic computing tasks on the Fire. I selected this case mainly for the included keyboard. The case is very nicely built, with precise cutouts for buttons, charging ports and speakers. It seems very protective, and I wouldn't be concerned if I somehow dropped the tablet. However it is very heavy and adds significant bulk. It's actually about 1/4 inch thicker than my laptop, and almost as heavy. The keyboard functions very well, especially given it's size. I don't find the keys to be cramped and there is good travel and feedback on key presses. I'm typing this review on the keyboard, and I've noticed some missed key presses, but I'm fairly sure that is operator error, as I'm not quite used to the keyboard yet. The major drawback is that it charges using a micro-USB cable. This causes it to be slow to charge.  I was extremely disappointed, especially given that the seller stated in an answer to a question that the keyboard charged with USB-C. If I had known that it came with the slower charging port, I would have selected a different keyboard case.  As it stands, given the good functioning, I'm not sure it would be worth the trouble to return it given its low price point. Overall, this isn't afairly nice keyboard with just a few quirks that keep it from being five stars.
