title: Not quite spy-gear
text:
First of all, the D-Link camera is relatively easy to set up - always the one to play with techie stuff first, my husband had it up and running in a flash (well almost a flash). Just attach the supplied cable to your computer, run the CD and follow the simple instructions and you're good to go. According to the instructions, you have two options to set up the camera: wirelessly or wired. Naturally, my husband tried the wireless option first, which didn't work because it claimed (spuriously, we believe) that it couldn't find the network, so he had to resort to the other method, which worked right away. We're using a Linksys wireless router.

The camera works quite well indoors where the intensity of the ambient light is generally much lower than outdoors. However, in the brighter outdoor light it is difficult to discern what you're looking at (is it a bird, is it a plane?). The colour is not the best, but then again, it ain't a Nikon 7000. There is some amount of adjustment that can be done online to change the settings, but you'll need to create an online account/register your camera first with D-Link at [...] This is also necessary if you want to view your camera remotely. Strange enough, whenever I try to access the camera online, I get a message telling me that the application needs an earlier version of Java. However, after hitting <Run> for the next three dialogue boxes or so that pop up, it will display the picture. I tried accessing the camera from outside my home network but was unable to do so. Maybe firewall issues?? (Too much effort required to check this). There is also an iPod app that is quite good, minus sound.

Night vision was surprisingly good too. In the dark, the images were shades of grey, but in brighter conditions, the colour returned. Four LED lights lit up whenever the night vision was activated (could be an issue if you wanted to place it somewhere discrete).

On the down side, the camera has to be plugged into an electrical socket to work, and the cord it came with is very short. This means you have to either place it near an electrical outlet or use an extension cord. This would obviously have limitations on where you can place it. It also has to be connected to your home network whether wired or wireless.

While in theory it could be used as a security camera, it has to be powered 24/7, so if you live in a country or area prone to an uneven power supply which could damage sensitive equipment, then you may want to consider that before getting it or you may need to install additional equipment such as line conditioners/UPS to protect your equipment.

The sound is not very good. In fact, after a few hours use it started to make a clicking sound in an endless loop.

Recommended for limited applications such as keeping an eye on kids (or pets, or pesky guests), or when you're avoiding (hiding from) certain people who come calling at your gate, but not as a dedicated security system.

Amanda Richards, June 29, 2011

title: Update: May work... or not -- and that's not a good thing.
text:
Update 12/10/19:
I was on the road yesterday when I got a message from my mesh network that there's a power outage in the house.
Came back 15 minutes later to find power restored and noticed that one of my APC 600VA units had done what it was supposed to do. My second unit one though was emitting a constant alert tone and everything attached to it had shut down including two 3D printers toward the end of 17 hour prints :-(

I don't know what the issue is. The unit is only a year old, so I don't believe it's the battery. I turned the unit off and on again, and now it's back to normal. When I pull the AC plug, it kicks in as expected. But what's the point of a UPS if you can't trust it to do its job when needed ???

Original review:
I'm pretty happy with this unit, compared to the UPS I used before. Slick looking, enough ports, widely enough spaced for bulky plugs. I haven't actually measured battery life but during a few outages I got at least 20 minutes, plenty of time to save files and shut things down properly. My main complaint is the hideous software that comes with this unit. Feels like written by a high school kid in the 90s. One weird thing: When I send a job to my printer, I get a power spike warning from the software even though the printer is not plugged into the UPS (it's plugged into a different outlet on on the other side of my office).

title: It must not be meant for music
text:
I agree with the minority of reviewers here who find it too rumbly and boomy, and not nearly tight and musical enough. It's fine if all you need is a device to shake the floor when watching Iron Man II on TV. For that purpose, it worked fine for me. But if you want to listen to music, well...
I was able to adjust the crossover and volume to make it sound acceptable for classical cello music -- to add some warmth, depth and resonance. It was actually quite nice for that. But for pop, rock, dance, etc, the way music is equalized, it simply demands more from a woofer than this is capable of providing. I had to turn the dials way down to keep it from muddying the sound completely. In the end, I just unplugged it for those types of music. If all you do is watch TV, then fine, it's a bargain and enjoy it. But if you listen critically and you don't want to have to fine-tune your subwoofer for each album, then move on, save your money up for something better. And let me know what you buy, because I will want one too.
Now my dilemma is: it was so cheap, it's hardly worth the cost of returning. But it's not really what I want, despite all the glowing reviews here that convinced me to buy it. Don't blindly trust reviewers here when it comes to high-end audio. Probably the folks with the true golden ears don't shop here much.

title: FINALLY figured out how to import playlists from iTunes onto this Walkman!
text:
Many people complained that there was no way to transfer Playlists from iTunes to this Walkman. I had the same problem, but I refused to give up. I finally figured it out after many trial and error attempts. It's a bit of a pain the first time, but it's pretty easy to do. It's better than having to recreate your playlists again. This information is for Window users:

1) Open iTunes and highlight the Playlist you want to transfer. Don’t open it, just highlight the name of the Playlist you want to transfer.

2) Click on FILE, LIBRARY, EXPORT PLAYLIST.

3) At this point Windows Explorer will pop up. You'll have to save the Playlist onto your hard drive. You can rename your Playlist here under File Name. IMPORTANT: Make sure you save the file with either an .m3u OR .m3u8 extension. You can find the correct extension in the drop down menu under "Save as type" just below the file name.

4) Note the folder where the Playlist is saved. I created a folder so I'll always know where they were saved in my hard drive.

Now open Sony Music Center (download program online for free). This is the program that the Walkman uses. From the Music Center:

5) Click on FILE which you will find under the 3 horizontal lines on upper left hand corner of screen.

6) Click on IMPORT PLAYLIST

7) Windows Explorer will pop up. Find the Playlist you want to transfer to the Walkman.

8) Click IMPORT.

Hope this helps!

title: Useful, but just OK for my purposes
text: I have an HP laptop I want to use in the field for running an all-day event stream without needing to tether to a wall. I thought something like this would be a good move to keep it charged since the battery only lasts about 2.5 hours running the stream (it's CPU intensive). However, this laptop does not support USB-C PD charging unfortunately (I was hoping it did, there is a USB-C port, but sadly only output is supported), so I had to resort to using the AC part. Now, I know converting DC from a battery to AC requires quite a bit of power loss, but one recharge of my laptop from single digits to 80% practically wiped the power supply out. I definitely would not be able to charge the laptop more than once off of this, and I have my doubts it would even make it all the way to 100% without dying honestly. I was really hoping it would last longer. If you have a PD-compatible laptop, this might work better for you. I DO love that it has an AC outlet for emergencies, and I'll probably take this with us camping because it is pretty cool to have. But the product description implies this is a good option for charging a laptop, but for the price I've seen better options I think. At the very least, I wish this had a automotive-style 12v DC port so I could try getting that kind of charger for my laptop (less power lost since not inverting to AC), but alas. The only real laptop charging options are AC and USB-C/PD, and if your laptop doesn't use the latter, the first is a pretty inefficient option.

title: For those concerned about cost, I wonder we have forgotten our love affair with reading books
text:
“I wonder how long it has been we readers have gazed at the young person sitting under a tree at night reading a book on the Kindle home screen..oh, our love affair with books and being able to read our stories late into the night…...by candlelight….anywhere.”

Pre-release technology reviewers commenting on the price of the Kindle Oasis are wrong. The new Kindle Oasis is worth the the price Amazon is charging, including cover it hardly represents at all an increase in price when compared with a Kindle Voyage with cover. Yet it provides the two most asked for improvements in mobile devices: increased battery life reducing the need to frequently recharge, and improved screen legibility (new sans-serif Ember font, and more LEDS that provide increased brightness).

“When we are immersed into the story of our favorite books, only that world matters.”

Pre-release technology reviewers have compared the Kindle as a single purpose e-reader, to multipurpose devices like in smartphones, tablets and computers. When we choose to read, we are seeking a bit of solitude in the day and night. Oh, how easy it is to remember being annoyed with yet another incoming phone call, text message or email. The power of focus!

“The tactile feel of a book”

Pre-release technology reviewer have labelled the Kindle as luxurious with it’s leather cover. How soon we forget our books covered with leather! And we are willing to pay an extra price for it!

As I sit across the street from the one and only Amazon retail store “in the world”, I have unboxed and set up my new Kindle Oasis. Maybe I am one of the few ordinary people outside of Amazon and the technology press in the world to have been able to purchase one so soon. The feeling reminds me of going to a release party in the same shopping center for the latest Harry Potter novel.

This Kindle is new, like the latest release from our favorite author.

It connects me to reading anywhere, late at night when there is little light.

The Kindle Oasis is magical.

title: Changing my Review From 3 stars to none
text:
UPDATE 4/14/21: I'm giving up on this watch. It's always something. The sleep mode is mostly better now but won't register some nights. Now the weather fails to sync so I have ghost clouds instead of weather forecasts for the week. When I try to sync it manually it just cycles and cycles for several minutes and still no weather. I've updated location to allow the watch full access and still nothing.
DON'T WASTE YOUR TIME WITH THIS WATCH. IT HAS MULTIPLE ISSUES DEPENDING ON THE LAST UPDATE. Now the battery has gone from 14 days to 3 1/2 days after one year.

PREVIOUS UPDATE: After switching to an iPhone this works better even though a previous update killed it on my Android phone. The Thing that irks me now after another update is that the sleep app is way off. Lately I am told I've been awake for 3-5 hours a night which earns me a 30 to 50 rating. Never got better than a 80 rating so far. They did include the REM sleep to the graph which is nice. Since they changed the app name to Zepp it hasn't really been the same. The few other things I use it for, steps and watch faces and time of day and compass work okay. Battery life is the best feature.

The price has gone down $40 from when I bought it; maybe because of the Zepp app you have to use on your mobile phone. It's not the best.

I bought this watch to use in counting laps while swimming, but the Covid has put the stops on that this year. It was the only watch in this price range--since reduced-- that offered a swim mode although it is GPS distance (miles) rather than laps counted.

The battery lasts 10-14 days. My wife's Fitbit Versa 2 needs charging every couple of days. I don't leave the face always on. If you leave it always on, you'll probably have to charge it in 3 days. In the econ mode you have to tilt it to your face or click on the stem to make the face visible. A good trade off for not having to charge your watch all the time.

My main gripe about this watch is that when someone sends me a text message, it repeats 3-4 times on my watch. This seems to be a problem with several of the Amazfit watches according to some of the forums I have visited to remedy the situation without success. It's annoying and difficult to see texts from others in the long line of repeat sms messages. UPDATE: Buying an iPhone to pair with this watch seems to have solved this problem for me.

I tried the music mode and it works if you already have music playing on your phone. It will display the song playing, the Album or CD Title, volume control, pause and play, next and previous song controls. However if you are on economy mode, the music face disappears and you have to search for the music control again.

I used the Find Phone and Found it easily, but your phone must have power obviously. It will ring or force volume higher if playing music, lol. UPDATE: This find phone function no longer works. Beware updates. It's like Microsoft. Everytime they update to make it better it causes glitches.

If they could fix the multiple repeat sms messages and tweak the sleep mode with more info this would be a pretty good watch. Right now its only good. Would I buy it again? Maybe, if the swim mode is good. I'll have to wait to find out.

title: Takes some getting used to, but the sound quality makes it worth the effort
text:
I use earbuds a lot since I typically prefer the lightness and ease of use compared with traditional headphones. Right out of the box these were a bit puzzling as to how to position them for use. But, after a bit of fiddling with the over-the-ear loop, it becomes clear.

The in-ear comfort is good. It comes with a variety of ear tips including two types I’ve not used before: a double flange silicon tip and a triple flange silicon tip. The flanges allow the ear bud to make a much better seal in your ear canal. That not only helps cut out ambient noise intruding, it also improves the bass response. I found the double flange works best for me, but the variety of tips included appears sufficient to fit pretty much any ear.

It also comes with an excellent case for storage, and adapters for airplane use and for 1/4 inch plugs. I especially like the case since it’s small enough to make it easy to carry along (roughly 3.5 inches by 3 by 1.5 inches thick) and is reinforced to avoid being crushed. It has mesh pockets to keep everything stowed, and looks nice to boot (black with red contrast in the middle). All-in-all, it’s a great kit in terms of useful accessories.

I’m not as pleased with the cord. While I like how sturdy it is, it has a “Y” link that always seems to be in the way when I’m working out. I got used to it eventually, but a more streamlined cord system would have been a better design approach. Another negative is the 3.5mm plug. It needs to be seated just so or you get sound cut-outs or static. I tried it with several devices to be sure the issue is with the plug and not the device. A more robust plug is needed for this – you shouldn’t have to fiddle with it to get it to seat properly.

The over-the-ear loops are also a bit annoying at first. Granted, that’s certainly due to the fact that I usually use standard in-ear buds without the loop, so any type of loop feels weird to me at first. The material is soft and bendy, so you can position it in any variety of ways. It could benefit from some additional padding. On the plus side, they do hold the buds in very well. Quick head movements that would have loosened an in-ear bud didn’t jar these loose at all.

Now for the really important feature: how they sound. In a word, excellent. My benchmark for moderately-priced earbuds has been units made by RHA out of the UK. These sound nearly as good. Very clean sound but still ample bass provided that you select the right tip. For me, the standard tip (the one installed as delivered) gave me very little in terms of bass. Selecting a different tip to provide a better ear fit did wonders for bass response.

They are a bit more airy than the RHA sound. That could be a plus or a minus depending on your preferred type of music. Very heavy bass music is not a good match for these. Pretty much everything else is, and I appreciated the enhanced clarity. It’s the type of sound that, when you hear it, the first word that would come to mind is “clean.”

They look odd, make take you a moment to figure out how to position them, but provide a very open, natural sound. It comes with a well-designed kit of useful extras. However, the plug issues, the cord, and the ear loops collectively knock it down a star. Still well worth considering, however, and I would certainly recommend them.

title: Fun, comfy way to listen in winter.
text:
This knit hat is a really comfortable, convenient way to listen to tunes when its chilly outside.

The gray beanie is pretty typical, as far as winter hats go. It isn't thick enough for Arctic expeditions, but its great for most winter days where most of us live. If the temperature is above about 20 or 25 Fahrenheitenheight (maybe -5C), this hat should keep you warm. Its small enough, though, to shove into your coat pocket when you aren't wearing it.

The cool thing about the hat, though, is that it has Bluetooth headphones inside the rim, that position nicely over your ears. They stay in place surprisingly well, which makes this a really easy, functional way to listen to your music with a warm hat on.

The instructions that come with the beanie are pretty minimal. To turn on the headphones and get them searching for a Bluetooth audio source, press and hold the hidden button at the center of the leather patch on the outside of the hat. Your phone or mp3 player should detect "Bluetooth Beanie". Select that, and you should be good to go. Mine paired up pretty quickly once I figured out how to turn on the earphones in the hat.

I like this hat and will use it from fall through winter. If you found anything in my review helpful, please let me know.

title: Great hub, perfect for extending the ports for my MacBook Pro
text:
When I first got this I thought it was interesting that the a/c power adapter weighed more than the hub itself. But that's really no big deal since this hub sits on my desk all day doing its thing. The cool thing about this is that there are 7 ports PLUS the 2 'always on' fast charging ports for iphones, ipads, etc.

I use this port with my MacBook Pro which, using bootcamp, has both OSX (yosemite) and Windows 7 on it. The port works fine with both and it worked right away after plugging it in. I have external hard drives plugged into it, a keyboard (for when the MacBook Pro is "docked" on the desk), a printer, and a wacom tablet. All work great with this.

The one thing you have to remember is the 2 charging ports are solely charging ports. You can't plug in a USB flash drive, external harddrive, or other peripheral device and access it through one of these 2 bonus ports. Which means you also cannot sync your iPhone, iPad, Android, etc when plugged into one of the 2 charging ports. This is perfectly fine by me because it gets annoying plugging in my iPhone to charge and the computer always wanting to access it, sync it, or whatever. Plus the fact that these charging ports are always on means I can shut down my computer but leave the devices I need charged plugged in and they continue to charge. No need to move them to a wall outlet charger.

I also have a 7-port Anker USB3 hub, which works great but it does not have the additional charging ports. Between that one and this TP-Link I have plenty of ports to plug in external harddrives (I use many of those for backups and portable data storage).

title: You may love it, but I found it just too hard to deal with it's problems
text:
This is a hard camera to review, as the strengths (low ISO image quality) are so strong and the weaknesses (they are legion) are so hard to cope with. If you've used a recent Sigma and more or less liked it, you probably will love this. Most other users however will likely return it.

I had the chance to use this as a part of a novel free trial program from Sigma. Basically you bought the camera with a prearranged return for a full refund. I suppose I could have kept it, but honestly, I was happy to return it. It was just too hard to use. Why was it hard to use? Horrible ergonomics, limited battery life, slow performance (though admittedly better than earlier Sigma/Foveon efforts), bad screen, no evf, no 3rd party RAW support (with none pending), and horrible software (needed because of the lack of 3rd party support).

Poor ergonomics: Sometimes weird designs are a form follows function fresh take. This isn't that. It's large, hard to hold, has uncomfortable edges, and get's rather warm. The buttons are in the wrong place or do the wrong thing.

Horrible battery life: Bad. 100-150 shots at best, and that's from a camera without a flash and with a screen I dreaded to use. Based on the heat and complicated sensor output, there must be some hard working processing. Either way, it's a bit of a pain.

It's slow: While it's faster than earlier bodies, it's still slow to process images. It's also slow to acquire AF, and as the screen is poor (horrible in in the bright light that the sensor craves), it can be hard to see what's in focus.

As noted above the screen is poor, especially in bright light. It also doesn't pivot or swivel, and there's no real EVF option. I'm starting to wonder who this camera is for. The slow moving deliberate artists who might make the most of this camera would benefit from an outstanding screen/EVF (ala Fuji X-T1) to verify critical focus in the field.

RAW support: Worst in class. While Nikon, Canon, Fuji, etc... users may be critical of the results of using one conversion program or another, they have choices. Most also have first party supported or built applications that are at least mediocre. Even Nikon's lamentable new raw software is a million times better than what Sigma offers, and here there is no support from Adobe, PhaseOne, Sillypix, etc... The good news is that the out of body JPGs are now rather nice.

There's a lot wrong with this camera, but the image quality is amazing. The transition to the new Foveon sensor design hasn't lost the special wonderful image quality of previous generations, and one can create images with this camera that few others, even medium format, could match. The lens is rather nice too.

Sadly this camera is a niche camera. The 5 star reviewers used the same camera, but if you're used to the Sigma workflow and love having the best image quality, this is a 5 star camera. For most photographers, you may be better off getting a Fuji X100s and take 2-3x as many pictures, pic the best, and use any number of editing tools to get great results. You'd be less frustrated, it would fit in a coat pocket, and you'd miss far fewer shots. If you can try it for yourself, go for it. You may love it.

title: Good, not great
text:
My 17" HP laptop died (CPU failure) and it really wasn't worth fixing. I looked around for a replacement and came up with this. I didn't really need another laptop, and the 20" screen on this all-in-one desktop seemed like it would be a big improvement.

And it was. And the touchscreen offers some extra ways of doing things that keep you from death-gripping a mouse and getting carpal tunnel syndrome. 1 TB of disk and 6 GB of memory makes it much faster than the old laptop, as does an Intel i3 vs. an AMD Turion 2 on the laptop.

All-in-all, the all-in-one is a very nice computer. Only having to hook up two wires (power and network) was most pleasant compared to previous desktops. I'm even getting used to the slightly cheesy wireless keyboard. Other reviewers have noted that the lack of a caps-lock light on the keyboard is a negative, but not a huge one for me. Since my laptop died from CPU failure, the hard drive was fine. I have an eSATA drive enclosure, so file transfer wasn't too onerous. Setting up and using the hardware was a cinch.

Windows 8, not so much. This machine is not suited for the Windows 8 notMetro ("Modern"*) UI because of the large screen. Take heart, though, you can arrange the "Desktop" button to take you back in time to Windows 7, or a close approximation thereof. After trying to be a good Windows 8 person, I gave up and installed a Start button replacement. There are several. The first one I'm trying is StartW8, which seems good enough. I may try a few more if this one annoys me, but for now, it's nice. If you want a computer specifically for W8 notMetro, get a tablet. The tiled interface should make a lot of sense there. MS really needs to offer a desktop-specific version of W8 with a more mundane UI. For now, though, do it yourself.

With that caveat, I recommend this computer. I haven't had it long enough to comment on durability, but after a month, so far, so good.

5 July 2013: The basic system is still working well. I finally settled on HP's Quick Start start menu replacement. It's simple and works well. The only negative item is the cheesy wireless keyboard. Eventually (i.e., today) I got tired of its lousy response, repeated letters and cheap feel. I dug out my old Dell L100 USB keyboard[[ASIN:B0037H8AB4 NEW, DELL USB L-100, SK-8115, RT7D50, KEYBOARD, 104 KEYS]] and hooked it up. Ahhh! The L100 has outlasted several computers and may outlast many more. It's small, sturdy and well laid-out. With this change to a Dell keyboard, I'm very satisfied with the HP computer.

title: Not very large, flimsy
text:
I own the Enthoo Pro II, so I was looking forward to building with this case. I do think it is sharp looking, but there are some problems. Let me start with the
PROS:

Good looking case
Great airflow
Mesh filters are easy to take on and off + clean
Lightweight
Decent cable management
Affordable

CONS:
Lightweight- makes the case flimsy. As I was building with it I did not want to lean on it because I was afraid to bend the frame. Everything flexes.

Poor quality components- Many parts in an effort to save money are made of plastic- and I mean junky plastic. The HDD sleds, wow! They feel like just pulling them out they will snap. I attempted to move the HDD cage over and it just fell apart. It is just two vertical panels between the PSU shroud and the case wall.
Many of the screws were overtightened and cause some little paint chips or divits in the steel.

Layout- The main compartment is nice and open, but behind the mobo the SSD trays and the HDD cage is too far apart. You cannot use the same power lead from the PSU for both. You will need separate leads for each.

Cables- it comes with a fan controller and they assume everyone will use it. The cables for the fan are much too long and is rather unsightly. However the power cable which your PSU will plug into is much too short. It took some finagling to get it to reach with the power lead plugged into the hard drives.

Size- while I like the size, the case is not wide enough. For a case that brags about airflow, you have to assume that users will be using enthusiast grade coolers like the NH-D15, or something similar. For this build I have a Silver Arrow and the side panel just misses clearing the top of the fan by a few mm- less than 5mm.

My overall impression is that I sort of like the case. Aesthetically it is pleasing which is what brought me to this. I spent about $89, but was willing to spend $150, so I just should have done that. My previous case was a Fractal Arc Midi and it was SOLID. I do have another Phanteks case- the Enthoo Pro II, which is why I purchased this. After using it however it just feels flimsy which does not give a pleasant feeling when using it. I was going to keep it, but my cooler does not fit so alas- I need to return it. If it tick the boxes you need, and will only have 1 or 2 HDD/SSD's, and don't have a humungous cooler then go for it. But if you are willing to spend more than do so- I think you will be happier.

title: This inexpensive item was a very simple fix for my broken blu ray player.
text:
On Black Friday, I managed to find a bunch of Blu Ray movies for $2 each...so I came home, hoping to enjoy a lot of good movies, only for my Blu Ray player to reject one after the other. I figured the movies couldn't be faulty. It would read regular DVDs just fine. After Googling this issue, I figured it was the firmware. I updated it, still had the problem. I called the manufacturer and they told me that the unit needed to be repaired and I would have to send it in to the tune of $69. Some new ones cost less, but I needed one that had component jacks. Finding none, I asked around if someone could help find out what was wrong with it. It was suggested that perhaps the pickup lens was dirty. I do have smokers in my home, as well as a wood stove. So that made logical sense that the player may have needed cleaning. I have had my player almost three years and had never thought to clean it. In the meantime it got choosy about which DVDs would read in it too. I was hoping this was a fix and yes....I had to run it through three or four times but it started reading Blu Rays again.

It was amazingly simple and inexpensive! Now every five or so movies, I will be doing this as part of the regular maintenance. It worked in a DVD player that caused discs to skip also. It may not work well for everyone's machines, but it saved me the cost of buying another player or sending off to get my machine fixed when it was not broken to begin with.

First I want to say that the first box I received did not work correctly immediately. (The ViewTV I received had software version installed from last month.)

I called the ViewTV company and they were really great. The nice tech support guy agreed I had to have something wrong with the unit...and he rushed me out a replacement. The replacement works much better...and interestingly its software version is dated 7 months ago.

I think the ViewTV at $50 is really a great value. (And I was impressed with the customer service the company provided.)

Running the antenna channel scan is relatively fast. The picture quality on my replacement box is stellar. Moving through all the settings menus is very easy and straightforward. Everything is easy to figure out.

When you think about the box's limitations, as pointed out by some very helpful reviews here, you must keep in mind the very reasonable price.

For $50 you get a good over the air box with a good tuner that sends a great picture via HDMI to your TV. You can time shift your viewing, if you plug in a drive to the USB port, and you can record programs to said drive.

For $50 you cannot expect multiple tuners or a great TV Guide. But at least you get to see the very basic guide info the broadcasters send down with their OTA signal. (My two HDTV's on their own do not show the OTA program info, which is very disappointing.)

For cable cutters out there on a budget, this box is definitely something you should consider. It delivers really well exactly what it promises.

title: With great sound...comes not great build quality
text:
[Great Sound]

As noted in some of the other reviews this pair of headphones has great sound for its price range. Sound is quite neutral, without the bass emphasis of a lot of headphones at this range. Highs are also good and not muted. The cable is also very generous in length, which is great as my computer is far away from my chair. Finally, the headband adjustment is exceptional. I have a fairly large skull and most headphones I've purchased have not fit well. However, this one fits perfectly and even has more room to expand. The only comfort downside is that the pads have quite a stiff covering material. This is not so great for comfort for long use sessions, but not too big of an issue as you can replace them eventually if needed. The thicker pad material would make the headphones last longer...if it were not for the major issue I describe below with build quality.

[Disappointing Build Quality]

I've had my pair for about 1.5 years now, and today the headphone snapped at the joint between the top band and where the extension band slides out. See attached photo. You can see that there is a metal band in the headband to provide elasticity and resistance. But the extension band (the part that slides in and out) doesn't have a metal band inside of it. This concentrates stress at this transition point, causing the plastic to snap here eventually. I noticed that the plastic on the other cup has also started cracking. The plastic itself feels quite brittle and is about as thick as the metal strip in the headband. I think the fact that I have a large head and had to extend the headphones out only hastened their demise as this put more stress on the plastic-only part of the headbands.

[Conclusion]

This is a great sounding pair of headphones for their price, but alas I cannot recommend them anymore due to the snapping of the headband. To fail after about a year of use is a bit on the low end. My previous pair of similarly priced headphones lasted over 10 years without the headband failing (only cable had become worn). I think you *might* be OK if you have a smaller head and don't have to extend the headphone band too much, but if you have to expand it to near its maximum, it will probably snap off like mine did.

I’ve needed a bed tray for the longest time, but after several attempts to buy one that would work for me, I gave up. First of all, my body is too wide for most of them, and my belly is too big. When I saw this bed tray, I thought “What a great idea for fat people.” It’s made out of plastic. It comes flat with the pieces snapped in to the tray part, showing how to fold it up when you want to so pay attention to that. The instructions in English were the tiniest type I’ve ever seen, so forget about reading them. But you can figure it out. I’m probably not going to be breaking it down to stow it in a backpack or on a shelf, so it doesn’t matter to me—why? Because it’s so darned useful! I mean, really.

It’s not a one-trick pony, an item to help you be more comfortable with your tablet or laptop in bed. On the contrary! It works great to hold cookbooks in the kitchen; the little rubber-tipped prong things on the bottom foldout tray shelf do a great job of holding a hardbound cookbook by its front and back boards, keeping it stable on the countertop but allowing for flipping through the pages. A binder clip or rubber band can hold the pages open if the book doesn’t tend to want to lie flat. You can see those prongs holding my Kindle Fire in one of the photos.

The tray adjusts to different angles, including flat for use as a little table for eating in bed. Hey, when you’ve decided to spend the day in bed because you just don’t feel well enough to get out of it, it’s nice to have a place to put a plate. My favorite use for it, though, is turned so the longest part of the bottom lip is tucked up under my bed bolster and the edge of the tray is resting against the bolster. This provides a very stable, sturdy, little bed table that can hold a phone or tablet upright in the top slot (cables can go through the bottom if needed) and an Apple TV remote plus a drinking glass and a big bowl of popcorn.

Such a simple little thing, but so great. I love it!

title: Here’s my practical review of the Acer Predator Triton 500
text:
The design aesthetics are subtle for a gaming laptop. This laptop sits at a sweet spot for the price/performance ratio using an 8750H processor and a GTX 2060 graphics card. Laptop is very well ventilated for cooling with perforated holes on top and bottom and has vents on the sides and back of laptop. It’s covered in mostly all aluminum for a premium feel. There are complaints of this being a fingerprint magnet but I take that any day for that premium feel. The AC adapter is one of the smaller 180w power bricks as compared to the competitors. Amazing how the webcam and the power supply shows the progress of miniaturization.

Durability: This laptop has a solid tank like construction comparable to the way Alien laptops are constructed. However, the display has some flex but that is to be said for a lot thin and light gaming laptops. Quality control issues are a concern from some posts, but these sound like issues that would present themselves right away once you boot up and can be returned or replaced in the event that should happen.

Noise: For basic daily non-gaming use, the fans runs fairly quiet even with 40 chrome tabs running. By comparison, my 9370 laptop has the fans running pretty noticeable with 40 chrome tabs. Fans run loud when turbo is enabled but the noise is on par or below comparable gaming laptop noise but most gamers wear headphones when playing games on a laptop.

Display: The 1080 IPS 144Hz near borderless display matches well for this tier of gaming laptops and is pretty decent, Although it was mentioned in other posts about brightness levels, it is plenty bright for indoor use. There are some screen backlight bleeding but it to be expected and is not noticeable or impacts my daily use.

Keyboard: One of the better keyboards for a thin and light along with good 1.7mm of travel and solid feedback. I was disappointed that I could not change the volume up, volume down, and mute key on the right to page up and page down.

Battery: Battery life is pretty good considering it’s a gaming laptop. I get around 4-6 hours from browsing the web. It runs only on Nvidia Optimus only on the rtx2060 model but the rtx2080 model has a software switch in the predator sense software to switch between GPUs.

Gaming Temperatures: The idle temps I was getting is between mid 40s to high 50s. Fan kicks in around mid 40s but is barely audible. My max Unigine Heaven benchmark max temps are 89c CPU and 75c GPU. However, average temps are around 5-15 degrees during the benchmark.
Upgrading the ram or SSD will be a pain due to the inverted motherboard. I hope this design trend does not continue with future laptops.
However, despite the difficulties involved in upgrading, there may be no need as the ram and drive space size should be sufficient for most people. The dual channel ram of 16GB is enough for most games and use cases, while the 512GB of NVM SSD drive is a pretty decent storage space by recent standards.

Should I buy now? For those on the border for buy a gaming laptop now or wait. I would say right now is the best time to buy a laptop based on current vs predicted future performance. The 8750H processor and 2060 graphics are both mature products from Intel and NVidia meaning the percentage gains from generation to generation will not be as high as they are with the current gen products. The increases will likely be in the single digit gains such as going from the 8750H to the 9750H (6% improvement) and that increase would not affect gaming (1-2 frame rate gain) in any perceptible way. Acer’s Helios 300 and Triton 500 are the best price/performance ratio for gaming around right now.

title: Buy a different Garmin!--turns itself back on after being turned off, constantly not recognized by Garmin website, battery life
text:
I did a lot of research before purchasing this expensive piece of equipment. I also purchased the accompanying heart rate monitor (more on that item below).

First up, the watch itself:

1. The watch does not hold it's charge as long as promised. It's constantly telling me it's about to die during a run. It SHOULD hold its charge for up to 8 hours according to the instructions but this has not been true in my experience. I've ran scared several times, hoping that my watch doesn't die (because I depend on it to tell me when I need to turn around based on mileage on several of my training runs in unfamiliar areas).

2. The watch turns itself back on anywhere from 1-3 times after being turned off. I have to check it twice after finishing a run to make sure it's turned off. Turning the unit completely off saves battery life and this is why I'm so concerned with this problem. Typically, when I press the button to turn it off, it acts like it senses the heart rate monitor right before turning off (even though I'm not wearing the monitor and it's not active). I then KNOW that it's going to turn itself back on within the next few minutes because it thinks the heart rate monitor is active. The reason why this is SO annoying is because sometimes I don't notice that the watch has turned itself back on until it's too late. I'm leaving for a run and I grab my Garmin and it has a 1/4 battery because it's been on for 20 hours without being used. This issue needs addressed. I believe it mostly has to do with the heart rate monitor function.

3. I've had to uninstall and reinstall the Garmin Connect software 3 times on my computer to get it to pair with my device. Every other time I connect the device, the software and computer do not recognize the device and I cannot download my runs. This feature is one of the reasons I purchased this watch in the first place. I like to be able to analyze the data from my runs online. It's free and it's a great service. I finally got it to work a 3rd time recently (I had my husband do it this time...I was too frustrated with it)...and now I'm nervous about the next time I plug it in...will my computer recognize it or not? I had to download 25 runs at one time because of this. The watch also pushes old data off of it when new data is recorded...so I'm sure I lost some runs as well.

4. The charging points on the back of the watch are finicky. They are difficult to pair with the charger correctly. This is another thing that has to be checked once or twice after plugging the watch in. Make sure to double check that the 4 metal dots are aligned correctly with the charging clip or you'll have a dead watch when it's time for your run (b/c you thought it was charging all along)! Do you see a theme here yet?!

5. I do like the strap on the watch. It has tons of adjustment holes and works well for my small wrists. I can wear it snug or a little loose if desired. Typically I cannot wear most watches and bracelets because they slide up to my elbow...this one is great! My wrists are about 6 inches around.

6. It is durable and comfortable. I've been using it consistently for 8 months and I haven't had any issues with the band cracking.

7. I love all the features. It's simple to use and it records what I want it to record. I cannot speak to it's water resistant capabilities because I've never put them to the test. The most I've ran in is a light mist.

8. The heart rate monitor...it works fine and it works correctly. It basically does its job. I'm not sure that I would buy one again. Here are the reasons why...

a. I bought it so I would know how many calories I was burning. Now that I've got a sense of how much I burn in 1 hour running, I don't need it anymore. I know about how many I burn because it's always around the same number based on the minutes I've ran. My heart rate is always around 160. The monitor adds $30 to your purchase.

b. My ribcage measures 34 inches. The monitor has fallen down at least 5 times during a run. Once was during a race and I had to finish the race with the monitor around my waist. Talk about useless. It doesn't seem to matter how much I tighten it or even if I secure it under my bra...it always kinda feels like it's going to fall down...and sometimes it does. I cannot wash it to shrink it up again due to the hard plastic piece on the front that holds the electrodes.

c. The hard plastic piece on the front is typically not uncomfortable during a SHORT run...for longer runs it has actually bruised my rib cage (5 or more miles). It also causes me to sweat more there (it's worn in the center, over your sternum, right under your breasts). Any woman knows that sweating any more than necessary in between your breasts or near them is just plain uncomfortable.

Overall, I've liked the product and I still use it and as of now, I'm not going to return it. I was really excited to purchase it and have been disappointed in the performance of it. If I continue to have issues, I may ask for a refund. Please note, this is my SECOND watch. The first one refused to charge the first time it died and I had to exchange it. Customer service was great and I didn't have any issues with the exchange

I would recommend purchasing a different, more expensive Garmin (as if this one isn't already expensive enough), or going with another brand.

For example, Cobo Vault Pro costs approx $150 and has a much larger touch screen and better overall build construction; look and feel wise. Would I buy another Model T? If the price point were around $100 I would definitely buy many more model Ts. As it is, with a price point of $165, I have opted to buy other competing hardware wallets, Cobo Vault, ColdCard, etc. as I don't think the price to value is quite right for the Model T.

title: Somewhat useful...
text:
The Gorillapod Video Tripod (Black/Blue) is a good idea on paper but in real life it just doesn't quite measure up.

The pan & tilt head is incredibly stiff which leads to jerky motion and bounce in your video. There also, on mine at least, appears to be a good bit of free play or slack in the vertical movement of the control arm. I've tried to tighten this down to no avail. The mounting screw seems to be a bit long. It wasn't bad mounting my RCA Small Wonder video camera but when I mounted my Kodak still camera the screw bottomed out and left the camera loose on the mount. The mount itself seems quite secure tight and sturdily attached to the tripod.

I like the adjustability of the legs but if you're not using the tripod on a metal surface for the magnetic feet to cling to it tends to just slide around when adjusting the pan or tilt. The magnets do appear to be strong for their size and will hold my RCA Small Wonder video camera fully horizontal on the 'fridge or door of my car. I tried this with my Kodak Z-650 still camera and it was too heavy for the magnets to support.

While on the subject of the magnetic feet I wanted to add a warning that if you're using an older CRT style monitor care should be taken to keep this tripod several feet away from your monitor. Even being more than a foot away from my 19" CRT cause distortion and image warping. There is the potential for damage to CRT monitors.

As a stationary camera mount this is a pretty cute product; easy to carry, lightweight with near infinitely adjustable legs. If you just want to plop down your camera so you don't have to hold it this product works fine. When you bring the flaws of the pan and tilt features into play the enjoyment goes downhill fast.

All in all it's not bad but it really isn't great.

title: A Harmony user and works with a mac
text:
Let me start by saying that my first universal remote was the Marantz RC2000. This thing was called the "Remote of the Gods" by Home Theater Magazine". This device could control all of my components and came with 4 macro buttons, which allowed me to turn on my TV then my cable box and then set the controls on the remote for that cable box. It was a great remote but not very "Wife" friendly. It was big, heavy and chewed through AA batteries.

That was then this is now. I just replaced my aging Logitech Harmony 880 (with failing button contacts) with the Logitech 900. The 880 was a fantastic leap forward with an activity "macro" based remote that walked you through the setup. The reason I know that the Harmony 880 was good was that once it was setup I never though about it again. It just worked.

The Logitech Harmony 900 builds on its predecessors. Unfortunately, you have to create a new account when setting up the Harmony 900. It cannot pick up your settings from an older Harmony remote. No a huge deal but if you haven't looked at the model numbers on your equipment in a few years this can be a bit of a pain. To ease that pain you should probably login to your original Harmony account and right down the make and model #s of all your equipment.

Initial setup was a bit different than the Harmony 880. No I should let you know that I setup the remote on Mac running OS X 10.6 (Snow Leopard). When connecting a Harmony 880 it gets detected and just works. The Harmony 900 gets detected as 2 devices. The first is the remote and the second is a network device. This surprised me at first but probably has something to do with the way the remote communicates with the RF receiver. Once you create your account and connect the unit it will download and update it's firmware. This will take a few minutes and then the remote will reboot.

It will then ask you to start listing your devices. In my case it was 7 (TV, DVD Player, TiVo Series 3, A/V Receiver, XBOX 360, a lighting controller and a Playstation 3. A special note about using a Playstation 3, the PS3 uses Bluetooth for its controllers and remote. It does not support Infrared. Logitech does sell an IR to Bluetooth transmitter for around $50. If you want to save some money pick up Nyko's Bluewave IR Dongle and Remote (for about $15). If you have the Bluewave don't add the Playstation 3 as a device, just add the Nyko Bluewave and system will understand that you have a PS3.

The setup was relatively painless. I had to manually setup the Lutron lighting controller. No when I say "manually" I don't mean that I had to have the Harmony 900 learn the commands. Logitech had the codes in its database. I mean that I had to go into the activities and add the "Lights On" and "Lights Off" to the Soft Buttons section.

The build quality of the 900 remote seems to be better than the 880. It has a sturdier feel with a rubber bottom for better grip. The screen and graphics are at a higher resolution and there is a nice bit of sliding animation when moving between pages. The remote fits in the charging cradle quite snugly with little room to miss the contacts (unlike early versions of the 880 charger).

I don't have any equipment at the moment that needs the RF portion of this remote so I can't comment on it. I'm sure there are several written and video reviews that cover this.

Over all I would recommend this remote for people who are somewhat technical. For people who have many components (and don't want to spend thousands on a Crestron controller) this is a must have.

title: Works as advertised
text:
I applied many screen protectors to many different cameras over the years. It's never a truly carefree process as the alignment and dust issues require attention. This Expert Shield is one of the easier ones to install. I have learned to wipe down the area around me where I will be working and I use an air blower to eliminate the dust particles that always will settle on the screen. I've read some reviews here claiming there are air bubbles and I must opine that what we are really talking about here is tiny dust particles under the screen that look like air bubbles. If you have the LCD screen clear and free of dust the protector will suck down onto it and leave no bubbles. If you do get one of these dust bubbles, use tape to lift the nearest edge of the protector and use another piece of tape wrapped as a tube sticky side out to pick up the offending piece of dust.

Since installation is more of an art than a science, it is disappointing that so many sellers of these savers do not put more than one in the package. Really, how much can the cost the manufacturer. I'd guess a nickel apiece. If a few were provided you can use one for practice and then have another if you need it.

Enough for the installation. Let's talk about how this one works. I like the matte finish. As has been said, it is just like one of those glare free glass frames. I think it enhances the view of the LCD so I am happy with it. It does not dim it at all. The touch screen works exactly as it did before with no change in responsiveness.

I feel that whatever the touted benefits of screen protector may be, the most important one is that it protects the resale value of the camera. A scratched screen may not bother the current owner, or affect the camera's operation, but it might discourage sale to a potential buyer.

title: Compact Attractive, Quiet Unit
text:
Several reviewers mentioned the difficulty in setting this up. It really wasn't that bad. The steps were pretty easy, at least on my system. The biggest issue I had was notifying my firewall that the software that was needed to map a drive for the unit was okay to run. There is no mention of firewall interference in the small quick install manual, but the Seagate on-line help is excellent and I was able to find the answer quickly. It was a bit confusing on how to identify the unit to the firewall, but I finally did get it set up. There were 3 pre-built folders on the unit: Download, Public and Wiki. I haven't yet figured out what Download and Wiki are for (or been able to access them), but the one called "Public" seems to contain most of the storage space and I was copying files to the unit in no time at all. The unit doesn't seem very fast, but that could in part be the speed of my network. You can use it with USB as an extension drive to one PC, rather than on a network, if you wish.

The fact that the install disk was a DVD threw me for a bit. I had expected a CD, but some vendors now use DVDs instead of CDs for install programs.

I was a little annoyed that I had to go through a complete registration process before the software install would proceed. When I went to a second PC and the registration process started again, I was more annoyed, but did discover that you can cancel out of the registration. It wasn't that obvious the first time through, so I guess they really want you to register.

You do need to know that by default the drive is configured for Raid-1 (mirroring), which means that you only have 2 terabytes of space; not 4. The second drive is used to mirror the first. You can switch it to Raid-0 and get the whole 4 terabytes, but then there is no redundancy, so if either drive fails you are out of luck and you lose all your data. With Raid-1, theoretically you can replace the failing drive (if only one fails at a time) and the system will rebuild the data. I haven't yet discovered how to change the drive setting from Raid-1 to Raid-0.

This is a very compact, quiet unit. It's totally black except for blue lights on the front that show power, status and drive activity.

I did not try the included backup program, as I prefer to use my own backup procedures.

Only time will tell if the unit stands up well or not. Seagate used to make the very best drives, but other companies surpassed them, at least for a time.

This is a nice unit for the price and I'm happy to have it.

title: ATIV Book 9 Plus Review
text:
I've now had this laptop for several months. I can't say better things about it!

The touchpad is sensitive, intuitive, and easy to use. This was important for me coming from a Mac, since their touch pads are amazing. Expectations exceeded. The touch-screen I thought would be more of a novelty, but I find myself using it more and more as I remember that I can actually touch the screen. I'm a graduate student, so it's perfect for scrolling while I have books covering the keyboard or while it's on my lap at an angle that makes it tough to get to the touchpad.

Operating system works well. Much much better than the ASUS Zenbook that I got previously when my Mac died. The ASUS had issues with scaling and screen resolution of many apps including the desktop itself, Chrome, Firefox, and Adobe programs. By this I mean that every time I opened the laptop after sleeping, the scaling and resolution were different than I left it, usually microscopically small, and I do mean TINY. Not just 10 point font...more like 2 point font. It was ridiculous. So as much as I loved the way it looked, I had to return it. This laptop has a less-sharp resolution (numerically, not really visibly), which makes the fonts (like in Adobe) much more legible, even though those (Adobe) are the only programs that do this on the ATIV Book 9 Plus.

Windows 8 is not this computer's fault, so I'm not going to talk about it. You can tweak a few things on Win8 and learn a few quick keyboard shortcuts and life is much better. I do not use the "apps" that Windows 8 touts. They're stupid--just avoid them if you don't like them. :)

Very portable laptop. Light, loud enough speakers that I can set it quite a distance away and still hear clearly, the screen sortof "locks" into position past about 100 degrees (like slightly more than a 90 degree angle), so there's not much jiggling past that point. However, I will note that sometimes, when it's right at 90 degrees or a bit less (like if I'm laying down with it on my stomach) and I move too quickly, it does tend to want to try and close on me. No biggie. Just be mindful.

Also no internet connection issues--again with the ASUS, the internet connection was spotty and would go out periodically (like every 20 minutes I had to restart the internet connection--sometimes it fixed it, sometimes not). My husband is a computer guru and tried everything that the ASUS forums suggested, from uninstalling and reinstalling to updating the drivers, and turning off settings that I never would have been able to find on my own. The ATIV is just peachy. :)

One more thing to note, and I'll update if anything comes of it: The fan, about a week ago, started making more audible noises. Not necessarily during "times of high stress" on the system, sometimes I'm just browsing Facebook with one tab open. I haven't dropped the computer or dinged it around unnecessarily. Husband-computer-guru said this just sometimes happens and isn't a sign that there's something wrong. His has been doing the same thing (he's got a Dell) since about 6 months after he got it.

BUT the fan issue for me only lasted that one day. Hasn't happened again since. So, like I said, I'll keep ya updated. Any more questions, feel free to comment and I'll answer ASAP!

title: one of the best pocket-sized big-zoom camera
text:
This is my second Sony HX camera. My first was a Sony HX-50 that died after several years of use (lens motor stopped working). This version is improved in a couple of important ways. Most importantly, the popup viewfinder is tremendously useful in daylight conditions. The viewscreen is often hard to see in sunlight, but that is never a problem with the viewfinder. Opening the viewfinder is a little clunky, but you get used to it. The viewfinder does have a focus lever so using it with glasses is no problem. I also like that the GPS locks on much more quickly than older cameras (that often had GPS that were too slow to be useful). Despite the features, this camera is slimmer than my old HX-50.

The main downside to this camera (and probably all compact big-zoom cameras) is that the image sensor is very small, which limits the quality of your images. Even in bright sunlight conditions, my photos are always grainy when viewed on a large screen. They may look fine on a cell phone screen or a low quality viewer (like Facebook or Instagram), but when viewed full-screen on a computer screen, the image quality is noticeably more grainy and less dynamic than photos from a better camera. Photos are still much better than any cell phone camera, of course.

A big zoom camera is great for sports and wildlife and if you want a big zoom in a pocket sized camera, you'll be hard pressed to find anything better than this. For sports and wildlife photos, getting closer to your subject is often not possible. I've taken usable wildlife and sports photos from hundreds of yards away, even miles away for landscape photos. If you don't need the big zoom or can tolerate a bigger camera (like a one-inch or micro-4/3 or APS-sized sensor), however, you can do much better than this (for a bigger price).

title: For The Price, These Are Great Quality With A Few Exceptions
text:
Two members of the family just told me that they had broken their headphones with this product came up to get. I decided it was worth a try, despite some previous experiences not being too great with cheaper headphones. Let's see what happened.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
These headphones make some claims. They come in a great box who for Carlos fans will be a thrill. It is well decorated and presentation is fabulous. That means they would be a nice gift in that respect.

LEATHER?
The case says that these are leather padded ear cups and underneath headband. I am still not sure about this. Perhaps it is that bonded leather that is made from leather residue chopped up and blended with binders to remake it into sheets which are printed with leather look imprinting. Technically that can be called leather, but it really is not as much leather as I would like.

EAR CUPS AND HEADBAND
Having said that, these white headphones are comfortable. I can wear them longer than some others that I have had which are a bit rough after only an hour. These can be worn for several hours without a problem.

CORD
This comes with a cord which is only 38 inches long. That is a bit short for me. I find it is annoying and not quite as long as I would prefer.

SOUND
The sound of these is surprisingly great. The bass is really good, and the mids and highs are definitely clear and not muddy.

CONTROLS
The controls on the white pair are awful in that they are nearly impossible to read. The buttons are white and the markings are just very thin raised white on the buttons. It should really be colored with marker- which I took care of. Using a very fine permanent marker I colored just the raised areas. The up/down and play pause buttons are separated by the noise cancellation button which is good.

ADJUSTABILITY
These are very adjustable. They go longer, tilt in and out and rotate from side to side.

COMPACT?
These do fold flat and compact if you need to travel with them or store them in a smaller place.

SOUND CANCELLATION
THAT is where we part ways with these headphones. The noise cancellation is awful. It barely works. When it is turned on, the sound gets really compromised too. It becomes almost muffled in a way.

OTHER FEATURES
The ability to know how much power is left on the headphones while using the phone is nice, but it does not help if you are not using it with a phone and some other bluetooth device. Calling, people hear just fine and we can hear them too (several of us tried this feature with our phones)

THE BOTTOM LINE
For the price, these headphones are a step up from what I usually get when I try them. The sound is very good and well balanced, the folding up for storage is great, and the comfort is also on the upper level. The only disappointments are noise cancellation, short cord for corded listening, and the hard to read buttons.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. If the noise cancellation worked better, these would be over the top amazing. As they are, they are still pretty great. I love the white color- it stands out from the rest, despite getting dirty faster. They are a great gift to yourself or someone else and are some of the nicer headphones I have used.

title: Couldn't get it to connect to my router for wireless control.
text: This is a good price for a starter kit of 5 devices.  The program you install on your Smartphone is easy to install and looks like it works as intended.  Here's the problem I encountered.  Every time I tried to connect to my router I would get the message "Only supported on 2.4 GHZ Wifi Networks".  My router is dual band and I believe it broadcasts WiFi both in 2.4 and 5 GHZ.  Apparently these devices are not seeing the 2.4 GHZ and are looking at 5 GHZ and aren't able to connect or the Smartphone is connecting at 5Ghz and the device won't pair with the phone unless it is connected via 2.4Ghz.  I contacted support and they gave me this answer:  "You will need to connect your mobile device to the 2.4Ghz Wifi for the app to connect to the devices when they are in the pairing modes. If you are unsure how to connect to the 2.4Ghz of the dual band router, you may need to log into the router to either turn on the 2.4Ghz WiFi or rename it so you know which connection is the 2.4Ghz. If you are unsure how to do so, you will need to contact your router manufacturer for assistance. Alternatively you can pair the devices via AP mode as indicated in the manuals of the devices."  I don't know how to make the necessary changes in my router to be able pair the smartphone with the 2.4Ghz connection and I didn't want to take the time to learn how and potentially mess up my router and/or the way the Smartphone connects to my router. (It seems like I would need to change both.)  I tried the AP Mode that support mentioned, but it still would not connect; it would fail every time.  The whole setup seems just too complicated.  Also, they fail to tell you that at least on the water sensor, you have to twist open the device and remove the paper tab that prevents the battery from making contact, before you can set it up.  Am disappointed and surprised that no other reviewers had the 2.4 vs. 5 Ghz issue.  Not recommended unless you know all about how to set up your smartphone and router to connect at 2.4Ghz or unless they already are.

Some appear to have had some difficulty or confusion with assembly, but I did it solo fairly quickly with no issues and found the instructions very clear. This isn’t really a problem per se, but it is quite finicky and it the only part of the operation my wife had to assist with. It definitely would’ve been nice if they’d just included both a spike and attached foot type tips with the stand especially at this price. The stand easily fits my vintage Sansui 661 receiver on the middle shelf and Audio Technica LP120 turntable on the top. I hope both this review and photos showing it with the perspective of having components on it help.

Edit: So, yea, I did dock a star due to the feet issue. As I noted they are finicky, but can quickly get frustrating. While I had to move the stand around getting my stereo stuff sorted the small discs constantly came off and you just really can’t put them back in solo. They will and did put small indentations on my floor with the discs off. My solution was to pick up a 4 pack of 1” sliders from WM that are plastic on the bottom with an adhesive disc on the top. I then stuck the small metal discs from the stand on the slider. Once my wife helped me place the discs back on the legs it could then slide pretty freely and they stayed on. It’s a shame they didn’t include a normal leg along with the pins. I still like the stand quite a bit, but I’d warn people with mobility issues against this one even as nice as it is.

I can not comment about mic or bluetooth quality as I did not use the headset long enough and I do not have a blue tooth supported device.

text:
THE GOOD:
---------------
* Braid type shields are much more flexible than the traditional vinyl, or thick rubber cables.
* 48gbps, 8K ready, HDCP 2.2, etc.
* 15 ft, and gold contacts.
* Customer service top notch. I "thought" the cable a I got was defective, and they sent me another one no questions asked. More on this below.

THE BAD:
------------
* This is the most difficult cable I've ever experience. It is very fickle. I have reproduced this fickleness with many gadgets, not just one. So, I am fairly certain this isn't user error. Now the first cable I got wouldn't give me any signal between my HDMI switch and my PS5. I wanted to make sure the Switcher isn't the problem, so I tested it with my Nvidia Shied directly to my 4k projector. Still no signal. Took it upstairs to test between Fire TV cube and another Switcher upstairs, still no signal. So it is reasonable for me to think the HDMI cable is defective. I asked for a replacement, and the seller sent me one quickly. With this new cable, I tested it with the Fire TV cube and switcher upstairs, and I got a signal. Great! So I took this new cable, and went downstairs back to the original location I wanted to use it... Guess what, no signal! LOL! This confused me, perhaps I mixed up the old cable, so I tried that cable as well, and guess what... I got a signal! But now I'm dubious of these cables because I'm fairly certain I did not mix up the cables. In any case, I took this cable that I just recently received signal, took upstairs to confirm, and guess what... no signal! LOL! See, what I'm trying to do to eliminate all doubts is for the cable to get a signal both upstairs and downstairs. Ultimately, I realized the original cable that I asked for a replacement for, I guess, was never defective. It is just fickle, like the new replacement.

Good customer service is why I won't rate this any lower than 3-Stars. I'm pretty tech savvy, and I've never had this much trouble with a cable. This might be a case of YMMV (your mileage may vary.)

title: Field of View
text:
These binoculars are all about quality in the largest field of view. If you want to see a wide expanse of nature or the heavens downrange from your position, these are the way to go. I got them specifically to frame smaller constellations and asterisms, the detail of which can be further examined with a scope. They help tremendously to put the object in the scope into context. Ordinarily, observing half a degree of field tends to abstract objects almost entirely from their surrounding. Since it's not practical to really "zoom" in using a single optical instrument, using these in combination with something of higher power is ideal. Don't get me wrong, I do have a zoom on the scope... it zooms from 25x to 50x -- amazing but you have to understand that this is a field of view of 2.4 to 1.5 degrees -- essentially like looking through a pipe to a drinkstraw. These Nikons however, show over 9 degrees field of view -- something which is unsurpassed in the highest-end binocular out there.

There are compromises necessitated by the optical principles used to make these function. They do not have a very flat field of view, meaning objects in the center of the field (circle) can be focused, but objects nearer the edge of the field are out of focus. This is because the focused field is curved not flat. This problem is also evident in most 10x50's for example. It's less of a problem in good quality 8x42's like Nikon's Monarch for example, and obviously the high end Swarovski, Leica, Zeiss etc. This problem matters more when you have a narrow field and highly magnified image where the subject tends to fill the field of view. It matters less when the subject is focused in the center of the field and the background surrounding it is slightly out of focus.

Still, even if you pay the biggest bucks for bright, flat, and sharp images from the top of the line binoculars, you'll still only see about 8 degrees true field of view, whereas these give you over 9 degrees. Furthermore, they give an apparent field of view of over 59 degrees, rivaling the top-of-the-line binoculars.

If you're looking for a handy, all-purpose binocular, the roof-prism 8x42's are proven to be far more popular for a number of good reasons (more compact, more magnification while not yet needing a tripod or IS like 10x does, more competition and choices etc.) But if you're looking for the best field of view with high quality optics, this is it, and fortunately it comes at a very reasonable cost. I don't know what other 7x35's are out there, but I can tell you this is far better than Celestron or Bushnell.

title: Exceedingly impressive for the price!
text:
I don't know how they can sell this flashlight for the current listed price of just under $85.00 US. This flashlight really belongs in a higher price point. This light has a typical soda-can shape and feels very solid. It's not a light-weight light. The charge port is accessed via a coin-slot keyed screw port with a rubber gasket to protect it from water entry; this is the only access port to the flashlight. For convenience, it comes with two coin-shaped "keys," but it nearly any similar sized coin would work just as well.

Being sold for use as a diving flashlight, I have to admit I have only tested it in shallow water so far, and not yet taken it on any real dives, but it does seem perfect for this use. However, it also seems like a great light for regular use as well. It does get warm, as would any flashlight of this power, but not as quickly as I would expect, even on the turbo setting. I think this is largely due to the sheer mass of this thing acting as a big heat sink.

It has a balance of both warm and neutral emitters, which allows you to switch up the color temperature as well as the brightness through various modes. It also has bright red and blue emitters, which you can use either alone or in conjunction with the white emitters to further adjust the color temperature. A quick double-click on one button takes you straight into the highest white setting. A double-click on the other takes you to an emergency function which flashes red and blue, exactly like a police light. In fact it is bright enough to easily be mistaken for one, so don't use this function from your vehicle or you could end up in some trouble!

When tested underwater, I found that the light stayed nice and cool, but it still went into automatic reduced output after a couple of minutes to protect the components from overheating. Whether this means that this function is dependent more on time than temperature I don't know, or perhaps the internal components still got warm enough to need protection even though the outside of the flashlight was still very cool to the touch.

Whatever the reason, I found that you can temporarily override this by double-clicking the button (which puts it back into turbo mode), so long as you hadn't used the double-click to get to that mode in the first place. In other words, if you started the light by double-clicking to go straight to turbo, then you can't double-click again to override the automatic power reduction. But if you cycled through the functions to get there, then you can. It will only last for about 5 to 10 seconds, and then it will automatically reduce the output again. You can repeat this procedure again and again, but I don't know if it's a good idea to push the automatic safety functions too hard or you could possibly end up ruining your flashlight. The truth is, even in reduced output it's still exceptionally bright, so I'd suggest only using the override turbo function when absolutely necessary.

This light is a real unit: the hard aluminum handle has a heavy, square knobby grip to make it easy to keep a hold on even when diving, and I also suspect that this helps it radiate heat more effectively. It has a mount option as well. The charge port feels like it would resist water entry to a pretty substantial depth, although as I said, I have only tested it in shallow water thus far.

This light has a very "floody" output, with a wide spread. It's not intended to throw a focused beam of light a quarter of a mile, but it will light up your general area very well. This makes a lot of sense for a diving light IMO.

I definitely recommend this flashlight. In fact, at this price, I will be recommending it to my friends and family as well.

I am a super-unorganized person, with ADHD. I have struggled my entire life to find a way to keep myself and my schedule organized. I sat down last week (the last week in December, perfect timing to do this!), surrounded by schedules, appointment cards, etc., and started putting my planner together. I can't believe how much more comfortable I am with a paper and pen planner than I was with the more high-tech version.

I highly recommend this set, especially if you are organizationally-challenged like I am. It will give you a comfort level with what's coming up that really takes the work out of staying on schedule, and let's you concentrate on the more important and rewarding things in life. Happy New Year!
