title: Additional Information
text:
My background with similar products is: Schwinn multi-function LED bike computer that I've used since I've started riding in my adult life, Garmin nuvi 1370 (automobile routing) that I've used constantly worldwide for years, and a Garmin GPSmap 62sc (hiking) that I use sporadically worldwide, and numerous proprietary rental car nav systems. Here's some random useful info about the Magellan Cyclo 315:

- Comes with an "up front" mount and a regular flat handlebar mount. That's great because then you can mount it on two bikes right off the bat.

The up front mount is for 31mm handlebars, and does not include the shim to make it work for ~28mm mountain bikes. You may have trouble using that mount for MTBs anyway because of the bend many have in their bars. You also need to take everything else off to get this mount on, as the ring only spreads slightly. However, this offers a variety of angles and mounting positions.

On my MTB, I mounted it on the stem using the regular mount and the look and fit at this location far exceeded my expectations. While I thought the size of this thing was generous - maybe too generous for mounting on a bike - it fills that location perfectly without getting in the way. It's angled slightly upward and is easy to see and access. When removed, you barely notice the small mounting bracket. How it is set up does not interfere with my existing mini bike computer (not that I need that anymore, but you never know).

- You can set up multiple profiles for yourself so that you can ride your street bike differently from your mountain bike, and even set the navigation options independently (for example, you can set it up to take you more often offroad on your MTB). But while you have two mounts in the package and the heart sensor can be used for all bikes, you may want to consider a second speed/cadence sensor if you're using more than one bike. I suspect the unit can read your speed by GPS, but it won't be as precise.

- Cadence sensor, which is wired in with the speed sensor, only shows you how fast you pedal. It can't draw any other conclusions from that like any sort of gearing ratio, because you don't need to pedal going downhill, which would ruin your ratio.

- The touch screen works really well, even with a glove. I know from my (older) driving Garmin how frustrating a poor touchscreen is, and I know from my hiking Garmin how obnoxious it is to have to type with arrow keys. Thankfully, I can easily move around and browse maps (no pinch to zoom, though) on this thing AND, when I want to go back to seeing myself in the middle of the screen, I can just hit that on-screen button. Nice.

Regarding this, one of the only imperfections I've found with the touch screen and/or software is how I cannot capitalize something in the middle of the word. Like, if I want to write an acronym, I'm out of luck. It does automatically capitalize the first letter of each word, though. Also worth noting is the keyboard is not QWERTY.

- But this reminds me that the software is very intuitive, easy to use, and has a whole lot of nice options. I LIKE that it does NOT use Android, as so many (even non-phone) devices do nowadays, but I'm thankful that it does seem mature and it's pretty easy to find anything you need after a few minutes of playing around. In comparison, both of my (older) Garmin units have quite a few annoying quirks that leave me looking for things that I know exist.

- Just a sampling of the many features and options worth noting are extreme customization of dashboards (putting 0 to 8 items on most screens, having up to three screens to page through when riding outdoors, putting up whichever info you want, clearing the map if you want, adjusting the map to be north- or rider-oriented, etc.), ability to see all sorts of graphs and data about past rides, surprise me function which takes you to a destination, completes a workout goal, or makes a loop of a certain length with the conditions you give it (this may show you some pathways you didn't know about).

- Uses regular Magellan maps (which I believe they actually source from another company and therefore share with many other products [whereas Garmin has their own]) and OSM maps, but focuses on OSM for bike riding. In my town, it (OSM) knows some, but not all, of the bike paths, college campus paths, and parking lots. It doesn't route me on them quite as much as I would like (even with that option set), but it recognizes them and starts routing on them once I turn down that way. It decides which is a "major road", so you don't always get what you expect, although it definitely changes the route if you are asking for car directions.

- Speaking of car directions, this can be your car navigator, but I wouldn't try to use it as your only car navigator; instead, just use it in a pinch. The features aren't set up for car navigating specifically, but it also has a 200km routing distance limit.

- Since the maps are open source, I suspect you can always load the rest of the world for free. I haven't figured out exactly how to do it yet because of some software issues I'm going to complain about in the next bullet.

- On my Garmin devices, loading new maps is super easy, but this one may be more complicated despite the open source maps used. And I suspect it's in an attempt to squash piracy of the other maps they have loaded. I suspect this because there is a software setup file on the device you can load onto your computer, but infuriatingly, it won't let you use it (well, I think you can still use it to backup your entire device) because it wants you to download new software instead. When you do, it won't let you in without an account, so this is "all online" software. It took them forever to actually send me the Email (they want to know who you are and your contact info) and once I got it, I couldn't sign in, it still didn't see my device, all sorts of annoying problems. ...When it comes right down to it, I really don't care. I can manage to just see the files if I try, and therefore I can load and download my own *.gpx files, and I'll figure out how to load maps eventually. This thing presumably came up to date and I don't take my bike overseas, so it's nothing I want to put any more time into for the moment.

To be fair, I suspect Magellan's servers were just having problems, which was what was causing me trouble. But why do I want any software that forces me to be online? Companies should not do stuff like this.

By the way, I'm a Communications Engineer, so - even though my scenario may be unique - I'm not having problems because of computer illiteracy.

But I'm not taking off a star for that because I really like everything else about this product. This is just me asking Magellan and other companies to give us simple, non-bloatware software. BTW, the first program allowed you to easily turn off the part where it ran when Windows started, but the second one did not, which is also infuriating.

- SD cards. It doesn't take them. On my other devices, I like to keep the whole world on SD card, but only load the parts I need. While this thing has 3+ GB of internal space, you'll have to remove some States temporarily if you want to add other countries. This could become tedious if you have to use their online based software to do it. Again, they shouldn't be so protective since the maps (the main biking maps) are open source (free) in the first place.

Despite ending on a sour note there, I really do like this device. The size, design, operating system, functions, and options appeal to my tech side and my outdoorsy bike rider side. I love to have a GPS with me not to be looking at a screen all day, but to find new trails and cool things to do, remember where I've been, give me even more reason to play outside, and generally enhance all the reasons I like to be riding. They did a great job with this product (and the software they can always update to be better). Highly recommended for bicyclists and lovers of solid GPS based gadgets.

title: Incredibly loud with above average sound quality
text:
There are a few things that set the review sample I received apart from most other bluetooth speakers. At the top of the list is sound pressure level because this is the loudest bluetooth speaker I have ever tested. Literally, this can compete with waves on a beach, which can get pretty loud when the tide is changing. I tested it from three rooms away from my writing desk and it could easily be heard. In that respect it could provide background music for a flash mob, which is way beyond the power of most other speakers, which are designed for personal listening on a desk or night stand.

The sound quality is also a cut above. While I have tested speakers that are better, this one is still on the short list of my favorites. The speakers are large and powerful, and they do a remarkable job of handling the high, mid and low frequency bands. As advertized the bass is pretty intense compared to ninety percent of the bluetooth speakers I have owned or tested (about fifty!)

In addition to volume and sound, this is ruggedized. I mentioned that it could compete with wave noise at the beach. It can also withstand moist and sandy environments and being banged around. It's not waterproof, but is designed to resist it.

While the product description and specs are complete I do want to highlight a few features that I personally love. First is ease of connecting this to my phone. When you turn it on it immediately beacons its presence (and announces it in a human voice.) Do a scan from your device for other bluetooth devices and this pops up immediately. A simple touch pairs and connects it. If you have an NFC-enabled phone like my Galaxy Note 3 it's even simpler. Just touch the device to the NFC logo on the speaker and you'll get a message on your screen asking if you want to connect to the speaker.

Finally, time and distance claims are accurate. This actually will play longer than most speakers. The claim is twelve hours. I had it on and playing for ten and it probably would have lasted another two hours. So say at least ten hours to set expectations. It also claims to work from 25 meters, which is significantly more than the normal 10 for bluetooth. I tested mine at about 18 meters and it did not falter - the music streamed with no breakup or dropouts.

Basically, if you want to play your music loud and still get decent sound this is the speaker for you. It has a lot of features that I did not mention (but are listed in the product description), but the defining one is sound pressure level.

title: A wonderful NVMe option at a good price
text:
I've used a variety of NVMe SSDs, including earlier WD Black drives, and this is among the best in terms of price/performance. Intel Optane (a completely different class of drive) and Samsung 960pro drives will beat these, and depending on the benchmark, as will some others, but in real world use, you're well into the crazy fast realm. That's what this drive is all about--getting into the crazy fast realm without breaking the bank!

In general, you will notice a speed difference between this and a SATA SSD, especially when launching huge applications/data sets (think Premier Pro, games, especially with 4k textures, and even Windows booting up). Most won't notice the difference between this and a Samsung 960pro (an Optane drive is a whole new level of fast). It was easy enough to setup, but YMMV. Due to the fact that this drive isn't SATA, you cannot slap it in a USB 3.1 enclosure, or even a 2.5" drive adapter. It will fit in a PCIe x4 card (not included), but otherwise, you'll have to do some juggling, especially if going from one NVMe drive to another in a PC with only one slot.

Intel and Toshiba drives have had some issues with newer Windows 10 builds (being fixed), and Samsung drives cost more, so this is a solid option for folks looking for NVMe performance without breaking the bank. 250GB is enough for many folks (especially if media on another drive, NAS, or the cloud), and 500GB gives you even more space. The lack of a 120GB option isn't a loss, as that's too small anyway.

title: Useful design that covers a range of applications
text:
This is probably one of the most useful surge protector power strips I’ve come across. It’s about the same size and shape as a small standard strip, measuring about 9 inches long and 2.25 inches wide. It has two power outlets that are unusually shaped – they appear to be designed so they can use both U.S.-standard 2 and 3 prong plus, plus a range of “overseas” plugs. They look weird, but they work fine with everything I plugged into it.

It also has 4 USB ports on the end so you can use the power strip to plug in a USB cable to charge a phone, tablet, etc. Two of the USB ports are rated at 2.4A; the other two are rated at 1A.

There’s an on/off switch at the top that powers down the full power strip. There is a separate power cord that attaches to the power strip to plug it into the wall outlet. That’s a very handy feature if you want to take this along on a trip, since it makes the power strip far easier to pack than if it had a permanently-connected power cord.

The case is plastic, but feels solid and durable. It has 4 non-skid pads on the base that grip the tabletop very well with no sliding when plugging things in and out.

While it would be nice if there were a third power outlet instead of just 2, this is a compact size that fits in well on my kitchen counter, and lets me plug in my phone and tablet for recharging, plus run a laptop off of AC power, with all outlets surge-protected. I also will be using this when traveling since the compact size and detachable cord make it easy to put into my laptop case.

Good design! Very pleased with this, and I would certainly recommend it.

I can access a single public smb shared folder through the device's local ip address but that folder is not accessible remotely in the cloud, and any private user folders are not accessible in normal windows networking. So far notwithstanding everything I've tried the "included(downloadable)" WD Backup App doesn't see the device and I have found no way through the WD Discovery App to sync or backup anything on my desktop with the device. My experience with WD Android Apps make me believe backing up from my phone would be much more functional. I can add users if they have email addresses and internet access but I will have zero control or oversight in what or how much they store.
Initial setup was very very simple but I quickly found a long list of limitations.

With so many things to complain about, why 4 stars? First it uses WD Red drives. Build quality seems good. It just works, with minimal technical knowledge required. As close to plug-and-play as I'd expect something like this to be. Uses the online WD website as a gateway which is much better than punching holes through my router's security. Attractive and easy to use web interface. Good price because mine was one that was used. I took one star away because I really wanted it to be able to automatically sync a few folders from my desktop.

A few uncategorized comments: Device only has Raid 1 (mirrored/half tb capacity) or what they call JBOD which is more like internally spanned drive configuration, possibly a Raid 0 type setup, but who knows. Switching requires a complete wipe of stored files. Can backup Google Drive if I allow WD App/Device access to my Google Account. Can share files with links for other people to access over internet. Cannot automatically sync local files from desktop pc. Use router DHCP to assign specific local IP if access to Public folder is desired. This Public folder is a non-password-protected Samba network share anyone on LAN has access to.

title: Excellent features & performance, with some problems
text:
Installation is easy and performance is solid. There are some nice features, such as the ability to use this router as an access point that can bridge systems operating under the older 802.11b standard (11 mbps), as well as the blazingly fast 802.11g standard.
It also comes with the usual features: DHCP server, NAT, and firewall. I also like the fact that the wired ports are based on switching instead of shared as a hub.
However, there is one major aspect of this router that you need to consider before purchasing - there is a firmware flaw (as of firmware version 2.02.7) that exposes the remote administration feature to hackers who will attempt to exploit ports 80 and 443. Worse, turning off the remote administration feature does not close the vulnerability of ports 80 and 443. This vulnerability was reported widely by Jason Meserve in the 6/3/04 NW Virus and Bug Patch Alert, and a workaround was provided by Alan W. Rateliff in a 4/31/04 port to the Security Focus bugtrack list. The workaround is to set the port forwarding to send ports 80 and 443 to non-existent hosts. Rateliff further noted that forwarding the ports to any hosts (including listening ones if you are actually running servers) will override the default behavior. He also recommended immediately changing the default admin and password before connecting this router on a live network.
There is another issue with Linksys in general, and that is the quality of their technical support, which I consider to be poor-to-mediocre, depending on how lucky you are when dealing with them.
Overall, this router has a lot of excellent features and performs very well. The downside is the security issue cited above and my opinion that they have less than great technical support. Therefore, if you are a highly technical user and can perform the workaround described above, and can solve most common problems without needing Linksys' tech support you'll probably like it. However, if you are a non- or quasi-technical user who wants something that works out of the box and does not expose your network to security problems, you may want to look elsewhere.

title: Great High Airflow Case for Mini and Micro ATX builds.
text:
I planned on upgrading my PC for a long time and I wasnt totally sure what case to get it, since my old case was a mid-range Thermaltake. After getting this case and setting it up, I dont think I will ever buy a Thermaltake case ever again.

The case was a bit bigger than I expected, but its fine, since it is still quite small compared to a mid or a full tower. The look of the case is very impressive, clean, but functional. The design does allow for quite a large amount of airflow through the case, and it comes with 3 free fans already set up to boot.

The ease of setting it up with all your parts is surprising, even coming from a case that had quick detachable pins for drives, this is even easier. You literally just pinch the hard drive tray to unlock it, pull it out, snap the hard drive in it, and shove it back in the slot. installing a hard drive takes all of 30 seconds if you have the case open, including the time required to plug in the cables. If you dont have the case, it takes all of 15 seconds to unlock and unlatch the side panels, which ALL of the panels come off easily.

The inside also is quite roomy, since it is a 2 compartment design, the main compartment is for your Mobo and other components that attach to it, and the second compartment is for your power supply and internal drives. it comes with room for 3 HDDs and 3 SSDs, and has slots for 4 expansion cards from your mobo.

I only have two minor gripes about the case, first is that the power button is quite small and has no real tactile feel, so feeling for it in the dark is a pain, and second, It would have been nice if they had just a single external drive bay.

Overall, if you are looking for a very good quality case for a Mini or Micro ATX build, then this is a solid choice, especially for the money.

title: This little radio is FUN
text:
This review might seem a little overly enthusiastic but I really like this little radio. The second product photo is accurate -- it's pretty much palm sized. But it has lots of fun features, including multi-band tuning and lots of LED indicators and surprisingly loud volume. It will even work as a wireless speaker, and has several EQ settings available when used in that mode. It will also play MP3s, WAVs, or WMA music files from a micro SD card (up to 256 gb capacity, card not included with radio).

It recharges via USB-C. The battery looks like an old-school flip phone Li-ion battery. Tuning performance is okay. The thumb wheel isn't going to give you fine control when shortwave listening, but the SW spectrum is divided into seven bands so it works. It's amazing this little radio even has SW. FM tuning seems to be assisted with AFC, so it automatically locks in on stronger signals on the band. The built in rod antenna is supplemented with an included clip-on wire extension for use on some bands.

You get FM, MW (medium wave, also known as AM), SW (shortwave in seven bands) , and weather band with several preset freqs. The LEDs indicate current band, power status, and can display battery charge, or function as a VU meter while listening.

It does come with an English language user guide that's pretty easy to understand. The selection buttons are all small (it's a small radio) and dark colored and have only embossed lettering so you pretty much need the guide or to memorize the functions and locations to operate everything.

It does not have a headphone jack or a line-in input. It will not transmit a wireless signal to other devices. But as I said it will function as a wireless speaker. It has a sleep timer, but no clock or alarm function.

It's a tiny speaker of course, but the sound quality and volume is impressive. On certain EQ settings it can get pretty loud. Don't expect full hi-fi audio from a speaker this small, but it is clear and has a decent sound. The sound quality reminds me of some of the better old school transistor radios (the ones that used 9V batteries).

And as I said in the title of this review, this little radio is fun.

text:
I bought this tablet to replace a Coby Kyros 7042 which fell off my desk and broke wide open, the screen cracking in half in the process. Since Coby Electronics is now out of business I had to replace the one I liked but unfortunately broke.

It comes nicely packaged including a quick start guide, a booklet of notices written by lawyers, the tablet, a DC wall adapter and a micro USB cable that plugs into the wall adapter or your computer. Unless you have wall outlets that are pretty high up on your wall, you will discover that the USB cable is too short. When you plug the cable into the wall adapter and then connect the tablet, you will find your tablet sitting at the edge of a desk or you may end up leaving the tablet to charge while it's sitting on the floor. Buy yourself a longer USB cable to avoid problems. The fastest way to charge the tablet is by using the wall adapter and I recommend you charge the tablet before you turn it on for the first time.

Once the battery is fully charged, which takes a few hours, start the tablet and answer the default questions. Then, it's very important that you find your way through the menu of the system settings because Lenovo has an UPDATE for the tablet which resets your tablet to "out of the box" condition. Do your customizations AFTER you update the tablet.

The tablet does NOT accept SIM cards, not the version of tablet that is sold in the USA. While the quick start guide refers to the tablet being able to accept SIM cards, it does NOT accept SIM cards, there are no sockets for SIM cards. There is one socket for a micro SD card. Use it.

The screen has beautiful color and images and text are sharp and clear. It's about as heavy as other seven inch tablets. The back cover of the tablet easily removes so you can see the slot for the SD card but nothing else is visible. The tablet easily connects to a wireless network and the antenna seems very potent and is able to quickly connect to wi-fi networks, even those with weak signals.

It comes with a lot of apps pre-installed including Google Play Store. Skype runs very well including the video chat. The microphone is sensitive, you don't have to scream to be heard. The tablet is not "rooted", if you want to root the tablet I'm sure there are methods available on the net. You know where to look ;)

title: Early adopters will love this
text:
Taken for what this is supposed to be, this is a fabulous machine. It's not a primary computer. It's not a laptop replacement. If you need a low power/ultra-portable computer, go with a netbook.

This is more of a mutt. It's a portable media player that doesn't have as much storage as an iPod or a Zen, but has a larger, higher quality screen and a kickstand, which makes it easier to watch movies at a desk.

It can read ebooks. It's not quite as light or comfortable for long term reading as a Kindle, but it can support full color images. It's far superior for this purpose than any of the other devices Amazon has put out an app for.

It can run Windows 7. It's not a full powered machine, but it's even smaller than a netbook.

It fits a slot somewhere between a PDA/smartphone and a netbook, and it's brilliant.

I would have liked a larger hard drive, an SD card (it would have gotten 5 stars if it had one) and more than one USB slot. There is no ethernet port. It only connects wirelessly. The optional port replicator gives you Ethernet and two more USB slots, but still no SD.

A few things to keep in mind. When you're first setting it up, you can't access the virtual keyboard button, so you need to use the Ease of Access icon to get to that. Windows will say to press the space bar to activate the feature. Use the mouse click button (marked +).

The design is very sleek. It's comfortable to hold and work with. The screen has an adjustable brightness, which is easier on the eyes, and easier to use in bright sunlight. The low glare screen helps with this as well.

Overall, this is bleeding edge, early adopter technology.

Nowadays phones, tablets, and laptops can lack ports, but they pack a lot of capabilities in a the few USB C ports they have. The USB C ports can not only carry USB, but they also can carry video, audio, and other signals on side bands. This is built to take advantage of that with a special focus on gaming systems like the Switch. The technology works the same no matter the device, but they each have their own needs.

As noted this markets itself as a compact solution for travel, but it's bigger than many compact solutions and it lacks the ports of some desktop oriented ones. It's very light weight (which can really be an issue when it gets tugged in every direction from attached cables), so that's a positive for portability. It also has all of the essential ports (not enough for a desktop replacement dock, but enough for basic computing), and it'll allow Dex mope in Samsung devices. I don't own a Switch, but I assume it does the same there.

I keep this in my travel bag for my laptop or even my phone in a pinch. It's lightweight, compact enough, and works. It's not the best device as it's an odd size (bigger with more ports would make a better desktop dock and smaller with the same ports exist for portability, and it really feels cheap (that light weight). You cannot do wrong with this, but there are many other docks that are every bit as good (unsure if all support the Switch as this one does--that could swap your choice if that's a need).

title: I’m okay, but not as happy with the Paperwhite as I was with my much older Kindle
text:
So far - after a few weeks - I’m lukewarm on the Kindle Paperwhite Essentials Bundle including Kindle Paperwhite. I had a Kindle for a number of years that I loved. It was back about 10-13 years ago and I used that one all the time. When that one finally was used up I got another, that should have been exactly like it. That one ended up with Ads and was horrible. I decided, rather than getting another Kindle - without Ads - I’d just go back to using my phone and the Kindle App. That was great until my aging eyes decided such small print - and readers - weren’t cutting it. So when Prime Days came around this year I took advantage of the day and got this Kindle Paperwhite Essentials Bundle including Kindle Paperwhite. I appreciate the Bundle, the cover, and the plug I bought extra. But this Paperwhite... I am just not on-board with it.

First, I DO like the size, shape, and weight. It is nice to hold and makes the older versions pale by comparison. I also like it compared to the size of my iPhone - too small and even as or heavier. Plus this size is easier to see and read and hold - with some decent edges to grip. The phone would grow tiring.

Second, like I said, I do like the cover - it looks nice and adds to the grip. (bought separately)

I love that I can adjust the size of the font and that I can do so as needed. There are times I’ll move it up or down accordingly.

What I am not a fan of at all:
I do NOT like the coloring. I prefer the ability to have the bright white - it helps me see better.
I do NOT like the softened element - that it’s like always at a soft color that ranges from a muted white to yellow. It is not at all comfortable or at least gets to a point I CAN see, but it is not nearly as nice or good for me as the original Kindle version.
I do NOT like the highlighting. I always highlight passages and this is a muted darker sort of gray, but not the yellow I prefer. It’s not all that hard to see, but certainly isn’t a nice way to delineate what’s desired. It’s frankly a lame choice.
I do NOT like how HARD and EASY it is to use the touchscreen. If you want something and need something it won’t work. if you do not want it to do something (open a page, change a page, highlight, whatever) it will keep doing it. Drives me nuts.
I HATE the way the library works, books line up, and access to the various areas. It is really BADLY coded and designed.

I decide against returning it for another Kindle. I’ll keep this one, use it until it too dies - or gets older - and then go back to what I THIIK is the same type of Kindle as I used to have - praying they still offer it. But this Paperwhite is really a bad option. I’m sure it has it’s fans, but I am NOT one of them. It’’ll get used, but along with a few unsavory words and desire for what’s next.

-----------------------------

WHAT I LIKE
Whoosh is definitely a reasonably good cleaner when it comes to removing those pesky fingerprints that water alone can't easily remove. The cleaner also uses a very good streak-free formula and this is a really nice feature for glossy screens that tend to show even the most minor of streaking. With it's safe formula, this product is appropriate for usage on many different types of delicate equipment. The bottles & sprayers are well-designed, and the smaller spray bottle is a great size for mobile usage, and are well made to withstand the beating that a product can be exposed to as an on-the-go item.
-----------------------------

WHAT I DID NOT LIKE AT ALL
Despite the above, I was VERY disappointed with the Whoosh cleaner. I can't speak to other people's experiences, but for me this Whoosh cleaner did NOT prevent fingerprints and did not perform any differently here than standard screen cleaners without this claim. Advertising this type of product as being able to reduce/prevent fingerprint buildup more or less allows this cleaner to be sold in a higher price-class than similar products because it sports a 'unique' feature to distinguish it from the competition. If it were sold without this feature being claimed, it would have to be sold for a lower price to compete with other similarly-performing screen cleaners.
-----------------------------

HOW DOES IT COMPARE TO A 'GOLDEN STANDARD' OF SCREEN CLEANERS???
Chances are you have heard of Rogge. Many electronics enthusiasts and something like 30+ major electronic manufacturers recommend Rogge as the premier screen cleaner on the market. There is good reason for this. Despite being as safe as this type of product can be, it rapidly removes the most stubborn of fingerprints & other oil stains, is as streak-free as streak-free can be, and is extremely versatile in that it not only can be used on screens but on numerous other delicate surfaces as well.
-----------------------------

CONCLUSION: I CANT JUSTIFY THE PRICE PREMIUM, AND THEREFORE CANNOT RECOMMEND THIS PRODUCT
When comparing ounce-to-ounce, Whoosh is priced almost double that of Rogge (less than 4 ounces of Whoosh is $13-20, and 8.5 ounces of Rogge is $17-20; both come with microfiber cloth/cloths.) As Whoosh does not seem to reduce or prevent fingerprints, it does not have a performance advantage to Rogge or other excellent-quality cleaners that are priced significantly lower.

This makes it difficult to justify paying twice as much for a product that is equally or less effective. If Whoosh was priced about 40-50% lower than it is, it would be an outstanding value. However, at its current price I recommend buying another brand because the same amount of money will get you a greater quantity of an equal- or superior-performing product.

title: This WILL Work To Bring Wired Ethernet To An Older TCL Roku TV
text:
I tried a couple of USB Ethernet adapters on an older TCL Roku TV (TCL 40FS3750) before settling on this unit. The chipsets on the other adapters were not recognized by the set.

However, this adapter (with chipset AX88772) was instantly recognized when it was plugged in. It appears that this may be the ONLY chipset that TCL Roku TV's will work with (based on other users sharing the same results). Or at least with an older set like mine which is a TCL Series 3.

Just make sure to restart your set (SETTINGS>POWER>RESTART) to allow the interface to transition from WiFi & pick up the wired configuration.

I was getting adequate speeds on WiFi (24MBps), but was having issues with Sling just freezing & timing out or kicking out completely & then restarting the TV.

After much troubleshooting, I was hoping it was b/c of my signal speed/quality. So, since I had the ability to go directly into a wired drop, I decide to try this adapter in hopes that I would get a speed bump as well as eliminate any WiFi bugginess.

Interestingly, my wired speeds were only slightly higher (around 27MBps), but this is most likely due to the USB interface (it's USB 3.0 on the TV, but only 2.0 on the adapter). I'm sure there are some other factors at play here as well. The set was never intended to be used with ethernet (only WiFi) so there could be some bottlenecking occurring just due to the aging firmware of the TV. I did have Roku version 9.0 running, but this did not seem to make much difference.

Unfortunately, Sling still randomly froze after the installation of this adapter. So I have to speculate the TV itself may be the issue or that there is still not enough bandwidth to accommodate Sling.

The adapter itself was not the issue. It was working just as intended.

As a comparison, I have no issues running Sling on a TCL Roku TCL 55S401 with INTEGRATED wired ethernet. I get roughly 75MBps to this set (which is also a much faster TV compared to the 40FS3750).

So, overall, the adapter did it's job, but the use of it didn't completely solve my particular problem. However, as noted, this was not the adapters fault. So it may still work for you in your setup. For under $12.00 it's definitely worth a shot!

title: Wow! Absolutely love, love, love it!!! (But buy the silver one)
text:
This is the most amazingly satisfying electronics product I have ever bought. The features are many and easy to learn. I especially enjoy some of the audio and video adjustment features: Audio: DRC setting helps bring up quieter sounds while controlling loud peaks. Great for taming those annoying audio surges in 'background' music or battle scenes, etc. The Dialog feature lets you adjust the dialog perception so that you can hear the voices better over the background sounds in the soundtracks. Video: You can adjust the Sharpness, Brightness, Contrast, Gamma, Hue, Chroma Level and BNR (block noise reduction). Each one has several levels to choose from and you get to sample it as it adjusts, so you can skip back and forth and compare the difference before you decide what to settle on. The USB mode has great, easy to navigate menus. You can also record to your thumb drive from a CD that you are playing. There is a choice of different bit rates to do this and you can record individual tracks or all tracks. Very user-friendly menus for all these choices. This unit has too many features to list, especially for someone like me, who is not quite fluent in tech terminology. Suffice it to say that it performs all the functions beautifully, the manual is very user-friendly and not only tells you how to adjust/change the various settings, but also explains the technical terminology in real English, so you know what those settings actually do when activated. I do love the region-free feature too. But for me, this is more ho-hum, since I already owned one - a far inferior quality Philips one. About the only thing I can think of to improve the user-friendliness of this product would be to have an alphabetized index in the manual. But, since it's only a 61 page manual, it's not such a big issue overall. Another suggestion I would have would be to allow to record audio from DVDs also. So often, the audio track on a DVD sounds so much better than the soundtrack that is published on CD (i.e.: Brassed Off, Eyes Wide Shut), although I recognize there may be some copyright issues with that concept. For the record: I am getting a second unit for my upstairs TV. Have I mentioned that I love it...? This is a really great product!!!

And yes, if you want to save some bucks, buy the silver one [[ASIN:B001PBQNPO Pioneer DV-610AVE PAL Multiformat DVD, SACD Player with HDMI and USB Host]]. It costs 30% less than the black one. I now own 2 of them.

text:

title: Excellent sound but a bit pricy
text:
To test the headphones I listened to about a dozen hours of movies, orchestral music, opera, jazz and solo piano.

The sound is clean, punchy, with a natural amount of bass. The quality was consistently excellent across all genres of music.

The headphones deliver a very upfront perspective which is particularly flattering to recordings of only several musicians — it creates the effect of it sounding like you're surrounding by them. The only downside is that the headphones amplify ambient sounds from the recording venue, such as noises from the audience.

The ear cups block out a good bit of ambient noise helping to minimize how much you need to turn the volume up to hear quieter passages of a recording. If you're hoping to use them at work to block out noisy co-workers they'll definitely do the trick (I tested the headphones at my office).

Overall the sound is pretty similar to Sennheiser over-ear headphones, which I regard as the best prosumer headphones for music. That being said, I do feel Sennheisers costing about one-third of the Monster Octagon deliver the same audio quality.

The construction of Monster feels pretty strong. While they are on the heavy side, they don't cause any pain when wearing for a while. It certainly helps that there is a good amount of padding on the cross strap that rests on your head.

My only complaint is that given the high cost the headphones should have come with a hardshell carrying case rather than a fabric bag. Even though they feel tough I still wouldn't want them flopping around in bag.

title: Isn't as Clean to Use as Pictures Indicate
text:
So, why 3 stars? The design. This adapter has a single USB-C port as a connector, and when used on the left side of a MacBook (as indicated in the promotional photos), it doesn't stay flush and kind of dangles down. This makes me worried that I'm going to accidentally snap off the connector inside of the computer. They do have a headphone jack if you use it on the right, which adds good stability, but then you have to use it upside down. This means that if you want to use the HDMI connector, it's facing towards you and the cable would have to wrap around in a big loop to the get to the monitor.

I've seen other models of this with two USB-C ports and would think those would be more stable. The actual build quality is good and I've never had any issues with the functionality. But the main reason you'd buy this instead of an ugly dongle hub is how clean a solution it's supposed to be. With the single port connector, that's not there.

title: A Chromebook is Essential for Online Financial Security
text: Anyone who does any online purchasing, banking or investing MUST buy a Chromebook, and use it for ALL their financial transactions.  Windows and Apple computers are way too vulnerable to malware.  Have you been reading the news about how ZeuS and other sophisticated password-stealing trojans and viruses are cleaning out bank accounts?  Do you want to be the next victim?  If you open an email or click a link on a website, you have to assume your computer might be infected with malware under the control of someone who intends to rip you off.  The last time my Windows computer got infected, the malware disabled my Trusteer Rapport security program and ran a fake dummy program which simulated that Rapport was still working.  Diabolical!  Microsoft Security Essentials was completely unable to even detect the malware, much less remove it.  Do you want to waste a week of your time reformatting your Windows hard drive every time it gets infected?  The solution is to use the Chromebook for all web financial transactions.  The Chromebook has no hard drive to get infected, and the Chrome operating system is hosted remotely and thus impervious to spyware.  You can still use your Windows or Apple computers to access the internet, just do not enter any passwords or personal data.  The bad guys will not be able to steal your credit card number or the passwords to your accounts if you only enter them when using your Chromebook.  As far as I can tell, the Chromebook is the best way to fend off the hackers and spyware criminals who are lurking on the internet these days.

title: Beautiful, powerful, fast. Making life and work enjoyable
text:
Skip to below the row of stars if you want the meat and no background "bun". I am not a gamer. Unless you count the fact that I still have SNES ROMs along with Doom, Panganitzu, Snarfs, etc on my hard drive that I haven't actually played in a decade but restore from computer to computer as I age out of a mixture of nostalgia and fantasy of free time suddenly spontaneously occuring in my life. With that disclaimer out of the way, I have purchased "gamer"-focused computers for the past 3 times now. This is my first AIO. This is also my first submission to the inevitability of horrid newer Windows versions (I was content with XP, thank you very much).

Almost 6 years ago my $1600 HP laptop died in a foreign land while I was starting vet school. I maniacally shopped- read reviews, created spreadsheets, poured over data as I do for all purchase from a $10 toaster to a vehicle. I chose an MSI GE70 2OC i7 laptop. I can't stand slow. The big turbo exhaust fan was attractive too, as I was at school near the equator and it was perpetually 88 degrees or higher. I was mocked by my classmates- literally all of which had macbook airs or whatever apple's slender little mass-produced silver computers were. They asked why I needed a computer like that. But as time went on on our mostly TV less island, my full size screen was envied to watch movies on and my processor handled ENORMOUS picture-saturated 500-plus slide Powerpoint presentation notes seamlessly while everyone else's struggled to load. I use my personal computer for work (I'm a veterinarian), for pleasure (I write, I still dabble with web and graphic design and art), and for storage (4 TB of vet school, pictures, videos, and fully scanned and digitized documents of my entire life).

My MSI was abused, traveled to and from the US twelve times, was exposed to excessive heat and humidity for 3 years, lugged to and from and around center city Philadelphia for my clinical year, was dropped, and infected with garbage third world school programs and systems. After 6 years the deciding factor for retirement was that for the past year it can't keep time. Every start up it reverts to a random day time way in the past. It loses time within minutes. I have to hard-set time and run 2 programs to keep it running correct... until the next restart or shutdown. (PS yes I've wiped and reinstalled this thing, changed main battery and internal battery, etc etc).

I started again maniacally researching options and initially wanted something more flexible. The flipping and convertible laptops were OK, but I already have a Note8 phone (long live the Note!) and had a Note 10.1 2014 edition tablet the second it was released in 2013. They definitely helped in vet school and clinical year and now in the real world both career and regular life-wise (what little there is). I somehow stumbled upon All-In-Ones and somehow they stayed as a viable option. I'm at the point where I really can go on vacation for a few days to a week or so and not actually need a laptop, I can catch up on work (online patient records etc, emails to patients' owners, etc) and can do it very efficiently on my phone, especially with a bluetooth keyboard. So it seemed like it would be OK to come full circle and back to a fairly stationary "desk top". So I took the plunge.

**************************************************************************************************************************************************************
Just kidding, more background about the hellacious ordering comedy of errors, skip ahead again to the actual product review....

I watched the price of this machine for months. It was not available through Lenovo itself with the enhanced SSD/HD size. Finally, a perfect storm of well-timed paycheck and $200 promotional discount on top of lowest price in 4 months pushed me to make the purchase. Oh what a can of worms. The first order (dramatic leading music here) shipped on time and then got stuck. It did not arrive the scheduled second day. UPS claimed holiday delay. I went to sleep that Friday night disgruntled I'd have to wait until Monday. Little did I know. I awoke Saturday am to an email from Amazon stating a refund had been issued as the item could not be delivered. (Record scratch noise). I simultaneously called UPS customer service (still showing in same place still in transit), and Amazon customer service chat. An hour later it was Amazon that informed me the item was damaged and being returned to them as the sender. I related this to the UPS dude on the phone and he was offended, saying, no proof or record of any damage and just a holiday delay, still in transit, don't worry my pretty little head. I left off with UPS and explained to Amazon that I need a computer not a refund. They instructed me to order a new one. I checked and the price had jacked up more than $200 and there were only two left and the original order's cost hadn't actually been refunded yet. I then proceeded to fall into a rabbit hole of customer service emails with Amazon. Eventually I was told to click on a provided link to purchase a new order and promised that if I purchased the computer again through Amazon through that link, they would knock off the price increase ($200) and refund shipping costs and I was told to choose expedited shipping and email them back when the order was placed so they could issue the reimbursements. I did so. They responded with "we don't do that". I responded to THAT. Eventually I was told that the order was still pending and things couldn't be adjusted until it was processed. It then showed processed and shipping label created. I contacted them again. Now I was told it was "too late to adjust as it was no longer pending but already shipped". (SERIOUSLY?) Back and forth 8 times, with seemingly every other person promising me refund interposed with those claiming "against" policy. On 12/5 I was told that it would be processed and would I like an immediate amazon credit or issued back to the card number. I responded. 36 hours later, nothing, not a word or a refund. I restarted customer service discussions. A dolt told me I had already been refunded the entire cost of the order. I wasted more time directing them to the provided new order number not the old. Another day of silence. Then, I was told I was given wrong information and no price adjustment could be made. It escalated between email and chat and eventually an awesome supervisor (thank YOU Anubha!) took care of everything which was a relief because I spent a day and a half setting up and transferring files and enjoying the new computer but I was ready to wipe it all and send it back rather than pay more than full price. Having 3 different agents corroborate what is apparently a malicious lie about a promised refund is very disappointing. I will never ever again take the chance or click on a link from an Amazon customer service rep or do anything with upfront pricing with an IOU promise. But thankfully, in the end Amazon came through and due to this I hope to remain an Prime member for another 12 years.

*********************************************************************************************************************************************************************

The item came in it's own obvious and exciting packaging. It is slightly over 39 lbs. The box dimensions are 801x282x590 mm (315.5 x 111 x 232.3 in for you majority Americans). The poor UPS guy looked absolutely frazzled with holiday spirit and asked if he could just slide it into my house. Box has nice hand-holes which made it easy to pick up. When you go to open this though, the push-through flaps for the hand-holes need to be pushed back out or you can't get your new computer out of its cocoon. It is well packaged. It could probably drop, get kneed, and tipped over without any concerns (don't test that). I don't see how my original order could've been damaged unless it was impaled by a forklift or fell out of a UPS truck on a highway and got hit by more than 2 armored cars.

The box includes the computer itself, the base to install on it, and a wired keyboard and mouse I immediately put to the side for CommunityAid. The bag the actual computer was in had clearly been opened before as the printed sticker holding it closed had been repositioned with residue glue and text from the label next to the current position. Computer itself was mint with all the protective stickers in place and not a mark. Beautiful, though I seem to be in a red and black schemed rut with my computer choices made solely on performance/power/storage.

The base is easy to install with the two included nice little screws- no tools required, reminds me of the handiness of Ikea, dare I say. The power plug is at the bottom of the back of the base. This prevents the device from being pushed absolutely flush against a wall due to the rigidity of the exiting cord. I immediately plugged in my Logitech wired backlit K740 slim keyboard and my wireless ancient $5 HP mouse. I started up the beast. Very quiet and everything was plug and play. Not a single click or install required for the mouse/keyboard. Set up was quick and easy with a lot of unchecking of bloatware (the stuff they openly identify anyway). Instead of using old discs, I downloaded the most current drivers for my (wired) Samsung CLP printer, (wireless) Canon Pixma IX 6800 printer, and (wired) Fujitsu ScanSnap S1300i scanner. So easy and smooth, no issues. They all worked like happy family members who could all finally be in one home now (not enough USB ports on previous machines for them all).

My first experience with Windows 10. Blech. Lots of deleting, uninstalling, and Cortana was exorcised before the immediately offered Windows update was at 2%. Mine turned on with version 10586 of Windows. It offered an update to the most current (15063) which would take up a gulp-inducing measly 40 plus GB. Sigh. They do this right at the beginning so that you're rendered more accepting and ambivalent by the amazing display.

It is gorgeous. Enormous. Sharp. Extremely bright. As others have discussed, changing brightness is annoying as it is not available through settings or as a hard button. You have to access it by opening Lenovo Nerve Center -> Display Settings. I'm not sure if a keyboard dedicated button would work, my keyboard's volume buttons work but it doesn't have display buttons. You can uncover a keyboard shortcut eventually in the Nerve Center: Alt + I increases brightness and Alt + D decreases. At the lowest setting it is comfortable even for my tired, dry, sensitive eyes, in the dark.

It is as fast and peppy as I had hoped. I can multitask writing emails, viewing huge digital radiographs ("xrays"), downloading/uploading photos or video, watching movies, and transferring gigs and gigs of files all at the same time elegantly. The radiographs look better on my screen then they do at work on the actual radiology viewing screen, and instead of crouching and angling myself to examine them I can smoothly and with the touch of a single finger, tilt this screen to the best angle.

Photo editing is amazing but I sadly couldn't bring my Adobe PS CS3 with me.

This machine is very quiet, although, on the second day I started to notice the fan running. It is a unique sound in my opinion compared to all the other towers and laptops I've ever experience. The best way I can describe it is, it sounds like you are hearing through closed windows, your neighbor down the street running a generator. I hope this is normal and not a sign of bad things. It's quiet but noticeable when its on.

The sound... I am by no means a sound system snob (except when it comes to my vehicles). This computer's sound is lacking. It's OK for movies and background sounds, it just resembles an inexpensive bluetooth speaker. The enhanced setting is a bit murky and the normal is fuzzy/dull. I haven't discovered if you can customize anything yet. I don't particularly care, just the price of this device made me hope for better. The sound in my car (2006 Volvo S60R with factory dolby surround sound 11-speaker using just a grom AUX input to listen to mp3s on my phone) sounds WAY better, but I do realize this computer is trying to put out "surround" sound from a single plane of speakers.

Although it's still the honeymoon I'm really hoping I continue to enjoy this computer and stay satisfied with having chosen an AIO. With the power, speed, and storage I am hoping to get many many many years out of it (with the cost, many many many many many years). I can't imagine ever wanting anything with a bigger screen or "better" picture. This thing is massive and I wasn't coming from a shrimp, my laptop was 17.3". My extra wide full size keyboard looks normal to small beneath this monster.

I did not purchase a secondary warranty at this time due to universally terrible reviews and jaded mistrust.

4/1/2018 update:
Two weeks ago a Windows update destroyed the built in bluetooth function of the the computer. I tried everything and could not resurrect it. I ended up buying an external USB bluetooth device and it works, but it doesn't function as well with the Echo Dots and Alexa ( I have to pair/unpair, connect/disconnect each Dot EACH TIME at the computer). Really really bummed.

9/2018 update offered and downloaded and the bluetooth capabilities are fixed! THANK GOODNESS! Very happy

title: Smooth Operator
text:
I have worked with GPS navigators from several manufacturers, including Garmin, Magellan and TomTom. Each unit has its strengths and weaknesses. My favorite GPS unit up this point has been another TomTom, an old Start 40 which served me well for several years. I was interested to see how much the series has changed since I got that older model. It has changed quite a bit – more than I expected. I like this navigator, though I can see a few things I’d change.

First off, I have the 6” model which is a beast. I am used to a 5” GPS which I have been using, and it took some time to adjust to the larger screen. This is not to say it bothers me; it just is enough of a difference to require getting used to it. If you are upsizing like that, be aware that it takes up more physical space and placing on the windshield might require replanning.

Out of the box, I powered it on, connected it to my WiFi network and downloaded over 6GB of updates. That’s a huge update. The map it holds is obviously the largest component to be updated, and it covers all of the US, Canada and Mexico. While it is nice to have all that coverage, I personally do not need that much map and would have liked the option of only having the US map on-board. That would cut memory requirements. My older model was limited in memory and the map grew until it could no longer fit; I can see the potential for that happening again.

For navigation, up to this point I have stuck with the default settings, except with the 2D/3D map setting.

My first trip with this unit was to work. I did not use it to navigate, I only used to to show the map as I drove. It found my fix quickly (one of the reasons I like TomTom navigators) and when I was driving it updated the map smoothly and quickly as I reached new features. It displayed road names, it showed the placement of certain POIs like gas stations, and because I was driving at sunrise the map switched from night mode to daytime so I got to see both maps.

I’ll state for the record, I am not fan of the daytime map’s default color scheme. I almost always use the 2D map, not the 3D one, and it uses a set of pastel colors that might be somewhat soothing on the eyes but they’re quite drab. I’d rather see a bolder map that makes features stand out more. Another thing this unit does not show is road symbols like the interstate shield, instead opting for just small-print words. I can live with that but I do prefer the symbols.

On the way home from work, I used the unit again, but this time to guide me on an alternate route. Friday afternoon traffic in this area is typically awful, and the route home is almost always snarled by at least one accident (sometimes as many as 4-5). I chose to follow a route I knew would take two hours to get home, though it moves the whole time. I loaded the first point into the GPS and it dutifully guided me there, taking me on a fairly optimal route. When I got there, I then told it to take me home and I was quite surprised – every other GPS unit I have used has tried to make me take a U-turn to go back the way I came to get back on the interstate (the source of the problem), but this one did not, instead taking me on a route that would connect me back to the interstate about 20 miles south. Knowing this was also a bad route traffic-wise, I made a planned turn in the middle of the route, skipping another 20 miles of interstate. Instead of insisting I turn around, the unit again adjusted my route and took me on almost the exact route I had planned to take anyway.

What impressed me is how quickly the unit rerouted me without trying to put me back on the original route it chose. This is quite different from most units. Normally I get “turn around when possible” or “recalculating” over and over – not this time.

I finally did let it put me on the interstate, about 5 miles from home. When I reached my exit is showed very clearly what lane it wanted me to use, and it was very obvious when I was to turn.

I use the American female voice that reads street names. She enunciates very clearly and is easy to understand. Many GPS units sound tinny or have a buzz when the voice is active, but this one does not. My old Start 40 sounded clear too and did not buzz. I think perhaps TomTom does a better job with designing their units for sound.

One thing I use my GPS for is speed tracking. When in an area where there are no posted speed limit signs, it is nice when the GPS shows the speed limit and your current speed. For this one, though, the speed display is very small. It’s out of the way which is good, but I’d prefer a larger display or at least some ability to make it bigger. If there is a setting for that I have not uncovered it yet.

My primary complaint with this GPS is actually the menu system, which I find to be very clunky and odd. I don’t like it, and preferred the older menu system. It is workable, regardless.

Most GPS units that offered traffic do so through a special antenna or attachment in the power connector. Rather than offer this, this unit instead gets traffic updates via your phone through a Bluetooth connection. This is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it does not require that the unit be plugged in all the time and it becomes much more portable. On the other hand, it means that it pulls data and if you’re in an area where there is no data connectivity your updates aren’t available. I’m still deciding if I like this arrangement or not.

This is a good GPS with a little room for improvement in a few areas. The screen real estate is nice, and it navigates very well (better than most others I have used). It enunciates clearly and updates en route smoothly and quickly. The menu system is a little clunky, and there are some display settings I think could be better. Overall, though, this unit gets the important things right. It’s a good unit at a competitive price.

text: I bought this to back up my LG phone because I was forced to buy a new phone since LG no longer supports their phones and I was already starting to have issues with mine.  In buying a new phone, I was particularly freaked out about the possibility of losing my photos and other important files since the newer phones no longer have MicroSD cards for backup.  This seemed like a great option--along with backing up to Google and Amazon cloud services, it added another layer of protection.  The problem is that the C port didn't even fit into the C port on my phone--even though I took the case off my phone.  After essentially having to cram it in the port, I kept getting a warning that my data would be corrupted if I kept "ejecting" it.  It also wanted to back everything up to a MicroSD card, since it did not recognize that the SanDisk was even inserted into the phone.  Since I'd spent a considerable amount of time moving everything from my SD card to the internal memory of my phone in anticipation of having to transfer it to a new phone without a card slot, I most definitely didn't want to back up everything back onto my card, so I took the card out.  Even so, it still took quite some time for the phone to recognize the SanDisk, and finally start the back up.  From there, the process was fairly easy, BUT it should have never been so difficult to get the phone to recognize the SanDisk in the first place.  After the backup, I of course plugged the SanDisk into my laptop (without issues) and everything was indeed backed up.  It should NOT have been that difficult to plug the device into my phone however!  I will also mention, not that it's a big deal, but the device is considerably smaller than it looks to be on the Amazon website (less than .75x1.5").  At least I have an additional backup, but not as easily as I would have liked.  Given the issues I had with it I don't think I would purchase this particular device again.

title: Better than my unamplified antenna, but no match for my other 50 mile amplified antenna
text:
I recently spent a similar amount of money on a refurbished Mohu that is very similar looking.

Both are similar looking amplified antennas, but they do not perform similarly.

The Mohu has a thicker cable. The Mohu has a longer cable. The Mohu's amplifier cable that connects to the TV is thicker. The 1byone amplifier makes a very soft (but detectable) audio buzz when connected. The 1byone is very slightly larger, and less flexible than the Mohu.

I tried positions both antennas in identical positions (Mohu, then 1byone, then reconfirmed the results after the replacing the Mohu), and the Mohu provided superior single quality and strength for all channels.

This does outperform the smaller, unamplified antenna that was bought this to replace, but my hope was that a similarly rated, similarly priced 50 mile range antenna would have similar performance to the Mohu.

My unamplified antenna got 28 channels, this got 32, and the Mohu got 42. While those numbers suggest that it's only a marginal improvement over the unamplified antenna, that is not true. This does make both ABC and CBS viewing consistent, while the unamplified was prone to "no signal" outages on those channels periodically.

Based on my experience with this antenna on two different TVs, and compared to two other antennas, I would call this middle of the road, and recommend people looking to pickup channels they might otherwise miss should spend a little extra on the Mohu 50 mile option. People who either have a coupon code or see this on sale and are looking for something that will get some local channels, this might offer good bang for their buck.

Update: I will say that 1byone's support is great. They commented on this review and answered my follow up questions through e-mail. While this antenna is not a match for the refurbed Mohu in my house, it is a good antenna with great service. If you're looking for bang for your buck, at the right price (and I've seen good sales for this), this is definitely a great option.

title: Maybe a nice learning toy . . . but way too expensive for such a cheap quality item.
text:
This is most definitely a toy microscope. The reason I say it's a toy is because it does magnify objects and comes with a set of accessories that can be used to study small objects and magnify them.

However, it's not that great as a microscope but it could be fun as a toy for kids who want to see certain things up close.

It has a nice sized view-screen and it's easy to charge and operate.

The main issues I have are a few. The included accessories are a set of 5 pre-prepared/stained slides of various things like cross-section slices of an earthworm, plant-stems, and the like. There are also 5 blank slides with 5 glass cover-slips. There's a pretty flimsy plastic tweezer that's a little larger than it probably should be, and a joke of a liquid dropper (see photos). It also comes with a small chunk of quartz crystal that isn't anything like the geode pictured on the box. It's just a chunk of crystal as far as I can tell -- might not even be quartz.

There is a 128 MB micro-SD card included (That's right, I said MB and it's not a typo). I didn't even know they made micro-SD cards with such a small amount of memory. The photos are 1920x1280 so it's not going to hold a lot, especially if you're taking videos. The good news it that it will accept larger micro-SD cards so you can just put in a larger one if that becomes a problem. I can confirm it works with a 4GB micro-SD card but didn't test anything higher.

This is clearly not intended for any serious use, but just as something for kids to play with to satisfy their curiosity by seeing what small objects look like up close -- but not too close. I've included a photo of two human hairs side-by-side at the 800x zoom. At that level of magnification, you can see a bit more detail, but you don't even see the bark-like layers that you would with a better microscope.

Which comes to the biggest drawback. The magnification is pretty low at I think about 200x optical with the packaging stating "800x Zoom". Clearly, it's still only a 200x picture that has been digitally zoomed 4x which basically gives you the same level of detail as the 200x picture, but it's 4 times the size, but the number of pixels hasn't changed so there isn't the same level of detail as if you had an *actual* 800x microscope.

I'm just not impressed by a 200x optical microscope even as a toy, especially at the current price of $90. That's an expensive magnifying glass with a few weak extras to jazz it up. You'd be much better off spending the $90 on a "real" microscope that has much better optical zoom. They can be found at a much better price.

But, it's National Geographic, so that might have some brand appeal, but I'm disappointed in the quality and National Geographic should be embarrassed at putting their name on this. At least they could have spent a bit more on the optics.

You can find pretty much this exact design in countless knock-offs which are typically used by coin or stamp collectors to get a better view of their stamps/coins. This one does have a view-screen which some of the others don't, so it might be just slightly more useful -- because as a toy a kid isn't going to want to wait until they're at a computer to see the photos.

There's nothing in the manual about being able to hook this up via USB so that you can use it to view objects directly on your computer in real time. HOWEVER, it

Pros:
- Nice packaging and graphic art on the box
- Giftable
- Better than a handheld magnifying glass
- When connected to a PC with the USB cable, you can copy pictures and videos from the microscope's micro-SD card right to the PC without having to remove the micro-SD card from the microscope. Save a little bit of time.
- Light from the LED's is fairly bright

Cons:
- Low magnification for a microsope. Optical magnification states 200x, but I'm dubious of that.
- Claims 800x zoom. That's like saying that if you watch a normal HD video on a 4K TV it becomes a 4K movie. Same concept here, the picture gets enlarged 4x, but there's no increase in the original 200x resolution, same number of pixels either way.
- Light only comes from above what you're viewing unless you rig up another light from below the slide. When looking at slides under a microscope, the images just aren't as good as when a slide is lit from below as well.
- Can't be used as a PC microscope. I tried a lot of solutions and I'm still working on being able to use it in that way, but for now only the attached 4"x3" screen will show a live image. There should be a way to connect it to a PC with the USB and view live images on the PC, but so far it seems like a complicated problem. But it would increase the useability of this microscope. If I find a way to get it to display on the PC screen live, I'll update this review.

So on to my conclusion. I really wanted to like this more, especially considering the NG brand, but . . . .

I have to subtract a star for the price, even if the National Geographic brand has some value, it's not enough to make up for the fact that this is a very-low end toy microscope and the current $90 price is not justifiable, IMO.

I have to subtract another star for the poor quality accessories that are included. Literally every accessory included is the cheapest thing they could find. The plastic is flimsy and the controls are clunky and the manual is dismal.

Overall, if you need a quick toy for a kid, it works, but you'd be better off spending the same amount on a much better microscope. It's got a lot of flash and marketing glitz, but the product is very sub-par and I definitely expect more from National Geographic. Think of the children, NG -- they are our future and they deserve a better effort than this.

title: This is all you need to get over the air HD TV
text:
Save your money. This basic indoor antenna may be all you need to receive over the air HD TV. Anything claiming to be an amplified antenna is a waste of money.

Let's go over some facts:

1) Unlike analog TV signals where the quality of the signal reception affects picture quality -- poor reception results in a snowy picture -- with digital the picture either comes in perfectly or not at all. It's like your cell phone -- the quality at one bar is the same as full bars. But when you're at one bar -- whether with your phone or TV -- there's a high likelihood that the signal will completely drop out for a few seconds and then come back. On TVs this results in pixelation because the tuner cannot decode the signal due to it being intermittent. So any antenna that claims to boost picture quality is just bogus. The real issue is having a good sightline.

2) What affects whether or not your can receive a signal is your antenna's sightline with the broadcast source, and the distance from the broadcast source. If you're not receiving a channel all you can do is adjust the position of the antenna to improve the sightline and/or buy a bigger antenna (which is why roof antennas are by far the best option). Any antenna that claims to somehow boost the signal is again bogus. An antenna has no way to bost the broadcast strength of the signal in order to overcome sightline or distance issues.

If you have no choice but to have an indoor antenna you simply may not be able to get every channel -- an expensive indoor antenna cannot move the buildings blocking the signal. But if sightlines and distance aren't an issue, this antenna will be good enough. (I'm in an apartment building in NYC. When I first plugged in the antenna and placed it behind my TV the only major network that always came in stably was Fox. I bought 18 feet of coax cable for $4 so that I could place the antenna by a window. I now get an extremely strong signal with CBS, NBC, FOX and PBS. Only ABC doesn't come through.)

Note on 5.1 sound: If you want to playback the audio in 5.1, you cannot connect the antenna to your receiver. What you have to do is run an optical (toslink) line out from your TV to your receiver, and make sure your TV is on mute. I know this sounds convoluted, but very few A/V receivers have built-in ATSC tuners.

The Oppo is worth some effort. If you know that Diva Plavalaguna was sung by Inva Mula and want to hear as well as see the glory, this is the player. Sadly, it won't make any Matrix sequels worth seeing... there's only so much technology can do.

And about those Netflix crashes... annoying, huh? Netflix looks good, though, and Vudu so good I'm actually paying for movies I could stream free. No HBO GO - nothing's perfect - but great DVD, BluRay, audio AND streaming quality? This rocks!

title: I like it but my neighbors may not
text:
When the huge box arrived, I thought I'd made a mistake by ordering the Altec Lansing VS4621 Octane 7, 2.1 Computer Speaker. Fortunately, the shipping box was much larger than the item, so my blood pressure was quickly reduced. The speakers do have a small footprint and the taller contemporary shape is quite attractive. The subwoofer size is compact enough and unobtrusive in it's solid black boxy shape. I now have it placed on the bare wood floor, so my downstairs neighbors are likely not too happy with me right now. I will be placing a small carpet beneath it this afternoon.

Installation was intuitive and quite simple -- the most time consuming aspect was removing all the plastic. I didn't even notice the visual directions for set up are imprinted on the inside top flaps of the box. Because there is no bottom covering on the speakers by design, I'm especially careful when moving the speakers from one position to another. You'll get a different sound depending upon what surface you place the speakers. In the past hour, I've listened to Bob Dylan, The Grateful Dead, Johnny Cash, Radiohead, Sigur Ros, M.I.A., my Dad's dictation of his life story, Charles Mingus Lama Karta, The Black Lips, David Sedaris and Luka Bloom. The least pleasing on these speakers was a classical piece by Schubert which demonstrated the "muddy" nature of this sort of speaker system. Now this is a wide variety of music and sounds and my impression is that this is a really nice system which for the most part I would recommend. There's also an AUX input on the front of the speaker with controls so it can be hooked up to another electronic device of choice. Being able to adjust the volume, treble and bass gives me simple control options but by using the iTunes Equalizer, I can adjust to my preference with each cut. Throughout the years, I've purchased and used various speakers for my stereo, iPod, computer and entertainment systems, and I'm very impressed with these! Can't now wait to watch a movie and hear how these speakers reproduce the sound!

title: Fastest, Most Reliable Home Network Performance Yet--Delivers Strong Signal Throughout Two-Story Condo
text:
When I first set up a home network, I selected a Cisco "Linkys" G router (EA1300) because I recognized the brand name. Later I upgraded to a Cisco dual-band N router ([[ASIN:B007IL7AKM Linksys EA4500]]), which was--and still is--a superb router. My latest upgrade, to this LINKSYS AC1900 (EA6900) DUAL BAND SMART WI-FI ROUTER, represents another leap forward in the performance of my home network.

The wireless signal is stronger in every corner of my two-story condo. All of my devices (some 25 computers, tablets, music players, Kindles, cellphones, Roku, etc.) connect very quickly. Best of all, I'm getting Comcast's promised high-speed Internet speeds of more than 50 Mbps with the Comcast-supplied new telephony modem. (An online speed test site just now clocked the download speed at 57 Mbps). In fact, my present home network is capable of even faster speeds--the home network is limited by the speed of the slower external Comcast network.

This router is extremely easy to set up. You just connect it, and follow the prompts from the built-in software. Whenever you access the router to adjust the settings, and click on some part of the Menu, you find excellent "contextual" help screens that fully explain the meaning of each of the settings. The Menu is set up differently from the menus for the EA4500 and EA1300, but the basic methodology for the settings is the same--the settings are just presented in a way that's easier for a non-techie user to understand.

I read a newspaper review that recommended NOT buying this excellent EA6900 router, because of testers' problems with the second band and with nonfunctioning USB ports. I think that the testers probably received a defective router--and should have requested a replacement. Even a reliable brand like Cisco may sometimes ship an occasional bad electronics device.

Because I only need a single-band router, I haven't tested the second band on my EA6900 router. (The second band did work fine on my EA4500 router, but using the second band didn't improve the signal strength, so I didn't continue using it.) However, I did test the USB ports on the EA6900, and both work really well. In fact, the router recognized and easily accessed a couple of external wireless storage drives--connected with a 100-foot (!) USB cable--when my PC was flakey about recognizing those same drives when they were connected directly to the PC with the long cable.

I absolutely love this EA6900 router, which I've been using for more than a month now. Because of my home wiring, the router is located a long way from any of my wireless devices, and I have a lot of nearby neighbors with competing wireless Internet connections. But with the EA6900, there have been virtually no dropped connections, and the strong signal is something that I've long been wishing for!
