title: The Best Blend of UltraBook and Multimedia Systems in One
text:
At first glance the Asus VivoBook V551LA-DS17T appears to be a nice touch-screen UltraBook-class computer, but it is a few steps beyond a typical UltraBook. Combining features of UltraBook systems and multimedia/entertainment workstations, this computer is what new systems ought to be. There are a couple of design decisions I would change and it's by no means a high-end gaming rig, but Asus got the important things right.

There are two things that set this system apart from a normal UltraBook. First is the inclusion of a slimline CD/DVD R/W drive. I have seen no other UltraBooks out there that include one, so finding one in this system was a very pleasant surprise. Carrying an external CD/DVD drive around can be inconvenient (especially when traveling) so having a built-in drive is a huge plus. Asus managed to include this drive in the system while still keeping the system to roughly an inch thick. The other differentiating factor that makes this system different than other UltraBooks I have seen (and not in a positive way) is the weight. This is a particularly heavy system and will make toting it around a chore.

I booted up the system and configured it for use and immediately went about looking for the utility for making recovery/restore DVD media. After searching the file system and the installed program list with no success I finally resorted to calling technical support. I spoke to a charming young lady who was exceptionally helpful and got me on my way to creating a recovery USB drive. So, from that experience I can say that technical support is courteous and helpful. However, I never did figure out how to make DVD media, but at least I can restore the system now should I have a need to do so.

After power-on for the first time it performed a bunch of hands-off updates and when it finished and finally allowed interaction with the OS it was loaded with Windows 8.1; it wasn't obvious if the initial OS install was 8 or 8.1 but that is irrelevant - 8.1 is what is there when the user can finally begin exploring the system. I spent a little time digging through the list of installed applications and was pleased to see that Asus did not load this system up with excessive bloatware. There are several applications I do not need and I intend to remove them - MS Office and McAfee protection services being among them - but at least what is there is not unreasonable. Interestingly, most new systems I have used have come with 1-2 years of internet security protection, but this system comes with just 30 days.

One design decision that really surprised me is that this system does not include a solid-state drive (SSD). I understand the reason - it drives up cost - but to me having an SSD in this system would make it even faster and make the battery last longer. This is by no means a deal-breaker but bootup times are slower as a result.

Asus makes a big deal about the touch screen on this system and touts it as more sensitive than most other touch screens. Asus' claims appear to be well-founded as the other touch screen systems available to me are nowhere near as responsive. After spending a couple of hours working with this system I unplugged my trackball and I don't think I will need it again for this particular system. If you are buying this system for the ability to use the touch screen, you will be pleased.

Battery life so far is excellent. I charged the system up completely and spent a good three hours using it for web surfing and typing up documents and the battery still maintains more than half of its charge. I plan to load up my development environment and see how the battery holds up under load, and I expect that to make the battery drain faster, but for typical use (surfing the web, writing document and watching online videos) the battery seems to be very much in the game.

The graphics system is provided by the Intel chipset and it is acceptable for most uses. It's not high end graphics but it's not terrible either. Serious gamers will not appreciate this system whereas most casual gamers and people using the system for more business-types of functions will be more than satisfied. As an experiment I had my teenage son load up Minecraft (an online game that uses 1st-person perspective) and test the graphics. He noticed that while the game played well enough it is not quite as smooth as a system that has a dedicated graphics card.

Wi-Fi connection speed seems to be about average with other wireless-n devices on the network.

One thing that really startled me is the quality of the sound system. Asus says that this is the best configuration for embedded sound available and I found the sound quality coming from the embedded speakers to be more than acceptable. The speakers are on the bottom of the unit and are visible via two inch-long slits in the case. In spite of the small aperture, the output is very good, better than one would expect.

With the slimline DVD and the decent sound quality, paired with the i7 processor and 8GB RAM this system is well-suited for multimedia tasks such as video production and music creation. It has the horsepower to handle the renders and so far has performed well while working on either audio or video composition. As I mentioned above I expect these types of activities to take more battery than less strenuous tasks but I have not spent enough time with these types of applications on this system yet to determine just how much they will impact battery life.

The touch pad is a bit better than average and is placed well. One issue I have with most laptops is that I tend to tap the touch pad while typing and on occasion I can highlight and delete a whole section of text unintentionally. So far this has not been a problem with this system and I think it has a lot to do with the way the touch pad is positioned relative to the open space on the keyboard. Asus includes a very nice utility (accessible by a special key on the keyboard) that makes turning the touch pad on and off very simple, so it's easy to eliminate any issue with it if it's "in the way" while typing.

The power adapter is odd and I am not sure I like it. The shape requires a little planning as it is a square block pressed against the wall when it is plugged in. Most adapters typically have the brick in the middle. So, plugging this adapter in when working in a cramped space could potentially pose a challenge. Another observation - the adapter gets rather warm.

I do not like the way the hard drive is partitioned right out of the box. It appears that the drive was simply chopped into two roughly equal partitions, the D: drive labeled as "data". I would rather have one large drive, instead of two smaller ones. This is a personal preference though and I am sure most will be indifferent.

I decided to toss in a Linux LiveCD and boot it up to see how well supported the touch screen is with a current distribution. The system refused to boot from it initially; to get it to boot I had to turn off Secure Boot in the BIOS after which I was able to boot up from the DVD. My distribution of choice for this experiment was Mint 16 with the Cinnamon Desktop. I found that there is basic support in place for the screen, though only as a standard pointing device (a lot like using a Wacom tablet) and not as a swipe and gesture interface. There are other distributions out now that are geared more towards tablets; I will try one of those and see how well it works out. That said, the fact that the desktop at least recognizes the screen as a pointing device and properly responds to it is a good thing.

A few other technical details: The system has 3 USB ports (two of them USB 3.0 and one of them USB 2.0), an HDMI port, an Ethernet port (which is not a given anymore when it comes to notebook computers), an audio out and a SD card reader. Given a choice I would have liked to have a VGA or DVI port to put the display on a second screen but that's not something I have seen on the most recent systems.

Asus has put together a very nice UltraBook-like system in this notebook. It's a nice workhorse for most uses and the touch screen is absolutely wonderful. The system's a bit hefty though and might prove to be cumbersome for those on the go, and the graphics system is not at serious gaming level, but the system is a solid performer and provides the best features of an UltraBook and a multimedia workstations in one place.

title: A super antenna
text:
There are already many reviews here but I like this antenna so much I feel I would like to say something. I had been using an old Channel Master "powerful" antenna in my attic. It did the job, but it was huge with many protruding elements. Also, aiming it was a finicky affair but as I've said, it did work. When I came across this 4V antenna, I could not resist. I could finally get the gigantic atrocity out from my attic and perhaps even get better reception with this smaller and less "stabby" antenna. This little beauty really pulls in the station. I'm getting all the channels intneded for me here in Houston.. I am very happy with this antenna. It is driving two TVs through a non-powered splitter and down two stories and there is no extra amplification at the TV end. All told, if this antenna cannot receive a station in your vicinity you probably will not receive it with anything other than a big "fringe" antenna.

My only gripe about this antenna is that I do not like tightening wingnuts directly onto the "buss" bars. There should be lock washers included. The wingnuts worked loose after mounting the antenna causing a minor annoyance. You have to make the wingnuts good and tight to endure the expansion and contraction due to changing attic temps. Not sure how they work outdoors. Just make em tight.

title: Very capable tablet
text:
I'm not going to delve into the technical aspects of the Fire as others have done an admirable job already. But as an alternative to other, more expensive tablets, the Fire is an amazing piece of tech.

I was almost getting ready to pull the trigger on the Google Pixel C or Samsung S3. A big leap for me as I didn't want to spend $500 plus on a tablet, but I wanted fast speed, large screen, and inexpensive aftermarket accessories.

The Fire is dual-core, so it flies through the games I play. A big plus. I know everyone hates when their game bogs down in the middle of a rousing Orc battle, or, even worse, won't even load. The Fire has run all the games I've thrown at it with no issues.

The 10" screen is heavenly, considering I came from a generic 7" tablet that was VGA on a good day. The text is crisp, the graphics flow as they should. HD movies and shows are freakin' excellent. The 10" format seems to be the best for this.

If you research well for accessories, you can find some nice deals. There was no way I was going to spring for a $30 case, when the $10 Fintie case works as good or better. More money saved for movies, games, and books!

Please don't spend the extra $15 on the 'without special offers' option. The only special offers thrown at you are when the tablet wakes from sleep. A quick swipe and they're gone. Save that money for a case!

And yes, Virginia, you can get the google play store. The easiest way is to install 4 app files and run them in order. No rooting, no PC hookups. Go to blog.ebook-reader dot com and search 'how to install google play on fire.' Easy peasy, just follow the instructions to the letter.

All-in-all this a capable tablet offered by Amazon. The price is right, the tech is excellent considering its price point. You can game like a madman, watch shows, and read War & Peace.

title: Affordable Coverage for Your Dot
text:
Here we have another case of purchasing an extended warranty being asked to provide a review but never having made use of (and hoping never to have to) the purchased coverage. The price was right but lower on SquareTrade's site (I'm signed up for the specials and such mailings so I should have been made aware of. But it's only a few dollars so its no big loss).

The plan covers up to three replacements of the covered item or the term of the warranty you purchased (two years in this case). After trying to troubleshoot your device over the phone they will make the decision to either repair or replace your item. If they decided to replace the item it's wholly their choice to either provide a new or newest model of your device or provide a refurbished model of what you have. They promise quick turn-around and cover shipping in both directions. If you do not return the defective model within in a certain time frame (I believe it's 30 days) of receiving your replacement your credit card (which you MUST have on file to file a claim) will be charged the full cost of the device when new.

I've heard nothing but good things about SquareTrade for years and almost all of the low-star reviews seem to be user's not understanding the plan or not making sure they would be covered for their purchases rather than anything to do with SquareTrade itself. While I hope I never need to use the plan it was affordable enough to make up for Amazon's fairly deplorable ninety day warranty (our refurbished PaperWhite came with a full year's coverage. A brand new Dot, like their seven and eight inch tablets (unlike their six or ten inch tablets, the Echo or Tap and their entire eReader line which all have one-year warranties) only has ninety days I don't know why. I've always trusted Amazon's electronics, I wonder at their apparent lack of faith.

But anyway. I've rambled on enough. The two years of coverage is comforting and was quite affordable. I'm happy with the purchase and honestly hope I never need to use it.

title: Happy with my new TomTom
text:
I just wanted to provide this small tip to new users of the TomTom. It's about the suction cup for the windshield - I've read review that it doesn't hold well, and one person said that if he wet the cup before sticking, that worked for a while. The windshield mount that comes with the TomTom actually is designed to hold - but the instructions aren't clear. So here's how you get it to hold really tight - you couldn't even pull it off.

You will need to figure out the position of the mount first, then separate it from your TomTom, since you can't do the rest of this with it attached. With the suction cup facing the windshield (away from you), turn the disk that is in the center all the way counter clockwise. Then stick the mount onto your windshield where you want it, and while you push it with your hand, use your other hand to turn the disk in the center all the way clockwise. That motion, turning it clockwise, makes the suction cup really tight. Then you can put your TomTom back onto the mount.

Hope this helps some folks. My mount fell off a couple of times, then I realized what I'd done wrong.

When I went to the web site to set up the My Tomtom account and check for updates, I have to say that it wasn't super intuitive - at first it wouldn't take my code. text:
“B A T T E R Y L O W”
“P O W E R O F F”
“P O W E R O N”

When you advertise “noise cancellation,” do you mean “make these headphones as loud as possible so that our customers can’t hear anything outside of what they’re listening to and then advertise it as noise cancellation?” I only have my volume up a single tick on my iPhone and these headphones blast sound through my ears.

I always get caught off guard when the headphone battery gets low. Even though I have a single tick on the volume while using these headphones, when the headphones tell me the battery is low it automatically turns the volume up to max and screams “BATTERY LOW” into my ears. If you like surprise jump scares then this product is for you.

When I bought these headphones Amazon advertised this product at 200+ dollars going on sale for 80-90%. I thought I was getting a great deal and buying some top notch headphones for a tenth of the price, but actually the product was worth 20 bucks. Maybe I should’ve known better, but apparently either amazon or SENSO advertised this product as being at an extremely high discount rate to get more sales. False advertising at its finest, or maybe that might be a trend with products sold on amazon in general. How unfortunate.

Now to get more into the technical side, the sound quality isn’t good or bad, which is appropriate since these headphones are only 20 dollars. They’ll get the job done. These aren’t a pair of Bose or Beats. However, when you advertise these headphones as 200+ dollars on sale for 80-90% which is the pricing range of Bose or Beats headphones, but in reality this is only a 20 dollar product, you’re expecting much more from these headphones. And obviously, since this is actually a 20 dollar product you just feel ripped off because it was advertised as really expensive.
Noise cancellation as stated previously is solved by Senso by blasting sound into your eardrums until you can’t hear your environment anymore. Not noise cancellation, but nice try.

tl;dr - these headphones are not as advertised because the noise cancellation is poor and sound quality isn’t good.

I’m buying a new set of headphones. I’m very disappointed, annoyed, and feel cheated.

title: Works good for me ...
text:
I've been using this fan controller for well over a year and have had no trouble with it at all. It's part of a high-end custom build.

The computer has 5 fans controlled by motherboard headers and 5 fans controlled by this device. The motherboard is an ASUS Sabertooth 990FX with "thermal radar" fan controls built in, CPU is an AMD FX8150 "Bulldozer" octocore. Everything is mounted in a Cooler Master 932 HAF case which has 3x240mm fans factory installed. CPU cooling is provided by a Corsair H70 water cooler with Delta fans in a push/pull configuration on the radiator.

Those Delta fans can get VERY loud at full power (3500 RPM @ 100+ CFM) and that is one of the main reasons I wanted a fan controller like this. @ 2000-2200 RPM they are nearly silent. This controller is very easy to adjust to get the performance you need without noise you don't need but still ramp up the fan RPMs when you really need the cooling power. The computer has a fairly serious overclock @ 4.0 GHz with a 4.6 GHz turbo. This works great BUT the VRMs tend to overheat (not the CPU) so I had to custom mod some smaller fans. I put a fan on the VRM heatsink, the RAM, and the North Bridge heatsink. The pump for the water cooling is on the motherboard CPU header, being a pump it needs to be at max. RPM constantly, CPU temp is controlled by the radiator fans.

I have the temp sensors strategically installed to run the fans. Here's my configuration-

TEMPS (Left side of controller) Fans (Right side of controller)

North Bridge Heatsink (110 F.) North Bridge Heatsink (2700 RPM)
RAM (105 F.) RAM (2000 RPM)
VRMs (Voltage Regulator Modules) (105 F.) VRMs (2000 RPM)
South Bridge Heatsink (125 F.) Radiator PUSH (2200 RPM Delta fan)
Radiator (105 F.) Radiator PULL (2000 RPM Delta fan)

At normal 24/7 operation the temps are set so that the fans are all cooling but quiet. When the temps approach the settings noted above they begin to ramp up the fan RPMs until the temps come back down below the set temperature. For a boost of cooling I switch the controller from manual to auto which at these settings boosts fan RPMs immediately to 25% and up MORE RPMs and then continues to ramp up the RPMS as things get hotter until all the fans are at 100% and max cooling is attained. Max cooling/RPMs NEVER happens with this configuration. The CPU idles at 100 F (38 C) and will climb to no higher than 122 F (50 C) under max load stress testing with AOD and Prime95.

This fan controller is perfect for my purposes and has worked flawlessly since it was installed over a year ago on a different motherboard/cpu which was recently upgraded to the Sabertooth 990FX/FX8150 current configuration. This system is on 24/7/365 and the controller is on when the system is on. I have had no problems with mine at all functionality-wise.

The controller board that goes in the case wants to occupy a card slot but all my slots have actual cards in them so I mounted it elsewhere in the case and ran the cable out under a mounted card with a rubber grommet to keep it from chafing. Though it is meant to mount in a card slot in the back of the case it doesn't actually require a PCI slot on the motherboard, that's just how it's designed to mount and it doesn't use the motherboard at all so you can mod it to mount where ever you want to put it as long as you can run the cable to the outside of the case.

The cable is plenty long enough to reach the top of my desk with plenty of slack to spare, rolling the computer in and out from under the desk is no problem, plenty of slack.

Having the fan controller on my desk instead of mounted in the case is why I bought this particular model. ALL my external drive bays are full with card reader, 3.0 USB, external SATA drive bays and DVD burners so I didn't want to take up real estate in my case with a fan controller mounted in the 5.25 drive bays. Sitting on my desk makes it a lot easier to read than a case mounted controller, the viewing angle on a case mounted controller can require some contortions to get down where it can be read, this obviates that problem. A glance at the controller sitting in front of my keyboard is all that's needed to monitor fans and temps. And it looks VERY high tech and cool also :)

I cannot speak for the other very negative reviews of this item but for my experience this is a very good compliment to a high-end expensive computer and a great way to keep track of what those high-end expensive parts are doing temperature-wise. If I need one I wouldn't hesitate to buy another one of these based on my personal experience.

I use this monitor for digital modeling in Blender, Autodesk, and UnReal. I was using a 32" and a 27" Dell 4k monitor for my set up. For me having everything on one screen is way more convenient. The backlight has a 135 cd/m2 output and 1500000:1 contrast ratio which is great for rendering accurate highlights and Shadows. The 48GQ900-B renders more than 100% sRGB and 98% DCI-P3 again which is fantastic for rendering. The monitor is really good to go out of the box. You can tweak it a bit, I calibrated the monitor for more color accuracy, but it was very close from the factory. One thing to be aware of is the monitor has built in burn protection. The individual pixels will dim when sitting idle. It's necessary to maintain the pixels health and this feature cannot be disabled. It's a bit jarring at first because the pixel dimming is very gradual and then as you slide the mouse across the screen the area brightens up quickly. The monitor also supports both FreeSync and G-Sync so you don’t lose VRR.

Overall, this is an outstanding monitor. I don't think I could game with this monitor but that mostly due to my gaming setup. I play FPS games and sit pretty close to my 32". I was worried about taking care of an Oled monitor but with this on it takes care of itself.

title: Great twig stove with one little criticism, late delivery by Amazon
text: As all Amazon deliveries have been for at least a month, since they dropped the USPS, this one was late.  Unacceptable performance.  This is a great twig stove.  Collapses into a small package and it use it burns hot and clean. Very efficient, leaving virtually no ash or charcoal.  I've had other similar stoves, including an Ohuhu (?) brand.  That one was nicer in one respect, it had no slotted cross pieces which this one has to space the pot above the flames.  In the dark, or when moving and setting up the stove several times a day these little bits could easily be lost.  the other stove had fold-out bits to support the pot. So, nothing to lose, but the folding part was slightly weak and could be broken or mis aligned.  So it's all about equal i suppose.  Anyway, filled with small fuel and started from the top this stove is very efficient and boils water at least as fast as any little gas stove i've used.  The "bio-fuel" system of heating the ignition air really does burn nearly smoke free.  If the stove is smoking you may have over-fed it or have fuel sticking above the hot-air feed holes.  I got at least 400 burns out of my last little SS twig stove and i never took any great care to be nice to it...and eventually wore it out.  If i get 400 burns out of this one i'll be a happy guy.  In short, if you are looking for a twig stove to burn what you find on the trail or around camp give this one a try, you'll probably like it.

title: Have To Work With It, But It Works For Jewelry
text:
We have a few photo boxes in our house. I got this one so that we could set up a small one just for earrings or small jewelry. My partner had to take a year or so off, so I have had to struggle with working with this by myself.

CONSTRUCTION
This goes up quickly, but to be honest with you, I need to support the edges with some clear tape sometimes. They don't always want to stay put even if I have to move it here or there.

LIGHTING
The light works, thankfully. I am thankful also that I have a USB port in my outlet board too. The lighting looks really bright at first, but when you photograph it, it can look a bit muted. I had to do some photo editing to get decent photos.

EASE OF USE
This is not too hard to use, but it does take some work to set it up and make it stay put for jewelry. A little tape helps, and also working with the backgrounds. They don't always look smooth, so I make my own too. The jewelry I am photographing works pretty well, but higher displays will put this near the logo on the back wall. That is fine unless there is daylight hitting the box from behind, then it can show through.

QUALITY OF PHOTOS
The photos I take with this seem a bit muted, but with some photo editing, they are acceptable. I am still not at the point where I have the right combo of settings for me that I am happy with. However, I can use this and get decent photos until I find the combination of lighting and background that works well for me as a formula.

CASE
The case is nice to carry this set around and keep it in one place. It is simple, not padded, just a drawstring, but it works.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a decent little photo box. It allows me to take photos of jewelry which I want to sell, and it also provides decent light so far. I am not fond of the USB plug (without outlet) but I made it work.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS for this. It is a decent little box and I like it. I just have not found the right combination of settings that thrill me yet.

PHOTOS
I have included three photos - 1 at each lighting temperature. They are marked so you can clearly see how the color is affected by the lighting.

title: Great fit and quality
text:
I needed covers for two different remotes; as a result, I got to do a general comparison of this cover to a unit from another manufacturer that sold in pairs. While the covers from the other manufacturer were of nominal quality and fit, this one easily it in a few important areas:
1) This skin seems only slightly thicker but holds its shape and resists deformation much better. The thickness matches the button height well, and the holes also have beveled/rounded edges rather than being cut straight through. The bevels provide a nice feel; It feels much more like a single unit when it's on the remote, and it's still easy to tell where the buttons are. The other cover was easier to stretch lending to obvious stress in a few narrow spots when putting it on the remote. Once on, felt too stretchy and mobile on the remote even though it technically fit and the straight hole edges were very distracting and much higher than the buttons.
2) The hole size and the thickness/location of the area for lanyard attachment on this unit is perfect for reasonably easy threading with the cover off or on the remote. The attachment feels like it would be tough to rip out accidentally or to loosen/slip. Due to materials, the lanyard attachment pulls the attachment point evently rather than threatening to cut through the material. The attachment site on the other cover was too thin and had holes that were difficult enough to thread when off the remote; the wiry attachment loop would only take a few hours to cut through the cover.
3) the lanyard seems to be good quality. The attachment loop is not too thin or wiry, and the wrist loop is a cord with a nice feel and enough body to it to keep a nice shape without being too chunky. When attached to the remote, it is secure and structurally sound. The ribbon loop lanyard that came with the other company's cover is obviously sub-par quality, even for bulk ribbon lanyards--enough said.

Overall, I am very happy with everything about this cover. When I find one from this mfr for my other remote, I'll be getting one for it.

title: Inexpensive but Fun Filter
text:
I recently purchased a new zoom lens for my camera after I broke the old one when I took a tumble. I had filters like these for my old lens but the thread size was different so my old filters were no longer useful. I selected this filter for my new lens, somewhat apprehensively because of the relatively low asking price. It has proven to be a decent filter but it is not useful in all situations.

The idea behind this filter is light diffusion which will give an image a very slight haze or softness, depending on the lighting and subject. This is an effect that can be emulated in software during post-processing but in doing this type of enhancement I have found it is sometimes unnatural. It certainly is less fun than making it happen while shooting, which is why these types of filters are available.

In use it works, though I have had mixed results. When using it with certain light sources, the filter seems to have no real effect at all, while with others it creates a subtle, soft glow around the subject. I am still working out the situations where it is most effective. I have had similar issues with filters like these with other lenses, and as such I assume the problem is in my lack of practice with them. It will take some time and practice to make my results more consistent, and for now I lay the fault on myself.

The build quality seems to be good. I have received filters in the past where the glass rattles in the frame which is unsettling. This one is tight and there is no play between the glass and the frame. It screws on to the lens securely and is easy to clean.

The asking price is quite reasonable. I have seen these filters priced much higher, and I have also seen much cheaper ones that do not work well. The pricing seems in line with the product, if not slightly low.

I have no complaints with this filter. The issues I have with it are probably my inexperience, and I will keep working with it to improve my results. I will return here and update my review if my impression changes. For now, though, I am satisfied.

title: wonderful, useful tablet
text:
I've a tablet for entertainment purposes, but nothing really beats a laptop when it comes to some tasks (writing, creating spreadsheets, presentations, etc). So when given a chance to get a Surface Pro at a great deal, I took it - I'd heard that this was a tablet that *could* do the work of a pc, that actually belonged in the workplace. After getting it in my hands and activating the Microsoft Office 2013 package, I have to say that I wasn't mislead on this matter.

The Pro is a bit heavier and a bit thicker than most tablets (which doesn't make it THAT heavy, it's still lighter than most netbooks out there, if not all). That thickness/heft gives you the processing ability to run multiple programs and software as well as a USB port and expand memory (more memory than other tablets out there, a friend who owns an iPad was *very* envious). The touch screen is very responsive and it takes just a little bit to figure out the new system of jumping back and forth between screens/desktop, and I think the detachable keyboard is a MUST if you're going to do any serious work on the Pro (I'd recommend the Type as opposed to the Touch as it has a more tactile feel). Response time has been very good on the Pro with the programs and the system not too difficult to figure out.

All in all, it's basically a computer in a tablet, nice and (relatively) light. Perhaps it's not as thin as some other tablets, or have as many apps, but it can out-work the heck out of them, which is a lot more important to me. If you want a tablet for doing something more than playing app-based games and updating your online status, this is the one to get.

title: Great Earbuds
text:
I've been using the LG Tone Ultras for about a year now, and decided to switch to these because of the external speakers.
Sound quality is about the same, both very good. I don't listen to anything with heavy bass, so these cover my music's full frequency range very effectively.
The external speakers are like having a cell phone speaker on each shoulder - not very loud or great range, but it's nice to be able to listen to music while still hearing my surroundings; I also like to leave the external speakers on when not listening to anything for the read-out alerts.
Step counter is a cool idea but compared to my fitbit and smartwatch, it's WAAAAY off - 1200 steps vs 3700 on fitbit and 3000 on the watch, and I only take the headphones off at night.
Battery life is excellent, I can listen to music more/less all day and they're still not dead when I plug them in at night.
I've been using necklace style headphones for about 2 years, so I'm very used to them, but I find these especially comfortable. They also resist rotating better than the Ultras.
The ends aren't as long as the Ultras so relearning muscle memory (button location) took a bit, but now that I'm used to them I prefer the smaller size, they're less in-the-way.
Only thing that disappoints me is the mic - when on a call the other party can barely understand me and usually complains of muffled-sound. Just a note to LG or any other manufacturers out there: combine this with a high-end headset for calls and I'd happily pay 200-300 for it, as is I wear these and carry a headset for calls in my pocket.

I want to note that I did not experience any drops in streaming as noted by other reviewers when using this with my Samsung Note 3 phone, but did have some issues with my Samsung Tab 3 10.1. The latter has some bluetooth problems that are well known, so I am attributing my issues with Tab 3 flaws and not this headband. I briefly tested this with an HTC One Remix with no problems either.

This headband is unique in that it was designed with real, strenuous sports in mind - or at least activities that make you work up a sweat. As such I tested my streaming as noted above with my source devices (phones and tablets) at least twenty feet away. That simulates where you would place those devices during a game of tennis.

It does seem impervious to sweat, although I would not call it sweat-proof. If you use it heavily and frequently you'll need to clean it at least weekly - see some of the top rated video reviews on this page for instructions for that because it is a bit tricky disassembling it the first time.

Also note that it's a snug fit on my head, which is size 6 7/8. I am guessing that if you wear a men's hat size above 7 1/4 it will be too snug. Take that into account.

Sound quality is excellent in my opinion. For the past nine months or so (at the time of this review) all brands or phones seem to have taken a major leap in that respect and these are no exception. The high frequency response of the phones is clear at max volume and the bass is deep (but not thumping). The mid range seems to be the sweet spot, and is rich and full. The volume itself is not super loud, and it is not noise-isolating. It does keep out most ambient noise though, and while these are not perfect for critical listening they are excellent for casual listening during sports and other strenuous activities.

If you want phones that stay in place regardless of that you are doing, and also demand respectable sound quality these merit consideration. I have not researched the market, but these are the only headband phones I have come across among the dozens I have tested to date.

title: One of the true 5.1 sound bars
text:
There are many sound bars out there, and while all generally will sound better than the crap in most TVs, most will exceed only in that context. Here we have a sound bar that aims for more. For me there are two criteria I use to separate the leaders from the pack: inputs, and outputs (as in speakers).

Inputs: here you have three HDMI inputs. Since everything runs off of HDMI these days, there's no reason not to have that as the main input. Many other units rely on one or two TOSLINK inputs, which require either separate wiring from input devices or using an optical out (if any) from your TV, which often is just 2.0 (stereo). I could wish for four inputs, but three is great. Now I can run my sources (DVR, Xbox360, and HTPC) through this then to my TV. Kudos DT for getting this right.

Outputs (speakers): 9 drivers plus a legit (by sound bar standards) sub. You'd be surprised how many sound bars have 2 speakers. Granted they are an upgrade over most TVs, but the 9 here allow for real audio wizardry you just can't fake with 2. Each has ample amplification, which supposedly benefits from better crossover options due to the discrete amps. The result is all that matters, and it's very good--perhaps the best all in one sound bar solution.

Misc: the learning IR receiver (that allows you to keep using your TV, DVR, or whatever remote you like, is uber cool. The slim design and well designed mounts are also a plus.

I guess my biggest misgiving is the price, which though somewhat justified by the features, is a bit hefty. Otherwise, the is rather awesome!

title: Like Fort Knox for your iPad
text:
I bought this case to use on my 8-year-old son's iPad mini. He is not known for taking great care of his electronics and I wasn't about to spend hundreds of dollars on an iPad for him only to see it bruised or broken. I heard of Otterbox cases before, but to me they were too bulky. However, this case is perfect for my son. It is a bit difficult to separate the case to insert the iPad, but that can be a good thing too. Once inside, it isn't coming out without significant effort.

The iPad is completely encased inside. It basically has a built-in screen protector, as the front of the case is a touch-sensitive plastic. So even though you are spending a bit more on the case, you don't need to purchase a separate screen protector.

It comes with 2 main pieces: the case itself and a cover that can double as a stand. If you use the additional hard plastic cover when storing/transporting, it adds additional security, as now the iPad is completely secured, including the screen (which already has the plastic protector). So it just adds another layer of security when you aren't using the device.

The materials are "hard core". I mean, this is heavy-duty plastic that is going to hold up really well. You could use both plastic pieces to encase the iPad and you've got great protection.

If you're looking for a slim, lightweight case, look elsewhere. But if you want something that you can give to a young kid and not worry about it getting scratched, dented, damaged, etc., this is perfect and worth the money.

title: Excellent tripod
text:
My son is very much into making stop-motion videos and he spends a great deal of time working with a camera on a tripod. Before we got this particular Vanguard Abeo tripod he used a very lightweight, no-frills tripod that eventually broke. This new tripod is a huge upgrade from what he was using.

The very first thing we noticed is that this is a heavy-duty tripod that is built to last. It is very well constructed and it has some heft to it - enough heft that it would not be the best choice for carrying any appreciable distance such as on a nature hike. For moving relatively short distances, though, this tripod is a winner.

This tripod has all manner of adjustments that can be made. Aside from the length of the legs, the angle of the legs is adjustable to the point that the camera can be lowered almost to ground level without ever removing it from the base. Of course the camera angle is easily adjustable, and unlike some other tripods we have used this particular tripod has tight settings that do not slip easily.

I especially like the bubble level, a feature lacking in some other tripods on the market. It makes getting the camera straight almost foolproof.

Not being a photography expert, I am no authority on cameras and tripods but from what experience I have I can say that this Vanguard Abeo tripod is a solid piece of equipment that works well. There are cheaper and lighter tripods on the market, and for snapping pictures from a camera that requires very little adjustment those may be fine. However, it's far better to have a heavier-duty tripod when the job requires some adjustment and movement, in which capacity this particular tripod will serve admirably.

The NVME throughput was about 2x the SATA-II interface on the board, so I think that it's running at Sata-III speeds through a PCI-e 2.0 x16 slot. I was hoping for faster performance (like 10x Sata-II) but it works perfectly and it's half the price of the next competitor.

I also tested the M.2 SSD piece and it works perfectly albeit at the motherboard's speed, so Sata-II speeds. I have another Sata-II SSD in the same computer and this board apparently made better use of the interface as the M.2 SSD was about 15% faster than an Intel SSD running through the same M/B IO controller. The M.2 SSD was recognized by the legacy BIOS but the NVME was not.

I had a problem with my card at about the 5 month mark (Sata stopped working). I got in touch with the seller and asked about a warranty replacement. They replied to my message via Amazon in one business day and, after gathering my address, mailed me a replacement that arrived three days later. For a relatively inexpensive product like this, the seller quickly made good on their warranty. This is the sort of reputable company that I like to deal with. I will look for them again, next time I want to buy computer electronics. Just awesome to get this sort of support! I don't write a ton of glowing reviews, but here's one: Highly recommended.

title: This is a 480p projector with an awesome on/off design...
text:
[[VIDEOID:a1ea9dee5ef92897a45e22f1f1942100]] When it comes to mini projectors, the Nebula Capsule 2 is still the best in my book, but you'll be spending more than twice the cost of this Walnutt DLP. If money is not an obstacle, then go check that one out. Who is Walnutt? I don't know, but I think even the big boys like Anker (who makes the Nebula) would be impressed by their design. This isn't quite small as a soda can, but it's still a nifty beautiful design. You twist the top to form a shape that looks like those right angle PVC elbows, and your projector turns on. Twist it back to form a cannister, and it turns off. That is a very neat design. It doesn't seem like it's a white label product either since I can't find any similar projectors under different brands. Walnutt is the only one selling this. So kudos to them for their unique product.

Because of the built in 3200mah battery as well as a USB port, you can be completely wireless watching the fire stick, the chromecast, etc. You simply use the USB port to power the fire stick. For how long, maybe just one movie, before you need to plug in the projector power adapter, but you'll never need to find a power source for your fire stick as long as you use the USB port. However, the native resolution is 854x480. I was completely fooled by the 1080p in their product headline, when it actually said "1080p supported." That's my fault for skimming, not reading. But this means you can play 1080p, it will just be scaled down. This is a 480p projector. The speakers are 2.5 watts x 2. There are no controls, other than the focus wheel, on the projector unit. So you better make sure you never lose your remote.

At this price point, you can't ask for the world. If you want to pay double and get the Nebula Capsule 2, that thing is 720p, has a 9700mah battery, android, and has 8w speaker.. all in a soda can size body. But for all that, you're paying over double. So at the end of the day, this is a good 480p projector, at a proper price with a nifty design. I'll give this 5 stars.

My video demo is in a garage with no white screen, just the garage door material, you can see the garage door hardware. LOL! It was about 4 pm, sun was still out. I simply turned off the lights.

title: Great Picture; Lots of available adjustments; low blue light emissions; auto adjustment to light levels
text: Maybe it is just because I haven't upgraded my monitor in a long time and maybe it is because this is the biggest monitor I have ever had on a computer, but I love this monitor.  Since I spend a lot of time on the computer, this has a feature that is very important to me, which is low blue light emissions.  The blue light that comes from monitors is not good for our eyes, so a monitor that claims to reduce that is a good thing, if it really works.  I don't know how to tell for sure, but after using the monitor for several days, it does seem that I suffer less eye fatigue.  The monitor also has a "bright intelligence" button that automatically dims or brightens the screen depending on light levels, which helps reduce eye fatigue.  This feature can be turned on or off to your preference.  There a number of different light adjustments on the monitor and they are not difficult to select, once you figure out the buttons to set them.  There are 5 adjustment buttons, but none are assigned to a specific function, but there is a way to assign some of the buttons, so they are configurable to some extent.  Initially, you press any one of the buttons to bring up a five selection menu on screen that allows you to adjust brightness, depending on what you are doing (web surfing, multimedia, office or reading) as well contrast and sharpness.  There are various other display adjustments for positioning the screen (which I had to use, since the screen was initially slightly off center at the highest resolution).  Also there are adjustments buttons for sound, if you use the built-in speakers and for auto shutoff time (choice of OFF, 10, 20 and 30 minutes).  There are various other settings.  I don't quite understand all the settings, but there is an included manual on the CD that comes with the monitor and the manual seems very complete, is well written and easy to understand.  My monitor also included an HDMI cable.  I tried using HDMI, but couldn't see much difference in that and the older type of connector (which they call D-Sub, also known as VGA, which is an analog connection vs. digital).  If you are watching Blu-Ray movies, HDMI should give you a better picture.  I don't have any Blu-Ray movies, nor a DVD drive that supports Blu-Ray, so no need for HDMI.  Also, I use a KVM switch to control several computers and that doesn't support HDMI connectors.  The included CD also has any drivers you might need, but the monitor worked perfectly on Windows 10 without the need to install any drivers.  The HDMI connection did bring sound to the built-in speakers, as well as the picture, but the sound volume was extremely low, even at 100%.  When I used the other connector (D-Sub), and a separate audio cable, the sound volume was much better.  Maybe something I am setting incorrectly?  Also, typical of speakers built-in to a monitor, the sound quality is very poor.  If you listen to music much at all, you will want to stick with external speakers.  This is probably typical of all monitors with built-in speakers.  It was disappointing, but not unexpected.  The monitor is very lightweight, so it is very easy to move.  Has a nice low profile base.  Can be tipped to a desirable viewing angle, but no height adjustment.  There is a lot to this monitor and to take full advantage of it, I will need to read the manual to understand all the available settings.  Requires a 2 step assembly of the base, but it is very easy; you should be up and running in mere minutes.  This can be wall mounted, but requires a separate wall mount kit, which is not included.  Overall, a great monitor that should meet the needs of just about anyone.  With a 3-year warranty, you can't go wrong.

title: Very strong alternative in the GPS market
text:
I purchased a Delorme PN-40 GPS for the purpose of geocaching. I already own a Garmin GPSMap 60CSx and a Garmin eTrex Legend, so although I did not really need another unit I wanted one so that when geocaching with my kids we would each be carrying a GPS and not reliant on one another. I have been very satisfied with my Garmin units but was impressed with the reviews and feature set of the Delorme, so I bought it with the expectation of it being acceptable for my uses as a backup unit. It has exceeded my expectations. It is not without flaws but it is a tremendous GPS that is very much worth every penny of the purchase price.

It is very similar in hard interface layout to my 60CSx, with the same buttons doing similar functions though in different locations. This makes working with the Delorme simple in that I immediately found myself familiar with how to work this GPS. The software interface is different, though, and is unlike any other unit with which I have worked. Different is not wrong, but it means a learning curve for those who use Garmin or Magellan units.

The first power-on of this unit is the most painful as it searches for the satellites. After this initial acquisition, however, power-up is always appreciably faster and the acquisition of satellites faster.

Once the GPS has acquired the satellites, it has proven itself to be very accurate and stable. It is not unusual to navigate to a location and have the unit lead me to a point less than a foot away from the lat/long specified. Reported accuracy on the screen is typically between 6 and 11 feet.

The accuracy does diminish under heavy canopy but no more so than my Garmins do. In dense tree cover I found that it maintains its location quite well most of the time, though it occasionally gets confused and leads me in circles. It seems to do this at times when my 60CSx is having no trouble, but it also seems to have no trouble when the Garmins are confused. This brings up a good point - different GPS manufacturers, using differing chip sets, will have varying environments in which their GPS units work better than others and sometimes not as well as others. It is important to keep this in mind and to select a unit that is best suited for the need.

The compass is excellent. Once calibrated it seems to be very accurate and does not need for the unit to be held level flat when in use in order to get a correct bearing. The 3D compass is something that is lacking in my Garmin units, but newer units have this feature now and it's wonderful. Manually calibrating the compass is easy and all you have to do is to follow the instructions on the screen (it equates to a series of arm motions).

This is a rugged and sturdy unit and can handle some jostling. It does as well in wet, rainy weather as it does on clear days. It is waterproof and can be submerged, but I am not daring enough to try this voluntarily.

One point on which many people complain is the screen size. Yes, it has a smaller screen than average units but it also seems to be bright and readable even in direct sunlight. Sure, larger would be nice but clear and readable is far preferable.

Delorme ships their Topo product with this GPS and it is the deal-maker that gives this GPS a decided edge. The maps may be cut and transferred to the PN-40 through Topo, or the pre-cut maps may be used instead. To get Garmin's MapSource costs an extra $100, which makes the PN-40 an even better deal. The maps are of good quality and are sufficient for hiking and driving alike. For most uses the pre-cup maps will be sufficient, but higher resolution images can be cut from Topo.

Right out of the box, my PN-40 was defective and had problem with the screen. I was not convinced that it was a problem until I called Delorme, and I was told to ship it back. In one week's time I had a completely new unit that has worked flawlessly ever since. While I was disappointed with the first unit being defective, I was shocked at how responsive Delorme is to customer requests for assistance. It is clear to me that they stand behind their product.

Less than three weeks after I purchased my PN-40, Delorme released Topo 8. My unit shipped with Topo 7. I called Delorme and asked about an upgrade, and for the cost of shipping a new Topo 8 DVD set was sent to me.

Map updates on the PN-40 are FAST. Scrolling is not exactly smooth but the dual-core processor embedded within keeps up quite admirably.

One drawback with this unit is that, at this time, importing waypoints and geocaches requires a different software set than can be used with Garmin and Magellan units. It can be done with Topo, and for geocachers there is Cache Register, but GSAK and other common tools do not transfer successfully at this time. Hopefully this will be remedied in the near future. Granted, this is easy enough to do, but one cannot have a single software application that can work with multiple units of different brand.

Another drawback is that this GPS loves batteries. On new, fully-charged NiMH batteries one can expect maybe 10 hours of operation before the unit gracefully turns itself off. On a long trek it is therefore a good idea to bring along extra batteries. Because alkalines tend to drain more quickly in electronics, I would recommend using either NiMH or lithium batteries.

The Delorme PN-40 is a very nice GPS for consumer use. It is accurate, it holds its signal well, has a great display and comes with Topo which combined all make this unit hard to pass up. It's not perfect by any means, but it is still excellent and should be considered when looking for a good handheld GPS.

title: Superb 12' Audio Extension Cable
text:
I work with a sound mixing board that is used to connect multiple instruments and sound inputs to an amplification system. The limitation of the system is the cabling which prevents relocating certain pieces of equipment. One of the biggest trouble spots in the system happens to be audio cabling between the mixing board and the computer used to process the data. This audio cable has helped remedy that situation.

This is one of the better-made cables I have used. Instead of a cheap, plastic-coated cable made of low-gauge wire, it is instead a heavy-gauge wire insulated in a thick nylon braid. I have had bad fortune with cheaper cables as they have a bad tendency to degrade when twisted or pulled tight. Another point of failure is the connection between the plug and the cable which is usually molded plastic that is much too flexible and allows the cable to break. This cable has a metal cap that screws down over the plug and adds a lot of stiffness to the connector. This is probably one of the heaviest audio cables I have used.

This particular cable is 12' and using it as an extension in the sound system it has added a lot of flexibility to the configuration.

This is a very good audio cable. It works as it is supposed to work and it is designed to last much longer than the average cable. This is an excellent choice if you need an audio cable that will not wear out or break quickly, and at 12' there is plenty of cable for almost any use.

Disclaimer: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at no cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

title: Installation Details Revealed
text:
I'll get right to some installation details that I didn't know until I unpackaged them:

INSTALLATION: To my surprise (disclaimer: these are my first in-wall speakers), these speakers install just like an "old work" electrical box. That is, they have screws accessed from the front that have plastic flaps on the far end that tighten around already-installed drywall/plaster/plywood/other. This actually makes installation extremely easy, assuming you can access your speaker wire through your new ceiling hole. The reason I'm mentioning this, though, is it actually makes my life slightly more difficult, as I was planning to install these in an as-of-yet unfinished attic room (no ceiling, just joists) so I can listen to my Death Metal through my whole-house-audio system without moving speakers attached to terminals around as I work.

FYI, per the manual, the cutout hole needed is 9-3/8" diameter, the outer diameter of the speaker frame is 10-3/4", and the mounting depth is 3-5/8". Obviously, you'll have to find space between joists.

Note that that mounting depth may not be enough if you are planning to put these in plaster walls. Ceilings I suspect will always be okay, but plaster walls have plaster seeping behind the lathe that makes your wall cavity too shallow, assuming 2x4 studs.

INSULATION & OPTIMAL SPEAKER VOLUME: Every driver (woofer or subwoofer) has a specific interior volume (of a box) that is optimal for getting the fullest sound and best bass. I tested these speakers right out of the box and of course they lack a little fullness in sound quality that way, but as you add barriers around the back, they sound better and better (I was looking in particular for a speaker with a low frequency range since I won't have a subwoofer in this room - and the quoted 40Hz is pretty darn good for a full range speaker - especially at this price). The manufacturer recommends - too vaguely - that you push your insulation back about a foot in all directions and add insulation if you have none to make a faux speaker box in the ceiling.

For me, I spent a lot of time insulating my old house, and I don't intend to make big holes in it to negate the positive effects. Also, I don't like "winging it" when trying to get the best sound out of a pair of speakers. I intend to make a box out of 1/2" sanded plywood (which should match up with the drywall I'll use on the attic ceiling), and mount the whole box in the ceiling, covering the whole thing with insulation. This should take care of both the insulation problem (as well as my specific installation problem) and maximize sound, specifically low frequencies.

I realize that most people's situations will be a bit different than mine, but you may be able to use this info to your advantage. Note that I think the insulation problem is inherent to all in-ceiling speakers, so I'm not blaming the manufacturer. If you are installing this on the first floor in a two+ story house, you'll probably have to add insulation or a box to get any bass out of the thing.

QUALITY: My main home stereo is a higher end Sony Amp with all Infinity towers and my main car stereo is all amplified Polk speakers, so I have pretty high standards. I don't think any in-ceiling/wall solution will ever be as good as a full-on tower speaker solution, but if you're going in-wall/ceiling, I can't imagine getting as much bang for the buck. In fact, as I cannot locate anywhere where they cut corners on manufacturing costs, I am still half thinking it's too good to be true, wondering when I will find out that it really is too good to be true. Even the circuitry looks well done and the spring terminals are much nicer than I'd expect.

CON: Even before these came, I knew I was going to want to do upgrade the rest of the second-floor rooms in my house. Addicting.

Highly recommended.

Update: With installation complete, the only other CON I can think of is that now my desire to stop and headbang is greater than before, eating up more time when I should be finishing the room!

title: GREAT Value and Seller! Poor Dell support.
text:
I have been an ASUS user for many years and there are still two in the house - my wife's 15.6" and my old 13". In my search I found that Dell offered more features for dollars spent. No issues right out of the box :) The setup took just a few minutes. However, the Windows 10 Home updates along with a few hardware and BIOS update took HOURS. OK ... just have some patience. Once that was done, I ran the Dell SupportAssist which took only a few minutes. The keyboard has a nice feel and is responsive. The touchpad isn't quite as sensitive as my ASUS, but more than acceptable. There were professional reviews that the touchscreen was not up to par. I find no lack of response. The fan is very quiet and unit seems to be running very cool, an issue I had with my ASUS.

The case feels a bit "plastic" which it is of course, and has a rough texture, which if you want to skin it, you may have an issue. A nice feature is that you don't have to remove the back if you need to replace the battery. An issue with my ASUS which is one reason for a new system, - batteries lasted less than a year. Not sure what life expectancy will be here - hopefully much better. It has a fair use time of 5 hours, which with the ability to replace the battery without removing the back is a big plus if you have need to be hours without AC.

It has a more than adequate HD at 2tb, and RAM at 8gb (upgradeable). The i5 7200u processor is not the fastest on the market, but at this price point is a great value. This is not a gamers system, but I understand that it can do a fair job with many games. Keep in mind that this is a NEW unit, not a refurbished. There were a lot of refurb with less features for the same dollars and more.

The seller, Trivalley, has the best rating of any Dell and HP laptop sellers on Amazon. They were a few dollars more than other sellers, but their customer service before the sale was excellent. I contacted them 6-8 times via email with various questions which were all answered promptly and completely.

All in all ... Super pleased with the Seller, the laptop, and Amazon.

EDIT: There is an issue with warranty. The Dell SupportAssist app installed shows that the warranty expires on 12/23/1018 even though it wasn't purchased until 2/14/2018. Called Dell and they said it was an Amazon issue and to contact them to make the correction. Guess what? Amazon said it was Dell's problem. Called and Chatted (both) with Dell and they said that they would not honor the one year warranty. Reason: the warranty starts when the unit leaves the warehouse since it was on a bulk purchase. REALLY? Contacted the Amazon Seller, Trivalley and they said that they would provide the 1 year warranty. Doesn't sound like a fair deal to me, but grateful for the coverage. Dell has probably lost a future customer even though this is a very nice laptop (see review above). If there were a rating here just for Dell, I would give them a one or two.

Additionally, I contacted Dell today regarding the HD being encrypted and unable to partition. Took two chats to resolve this. No help from the first other than a phone number. Called and this tech wanted my life history before helping even though he had my system information.
He was a bit irritating and I told him I was going to hang-up and try later. I did a chat again. This chat tech was even willing to do a remote to help out. I didn't have the time for that - so the email route. I got all the information I needed and all is well.

title: Survived the wash, but I wouldn't suggest that you try it yourself!
text:
These Omidyi True Wireless Sleep Earbuds are my second pair because I accidentally threw my previous pair in the wash. Surprisingly, my original pair survived and this pair is now my backup.

Here is my original review:
These earbuds aren't bad at all, if you use earbuds to fall asleep. The advantages these earbuds have over wired ones are, of course, the wires. I used to go through wired sleep earbuds fairly quickly because I tend to pull on them quite a bit when I sleep. There are no wires to tangle here.

What makes these earbuds "sleep" earbuds are that they are much smaller than normal wireless earbuds (see my picture). They sit flush in my ears and don't protrude. In general, depending on your ears, these may actually allow you to lay sideways and still be comfortable. In my case, I can lay against my right ear without it hurting me but I can't do the same with the left. I often end up using only the right bud.

In terms of sound quality, due to their size, these earbuds will not be loud nor will they have great sound depth. The battery life also lasts about 5 hours due to their size.

I still really like these buds because I do like them more than wired ones but I don't use them any other time.

title: I would recommend it, but be aware of the time it ...
text: Bought this to go with a TP Link T8E wireless card in a new build. Set up the router according to the instructions. Did everything in order. Router would not recognize IPV6 connectivity. Went to the download site and followed the instructions for setting up IPV6 with Comcast. Nothing. Still no IPV6 recognition. Noticed two firmware upgrades available. Downloaded both. Installing them was a nightmare. The factory website only shows the progression of the download to the router. Then you sit and wait while staring at a screen that says, effectively, wait for reboot. The reboot never comes. I waited over 30 minutes for the reboot on the first update, finally just ended the connection. Did the second update the same way. Waited for the 100% on the site and ended the connection. No reboot was ever shown or witnessed on the router itself. But it finally recognized IPV6. After that was over, I checked the wired and wireless speed. With some minor tweaking of the antennae on the T8E, it shows the full 1.3GB connection. The wired speed is hovering around 214Mbps. Far faster than anything that preceded it, on any of my computers. I would recommend it, but be aware of the time it will take to set it up. title: Great for graphics
text:
I'm not a gamer. I wanted to try this mouse pad out for graphics (photo editing, vector graphics, and so forth). I'm not a big fan of pen-type tablet input devices. I've always preferred working with a mouse. (To me, the only real down side to using a mouse instead of a tablet input is loss of pressure sensitivity, but there are plenty of workarounds.)

This pad works great. An optical/laser mouse reads it very well, with the slightest movements picked up. The bottom of the pad is grippy enough for the pad to stay put, and the surface, while satin-like, still has enough resistance to provide a lot of fine control.

It's also larger than I expected. It's 11 inches by 13.5 inches. And it is quite flexible and rolls up easily for storage or transport.

Here are some tips for getting precise mouse control:

First of all understand that a low-DPI setting means your pointer doesn't move far when you move the mouse. This enables gamers to aim and target precisely in-game. It also enables artists to precisely move the pointers when working on graphics. How far your cursor/pointer moves is entirely up to you and can be adjusted in your control panel for pointer settings (or, depending on the game, possibly can be adjusted in your game settings).

In that control panel, uncheck "enhance pointer precision." This will turn off pointer acceleration, which can adversely affect control. If the software (or game) you're using overrides this (rare in graphics software, but more common in games), you may have to employ a fix. Just do a search for "Windows 7/8 mouse fix" and you'll find plenty of information on how to do this.

Anyway, it's a great pad for precision cursor control with a mouse, whether for gaming or graphics.

title: Works extremely well with Dragon NaturallySpeaking
text:
I got this recorder for one purpose only, because it is at the top of the list of compatible recorders for Dragon NaturallySpeaking. It works extremely well for that purpose.

Besides that, I like these features in general:

--It is small and light, using two AAA batteries.
--The unit comes with a USB cable and batteries, which are (rationally enough) not pre-installed in the device (to avoid potential damage from battery-acid leakage).
--When I listen to recordings I have made, rather than simply using them for Dragon voice-recognition transcription, the sound quality of the recording is exceptional.
--The unit has an LED display, which makes reading the very small screen much easier.
--There is an alarm feature, which I don't personally need, but others might.
--Much like a camera, this device has a date and time feature that you set, and it is used to date stamp all recording files.
--There are advanced features that some may want to use, which I do not, including voice-activated recording, timer-based recording, and an indexing feature to "bookmark" particular spots in a given recording.
--This device can be connected via USB cable to a laptop or desktop, and thereby move, copy, delete, or save files. These files can be emailed or transferred to other computers.
--The device itself has, internally, 2GB storage. If you want more than that, it can hold a 32GB microSD card to expand storage. This card has to be purchased separately and formatted to the unit.
--You can program the unit to automatically stop recording at either 5 minutes or 15 minutes when nothing is recording.
--You can lock the keypad.
--This recorder is useful for recording meetings or lectures, and there are specific settings for various needs, including: speech-to-text, dictation, lecture and conversation.
--There is a one-year limited warranty.

I have a few small complaints:
--I had to download a manual online on the Philips website.
--There are four preset folders, A, B, C, D, that the device automatically records in, using one folder per session. You cannot create additional folders of your own. I have to make a point to move files off the recorder after I have run them through Dragon and transcribed them so the recorder's folders don't get cluttered.
--The USB cable is very, very short. When I use it, I have to hook it to an adjunct cable to extend the length.

title: Would have been at least a 3-star without the price increase
text:
[[VIDEOID:6540c157c9d93155ffc182c5962a015e]] This is essentially the same function and value of a chalk-slate without the chalk. But what you might save on chalk you might eventually spend on batteries.

When I first got this, it was priced at less than half the current price of $23 which is why I had to drop my review to a 2 instead of a 4. It will never warrant a 5-star review in my opinion because of the quality of the drawing and the cheap, flimsy feel of the plastic. If you're looking for something to replace paper and get a lot of other extras, check out Remarkable™. Pass on this unless there's a coupon or price drop.

The on/off switch is confusing and there's no manual to explain. I thought mine was broken because no matter the position of the on/off switch, you can still make markings on the screen with any object that is pointy enough to trigger the pressure sensitive LCD. There's a tiny hint on the packaging. The on/off switch actually is used to enable or disable the delete button -- which clears the screen. If you don't want to accidentally erase your masterpiece, set the switch to "OFF" and the delete button won't delete your work if you accidentally hit it.

The stylus included is awkward and shaped like a plastic popsicle-stick. A popsicle stick would also work.

One issue is that normal writing pressure creates very thick lines that are about 3 times the size of the point that you use to write with. To make a thin line, you can use the stylus and apply almost zero downward pressure, but that's not how most people write with pen and paper.

There's a huge brand-name up in the top corner that seems obtrusive and unnecessary. It could have been four font-sizes smaller and still have been fine.

Overall, because of the big price increase and the poor quality of the material and the single color along with the inconsistent thickness of the lines, this is only a 2-star review right now. If the price drops back to the original $11, then it might be a 3 or 4 stars for use as a scratch-paper alternative. But at the current price of $23, it's not worth it and I can only give it 2-stars.

title: Reliably steps up voltage to desired output

The power delivery is relatively clean, I have some flicker on the LED strip, but that seems to resolve itself fairly rapidly - for sensitive applications you might want to run through a capacitor to clean things up a bit.

The unit is moderately efficient, but becomes quite warm - when converting from 2xAAA Lithium batteries (3v) to 12v, with an approximate draw of 200mA the converter (both the top of the transformer and bottom of the board) temps at about 116F within three minutes or so of operation. Pretty warm, warmer than I would typically like. I might try hooking up a 9v instead to see if this knocks the temps down a bit, or if that fails, adding a thermistor to mitigate the risk of a thermal event.

Would recommend for general experimentation though.

text:
I have a Chromebook that I use for business. That means that I have a few small spiral notebooks I need to keep with it and some paperwork. The problem is that I store it in a small area. When I saw this, I was hoping for the best. I got it!

FABRIC
The fabric on this bag is fantastic. It is very heavy duty and repels water too. the gray color makes it much easier to find than black.

INSIDE
The inside has two padded sections- one for the Chromebook and one for the pad. Both fit perfectly. These pockets have a tab that closes on them to hold the pieces in place. They are well padded too. My Chromebook is a 14 inch one and it fits perfectly.

OTHER STORAGE
In between the two side areas of the inside which holds the tablet and the Chromebook, there is a storage area that I can put my spiral notebook and papers on.

FRONT POCKET
The front pocket has pleats in it so it will hold cords, etc. It also has two small compartments that will hold a cell phone and pens, pencils, etc.

FOOTPRINT
What I love about this is that it is slim in profile. I can fit what I need in it, but it will slide onto a bookshelf, or in a slim spot that I need to put it into. This is perfect for me. My other bag was too bulky.

SHOULDER STRAP
The shoulder strap is nicely padded and adjustable.

HANDLES
The handles are covered in faux leather and are easy to grip and comfortable too. The bright tan color is a plus- it helps me find the bag when I need it quickly in a pile of things!

ZIPPER
I am mentioning these because they are unique zippers. The top zipper closes itself in with the zipper tape in a sort of invisible zipper fashion but it is a big heavy duty zipper. The front pocket zipper appears to be waterproof. It closes underneath a rubberized tape. It looks water resistant at least when closed.

DOES IT STAND UP ON ITS OWN?
Because it is so slim, it does not stand up on its own, but most of my cases don't.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is the perfect bag for my business Chromebook and materials. I love that it is slim yet holds what I need it to. The color is great and the fabric does seem to have water repellent goal in mind.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. I am so very happy with this. It really love it.

title: Impressive
text:
After 40-some years on the technical side of electrochemical fabrication (12" wafer fab) and manufacturing that included the IBM PS1 & PS2 birth … cleanliness is Godliness. I've likely tried every chemical variant of cleaner ever invented, though many fewer are now permitted for USA use.

Though impractical for the laptop, some excellent cleaners in the $1000/gal category might be suggested for cleansing strategic missile-related monitors and surfaces. The value and reliability of what device you are cleaning is the most critical consideration when choosing a cleaner. A wrong choice might pay back immediately with bad results, dissolving the anti-reflective coating or lamination of the touch screen overlay, removing specialized keyboard paints, ruining distinctive finishes, etc. For another, that same choice might do a bang-up job on the big screen at home, but when used on a laptop, it slowly dissolves and/or corrodes critical interconnects as you pass through dewpoints on that 17-hour airplane ride to Sydney.

Q: What is the best cleaner to shine on my $1500 laptop?

A: Not the cheapest $4/qt cleaner. Not one of grandma's window elixirs.

Behind the scenes, there is likely no other technical discussion as critical as cleaning and cleaners. Billions are spent every year on the problem. What I know from experience is that an alcohol solvent-based cleaner does a pretty good job erasing the symbology that makes my lighted keyboard legible. I look for a cleaner to remove the latent crusty-goo residue left by that anti-viral covid computer cleaner six months ago. Some cleaners with notionally benign saponifiers that sell under the enviro-friendly, "Green!", "non-GMO!" moniker is known to corrode solder joints and electro-plating to short the keyboard and LCD/OLED out.

Finding the right balance between solvent and saponifiers has not evolved smoothly. Saponifiers remove organics. The stuff that sprays out of your mouth and nose when yelling at the laptop. Solvents remove inorganics like hand cream, french fry grease, and Cheeto dust. I've rolled up all of this wisdom in my 'Rule #446 - Do not buy the cheapest electronics cleaner. Ever.'

This Monster cleaner is not cheap. It's a premium cleaner under a known premium brand. Given Monster brands, cleaning processes are the #1 priority for their established long-lived high-fidelity interconnection. My laptop has a touch screen that demands a non-delaminating cleaner and a lighted keyboard with that funky paint and laser-etched symbology. This Monster cleaner did an unexpectedly quick, no-smudge job on the laptop. All is good.
