title: Love this case - exactly what I wanted.
text:
This case is exactly what I wanted: extremely durable shock-absorbing (read: drop-proof) protection without screen protection. Let me qualify that statement: I did *not* want screen protection. I love the pearl eink display on my graphite Kindle Keyboard, and it now has a big brother. I do not want a screen cover, as this would greatly reduce the screen's otherwise remarkable clarity, adding unwanted elements such as bubbles, surface scratches, and glare to the mix--no thank you. There is a reason I disliked reading on the iPad so much I gave it back (very reflective!). In fact, this OtterBox defender case came with a stick-on screen protector--no way. It would ruin that big, glorious pearl eink display.

A screen cover serves no purpose once you remove the device from your backpack/messenger/tote/briefcase for use. Assuming you transport your Kindle device safely in an appropriate sleeve (you put your other expensive electronic equipment--your laptop/tablet in one; your Kindle deserves the same amount of respect), the screen protector is completely unnecessary--the sleeve protects the screen during travel. THAT is when the screen needs protecting--when you are not using it, from the other goodies in your messenger bag/backpack (keys, pens, earbuds, and anything else rattling around in there). Yes, that's right--I'm talking about a Kindle in an Otterbox Inside a sleeve inside your briefcase. ...Inception-level protection. You got it. Better safe than sorry, right? What if they once again stop producing our beloved Kindle DX and something happens to yours? I do not want to have to replace my DX--especially if it has to be with a Fire device (5% the battery life, reflective, heavy, expensive--no thanks!). When you are holding your Kindle in your hand, reading, a screen cover only detracts from the experience.

What you see in my pictures is exactly what you get: a beefy, black rubber (not silicone--too easily torn; rubber is much stronger) form-fitting sleeve with an equally form-fitting outer plastic shell. Science geeks like me understand how this works, and just in case you are not one, here is the idea: if you drop your device onto the floor, the outer shell absorbs some of the impact energy generated by the device hitting the floor. It then disburses the remaining energy of the impact broadly into the rubber inner lining. The rubber lining then in turn disburses the now greatly-reduced impact energy into the device. In other words, by the time the force of the impact is filtered through two layers of protection, the second of which is very absorbent and resilient (rubber) the device inside absorbs little if anything of the original impact.

I feel very good about having my Kindle DX in an Otterbox Commuter. If I ever had one of those incredibly poorly-designed (read: seriously fragile) apple devices, such as an iPad or iPhone (which I do not, and am not ever likely to), it too would live in an OtterBox Commuter case. OtterBox = the best protection a device can get. I paid $18 including shipping for this. A great price, and worth much more in terms of peace of mind.

title: Perfect for Amazon Fire TV Centric homes
text:
I have an Amazon Fire TV stick on all three televisions in my house. When I decided to cut the cable, I started looking for solutions to get OTA (antenna) signal to all of my TVs. I had the cables from Cable TV already in place, so I ran the Antenna cable through those. That is a solution if you have good signal from the antenna and a powered amplifier so a 3 way splitter isn't needed because the splitter eats signal. and it is kind of clunky to have to change the TV input from the Fire TV Stick to the antenna input every time I wanted to switch between streaming and local channels.

I am still working on improving my antenna and have a powered amp on the way. But The Fire TV recast removed the need for more than one cable from the antenna, which plugs into the recast. The recast sends the signal to my 3 Fire TV sticks via wifi and integrates the OTA channels into the Fire Stick Menu and it works flawless across my three TVs.

There may be better solutions for other streaming devices like Roku, but for a Fire TV home, this is the answer. Plus its a DVR. Even better. No need for an external hard drive unless you plan on recording and storing tons of programing. But as I understand it, you can plug in an external Hard Drive if you wish.

It is super easy to set up. All you need is some way to download the Fire TV app; phone, tablet etc, that is connected to your home network. I used my iphone.

Highly recommend for any cord cutting Amazon Fire TV households.

title: Amazing Keyboard Cover
text:
This is the best keyboard I have found for the iPad, and I've used a lot of them. In terms of the usability and comfort of the keyboard itself, the quality is simply unmatched. My last keyboard had flimsy keys and would sometimes type 2 or 3 letters with one keystroke, while other keys didn't seem to work at all. This one is exactly the opposite - it feels great to type on even if it's a little undersized, and all the keys are exactly where you'd expect them to be. Having two shift keys is also quite nice, that's one of my main gripes with every other iPad keyboard.

The cover feature is also very good, though the hinge magnet does seem a little bit less "snappy" than the smart cover. It works fine, but it just seems a little bit lower quality. When closed, it blends perfectly with the iPad itself and creates a seamless brushed metal case all the way around, aside from the two ends of the slot that the iPad fits into during use. It is slightly thicker than the iPad 2. One thing this product has over many other keyboard covers is that you can use portrait mode, though as stated in other reviews, that position is not quite as steady as the magnet in the holding slot does not work in portrait orientation.

The battery life is also quite impressive. The manual claims 6 months (2 hrs/day usage) on a single charge. I can attest to that since I've had it for several months and have yet to charge it a second time (although I use it probably an hour a day, if that).

The last point is the price. Having used it, I'm confident it's a good buy. Might be a bit on the expensive side, but you're getting your money's worth - it does not seem rinky-dink like a lot of these other keyboards. This is clearly a professional, high-quality product.

For me it's turned typing on the iPad from a headache/nightmare into, basically, using a normal keyboard. I've seen a couple other reviews that complained about the protective edges getting in the way, but I keep my wrists up when I type so it's not a problem for me. The only thing I miss from a normal keyboard is a delete button (the 'delete' on this keyboard is backspace) and the home/end keys. There may be a way to do those, but I haven't used it long enough to find out.

I'm a software developer with roughly 10 years of solid typing experience, and this is not just a great iPad keyboard, but in itself a very nice keyboard, period. I wouldn't mind having to use it on a normal computer. Overall, it's simply amazing. I typed this entire review with it and had no problems whatsoever. I highly recommend it.

title: Precise, but has a learning curve
text:
I received a review sample and after I got this up and running there was a slight learning curve before it felt natural. After I did become accustomed to it, going back to a regular mouse was a slight letdown.

While the instructions are a bit terse I am still giving this four stars because it's easy to set up. The subtracted star is for lack of clear explanations in the quick start guide for how to precharge the unit or even for explaining that the retractable USB cable that ships with it is only for charging and will not connect the mouse interface to the host system.

This mouse operates wirelessly via an included dongle. My old ThinkPad running Windows XP immediately recognized the dongle when I plugged it in, and the mouse as soon as I inserted the included battery and charged it up.

Once I became comfortable with the mouse I found that it was a lot more precise for graphics applications and games than a regular mouse. Note that the base is fixed to the pen-style handle. You move it as though it's a pen affixed to a sled. After you become accustomed to the buttons and the wheel placement you will be using this like a pro.

There is a LED on the top of the unit that shows the charging state. Once that light turns green you can disconnect the USB charging cable. I initially did not like this feature, but have grown to love it because the battery is rechargeable. Other wireless mice I have used in the past seemed to have a voracious appetite for batteries, so plus one for the rechargeable feature.

Bottom line: this is an excellent mouse that is less stressful than using a normal one. Set-up is a bit confusing, but if you have issues leave questions in a comment to this review and I will answer them to the best of my ability. If the company redesigns the documentation to make it clear to complete novices this would be a five star product.

title: Good concept, but bizarre bugs
text:
I've tried a similar box to this one, I'm familiar with the concept and I really REALLY wanted to like it. But sadly, it needs some more quality control.
I've always loved the idea of a Android powered head unit, I've seen aftermarket ones sold for popular car models, and I was hoping this would give me that functionality without having to replace my radio. But sadly, I can't use this.
For starters, it takes a long time to boot. That means you are first going to be greeted with your car's normal radio display, connected to my phone over bluetooth, and then once I've already pulled out of my driveway and started down the road, THEN it finally shows up on my display.
That is, if it displays at all. It seems to do this thing in which is boots up, checks for display info, then reboots in the proper resolution. The instructions even imply it does this. The problem is, most of the time my carplay radio will freeze up when it does this. Not only will it get stuck and not display anything, but my radio locks up and MY TIME RESETS. It's the strangest thing. After looking at reviews here, it seems at least one other reviewer said it make his car radio go crazy, so I don't really understand what this thing is doing that might cause that, but at least it isn't just me!
And even when it DOES work, it has a similar problem to other Android-powered adapters like this: it is a cold boot every time, with no idea what the time/date is. This is a major issue because if I don't supply an internet connection, the mini computer in this reverts to the wrong date/time on the display which is SUPER annoying. Ideally, they should design this to have a small battery to "sleep" like a phone, so it can retain time/date function and wake up faster than a complete boot. The way this is designed right now is really a subpar experience, assuming you can get it to boot up at all on your system.

title: Excellent Cables at a Great Price
text:
I have a good tangle of cables in my home office for a variety of devices that require a micro-USB cable. Most of these cables are very nondescript and I have no idea who made them, though there are a couple of them that have manufacturer names printed on the plugs on the end. Most are plain black and are mostly indistinguishable from one another. These cables from Magic-T are absolutely the most easily identifiable cables on the desk and it has made it very easy to assign cables to every device on the desk. But, there is more to these cables than just pretty colors.

The most obvious advantage of this cable set is the colors. Each of these cables is a different color and none of them are black or gray - there’s blue, pink, orange and green. And, even more important than the color is the fact that they are insulated in nylon weave, not plastic coating, which in my experience holds up a bit better under stress and the result is a more reliable cable.

The plugs on both ends are metal shielding with a plastic base, sufficient to give these strength for the connections. The cables have been inserted in the bases and attached within, not attached to the plug base, but those connections are very tight and seem to be solid so I am not concerned about them pulling loose.

Each cable is about six and a half feet in length which is much more convenient for me than the regular 3' cables.

These cables are capable of high-speed charging so if you have a device and a charger that are both capable of high-speed charging then these cables will work well for you. I used one for my tablet and a high-speed USB charger and the tablet did charge faster than when using a lower-grade cable.

I want to mention the pricing. As I write this, the price on this set of four cables is about $9. That’s about $2.25 per cable, and the cables are of good quality. The price can change of course, but at the current price this is an absolute bargain.

There’s something else I need to mention. The manufacturer offers a 12-month warranty on these cables, and to me that’s just amazing. For a cable that costs less than $2.50 per individual cable the manufacturer thinks enough of their product to back it with a 12-month warranty. I doubt I would ever need to use the warranty for one of these, but it’s reassuring to know the manufacturer believes in their products.

It is hard to find fault with these cables. They are made well, they are easily identifiable and they are very inexpensive. This is a fine set at a great price.

text:
Black Friday sales have brought the Echo Dot to under $30, and that is how I am now buying my second one.

So yes, often times you do need to formulate your requests in a certain way (for instance, try asking Alexa how much time it will take to go to work... I gave up on this...) and enunciate them more clearly if you missed, but in general, this technology is just amazing.
Sometimes I even ask Alexa for information I don't need, just for fun.

I like that they named it Alexa. That's so much better than "Okay Google." It feels like a real person. Who in hell at Google thought it's a good idea to force users to use their company name, and thus remind them that their huge creepy analytics private data gathering network is behind it?

Possible improvements:
* Bring back the matte finish from 1st gen. I shouldn't have to pay more to not have it shiny...
* Listen to the word "stop" when the alarm is ringing. Currently you need to wait until it's not ringing and then say "Alexa, stop."
* Add confirmation and modification prompts to "Add a new event to the calendar." Currently if she misunderstood one word, you have to start all over again.
* Alexa bluntly tells you that she cannot tell you about the events in your calendar on a specific date... C'mon guys...
* Implement the word "Repeat": sometimes you didn't hear or didn't catch the information you were looking for, and currently you have to formulate your request again
* Only gives info about the last Amazon order. She can retrieve more order but you have to be very specific about what they contain.
* I wish Alexa could Google more stuff.
* Choose your own wake up word

I never use Siri on my iPhone, but for some reason it feels very natural to use Alexa, maybe because the device is more "fixed" whereas my phone could be in a backpack, in the other room...

The Killer App is MUSIC. We have an Echo Dot in the bedroom, and my wife just loves to ask Alexa for tunes. We have it linked to Spotify.

Also, I am a software engineer, and I have added some custom features through my own skills. I wish somebody came up with something simple to add your own skills, because this is really useful. For instance, the bus comes in front of my house at the most random times, so I developed a skill that tells me in how many minutes the next buses will come. title: Huge improvement in 4K HDR image
text:
Panasonic DP-UB9000P1K Reference Class 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray Player with HDR10+ and Dolby Vision Playback

This has replaced my OPPO 203 for one reason, the HDR Optimizer for my OLED TV. It preserves the entire HDR dynamic tonal range and 100% of the color volume on low peak luminance level displays. Projectors and OLED tv's will see the biggest improvements over the OPPO. The "UB9000 correctly sends along static HDR metadata to your display. Many players out there still don't support this feature." From HomeTheaterReview. This means it can accurately recreate the light levels, black levels and peak luminance based on this mastering metadata. This has been a huge improvement when watching 4K HDR content. You can read about all of the connectors and XLR outputs in the product description. If you use those connections, then you know what you are looking for.

The downsides:
The Panasonic UB9000 does not play region free discs like the OPPO's did. There's no support for SACD or DVD-Audio disc playback. I haven't really found myself going back to my old Region Free movies or old DVD audio discs over the last few years so this is not an issue for me.

Basically, I have nothing negative to say. It's been a positive experience using this player and the old OPPO has been sold.

title: Great sounding wireless headphones...
text:
I'm a musician with a home studio. With several sets of headphones all getting old, I decided to invest in some new ones. I've had good luck with Sennheiser in the past so I wanted to check out what they were currently offering. After reading lots of reviews, I decided to give these rs175 rf's a try. I was a little leery of them being wireless but trusting in the Sennheiser name, bought them anyway. I wanted them for general recording and playback.

Pros: Excellent sound... flat, uncolored. Clear detailed, etc. All the qualities I've come to expect from Sennheiser. Wireless setup was virtually nothing... plug in the base where you'd plug in the headphones and you're done. Turn on the headphones and start listening. The stand serves as the charging station and placing the headphones on it is straightforward and secure... not clumsy at all. I have a fairly large head with proportional sized ears... (size xxl hat). The ear pads fit completely over my ears and completely seal very nicely around them. You won't be bothered by outside sounds, nor will your spouse be bothered by what you're listening to. A quick check of the range shows I can go anywhere in my average size home without losing the signal. (I didn't try going outside).

Cons: The only negative is that there is a bit of latency. If you use them for listening to music or even tv, you won't notice it... but if you turn on speakers at the same time and listen to both, you'll notice a very slight lag in the headphones.

Bottom line: these are excellent headphones, quality of build and quality of sound are both first rate. But if that latency is an issue, you probably shouldn't be looking at wireless anyway (I suspect this occurs on any wireless system).

title: Absolutely perfect for my office
text:
This is a fantastic emergency radio with lots of great features. I had been going between this and another. Glad I decided on this one. For the price you get a LOT of bang for your buck.

This features two flashlights - one at the end, one under the solar panel. While neither are exactly the brightest, they do provide enough light to make this useful. The one under the solar panel is activated as soon as you lift the panel.

There are three ways to keep the device charged: USB, Solar, and Crank. USB is obviously the easiest. Accepts charge from the outlet or from a battery pack. The solar charger does work, but is extremely slow. In a situation where you needed to use the device and keep it running, solar would work...just don't expect to charge it in one sitting. The crank actually does a decent job. On a dead battery, you can crank for about a minute and get ten to fifteen minutes of light. If you crank for about five minutes you can get about five minutes of the radio on low volume. It's effective, but you're not going to want to charge the battery this way. Haha

This covers AM, FM, NOAA, and BLUETOOTH! That was the main selling point for me is to have this as a small Bluetooth speaker in my office. It works great, connects quickly, and sounds very good. It's not going to beat a fancy home stereo in terms of loudness or sound clarity, but for a tiny emergency radio it is perfect.

This radio is worth it just as a Bluetooth speaker. It's loud enough to fill a room and is well sealed and rugged to keep on the back porch or by the pool. The locking carabiner to attach to my backpack is also a nice touch. A little rain or water isn't going to hurt it.

This is possibly my favorite emergency radio I've owned. No complaints.

title: USB C adapter defective, horrible customer service, tablet OK
text:
UPDATE Jan 20, 2021: I contacted HUION (their customer service appears to be in China) about the defective USB C adapter and send them a video at their request showing it did not fit into the USB C port on my laptop. They then asked if it fit my phone and I said it did not. After going back and forth (their replies are not all that quick) they finally said they would send a new adapter with a tracking number. Then around 2 weeks later after saying they would be sending a new adapter, they said would not send a new adapter because it was only for phones which is ridiculous. If I owned a MAC, which I am switching to later, how would I plug it in without a USB C adapter since they only have USB C plugs? My request has been going for around a month just to replace a defective adapter and after promising to send the adapter they have gone back on their word. Forget it, I have decided to return this tablet. Makes me wonder if they would honor their warranty if something went wrong with the tablet and how long this tablet will last if the adapter is defective right out of the box. I did not test the mini USB adapter. I have also found the mouse functions a bit sticky on the one I received. The tilt function also wasn't so great. Overall the tablet itself has some flaws but works okay. I think next time around I'll try X-Pen or maybe I'll go back to Wacom.

ORIGINAL: I have just received this tablet. I'm on a Dell XPS with Windows 10 Pro. I didn't realize this was marked as a 2019 tablet, not that it's a big deal. I got an extra $10 on Amazon so I was able to get this tablet for around $58 not including the tax. The box is great, sturdy with padding in the cover and molded plastic to hold all the parts. I downloaded the drivers and full manual from the Huion website. I followed the instructions and removed my Wacom tablet drivers before installing the Huion drivers and using the tablet. Huion software is easy to use to set keys and preferences.

What was not so good was the USB-to-USB C adapter does not work and doesn't fit properly in the USB C port in my laptop or phone. I am not sure about the mini-USB adapter as I don't have anything to use that with. If you need a working adapter just be aware the one I received was defective. Some complained about the pen. I prefer the lightweight pen included as I feel it's easier on my small hands. text:
Regarding the Linksys AC2600 4 x 4 MU-MIMO Dual-Band Gigabit Router with USB 3.0 and eSATA (EA8500) -- this is by far, the easiest to set-up router I've ever used.

What I love about it:
* Multiple networks. You've got a 2.4 GHz one (good if you live in a huge house) and a 5.0 GHz one, as well as one for guests.

* Four data streams. My previous one (a TP-Link -- a fine device, but simply hasn't the firepower) had two. Two is an industry standard.

I'm using it to the hilt. Two smart phones, two laptops, and TV running Netflix at the moment. All are quick enough. What's more: I'm doing all of this only on DSL. Cool, huh?

Note: This is just a router, not a router-modem.

I fully recommend the Linksys AC2600. Sure, mine came as a result of a review program sponsored by Amazon, but I'm extremely happy to have this.

title: This is the 24" you've been waiting for..
text:
This is the first high quality 24" I have seen for under $500. Yes, this is one of the new 24" TN (twisted neumatic) panels, but don't let that dissuade you. The 22" TN panels have gotten a bad rap due to their poor performance, most of them have issues with bad color banding and lots of light bleeding at the edges. I should know as I have owned several 22" TN panels (mostly Viewsonic VX2235WM).

This 24" TN panel is far and away superior to any previous TN panels I have seen, it is almost laughable how bad my old 22" TN panel looks up next to this one. I would challenge you to put this 24" TN up against any of the more expensive 24" IPS or S-PVA panels and see the difference for yourself, I doubt you will be able to tell which is which unless you are using a specialized image for gamut testing or you are a graphic designer with an extremely keen eye.

The only downsides that some people may find with this monitor compared to other (usually more expensive) 24" panels are: less inputs, no portrait mode. This monitor only has VGA and DVI(+hdcp) inputs, no component or hdmi, this is not really an issue if you are using it as a computer monitor but may turn off some people who wish to hook up other media devices. Also there is no portrait mode like the other 24" samsung 244T series; however, the stand on this monitor is still extremely high quality and height adjustable.

I would very highly recommend this LCD, better yet, I'd recommend 2 or 3. Why buy a 30" when you could have 3 of these for the same price?!

title: Most silent drive I have ever owned!
text:
I purchased this as a data storage/backup drive for my desktop PC. My main drive is a1TB NVME drive. The data drive I use for movies, songs, and backups and digital images. Since I am not booting with the drive I don't care about raw performance, nor will I pay for it. With that said I am VERY happy with this drive. It only spins at 5400 RPM, so the access time is slightly slower, but it makes no difference to me. Maximum transfer rate is nearly 200MB/sec. High capacity drives have dense platters and are able to pull data faster.

I am a Nazi for eliminating extraneous sound and used to keep my drives inside enclosures to reduce sound. My quietest drive to date is the Samsung HD 503HI, and this is even quieter. I have several large case fans spinning slowly and if I turn them off I can ever so slightly hear a faint humming or click, but otherwise I hear NOTHING.

This is my first WD drive (have always used Samsung). I cannot speak to the drive's reliability as I've only had it for one month. It is labeled for "Surveillance," so if it's meant to be running 24/7- 365 it is meant to get use in commercial/industrial environments.

I think everyone with a desktop PC should adopt this system. It is very easy to backup anything important- save it to your C: drive as well as your backup E: drive or whatever. If one your main drive goes kaput you have the backup to pull your saved data from. You can use flash drives for additional redundancy and portability, but in my experience they are not so reliable.

title: The best camera is the one you have with you
text:
I was not happy with my "little" camera: just not enough image quality. I like to use my Nikon D700/24-70mm and some prime lenses as well as a medium format camera (film + scans) - so it is not easy to live with the smaller formats. After looking at consumer DSLRs like the Nikon d5000, I would still be stuck with a too-large camera for all-day carrying around.

The GF-1 with the micro 4/3s format just met my criteria and it hasn't disappointed me. It is smaller but has a lot of features that permit manual control when needed. The 20mm lens is really nice: small and sharp. I have spent a week playing with it, using it and messing around with Silkypix RAW converter software. I use 64 bit Windows so I had to spring for version 4 which cost me $149. In addition, like all cameras using LCDs, the GF-1 was not very useful in bright sunlight so I had to spring for the accessory viewfinder - another $159 (Amazon). All in all it added up to a bit of change, but I am not reqretting it. I am excited to be able to carry a camera around. Frankly, the D700, even with a small prime is just too big to lug around on long trips. Theft is also a concern.

As to the RAW converter, Silkypix, it seems to work well but takes a bit of work to figure it out. I has a number of controls. If I used Photoshop with its Adobe Camera Raw (ACR) converter, then things might be easier. For now I still use Nikon's NX2 software for editing, which I feel very confortable using so I'll stick with Silkypix and TIFF files from that software.

All in all, I recommend this camera. It is a bit pricey for a travel camera but I definitly preferred it to the Oympus E-PL1 or the E-P1/2.

title: Exactly What Our Family Needed
text:
I live in a family compound which is an old house divided up into several apartments. What makes these walkie talkies useful on a daily basis is the water situation in the compound. All the apartments are connected to the cold water line and a couple of the apartments share a hot water line. That means if you are taking a shower and anyone anywhere in the house turns on a cold water tap, not only will your shower lose water pressure but the cold water flow will abruptly decrease, leaving the hot water hotter than ever. For the apartments that share a hot water line, the same kind of thing happens. Suddenly you are taking a cold shower in a a trickle of water. These walkie talkies have solved that problem. With the group call button you can let the whole house know you are going to take a shower so no one will use any water till you call in that you are done.

Nor is that their only use. Several times a year our town will get a tornado alert. Should a tornado actually appear in our area, the whole family will head down to the storm shelter behind the basement apartment. With the walkie talkies we can make sure everyone got the emergency alert and knows that they need to be ready to move fast if the sirens go off.

One our family members has been sick the last couple of days and these units were in an easy way to check in on her throughout the day to see if there was anything she needed. By assigning each apartment its own channel and having everyone on the same group channel, it is easy to call one apartment or to reach them all, whichever is appropriate for a given message.

The units are easy to use and even our least techie family member quickly got the hang of it. The sound is clear even when calling from apartment to apartment. There is a flashlight function that is fairly bright, one that will come in handy in case of emergency. All in all, our whole family is well satisfied with this product and it deserves a 5 star rating.

title: A simple yet rather useful adapter (no electronics--just a form factor change)
text:
This is a relatively basic yet rather useful gizmo. Basically it allows you to use SATA M.2 cards in a 3.5" internal bay (like you use for a HD). There's no controller or really any logic--just an adapter. As such, even StarTech skeptics should be able to buy this without fear (note that various products are bundled in this review section, and I'm referring to the StarTech.com 4x M.2 Mounting Adapter for 3.5-Inch Drive Bay).

The box was rather hefty, and in side was a well made adapter and all needed cables. Depending on your situation, you may not need all 4 slots (or have that many free SATA connections), and you can use them as needed. I found this useful as I'm replacing older Samsung 850 EVO m.2 drives using SATA with newer (and zippier) NVMe drives from Intel and Toshiba. Thus my "older" (yet still darn fast drives) can still be used for other purposes in here. Depending on your case, you may want or need heatsinks on your drives (they can throttle when hot) and they can fit in this enclosure.

Do note that this is not a SATA controller, nor will it convert PCIe based drives to SATA. It's just a "dumb" adapter, but it's a rather useful one.

title: Dreamy macro, versatile.
text:
Although this lens is intended for macro photography, it's also a great lens for general purpose shots, or portrait shots. The lens produces beautiful sharp images and is a fast, accurate focuser. The lens is moderately heavy and bulky, so I wouldn't classify it as eminently carryable, and without image stabilization, you might suffer hand shake blur if you're not shooting at the wide end; at smaller apertures, using it with a tripod is highly recommended. But if you're buying it primarily to get into macro this shouldn't much matter as tripod shooting with macro is virtually a necessity, and completely expected.

The 100mm focal length is a nice compromise when you want to get close to small subjects (particularly insects) but are limited to how close you can get before scaring the subject off - as a comparison with the 180mm macro, you would want to factor in a consideration as to what you might like to shoot most of the time - big spiders that you'd rather stay well away from might be an application more suited to the 180mm, for instance, but if you are keen to shoot mostly flowers, the 180 might be more length than you really need.

In short, the 100mm macro is one of my "keeper" lenses, a real performer.

title: You will need a HDMI splitter....
text:
THINGS YOU WILL NEED:
----------------------------
-HDMI Splitter that can bypass HDCP (For digital caputuring. What device isn't digital nowadays?)
-Flash drive or Hard Drive: Maximum flash drive space is 256gb. Maximum hard drive is 8tb.

As a kid, I used to love recording tv or cable to VHS. Then in the late 90's and early 2000's, I was into those Hard Drive recorders with built in dvd-r burners by Pioneer and Philips, remember those? But then Tivo and Cable DVR really took off and made recording to actual dvds a thing of the past. So what we have here with the ClearClick is simply a device that brings the "old way" of archiving to 2020, but instead of VHS and DVR-Rs, it will record as MP4 files into your flash drive. I also think the reason these devices are still relevant is due to the phenomenon of gamers who love to record all their game-play. Anyway, I'm happy to report it does exactly what it advertises brilliantly. However, unless you're only capturing analog signals (VHS transers), you will need a HDMI splitter that can bypass HDCP. In my use case scenario... I have a Caavo Universal Remote/HDMI Switcher. The Caavo has four HDMI inputs. I have my Tivo, a Fire TV, a Android TV box, and the Nintendo Switch hooked to it. Then it has one HDMI output. This output normally goes to the TV. So that's my set-up...

Now to hook up this ClearClick, I remove the HDMI that connects to the TV from the Caavo, and instead, I connect it to the Input of the special HDMI Splitter. Then HDMI OUT from this splitter to the input of the ClearClick. Finally, HDMI OUT from the ClearClick to an input on my TV. This way, I can capture from any device I want that's connected to my Caavo. Of course, you can just connect one source at a time too if you don't have a hub like I do. But remember, you need to connect your source to the HDMI splitter first. If you don't, you will just get a black screen that says "unsupported format." One more thing, the HDMI splitter obviously has 2 HDMI outs, one of which is going to the ClearClick. I also use the second HDMI out to connect directly to another input on my TV. The reason is to avoid having to turn on the ClearClick when I'm not recording.

The spliiter I use is called the ViewHD Model: VHD-1X2MN3D. You can find this on Amazon. However, I believe it is still YMMV (your mileage may vary.) I bought that years ago and it still works. But if you search in the reviews for that splliter, some do complain it didn't work for them. Sometimes a different batch has different chipsets, I dunno. So it may take trial and error before you get a splitter that works. I also have a 4tb Western Digital passport connected the ClearClick, and it works perfectly.

Lastly, inside the box, they give you a free license of Videopad software. This is so you can touch up your recordings, add effects, transitions, or even output to DVD. Before I registered my copy, I wanted to see how much this software cost, so I proceeded to purchase as if I didn't have a code. So currently, it's listed as $99, but it is on sale for $35 until August 15. We get it free!

However, after just a couple months I'm noticing that the balance is very uneven. At low volume the left channel is significantly louder than the right channel, regardless of the audio source or speakers used. As you turn up the volume, the balance returns to normal. Essentially if you want to listen to something quietly you'll be listening to the left channel only, and if you need to attenuate quickly the audio moves off to your left before fading out.

I've babied the unit and never turned it up more than about 1/3rd of the way so it's hard to imagine that it could be damaged or blown out.

Update: A year later the balance issue is much worse AND this thing is emitting a constant high-pitch whine. Time to shop for another replacement... Overpriced junk.

title: A great fit for workouts; some usability issues and short battery life
text:
Overall I'm very pleased with these ear buds. They are my first pair of bluetooth buds and it has been wonderful to not have to deal with cords, especially when working out. I can't tell you how many times I've hit an earbud cord while exercising and ripped the ear bud from my ear. A real pain in the neck (and ear!).

>>>Pros:

Comfort - These fit very well in my ear. There are different tip sizes to create a good fit and, after trying them all out, I went with the medium size. Very comfortable to wear even for long periods of time.

Stay put - I've yet to have them fall out even when doing aerobic exercises or while on the treadmill.

Sound - they sound pretty good. The sound is not as good as my favorite (and inexpensive) corded buds ([[ASIN:B0053R0WWG RHA MA-350 Aluminium Noise Isolating In-Ear Earphones]]) but they are a solid B+ performer with regard to bass response and overall clarity. Keep in mind that good bass response is affected by how the buds fit in your ear, so it's important to try out different tip sizes to see how they affect sound quality. They do get harsh at loud volumes, but for normal listening they are more than fine for my non-audiophile ears. They do reasonably well at blocking out ambient noise.

Setup - I found it straightforward even though I've never had any experience with setting up bluetooth earbuds.

Size - nice and compact so you don't get the "radar dish" look that larger units can have.

Durability - they have a "sweat proof" guarantee which is nice (although I imagine, like most guarantees, there are some loopholes). Overall build quality is good, with a very solid feel to all components.

>>>Cons:

Battery life - The manufacturer claims a battery life of 4.5 hours but I've yet to get more than 3 hours off a single charge. Plus there's no warning about battery life (until you're almost fully discharged) or a visual indicator of how much charge there is left.

Usability - the buttons on the buds are too small, making it difficult for me to push the right one. A lot of fumbling and mis-presses, making it often easier to deal with volume changes on the device, which kills some of the value of having wireless buds. I guess I lack the nimble fingers of the primary target market.

But overall, I'm pleased. The pros outweigh the cons, and I think this is a solid 4-star device.

title: Vs. Alienware 17 w/ GTX 880M
text:
I also have an Alienware 17 with GTX 880M GPU. Comparisons are somewhat unfair considering the nearly $1000 price difference, but I believe they may be helpful to a prospective buyer:

You can look at specs and framerate comparisons of the GPUs all over the web, but my experience is that both deliver seamless perfection in the newest games. If I'm dropping some frames with either, I don't notice, but I often like to play on my TV, and I know I lose something there. I am also not obsessed with gaming like some, so I'll concentrate on some of the other factors.

The displays themselves are both fantastic, and I cannot distinguish a huge difference there.

The GTX970M included with this machine does make a noticeable difference in terms of power consumption, as this machine is much thinner and lighter than the AW. At the same time, it feels slightly less robust because the entire chassis is not metal.

I don't like the CD drive placement on this machine, as I keep popping the slot open from time to time.

USB 3.0 is on only one side of the machine (2.0 port and card reader on the other side). AW has two ports on each side.

What I really like about the AW is that it has a second full size HDD slot for added versatility. It's the only laptop I've ever seen with that.

There are no obvious annoyances with the touchpad or keyboard as far as accidental hitting a key or something not working correctly, which I've seen with other laptops. I am not thrilled with the placement of the delete key on this laptop, and I don't really like the fact that the arrow keys are scrunched up with the numbers and other keys, either. By contrast, I believe AW got their layout perfect, including their four programmable keys.

Lights. The keyboard by itself may actually look cooler on the Apache because the lights are in the height of the keys. BUT, there are only three zones, compared to AW's four, plus multiple chassis zones. I really love the light-up touchpad on the AW. What really annoys me about the lights on this keyboard is that despite the controller software that allows lots of per-key and per-game customization, there is no setting that allows the keyboard to turn off at the same time that the screen goes blank (or any time for that matter; you have to wait until the computer goes to sleep). I have it rigged to change from one profile to a dark profile when I press the special command button, but that's not seamless.

Windows 10. Actually, I love that I got the AW at the time when they were still loading Win7 (Win 8.1 was out, but nobody wanted it). I'm still not thrilled with Win10 due to their moving some settings out of control panel and into settings, getting rid of other settings altogether, still having a ridiculous start menu, and wanting to control your life as if you're some dumb tablet/phone user. I installed Classic Shell to get my start menu back, messed with the control panel and settings for a long time, turned off everything they were "offering" me, and I have this working just about as good as a Win7 machine. Oh yeah, and I ditched MS Edge; God, what was wrong with Explorer? Anyway, if we're stuck with it, may as well make the best of it.

Very little crapware on this machine. On most computers, I disable even the proprietary controls since most of them do nothing. This machine has a System Control Manager that doesn't do anything that Windows Power settings cannot do, but it confuses things and messes up my settings, so it will be turned off. The other stuff seems harmless so far.

I was telling someone that computers like this are a status symbol to some people (like cars are to some people). And it came with a key fob, like a car... Oh yeah, this and the AW both come in fancy packaging, including a suitcase-style box that you'll be tempted to keep, but practicality keeps me from doing so. However, you may want it if you frequently transport your machine. Also comes with the largest - but not softest - microfiber cloth I've ever seen (the size of the screen).

In conclusion, you can see that there are a few minor things I prefer about the AW. Are they worth an extra thousand bucks? No. This is an impressive machine that can handle anything I throw at it. It should definitely be on your consideration list.

title: Interesting technology with potential--not there yet
text:
This is a pretty mixed review of an interesting concept that is pretty good right now, but has the potential to be great in the near future. At the current price of about $150, this is ok+ based on the following criteria:

Sound Quality: 2.5-3 stars
For the size, it's ok
When reviewing for sound quality, I compare speakers (and headphones) to comparably sized items, based on speakers I currently or previously have owned. I take price range *somewhat* into account (I don't expect $15 headphones to sound like $500 ones), but for anything over $100, I use the full range from the cheapest stuff I have, to my favorite brand, Bose.
So with that in mind, I have a portable wireless Bose speaker that is smaller and acts as the "5" on the scale.
The sound on this can get loud enough to not distort and still fill a smallish room or normal bedroom fine. The treble and bass are ok, though the higher ranges are tinny and the bass lacks depth. Overall sound from high to low and throughout the mid range lack definition. It's good enough for very casual background listening and for podcasts.

Alexa Feature: 4 stars
I have an iPhone and think Alexa has quite a bit more understanding and skill than Siri. When asked questions, from simple stuff like "what's the weather" to more complicated stuff like "I'm hungry. What can I make in half an hour?", the answers and follow-up questions are highly intuitive and thorough. Does she get everything all the time? No. But she does a much better job than Siri.

User-Friendliness: 2.5 stars
I didn't like the process of figuring out how this works, particularly the part of pairing with more than one device and also Having to use an app to make most of it work. It was a clunky, irritating process that more or less stayed that way every time I wanted to use this thing, especially for listening to music. It should be able to just play from your iTunes through the iTunes app and bluetooth, and instead, I was only able to make it play iTunes though Their App, which sucks when it comes to my music. And that brings us to the App..

App: 2 stars
No. Just no. Bluetooth exists for a reason, and if a speaker has bluetooth, you should be able to just pair and play. I had to use the app to play from my iTunes, and because I have a very specific way of organizing things, I was incredibly annoyed that something didn't translate, and my music was disorganized and basically impossible to search for with this app. Instead of being able to play what I want from one of my playlist subfolders, it disregarded my way of organizing things, and I ended up giving up. If I can't listen to my stuff easily with this, then like 75% of the reason to use this disappears, leaving me with an expensive alarm clock with weather report, recipe ideas, and some cool internet stuff. That's cool, but it's quite incomplete for what I need, and what I suspect many people want.

tl;dr version: sound is mediocre but doable, app is bad, Alexa is super clever and smart, and the experience has a lot of frustrating aspects.

title: Best m-ITX case so far
text:
I am in love with SFF gaming PCs. Originally I built my PC using the SilverStone RVZ02. I liked that case but I found that it generated a lot of heat on components that can't cool themselves. My SSDs were hitting 65+ Celsius. Not sure if that's really an issue, but I didn't like it. To help with the heat, I created this monstrosity with tiny 40mm fans all around the case and drilled some holes. It worked but boy oh boy did it look ugly.

Enter the Node 202. I built a monster system in this computer. The Node 202 actually seems a little smaller than the SilverStone and it feels a lot sturdier. I was able to fit an SFX-L power supply in my system, 2 slim case fans inside with the GPU, as well as a 58mm high CPU cooler. All of that makes for an extremely cool and moderately quiet PC (the GTX 1080 FE tends to be loud under load). Building this was no easy task as I used components that are not really supposed to go in there. But I love the design of the SFX-L PSU and I love the Scythe Big Shuriken 2 rev. b cooler. So I needed to have those. The thin case fans inside next to the GPU are a dream. They run at 700 rpm and keep all of the heat out of the case. Even though I have the blower style Founder Edition, it still made a lot of heat behind it and right above where it exhausts the air. The slim fans work so well that I would wager a normal aftermarket GPU cooler would be fine in there and wouldn't heat up the rest of the case. The SSDs are now nice and cool too since they are sitting away from the graphics card (rather than behind it in the SilverStone case).

I noticed some reviews around complained about the cable managements. That's just a fact of life for SFF cases. It was difficult, but I was able to cleanly install all of my cables and route them relatively out of the way while still using really beefy components. If my wallet ever stops hurting I might buy custom length cables as I don't see someone making a better case than this.

Overall, I have yet to find something that I think will beat this is size and cooling. I don't like the cube style m-ITX cases since I need tall and skinny in order for this to fit next to my couch or in my TV stand. I'll try to post some pictures when I'm not feeling lazy :)

title: Performs as Advertised--Turns PS4, Other Devices On/Off; Controls, Navigates PS4 "Media"
text:
If you read the product description carefully, you won't waste time (as I did) trying to use this PLAYSTATION 4 UNIVERSAL MEDIA REMOTE to navigate PS4 games (e.g., Journey, Minecraft). The PS4 remote uses Bluetooth to turn your PS4 on and off, and to control and navigate PS4 media (e.g., DVDs), but only controls PS4 media. The PS4 remote can also be programmed to turn your TV, Cable Box, and Audio Receiver on and off, and to control and navigate those devices (assuming they accept remote Bluetooth operation).

The PS4 remote performs the advertised functions very well, and I'm happy with it. The main thing I wanted was the PS4 on/off feature, so that I wouldn't have to fool with the skinny button on the PS4 box when I wanted to play a DVD. But I also wanted something that would make it easier to navigate DVDs. I'm not much of a gamer, and I find the game controllers awkward to use. With the PS4 remote, the forward, back, play, and arrow buttons work "normally" (like any TV remote).

NOTE THAT once the PS4 remote is paired, you will turn the playstation "on" by pressing the big PS4 button, but you will turn it "off" by navigating to the PS4's power settings (in the display). (The PS4 remote doesn't have a "sources" button for bringing up the output options on my Samsung Smart TV, so I still need a second remote for selecting the PS4 output.)

The Bluetooth pairing and setup for the PS4 remote is straightforward, but you need to follow the directions in the accompanying booklet "to the letter". You have to visit several locations in the PS4 settings to add the remote to the PS4 device list, and then complete the setup.

Programming the remote to turn on another device (TV, Cable Box, Amplifier, etc.) is exactly the same as programming any universal remote. You turn on the device you're programming, put the remote into learning mode, point it at the device, and wait for the remote to find, recognize, and turn off the device. If the remote doesn't recognize the device, you must perform the device code programming manually (lots of codes are listed in the instruction booklet). The PS4 remote recognized my TV without difficulty, but my sound bar required manual programming.

Once you've programmed the various other devices, you switch between those devices by pressing the little labeled buttons (PS4, TV, AMP, CBL). Which brings me to the only thing that I don't like about the PS4 remote--the buttons (especially the switching buttons) are quite small, because there are so many of them packed onto this rather narrow remote.

title: A Good Battery Pack with a Few Minor Flaws
text:
I bought this to power two small (~3"x3") 12 volt heating pads to help keep me warm while working outside at night during a Colorado winter, and for that it performs admirably. While my use case is rather atypical, it should highlight just how flexible this rechargeable power supply is--anything that needs 12 volts and less than 3 amps is good to go.

The build quality is better than I was expecting, in all honesty, and for once I applaud the use of plastic over something like aluminum because the battery pack is already a bit on the heavy side and for something portable like this, every ounce counts.

I marked it down a star for a couple reasons:
1) The documentation that accompanied it was minimal and suffered from some translation issues (though I've come to expect that for products such as this). If not for reviews/questions here on Amazon, I wouldn't have known that the Red/Green LED indicator for charging is on the charger and not the battery pack. The battery pack LED is always Blue.
2) The Li Ion Charging/Protection Circuit is contained in the "wall wart" charger that comes with it. While I understand that this saves space in the battery pack itself (and I did just make the comment about every ounce counting), it also means that if I should lose the charger, I have to get another one to continue using the battery pack (the 18650 batteries used here are unprotected, I believe). For convenience, it would be nice to be able to plug the pack into any 12 volt power supply of sufficient amperage and have it charge without exploding.

These are truly minor gripes, though, and I am overall quite happy with this battery pack and its performance. I imagine I'll find another use for it when I no longer need it to provide life-saving warmth.

title: Wonderful Sound Quality, Lady's Voice Creeps Daughter Out
text:
There is always a run on headphones in our house. Not only are they being lost or dying, but everyone is on a constant quest for the best design and sound they can find in a bluetooth headphone. Let's see how these measure up.

WHAT ARE THESE HEADPHONES LIKE?
These headphones have a long sturdy neck band which means they will fit a variety of neck sizes. Each ear piece has a magnet on it so that when you are not using them, they will close in front of you so you won't lose them. The controls are at the end of the neck band on the right side.

ON/OFF BUTTON
Play, pause, on/off, pair can be done with this button.

VOLUME
The minus and plus of volume control is also used for skipping songs- + skip forward, - skip backward.

ANC
There is an ANC button on the right side directly behind the negative volume button which makes it easy to press them both at the same time. It does do noise canceling, but it is frustrating because it is easy to press the ANC button by mistake when also pressing the middle button.

CHARGING PORT
Charging port is on the edge of the control button area.

AI INDICATOR VOICE
The automatic voice is very dysfunctional. It only says part of words, and seems to be a bit mean sounding which makes my daughter say it feels creepy.

NOISE CANCELING
The noise canceling works beautifully on these headphones.

SOUND QUALITY
The sound quality is awesome. Highs and mids are where they should be. Bass is very good. It is not overdone but it is in balance and does not distract from the music. There are not any breakups in sound unless you walk away from the device.

BLUETOOTH RANGE
The bluetooth range seems to be good up to about 35 feet or so.

PHONE CALL QUALITY
The calls go through very well and people can hear just fine on phone calls.

BATTERY PERCENTAGE
There is no physical light indicator to tell you how much battery power you have left.

THE BOTTOM LINE
If you want a good solid set of headphones to use with phone and music that work well, are in balance, and great for listening. The controls are not as convenient as they could be, which can be frustrating at times.

MY RATING
Four stars. If the control area was set up just a little more conveniently so that you can not accidentally press the wrong buttons all of the time, they would probably be five stars.

I don't know how it happens but I somehow ended up buying over 20 pairs of bluetooth headphones over the course of my life. I'm also finding that I can't pass up a good pair of bluetooth headphones.

So of the over-head style bluetooth headphones, I've run across problems with short battery life (had one pair that lasts only 3 hours), too tight against the head, presses on the ear (supra-aural) and gets sweaty, active noise cancelling that can't turn on independently of the bluetooth function, and no carrying case.

This pair of RCA Active noise cancelling headphones don't have any of those problems. I sit at my desk all day with an air outlet behind me that is constantly blowing. I'm able to use them the entire day with music playing without the batteries running down. I don't keep the noise cancelling on the entire time but when I do, the fan noise is completely blocked out. Being circumaural headphones, the ear cups completely surround my ears and do not press on them. In addition, the spring isn't too tight to make me feel like my head is being squeezed in a vice.

As far as sound quality, because the speakers are not pressing against the ear, the sound seems to have a wider-room feel, making me feel even more like I don't have headphones on.

Overall, I'm quite satisfied with this purchase and don't feel the need to splurge and buy the much more expensive Sony and Bose products.

title: Really impressive sound!
text:
If you ask my wife, I've gone through too many MP3 players looking for the best one for my needs. I've had a lot of the unknown brands and some are actually really good..just not exactly what I wanted. The one I've been using since summer goes everywhere with me...but I needed something BETTER. Got it with this.

Let me preface this by saying this is not for beginners. If the extent of your music playing comes from apps on your phone, you might be lost in the beginning. If you're looking for a touch screen with big pretty buttons, this isn't it. I read another review saying the user experience is bad. I think that's absurd. If you're serious about music but on a tight budget, this has an experience you will appreciate. The UI is extremely intuitive and there are a lot of options and settings to fiddle with to get this set up exactly the way you want it.

DAC - This has a great DAC for the price. It's not the most current generation, but at this price point that is to be expected. It does the job and does it well. My FLAC and MP3 sound fantastic pumped through a solid pair of IEM headphones. Blows away other DACs in the next tier down. TI makes a really great DAC!

Sound - Even my lower quality MP3s I've been keeping since the days of Napster sound great. Obviously you can tell the difference in quality when one of the old files pops up on the shuffle, but it doesn't sound grainy or glitchy. My high quality 320kbps files and the few albums I've ripped from CD to FLAC are where this shines. It is absolutely phenomenal to listen to hi res audio on this device. I am really impressed at the sound for the price.

Build - Another review says this device is lacking in build quality. This is an aluminum brick. The buttons are plastic but seem completely solid. The scrolling wheel is textured plastic but feels very sturdy. I had no problems navigating the menus with it. The buttons are all perfectly labeled and make navigating the interface that much easier. The screen is of a decent resolution for this type of device as well.

EQ - This has a very competent 10 band equalizer with lots of presets. Unlike in low-end hi-res players, the equalizer here makes a difference. I've got it set on Rock and it sounds fantastic.

I/O - I've used this device with bluetooth headphones, bluetooth earbuds, a bluetooth stereo, single bluetooth speaker, and my car bluetooth. No connectivity problems at all. I get the best sound out of my wired IEMs, though. Bluetooth is fine, but nothing compares to a decent pair of headphones. You can also connect external devices (I used a generic USB stick connected with a micro-USB OTG cable) and get music from those. I've got a 128GB MicroSD card installed and am listening to this device streaming through an Anker Soundcore about 25 feet away as I type this review. The HiBy Music app works as expected, and streaming from my phone through this is really a simple process IF YOU READ THE INSTRUCTIONS. Haha

Interface - Three themes to choose from..Doesn't do much but change the color scheme. What I LOVE about the interface is that you can access important settings from the now playing screen. Turn on and off bluetooth, display lyrics, show album art (looks great), and access the EQ. The back button does what it says, and the menu button does what it says. There is literally no issue with the UI for someone who understands file structure or has ever used a computer. There are two other settings menus accessed from the home screen. You can customize nearly everything.

Battery - I fully charged this after receiving. Took about 1.5 hours to fully charge. As of this moment, I've listened to music either through headphones or streaming through bluetooth for about sixteen hours. Mostly streaming to bluetooth. Battery bar shown in the photos is showing about 50%. In real world use, this device might need to be charged once a week, especially if you're mainly listening through wired headphones.

Overall impressions: THIS is the MP3 player I've been looking for. It's inexpensive, built like a truck, looks good, and has more settings than I can shake a stick at. I am extremely pleased with my purchase.

title: Truly international adapter for low-wattage devices!
text: Truly worldwide!  This travel adapter plugs in to European, British Empire (UK, AU), Asian AND North American (female) outlets, and accepts (male) plugs from those countries as well.  So, it's great when you travel from US to overseas, but also can be used by visitors to the US from overseas.  This is an adapter, not a converter.  What's the difference?  An adapter adapts between different shapes of plugs and sockets.  A converter (or transformer) changes one voltage to another, like allowing you to plug a US (110 - 120 Volt) appliance into a European (220 - 240 V -- also found on most cruise ships, by the way) power supply.  (By the way, there are also inverters, that change DC current (from a car or battery) into AC current.)  Do you need an adapter or a converter? You probably only need an adapter because most new-ish devices (like the iPhone) and most small appliances (like a shaver or toothbrush) accept both 110-120 and 220-240 V.  The device or appliance will either automatically switch between each type of power supply, or there will be a small switch (usually a slider switch on the bottom of the device or appliance).

title: Great sound, crappy UI
text:
The Vizio SB3821 has a few great points: it's very narrow and discrete, so it fits in tight places. It sounds good. It has quite a few inputs you can easily switch between, a feature usually lacking on sound bars.

And it has some massive flaws... the IR remote is picky and won't work if blocked. You can't jump directly between inputs; you have to iterate between them. And the UI consists of 12 tiny LEDs in a column, on the far left edge, while the control buttons and remote sensor are in the middle.

Think about that. You not only have to remember patterns to know what you've told it to do... example - if you use the analog cable it came with to connect to your TV, those are LEDs 9/10 from the top when switching inputs. The Toslink digital is LEDs 5/6. The signal for turning DTS, TruVolume and Power Saver on/off are EXACTLY the same. And aren't near the controls.

This is more inconvenient than it sounds if you switch inputs regularly. You have to keep the left end and the middle of the sound bar in line-of-sight, and use both.

Other than that, it's great. But that's a pretty significant demerit.

Update: I wanted to upgrade to a soundbar with rear speakes, so I compared the [[ASIN:B00SMBGP76 VIZIO SB4051-C0 40-Inch 5.1 Channel Sound Bar with Wireless Subwoofer and Satellite Speakers]] to the [[ASIN:B00VNHE26W Samsung HW-J470 4.1 Channel 460 Watt Wireless Audio Soundbar (2015 Model)]], those being the only soundbars I could find with rear speakers. And they're about the same price. Unfortunately, they're not very close.

I've already mentioned the Vizio U.I. Not a fan. The Samsung looks nicer, it's a lot smaller (so it won't block as much of a TV) and it has a nice alpha-numeric panel in the middle telling you what it's doing. Much more usable. But it's also got sound matching the smaller size - it's comparatively tinny sounding and less full. Those are two different things. Tinny perhaps because it's so much smaller. But it also doesn't fill the space as well, perhaps because there are so many fewer drivers. The Vizio has three driver-sets in the sound-bar, including for the center. The Samsung only has left and right in it, no center. And it makes a pretty big difference.

Side by side, the Samsung looks a lot nicer, but the Vizio sounds a lot better.

title: Small and Fast Storage for PC and Android
text:
I like SanDisk storage devices and have used a variety of their products with my electronic devices. I was intrigued by this one because of the small size relative to the capacity. The fact that it can talk to an Android phone as well as a PC is an interesting feature. So far, I am pleased with it.

I have the 128GB version and it is more than large enough for my needs, though there is a 256GB version for those that need more space. 20 years ago this kind of space would have been on a large hard drive and cost hundreds if not thousands. This one fits in my pocket and costs less than $20. Times have changed.

This device connects to my PC with a USB Type A connector but at 3.0 speeds, meaning I can transfer plenty of data quickly without waiting half the day for it all to transfer. This is handy for moving picture archives or movie files which tend to be large. Both my Windows and my Linux systems see this device and are able to communicate with it.

The other interface to this device is a MicroUSB connector, which works for older Android phones. Newer phones have a USB-C connector so be sure that your phone can use this device if that is your intended purpose. It comes with an app for installing on your Android phone to make it easier to manage. I don't have an Android phone anymore but I do have a tablet that runs Android, and this device connects to it without issue.

text:
From what I’ve read, there are many factors that contribute to the success of an instant photo: the camera, the lighting, the temperature, the subject, how still you are when shopting, the film itself and how careful you are to keep it in the dark during its developing. That said, you will just have to try it out for yourself!

I’m new to the vintage instant camera scene, but I’ve already learned how easy it is to mess up a shot.

My only complaint is the price, but it’s not like there is any other option. Hopefully some day, they will be able to produce it more efficiently and thus cheaper. Until then... I’ll be very choosy about taking a snap.

Oh! And it might be helpful to note that my camera didn’t want to eject the film after the dark slide. To fix this, I found a resource online that suggested the following:

—Open the camera to reveal the film cartridge.

—Locate the thin, long strip of plastic (on the cartridge) right in front of where the film would come out. Just beneath this strip is a thin black Mylar sheet.

—Carefully bend back on that plastic bit to remove it. Might take a little rocking back and forth. It will snap right off.

—If the film is still not ejecting once you close up the camera and go to take another photo, you can open the camera again and fold back the little Mylar sheet to eliminate the resistance of the photo popping out. I used my nail to fold it (bend it back then fold it to keep it down and away from where the film pops out).

^I realize these pieces are there to keep the film dark and being contaminated with light, but this has caused me no problems thus far. I have done this with 3 of my vintage cameras and film. Do so at your own risk, of course!

Hope this helps. (:

title: An Excellent Touchpad
text:
I am loving the Logitech Rechargeable Touchpad T650 with its user-friendly ease of use and many great features. The small size of 5 1/4" width x 5" length, smooth surface, rechargeable battery, very responsive with light-touch to activate gestures, on/off switch, place anywhere to use and sturdy design makes this the perfect touchpad for me. I got this touchpad as my computer mouse stopped working. I thought about a touchscreen monitor, but opted for this touchpad instead as it would be so nice to not have to stretch and fatigue my arm with the actions needed with a touchscreen monitor. The touchpad only needs a very light touch of the fingers to click, slide and navigate the gestures to activate the product features, which is most excellent to keep stress off the fingers. I have a desktop computer with Windows 7 right now, but this touchpad supports Windows 8 when I make the change which is another plus for me. Note a gesture not listed on the Logitech site that I just happen to notice worked to activate the right mouse click is a very light tap of two fingers in the middle of the touchpad. Also, note that a two-handed gesture not listed on the Logitech site that I found useful to highlight is to apply pressure to the left-hand bottom corner of the touchpad with the other hand lightly touch the touchpad with a smooth move of the cursor to highlight, then release the pressure on the touchpad to end highlighting-- after you have finished with copy and paste or drag and drop, to release the highlighted text--place the cursor on the highlighted area then lightly tap anywhere on the touchpad with one finger. Make sure to download the latest version of software for this touchpad to avoid possible glitches. It took me less than a day to get used to using this touchpad, and I find this touchpad superior to a mouse. I highly recommend this rechargeable touchpad and hope this review is helpful to others.

Tips for this touchpad's gestures (includes some that I wrote above):

(1.) To activate the right mouse click is a very light tap of two fingers in the middle of the touchpad.

(2.) A two-handed gesture to highlight is to apply pressure to the left-hand bottom corner of the touchpad and with the other hand lightly touch the touchpad with a smooth move of the cursor to highlight, then release the pressure on the touchpad to end highlighting-- after you have finished with copy and paste or drag and drop, to release the highlighted text--place the cursor on the highlighted area then lightly tap anywhere on the touchpad with one finger.

(3.) Download the latest version of software for this touchpad to avoid possible glitches.

(4.) Use the on/off switch on the top right side of touchpad to turn off when not in use for a long period of time to save the rechargeable battery.

I had also had countless thoughts about the negative review I would write on Amazon when I'd returned home.

I considered writing about the design and functionality of the bag, but there's really no point in doing so.

This bag is a worthless piece of junk. It's amazing that they get away with charging almost $80 for this. title: Badly Designed, Bulky, Lousy software, Defective unit too
text:
I am now a total expert on Bushnell Golf GPS's having owned the Yardage Pros XG, XGC and Neo.
Of these, the XGC was the only one that worked properly. It has problems, but I was able to read yardage.

But this is an XG Review:
Pros:
Good Satellite Reception.
Good data (with $35 subscription to iGolf - annual. But you can cancel after a year if you've already downloaded all the courses you want)
Solidly made (though very bulky)
Good Buttons

Cons:
Did not work on the first course I tried it on ("No Tee Box Found" error)
The Display is low contrast. Some of the menus are impossible to read in sunlight because of their truly moronic interface design (highlighting black text with dark gray instead of using white text on dark).

The Bottom Line: If this unit worked, I would've kept it, But the NEO or XGC are probably better choices.
I think if the NEO actually worked that'd be my top pick(I had an issue with Windows 7x64 - or something - and it wouldn't load courses). Bushnell thought my problem was weird, so maybe it'll be better for you.
BUT since the XGC DID work and seems to be a little bit more modern electronically (e.g. seems to recognize USB natively without pretending it's an old fashioned 1980s serial port), I think I may have to go back to the XGC.

ALL I really want is something that tells me how far to the pin. How far to hazards or dog legs would be nice, but mostly I want distance to pin. Maybe I need a rangefinder, but I don't want to slow down play by pulling out a rangefinder on every shot. I want something where I can just glance at my bag and see the yardage. That's it. The NEO has its own issues, but if it worked, I think it's the most sensible tool for most golfers simply because it is the least intrusive.

CUSTOMER SUPPORT: AWFUL!!! Bushnell provides no support email on their website. It takes at least 10 minutes to get someone on the phone. If you do get someone on the phone, they'll be able to answer routine questions, but not much else. They were supposed to get back to me about my defective unit.
No call or email back. I get the feeling Bushnell simply doesn't want you to bother them.
