The foam eartips are very comfortable (very similar to the nice comply TX-100 eartips) and isolate very well. The two silicone options are also very good, but a few more tips would have been nice, even if it cost a dollar more.

They're quite light and don't weight down your ears.

I like the over ear wire, it's very unintrusive. I find the ones with little wire ear pieces to get REALLY painful, but the thin, light wire is completely unnoticeable. instead of the earpiece, it has a tiny brass weight that just holds the wires down, which winds up working REALLY well.

I don't plan on using them for workouts, but if I were, the only thing I'd want is a chin cinch. That's the only thing these are missing. Running is probably fine, but if you're a jumpy crossfit type, you might be able to bounce the wires off your ears.

The fit and finish is quite nice, though the parts are built down to a price. Not the greatest wire, but it seems serviceable, there's good stress relief on the plug and Y, and there's no rough or sharp edges.

The sound quality is exceptional. I'd say that I have a hard time telling these apart from my $100 klipsch IEM's. It's a nice moderate tone, there's plenty of base but it's not muddy or overhwhelming. Very tight and clean. The mids are the only place you can hear any faltering, and it's just a TINY bit muted. Highs are plenty clear and clean. And that's without any burn-in.

Can't speak to the in-line mic, but it responds to google voice commands just fine. It's just a one-button remote, so you only have a pause/play option. No volume control. double click it to skip a song, hold to enable voice commands, Voice commands can be used to set volume, but it's more than just a click.

My only four small gripes are the small number of earpieces (the foam tips do kinda make up for it, but the other two are great if they fit your ears. I have medium sized ear-canals and the smaller silicone tips are perfect), I wish it had volume controls on the mic, a chin cinch for exercise, and that it doesn't come with a case of any sort. I'd have gladly paid an extra few bucks for those things.

Also not great option for motorcycle helmets, they stick out a little far for that.

Overall, I highly recommend these though. The user manual is a hilariously badly translated mess, well worth the read. "To get your earbuds fit perfectly, require and error."

Now, here is one myth that all HDMI cable buyers should know.
Not all HDMI cables are equal. There are people making adequate HDMI cables on the cheap- by adequate I mean that they do work and for those people who don't care much about picture and sound quality they will be happy with the results. You can find these cheaper cables on auction sites and closeout retail outlets.
BUT
The cables are basically junk- they wont last long, the connectors are weak and prone to bending, crimping, etc.
On the other hand, high price HDMI cables are also somewhat of a myth. Anyone selling a cable with "gold" connectors is not selling you a cable with "gold" connectors- the "gold" is plated on tin or aluminum or sheet metal and amounts to much less than a milligram's worth. the difference in connection is marginal at best.
The cables that Amazon is providing is all you really need. Don't spend $45 plus on a calbe that only cost $8 to make (at best).

title: Jabra 85h head-to-head with Bose 35
text:
If you’re looking for unmatched sound reproduction in a very quiet music room, neither the Bose 35 nor the Jabra 85h is competing in that studio monitor class.

These are yeoman everyday transit use with great sound quality. It’s the noise cancelling depth that shuts out the chaos that makes the two exceptional. Ambient sustained engine/crowd noise will wear you out. That’s what makes noise cancelling central for me.

Noise cancelling – Jabra is the first headphone experience every bit the equal with the Bose 35. Other noise reduction players competing in the price bracket don’t come close. The Jabra and Bose cancellation are different. Audible net cancellation is so close to the same that I can’t discriminate. Bose noise cancelling has a sort of over-pressure feeling that I don’t notice in the Jabra. It’s not a discriminator or fatigue element either way for me. If you know what I mean, you will notice it.

Bass – Jabra by a hair

Treble – Jabra wins

Clarity – Bose by a hair

Comfort – High personal importance for air travel. Bose passes the 8-hour flight test. I believe the Jabra will too.

The Jabra 85h is incredibly impressive. It’s a competitive break-through from my perspective. The same price range as Bose 35. Overall the same with very subtle differences that make a winner impossible to my ear. I’d need an acoustics lab to compare the 2 in detail and that degree of detail would be irrelevant for me or the typical user in the price bracket.
Nobody’s going to go wrong with the Jabra 85h. Bose has the first genuine competitor in the price range. That’s good for everybody.

It's super lightweight and airy and I'm finding that I seldom even have to run the fan - just having this under the laptop works great! title: This one is difficult to rate; definitely not a NOAA alert radio exactly.
text:
Basically the radio is pretty sound (we bought 3 at once). The Weather broadcast works fine; the NOAA selection has no instruction in the manual at all - there were no options on the radio when it was selected. Today this county had its first NOAA test broadcast, made to activate all working NOAA radios. We have two Midland emergency radios that turned themselves on and gave the alert. These 3 Kayinow radios did not respond to the test broadcast, unless fully turned on and on the Weather alert channel (we set up one on the Weather ("WD"), one on NOAA, and one turned off). Only the Weather (WD) selected one played the broadcast. The NOAA set one did nothing at all. SO they work fine if you are on the Alert channel already, but unless you are, they will not alert you to danger (we've lived through 2, and almost 3 evacuations in 3 years).
The reception of the radio is decent (sometimes the antenna isn't enough - its about as long as your hand and fingers), but the biggest issue is the radio tuning; you have to depend on the radio to preselect your stations (it'll skip local stations if you are in a bad reception spot of your home). It creates channels you can jump to by pushing a button to index through; our local news/talk channel (which is the best for emergencies) requires 18 button pushes to get to it each time. You can change the station frequency, but it is a laborious amount of single button pushes to change much. The reception is good once you labor to your channel, but the chipset in this radio is lacking any quick way to achieve your goal.

title: Initial Reaction: Excellent! (See Updates Below)
text:
Believe me when I tell you I read and read and read about these high-end RDs before making my choice. After reading the reviews on Amazon, I was very uncertain. But after looking at reviews by people in the tech biz, I decided to take the plunge and so far I am very glad I did.

After very limited usage, this is what I have found (all I can do is speak for the unit I own):
1. the suction cups that came with the unit adhere to my windshield. The connection seems strong and tight. I left the cups on the windshield in 20-degree weather -- they have not budged. So far I see no need to buy a more deluxe suction device. I do remove the unit itself when I am out of the vehicle;

2. the manual indicates that the RD is to be positioned flush against the windshield. So far I do not see a problem with that position. As I drive I have been keeping an eye on the unit. It remains steady, it shows no signs of movement on local streets (not the smoothest on God's earth, either);

3. I was able to update the database of cameras by downloading the detector tools from the mfg. website. Since mine is a newer unit, I connected the unit via USB to a netbook, powered up the RD, clicked on the icons in the downloaded software, and was finished this process in about 15-20 mins. I did NOT have to do this download in my vehicle. The USB connection (netbook-to-RD) was all that was necessary; Note: until I turned the unit ON during the software update installation, the detector tools could not verify my serial number and the install would not proceed. (See my review of the AmazonBasics cable, which is the one you want for this RD.)

4. so far the unit has functioned as described in the manual: it has very, very few false alarms, it stores detected points as I drive, I have it set on AUTO as recommended for the best hiway-city setting;

5. compared to other detectors I have owned, which have all been in the $150 range, the Passport is by far the best at this early stage;

I have yet to see how this baby behaves when I am on turnpikes and other places under surveillance by the good folks in blue. I am not a lead-foot particularly, I just love electronics; but there are times when the lull of the road will cause excessive speed. I like to be prepared.

As I get more experience with this unit on the road, I will update this review. For now, I can honestly say this unit deserves the very high marks it has received on tech review websites. It looks and feels very well made.

I am glad I made the move upward. I encourage you to do the same!

First Update:
So far I have had no problems with the windshield suction cups adhering to the glass. The temperatures here have been between 20 and 50 degrees. From time to time I will press on the nubs to check the strength of the grip, and sometimes I will hear a "clicking" sound which "resets" the cups to full strength.

I have been doing local driving only and there is very little "chatter" from the unit. I can only assume it is doing its job. It goes through the power up sequence just fine. I have not passed any stationary police vehicles. Another update will follow when I have somethinbg significant to report.

Second Update: (April 21)
I finally had a chance to drive on the open road on a 4-hour round-trip. I can only assume that this detector is doing its job. True, I did not eyeball ANY police vehicles on my trip. The detector did not report any, either. So, is it working? As I say, I can only assume so. It did fire off several K-band alerts along the route, but nothing more.

In my home area there are many speed cameras installed. My detector would have me believe than none are operative, since I have yet to receive a single camera alert. BTW, I am current on all updates via USB. I have nothing else to report, other than the fact that the unit powers up and self-tests as it should.

Third Update May 14, 2013
For the first time since purchasing this detector it identified red light camera locations. I am now satisfied that this function is working properly.

Fourth Update July 14, 2013
Even in extremely hot vehicle interior temperatures, the windshield suction cups have remained in place. As a matter of fact, the clip has not moved since I first attached it back in February.

title: Dell i3464-3000BLK-PUS Inspiron AIO, 23.8" AIO, (7th Gen Core i3 (up to 2.40 GHz), 8GB, 1TB HDD, Intel HD Graphics 620, Black
text:
My daughter and I set this computer up yesterday so my review is not based on weeks/months use of it. However, I can probably tell you some things that might be good to know. First of all, I am NOT computer techy and will not delve into the specs. Besides, all that is already listed in the product description. It runs on Windows 10, 64-bit. I'm not super-fond of any Windows platform for privacy reasons, but overall it seems to function well with few problems thus far.

The set up was very easy. Actually the most difficult part was clearing away the previous computer and all it's various components. There is no separate CPU which I find to be absolutely delightful. I actually have a nice, open space on the floor where the old one sat. The CPU is inside the monitor, as well as the DVD drive. It comes with all the cords you need, including a wireless mouse and keypad. I was surprised that the sound from the monitor was much better than any other monitor with speakers I've ever used. It wasn't nearly what an audiophile would want, but good enough for basic listening needs. I still attached my separate sound system because I love really good sound. The Bluetooth function connected quickly to all my devices.

The colors are vivid and defined, the monitor can be angled for different views, and everything is adjustable. The included instruction showed a base plate for the monitor but mine did not have one. The monitor stands just fine none-the-less. The DVD drive is mounted on the right-side of the monitor and seems to work very well. We had this up and running in about 20 minutes and we were moving kind of slowly.

What did not work at all was the Netflix app. It needs to be uninstalled and re-installed from the Google Play Store. It will give an error code but it was an easy fix. The Cortana feature on this computer only works when the computer is initially booted. Afterwards it fails to hear although I have gone through the mike wizard set-up several times. I don't know what is wrong with that but it might be something most people would like have working well. Also, the mouse "copy/paste" function doesn't work. It will copy but you have physically hit "control V" to get it to paste. It seems to be fast - it moves from webpage to webpage rapidly, movies and videos have yet to glitch, and......it' so quiet. My previous computer was noisy all the time. This one is so very, quite.....no cpu sounds at all.

Overall so far: I like it, I wish the Cortana worked like it's supposed too, it's fast and the monitor is large and clear. Also it's touch screen so you can just touch any app on it to open it up. I'm actually to lazy to lean that far and prefer to use my mouse, but it seems to be a reliably working feature. However, the touch screen makes it really easy and fast to delete a bunch of pictures. I had a LOT of pictures from my kid's various science projects that I no longer needed and just touching the screen marking them for deletion was about 20x faster than using a mouse. I will definitely update this review as I use this computer more. If anything malfunctions or is super wonderful I'll report back. As of this review this computer costs $729.99. It also has many various ports on the sides and rear and are very easy to access.

title: Pretty good but for one omission
text:
I like this router.

Pros:
1. Very easy setup
2. Fairly nice web interface
3. Changes to settings are very quick and reboots are seldom required.

Cons:
The only fault I find is you can't set client IPs based on their MACs. I think this is usual for Cisco/Linksys routers though I don't know why they don't provide this important feature. Without it client IPs seem to change randomly. Maybe only when rebooting the router but I'm not sure of that. Some routers, even if they don't have this feature, at least remember the IPs they offered previously. This one doesn't appear to do that.

This would probably not be a problem unless you run simple servers, remote control clients, bittorrent clients etc. I think many users do at least a bit of this.

The alternative is to set the IP individually on each client. This is a PITA and cannot be done on some devices such as some printers, access points, game consoles, DVRs, etc. It may also be a problem for portable devices that try to make connections to multiple routers.

title: Spacious and Well-Designed Backpack Camera Bag
text:
I have a growing interest in photography and I have been learning as I go. One of the things I have discovered is that a good camera bag – sufficiently large to hold the camera, lenses you need and any accessories – is absolutely essential. I have a messenger-style camera bag that works well enough but I have run out of room in it and it does not have the capacity to hold all of my extra lenses and filters. I looked to this camera bag as a solution. It definitely holds more than my old bag, it seems to be made well and there are some nice features to this bag.

This is a backpack style bag and it is about the same size as a small travel backpack, though it is an order of magnitude thicker. There are zippers and pockets everywhere. There's a lot of padding to protect the camera and multiple movable partitions.

The main compartment is large enough to hold a small laptop if all of the partitions are pulled out. There are three small partitions and two large ones and these can be arranged in any configuration to accommodate a wide array of accessories. As shipped, the partitions are arranged to allow for the camera lens and camera to sit through the middle of the pack which maximizes the padding and protection for the most valuable parts of your setup, and the smaller partitions are about right for 2-3 lens kits. I have a smaller camera – a Samsung NX300 with the 18-55mm lens – so I need less room for my camera and rearranged the configuration to permit room for several filter kits, a telephoto lens, a fisheye lens and a few smaller accessories, all in the main compartment. I have not yet purchased additional lenses but will rearrange when I do.

The main compartment also has a pocket that is suitable for either a thin book or a tablet. So, even with all of my other gear in the main compartment, I still have room for my tablet. I really can't ask for much more than that.

There is a smaller zippered compartment on the front that has room for even more accessories. In this I have loaded up a spare set of macro lenses that would not fit in the main compartment. Inside this compartment there is yet another pocket suitable for holding a tablet as well as a mesh pocket for loose items, my choice being a couple of pens. However, the most interesting item in there, attached by a tether, is a waterproof nylon cover for the whole bag. So, if you need to go out in the rain with this backpack, you can do so without fear of getting your equipment wet.

On the sides there are two small pockets, sufficient for holding a couple of small items like a filter or two or even a very small flashlight.

On the front there is one more zippered pocket that is well suited for thin items, like a map, magazine or papers.

The shoulder straps are adjustable and padded so getting the pack to fit just right is not an issue. However, there is a carrying handle loop on the top of this bag and I prefer carrying this bag using that instead (I have always preferred carrying backpacks this way).

This is a very nice camera bag. A lot of thought went into the design and it can hold a lot of equipment for its size. It has replaced my other camera bag outright.

Disclaimer: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at no cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

title: GREAT STAND!! - The L3 has both great aesthetics & great function. This solid stand reduces the temperature of my MacBook Pro-r
text:
This Elago L3 stand is a fantastic product: it is strong, light, attractive, and functional. The aluminum construction helps to transfer heat away from the laptop, allowing it to run at a cooler temperature. With a silver color that matches the silver used by Apple, this stand is the perfect companion for the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. I was torn between a few different stands for my r-MacBook Pro, but I am glad that I decided to go with this Elago L3 over others. I highly recommend this product!
------------------------------------------------

WHY I WANTED A STAND
[While this stand can be used with many computers, my specific usage is with two MacBook Pros and since my review discusses my own needs & preferences, some of it will pertain specifically to usage with the MacBook Pro.]

If you own a MacBook Pro, then you are likely aware that they do tend to operate on the hotter side. While not normally a functional concern, sitting a MacBook Pro on an insulated surface (like a leather couch) could result in accelerated wear from abnormally high temperatures. Additionally, the palm rest of the MacBook Pro can get almost uncomfortably hot when under a sustained & intense processor load. So I wanted a stand that, 1) contributes to reducing heat, and 2) I can set both on a hard surface and on a couch. This Elago L3 stand does both very well.
------------------------------------------------

DESCRIPTION
The Elago L3 is a one-piece aluminum stand that is designed to elevate a laptop computer. At only about 18 ounces, this stand is both strong and lightweight. While it will work with many different laptops, it is often marketed as a product for Apple’s MacBook Pro or MacBook Air, and the silver L3 stand uses the same color, matte, and texture used on the current MacBook models (it is also available in a few other colors.) The stand itself is about 7.25 inches wide, 10 inches in depth, and at the tallest point the height is about 3 inches tall (meaning that the computer screen itself will usually be elevated in height an additional 3 or more inches, depending on how deep the computer is.) The L3 is manufactured in South Korea.

The points of the stand that make contact with the surface the L3 is placed on, and the surface that contacts the laptop, are both lined with a black no-slip, no-scratch silicone material. The edges on the stand have been slightly rounded so that they are not sharp.

The rear of the stand has two cutouts for cables. This feature not only looks neater when used, but it can also help avoid accidental snagging of the cords (which can cause damage to the cords.) As another Reviewer noted, these cutouts are on the small side, and so larger cables may not work with them. The larger of the two cutouts is only about 1 inch by .5 inch.
------------------------------------------------

TEMPERATURE BENEFITS
Aluminum is a very effective material for heat transfer & dissipation. This stand operates as a giant heat sink, pulling the heat away from the bottom of the computer and moving it to the base of the stand where there is improved airflow, which then helps the heat more rapidly dissipate. I find my MacBook Pro Retina runs MUCH COOLER when sitting on this stand than on other surfaces. Given the palm rest of the MacBook Pro can get rather hot when the CPU is being heavily utilized, this stand makes a big difference in preventing the palm rest from becoming uncomfortably hot.
------------------------------------------------

MY OBSERVATIONS WITH USAGE
I enjoy using this product every single day. I really like the angle & amount this stand elevates. It’s tall enough to allow excellent airflow but is not so tall that the stand is inherently unstable or awkward. I find typing is comfortable as is the viewing angle.

The single-piece design is great because it minimizes form-factor, adds durability, saves weight, and improves stability. This stand sits sturdy whether I put it on my couch or on my table. It’s solid, it is not prone to rocking, and the non-slip material prevents the stand from sliding around and prevents the computer from sliding off of the stand.

Because the material used is aluminum, this stand CAN have the potential to scratch other surfaces, especially surfaces which are softer. A careful eye can minimize this, however. When placing a laptop on or removing it from the stand, doing so gently to avoid the computer banging or rubbing against the stand will avoid scratching.

While I am not sure how well this stand will work with extra-large laptops (over 15.5 inch screen), I have used this stand with a 15 inch MacBook Pro, a 13 inch MacBook Pro, and a 15 inch MacBook Pro Retina. All of those sizes work great with the L3.
------------------------------------------------

CONCLUSION
Overall, I am really glad I purchased the Elago L3 over the other stands I was considering (most of which were more expensive.) I am impressed by the performance, style, and fit & finish of the Elago L3, and I could not ask for more. This stand looks great and functions well. I highly recommend it.

Upon exchanging the battery, I charged it to full capacity, but the battery quickly lost power and drained in under an hour. Not only that but my screen flickered and would display colored lines. I reinstalled my old battery and the lines and flicker disappeared. I tried reinstalling the new battery and got the same result. Based on that I realized that I might have received a defective battery, which I understand can happen, so I requested a replacement.

When I had requested a replacement in the past, I was always sent a replacement immediately. This time however, I was told that upon return and receipt of the battery, a replacement would be shipped. Amazon was touting their partnership with Kohl's for returns and since it was close, I took the battery to them. The handoff went smoothly, but the receipt I received indicated that it could take 21 days for the return, which had not been disclosed to me previously. Had I known I would have gone to a FedEx location for a more speedy return, since I was counting on receiving a replacement timely. Checking on the status over the next two weeks was impossible, so after 21 days I was able to chat with Amazon,, and things got even more wonky. I was told it could take 1 to 3 weeks to show up in facilities. When I finally got them to understand it was over 3 weeks, they offered a $5 credit on book purchases for my trouble, but it was still another week before they knew they had received the battery, and then they told me they got it 7 days ago. The only good thing is that I was able to get my money refunded, as by then I had gone another route to get a replacement battery, with far less inconvenience. Normally Amazon is great to work with and their vendors are as well, but this reminded me that things can go very wrong as well. I know that I will not use Kohl's for returns again.

title: Decent assortment of parts without having to buy in bulk
text:
This is a nice set of parts for what you get. There are a lot of individual parts that usually are fairly cheap, but you can usually only find them in bulk quantities.

In other words, it's a little pricey compared to the bulk pricing of everything included, but it's nice to have a small assortment if you don't have room for a whole electronics shop in your house.

The cost per item is a lot more than if you were to buy any of them in bulk, but a lot less if you were to buy each of the items in this kit one at a time.

So overall, it's a good set of parts for the Raspberry Pi, but just for electronic components in general for things besides Raspberry Pi -- like an Arduino project kit or things like that.

It comes with a very nice box that is a step above the others that I've seen. I have another RexQualis kit that is also of the same quality.

I want to point out the latch for the box is much better than a lot of the other alternatives I've seen. It's an actual clasp that stays shut much better than the simple flap-clasp of some other kits that are out there. It won't just pop open and spill out if you accidentally drop it. Within reason of course, I'm sure you could break it if you tried because it's not armor-plated.

The assortment is good for most projects and there's a CD included that is helpful if you still have a CD-ROM drive in your computer -- otherwise anything on the CD is easily found online as well as newer projects.

For the price, it's not bad for anyone who just wants to play around with a Raspberry Pi in their spare time as a beginner to see if they want to get more involved.

Overall, a good assortment of components, especially if you want to try a lot of different parts and experiment with a lot of different applications that can be done with a Raspberry Pi or similar single-board controller/computer. This gets a so-so five stars because the price is a little high, but it makes up for it by not being that expensive for a starter kit with a good assortment.

title: Comfy, decent sound quality, calls just okay
text:
First things first, these have awesome packaging in that they're easy to open. I feel the need to mention this because some things are so crazy, that easy open stuff makes me happy.

Okay onto the real issue at hand, the headset. To me it just looks like an old school set of headphones but with a slimmed down band which feels almost flimsy because it has quite a bit of give to it. The wireless aspect means that there is a detachable dongle connected to the left earcup.

These are really light with or without the dongle attached. If you remove the dongle you can use them wired, but you lose the ability to make calls and there are the usual playback controls on the dongle, well you obviously lose those too.

I had two main sets of heaphones I was using when they arrived -- both with mic capabilities but I only cared that one had a mic as it was paired with my phone, the other was paired with a computer being used as headphones for music and videos. One, [[ASIN:B0070UKBO8 MEElectronics Air Fi Runaway Bluetooth Stereo Wireless Headphones with Microphone (Black/Red)]], I was happy with. The other, not so much. I figured this could replace the pair I was unhappy with. The only question for me was would it end up on the computer where the mic doesn't matter or with the phone where it does? The truth is the jury is still out on that. So far the MeElectronics seems to be winning mic wise as the person I actually talk to the most and the longest noticed a difference. She wondered what had changed. When I explained I was calling to test a new set of headphones, I had to explain I wanted to see if they were better/worse/no different from the ones I usually used. The first call was a disaster but she was in a loud place so we chalked that up to issues on her end. When she called back it was better but she still felt it was different - she could hear me but she felt like it was as though I had her on speakerphone. With the AirFi she said she had no clue that I was anything other than the phone's direct mic. Since she could actually hear me it's not an issue, I chalk it up to the mic being better placed on the other brand.

When it comes to audio, I've had no complaints whether I was listening to various types or music or audiobooks though I am not some crazed audiophile who can tell you how much more of this setting or that something needs to be "right" or "perfect" or whatever.

These are as comfortable as the MeElectronics (my faves comfort wise). They're light, should fit just about any adult. Decent sized earcups. Although I was a little taken aback by the whole dongle thing at first, being set up there is nice in that unlike some other headphones I have, they don't necessarily become useless when they need to charge. You can disconnect the dongle and charge it while using them wired.

The controls are easy to use / figure out, the manual is possibly not even needed as they're pretty standard (up and down volume buttons and then one button for everything else).

Of the headphone/headsets I own, they're tied with MEElectronics AirFi as my new faves. They're both really comfortable (a huge deal to me as I have frequent headaches and ear infections, etc). This has a slight advantage soundwise and it keeps sound both in and out better. AirFi has a slight advantage when it comes to the mic. If the two were to somehow merge, they'd be perfect. As it is, this pair is really decent.

title: EXCELLENT VALUE PRICED OUTDOOR WiFi CAMERA
text:
I have been testing and reviewing WiFi cameras for the last five years. Over that time the industry has seen major advances which has led to incredible availability of high quality cameras at very reasonable costs.

I had no problem setting this camera up on my network. I set it up vis Ethernet cable and WiFi and each time it connected without any issue.

Due to security precautions I never use cloud based storage in relation to WiFi cameras because that amount of constant data transfer opens your network to unnecessary hacking. The only cameras that I employ in my home allow for local storage - whether to a dedicated hard drive / served or individual micro SD held within each camera. This camera can hold up to a 128 Gb micro SD card. The card will over write the oldest data first - how much the card holds is dictated by the settings you select.

It’s important to know that by default the camera is set to record and save to the cloud. That can easily be reset in preference settings.

The camera provides a crystal clear 1080p image. I found little to no lag with my mesh WiFi network - typically camera lag has to do with individual network properties rather than the camera itself. As with the vast majority of outdoor cameras pan and tilt controls are not possible with this camera as it has a fixed lens.

This camera has a built in microphone and speaker allowing for 2 way communication making it ideal for placement at home entrances. In addition it has motion detection and an alarm function that can be set when you are away. If motion is detected you can have it set to alert your phone, record and / or record the action.

I found all of the controls intuitive and easy to control. The app is well designed allowing for the installation of multiple cameras and easy switching between multiple camera views.

In my tests I found this to be an excellent budget friendly WiFi camera that as long as you utilize the micro SD card feature is quite secure.

This is a camera I would recommend.

title: Newbie's first impressions of digital tv and this box.
text:
Firstly, you can take advantage immediately of the new digital transition. Extra channels are already up and running. The FCC allowed each station to broadcast up to four stations at a time. Here in So Cal PBS now has an all Spanish broadcast, NBC weather & sports rebroadcasts. So there will be programs/stations that your cable subscription just won't cover.
Here are a couple of links to get you on your way to making a decision:

[...]

click on the first PDF and you might figure out how to get the Consumer Reports ratings for the convereter boxes. Apparently what's availible now on Amazon are one's with the best picture. But digital pictures are ghost-free so the pictures will look better regardless.

[...]

This should help a little to alot as well.

As for functionality/set-up of this particular unit let's just say reading the instructions was not even a consideration. You hook your antenna F connector to the box, hook the included F cable from the box to the TV, plug the included 'wall wart' ie voltage adapter to the ac source & converter box, once you have a green led glowing, push menu on the very ergonomic remote control and have the box automatically look for digital stations. If you had to put up with snowy pictures in the past you should be impressed with the difference in picture quality. However, pictures from extra weak signals will stall & pixelate. Satellite transmissions did the same thing so this anomaly should be rather familiar to long-term tv watchers.

There is also composite audio/video rca jacks for hooking up to an AV receiver, so you should get Dolby digital fidelity, However surround 5.1 sound would come from an optical/digital co-ax jack which this unit does not have, and I don't think any Government paid units have s/pdif jacks either. The AV receiver would do simulated surround sound which should suffice should you so choose to engage. But good ol' plain ol' stereo still has it's merits, trust me. Clarity might be one virtue.

This 'not being sold right now' unit also has pass-through. Just turn it off and the old familiar analog stations should come through to the tv even though the box is off. After February they won't be there; however.

Like I indicated, remote is as simple as it gets but I like it. Batteries for it included.

I don't expect this review to be viewed much, but hopefully the links will get you going in the right direction.

Good Luck. I think you'll like the transition.

text:
I own a a streaming device from each major brand and I'd only put the Fire TV Stick ahead of the Google Chromecast. And that's mostly only because the Chromecast has no remote, which some consider an advantage.

The remote for the Fire TV Stick is decent, although it has no volume buttons for the TV, unlike some others. I like it better than the Roku remote, but the remote is the worst problem with the Roku.

I'm not a fan of voice commands, because they're so unreliable, and Alexa is no different with it's wonky behavior. I asked Alexa to change the channel last night, but it instead sent me to the home screen, where an ironic advert was boasting about this very capability. Voice command technology has been about the same for over 20 years now, so I'm not sure why it's suddenly considered cute and useful.

However, the main problem with the Fire TV Stick is the interface. There is no organization, so it's really difficult to find specific programming. It just seems like Amazon is trying to sell you stuff, rather than offering the service you paid to receive. I recently read that Amazon is working on improving the interface and it needs it really bad.

Update: I forgot to mention the network latency. Apparently Amazon sells a more expensive version with a faster network card, which is needed, because the Fire TV Stick is SLOW. My home network is great and other streaming devices have no trouble, but the Fire TV stick regularly buffers and has other errors that I suspect are network related. Which begs the question "Why sell a streaming device that's too slow to stream?"

also there are time limits to back up and again the default is bad, only 15 minutes. so at 15 minutes it just stops and you don't know what backed up and what did not. the max setting is an hour and a its easy over 2 days to collect photos and video clips that can take an more than an hour to backup so it can still drop mid-sync. also, if it does fail before complete it tells it failed but again you have no idea what was backed up and what was not. it does not seem to back up/upload to the drive in sequence.

title: Pocket-Sized Telescope Delivers Bang for Your Bucks
text:
This BARONAGE MONOCULAR TELESCOPE (12X42 High Power BAK4 Prism, with Tripod and Phone Mount Adapter) delivers a lot of bang for the bucks (it costs about $30 on Amazon). It’s pocket-sized (about 6” long, 4” wide), provides good magnification, and comes with both a mini-tripod and a smartphone mount.

The magnification is quite good. The little telescope is great for hand-held viewing of nearby objects of interest. The focus wheel works smoothly, and it is positioned to be very easy to use.

You’ll probably want to use a tripod for taking smartphone photos (though I took some decent photos without one). The photos are pretty good, even if all you do is point, focus (looking at the smartphone display), and shoot. (You won’t be taking prize-winning nature photos with this monocular telescope, but the photos are fine for documenting a trip or other interesting sightings.)

In the attached photos, the tree closeup shows the tree seen in the top center of the second photo (which was taken from the same spot with the smartphone camera alone). The tree closeup appears more sharply focused in my camera gallery than it does here on Amazon; some of the detail was dropped during Amazon's processing.

MOUNTING NOTES: The telescope doesn’t come with instructions for assembling the smartphone mount, or for attaching the telescope to the tripod (see the product page for these). Note that the little projection on the telescope (actually a loop for attaching a lanyard) can be unscrewed to reveal a threaded hole for attaching the tripod.

Also, note that the smartphone mount uses a threaded piece (a round cap with a threaded hole) that screws onto the flat positioning bar that allows you to adjust the position of your smartphone and its camera lens. It’s easy to overlook the cap’s fine threads. The round cap piece fits over the viewer end of the telescope to hold the smartphone clamped in the mount’s pull-out jaws. The mount worked fine with my Samsung Galaxy S7 Edge, and I didn’t even have to take the phone out of its Otterbox Symmetry case.

Both brought in most of the local stations, but I could not get CBS (no NCIS!) nor NBC, which are broadcast from the top of a high mountain range that blocks reception for much of the metro area (most stations are broadcast from a low mountain that is line-of-sight for most of the city).

The Winegard FreeVision antenna picked up all with excellent signal quality. Yes, everyone says that digital signals are all or nothing, but my experience with the other antennas showed that they could flip between all and nothing many times a second, providing the digital audio and video equivalent of old-fashioned bad, snowy analog reception. Some more distant stations are still problematic at times, but now I have the possibility of watching them most of the time. All this with the antenna just propped up on a high shelf in my living room!

I'm very pleased with this product, and it costs less than one month of basic cable.

title: Just what I was looking for
text:
One of the first purchases I make these days whenever I get a new phone or computer is a case. I made the mistake of not getting one for my last macbook and lost it to an unfortunate (and what turned out to be a very expensive) accident.

When I finally got around to getting it replaced, I was looking for a case to provide some adequate protection but that also wouldn't risk screwing up the computer. I was worried about the cases that "clamp on" to the computer either because I could see the possibly of accidentally cracking the screen myself when putting the case on, or the case potentially warping the shape of parts of the computer over time. I had tried a couple of the plastic shell cases in the past but they basically broke apart over time because of how cheaply made they were.

I finally decided on this case as it seemed to be what I was looking for.

The computer very easily slides in and stays put. The lower part of the case covers the entire bottom section around the trackpad and below the keyboard, while two little tabs at the top hold the upper part of the case in place. The case is pretty thick as is the leather covering it.

What I like most about it is that it covers the entire computer without needed to clamp anything into place. I also like that it covers the entire bottom section of the laptop, the area where I usually keep my hands when I'm typing or using the trackpad, so it seems less likely that it will get worn over time.

I'm not sure how much protection there would be if literally dropping the computer from some type of significant height, but I imagine most cases wouldn't do much to protect in those situations. It does seem like it'll provide pretty adequate protection with general use though.

I've only been using it a few weeks so far, but it seems like it will probably last a good amount of time. For this price range, even if it only lasts for a year or two, I would feel absolutely fine purchasing the same one as a replacement at that point.

title: Superior sound, but not so good app and instructions
text:
I received one of these as a free review sample. Up front, the reason I subtracted a star is the set-up using the libratone app is maddening (to say the least.) On the other hand the sound quality is simply the best I have come across for a wireless speaker. That means I have to eat some recent words along the lines of there is no bluetooth speaker that is truly audiophile quality. This speaker disproves that.

Out of the box this quickly pairs and connects to bluetooth devices. I tested mine with a Note 4 phone and it took literally seconds to have it up and running. I was so blown away by the fact that this speaker reproduces music in a neutral manner by default that I was ready to sit down and give it a glowing review. Then I downloaded and installed the app.

The app is the Achilles heel. It had trouble finding the speaker, and the scant instructions were not very helpful either. Some how, some way it finally found the speaker, then was totally confusing when it came to setting up my personal profile (speaker location, bias and other features.) It also presented me with radio stations that were accessible via WiFi, and after connecting to my router I was able to access those. However, I am not personally interested in those offerings so did not explore them too deeply.

Basically, the app is good for linking multiple speakers, and some basic controls. Since I still cannot get the profiles set correctly I cannot speak about those. I will say that out of the box, without the libratone app and just connecting from my phone via bluetooth this speaker is spectacular. That is why I gave it the four stars that I did.

Bottom line: if you are looking for [possibly] the best bluetooth speaker on the market (and, yes, that includes Bose), this is it. If you want a speaker that can do everything this one is supposed to do, including fine tuning it for your room and musical tastes, you may be disappointed or frustrated. With a more intuitive app and more detailed instructions this would easily be a solid five star product that would keep Bose engineers and marketing up late at night. Until that happens, though, it's merely a superior bluetooth speaker that has crossed over into audiophile country.

title: Picture is beautiful & truly plug & play but..
text:
First off I was a little irate with this product. I was so excited when it arrived today, that I was tracking Amazon. Okay upon opening this monitor the packaging was done right. Everything you need is in the box.

I am a coder and I needed this monitor to work perfectly with my Macbook Pro 2020 version.
This is from my experience others may have not experiences the trails and frustration I dealt with. I was seriously debating on returning it to the UPS store.
I couldn't get the picture to work. I worked on it for about 30 minutes and started surfing the web. I came across a video and watched this guy plug it in on the left side and it worked. So it will help to read and look at the pictures in the booklet first.

To save you the hours of frustration I experienced with this product, I will give you the information you need for this to work minutes out of the box. If you want to read this instead of the book.

1. Plug the USB-C port into the left side of the monitor. (I did all the other ports except that one.)

2. Plug into your USB-C port and the picture will work. No stand by or black-outs unless you use all the other ports besides the one on the left.

3. Issue: How do you have more than one thing on the screen?
System preferences>display>arrangement (important!)
The white box in the arrangement tab above the box, that is your Macbook. The second box is your monitor. If you want the monitor on the right side, move the box without the white bar over to the right. The same goes for the left. Now drag that picture over to the side your monitor is on and Bam!!! Beauty!

4. Problem: You don't want to use the volume on the monitor you'd rather listen on your Macbook.
System preferences>sound>output>slide that over to MacBook Pro speakers and take it off that Z1 crap. (That took me a while too.)
Overall, after the stress and migraine, I endured trying to figure this product out. I will have to say it works perfectly for my needs for now.
You better bet your bottom dollar if I have one issue with this product I will be returning it ASAP! Spending more than a hundred dollars on any product during COVID 19 is too much.

Overall I am glad I made this purchase and I'm glad I didn't take it to the UPS store to return it.

title: Not perfect but very good for the money
text:
For the price this is a very nice USB microphone, I would agree with other reviewers that it performs on par with or better than similar competing USB condenser mics in this price range such as Blue Snowball or the Behringer C1.

I do wish it came with more accessories though similar to the non-USB version. The Aokeo AK-60 XLR version comes with a scissor boom arm, shock mount and pop filter for the same price.. so if you do happen to have a compatible audio interface with phantom power then I would recommend the XLR version.

The main annoyance with this mic is that when using it in windows 10 the driver does not have native mic gain control option. In many recording programs you can boost the mic gain via other means but if using this mic for gaming or other purposes through the native drivers then you will have to be very close to the mic to produce adequate volume (ie you pretty much need a boom arm) or otherwise you will need to boost gain via external passthrough program such as APO equalizer. I have also tried this mic in linux and the drivers there do have native gain control.

Overall I do think the sound quality and construction of the mic is good for the price and I would recommend it .. just note that if using windows 10 you will probably either need a boom arm or need to use external software to boost the mic gain. A boom arm is strongly recommended anyways to prevent extraneous noises like keyboard clacking, etc..

title: Very impressive!
text:
Fastest new computer start-up ever. From box to MS Outlook inbox in 6-7 minutes … including iPhone contacts & calendar sync, including Cloud sync. This used to take time, hours … days of downloads and starts and restarts. Dell has laced up Cortana to verbally walk through the setup process with the clearest voice and response I’ve seen. Very impressive! Dell is hands down the best I’ve experienced at getting you up and running fast. Minimal bloatware.

My application is business/internet from lap/table to car seat to site. I tote my computer walking miles on the job using various power modes.

I’ve been sold on the 13.3” size by day and switch to my engineering work station by night. If you are looking at a 13.3”, Asus and Dell are the leaders duking it out for market. As I have both, I’ll compare and contrast to answer questions regarding stuff I’ve found important between them

Newest Dell …
- Extraordinarily fast … speed has not been a discriminator for non-game use for some years. I can’t detect one faster than another. It’s just really fast. It behaves like MS and Dell are better integrated behind the scene than Asus.
- Dell is physically smaller and presents a ¼” display bezel to reduce the footprint and shave about ½” off the external X and Y.
- Dell’s LED-backlit display appearance is superb. The 4000:1 contrast is a noticeable attribute. Viewing angles appear to be like >60 degrees all around (outstanding!). It seems unusual that Dell incorporates a UHD graphics card to drive an FHD display ... I suspect a UHD display is coming when competition demands.
- No touch screen. I don’t like the touch screen 95% of the time (thin film over LCD, busy pointy fingers on the screen make stuff happen) … but you pick’um.
- Keyboard illumination has moved into my must-haves. The Dell delivers a different take in light piping. It works OK. In daylight, the Dell keyboard has to be turned off if you want to read the keys. Could be the color or light pipe strategy, the illumination obscures the key characters like an optical illusion. The Asus keyboard lighting is better.
- The keyboard of course feels different. Asus uses membrane switches offering minimal tactile feedback and less noise (I think it’s faster). The Dell is using a spring key switch to provide more tactile feel and audible ‘click’ feedback. User decide. Both work fine for me.
- Integral sound quality is comparatively outstanding from the uber-tiny speakers. Dell has fixed the typical awful anemic 13.3” sound quality.
- The Skype view camera is at the bottom of the Dell display providing crisp up the nose hole vision. Come on Dell! You gotta be kidding! It’s awful. This is not a Skype’r PC.
- Very responsive touchpad. Better than Asus.
- Face recognition is by True Key and works fine. After a couple initial failures, the fingerprint reader works great ... faster than the FRT.
- The 128G SSD might have concerned me a couple years ago. Asus standard is 256G. However, cloud and share applications have become so good and so responsive that I simply don’t store data locally from the start. The paradigm that more SSD is better is obsolete for me. I’m not going to suck up 128G.
- Not initially obvious, the Dell keyboard deck is made from an excellent composite. Water beads up on it, great for sneezes and general hygiene. Easier to keep clean than the anodized metal Asus top deck.

I'd say the chief consideration for the Dell is the USB-C only connectivity that for the moment, must be dongle/hub adapted to your USB A-B, HDMI peripherals. As these 13.3” offerings get faster and lighter, they have to get thinner. This Dell is the thinnest I’ve seen and too thin to even fit a USB-A port in it. USB-C thin is the tech trajectory so get with the program.

So my wireless mouse here is hanging off an adapter dongle. Who among typical users even have a USB-C Thunderbolt device to plug in? The Thunderbolt 3 Type-C ports run at a blazing 40Gb/s transfer rate and support full 4K TV and more … for now, you will need to buy an adapter hub to plug your HDMI, and various collections of USB A and B peripherals. The Dell is significantly ahead of the market here. On the plus side, it’s been a while since I’ve had to do some uncharted pathfinding and the USB-C, Thunderbolt 3 connectivity is going to be interesting for me.

The bottom line … if I need a day with the best display and no mini-mouse, I’ll take this Dell. If I need to be flexibly capable for connecting HDMI and USB A/B on the fly, I’m going to use the Asus. If the newest Asus display stepped up to this Dell performance level, it would be a toss-up. For now, 95% of my ‘joy!’ is in the display and sound quality. The 5% negative includes the nose-hole-cam and its incompatibility with an adult video conference.

Overall very impressive, excellent value for money. Kudo's to the Dell team for this CES 2018 winner!

title: solid product if a bit kludgy
text:
The home is a decent little alarm clock/speaker, though not always the finest in terms of design.

What does it do?
Acts as an alarm. Some people I noted were annoyed that you had to cycle through the minutes to set the time and alarm and while an hour button is easier, if you hold down the button it really zips through pretty quickly. In other words, you really don't have to plod through minute by minute. To give a sense of that, it took me 10 seconds to speed from 6:00 am to 10:00 am. So really, this isn't much of an issue in my mind. It has two alarms, which is a nice touch. The alarm can go to either the radio or to your input device, though that is a bit iffy depending on your device. It worked with my ipod touch but you're going to want to make sure your device works as it should. One problem is that it is not very easy to see in the dark.

Acts as a radio: the reception was quite good; I had no trouble with local stations. All tuned in well.

Acts as a speaker: the sound is decent for what it is. It certainly isn't going to replace your stereo or even a set of decent bluetooth speakers, but that isn't really its goal and for what it's meant to do, and what its probably target audience is (children, tweens, young teen) I'm sure it's fine.

Work with audio devices--this is a bit mixed. I've had variability with a range of Apple products. They all work in terms of producing sound, but the volume varied amongst them at times so that even with the volume all the way up on both devices it was surprisingly low. Not inaudible or anything, but not loud enough for good entertainment (probably OK for an alarm). You also just basically sit your device atop between two plastic "walls"--there's no cradle or anything and so there isn't much difference between that and just lying it flat next to or atop it. It charged my devices, but it's not a charging cradle, which would have been nicer. Instead there is a USB charge slot on the bottom of the device and you use your own charging cable. The same is true for the audio--you use a cable jack into your device (this one is provided) to link the two. It's an adequate design, if not an elegant one.

Glow/change colors: Well, it does do this. My response? Meh. But then, again, I'm really not I'm assuming the target audience. It doesn't do a anything for me, but kids and tweens might find it interesting. At the least, it isn't obnoxious (not too bright, not too fast-changing, etc.)

it's plastic, but it feels pretty hefty and the build seems decent if a little cheap. I certainly didn't have the sense that it would be fragile or break down soon or anything.

in the end, I'd say it's a decent little device for a tween sort. Not sure it's worth 50 dollars, but it's not exorbitant, just maybe a little pricey. If you're just looking for a speaker, I'd say there are bluetooth ones out there that provide better sound for the price. But if you want a speaker/alarm/radio/something to look at now and then, it's a decent purchase.

title: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are Reliable!
text:
Since I am a fan of audio equipment, I usually replace my receiver every 2-3 years. I purchased the Onkyo TX-NR626 on WOOT a little over a year ago. This unit replaced a Yamaha RX-V671.  I will try to leave things out of this review that other reviews have already talked about.

Wi-Fi and Bluetooth
To my surprise, I have never had any issues with Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. My Wi-Fi network uses WPA2, and I use a variety of Android devices to Bluetooth to the receiver. This means that from a back room of the house, I can turn the receiver on via the Android App, and Bluetooth whatever I want to whoever is in the living room.  One time out of the blue I made thunder play loudly to an unsuspecting room full of people and animals. The pandemonium that was created as a result of that, was both memorable and delightful.

Remote
The remote on my RX-V671 never saw much use, due to how cumbersome it was to use  The remote on this Onkyo is so easy to use, that I now use it instead of my Logitech Harmony.  I use the Onkyo remote to control my receiver (of course), the TV set, the xBox, and the LG Blu-ray player.

Sound / Setup
It sounds as good as the RX-V671, but is easier to use.  I felt that the Yamaha had too many unnecessary settings, which actually made me want to play with it less.  What I don’t like about the Onkyo though, is that the labels for the buttons on the front of the receiver are hard to see.

The famous HDMI sound issue
This happened to me twice over the last year.  Each time I needed to unplug it, and plug it back in to resolve the issue.  I don’t think this is related to heat, at least in my case, as I have plenty of room on top for ventilation which is open on either end to enable a cross draft.

title: They're okay, but won't be my main headphones
text:
Let's start with the positives:
- Nice carrying case
- Stylish headphones
- As soon as you put these on, you'll notice sounds are already very muffled. Turn on your music and, well, you're pretty much set. If you want to get lost in your music, you will.
- Easy to use controls. You likely already know how to use them, without needing the manual (volume +/- buttons and a center button for call control / playback functions).
- Decent sound (sorry, I'm not audiophile enough to get into details, I was satisfied enough with the sound quality with several different types of music and audiobooks).

The negatives:
- Ear cups seem slightly smaller than on my other headphones.
- Headphones overall seem either smaller than all of my other headphones, I had to wear them awhile to feel comfortable in them (for the first 20 minutes or so, I kept adjusting them) but if I wear them much longer they'll start to feel a bit heavy. They definitely will not win the comfort test.
- They're not just corded, they have a cord that is hardwired into them. So, if something happens to that, good luck, hopefully it will be minor enough to tape up I guess? Otherwise it's a new pair of headphones.
- The controls seem a bit high on the cord, I suppose because of the mic, but if you use them primarily for music it's a little awkward to use.

Overall, they're actually a good pair of headphones they're just fairly small and not the most comfortable pair I own because of that. I'll definitely use them, they just won't be my primary pair.

title: Works great, but company needs to clarify and enable cable length options @ time of ordering.
text:
The camera and kit are a superb value. Installation was not difficult (including BOTH TIMES, I had to install the cable). Let me explain: When ordering it doesn't tell you what size cable comes with it, which is a 23 ft. cable. I found this out the hard and dirty way after a couple of hours on a winter Sunday afternoon painstakingly dragging myself underneath my truck; routing, securing, and cable-tying the camera cable from the back of my 2009 Ram 1500 (crew cab short bed) to the front, just to find out when I went to bring it through the firewall, I was about 5-7ft too short to reach the middle of my trucks console and mounting location. Pretty frustrating after spending hours to install and come up short. On re-reading the instructions by LKL they advised 'if cable too short, contact us for the longer 33ft. or 50ft cable'. Uhm OK, and I sent an email, and to their credit, they responded within a couple of hours asking for the size I wanted that would work. Unfortunately, a "short splicer" cable wasn't an option with both male finish end couplers on their cables to simply "Splice" into what was already routed 95% of the way already, so I asked for the 33ft. one. They sent it immediately, and I got it a few days later with plans to complete installation the following weekend from my original effort. So, new cable in hand I had to re-route the new cable basically starting over. A bit frustrating BUT hopefully this post will change their ordering system to ask "cable size" based upon application upfront; like for a car. SUV, truck, or RV. If, not simply message them ahead of time to install to see if they can send you a longer cable. not as efficient, but will save you the double-install time.

That said, I really like my camera. It has great clarity, good screen size, and detail. I like the flexible options for 16:9 vs. Narrower field, grid options and adjustments, etc. I also recommend adding LED back up lights to improve the night view of the camera which already includes some LEDs to help with night safety (you are likely reading this because you want better safety, and rearview vision, especially at night, correct?) You will already be removing one taillight assembly installing the splice-in to power the camera with the backup light wire, so you might as well install LED Backup bulbs both sides of the taillamp assembly.

I had a perfect spot in mind to install my camera in the center on top of my dash above the radio into a little "coin tray" recess. I had to snip about a half-inch off the camera holder base front and back to make it nestle in the bottom and adhere with the provided mounting tap securely. If I had it to do over again I likely would get their wireless camera product first, then see if the wireless signal worked OK given the length of the truck. (They don't recommend their wireless version for larger vehicles, like full-sized SUV's, trucks, or RV's but reviewers have reported satisfactory results with trucks and SUVs) Although it's a bit more $$ for wireless the amount of install time required for do-it-yourselfer's, or professional installation would be well worth it. If the wireless signal isn't good enough, return it since it wouldn't have been installed fully; then just order up this wired option. Good luck and happy backing up!

title: Just Like The More Expensive Wire Without The Insulation
text:
I've always wanted to know if the much more expensive wires are really better than basic 16 gauge wire. Our electrician always said that 16 gauge wire is 16 gauge wire. The only difference in the heavy duty wires is the insulation that makes the wire look thicker, along with a flux tube.

To find out for myself, I compared our much thicker Monster speaker wires to this Amazon basic wire. I can't hear any difference in the sound at all, but our large Definitive Speakers are in the basement, where it is not a perfect environment for wires to be on a damp cold floor. Our electrician said that's probably why the store told us we needed the expensive Monster wires. He said the insulation would be a good thing in a damp, cold space.

As for the actual sound this Amazon Basics 16 gauge wire gives- it is no different than the expensive Monster insulated wire we have on the basement floor. Our electrician was right, 16 gauge wire is 16 gauge wire, and adding insulation doesn't change the sound at all, but if you have a damp basement, then the insulation is a plus. This Amazon Basics 16 gauge wire is exactly the same as the Monster insulated wire in sound and we will use it everywhere in our house, except the basement. It's a fantastic buy for the price and sounds exactly like the expensive brands.

title: limited battery life, but great gaming laptop for the money
text:
Like all dedicated gaming laptops, this is a big heavy high-powered machine. It is portable enough to lug over to your buddy's house for play dates, but it is too bulky and heavy to carry to work everyday. Construction is very good with an aggressive-looking aluminum case to match the aggressive-sounding "Legion" product name. Mechanical keyboard has decent (but not the best) travel and the large keys are backlit so you can easily play your games in the dark. Dolby Atmos audio works well for games, but is kind of thin for music or movies unless you hook it up to external speakers. This Y720 version has a 1080p IPS display, which is OK but not as bright or contrasty as some other laptops I have used. There is also a more expensive 4K display available, but I have not tried that.

Core i7 CPU with 16GB of RAm gives you really great performance. This machine is easily powerful enough for any games I tried on it. Even though performance is throttled somewhat when run off the battery, battery life is still less than 2 hours under heavy use (maybe 6 hours with light use).

For the money, it is hard to go wrong with these Lenovo Legions. If you don't want to spend more than $1000, the cheaper Legion Y520 is almost as good for most types of games and costs $300 less.

title: Quite a unique system that's not for everyone, but it's pretty cool for those who appreciate it
text:
I've owned a variety of home audio, home theater, and soundbar setups over the years. The former two categories are a bit easier to evaluate than soundbars for a variety of reasons, but I'll do my best here. Soundbars are seeming a commodity, but many try to offer something unique which can make comparisons a bit indirect, as we have here.

This unit comes swinging with a few clear positives:
* wireless rear units
* some HDMI support (2 barely scratches the surface for me, but for many users that's enough)
* ARC support on the HDMI (if your TV is less than 2 years old this can be very handy)
* Bluetooth with some enhanced protocols and NFC to boot
* You can use as three separate Bluetooth speakers
* limited room correction (spacial calibration) and some enhanced DSP modes

It also starts off with some limitations
* relatively small sound bar (no room for larger drivers or greater spacing)
* small sub (physics are what they are)
* battery powered portable speakers more of an as needed satellite than a permanent solution
* only 2 HDMI (ARC may help, but not with my TV)
* no USB for media (firmware only)
* many users may not get the most out of it

FYI it does come with a wall mount

If I had to some up my impressions of this unit, I'd say it was clever. It's not the best sounding unit, but it does a lot with a little (quite literally in the case of the overall volume of space this tiny setup uses). The dockable and removable satellite speakers that can work as standalone Bluetooth speakers as well as the mic for the spatial calibration is rather clever. The audio processing that happens to give this unit a larger than reality feel is clever, and the overall experience is a bit unique from other sound bars. It doesn't so much work the way you expect it to, and you need to work on its terms. That being said, the flexibility is there. It can work with HDMI, either as a two way switch or using ARC, but it can also work with digital coax, optical digital, and analog in. Bluetooth works in a few ways, and you can use the portable wireless speakers as you see fit. You actually have three separate Bluetooth speakers!

In the end this is all a great way to make the most of a modest system, but there are always compromises. The battery powered satellites limit their use as a permanent home theater setup and the main sound bar is a bit week too. If you appreciate the variety of uses this offers and make the most of it, it's a great system. Many users simply want a good soundbar, and for the price, it's not that good (in that traditional role). The sound quality is good, but far from great. If you want a great sound get a [[ASIN:B007WLQNUQ BIC America FH-56 Surround Sound Bar with BIC Acoustech PL-200]] and a decent 5.1 or 7.1 receiver (it's not a powered sound bar).

If you've read this or otherwise familiarized yourself with what it does and how it works and it all sounds good--I recommend this. It's really novel and well thought out. If this seems confusing or has stuff you don't think you'd use, well you may want to try something else.

text:
Hands down the best headphones I've ever put on for bass. I ran them through my audio tester and these picked up way lower tones than my Senn's which have been my long standing pair for bass. It does seem to come at that cost of picking up the higher notes, but honestly when pitches are that high, they are annoying and I'm fine with the headphones not picking them up. I don't need to hear a dog whistle...

Mid-range was true, sound was immersive, the headset was light and comfortable. A bit warm on the ears but pretty much all closed style headsets are.
So why the three stars?
OMG the constant never ending hissing. Unless you are playing something loud enough to cover it up, it is always there. Even when I turned off ANC, even when I switched to ambient mode. HIIIISSSSSSSSSSSSS. I tried to ignore it but it was always there. I work on the computer and sometimes I have to hear audio tracks and othertimes there is silence, I have to physically remove these every time I am not playing something or HIIIIISSSSSSSSSSSSSS. Honestly have no idea how other reviews aren't bothered by this, its the loudest hissing static I've ever heard coming through headsets.

If you are like me and do not have sound coming out the entire time you are wearing them, do not buy. They will make you insane with rage, RAAWWRRR.

If you are only going to wear them while listening to music, and want the best bass you can find, buy these they are AMAZING for that, seriously. But ugh that hissing.

title: Give and Take: A Different Perspective
text:
Let me begin by saying that I am not gifted in the arena of art. I am more technically oriented and as such I use tablets in different ways than most people. For that reason, this is likely going to be a very different review than that of most others on here.

I use pen tablets for handwriting and as general pointing devices as I find them to be more comfortable than mice and trackballs. I started experimenting with tablets a couple of years ago with a Bamboo small, which worked well but was just too small for me. I then compared a Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch to an Intuos4 and it took no time at all to determine that for me, the Intuos4 was a much better choice. With the release of the Intuos5 I jumped at the chance to compare it to the Intuos4, and so far I like it but I have found a couple of things about it that are, in my opinion, less than ideal.

I am using an Intuos5 on a Core i7-based laptop with 8 GB RAM and Windows 7 64-bit.

The very first thing - installation. Installation was about as painless as could be. I plugged in the tablet, installed the drivers and I was able to start using my tablet immediately without any issue. That's a big plus right off the bat. I have had trouble with installs in the past, in particular with the Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch, so having a smooth install is a great relief.

There is one thing about the install that troubles me, though. This tablet is capable of left- or right-handed use, so by simply rotating the tablet it is easy for anyone to use it. However, unlike the Intuos4 the Intuos5 only has a USB plug on one side, and it's the edge that always faces away from the computer. This means that the cord will always run above or below the tablet when plugged in unless it's plugged in to a USB hub of some sort. Perhaps that is not a big deal to some, but to me it is a minor irritant. The included USB cable is long enough, though, that I can hang most of it off the far edge of my desk. I suppose it's a good thing that my desk faces the wall.

I immediately grabbed the pen and started writing, and what I have found is that the Intuos5 seems to be a little more sensitive than the Intuos4, which means I can write a little more softly and still get what I want from it. Wacom did a good job of adjusting the sensitivity to the pen and subsequently turning off the touch feature. With my Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch the pen had to be very, very close to the surface of the tablet before touch was disabled, and even then the tablet kept trying to zoom on me as I wrote. Not so with the Intuos5 - the sensitivity to the pen seems to be good up to about an inch from the surface, which is fine for my purposes.

The surface of the Intuos5 does seem to be a little rougher than that of the Intuos4, so expect the nibs to wear more quickly. Though it has more texture it still feels very natural to me and I have no issue with writing on the surface. That said, why make it rougher so that it eats the nibs faster?

While the buttons along the side are configurable, I don't mess with them. I do use the scroll ring though and it works well. It is sensitive to light touch and so far has given me no trouble at all.

For a good graphics test I brought up Corel Painter and did a little doodling. The tablet and Painter work together quite well. Painter was able to determine at what angle I held the pen and it allowed me to make nice strokes and then reverse the pen to erase without any hassle. I really have not tried to push the tablet through all of Painter's features (which would do a great job of showcasing what the tablet can do) but I did enough to convince myself that the Intuos5 is a strong tool for the really artistic individual.

The Intuos4 has a small, no-frills 3-button mouse where the Intuos5 has touch features that make it work like a giant laptop touchpad. This comes down to personal preference. I never use the mouse on my Intuos4 but the touch features on the Intuos5 are very handy and convenient. Others may find the removal of the mouse to be a deal-breaker.

So far, the handwriting recognition seems to be about equivalent to that with the Intuos4. I have had to adjust my writing habits because of my using tablets for this, so a lot of the retraining took place long before the Intuos5 came. The recognition software does a reasonable job of reading my handwriting but it still makes mistakes and requires more patience.

The Intuos5 is a really nice pen tablet. It is comfortable, it is sensitive and it has two modes for accepting input. I question why Wacom placed the USB port on the outside edge of the tablet, and I also wonder why the surface is more rough than the Intuos4, but of all the current tablet offerings on the market right now this one is the best. It's not perfect, but it does try hard. I'm satisfied.

title: 99.999999995% terrific
text:
I've had these for about 2 weeks now. For the first few days I didn't like them much, then the next few days I liked them more, and now you'd have to pry them loose from my cold lifeless fingers.

I use mine with a BlackJack II, so I don't know how well the iPod adapter does or doesn't work. With the BlackJack, at first I was frustrated because it seemed that although the pairing went well, my phone was not 'automatically' connecting to the earphones when I turned them on. I've since found that if I turn on the earphones and then hit 'play/pause' twice, VOILA!!, I'm suddenly hearing beautiful music (through the earphones, and not on my phone which gets some very annoyed looks from fellow commuters).

I do look a bit like the bride of Frankenstein wearing these things, but the sound quality is so good that I don't care. I haven't gotten too many strange looks, or at least not stranger than usual. I love the size, and the cute little leather carrying case. I haven't had any problems with the cord going across the back of my neck, and I find the earbuds pretty comfortable. The buttons are indeed small, but fingernails work well.

The only down-side to these phones (and it's probably some secret I've yet to uncover) is that sometimes, when I adjust the position of the right phone in my ear, the unit will power off. I don't know if I'm jiggling the cord in a certain way, or if I'm hitting a button (though I don't think I am). Doesn't seem to happen all the time, so I'm still narrowing down the cause. Other than that, these things are great.

Best thing about these earphones is that I am the only one that can hear them. Even when they are not in my ears, these phones can't be heard - you need to get them pretty close to your ear before you will hear sound. Ever sat next to someone on a train or a bus and their headphones are so lousy that you're bopping along with P Diddy whether you want to or not? Not a problem with these. The sound quality is superb, particularly the low tones that can be hard to hear without overdoing the bass. Love em, love em, love em (except for that powering off thing).
