title: Crystal clear networks channels was what we wanted, and what we got!
text:
Trying to decide if we were ready to cut the cord, we installed this antenna to see if we could get all the local channels. We got 40 digital channels about 20 miles west of Washington DC and the major networks are crystal clear.

The network towers we use are clustered together about 20 miles away. We have 2 or more topographical obstructions between our house and the towers (no line of sight). The Noise Margin on the networks is 35-40 dB. TVFool.com listed my location as "yellow" (which means use an attic antenna or higher). The cable drop is about 25 feet and I did not use an amplifier.

This antenna is supposed to be omni-directional but we did experience occasional signal drop on the networks with the initial "eyeball" installation (which was off about 15 degrees). Standing directly under the antenna and looking through a compass I had my son walk through the yard until he stepped into the path to the towers. Then I had him stand still, facing the antenna, and rotated it until he told me it was pointed straight over his head. That seemed to fix the signal drops. Given all the factors of our situation, I am probably maxing out the performance of this antenna. If I have any issues I'll just buy the add-on the reflector shield to increase directional performance...but for right now I don't need it.

Installation was easy (I just mounted it to the Direct TV mast). This antenna is small and light which was a big plus when climbing up a 25 foot ladder.

So far so good!

title: Sturdy, Light, Stores Flat, No Little Parts but Does Require a Bowen Speedring
text:
This S-Type Bracket is simply brilliant. It has no arms or parts to lose and packs flat. It's all plastic but is very sturdy. It has an umbrella port if you want it to shoot into an umbrella as is or it can be attached to a softbox as long as your speedring has a Bowen three-lug adapter on it. This is the part I didn't understand before I bought it. I thought I'd have to bolt the large round black flange into a speed ring. But it's easier than that.

That large 6" black ring/flange that surrounds the flash port is actually a socket that receives the Bowen ring. The ring pushes into the flange and twists to lock in place. The tolerances are loose and the speedring moves about a bit after it's locked in place, but it's not a big deal. It's just holding a softbox. You spin and aim it and then never touch it again. Besides, the loose tolerances allow the ring to mount and unmount easily and quickly. There is a sliding lock button on the back of the flange that securely holds the Bowen ring in.

The reason the flange is so big (6" diameter) and doesn't seem to be needed is because it's designed to hold the Neewer 24"x24" softbox and replace the L-shaped strobe holder that comes with that unit. [[ASIN:B004XY65WQ Neewer® 24"x24"/60cmx60cm Professional Protable Foldable Off-Camera Flash Photography Studio, Portrait Soft Box with L-shaped bracket & flash Ring, Outer Diffuser and Carrying Case for Nikon SB900 SB800 SB600, Canon 580EXII 580EX 430EXII 430EX, Neewer T...]] That very popular box does not need the Bowen adapter to attach to this S-Type bracket.

Fits on standard 5/8" baby spud light stands. The large plastic tightening handle is spring-loaded so you can pull outward and reposition the handle as needed if it hits anything.

A shoe-mount flash like a Nikon SB-800 or similar on-camera flash is gently but securely held in place in vise-like padded jaws. This means you're not trusting a tiny cold-shoe to hold your $400 strobe up in the air. It's elegant in its simplicity and function. Treat this right and it'll do the job for years.

title: Working well for listening to music off my tablet while I work around the house
text:
I haven't previously owned Bluetooth headphones, so I can't compare them with others. I followed the directions and had no problem connecting the ear buds to my tablet. I did have to change the ear pieces for the smallest pair as the medium size wouldn't fit properly and the ear buds kept falling out. I could walk about 30 feet from the tablet before the music started to break up due to reaching the connection limits. However, just turning around and walking back toward the tablet restored the connection. I found it awkward to use the buttons on the right ear bud to turn up or down the volume and skip forward to the next song, but I could do so. I expect it'll be easier as I get used to it. I wear glasses, but the over-ear holders still worked fine and were comfortable. These hooks and the band that goes behind your neck made me feel confident that the ear buds wouldn't drop far if they fell out. My only irritation was that you must charge the ear buds using a short USB connector, so I had to charge them using my computer. Charging can take up to 1.5 to 2 hours. An LED light indicates when the battery is fully charged. However, you can't just plug in and charge overnight as you can overcharge the battery. You need to charge your headphones at least once every 6 months to keep the battery working.

I deliberately listen to music at the lowest volume that I can hear. This may be why I didn't notice any background noise reduction occurring. The battery run time is listed as up to 8 hours. I've only used them for 1.5 hours so far, and it's still working fine. The set comes with the earbuds, a carry case with carbine, a smart phone sports armband, USB charging cable, small, medium, and large silicone earbuds, and instructions.

The wireless connection is Bluetooth 4.1. Transmission range is up to 30 feet. Waterproof rating IPX7 (withstand immersion in water up to 1 meter for up to 30 minutes). Built-in microphone. Noise reduction is CVC6.0 digital noise cancelling technology. Battery is 100mAh rechargeable Lithium-Ion. Charge take 1-2 hours via micro-USB cable. Standby time up to 240 hours. Weight 20g/0.7 ounces.

You can clean the earphones with a soft cloth, damp with diluted soap water solution if necessary. Never use chemical cleaners. Do not charge earphones when wet with sweat, etc. and wipe off the headphones if they get sweaty or wet. Quick/Fast chargers are not recommended for use with these earphones.

The multi-function button on the right ear phone has music playback functions (power on/off, play/pause, next/previous song), phone calling functions (pick up or end calls, redial), and enable Siri for the latest Apple device only.

title: Made in China.  Great picture quality. . . Easy to set-up. . . Fun to use!
text:
It DEFINITELY is very easy with very few steps to set it up. It portrays the pictures with amazing resolution--2048X1536 pixels.

With your phone, just download the small Frameo app. On the digital frame itself, click the + friend to get the number code. Enter the code on the phone app then click the pictures you want, write a caption, center the image and send! Bam, it showed up on the digital photo frame.

If you have the frame set horizontally but a picture is vertical, you can easily click on the picture, click to make it fit, suddenly it fits with faded colors in the void spaces. Also if a picture is zoomed in too much because of the alignment, just do the same thing, click it and fix it in an instant.

There are multiple settings and methods:
1. You can also just scroll through the pictures without the slideshow.
2. You can set the speed for the slideshow.
3. You can set how long the frame will stay on during the day. If you want it on only when you are home, let's say from 5 to 9pm, you can set it so the frame is on only during that time.
4. You can also set the brightness of the screen.
5. You can choose to have the captions show, or not, and many more.

Directions say your friends have to have the app to send the picture to your frame, but honestly, I think Frameo just wants many people to have their app--understandable, but some of your friends cannot add anymore apps and they can just text the picture(s) to you, then you can send it to the digital frame.

The cord to plug the frame is a little short, but it worked just fine for me!

You must buy a micro SD card and use it for backup.
Reason: anyone could click it and possibly mess up your settings or even reset it by accident...young kids...or maybe imagine your crazy in-laws during the holidays...? It would be nice to have a password to prevent accidents...but that is what the back-up is for.

This frame does not offer "motion detection", which some others do.

This photo frame is Made in China and being sold by a Chinese company on Amazon.

title: Long-lasting, privacy-protecting device
text:
I have owned this shredder for over six years, and it has endured some heavy use. It is the second home-shredder I've owned, and it is much the better of the two. It is heavy enough that it doesn't tip over, but not so heavy it can't be hauled from room to room by someone moderately strong. The front compartment holding the shredded paper is easily removed--in an identical fashion to our dehumidifier's bucket. You pull on it and the bucket comes out with a forward motion. The sound the shredder makes when in action is loud, as one would expect, but not so loud that you need protective ear plugs, such as for when you are near a kitchen blender, blow dryer, leaf blower or lawn mower.

The main thing to be careful about is to not get impatient and overload the shredder blades. Yes, you can use the backup function to try and back out paper you have overloaded it with, but it is a pain. Secondly, be sure and feed paper in straight. If you feed it in crooked, that, too, is a prescription for a jam.

When I am shredding, I lay down either a bed sheet or a tarp and set the shredder in the middle of it. This helps me corral the scraps of shredded paper flying around when I empty the bucket into a trash bag. Another option is to shred in your garage or basement, if you have such spaces, and use a [[ASIN:B00005AXI1 Shop-Vac]] to clean up afterwards. If you do it inside your house, plan on having to use a regular vacuum to clean up after each use, because a mess is almost unavoidable no matter how careful you are since this shredder is turning private papers into confetti. That's great for the shredder's intended purpose, but it does have a tendency to give whatever room you are using a strong resemblance to Times Square on New Year's Eve.

title: Good Add-On Kit
text:
This is a 3-piece accessory kit for a camera with a threaded lens (in my case, a 58mm thread). I use this kit with a Samsung NX-300 with the 18-55mm zoom lens and it fits that lens well. My experience with this kit has been mostly positive.

Included in the kit are two lens hoods and one lens cap. I will discuss each separately.

The lens cap is, to me, the best component in the kit. It does not look like a particularly exciting item, but in this case this lens cap actually fits my lens better than the original cap from the manufacturer. It is tight and is seated evenly on the lens assembly. As an added bonus is has a lanyard that allows it to hang on the lens barrel so it does not need to be specifically tracked when it is not in place covering the lens.

The second item in the kit is a tulip hood for the lens and it is neither better nor worse than the one that came with the camera. It does an acceptable job of keeping the lens in the shade instead of allowing sunlight to hit it directly. Note that when the tulip cover is in place the lens cap will not fit.

The last item in this kit is a rubber hood that works similarly to the tulip hood and it helps prevents direct light from angling in to hit the lens. This one component is the only one in the kit about which I have anything critical to say, and it’s this: when the lens is zoomed all the way in the edges of the hood can be seen in the picture. It does not take much to zoom out past it but it still merits some mention.

I am satisfied with this kit. It includes two hoods and a lens cap that in my case is better than the original that came with my lens. This is a decent kit at a good price.

They only include a slightly tapered nozzle, which doesnt allow you to get the pressure and precision you need to clean as well as a can of compressed air, even if you blast the thing using the high-power setting. If only they included a nozzle that tapers down to a tiny straw, I would love this thing. Dont buy this thinking its a complete replacement for compressed air cans.

title: A great idea that will get better over time
text:
When I was shopping around for hi-def-capable video cameras, I wanted to avoid the pitfalls that plagued previous video cameras I had purchased. Ergonomics, picture quality, ease of use, storage and especially weight were all important factors. I tried several cameras that were hi-def capable that used tapes and hard disks, but found those things to just add weight to the body. I have weakness in my right wrist that makes holding a 2 pound camera for an hour really painful. No matter how awesome the camera is, I end up leaving it at home and taking videos on a tiny point-and-shoot digital camera because it's just not worth it unless I lug around a heavy tripod or monopod. Fortunately, this unit is light and designed perfectly around the average adult-sized hand. The controls are easy to reach and the touch screen is great. I put a clear contact protector over mine to ward off fingerprints. Note that there is no electronic viewfinder on this unit...and when was the last time you used an EVF on a small video camera? Right. It saves weight!

As for the quality, it looks good on a large hi-def unit, but be aware that the AVCHD codec compresses the video quite a bit. The 15 MBps setting gives great quality, but I found the 9MBps setting to be a good compromise between space and quality. The CMOS sensor can include some graininess in the video, but you've got lighter weight when compared to a 3CCD camera. Of course, the 5.1 sound is great and the camera picks up ambience well. You have to be aware that, like all of the hi-def cameras, the real problems come during editing because simple video editors can't handle AVCHD video natively (expensive ones can and upgrades can be bought), so you're stuck with the relatively basic manufacturer software. A hard disk camera would allow for more storage, delaying the inevitable, but investing in the DVD recorder unit that is now available is a good idea. Also note that decoding and playback of the HD video signal can slow down some computers considerably...fortunately, the video looks awesome when played back through the camera to the TV via an HDMI cable.

Battery life on the included battery is not bad. It will allow for more recording time than the average user will have Memory Stick space. Long-play batteries are available, but I've found that 4GB of memory stick and the kit battery are fine for most things. If you have the portable DVD recorder unit, you can offload as you wish to regular DVDs. You can also insert the stick directly into the PS3 for hi-def playback. Note that the AVCHD codec is also used for standard definition recording and the highest standard def setting (9M) is the second-highest hi-def setting...so I just leave it in hi-def mode.

Hi-def video cameras are becoming more mainstream, but the manufacturers seem to be pushing 2 main formats. One is the AVCHD hi-compression codec that allows for longer recording at the expense of quality and the other is the HD codec (using MPEG encoding) that allows for great quality but requires bulky media like DV tapes.

Sony has a large camera that does HD very well, but it costs three times as much as this unit and has bells and whistles the average user will never even touch.

I would say that this camera addresses the large part of the market that wants something light and easy to use with good video quality. It's not going to win any awards and I'm sure next year's model will be improved on 100000000 points, but for what it is, this camera works well and I've caught some great video on it.

I recommend it, but only if you try it first and compare it to others in a brick-and-mortar store, first.

title: Audio recorded with high gain become profoundly distorted
text:
When I received this DAC adaptor I was really ready to love it. Like many other late-model iPhone owners I was disappointed in the signal reproduction of Apple's stock Lightening-to-Headphone-Plug adaptor with its cheap DAC and was trying to find a replacement that had a better frequency response and sampling rate. This device, while oddly bulky, seemed to fit the bill. The device has controls for volume and track selection like pretty much all headphones that are designed to be used with smartphones so unless you are using old-school or audiophile headphones all these controls manage to do is render the controls on your headphones inoperable. Considering this means you a reaching for controls that are going to be right next to your phone anyway, it definitely reduces the convenience factor in your controls are located up the wire near so you don't have to fishing for it in your pocket. The devices is well built out of machines aluminum, it's unnecessarily bulky and the short lightening cord makes it awkward and likely to put torsional strain on the lightening port of your iPhone- something you really don't want to do.

But how does it sound?

Initially, I was really impressed with the sound reproduction playing an album that was mixed at a lower gain amplitude, like what you'd find from a streaming service or Apple Music. In combination with my Ultimate Ears TripleFi 10s I was pleased to finally hear the full sound reproduction so that trouble of encoding my music at a 320k bitrate finally wasn't a complete waste of storage space as it was before since the stock adaptor steps bitrate down to something like 192k. (Don't quote me on that.) Anyway, all seemed well, even if the device was kind of bulky and the black finish on the aluminum started to rub off after the first day, until I played some music that was encoded with an unusually high gain. The sounds was UNLISTENABLE. It was so distorted that I was worried I was damaging my headphones. I checked the SoundWise App that you can download to update firmware and boost the signal if need be, but none of that was in use. The DAC simply couldn't handle the signal! Even the cheap Apple adaptor could play that signal without butchering the sound, albeit it in its flat, lossy way that it usually does.

Therefore, I do not recommend this product. I was really hoping to love it and that it would solve the crappy DAC problem Apple created, but it simply was not designed well. Keep looking...

title: Best mouse for precision photo work
text:
I hate trackpads and since I do a lot of editing in photoshop, I've found that this type of trackball mouse is the absolute best for precision and ease. The best thing about the ball style mice is that you never run out of room on your desk and never have to pick up the mouse to reposition it lower on the mouse pad. It also feels more comfortable than thumb-controlled trackball mice. If I'm doing a lot of scrolling, I can "walk" my first and middle fingers on the wheel to continuously scroll.

This particular mouse come with four programmable buttons. Really it's just two if you keep the standard right and left click. I programmed one of the smaller buttons on top to use a shortcut for my RSS reader. It lets me click to the next article without having to use my keyboard. I programmed the other small button to activate the scroll wheel, so I can turn that on and use the trackball to quickly scroll up and down on any website.

I've bought three of these mice over the years. All three of them work, but I've literally "dropped the ball" several times on my tile floor and it creates little dents that catch on scroll cradle. Since the balls cost almost as much as the mouse itself, I just end up replacing the whole unit. I've learned to be a lot more careful with this third one. You also need to remove the trackball every once and while to clean it since it does gather dirt and grime and can make the trackball feel like has more friction. That's easy though. You can either clean it off with your finger, or for a more thorough cleaning, just remove the ball, wet a paper towel and wipe the whole thing down.

- They produce better sound than my tablet or phone.

-The sound is tinny, and I had a hard time getting any mid or lower tones out of them. You can feel the bass when you are up close to the speaker, but it's hard finding an appropriate surface to set them on to get it to resonate.
-Cables. Comes with a mini-A/mini-A/USB-A Y-cable used for both charging and play, along with a 3.5mm M-M stereo cable for audio. I like the audio cable, but the specialized charging/connection cable could render these speakers useless if it ever goes bad. Out of the box, mine already has some flaky positions...

Overall, it's okay. Better than my tablet speakers, and definitely better than my phone, but not better than a pair of ear-buds at a comparable price point. It's a good start though, and I'll stay tuned to see what MonoPrice has coming up down the road.

I prefer analog to digital because digital electronics has to be reset every time the power drops to zero, so the analog tuner on this radio is perfect for me. title: Worth it
text: OK, it's pricey.  OK, it's a fixed lens.  I shot about 200 pictures around a golf course and duplicated every shot with my Nikon P7100.  The P7100 is an awesome camera and the 28-120 effective zoom range is handy, but for this outing I set the Nikon to the same focal length of the Fuji, about 35 mm.  I shot landscapes with sky dominate, with land dominate, water scenes, close ups of flowers, I shot using both standard and vibrant settings, I used the flash fill for portraits of my wife in full sun, half shadowed face, and full shadow.  Result:  I like the Fuji color and details in the shadowy areas better.  I like the controls better on the Fuji.  I like the old time move-yourself-to-get-the-right-composition mode of the Fuji fixed lens rather than the just zoom in or out of the Nikon.  You can set it to aperture preferred, shutter preferred, or programmed -- nothing different than on the Nikon, EXCEPT if you go aperture preferred (my preference in order to control depth of field) you move the aperture ring on the lens mount and you set the shutter speed dial to "A" (for Automatic); or if you prefer shutter preferred you set the aperture ring to "A" and rotate the shutter speed dial. On the Nikon, if you go manual or semi manual, the control rings are in places that don't make sense -- in the traditional old style sense.  OK, I'm an old guy and have been doing landscape photography since the early 70's, originally with a hand held light meter.  Now my main landscape camera is a Nikon D700 and 11 lenses and all the "modern stuff."  Still, the Fuji is a neat camera and I felt "closer" to photography by using it.

title: Outstanding Durable Cat5e Cable
text:
I have used and tested more Ethernet cables than I can remember and there is no question, all Ethernet cables are not created equally. While I had no experience with the ZOSI brand prior to testing their Ethernet cables, after thoroughly testing them I have been thoroughly impressed.

Typically any device requiring an Ethernet cable will come with one in the packaging - it will work (usually). A good comparison is those cables are much like an old car - it should get you there, whereas this cable is like a high end sports car - it will get you there lightning fast, without fail.

This Cat5e is designed to be thin, but don’t let that fool you into thinking that it lacks capacity - within the ample PVC covering contains 4 pairs of twisted 100% bare copper wires for fast transfer speeds. The connector bases are reinforced at each end of the wire which really help hold all of the wires in place even if you have to bend and twist it to fit it within the plug.

One area where this cable could use improvement is the plug hood lacks a protective rubber boot guard that protects the clip on the plug - this becomes very important when snaking the cable through walls and tight spaces. Due to not having this feature it is critical to wrap the boot and plug with a small piece of electrical tape to make sure not to unintentionally snag anything as the cable is being snaked.

I love the grey PVC shielding on this cable - not only is it waterproof, durable and will help the cable withstand damage but it can be run along a wall and then painted to match the wall color.

I used this 65 foot cable to run between a PoE switch and an external security camera, this cable supplies power and transmits data to and from that security cameras - after thoroughly testing this cable over the last 3 months I’ve been nothing but impressed by this product.

This has proven to be an outstanding, dependable Ethernet Cable - this is really a top of the line cable that you’ll love.

This is a purchase that you’ll never regret. I’ve been utilizing two ZOSI cables for a3 months now and I’ve had nothing but outstanding results from them.

This is definitely a brand and product I recommend.

title: Fantastic product for workflow optimization
text:
I have a few notes about quirks/things that I wish were different, but I wanted to start by saying that I love this thing and it has drastically improved my workflow, such that I rarely touch my keyboard anymore. As a note, I only use the key dial for Adobe After Effects since that’s where I spend 98% of my time, but I’m sure it works great for other programs as well and I like that the keys can be set up to change based on which program is active! Also, the battery life is crazy good. Thank you Huion! In case anyone is interested, I’ve included a photo of how I have mine set up for Ae. I would highly recommend this to anyone who is on the fence about it.

A few notes/quirks:
- I love that you can set the dial for up to 3 different functions and easily switch between them and also that if you only have 1 or 2 functions set up, it doesn’t make you switch through a blank function. BUT! It is a *slight* inconvenience that you have to wait for the on-screen-display to clear off before you can start using the selected function. Because of that, I rarely if ever switch functions (which really isn’t a big deal because my other hand is always on my mouse, which has a scroll wheel). Also, I wish you could swap the scroll direction, but that’s not a deal breaker.
- The keys can be set up as modifier keys (CTRL/ALT/SHIFT/etc) which is nice and those seem to work well with the keyboard and mouse for the most part, but have some weird behaviors with the other keys on the key dial. Certain keys only seem to work with other keys on the keydial, but it seems really inconsistent. For example, I have the large lower-right key set up as ALT which works to modify the first key on the second row but not the 3rd key on the second row. There are also a few keys that have a really subtle mark on them (either a dot or an arrow) and those keys never seem to work in combination with each other. As before, this isn’t a deal-breaker, but it is a slight inconvenience.
- When using a modifier key with another function, if you release the function first everything continues as expected. If you release the modifier key first, it seems to lock that key down. For example, when I’m using alt+wheel, if I accidentally release the alt key first my computer acts as though the alt key is still pressed. This happens with other peripherals as well, so it’s not an issue with Huion, just something to note if you pick this thing up (which you should)

title: Fits Sony A7s battery door, and most any camera I've tried from Canon and Panasonic! Lots of mounting options!
text:
I got sick and tired of buying unique cages for each camera I use. This cage is great because it is the most universal design I've seen while still being solid and relatively compact, and most importantly: THE BATTERY DOOR CUTOUT FITS VIRTUALLY ANY CAMERA I'VE TRIED WITH IT! This was the biggest reason I wanted it. I happen to own many different types of cameras (Canon, Panasonic, Sony, etc) and all of them occasionally get used on jobs that require attached recorders, microphones, power supplies, etc. But until I found this, I needed specific cages that allowed access to the battery on each one, otherwise I'd have to remove the camera during a shoot to replace a dead battery, which is just unnecessarily complicated. I feel like this cage is a great addition to whatever I'm using now, and likely whatever I end up using in the near future.

As a few people pointed out, the rail system on the bottom has a knob that somewhat obstructs part of the battery door opening on some cameras (I noticed this on my A7s, other types of cameras may still get enough clearance). Someone on youtube showed that they were able to remove the knob to keep it accessible, but personally I just wanted the cage part. The cage itself has the same mounting holes as the bottom of the rail adapter, so you can just leave the rails off and attach a tripod QR plate directly to the bottom of the cage, which is what I usually do. I did one time try using the entire package decked out, with the rails, a matte box and follow focus attached... I got around the battery door problem by using a dummy battery with a DC wire that attached to an external power supply (I built my own adapter, I won't go into the details now but I'm pretty proud of it!). So I was able to swap batteries via an adapter mounted on the cage instead of under the camera. But this was a much more complicated setup than I usually work with. For normally daily use, I use the cage without the handle or rails, and with the camera attached it actually fits where my camera usually goes in my gearbag. I have the handle and rails handy if I ever need them, but the price is great for the cage alone!

title: FRAUDULENT GARBAGE - AVOID - the actual size of the drive is less than 1% of the advertised size
text:
The drive was provided free of charge for review purposes.

I do not recommend this product. I cannot recommend any of the merchants who sell this product. And I cannot even recommend Amazon for purchasing this type of product. Simply said, the "512gb" advertisement is fraud, and until Amazon takes meaningful action against the Sellers committing this type of fraud, Amazon will remain the go-to place for unethical Sellers to push their fake USB drives and SD cards, at your expense.

This is not a 512gb flash drive. The few 512gb models on the market currently start at around $300. Your computer may show the size of this drive as being 512gb, but the drive has been "tricked" into displaying this inflated number. What is happening here is the same as has become commonplace on Amazon. A Seller of poor morals modifies the firmware code of the USB flash drive so that the drive is "tricked" into showing a size of 512gb, despite the fact that the drive's actual capacity is generally between 4-8gb. In other words, if you try to write 512gb of data on this drive, you will almost certainly lose at least 500gb of that data. In other words, the drive you get will be roughly 1% the size of what is advertised, and it will most likely have serious reliability problems down the road.

With any flash media purchased on Amazon (USB flash drives, SD cards, Solid State Drives, etc.), be VERY weary because there are TONS of fake products, many of which come from Amazon through their Fulfilled-by-Amazon program. Upon receiving the drive, you should manually verify that the drive is indeed what is advertised. You can use a free program like H2TestW, which tests drives by first writing X amount of data to the drive, and then verifying that X amount of data still remains after the drive is filled (with X being the advertised size of the flash drive or SD card.) Additionally, perform several checks on the health of the media, and if this is a solid state drive (or a hard disk drive for that matter), manually review the SMART data because it will show you whether or not the product you purchased is actually new.

Finally, while Amazon User Reviews can be of great benefit, there appears to be cause for concern here as well. It appears that many Sellers of these fraudulent flash drives and SD cards send boatloads of these fake products out to ranked Amazon Reviewers, and in many cases will get a positive review even if the product they sent is total garbage. It also appears that some Sellers go as far to create Amazon User Accounts and then publish a positive review on their own junk product to give it a higher rating than it deserves. So while Amazon reviews are certainly beneficial, there are limitations and this particular type of product seems very prone to abuse. YMMV.

title: Great extras but not a good typing experience
text:
I'm yet another Natural Elite fan saddened by the fact that Microsoft no longer makes it. If they started making it again and added some of the features this one has, I'd buy a lifetime supply.

I had this for about a week and really, really wanted to keep it. Having a dedicated calculator key was great, but even more useful were the page back and forward buttons and the toggle switch to change magnification. That toggle made my life much easier at work; I wish every keyboard had it.

I didn't use the riser for the front of the keyboard, though I would have used it more had I kept it just to see if it made typing more comfortable. The padded wrist rest was nice, and the keyboard itself was easy to clean. And although I don't care much about aesthetics, my colleagues all commented positively on the keyboard's appearance.

Unfortunately, the negatives outweighed all of that. The biggest problem was that the typing experience just wasn't that good. I've been using a split keyboard for years -- a Natural Elite, as it happens -- but having the center keys be larger than regular keys threw me off. Maybe it shouldn't matter, but it slowed me down and was very frustrating. Also, as noted by others, it is loud. My office has rather close quarters and everyone hears some noise from others, but my keyboard was far louder than other keyboards. Nobody complained, but I was bothered by the idea that I might be bothering others.

Then there were the customizable hotkeys that never worked. I would seem to have them set one day, but they wouldn't work the next, and searching for help online didn't yield any useful advice.

And then there was the fact that it came without instructions, not even so much as a slip of paper directing users to a web page for more info. That's absurd. Even the cheapest electronic items I've purchased have had a manual of sorts, either printed or online. It makes me wonder whether I got a legitimate product, a knockoff, or a refurbished model.

After returning this one, I got a Perixx Periboard-512. It's not a sexy looking and it doesn't come with the awesome extras that the 4000 has, but it's a smooth typing experience and I can type a report without everyone on my floor hearing me bang each letter. Ideally, Microsoft will someday resurrect the Natural Elite and add those oh-so-useful extras, but this is okay for now.

title: Excellent HDMI to SPDIF optical and analog converter
text:
This is an excellent HDMI to optical digital & analog converter. Sound & video output are excellent.

Pluses
1. Very simple, straightforward setup
2. Clear, easy-to-understand, instruction manual
3. Power adapter connector screws onto the back of the converter
4. HDMI video output is just pass-through, no visible (that I can see) video distortion
5. Supports 120Hz/4k output, which matches the output of the Sony PS5
6. The HDMI audio output is converted to both optical digital (SPDIF) and analog (3.5mm stereo) output, providing great flexibility
7. Audio & video sync is great

Minuses
1. None!

I needed an HDMI converter to pass video & sound from a Sony PS5 to a Bose soundbar (optical in) and 27 in. HP gaming monitor (HDMI in). This HDMI converter fits the bill perfectly.
The setup is easy. Video will simply pass-through, allows the full 4k/120Hz video signal from the PS5 to be displayed without distortion; video looked great on the gaming monitor.

The audio output is really the only thing that needs to be configured. If, like my setup, you are connecting the optical out to a soundbar, receiver or other speakers that don't multi-channel sound output, press the "EDID" button until you see the "4k@120Hz, 2.1CH" lit up. The optical out from the converter to the soundbar is excellent. Audio & video play back in sync.

This is an excellent converter. I highly recommend it.

title: Very happy with this tablet
text:
I am relatively inexperienced with tablets, having spent the majority of my time working with laptops. That said, I started looking for a tablet about a year ago with the intent of using one as an e-reader and I finally found a white Sony Xperia Z for a really good deal and snapped it up. I have had it for over a month now and so far I am pleased with it. There are a couple of little minor quirks that I would change but those are outweighed by the positives.

This particular tablet has a 10.1” screen with better resolution than the best 15” laptop I own. Images are very bright, crisp and clear. I don’t think I could ask for a better display in terms of image and color quality. The size is right for me, too – I had originally considered a smaller tablet which would have cost less but would have been a little harder on my eyes. Also, the screen is very responsive and has worked without any serious issue up to this point.

I have had one issue with the screen, though, and I have seen others mention this in the forums online. As I type, sometimes the screen will flicker. It does not do this every time and it is not a major problem but it is an annoyance. This is apparently an issue with this model and I read somewhere online that there is a firmware update that fixes this. I haven’t had the time to pursue this yet.

Battery life thus far has been very good. I usually have the tablet in standby when I am not using it (which to be honest is a majority of the time) and I have let it go for a couple of weeks without charging and still had enough power to work. I can’t really find any reason to complain about the battery life.

The sound quality is surprisingly good! When I have brought up anything that involved sound (such as an online video) I have been started by how well it sounds on this tablet even when I am not wearing headphones. I would expect the sound quality to be passable in a tablet but I have been pleasantly surprised.

Weight-wise, this tablet is a little heavier than I would expect but it’s not an unreasonable amount of weight. It is not uncomfortable to carry it around for extended periods or to use it as a reader for a while.

I am not really very savvy on the differences between Android versions but so far I have had no real complaints, both before and after upgrading. It has provided everything I want and need and has been very stable for me. I had a first-generation Droid phone for a long time and the Android version on that phone was nowhere near as advanced as what’s on this tablet, but it is similar enough to make using this tablet a very familiar experience.

I can’t find any real major complaints with the Xperia Z and I am happy with it. Other than the screen flicker issue when typing it’s about as perfect a device as I could want (and if there's a fix for it via firmware update then it's a problem only because I am lazy). The price is a little high – especially when not on sale – but so far it has been worth it.

title: Excellent Value
text:
I purchased 300N to extend the wireless signal for second floor about a month ago. The set up is easy. I followed one of the reviews to log in via IP address and did not use the CD. The interface is intuitive and 300N works as it was advertised.

I have a Linksys WRT610N wireless router connecting to Charter Communications cable modem. The router is in downstairs library close to front door. The room I am not getting strong signal is the second floor study at the back of the house. The distance is over 100 feet, I barely get 1 bar from Linksys router in the second floor study. I placed 300N on the second floor wall near the stairs, which about the center of the house. 300N has excellent coverage. Even it is on the second floor, I can get close to 4 bar most rooms downstairs, and 3 bar in the back porch. Speed is very good, no noticeable difference between downloading from 300N vs. Linksys.

The gears I connected to wireless network are:
1. 2 Alienware laptops running Windows 7
2. 2 Sony VAIO laptops running Vista
3. 1 Sony VAIO laptop running XP
4. 1 Sony LocationFree(watch TV from computer anywhere)
5. 1 Xbox
6. 1 PS3

All the laptops operate downatairs and upstairs so they switch between 300N and Linksys wiht ease. Xbox & PS3 connect to 300N only upstairs. LocationFree is in a room upstairs directly above the library and connects to Linksys instead of 300N.

There are two issues that prevented me from awarding 300N 5 stars:
1. Unfortunatley Charter cable drops internet connection once awhile. Rarely, I need to reboot the Linksys to restore connection and 300N will need to be reconnected to Linksys via cable. I have done so twice since I purchased the product.
2. The Sony LocationFree will not talk to 300N. Be fair, this may not be 300N's issue.

In general, I am very pleased with the product. I have been using exclusely Linksys products for 10 years and have tried their signal extender which did not work at all. I am pleasantly surprised by the friendliness of and the simplicity of Hawking 300N.

title: Great Item to Use Within Limited Parameters
text:
These color coordinated wire sleeves are nice for taming stray cords and prevent tangling, while making it easy to neatly fold wires when not in use. They are nice quality, attractive, and easy to use.

I like that you can buy individual cords in different colors so that you will always know what you have and where to attach it. This is a huge plus. And for traveling, I love how they keep my cord from knotting up in difficult spaces like an airplane seat. I used to dread the end of a long flight because after several hours of flying, my headset cord was always knotted up in such a way that threatened the integrity of the cord. The Cable Keeper is an excellent solution for cords that turn into a mass of tangles when the device is constantly being moved about. I think this item significantly lengthens the useful lifespan of a portable device cord when out and about in circumstances that put stress on cords. I find that my cords are much easier to handle when couched safely within these protectors and the colorful and flexible wires make them hard to lose and easy to manage.

However they are limited as it isn't really easy to use them except with wires that are exactly the length of the Cable Keeper! Even though the instructions give a way to shorten your cords to fit into the sleeve, it is kind of hard to do because the interior space is SO small that any extra bulk inside the sleeve just isn't really practical. In addition to that, there really is no way to shorten the sleeve if your cords are too short for the Cable Keeper, so there is a good chance that you might need to buy extra device cords just so you can fit them to the Cable Keeper. And, if you need to manage more than one cord, you will have a hard time getting more than two into the sleeve, and when you start using multiple Cable Keepers, you will still be wrangling a lot of cords that (while no longer tangled) will still be unwieldy and unsightly, especially since the loud, garish colors seem to belong in a child's playroom and not in an office or home environment. So if you have one or two small cords that will fit within the Cable Keeper, and both cords are exactly the correct length, this could be a lifesaver. If not, you could end up with a mess.

And while this could be useful if you are using it with single portable devices, but don't buy this if you are trying to invent a way to de-clutter your home or office. I still think large cable organizers like Legrand, Omni Mount or UT Wire is better for large component systems in the home or office. The Cable Keeper is great for portables but probably not the best choice for systems. Used in the right circumstances I would not hesitate to recommend it. Used in an application where is doesn't fit could end up being an expensive frustration.

title: Better than ATH Ad700x
text:
I purchased the Tygr 300r headphones by themselves through Beyerdynamic's website a couple weeks ago, so I won't be speaking for the microphone in this review.
Also, I'm not an audiophile by any means. I just like good headphones.

Comfort:
-I have a very large head. The clamp force on the Tygr is very light and pleasant. The padding on the headband is very thick and cushiony. The only thing I'm not a big fan of are the earpads. They look like they'd be really comfortable, and they are initially. However, after about fifteen minutes, the velour material begins to irritate the area around where my jaw and ear meet. It's possible I still need to wear these headphones in and I will get used to them, but as of now, the earpads are a little stiff and the material isn't as soft as you might believe from looking at it. Also, I don't have very big ears and my right ear touches up against the drivers a little bit. It's not irritating by any means, just something I thought I would mention.
-The Ad700x, on the other had, are hands down the most comfortable headphones I have ever owned. The pads on those are UNBELIEVABLY soft and large and comfortable. I wish I could put them on the Tygr. The headband actually isn't great, but to easily make up for it, grab one of those little black hair band things girl use to put their hair in ponytails and wrap it around both the support wings. Voila. Fixed. They're also incredibly light. You will forget you're wearing them. The drivers on this headphone are angled so your ear doesn't really make contact with them at all. A+.

Sound:
-The Tygr 300r have a very nice and warm sound- at least coming from the ath ad700x, they do. The bass is definitely present and it's very nice and warm. Mids are good. Highs are great- and not sibilant at all in my opinion. I know Beyer is known for their controversial high end, but I don't feel it on this headphone. Everything comes together nicely. These headphones make me smile when I listen to music.
-The ath ad700x are more analytical in comparison. The bass is anemic. Present, but anemic. Mids are very clear as well as the highs. I feel like there is more detail in the ad700x, and perhaps it is because of the recessed bass. It's a nice sound, but I don't smile like I do with the Tygr 300 when music is playing.

For gamers, I don't think you can go wrong with either. If I HAD to suggest one for gaming, it would be the ATH AD700x if you strictly play fps games and are really competitive. If you play other games, like the Witcher or Fallout- I'd definitely go for the Tygrs. Although, the imaging on the Tygrs is INSANE, so there is that. You can't lose either way.

Ease of Driving:
I currently use a soundblasterx g6 dac/amp powered by usb off of my computer motherboard.

-Tygrs are a little less sensitive than the Ad700x, so I would recommend an amp even though they're only 32 ohm. I'm sure you could get away using them without an amp, but the headphones probably won't be as loud as you would like them to be. I run high gain on about ~40 windows volume and I'm happy with them there.
-The ad700x are very easy to drive. I can run them on low gain with my amp and they sound great.

TLDR; IN MY OPINION
Tygr-
Sound better
Look better
Warm

Ad700x-
More comfortable
More detailed
Analytical

you can't go wrong with either.

UPDATE:
I've put a good 30 hours or so into this headphone and it has only gotten better. The earpads have become much more comfortable and the sound is just so solid. I recently got the Sennheiser hd 560s thinking I would like them more because, well, they're Sennheisers. I actually prefer the Tygrs. They're more comfortable for people that wear glasses (I do) and the sound is more impactful. You really feel the music in the Tygrs. The Sennheiser hd 560s is not a bad headphone by any stretch of the imagination. It's just super, super neutral and not very exciting to listen to music with.
So, I can say of all the headphones I have ever purchased in rather short 21 years on Earth, the Tygr 300r is my favorite headphone and I say that with no hesitation.

title: The most inaccurate GPS device I have ever tested
text:
I had high hopes for the Magellan Switch Up. Since Magellan has been producing various GPS devices for many years, I figured that they must have a team of designers who could pull off a new fitness device with as many features as the pre-release hype described. Unfortunately, the features are there, but the all important GPS is not!

While the Switch Up has a marvelous display, and a feature set that is enough to make even the most seasoned endurance athlete's jaw go slack and agape, the one thing that drives all of those features is completely absent - an accurate GPS. Lacking the ability to very accurately determine distance renders all of the seemingly impressive features, save the clock function, completely useless.

To all of those who gave the Switch up a glowing review, I challenge you to take it out and compare the distance that the device is telling you with an actual, measured course. How it "feels" or "seems" is completely irrelevant. Test it against a hard measured distance, and I wager that you will be shocked at the devices inability to properly calculate distance. It really is THAT bad!

While many first generation devices have been "fixed" through firmware updates, the updates to the Switch Up have done nothing to fix the accuracy of the GPS of this device. Since the heart and soul of a fitness device is an accurate GPS, the Switch Up is a zombie amongst a throng of real fitness devices.

Will Magellan do better next time? Let's hope so, because the Switch Up is completely useless in its current state.

title: Buying this was a huge mistake. Samsung service is as bad as they say. Tablet is flawed and Samsung doesn't care.
text:
I purchased this from amazon right after they came out. After a few weeks the screen started to distort in the middle. I called Samsung service and they refused to deal with it. All the rep said was "out of warranty." Nothing I could say would change his mind that it was not a warranty covered failure. How in the world can a fuzzy screen not be covered by the warranty? What is covered if not the screen? Doesn't make any sense. When I asked to speak to someone who actually understood something, he told me someone would call me back in, get this, THREE DAYS.

I've heard terrible things about Samsung service in the past, but I ignored it and bought this anyway because I have an Android phone (droid x), like it a lot more than my old iPhone, and wanted an Android tablet. Bad call. Samsung more than lived up to its reputation of treating customers like they despise them. I am still in shock about how badly they responded.

I could understand this if it was a cheapo tab, but this thing costs as much as an iPad and is designed to compete with Apples. Much as I did not want an Apple tablet, I am fully aware that Apple would have responded quickly and cooperatively, in person at the store. Samsung, on the other hand, basically said "Too bad, sucker" without even seeing the thing.

While I'll admit it is a nice tablet and I enjoyed using it while it worked, Samsung's reputation for atrocious service is an unfortunate reality. Please do yourself a favor and before you buy one of these consider seriously what will happen if you get a bad item. Check the reviews on not only this item, but any Samsung gadget. The overwhelming point to the negative reviews on all of them involves how bad Samsung service is. Do you really want to take a chance with your $600?

_________________

New information since posting review: I now know that the issue is a known problem with the tablet. Samsung clearly knew this when I talked to them, but still just blew me off. Guess they cannot fix it and simply do not know how to deal with the fact that there are so many bad tablets out there, so they simply claim it's not a warranty item.

title: Keeps up with the competition, but half the price!
text:
Photo: a comparison of the uni adapter, a Samsung adapter and another brand bought from Amazon. The other brand is a little longer and a little bigger. The Samsung is shorter, but thicker. The Uni is in the middle, size wise.

I've had the Uni adapter for a couple weeks now and have run it through some paces. We use these adapters to run Netflix and other streaming services from our phones to our big screen TV.

In short: the Uni adapter has done just as well as any that we've ever bought, and is constructed better than the "name-brand" adapter (it has a simple plastic cable and started breaking down pretty quickly, whereas the Uni has a nice braided cable). I kept the name brand cable as an emergency backup, and then forgot about it in the console for a long while. Will probably toss it now that I have the Uni cable.

All of these adapters will overheat after a while. It's just a matter of fact. Which is why you want a few on hand to switch out if you use them very heavily. Every. Single. One. Name brand, off brand, doesn't matter. But the Uni lasts as well as any of them. And at literally 1/3 to 1/2 the price of the competition? That makes it a good buy.

If you're looking for an adapter to run HD from a phone to a tv, I'd recommend this one. Keep in mind, if you run movies, you might want to buy two.

title: Feels Undone Beta and Unstable
text:
I had my eye on a nixplay wifi photo frame for almost 6 months before plunging into the 10.1 inch seed version. I initially had purchased their largest 18 inch original model and found the entire thing to be ugly, bulky, and resembling that of an older model computer screen. I just couldn't work with it so I returned it for a sleeker version. The 10.1 widescreen seed.

First impressions are a beast, and when I unboxed the seed my first thoughts where that it looked like an Amazon Kindle. Yikes! I wasn't to happy with how long and awkward it felt. Even set in landscape it felt too long but not wide enough. I wish it was a 10 by 10, but it's not, so you're left feeling as if it's too narrow when in both landscape placement or vertical. The shape just feels off by an inch when held vertically and horizontally.
The next big, what the heck moment was when I realized that the power adapter is also built into the frames kickstand. It makes for a flimsy bendable kickstand, and if someine bumps the chord it can send your prized frame hurdling to its death. Not sure what the developers were thinking here, but it made the frame feel like it was rushed right at the end. God forbid you add a built in kickstand.

The deal breaker for me was the online website and the app.

I installed the nixplay app and right off the bat couldnt sync my social media with it. That's because this feature is not available on the app. For me that was a deal killer as I had to contact customer service to figure this out, to make matters worse they kept telling me to sign in on the website to link my social media. Unfortunatley you cannot do this on a mobile device and this must be done only using a pc or laptop.
What a stupid archaic method of execution.
If you have an app make the app fully functional as to where I won't need pc access for full use of my frame.

Until those kinks are ironed out, nixplay in general feels too new and undone, as if I bought into a high end company that barely launched and is in a very uncomfortable and unstable beta stage.

I wish this company the best though, it needs work.
I came from the first estarling wifi frame about 10 years ago, and this frame doesn't feel much better than the one I picked up 10 years ago. For me that just reeks of trouble.

UPDATE
Not even a week later and already acting up. The frame drops my wifi signal every single day. I have to unplug the frame for it to catch a signal again. I imagine this cannot be good for the frame. I have contacted the company and am hoping they can address this issue, because this is unacceptable

Update

I bought another used nixplay a day after buying the 10.1 seed and learned the hard way to never ever ever buy one of these frames if it was already used.
I picked up the 12 inch model and the original owner never unpaired the frame from the original account. Customer service will not help and I basically own a brick. Working with seller for refund but what a stupid nightmare this entire thing has been. I regret ever buying it. Too bad too, it was so neat for a few hours. Pure garbage

Update

After about 2 weeks of non stop back and forth with customer service I'm ready to spike the 10 inch frame.
The unit will not stay connected to my wifi. I tried everything the company asked of me and still no connection. The worst part is that when it drops connection the only way to reconnect it is to unplug it from the outlet. This will eventually brick the frame.
Customer service closed my case for no reason and I had to reopen it because the frame still doesn't work and even being under warranty they seem ljke they don't care or want to fix the issue. I'll likely have to call the FTC because this is awful, and they should not be dragging their knuckles on a replacement since it's still under warranty

title: Wish it could be 0 stars
text: I heard Jeff Bezos on Charlie Rose last night and his enthusiasm is great. If you love all tech stuff, this may be for you. You can love to read without loving books. Bezos said the important thing about reading is that you get lost in the reading and forget the book. Well . . . sort of. Certainly, I disappear in stories. But I love the book. I want the 2 'pages' in my hand(s). When I have to stop reading, I want the feel of the book in my hand, even if it is 1000 pages. I want to look at the closed book and see how far the bookmark has moved. When I get a book, I look it over carefully. Then I savor opening it for the first time. I remove the jacket and look at the binding. Yes, I read the copyright page. And I love it when there's a paragraph, usually at the end about the font that was used. There's a whole tactile-visual experience before I start reading. I can live without an author picture and, for fiction books, without any personal info about the author other than other books written. I love the pages. In 1979, I found a sale book. It introduced me to Sigurd F. Olson, whose books are now in abundance at amazon. I didn't know who he was. The jacket photo was beautiful. But what sold me was the paper. It's a beautiful, textured paper that's absolutely perfect for his essays. (That book was WILDERNESS DAYS.)  And what a person to meet! That I'm not an outdoor/camping person was and is irrelevant. His writing is glorious. But if all I had was a Kindle, I'd never know any of that. I think all this has a lot to do with why ebooks aren't tremendously popular. My guess is that, in the end, the Kindle will be a success. Generations of children won't grow up knowing anything else, unless their parents or grandparents loved books and showed them the total joy of a real book. I do love trees and the Kindle is certainly kind to them. When I read a bad book, I tell it it should apologize to the trees it has killed. I also like picking up a pencil and making my notes in the margins. In fiction, it may just be a small arrow to highlight a beautifully written sentence or paragraph. In non-fiction books, I usually carry on a running dialog with what's written. I'm more glad than ever that I have my own library. And more than ever, I wish it was much, much larger. When I started using the Wish List at amazon, I felt guilty when I had 35 books on it. Now, I have to edit it occasionally because the number is more like 200. May Kindle wait until I die, before it is a blow away success. With my family's history, that may be another 40 years! Sorry, Jeff.

title: Excellent Chromebook
text:
This is my first time using a Chromebook and I didn't know what to expect. I mean it's sort of like a laptop in size but it runs on Chrome, not Windows.

Start-up was fast, almost super fast. You open the cover and BAM, within seconds, you're online. Very cool.

The display is HD and very crisp. I viewed a couple of Netflix nature movies and the display was stunning. No lag or fuzziness. There's a Micro HDMI so you can view on a big screen, but a cable is not included.

The wi-fi is dual-band 802.11 and is fast as well. I had no issues connecting at home, work, or the local coffee shop.

There is 16gb of local storage, but Google includes 100gb of Google Drive storage for 2 years. Personally I've never used more than 3gb of storage, so 100gb should be adequate for most people.

The internal speakers weren't great, but they didn't suck either. Sound was crisp but slightly muted. A pair of USB speakers took care of this. Soon I was rocking in the coffee shop (i forgot my headphones).

Because of my big fingers I'm not a fan of the pad thingy. I was able to plug in a bluetooth mouse and was up and running within 30 seconds. At first I wasn't sure if the Chromebook would allow peripherals, but it did with no issues.

The battery is stated to last 13 hours. I haven't gone that far yet, but I've gotten a solid 5 hours of mixed internet/video streaming use and still had 50% battery left.

title: How to program a macro button to make the computer sleep (Windows 10 instructions)
text:
I figured out how to create a sleep button by programming a macro key like this in Window 10:
1. Open Start --> All Apps --> Microsoft Mouse and Keyboard (the software installed with the keyboard, download from microsoft.com if you don't have it)
2. Open the keyboard settings, then select a button to assign a macro for (e.g. for the Web / Home button)
3. Select the "Macro" radio button and click to create a new one, name the new macro "sleep"
4. Insert the Windows Key via the "Insert Special Keys" droplist
5. Double click the Windows key to select it, then right click and choose "split"
6. Insert an "X" between the Windows Keys- this will open the right click start menu
7. Move to the end of the macro, then type arrow keys up, up, right, down, and then press enter- this selects the "sleep" menu item
8. See the picture for how things should look in your editor when done
9. Exit the macro editor and test your new sleep key!

Please click on the helpful link so that other people can find this info. It took me a while to figure out- there's no command line task to make this happen- only to hibernate- and 3rd party software isn't safe.

Oh yeah, and as this is a review- the keyboard is great otherwise, been using it for years.

title: Works Well with Canon 50D
text:
I have been shooting a Canon 50D DSLR for several years, mostly outside or with stage lighting. Occasionally, I also have been using a small camera-mounted flash, but it is weak and very limited. To improve my flash photography, I decided to try the Mago Speedlight by Pixel. This is an excellent, mid-priced flash with loads of features.

The Mago Speedlight comes with a nice soft case and a fold-out manual which guides you through the setup of the flash and includes screenshots of the back LCD. It also includes a small stand which is great for use in slave mode, and a clip-on flash defuser. The flash uses 4 AA batteries or an external power supply (not provided). It is even upgradable via a USB port hidden in the battery compartment (not tested).

The controls are easy to use after some experimenting. The manual really helps as there are so many features. The buttons are solid and the display is easy to read, with an optional green backlight.

The flash head can be tilted up and down, or rotated left or right. It also includes a built-in defuser and a white card reflector. These are very useful if you are not bouncing the flash off of a ceiling or reflector.

One interesting feature is an LED model light that can be turned on/off easily via a dedicated button. This light is quite bright and very useful for setting up your shots.

I tested the flash on a Canon 50D with 20mm and 50mm lenses and somewhat cooperative subjects (my kids). After learning the controls, I took several excellent pictures.

The flash supports E-TTL mode, manual mode, and multi-flash mode. I tested all three.

To test the multi-flash mode, I set the flash to 5 bursts at 500 HZ and took a picture of fan blades, resulting in a very interesting effect.

As a final test, I put the flash in slave move (S1) and put my old flash on the camera. This flash worked great as a slave flash and I took some interesting pictures using both flashes. I also used S1 mode to slave the this flash to the camera's on-board flash. Note, I did not test the wireless flash mode (a smart slave mode) as I do not have another flash that supports that feature.

Disclaimer: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at no cost, I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

title: Pretty watch, but not reliable
text:
It took me a really long time to review this watch because I am not great at removing links. They do provide you with a tool, but I’m almost 50, and trying to see tiny screws is much harder for me these days. And I also have anxiety issues that make it hard for me to do small detail work that requires a patient and steady hand. I ended up having to go to a watch repair place and pay $20 to have someone remove the links. And I actually have to go back because he removed them unevenly so it pulls to one side.

So this watch has given me a lot of issues before I even started using it. There are watches with links that have clip on links at the end so that they become adjustable. It would have been So much easier if this had had those type of links.

The most frustrating thing is that, after all the struggle just to get the watch to fit, it just has a pretty terrible battery life. Perhaps it’s just this smaller watch face? I’m not really sure but if I’m getting a lot of alerts (it’s not even automatically running the health scans because that would take too much energy- I have to manually request the scan each time for blood pressure, O2, etc.) it can run out in 2 days easily.

And most annoying thing of all is that the alerts from my phone only work sporadically. I think I usually do get the phone calls. But some messages never make it through. And the only other thing I have linked to it is Facebook messenger. Initially that worked. However, it stopped working very shortly afterwards. I tried to reset everything and then it worked again for a bit. And then it stopped working again.

This is a much more attractive smart watch than the normal type, with the huge watch face. That is the one thing that this smart watch has going for it. Everything else is patchy and frustrating, in comparison to my other smart watch with the huge watch face. So even though I like the look of this watch better, I find myself reaching for my old watch each day. I just don’t want to rely on the nicer looking watch and miss important calls or messages. I actually wore them both at the same time for a couple of weeks. So I could feel and see clearly when my old watch would buzz me for calls or messages and this new watch would stay silent. It happened too many times for me to feel like I can really trust the new watch.

text:
I ordered this 'Plugable 512GB Thunderbolt 3 External SSD NVMe Drive (Up to 2400MBs/1800MBs R/W)' for review.

I ordered this Plugable drive to use as a backup drive for my Alienware 17R5 gaming laptop. I use it mainly for video and photo editing and needed a fast drive. This is my first Thunderbolt drive and I must say that it has blown away my other external physical hard drives by a long shot. I couldn't tell you if the speeds are up to par with what Plugable claims so I will leave that up to the experts, but for my use and needs this one has been amazing. I do think that it is a bit overpriced however, but this is Thunderbolt 3 and SSD NVMe at that, so I suppose that it to be expected. I do love how small and compact this thing is. It comes with a soft cloth pouch which is nice but I would like to have seen a padded hard case or even a soft padded neoprene case but with it being an SSD drive and with how solid the shell is, the soft cloth case should be sufficient. Still, a more padded case would have really made me happy haha. I do notice that after a bit of use this drive does get hot, but I think (and hope) that the way the case is designed (with the heat fins) it should be fine. At least I hope so. Overall after several weeks of use, I am pretty happy with this drive and think it is of good quality and value. It is quite solid!

title: Pretty straightforward settings, easy-to-read display
text:
This timer is a good size with a very readable LED display and a strong magnet on the clip on the back to hold it to your fridge or whatever a magnet will stick to. The buttons are large and accessible, and it's really no problem to set it up. It beeps loudly when the time is up, so there's little danger you're not going to hear it from an adjoining room.

Strangely, on day one (unlike with some timers I've used), the first three or four times that I held down the hour, minute, or second buttons to speed up the counting and turn off the beeps, it just froze and stopped counting. If I pressed the button over and over to advance the counter by one, it worked—beeping annoyingly loudly each time, of course. I was about to give it a two-star review and throw it away because I couldn't stand it, but I put off doing it and just stuck it to the top of my stove. A week later, after I'd used the stove several times and the timer probably got exposed to some heat, I went back to try it again so I could write this review and the fast-count sans beeps feature worked. Weird. Maybe it was just stressed in shipping and needed time to settle down....

A few things I really do dislike is that it's easy to reset the time by mistake if the grey button on the left gets slid up; the modes are manually set with this button. (That approach to the modes could be good for the technologically challenged, though.) Also, if you overshoot your mark on the time, there is no way to go backward; you have to go forward until you come back around to where you were supposed to have stopped the first time. The clip is a little too sharply angled, so when you stick the timer to a surface with the magnet, the face slants down somewhat, but it's still visible; really not that big of a deal.

Another thing, as I've remarked about another MeasuPro product: the how-to info on the packaging is white letters on light grey, which is practically unreadable for anyone, not just people like me with old eyes. (The company told me they were correcting that with the other product, so I expect they will do the same with this one.)

title: Gives my iPad that laptop feel - 4 out of 5
text:
I have been using the Belkin _____ keyboard for a little while now, so I have a pretty good basis for this review. As far as the look of this keyboard, it is absolutely second to none. The silver and white color of the keyboard matches beautifully with the silver and white of my iPad mini. It locks magnetically to the side of the iPad, as Apple's Smart Cover does. The keyboard puts the iPad to sleep and wakes it up, again just like the Smart Cover. With the color, style, form factor, and magnetic integration you can certainly see that belkin took their time to get the physical design just right.

From a functional standpoint, I am thrilled to have a keyboard attachment for my iPad. The keyboard's bluetooth connection works seamlessly with the iPad. the iPad mini itself can be moved from the magnetic attachment to a groove in the keyboard, so it stands up like a laptop. This gives you a good working feeling. The only problem I had at first was that the screen was so close to the keyboard, i would tap the screen from time to time which can be an issue with a touchscreen. As for the keyboard size/layout the button layout does feel a little condensed, especially on the right hand side. When you are typing with your fingers in the "home" position (index fingers on F and J) your right little finger is on the enter button. That, for me, took some getting used to.

All in all, the keyboard made my iPad mini more of a usable device for me, when it came to business at least. I feel that I can type much quicker with a keyboard than i can with the touchscreen. The way that it attaches does not take away from the small, portable size of the iPad. In fact, I don't even think it doubles the thickness. The keyboard folds up on the iPad and you would never really tell that they weren't made for each other.

title: Lots of hype but really just average
text: This hub is nothing special but it does seem to work fine. I am not happy with several aspects. First, if you place the device next to your computer with the power cord facing away from you, you can't see the activity lights on your flash drives. The USB ports should be the other way around so you can see these lights. This is a major design miscalculation, in my opinion. Also, Anker makes a big deal that the charging ports provide lots of power. Perhaps they do, but if you are expecting them to fast charge a so-equipped Samsung phone it does not kick up to fast charge mode at all. You only get the usual charge speed. The supplied USB 3.0 cable is very thick and not very flexible. The hub does not want to stay where you put it as it is constantly being torqued by the heavy cable. It would be nice if this expensive thing had a little more mass so it does not flop around all over the desk. A bit wider base, some rubber feet (instead of the Nothing supplied), and a more flexible USB cable would be nice. The distracting blue lights are pretty, but mostly useless. If I have a device plugged in, I expect it to be active, so what good is the blue light. It would be better if the ports themselves were illuminated so you could have a little help on trying to find the opening when attempting to attach a device. On some of my SanDisk thumb drives the blue lights turn off after a few minutes when idle but the drive is still available for use in Windows. I don't know if that's a weird thing caused by the hardware in the drive or a weird thing with the hub. The main thing is that it works so once again, what is the blue light for? Having said all of that, I don't hate this hub. If you need all these ports plus some charging capability this is a fine choice. It is just that, for the price, it could be so much better.

title: One of the best in this price range
text:
We have tried several projectors in this range and found this WEWATCH model to be much better than any we have personally used. It's noticably brighter than the others and its 4 Point Keystone Correction (plus rotation) makes exact projector placement slightly less critical.

I like that it comes with dual band WiFi, so it allows us to more target which band to use. If we have the projector set up in close proximity, we use the 5G connection since it has a faster data tranfer for streaming movies over our network and if we are using it in the yard for outdoor fun times, we'll hook it up to the 2.4G band for the extended range capability. Of course, connecting this to our Firestick gives us many more options to watch and has worked flawlessly for us. We hooked it directly to our laptops and PCs and have found no compatibility issues there.

The built-in speaker is adequate, but we prefer to hook it to an external speaker source. You also have the option to connect to your headphones which may be convenient at times when wanting to watch something without disturbing anyone else with the sound.

The product description shows that it has a range of viewing sizes from 30" (about 3.7 feet from the screen) to 230" (about 29 from the screen) but be careful at the larger end as you do obviously lose image quality, but it's nice to have the option. WEWATCH customer service recommends a viewing placement of approximately the 8 feet to 15 feet range for optimal viewing. We placed ours about 12 feet from our screen here in the house and found the image quality to be excellent.

Other features that we liked were the native 1080P support, the zoom function and the screen mirroring ability. We had some random questions about the unit, so we contacted WEWATCH support a couple of times. Each time, they were quick to respond and very helpful and informative. It seems that their customer support is very good, and that's a bonus every time.

Overall, we have been very pleased with this unit. For our money, it's an outstanding value at this price point.

We had been using one of the flat amplified antennas, and it just couldn't get the distant station. I don't know if the signals didn't want to go through too many walls, or if the high voltage electric transmission line running along the east edge of our front yard was responsible.

When I installed this antenna, I still couldn't get CBS. With the nice long piece of coax attached to it, I experimented with various places. The window was a no go, no matter where it was placed, giving my power line hypothesis some points. Holding it high its full distance to the west worked.
