text:
I received exactly what was pictured along with some cable routing clips. Overall, it was a nice combination and well packaged. The description is a little bit misleading since it mentions the flat design of the cable. This cable is round, like a standard TV cable round. Probably a copy and paste typo, but if you're expecting a flat cable, just fyi.

It's very thick and rated for outdoor usage, but I can't think of any outdoor use at the moment except for a patio big-screen TV -- which is a pretty good reason to get this.

I don't think it would be a good idea to consider this cable completely waterproof/weatherproof because it wouldn't be at the end that's plugged into an outdoor device. Most people with a patio TV would know that you need to cover up the TV and the cable connection from the elements, so probably not a big deal.

Just use a bit of common sense with it and it should work for outdoor uses . . . I just can't think of anything besides a patio big-screen right off the top of my head . . . welll, maybe you could use it to connect to a laptop so you could work outside on your deck, then take your laptop back inside and leave the cable out for the next time. But you'd still want to cover the exposed end to prevent plugging in a wet cable to your laptop.

I maxed out the speed in my tests (caveat is that I only have 1 device that is capable of Cat-8 speeds and any speed test will only measure the slowest device in the link). I was able to get nearly Cat-7 speeds on a Cat-8 modem to a Cat-7 device. It actually did marginally better than a Cat-7 cable, but it's not enough to reach any conclusions.

Overall, this is a great product as long as you don't need truly outdoor waterproof/weatherproof connections.

- Tech support is awful. My latest call to them were a waste of time. I couldn't understand what the tech support person was saying due to her very poor English. She didn't seem to understand me either.

- The software utility tool is poor and most of the time has trouble finding the extender (even though I'm sitting about a foot away from it)

title: Best USB hub I've tried so far
text:
Love this hub. Lots of performance, lots of flexibility. You don't need external power for this hub, unless you want it; in which case you need to provide your own power source (there is a USB-C port on the side that you can plug the power source into). If you are going to be using this hub for everyday devices (flash drives, mouse/keyboard, etc.), you don't need external power anyway.

Having 7 (!) expansion USB 3.2 ports sitting on your desk is a game changer. Much easier than plugging directly into your computer. The high transfer speed is SO nice. Most (newer) PCs only have 1 or 2 USB 3.2 ports, so getting 7 with this hub is awesome.

It seems like a selling point for this hub is the 32 degree angle that it sits at, which at first I didn't think would be a big deal at first, but it is definitely better than a lay-flat hub (i.e., every other hub I've had). Makes it quite easy to plug in/out of.

The only thing I'd wish for is faster charging (even with external power plugged in, it's not very fast).

Bottom line: a great hub.

title: Basically works.  Not well designed. Maps are iffy
text:
I am now a total expert on Bushnell Golf GPS's having owned the Yardage Pros XG, XGC and Neo.
Of these, the XGC was the only one that worked properly. It has problems, but I was able to read yardage.

Pros:
Good Satellite Reception.
Good data (with $35 subscription to iGolf - annual. But you can cancel after a year if you've already downloaded all the courses you want)
Solidly made (though very bulky)
Good Buttons
Works! (more than I can say for my experience w the Neo and XG models)

Cons:
About 3x bigger than my cellphone (why? My phone has a gps...)
A lot of extra crap menus (do you really need an option for News and for course Reviews on this device? Even if you did, the content is totally worthless)
BIG CON: The map function didn't really work on the courses I tried. Sometimes the unit would display the correct yardage to the pin in the main display, but the map didn't match the hole. It would show 800 yards because the map would actually be for a different hole). I returned it because I figured if the maps didn't work, I may as well have a NEO which has bigger yardage display and is smaller.
TERRIBLE Menu Display: Why would anyone choose to highlight a black menu with dark gray? You can't tell which selection is highlighted in sunlight. Period. Fortunately, you don't really need to choose from those menus during play. Still - the interface options were designed by a lab rat.

The Bottom Line: If the NEO actually worked for me (mine wouldn't let me install course data) I would buy a NEO over this in a heart beat. I'm sure the NEO does work for some people, so it might be worth your time to give it a try.

BUT since the XGC DID work and seems to be a little bit more modern electronically (e.g. seems to recognize USB natively without pretending it's an old fashioned 1980s serial port), I think I may have to go back to the XGC if I want a golf GPS. As stupidly designed and old fashioned as this device is, it may still be the best out there in terms of simply being a good tool to have on the course without being a hassle.

ALL I really want is something that tells me how far to the pin. How far to hazards or dog legs would be nice, but mostly I want distance to pin. Maybe I need a rangefinder, but I don't want to slow down play by pulling out a rangefinder on every shot. I want something where I can just glance at my bag and see the yardage. That's it. The NEO has its own issues, but if it worked, I think it's the most sensible tool for most golfers simply because it is the least intrusive.

CUSTOMER SUPPORT: AWFUL!!! Bushnell provides no support email on their website. It takes at least 10 minutes to get someone on the phone. If you do get someone on the phone, they'll be able to answer routine questions, but not much else. They were supposed to get back to me about my defective unit.
No call or email back. I get the feeling Bushnell simply doesn't want you to bother them.

title: Simply Works. Linux & Windows Compatible
text:
An air mouse is not something you would normally use with a PC-based system unless you are trying to save space or are giving a presentation in which case it is a convenient accessory. Such a mouse is a lot more useful for things like Smart TVs, though it is also useful for embedded systems like a Raspberry Pi. I have used several air mice and I was curious to see how well this one would compare to others I have used. So far it has worked well, under both Linux as well as Windows. I will state up front that I have not used it with a Smart TV.

At a glance, this little device looks like a TV remote and little more, but it is quite a bit more than that. It does work as a remote, of course, but it also works as a mouse with a full-up keyboard. On one side of this device there are all of the controls you would expect to find on a remote for a Smart TV remote – volume control, channel settings, mode buttons, play, search and more. Flip the unit over and there is a keyboard, with 38 keys and most regular keyboard functions accessible through function key settings.

The unit requires two AAA batteries, not included.

I decided to try it with my Linux workstation, running CentOS 7 with a 64-bit 3.10.0-series kernel. I did not have to load special drivers and I did not need to do any special configuration at all, it was just plug and play. I was able to move the mouse just by waving the device in front of the screen and several of the buttons on the remote side worked as I would have hoped – Home took me to the browser home page, volume controls worked, Search worked, the menu button brought up the menu for the current application with focus and more. The keyboard portion worked as it should and I was able to type, though I found it a little awkward after being used to a full-sized keyboard for so long.

I also tried it with my Windows 10 system and I got nearly identical results. It required no drivers, no special configuration, no extra set-up – it just works as expected. The buttons works the same under Windows as they did under Linux for me and I was able to navigate as desired.

This is a good air mouse that works well under Linux and Windows. It should work fine with smaller systems like the Raspberry Pi (which uses a derivative of the Linux kernel). As an added bonus, it is relatively inexpensive. If you need an air mouse, this one is worth some consideration.

Disclosure: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at minimal or no cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

title: Very cool 4k recorder if you know what you're doing
text:
I've been doing a lot of live event streaming and usually have OBS software running to also record. Having this device however means I don't need to record in the software and/or use it as a backup, as this will offload the recording directly to my SSD drive I have plugged into it!
I have an Atmos Ninja recorder I sometimes use as well, however it is picky about the source (if there's a splitter or adapter in the middle, it doesn't like it), whereas this seems to accept almost anything I throw at it so far. I like that. Also, the fact that it can bump all the way to 4K is pretty sweet too, as I can even use the original Sony A7S (which only recorded 1080 internally) as a full 4K recorder now! Cons are that it doesn't really have a display to tell you what's going on so you need to rely on the little LED colors to figure it out. Plugging a field monitor into the HDMI out helps, as you can see the output as well as the "rec" label on-screen.
NOTE: DO NOT use the output of this box as your stream or other devices in a chain, as the output is NOT a clean copy of the original! Imagine that this box is using your monitor/TV/output as its own screen, with its own overlays and all. One other reviewer mentioned that it appeared cropped on the output versus what his camera showed. That is acceptable with using this with a field monitor to keep tabs on what it is doing, however, if you wanted to go straight from this box to an OBS stream or projector for a wall at an event, you're going to see the overlays. It does NOT support clean HDMI out.
I intend to use it with an HDMI splitter as a backup stream, or with my A7S mark i as a 4K recorder, and for that it is perfect.

text:

I like the fact that you can re-charge it easily with AAA batteries (not included). I have found that re-charging with a hand-crank is too slow. Solar re-charging works well on most devices if you keep the device stored on a windowsill for the year so that it is fully charged during a weather event. Having the option to use three AAA batteries is great because the radio can be ready to use immediately. Another feature that I like is that no screwdriver is needed in order to open the compartment in order to change-out the batteries. This is important when evacuating and also when the power goes out.

During Hurricane Ike, I evacuated to a friend's home. The storm made landfall around midnight or so. In the dark, it is hard to find anything, so it's good to be ready before the lights go out. I can remember lying in bed alone listening to my friend's radio (not this radio) in the dark as the NOAA forecaster reported the progress of the surge up through Galveston Bay and into the bayous, lakes, and streams inland. It was so helpful to know exactly what was happening to the area in which I lived.

My friend's radio was a very expensive radio, and the main difference between her radio and this radio seems to be the reception.

Hers ran all night with no interruption with reception. With this radio, I do have to turn the radio off and then back on if I lose reception to the channel. A really expensive weather radio would probably have better reception if you want to listen non-stop.

For my needs, however, this radio is excellent and is the best that I have owned in its price range.

title: Outstanding 70-200mm lens goes toe to toe with Nikon and you win
text:
I've used both Nikon 70-200 f/2.8 VR zooms, and I prefer this to both Nikons. Price definitely plays a role in that decision, but looking at the pictures, I'm not losing anything in regards to sharpness or contrast, and the overall experience (ergonomics, AF speed, AF accuracy, AF noise, VR/VC, etc...) is similar or even slightly favors the Tamron. The Nikon does win in regards to build quality and tripod food (especially in regards to mounting an ARCA Swiss plate). Having also owned the earlier Tamron 70-200 f/2.8 (without VC or USD), one must say this is a huge improvement. It focused slowly, with a fair amount of noise, and lacked critical performance at 200mm. It also showed a need for stabilization, and this new lens addresses all areas. In short, this is the 70-200mm f/2.8 lens to get unless you need the Nikon durability.

If anything, this lens is lacking a bit in color rendition. It's very subtle, and like many color subtleties is a matter of preference, but I do wish it were a bit less muted compared with my Nikons. That being said, it's very subtle, easy to fix, and pales in comparison with the other strengths of this great lens. Do note that 200mm performance wide open does lack a bit, but I've experienced this with both Nikons and the earlier Tamron, and this outperforms all at 200mm, and it's quite remarkable at f/4.

if you've never used a top line 70-200 f/2.8 lens, it's a step above most other lenses. The solid build of a lens that doesn't change external dimensions when zoomed is a nice feeling, the instant AF is stunning, and the critical sharpness edge to edge (I use a D90 with a 12mp DX sensor) is empowering. This lens excels in these areas, and it offers it all at a great price.

title: After nearly a year, loving it even more
text:
How many products get better a year later?

I was having some ergonomic issues using the Kangaroo Pro. Placing it on my desktop, and my keyboard and trackball on top of it, in the seated position it required my chair to be higher than it can (in order for my arms to be level while typing or using the trackball). So I bought a cushion which raised me higher in the chair, but that required me using a foot rest as my feet were now off the ground. But, ok, workable while seated. (In a standing position, the KP has always been fine for me.) But after about 6 months of this, I really started to be bothered with the whole setup. I just wasn't comfortable when seated.

So back to my original position (which I had abandoned on day one as I thought it unworkable), which was using a drop down keyboard shelf which fits under my desk. So my seated position could be brought down to a normal level -- no more seat cushion, no more foot rest. But the keyboard shelf extends in front of the desk, which means I have to sit further away from the desk and monitor than before. However, the KP does not have any way of adjusting the monitor horizontally (that is, to bring it closer in, as I now needed it to be). So I used it like that for several months, always wishing the monitor could be about 6" closer to me (when seated).

Finally I decided to write Ergo Desktop, to see if I could replace the monitor arm with one that could adjust horizontally. It turns out that there are inexpensive monitor arm extensions that can bring the monitor closer by 4" or 8". But what about while I was standing? I didn't want the monitor closer when standing -- it was already close enough. Solution again provided by Ergo Desktop: 2 extensions of the same size (in my case, 4") can be folded in on each other, bringing the monitor back to where it would be without the extensions. After using the extensions for a few weeks, I found the KP now almost perfect for me. The only remaining nit was that when seated, the monitor was now a little too high, as the monitor extensions added about 3" vertically. So even adjusting the monitor down all the way on the KP, the monitor was just a few inches higher than I'd like. I wrote Ergo Desktop, just to let them know the extensions were working out well for me, and mentioned this. And was surprised to find there was a solution for this problem, too! A little adjustment on the KP itself brought the minimum monitor height down about 2", which means it's now perfect for me.

The quality of the KP itself is very high. It seems like it will withstand years (if not decades) of use. Now I know the customer service of Ergo Desktop is also outstanding, and I am one very happy customer!

title: Amazingly thin
text:
When buying filters, I've found two criteria stand out more than all the rest: coatings and thinness. This filter is awesome in both regards.

While the fine German optical glass is certainly a plus, B+W amazing coatings to reduce haze and any unwanted glare induced by the filter itself (the MRC in this filter's name) assure you top notch results--this filter won't hold back even the finest lenses out there. Most B+W filters have these coatings and all use the fine German optical glass, this line of filters (XS-Pro) adds a few pluses--notably uncanny thinness. Some lenses make you wonder why there are threads (apart from using a lens cap), as most filters will cause some form of vignetting (darkness in corners) on these demanding (typically wide angle) lenses. My old [[ASIN:B0007U00XK Sigma 10-20mm f/4-5.6 EX DC HSM Lens for Nikon Digital SLR Cameras]] comes to mind, but many other lenses fall into this boat. Some photographers resort to older slim filter designs without front threads (thus the explicit reference to them in this item's title), but these require odd lens caps and cannot allow filter stacking (well you can still stack in the right sequence assuming your other filters do have front threads). The lens cap issue is particularly challenging, as the caps that do work with these filters simply suck. Anyway, no worries here, as they somehow squeezed threads into a compact frame. Even if you don't have an ultra-wide angle lens, you can safely stack a polarizer or graduated ND filter on this without vignetting. Also new to this line of filters is an enhanced scratch-proofing treatment that also is easier to keep clean. For those of you who haven't had the pleasure of using a B+W filter, they're top quality in all regards, including non-binding threads, durability (no rattling glass), and are always free of imperfections.

Basically this is the best UV filter out there.

title: Not good for big spaces/houses
text:
We couldn't find a way to set this up because of logistics, which is unfortunate. Wireless or Bluetooth options would have worked better for this, not only because of distances, but because having to work with wires at such lengths and hide them in a home would have been beyond unwieldy.

Problem 1: drilling from the exterior of the house to the inside in Florida, unless done by a professional, likely means you created a place for water and moisture to leak in, which inevitably means mold and other issues. Even so, it's understandable that this may be necessary pretty much every time, and perhaps that wouldn't be such a big deal if it weren't for problem 2.

Problem 2: for this to work, you need to have a tv or monitor setup. If you have a bigger space, the distance might be further to get from where you want to record to the place where you have those things.

Here's what would have worked to let us set this up:
Have a hub of some sort that can be put anywhere nearish to the cameras, and then that can connect wirelessly to an app, computer, or monitor on the same network, not just for setup, but in general.

We would have had to go from the garage area to the inside part of the house, somewhere over 70 feet? To get to the nearest tv or monitor.

I'll try again for my small business if we ever change locations, but having to attach to a monitor is a pain. It should be able to work directly from the hub/DVR to an app.

title: Good HDMI-CEC support; unimportant to most, important to me.
text:
I purchased this Panasonic Soundbar in June of 2013. At the time, my requirements were:
- Good sound (can't afford GREAT sound)
- Wireless Subwoofer
- HDMI input and good HDMI-CEC support
- Bluetooth support

In my search, I tested the [[ASIN:B00811NMMI Toshiba SBX4250]] and the [[ASIN:B00BLX9510 Samsung HW-F450]] from my local Costco. My final choice was the Panasonic.

Sound:
- Acceptable sound -- The front speakers are not a big improvement over the built-ins. With the subwoofer turned off, it is easy to mistake the Panasonic sound bar with the speakers from the Television.
- Good subwoofer -- The sub sounds good even at high volumes and fills out the overall sound from the sound bar.
- The Samsung has clearer mid and high ranges so the Panasonic seems slightly muffled in comparison.
- Overall sound better than the Toshiba.
- Wireless range for the subwoofer is short -- especially if placed behind the sofa (interference from people sitting in front of it). Range is about 15 feet with clear line of sight.

Decoders and Passthrough:
- AC3 and DTS Decoder (Toshiba lacks DTS)
- ARC (Audio Return Channel) -- If you use the Netflix app built in to your TV, audio is generated by your TV. Normally, an "optical out" cable from the TV back to the sound bar is necessary. ARC removes that need.

HDMI-CEC (also Aquos Link, Anynet+, Bravia LinkSync, Regza Link, etc):
This is where the Panasonic beats the Samsung. HDMI-CEC allows Televisions to control a connected device -- no matter the brand; The TV remote should be able to turn on a bluray player and send navigation (up/down/etc) and standard playback buttons without the need for a second remote control.

In the case of a sound bar, through HDMI-CEC:
1. The sound bar should turn on when the TV turns on -- Panasonic does this, Samsung does not.
2. The TV should play all sound through the sound bar and volume buttons on the TV remote should control volume on the sound bar -- Panasonic does this.
3. Turning on a bluray player, the sound bar should turn on and switch to the correct input automatically. The TV should also turn on and switch to the correct input -- Panasonic does this. It's then up to your TV do its part.

In conclusion, I chose the Panasonic because it gave me the ability to eliminate a remote control through HDMI-CEC (which Samsung didn't) and it had both AC3 and DTS decoders (which Toshiba didn't). With the added ability to play music from my phone through bluetooth, I'm still happy with my purchase one year later.

Tip: Unlike the Samsung and Toshiba, the Panasonic has a small "receiver" unit that adds another machine to your entertainment center. For me, I use some velcro strips and attach the "receiver" to the back of my TV. It is only 1 ¾" thick which was thinner than my wall mount.

title: A decent deal, with some simple "issues"
text:
UPDATE 9/4: everything with the kit is fine but 4 of the CFL bulbs broke, either they stopped working or they broke in the process of screwing them in. Do yourself a favor and go out and get a 12 pack of 5000k LED bulbs, I did a side-by-side and they are almost indistinguishable from the included CFL bulbs in terms of output, and while there are much more expensive photography grade bulbs out there, I'm fairly certain that those are not what are included, and the bulbs that I got that were comparable ran me $20 for a 12 pack; plus now I don't have to worry about handling them like eggshells, and as a side benefit the lower power draw might be less likely to cause fuse issues. We'll see.

Original review:
So first off, after comparison shopping for a while it became clear that there are 2-3 "types" of this kit around, with the main difference seeming to be how they are branded and the size of the softbox...in the end, they are all very similar, if not identical. I think that a lot of the complaints come from confusion about certain aspects of use from people who are first-time users, but that being said....if I have any catastrophic failures in the next few months, I will come and update my review.

The stands: Yes, they are inexpensively made; light and a bit flimsy. If you screw the thumbscrews down too hard in the plastic, you will probably split it. Don't white-knuckle tighten and you should be fine, it's "tight" even when it still feels a little loose.
I think some of the complaints about the stands collapsing and the legs breaking might be because people are not fully extending the stand...when you unfold it, it sort of...turns back on itself. It would be easy to assume that the full extension is at a point when it's only 1/2 unfolded, if you haven't used tripod-type stands before, but if you stand it like that it will be putting a lot of strain on a relatively weak point. In addition, you must use the sandbag as a counterweight for the boom light, which means it's up to you to put some sort of weights in it (as others have mentioned, the little cloth bag with an eyescrew on it), and it will require a little fiddling to get the optimal balance....that's just how counterweights work. If you have the pole extended far and high, you may also need to weight it at the base, but do so cautiously, because if you put too heavy of a weight on one of the crossbars, you will bend it or pop out one of the fittings.

The lights. I saw a lot of complaints about how they stop working, and I suspect a LOT of that is fuse or bulb related. Not only is there a fuse, but they include an extra one with each light head unit. I suspect that SOME of that may be bulb-related, CFL bulbs can cause momentary surges in power, especially inexpensive ones, and especially when they begin to fail, and the included ones feel fairly inexpensive...very light in my hand, compared to nicer ones that I have used. I know that a lot of people will replace the fast blow (F3AL250V) fuses in their photo lights with slow blow type (T3AL250V) to help with blown fuses...but I'm not sure if I recommend that, if we don't know exactly why the fuses are blowing. On one hand, there's not much delicate in the way of electronics with a basic light bulb socket, which is typically why fast blow fuses are used, but I also wonder if the fuse is there to help with a design flaw, and using a fuse that takes longer to blow will cause a safety issue. Before I messed with any of that, I think I'll try it with nice bulbs, possibly even LED. Also, the sockets are a little fiddly, 2 of them started to bind when I was screwing the bulb in, if you feel the bulb snag, don't just screw harder, back it out and try again. The last thing you want to do is twist the socket inside its housing, which can cause damage that will lead to short circuits or dead sockets, because it will just get worse each time, or you'll crack the bulb at its base.

The softboxes; The main advice I can give with these is don't follow their illustration, because it will be extra annoying as you try and pass the box over the light without knocking the rods out. What I did was put the lower 2 rods into the sleeves on the reflector, and the top two into the light, and held the lower part including the rods in my hand, as I passed it onto the light, then you can let it freely hang in place without anything slipping out as it rests on the top rods while you feed the top two rods into the sleeves, and then the bottom two into the socket on the light unit, and then finally do the velcro.

The carrying bag is a bag, nothing remarkable. I would recommend not storing the lights with the bulbs still in them, because you will most likely eventually break some, or at least render them inoperable; they stick out at angles so that 1-2 of them will always be bearing some weight at rest. Take them out and store them all separately in a small plastic tote, or something like that.

text:

The price is also impressive for a name brand product with this kind of build quality. However, I had almost forgotten how slow USB2.0 can be. I'm so used to USB3 storage speeds of easily over 150MB/s, that the benchmarks on this one seem almost painfully slow at around the 20MB/s mark. But, that's par for the course with the older standard, so I can't really fault the product for it. This is a great value but you could easily get a much faster storage stick for a bit more money. I could see this being useful for someone who wants to distribute a hard-copy of something by hand and would like to order a bulk supply of durable and fast-enough but still affordable media. Otherwise, I think I'd recommend one that is USB 3 compatible at least since you can always be backwards compatible with 2.0 if necessary, but have the increased speed when available.

title: I am NOT a Pro - so this is my review as such
text:
I am not a professional photographer. I can not go into great detail about all of the settings and fancy terminology that others can do so if that is what you are looking for, you won't find it in this review.

I AM an artist, however. I have spent the last 20 years taking accurate color specific photos which need to have accurate texture as much as possible for posting photos of my art in many different media.

When I was younger, I used to devour every inch of every tool that I had. I would learn it inside out and study it until it became like an extension of my hands. Unfortunately life has crowded out my time and ability to study things so I am forced to learn things off the cuff and fly by the seat of my pants.

This can be a problem, however, when it comes to having a very refined taste in photos with color and accurate texture, but only the time to run a quick set of photos.

When my Kodak camera broke, I was very upset. I had one of the nice Z series of Kodak cameras. Although low light photos were a nightmare, the color intensity and accuracy always delighted my senses- especially when taken outdoors.

The Canon G12 is both a huge step forward and a step back.

WHAT I LIKE

The step forward is that in low light, this camera is unbelievable! I can capture a photo in a pure dark room with a flash that I can not capture with most cameras in good artificial light.
There are a ton of settings with the G12. I can set them any way that I want to and that is really nice- except when I am in a hurry.

The auto setting is adequate, but not quite as colorful as I would have hoped.

The camera is solid and can stand on its own for self portraits and a timer.

The intense color setting does a great job in some instances

The camera is easy to hold and I have no problems adjusting to it

The back screen flipping around for self portraits is fabulous- I take a ton of those and this is a huge help.

The lens is FAST- retracts and goes out really quickly.

After not using the camera for a few moments, the lens does retract back again into the camera, but if you press the button lightly that takes photos, it comes out quickly again.

WHAT I DON'T LIKE
The camera can be a bit heavy and cumbersome when I am attempting to hold it with one hand out of necessity (when photographing my arm or hand).

The color capture of this camera is nice outside but in subdued light- photos look washed out. I am well acquainted with photo editing and do use it, but it is a bit more challenging with the G12.

The neck strap can sometimes get in the way when using one hand for photos- but it is a bit too heavy for a wrist strap- although I would like to have that security in case I drop it like I did my other camera.

The manual has to be printed out which annoys me to no end. For a camera this expensive, you would think they would include a manual. This makes it really hard to learn how to use this camera.

I know that some people feel you need to know photography rather than a manual, but I find that I would like to learn this tool, and am very frustrated without inclusion of a manual.

I have not used this camera at all near to its potential. As a point and shoot camera on auto- it is adequate and for most people would probably be just fine. For the other features, there is no manual at all, unless you print it out, which takes ink and paper.

I do love the camera so far, although the color saturation is not quite what I am used to, I will learn to work with it. The lovely low light capacity of this camera makes up for it, I guess.

I have given this four stars because of the lack of manual mostly and the auto mode not being quite as accurate as I would have hoped.

But the G12 is such a nice camera in other ways, it is still close to five stars despite my disappointments.

title: A Warning for Mac Users
text:
I bought one of these to use with my iMac. It works fine for a keyboard, mouse or other low data rate devices, but like many Mac owners, I found that once I use more than four of the available ports data transmission rates max out at USB 2.0 speeds. This apparently had something to do with the the Anker's circuit design. The consequence is that hard drives and even memory sticks or flash drives operate at far below their best possible speeds. If the data is being used by an undemanding application – word processing for instance – the user might not even notice. But if you are running programs that make more of a demand on a hard drive, for example 3D rendering, video or music creation applications then you will surely note the difference.

For me it meant that an SSD drive that typically communicated with my computer at better than 700 MB/s when plugged into one of the computer's ports began to function at less than one third that speed. When I looked at my computer's System Report (found under the Apple menu after you press "About this Mac"), I found that the Anker was being recognized as a USB 2.0 device.

title: Lens Ring does not adjust Focus
text:
I really love my camera, it feels solid and well made and I'm nostalgic about the silver trim as it reminds me of my old film Minolta. The menu is easy enough to navigate, and the pictures I've taken are very clear, with a really amazing image stabilization. The zoom is also amazing, having a viewfinder is life changing (on a point and shoot anyway), and it fits well in my pocket... But...
The control ring on the lens cannot be programmed to control manual focus. I work for a camera manufacturer and when I brought my new toy in to work my boss was very excited about the control ring, and we played with the menu for a while to try and find how to program it to control the focus on the camera. No luck. Why would Panasonic drop the ball here? Why make a camera that obviously appeals to the DSLR crowd, include a feature which ostensibly appears to be a manual focus ring, and then make it (at best) an iso or zoom toggle? It's really disappointing. Also, I have yet to get this to connect to my wifi, and its been difficult to locate a compatible replacement cable on amazon.
Dont let this deter you, though, if you want a solid pocket camera with amazing zoom and some other nifty features. I'm planning on testing out the GPS while hiking in Peru this summer, and while conducting a preliminary archaeological survey (accuracy is +/- 5m, so this is not a research level GPS device, but the metadata is awesome for organizing photos later on). Also, this camera takes very nice macro photos.

Though I received this Acer Chromebook for review, I have another one exactly like it that I bought refurbished about a month ago and have been using it a lot. They are both the same make and model. What I like:

But, for the price of this chrombook (as of this review it's around $179.00) I think it's an excellent buy. It comes with a power cord (of course) but that's it. It would be great for college/high school students and anyone who doesn't mind storing their data in the cloud. My main reason for using Chromebooks is that you don't have to buy anti-virus for them since they can't download any data so working off line is not feasible.

title: As is said in Engineering: "It's Cookbook!" Just Follow the Steps.
text: This was quite easy to setup as far as the SSD is concerned. I cleaned up my Desktop and emptied my Recycle Bin so as not to bring all that to the SSD when cloning. The software I used was the free version of AOMEI Backupper Standard. It's straightforward. I have found this the best software to clone SSDs. First, install mSATA SSD into the empty mSATA slot (#11 on my motherboard) and do yourself a favor. Buy a set of Motherboard Screws like [[ASIN:B011EFAB8K Mcsher 300pcs Laptop Notebook Screws Kit Set]]. These were $9.99. You can never expect screws to come with these things, so be proactive. Once installed, the system will recognize it after you boot it and at some point Windows will show “You must initialize a disk before Logical Disk Manager can access it” i.e. make it an MBR or GPT disk. Mine is an older legacy Booting System, so I made it an MBR. I’m not going to use more than 2TB disks. It's quick (there are brief articles explaining this). Then run AOMEI. Select the disks and it does the rest. I cloned my HDD to the SSD. AOMEI did everything and made it bootable and entered into the boot options in SETUP (F2). You can boot the SDD the first time by hitting F12 during the boot process and it will display a menu of options. You can choose the SSD and make sure it’s all working. Then the next time you boot you can choose the permanent boot order you want in the BIOS SETUP and give the SSD the first option. The whole process took only 15-20 minutes.

title: Setup is a little confusing but a really nice dashcam
text:
First have to say to get a SD card right away! I didn't realize I needed one so had to wait a day to finally sit and try to set this up.
I read the instructions a few times before I began setting this dashcam up. I tried going to the support page they have listed in the booklet but, every time I tried I got this message.."Your connection is not secure
The owner of support.zenfox.com has configured their website improperly. To protect your information from being stolen, Waterfox has not connected to this website. (I did this with Firefox and Chrome also with same results)
After the SD card was formatted and put in the unit, I installed this on my windshield with no problem at all.
I also downloaded the Zenfox app onto my Android phone. But, will go into that in a bit.
Setting this up wasn't too hard. It's SO hard to see the little screen and the little icons on it. Wish they had the icons in a different brighter color so they stand out a bit more. So, until I go back out with a magnifying glass and a flashlight, I'll have to wait to get it completely set up the way I want it.
Did drive with it on last night. The inside camera picture covers up the front view a little so you don't get a clear view of what's in front of you looking at the little screen. Looked really nice and clear!
When the record function is working, the light on it stays red. It's a very light light so it's hard to see if it's light outside. If it isn't working then it'll blink and you'll hear a beeping sound. The microphone is red when working, off when it's not. Again, it's hard to see the light when it's daytime.
One thing I noticed is that the screen goes dark after a certain amount of time. It looks like it's off. I did open the phone app and saw that I could see the pictures so I figured it was still recording. Could be a setting I need to change?
Now with the phone app. What I like about it first. I like that I can open the app and see what the camera is seeing. I can also change any settings using the app. Very nice and convenient. So much easier than doing it with the dashcam itself.
What I don't like about it is that the dashcam has to be turned on, by means of turning the car on, to be able to use the app. Tried it out the first time last night and getting past the WiFi setting was a pain. I don't have WiFi when I'm driving so there's no way to connect to it. After 7 mins of fiddling around with it, I finally got past that part (don't know how) and saw the camera view on my phone.
I was going to try to check out the different settings but couldn't until I turned the camera off. Because I didn't want to turn the dashcam off, change a setting, then turn it back on to see the difference over and over again, I just gave up and let it be. Should be able to change a view setting or any setting with the camera running so we can see what the difference is and see if we want to keep it changed.
Over with the confusing part of setting this up, I'll state what I really love about this dash cam.
If I'm in an accident, it will automatically lock that particular time in the loop program so that it won't be over written with new coverage. I can also hit the OK button to lock a particular time so that it won't be destroyed or overwritten. I love how clear the picture is. May look small on the small screen but, it's even better when you view it through your phone. And I'm sure much better if you view it through your tv or computer screen.
I like the peace it gives me that if I am in an accident, I have proof of it on film. Just a nice peace of mind when I'm driving now.
Now that this is completely installed and running great, I'll have to take the time and look at all the setup options I have in the phone app. I think I saw where I can format the SD card and maybe download updates using the app.
For someone not really tech smart with devices like this, I can't really tell you what is the best in the option settings they have. But like anything, what is good for me might not be the best setting for you.
I'll have to keep testing different settings with this to see what is what and what best fits my needs.
Overall it's a really nice dashcam with a nice clear picture. This is something I'll be using every time I have my vehicle on the road.

title: Definitely NOT 3x Faster than USB 2.0
text:
This is a nice little thumbdrive (jumpdrive) and a decent size at 32GB - however it's not USB 3 speed. If you don't really care about speed, it's fine as a USB 2 drive and stores plenty of files but for being advertised as USB 3.0 it's a one-star at best. I gave it three stars because it is a 32GB drive and useful, but since it's advertised at USB 3.0 it should work at that speed.

First I tested the drive in my USB 2 slot to get a baseline and see how much faster it would be when I put it in my USB 3 slot.

To test I used a 3.76 GB file. I renamed the file so that I would end up with two files on the drive. Basically I just called one "USB2" and the other "USB3"

Results:
In the USB 2.0 slot:
+ the 3.76 GB file copied TO (write speed) the Lexar drive in 1:54 (114 seconds = 33.77 MB/Sec);
+ the 3.76 GB file copied FROM (read speed) the Lexar drive in 1:37 (97 seconds = 39.69 MB/Sec);

In the USB 3.0 slot:
+ the 3.76 GB file copied TO (write speed) the Lexar drive in 1:41 (101 seconds = 38.12 MB/Sec);
+ the 3.76 GB file copied FROM (read speed) the Lexar drive in 1:22 (82 seconds = 46.95 MB/Sec);

Okay, so the advertised speed is "up to 45MB/s read and 20MB/s write" -- but USB 3.0 should be much faster than that - speeds up to 640 MB/Sec. USB 2.0 is speeds up to 60 MB/Sec. So you can see by these numbers that this drive is closer to USB 2.0.

Really, it's not that bad of a drive if you're not having to copy really large files. But don't expect USB 3.0 speeds from it and don't buy it if you can get a 32GB USB2.0 drive for cheaper.

title: I'm Addicted
text:
I received a Kindle as a gift, and it has taken over my reading life. I'm sad when a book is only available in print and delighted when there is a Kindle version. It's not AS comfortable as a print book, it's MORE comfortable than a print book. The font is amazing. It's easy to use, and for people who knit, it sits nicely in a bookstand on or a reader's pillow to read while knitting.

I have the Sony eReader. I used to own the rocket. I see the Kindle as the real future of ebooks, and I really want ebooks to succeed for a few reasons.

One is storage. If you are a bibliophile, you probably have a book army ready to take over your home. We avid readers are forced to cull our libraries to make room for new books. No more. I would suggest opening a free account with a service like Goodreads to categorize books, since with the Kindle you can't set up a "history" section and a "fantasy" section, but that's so minor. I never could keep those organized in my print library as well, and many books fall into multiple categories anyway. Do I need to mention that ebooks don't yellow and decay over time?

Two is portability. If you are the type to carry many books at once (I am--some for study and some for pleasure reading along with a newspaper) then this is the easiest way to do it.

Three is the glorious possibility that books will never go "out of print" again, because there is no "print" overhead, just a little meg sitting in a several terrabyte raid array somewhere. Books will always be a minute away.

Four is the idea that books will be instantly large print and still small, and easy to tote around. My eyes are still quite good, but I'd love to think, when age degrades them someday, I'll still be able to read the latest releases easily.

Five is the instant availability of hot books. When Brisingr came out, it was sitting on my Kindle that morning. Compare that to the sometimes day-long wait we went through for the Harry Potter books (and books that size are yet another reason ebooks rock). I love having the New York Times delivered, but can't stand it when the delivery boy loses the key and rings my bell at 4 in the morning. This is the best of both worlds.

Six is the ease of reading large online documents, such as those from Gutenberg or a friend's novel (and don't we all have someone who sends us large files to read from time to time?)

Seven is the price of the books. Everything is cheaper on the Kindle and some books are frighteningly inexpensive. I bought the Talmud for 99 cents. A collection of the first five books in the John Carter on Mars series for 99 cents. And the entire collection of the Wizard of Oz books for, you guessed it, 99 cents.

Other e-readers hit close to the mark; the Kindle got it right. I only want two things. I want color and I want Amazon to hit that goal of having every book (including comics and manga please) available for the Kindle. Overall, the day of the ebook truly arrived with the Kindle and I couldn't be happier.

title: A good product that's getting better
text:
I've been obsessed with fully wireless earbuds for years and have tried out at least a dozen different ones throughout.

I fully support some in the $30 range, I had a pair of old soundcores that worked great. I've also tried the more expensive Samsung Galaxy Buds (2018 version), which worked well enough. I've also tried some mid-range ear buds in the $70 range. Earbuds have gone through some growing pains with drop off issues between the left and right buds and battery life. In my experience, I believe the $30 buds are great value and >$100 buds are worth it only if they have good sound and good app support. For me every one of the $70 buds that I have purchased have broken down in less than three months, so I'd say stay away from those.

Now on to the review:
The Cleer Audio, Ally Plus II True Wireless Noise Cancelling Earbuds are in the >$100 range (although just barely) but in the last few weeks that I've used them, I truly believe they are worth their asking price. I will of course update this review if they break down in a few months.

There are so many wireless earbuds being produced these days, which most imitating the airbuds with their ugly stalks in one form or another, Cleer has gone with a tear-drop shape and capacitive controls that I appreciate. I purchased the tan-colored buds and they don't stand out like a pair of white or black buds would. There is only a single dim light on the earbuds to indicate charging status and they are the in-ear-canal style of earbuds.

Features:
- Light-weight.
- Charging/carrying case supports type-c connection as well as wireless charging. Interoperable with products designed for airbuds wireless charging.
- Long battery life. I listen to audiobooks and they have lasted for hours while I worked on chores around the house.
- Passthrough with good app support (more on it later)
- Active Noise cancellation
- Can be used as a single earbud without having to pair each separately
- Touch controls: Only tap, double tap, and triple tap are supported. Configurable through the app.

The App:
When I first received the Cleer earbuds, the app was unimpressive. There was a single slide bar that changed the balance between noise cancellation and passthrough, a equalizer with no presets (and no reset for that matter), and there was limited control over what the tap functions did.

Since then, the app has been updated and the earbuds had a firmware upgrade. While the app still has room for more improvement, they did separate the passthrough, normal, and noise cancellation modes into separate controls. Passthrough now has a slider to control the strength of the surrounding noise and the noise cancelling has a "smart noise cancel" mode. In addition, a new personalized audio feature was added. The app takes you through a hearing test and adjusts the sound to your hearing levels. Quite cool.

The limited controls over the touch function is still there and the barely passable equalizer is still there but I'm hoping that they will be improved in future updates.

title: Heavy but good protection against light damage.
text:
I was very pleased with how easy it was to install, and how well it fit my new MacBook Air M2. Simple as wipe the MBA down with the supplied cloth, unwrap everything and it just snaps into place. The keyboard cover is barely noticeable when I type. The case is very clear and bright and still shows off the beautiful new MacBook Air black color.

It is a hard acrylic case and it will protect your laptop from scratches, scrapes, bumps and bruises. However I don't think it is going to offer much protection to a drop. It might mitigate a dent, but there is no silicone middle layer so there is nothing to absorb the energy of impact and it will be transmitted right into the screen/computer itself. So if this were dropped on an edge or corner I would not be surprised if the screen or internals did not get damaged. It is obviously better than nothing at all, but definitely not Otterbox level of protection. I still recommend AppleCare regardless of case choice.

Be Aware: This case is going to double the weight of your MacBook. I love how light the MacBook is out of the box and if I did not have to return it in 3 months with zero blemishes, I might not use this case due to the weight increase.

So in summary this is a good case to protect against scratches, scrapes & dents, but not drops. Pretty heavy but that is expected for this type of acrylic case.

title: Better for Business; Graphics Card is Mediocre
text:
I have a Dell laptop that has served me well and I also have an older Dell workstation that has been great. I had high hoped for this tower system, and unfortunately it doesn’t quite meet expectations. If you are looking for an affordable gaming system, this one will work on the lower end.

I’ll start with the positives.

It comes with a 7th-generation core i7 processor and it is definitely fast. It is not one of the low power consumption processors, so when you look at the CPU in the device manager you see 8 of them reported - this is a good thing.

Everything is integrated with this system and there are plenty of ports. You don’t need a separate graphics card (though you can add one - more on that in a minute), sound is built in, Bluetooth is built in too and it even has integrated wireless networking.

This is a very attractive system too, and it’s quiet. If you don’t like a noisy system\, this one has you covered.

It comes with 1TB storage. It’s disk-based so it’s slower than an SSD but with that amount of space you have more than enough space for most uses.

And, it’s affordable. It will not break the bank if you already have a monitor and keyboard/mouse combo.

And now for the bad news.

I am not the least bit impressed with the graphics card. With modern games the more graphics memory you have the better, and having only 2GB video RAM is not enough to get it done anymore. My son is an avid gamer and has demonstrated to me that his business-grade laptop gets better frame rates. So, we are shopping for a better and more generous graphics card.

Another area where we will be expanding is the system RAM. The RAM is DDR4 and it’s fast, but the system comes with only 8GB. Our present plan is to double it.

No documentation? I know that the trend is to not include install/recovery media, but come on - there should be more than just a quick start in the box.

This is a decent desktop system that would be find in a business environment, but it falls a little flat when it comes to gaming. It needs a better graphics card (well, at least more video RAM) and it needs more system RAM to be a respectable gaming system.

title: This fan heats up my laptop because the fan is reversed, temperature is only displayed in Celsius, & instructions are horrendous
text:
I selected this because my work computer runs hot and this fan is supposed to cool down a laptop by attaching it to the vent. I tried this on a Dell Latitude E6430 and the LED temperature reading climbs and my laptop heats up when connected. In fact, there's nothing about this product that would make me recommend it. Read on to see what is provided and what about this product is so wrong.

WHAT COMES IN THE PACKAGE:
- 1 laptop cooler fan
- 1 USB cable
- 1 plastic connector plate
- 4 rubber sticky feet and 3 (not 4 as specified) tiny silicone suction cups
- 1 instruction sheet
- 4 silicon mouthpieces to connect the fan to the laptop vent

WHAT IS WRONG WITH THIS PRODUCT:

- The instructions (picture attached) are incredibly poor and barely make any sense at all. Here are three sentences that I copied below exactly as written including punctuation and wording (except for the quotes I put around those sentences to indicate they were verbatim).

"Products with a bottom bracket accessories, and comes with three super sucker."
"Qingtai outlet end notebook, the silicone radiator outlet to trap the notebooks vents guide."
"According to the books of the heat, free adjustment"

- Assembly is slightly required and I had to figure it out on my own because the instructions were so poor.

* To assemble, I took the plastic black connector plate and snapped that into the three holes on the bottom front of the unit; the side closest to the on / off knob.

* I inserted the suction cups into the three holes in the front of the plate with the suction cups side down. Perhaps I could have used the rubber sticky feet but I'm not sure where to put those. I think the installation of those cushions is optional and I suspect they go either on the bottom of the connector plate or the unit.

* I attached one of the four silicone "mouth guards" to the front of the unit. I was sure to use the one that best fit the shape of the laptop vent so that it created a tight seal. Once assembled, I plugged one end of the USB cable into the side of the unit and the other end to a free USB port on my laptop.

* After the USB was connected, the temperature is displayed without ever having to turn on the unit or connect it to a laptop. I noted that the temperature without connecting the fan to my vent and with the fan off read 26.0 C. The LED is only in Celsius so I had to convert the numbers to Fahrenheit because I am not fluent in Celsius. I do know that the temperature is supposed to go down and not up so I turned on the fan but still did not connect the fan to my vent and the temperature started decreasing to 24.0 C and lower. However, once I connected the fan to the vent the temperature steadily increased to 31, 33, 36, 36.5 C, etc. I repeated all these steps on six separate occasions and got the same results. In exasperation, I decided to turn the unit around by facing the back of the unit toward the laptop vent. Once I did this, the temperature decreased slightly. This means that the fan is rotating the wrong way making this device useless.

In summary, this fan heats up the laptop. I suspect the reason for this is because the fan is rotating the wrong way so it is not drawing the heat away from the laptop vent. The temperature LED is only in Celsius which is great for Europeans fluent in that temperature but is not great for the majority of Americans. Also, the instructions are horrendous. My recommendation is to pass on this one.

UPDATE Jan 24, 2017 - I tried to see if I could fix this fan but could not. There are three tiny screws holding the body together. One screw is located underneath one of the rubber feet. Once I got it open, I had no way of knowing if the connectors are correct or not. The ribbons inside only go one way and reversing the fan doesn't seem to be an option. Therefore, I decided to throw the unit out since Vine reviewers have no warranty on the products they receive. What a waste.

title: Great Antenna Kit!  (And I Did Not Use The Rotor Or Pre-Amp)
text:
If you're looking for an affordable OTA antenna, then you've probably seen A LOT of them over the course of your research. I went back & forth on a few, but finally pulled the trigger & went with this unit. And I'm glad I did! After using for almost one month, it has exceeded my expectations.

The unit came well packed from the vendor with all of the parts needed for the installation. You will need a few tools for the mounting portion of your install, but these will be determined by where you mount (indoors or outdoors). The manual will explain further. The documentation is OK (not great), but you will be able to complete the project from what is provided.

This kit ships with a mounting pole, 40' RG6 coax, a rotor control (to remotely turn the antenna), a pre-amp, the antenna & mounting hardware. Some light assembly is required, but it's very straightforward.

**There is a model of this antenna that is cheaper, but DOES NOT SHIP with a mounting pole. So make sure you select the correct version for your application.**

Also, some OTA antennas DO NOT included coax, a mounting pole or a pre-amp. These will be additional expenses on top of the purchase of your antenna. So make sure you read the details on any antenna that you consider purchasing. This model includes all of these items.

Of course, for the price, you're not receiving a top of the line pre-amp, or for that matter high quality RG6, but for most applications it should suffice just fine. Especially if you install indoors (mine was an attic install) where it will be protected from the elements.

And for anyone wondering, the pre-amp IS powered by the rotor control box (not by the coax feed). So if you opt not to use the rotor (to turn the antenna on demand) then you will not be able to use the pre-amp.

So if you need the pre-amp, you will have to connect up the rotor control even if it won't be used. However, if neither are needed, then they can be bypassed entirely.

Also, you can run this antenna directly into a signal booster (drop amplifier) like a PCT (PCT-VC-9U). These can be found on Amazon for around $50.00 - $100.00 depending on size & features you need. So if you already have coax jacks in your house that are in place from previous cable or satellite TV, then you can repurpose those jacks for your new antenna. This way you can distribute your antenna signal to all (or most) of the TV's in your house!

Please note that your location, proximity to your broadcast towers, potential points of interference (trees, building, mountains, etc..) & height of your mount are a HUGE DEAL when using ANY OTA antenna.

I'm located in FL, so it's pretty flat. However, most of the broadcast towers are 30-45 miles away. As well, the antenna was mounted indoors & at the most 15' to 16' in the air. So it is fairly low. However, even with an indoor installation (and not using the pre-amp) , this antenna easily picked up 57 OTA channels!

So while some people blame the antenna when they can only pick up a few stations, there are many other moving parts involved to get this all to work.

If this is your first time installing an OTA antenna, then PLEASE use a free site like "tvfool" or "antennaweb" (Google these) to determine what direction your broadcast towers are in relation to where you will be mounting your antenna. These services will also tell you what channels are going to be achievable with the antenna of your choosing. All you do is plug in your address & the site will serve up all of the info that you need. Do this BEFORE you buy any antenna to make sure it's even worth your time.

One last thing, be sure to re-scan your channels on your TV every now & again. Channels get repacked (put under different channel assignments) & new channels get added. So if a channel that was coming in suddenly disappears, it may not be your antenna, but the broadcast signal itself.

Overall, this antenna was easy to install. Since I mounted indoors, I used two 2" wood screws with washers right into a truss to mount the mast. The antenna goes on with 2 bolts (ratchet & socket do well here) & you're done. I can't personally speak to an outdoor installation, but would have to assume that it would be a bit more involved.

I shortened the included RG6 cable (only dual shield not quad shield) to around 15' as my equipment panel was directly below the antenna in the laundry room. If you decide to do this, then you will need to crimp on a new compression connector on one end of the cable. However, you can purchase an entire kit on Amazon (with F connectors, coax stripper & the crimp tool) for under $20.00 (Bestar #3189 (Blue-F) ). It's VERY easy. You can do it!

As well, having a shorter run can only help your signal performance. So if you have excess cable after your install, consider shortening it to the exact length that you need.

The hardest part of the install is dialing in the perfect sweet spot for your broadcast towers. The best thing you can do is use the websites noted above to get the direction of the towers BEFORE you do your install. Then bring a compass (yes, a real compass) or use a compass on your smartphone (this is what I did & it worked perfectly) to help point your antenna in the correct direction. If you have a helper, then have them scan the channels once you lock on to your desired direction. It may take a few attempts, but it's worth it (especially if you don't use the rotor function). Cell phones or walkie talkies do nicely here :-)

And if you ever need it, their support was great. It's only email based, but they responded within 24 hrs. Very willing to help & get any questions answered.

If things change, I will update this review. However, after almost a month of use, I've been very happy with this kit. It feels great not paying the cable company to provide stations that are otherwise floating around us for free -in uncompressed HD!

text:
Wanted something to take on vacation to Europe - river cruise and wanted to see castles and such off in distance.

The binoculars are very simple to use and provide good viewing from moving boat on a stable image off at a distance. Extremely simple toggle system let me get right on the best focus. The case is a soft material and I would be careful packing them with anything that might damage the binoculars. The case gives some protection from damage and has straps, so I carried them in the case at times around neck. There are also straps for the binoculars. I would not carry them for long around neck as I'd worry about damage. The case closes with a single velcro fastener and anything small could easily fall out and get lost. This is probably the only downside on this buy. I am looking for some additional velcro I can attach to the case.

There are four lens covers and they do the job, but would fall off easy were you carrying the binoculars around neck or otherwise not attending close. I only use the covers when the glasses are inside case. I suspect these covers will get lost easy, especially as the soft sided case does not zip.

I don't know the material used for these glasses and was shocked at the price for the quality. Clearly, these are not the high quality glasses a professional may want. But, for travel, hunting or backpacking, or such use once in a while, these do a great job.

My speeds are a little better, and my connection seems more stable, although I have experienced disconnects with 5G (this may be due to proximity, since I haven't experienced trouble with devices that are closer ). The setup would have been a breeze, except that the instructions were wrong for setting it up as an AP. If I'd had previous experience with TP-Link routers, so I knew how to load the server interface, that probably wouldn't have mattered, but this was my first for this brand. After trying nearly everything possible, I eventually ignored the instructions and it was a breeze (why is it that everything made to be more simple, always ends up being harder?)

Overall, I'm a little disappointed in the basic features, and the quality doesn't seem great, but it's fairly easy to use and it seems stable. However, I wouldn't recommend it to those who want more from their router and I wouldn't buy it again.

title: Recordings Are Stored in Canary Cloud; Full Replay Access Requires Paid Membership
text:
When I ordered this CANARY VIEW INDOOR 1080p HD SECURITY CAMERA (with Wide-Angle Lens, Motion/Person Alerts, Works with Alexa, Pets/Elder/Baby Monitoring), there was one very important thing that I didn’t understand. To wit, the camera has zero internal storage--everything is uploaded to Canary Cloud, which costs $89 a year for full-featured camera access and video replays.

It is possible to set up the camera without signing up for a free 30-day trial membership (which requires entering a credit card that will automatically be charged after 30 days unless you cancel the membership). You do this by accepting the $0.00 monthly charge option, and scrolling on down past the place where you enter the credit card info.

However, most of the playback and customizing features in the Canary app (the only way to access the camera) are inoperable without a membership. When you’re at home, you can “Watch Live” if you tinker with the available settings. However, you can’t play back motion events without a membership unless they happen while you’re away--and you can’t trick the camera into thinking you’re away, because the app determines your location by the location of your tablet or smartphone. (And you can’t turn the phone off, because you need the app to access the camera.)

The camera sells for about $80 on Amazon, and that’s a lot to pay for a device that’s almost useless unless you add a “membership” that costs another $89 a year. Should the company go out of business, your device will, too. Also, all of your recordings are stored in Canary Cloud, so you need to trust the company to keep the site secure and private.

As for the camera itself, it’s fairly low resolution, but reasonably wide-angle. Without the membership, the camera will works as a real-time spy camera for the room it’s in (it does resemble an Amazon Echo). The camera is fixed in one position, and only records what is directly in front, so you need to place it in a spot where it will cover as much area as possible.

When I think about it, I don’t really need an indoor security camera, because my Comcast home security system monitors all the doors and windows of my condo. Given that this device costs $89 a year, it makes more sense for me to add another camera to my existing system ($95) and then accept the extra Comcast monthly charge, so that I don’t have to fool with the awkward Canary app settings.

Overall I'm satisfied. It does what I need it to do and for not a lot of money, and some channels look better than my Samsung that cost more than twice as much. This is a high-quality cable. I wasn't sure how well it would work since it's 65 feet long, but it's well-made unlike some of the other cables.

I wanted to be able to use a single cable box in two different rooms. Not so that they could be used at the same time, but because I didn't want to pay the fee that the cable company charges for "additional cable boxes". I could just get an HDMI splitter and connect it to both of the 4K sets.

This cable allowed me to have one TV in the living-room and another in the bedroom using only a single box. One obvious problem I thought might be a problem was the remote. However, I'd heard that if your devices have HDMI-CEC abilities, then you can control them over HDMI. That didn't work for my setup.

But, getting another universal remote and a remote extender worked. It picks up the signals from the remote in one room and relays them to the other room as if the remote were in the other room. It was probably the easiest way to do it.

The signal works fine over the 65-foot length. And for my case, it made things a little better.

It might not be something you'll need except in similar situations, but I can say it does a great job.

Overall, a high-quality cable that works, for a decent price without having to resort to one of those RF extenders that just add extra wireless noise to your home.

title: Keyboard feels great to use, the case has made my iPad more functional; don't like the trackpad
text:
The Logitech Folio Touch is a JOY to type on. I really love typing on it — I’m writing this review using the case. I’ve typed quite a few long documents on it. I turn to this keyboard when I want distraction-free writing.

The keyboard reminds me of Apple laptop keyboards before the disastrous butterfly keyboards. The keyboard is backlit, and the brightness of the backlighting can be adjusted via the function keys. The row of function keys is another good feature for me. I find it much faster and easier to adjust the iPad’s brightness or volume using the function keys.

I downloaded the Logitech Control app, but it doesn’t seem to give any options for customizing the keyboard. All I see the app do is check for keyboard firmware updates. When I wanted to change the trackpad scrolling direction, I had to hunt through the iPad’s settings — I thought that would be in the Logitech app. (I learned those settings became part of iOS, so the Logitech app seems … unnecessary.)

I don’t really like the trackpad. I’ve used Logitech mice for years. My current daily mouse is the Logitech MX Master 3, so I *know* they can do a good Mac mouse. But I just feel like they dropped the ball with this trackpad. The trackpad works but it could be better. I notice drag at times, and I don’t like the noise or tactile feedback when I click it. I can adjust a few settings (scrolling direction, tracking speed, tap to click, and two finger secondary click) in the iPad’s General Settings, but I want to be able to customize more through Logitech.

The corners of the case are reinforced. The bumper is a bit thick, too thick for some hubs or USB-C cables to fit without using an extension cable. There is a cutout for the power button so Touch ID can be used. There’s a spot for the Apple Pencil, it can rest inside the bumper or fit through a slot on the latch.

The Folio Touch pairs via the Smart Connector, so it’s super easy to set up: just stick your iPad inside and it’s ready to go. The iPad powers the keyboard, so I don’t have to remember to charge it, which I like. I haven’t noticed it being a battery hog.

Overall, I really like the Logitech Folio Touch. I actually use my iPad more now, since I like typing on the keyboard so much. The case has made my iPad more functional for me.

title: Great Receiver, A Few Imperfections
text:
I bought this receiver from Best Buy and not Amazon only because I absolutely had to have convenient nearby service, after a horrible experience with my prior Samsung monstrosity home theater that I had bought along with a side market service plan. (No fault of Amazon or the service plan, just Samsung.)

This is a terrific receiver. The fidelity is excellent, plenty of power, although I'd like it if the rear channels were stronger; even at 10 they are kind of weak for my taste. Unlike other commenters, I don't mind the large, loaded remote control. It's always better to have more control than less. However, the Mute button is tiny and located in an inconvenient position next to the main volume rocker control, and I have bumbled with one when I wanted the other, numerous times.

It was very easy to get the unit connected to my home WiFi, went smoothly.

The receiver is large and heavy, so you need plenty of room for it.

The system has a capability for the user to set the time difference between audio and video, in milliseconds. I don't understand why there should EVER be asynchrony between audio and video in the first place, since the HDMI signal carries both of them perfectly synchronized, and this issue drove me crazy on my prior Samsung, but it seems that I hardly need to use it in the Sony, so I guess it's okay.

I'd have to grasp at straws to find something to criticize. Here's one -- although it has built-in apps for streaming music, it should also have them for streaming video. I know, I know, most products in this class concentrate on audio and not video, but it would be a much better product, and could stand out in its class, if it had this functionality, which much cheaper home theater systems DO have somehow. Without it, to watch Netflix I have to use a DVD receiver that DOES have it, connected to the Sony and selected for viewing, kind of an awkward arrangement when it could be just as easy for them to have included this in the Sony, I don't think it would have necessitated any additional hardware.

Likewise, although the unit wll play audio files and dislay JPGs and other images, from a flash drive plugged into ts USB port, it will not play video files, and could have if they had designed it that way.

Another issue -- although the binding posts for speaker wires in the rear work well, they are jammed in close together and this makes it very difficult to connect multiple wires on nearby posts. They should have spread them out some more.

Unless I'm misunderstanding how to use it, you are not able to view DirecTV or other external sources on your TV set thru this product unless the Sony is itself turned on. There are many occasions where we don't need the full capability of Surround Sound, like when watching the Sunday morning talk shows, and the TV speakers would be fine. But you have to turn on the Sony any time you watch TV whether you need Surround Sound or not. It should be easy for them to allow for full pass-thru of audio and video when the unit is powered off.

I also agree with other commenters that the Sony should have included an on-TV volume indicator for when you change the volume on the Sony. At moderate viewing distances the volume indication on the Sony front display is too tiny for me to see easily.

And one other thing -- the use of ancient dot-matrix display technology on a brand new hi-tech product like this one just introduced in 2013 is ridiculous. Sony SHOULD be able to provide a modern, larger, colorful, easier to see front display than this artifact. I feel like an archaeologist reading from it. It belongs in the Smithsonian and not on this otherwise splendid new product.
