title: Paired with Amazon’s Unlimited Music service, these are awesome!
text:
I love the look of this newer generation Echo Alexa. I like that it’s shorter and wider, making it feel more stable and the fabric is really nice looking. Echo Alexa’s are incredibly easy to set up yourself... even the most technologically challenged should be able to do it themselves if they just have a device where they can add the Alexa App. Turns out our old Echo is MUCH more consistent, and much more reliable but it is really nice to have two and we mostly only use this second one for a timer in the kitchen, and for music. The speaker appears to be a little louder and more clear but it’s not a huge difference... both sound really good. Both play the soundtrack for Hamilton 20 times a day beautifully for my little person who is obsessed with all things Hamilton. Sometimes I laugh when I look on the app and see our history.... Hamilton, Hamilton, Hamilton... a few other favorite songs here and there, Disney Storyteller Version books,daily alarms, and “ask for a fart” over and over. Hahahahaha! Are we really utilizing our devices to the fullest? Well that is a resounding “NO” but we are very happy with what we do use and can’t inagine life without them at this point. One big complaint... this device ( which was a new device, not certified refurbished) has LOTS of delays after you ask for something. She lights up and thinks and sometimes she will respond after a pause, but sometimes you get nothing at all and have to ask again. Our first device never dies that and in fact... will answer to the tv or anyone you says the wale word even if it’s all the way in the other room. This second generation seems to be far less sensitive and may even have some connectivity issues. I probably should have sent it back but it works for the most part and honestly I felt bad doing that because then it has to be sold as a refurb unit. I got two new 2nd generations in a multi-buy deal, for far less than you’d even pay for one by buying them on Prime Day. One is a gift for family. The deal was so good my mind was blown after having previously paid full price for our first generation Echo Alexa.

Update August 2020. We still have both Alexa/Echo devices mentioned here and both are still the same as I described. Our first device works relatively well, is loud and clear, and is able to produce somewhat correct results for most of the music I ask for using our Amazon Unlimited Music account. But the second, newer version is so lacking it seems crazy to me that this was considered and upgraded/updated version. Yes, it does look less plasticky.... less like a computer component (although the fabric attracts dust and the plastic does not) but other than the appearance, I don’t find one area where the newer version is better than the older one. The older version is in the room where our Echo gets the most use anyway, and truthfully we almost forget we have the other one so it’s not a huge deal, but for people who only have one at their disposal...I can’t imagine being happy with the newer version. BTW, I did get two of the newer version Alexa/Echo’s on Prime Day for an absolutely stellar price in a “buy two” deal. I gave one away and kept one. The person I gave the other one yo says theirs works well, so, it looks like I should have returned ours for a replacement. Live and learn.
At any rate, I am very impressed that our original Alexa/Echo, purchased in store for $179.99 black when this was new technology, is still going strong. It doesn’t always have an answer, and sometimes the answer is wrong, but it’s still great to have music at the ready, volume control from anywhere the device can hear your voice, and silly things like farts and games. I know we don’t use it to it’s full capacity, but even just for the music, it adds much enjoyment to our lives. I didn’t mention that the two devices appear to operate completely separately of each other and can not find the same music or information even if it’s been accessed hundreds of times before on the other device, which I find odd, but we’ve gotten used to. Haha

title: Here’s my practical review of the Acer Predator Triton 500
text:
Here’s my practical review of the Acer Predator Triton 500

As a disclaimer I own the 8750H model not the 9750H but all else aside everything should apply to this model as well. The design aesthetics are subtle for a gaming laptop. This laptop sits at a sweet spot for the price/performance ratio using an 8750H processor and a GTX 2060 graphics card. Laptop is very well ventilated for cooling with perforated holes on top and bottom and has vents on the sides and back of laptop. It’s covered in mostly all aluminum for a premium feel. There are complaints of this being a fingerprint magnet but I take that any day for that premium feel. The AC adapter is one of the smaller 180w power bricks as compared to the competitors. Amazing how the webcam and the power supply shows the progress of miniaturization.

Durability: This laptop has a solid tank like construction comparable to the way Alien laptops are constructed. However, the display has some flex but that is to be said for a lot thin and light gaming laptops. Quality control issues are a concern from some posts, but these sound like issues that would present themselves right away once you boot up and can be returned or replaced in the event that should happen.

Noise: For basic daily non-gaming use, the fans runs fairly quiet even with 40 chrome tabs running. By comparison, my 9370 laptop has the fans running pretty noticeable with 40 chrome tabs. Fans run loud when turbo is enabled but the noise is on par or below comparable gaming laptop noise but most gamers wear headphones when playing games on a laptop.

Display: The 1080 IPS 144Hz near borderless display matches well for this tier of gaming laptops and is pretty decent, Although it was mentioned in other posts about brightness levels, it is plenty bright for indoor use. There are some screen backlight bleeding but it to be expected and is not noticeable or impacts my daily use.

Keyboard: One of the better keyboards for a thin and light along with good 1.7mm of travel and solid feedback. I was disappointed that I could not change the volume up, volume down, and mute key on the right to page up and page down.

The dual channel ram of 16GB is enough for most games and use cases, while the 512GB of NVM SSD drive is sufficient for most people and pretty decent storage space by recent standards.

Should I buy now? For those on the border for buy a gaming laptop now or wait. I would say right now is the best time to buy a laptop based on current vs predicted future performance. The 8750H processor and 2060 graphics are both mature products from Intel and NVidia meaning the percentage gains from generation to generation will not be as high as they are with the current gen products. The increases will likely be in the single digit gains such as going from the 8750H to the 9750H (6% improvement) and that increase would not affect gaming (1-2 frame rate gain) in any perceptible way. Acer’s Helios 300 and Triton 500 are the best price/performance ratio for gaming around right now.

Notes:

Changed the base speed of the CPU when plugged in to 2.2GHz under power options, advanced settings, intel dynamic platform and thermal framework, config TDP level to maximize CPU potential when its plugged in.

Apparently, CPU comes undervolted with an offset of -0.100 V.

Downloaded and Updated bios to 1.06 from Acer’s website but found out there is no options on the 2060 model to switch G Sync and Optimus.

Be sure to turn off Waves Nx from Waves Maxxaudio when listening to audio from your headphones else the camera turns on all the time to track your head movement for virtual sound spacing.

I contacted Acer tech support and due to their internal policy before I could talk to them about my laptop, I had to allow them to register my laptop. By doing this, I was prevented from registering and associating my serial number when self-registering on the Acer site. A fix I found was to log into the Acer product registration app from the start menu which did fix my problem.

An inherent problem with laptops and monitors, are the very bright power indicator led lights are always on at night. This laptop is no different and I have not found a software solution to turn it off, although it does serve a purpose it is annoyingly on at night. I probably will sharpie with a black marker or black removable tape.

title: Good device - better than the Jawbone!
text:
I acquired one of these to replace the Jawbone 1 I had been using. I liked the Jawbone 1, in fact, I liked it so much I bought three - one to replace the one I broke, and one to replace the one I lost. The one niggling problem I had always had with the Jawbone, however, was that the incoming audio was just never quite loud enough. This is a puzzling flaw, because the Jawbone 1 is specifically designed to work well in noisy environments, and in fact it almost always excelled at allowing my callers to hear me well. However, since I couldn't always hear my callers well when I was in noisy environments because the earpiece just wasn't loud enough, and I read reviews of the Griffin that specifically mentioned its loud, clear audio, I decided to get one.

I've only had it a couple of days now but I can definitely say that I can hear my callers better; it's probably partly due to better sound isolation from the silicone rubber earplug part that very effectively blocks the entrance to the ear canal, but also because the speaker inside the unit is just more capable of producing a nice, loud signal.

The unit itself is significantly lighter and more svelte than the Jawbone 1 and the swiveling ear hook allows for better & easier alignment of the earpiece to the face. The recharging cord is a little more fiddly to attach than the Jawbone 1's, but early samples of the Jawbone 1 often had some difficulty in making and sustaining a charging connection, which the Griffin does not seem like it will. The voice prompts are a nice touch, but are, themselves, curiously muffled in quality, and the start of each phrase seems to be mysteriously clipped off, so I felt I had to deduct one star in my rating for this reason.

Otherwise, a very solid product, and a definite improvement over my beloved Jawbone 1.

title: UPDATE REDUCED TO 2 STARS Beautiful sound, amazing with the 500 as a group.
text:
UPDATED REVIEW REDUCED TO TWO STARS JUNE 2019

We've had trouble with the remote for three months now. It works sporadically at best and has finally died entirely. This is a major problem because you cannot do important stuff with the sound bar without the original remote control. Such as.... rebooting it. If you change your WiFi network like.... getting a new router, then you cannot simply go to the app and update the connection. You must reboot the entire sound bar via the remote control only. WHICH DOES NOT WORK AT ALL. This design flaw has rendered the entire sound bar none functional because it cannot connect to the new Wi-Fi - going back to our old router isn't an option because it died. So now I have a sound bar that technically is operational, yet cannot be used. Our Bose 500 sound bar was able to be reconfigured for the Wi-Fi swap because it's remote works like a champ - it's also significantly simpler in design than the 700 remote. (I'll end up spending fifty bucks for a new 700 remote and that really aggravates me)

******* Original review before the drama*******

We've had an older Bose Solo 15 Series II TV Sound System in our living room for a couple of years and we've been pretty happy overall. I recently put the Bose 500 version of this sound bar in our master bedroom and was amazed at the difference, so getting this 700 for the living room was a no brainer. I mostly just expected them to connect as a group and have the same sound, but this 700 is better than the 500.

It's a long, narrow, sleek looking unit with glass finishes that makes it almost invisible in front of the Tv. Our Roku fits alongside without drama. The connections are via digital optical cable or the HDMI. Just turn off your TV speakers - not mute, off from the tv settings. You need to use the included wired headset to fully set the speakers for your room's accoustics. I'm using this bar with a 55", 3 years old, Sceptre dumb tv and a Room streaming stick - the connection was immediate and drama free.

You must use the Bose app to get full functionality out of the sound bar. The app let's you connect two or more Bose speakers with the tech and use them all simultaneously as a group to play music or audiobooks etc. The app also starts the set up for the Alexa link and the streaming services like Prime, Tune In, Bluetooth streaming and others. You can also set 6 favorites as one touch launch options.

Alexa works fine through the sound bar, but the response speed is noticably slower than through a regular Echo. I get a glitchy message saying "This unit is unable to perform routines" every time I say "Good morning". Good morning triggers a specific set of actions from Alexa to turn on our bedside lamps, the bathroom lights, turn off our porch lights, give me the weather and then our daily news brief. Despite that glitchy message, every morning, the Bose performs our routine flawlessly. It's weird, but not a big deal really.

The sound quality is excellent and immersive in multiple settings from music to a movie. The app let's you adjust the sound quality and balance with bass, treble and center. You can also set it for dialogue mode to enhance/clarify voices and reduce background noise - this is very handy for the news or a talk show. Take some time to adjust the settings for what your ear really likes and you'll be amazed at the fullness of sound and all the background details.

After two weeks, I'm incredibly pleased with the build quality, looks, sound and full functionality of both the 500 and 700 units. The 700 wins out by a nose over the 500 for us because the sound is bigger, but mostly because the remote control is better. The remote lights up when you lift it and you can find the buttons instantly. I programmed our TV to the Bose remote and it controls the sound bar, channels up and down and power for both the tv and the sound bar. title: Excellent Optics, Great Price, Unique in the Market for SuperWide EF-S Stabilized Quiet Focus lenses
text:
I really bought a Canon DSLR (vs Nikon, or any of the mirrorless Cameras) for this lens. I needed a low distortion very wide lens for real estate videos and I also needed image stabilization and quiet focusing. I don't think there is any other lens from any manufacturer that satisfies all of those things except this one. (Sigma has the 10-20mm but no stabilization, lower optical quality, and more money! Tamaron - 10-24 - same story. And so on ).
GOOD: Excellent optical quality for the price. This lens is noticeably sharper and has less distortion at 10mm than my kit lens 18-135mm has at 18mm. Stabilization works very well. Focusing is very fast and silent. I don't hear it even with the built in mic when shooting video (on a Canon 70D). Extremely lightweight and fairly compact.

BAD: Maximum Aperture. This is NOT a fast lens. F/4.5 maximum is not that great and you lose it pretty quickly as you zoom in since the max aperture ranges from 4.5 - 5.6. You need to have some decent light to shoot with this lens. But given the lack of competition in super wide stabilized silent EF-S lenses (or any Canon mount lens) and the price of anything vaguely similar, I think it's a reasonable compromise.

Note: At this price, you can't really call it a knock, but it'd be nice if it came with the lens hood. You can get a clone lens hood for $10 or so.

ALSO: Canon has now updated their EOS Utility software for this lens.

title: Don't waste your money.
text:
OK, take 2. My original review of this product got hijacked somehow. After writing it, I checked back a couple hours later and my screen name and original title were there, but my review got replaced with what seemed like some guy's journal entry. It had absoluterly nothing to do with this or any other product. Strange.

Anyway - as mentioned in my original posting, this review is more a condemnation or earbud headphones in general than the Sennheiser CX300-B, which I decided to try after my "over ear" style Sony noise canceling headphones went on the fritz. My past experience with earbuds was not good, although I had only ever tried the type that come with the iPod and not the "ear plug" type that go in the ear canal, like the Sennheiser CX300-B. However, having owned a pair of Sennheiser over the ear headphones back in the 70's, my impression of the company and their products was good. So, I decided to take the plunge. What a mistake.

After opening the package (no easy feat - damn sound welded plastic clamshells!), I popped on the medium-sized bud covers (appropriate for my size ears) and inserted them into my ears. I turned on my mp3 player and listened for a few minutes. The sound was adequate - nothing spectacular. I did notice they had decent bass and did block some external noise. I kept listening as I stepped outside to go to the store. I couldn't believe what I heard. Every step I took was amplified in my head - like a booming bass drum. Even the gentle bumping of the cord against my chest was amplified - a constant thump, thump, thump that was impossible to ignore. As it turns out, the very feature that blocks a modicum of external noise, also amplifies any sound that travels through the body. Even breathing is amplified! As I walked, it sounded as though I was listening to someone breathe over a PA system! I had hoped to use these while running, but there's no way that's going to happen. In fact, the problem with amplified sound is so bad, I won't use them at all.

I am very disappointed in this product and will never buy any ear plug style headphones again. I don't understand why anyone would sell them, let alone use them. They may have great sound reproduction, but the listening experience is totally ruined by the sounds that get amplified through the body. It amazes me that people buy similar style products that sell for hundreds of dollars. The only way you can enjoy the sound they produce is to sit perfectly still. I'm glad I only paid about $16 for these things. I won't return them because it'll be too much of a hassle - probably cost more to ship them back than I paid.

BTW - The photo of the product is misleading. The cord looks thicker than it actually is and there's no way it can be coiled as is shown in the photo. It gives the impression the cord is more supple and flexible that it really is. Also, one end of the cord is longer than the other. Not sure why this is, but the thinness of the cord makes it prone to kinking and tangling. In fact, since one side of the cord is longer than the other, it makes it even more prone to tangling.

Bottom line - steer clear of the Sennheiser CX300-B and all ear plug style earbuds.

title: Very Very SLOW for sequential writes with Common Scenarios. AVOID
text:
This is my 5th SSD (in several computers). The performance is so poor that I was sure there was something wrong with my connectors or something until I looked at other reviews on Amazon.

Using this in a USB3 enclosure designed for SSDs, if I tried to copy an 11GB file to this SSD from a very fast SSD (Intel 750 that can do almost 2GB/s reads), at first I got up to 320MB/s, but then after about 1/5th of the file it very quickly ramped down to 50MB/s. That's terrible. REALLY terrible. The drive was formatted correctly, but I tried reformatting it anyway. No improvement.

Since this complaint is common in other reviews, it seems that this drive is just a sinker.

While it's not a completely fair test, I tested the drive with CrystalMark and found that for sequential reads and writes, it's capable of 450MB/s, but random performance was horrible. (sequential - about 80% the performance of a Samsung Pro series 540 SSD. Random 1/2 to 1/3rd the performance. The Samsung was internal/SATA3 - so not a fair comparison. But there's no reason for the Random performance to be so bad.

The bottom line: AVOID This Drive.

title: Samsung UN55C8000 3D LED TV
text: Great product!!! I have had this TV for aproximately 6 months, and waited to see if there were any problems before I wrote my review, and I can happily say that the TV works great! We don't use the 3D feature a lot but it works great, no problems at all. Colors are brilliant, it looks great on the wall, super thin and I have all the wires hidden. It looks like a picture on the wall. I only have one suggestion. I received this TV in February in Pittsburgh, the temperature was 22 degrees, and that thing was on the truck till 4PM. Please do not have the delivery guy take it apart and plug it in to see if it works. Inspect it visually, see if the box is dingged up, check the glass for any visible cracks and if that's ok, just leave it at that. I called Samsung and asked, they said that the operating temp. is supposed to be above I believe 50 degrees(it's been a while). They suggested I let it sit @ room temp. for 24 hrs., which I did. No problems, no cracking - ever. I work on and build computers and I know that it is a big no-no, to plug them in if they have been in the cold. The circuitry on the motherboard and other boards is very sensitive, and then you have condensation from the heat of electricity warming the boards up, but they are very cold. Bad scinerio. Be patient and let the TV warm up, you'll be happy you did!! It was delivered by Pilot. TV was nicely secured to the side of the trailer, which made me comfortable! The delivery man was very nice, but he was by himself. I was glad that i was there to help him take the thing off the truck. I don't know how he would have done this by himself without smacking the TV once or twice, eek? I have read some reviews that complain about the sound. I think the sound for the one inch thick TV is great. I have a home theater system hooked up to it but we generally only use it for the movies. You really do not need it, honest! The whole family loves the TV and we get many great compliments from our guests!

title: Awesome Concept - Execution Needs Fine-Tuning
text:
Being both an audiophile and a lover of all new tech when I first read about this technology coming out a few years ago I started looking forward to testing it.

So what are the potential advantages of bone conduction earphones? I’m glad you asked. When properly adjusted they allow the user to enjoy listening to whatever they choose while not blocking external noises, thus allowing the user to react to ambient noises. This should make them safe to use while driving or doing other activities that require hearing ambient noise in order to conduct safely.

Unfortunately these R9 headphones allow for very little fine adjustment. In order for this type of headphones to work properly and provide the highest sound quality they should rest flat, or almost flat against the skin between the front of the ear and the rear part of the cheek bone. When adjusting the speaker it is clear when the speaker is properly adjusted. The adjustment that I was able to do came from working the rubber casing and sliding the speaker further onto the arm that wraps around the back of the head. By twisting the speaker inward I was able to get the speaker closer to the proper location but not exactly correct. Due to this, sound quality is not optimal and surrounding people are able to hear what the listener is playing.

In terms of design choices I find it odd that while it’s estimated between 70-95% of the population of any ethnicity is right handed this manufacturer chose to place the controls on the left side. This makes controlling them both awkward and difficult. While the buttons operate in a standard press and double press pattern it is awkward reaching across and doing it on the left side.

In terms of operation these headphones maintain a solid connection for the full 33 feet they are rated for and the batteries lasted approximately 6.25 hours on the first full charge cycle. Sound quality is middle of the road especially due to not allowing for fine adjusting of the speakers.

With a couple of minor changes these headphones would be a much better product. If the speakers are held in the correct positions it is much better - if an adjustment system were added these could potentially have much higher sound quality. In addition, obviously the controls should be placed on the right side for ease and regularity of access.

This is a great technology with a lot of potential. These headphones while not capable of fine adjustments would probably fit someone with an average sized head better. My head is a bit smaller than average which made these fit a bit too large for me.

title: Problems with navigation and estimated drive times.
text:
UPDATE 5/6/17: I have upped my rating to 4 stars. This unit learns your driving habits and adjusts drive time accordingly. For whatever reason (at least so far) it is better at this on major highways than it is on secondary roads. The unit still sometimes chooses slower routes than previous Garmin GPS's but I plan to call technical support and hopefully they can resolve this.

This is the 6th Garmin Nuvi that I have purchase for myself and other family members. The unit has a nice metal case, high resolution glass screen and great magnetic mount (available only on the Drivelux model). The map info is good and there are useful warning such as speed limit changes and school zones that can be disabled by user if desired.

So whats not to like?? To call the software programming a disappointment would be an understatement. The estimated arrival times of this unit on average is 25% higher that actual driving time and in some cases as much as 30%. Like most people I drive about 10 mph over the speed limit, sometimes faster if I think I can get away with it. That said I have no speeding tickets in over 15 years and no radar detector. Worth noting is that the while the drive time on major highways is slow its not ridiculous while back roads are most definitely ridiculous. I can hit every stop light and get stuck behind a school bus and still arrive ahead of schedule. The drive time estimates on all my previous Nuvi's were much more realistic. Usually within 10%

Just a bit of prospective, I am a real estate appraiser and have covered the same surrounding 20 or so cities and towns for the past 25 years. I drive about 25,000 miles a year and the GPS is always on when I am working because if for no other reason, its handy to know exactly where on a busy street a house is located as I usually have someone tailgating me. I purchased my first Nuvi (350) about 10 years ago.

All of this was no big deal until I fed an address into the unit and ended up with directions that seemed odd but I began following them just because in 10 years and a handful of Nuvi's I had never been seriously let down. I just assumed it was a shortcut that I had yet to discover. Not this time, I ended up driving and additional 10 miles and drive time was at least 11 minutes longer on what should have been a 50 minute trip.

When I returned home I checked Google Maps, Waze and MapQuest and they all showed the same 2 routes which happen to match my old Garmin 3760 and 760. Even my wife's low cost 52 LM came up with the same route. Hard as I tried I could not get any navigation software or other GPS to duplicate the crazy route this GPS gave me either as primary or alternate route.

I don't understand how this is possible after 10 successful years with Garmin products. I seems to me that perhaps the estimated drive time on back roads is so unreasonably slow that the unit likes to include a highway even when secondary roads would be much faster One solution might be to include a slide control (similar to volume and brightness controls) that allows the user to speed up or slow down the estimated drive times. One control for highway and a second for all other roads. The other obvious solution would be for Garmin to reprogram the software and or maps to correct the problem.

title: Highly recommended. Best eReader I've owned to date. But still want an Oasis.
text:
I used to have shelves of books taking up space in my home. Now, I can get nearly every book in one tiny device. As a bit of background, I'm a "gadget geek" but I'm not on the bleeding edge of technology as much as I used to be. My last e-reader was the Sony Reader bought in 2006. I have to say that the Paperwhite blows it away.

First, it's surprisingly light. Even with an aftermarket cover it weighs about the same as an average paperback and is nearly the same size (unless you're taking about the paperback version of War & Peace.

Second, the print is great, perfectly white to my eyes and the built-in night reading is a great bonus. In the past I've bought at least a half-dozen clip-on book lights for night reading and they are always odd and unwieldy. Paperwhite solves that problem.

Third, even though it has a limited amount of internal memory, it's more than enough for a year's worth of books for me. Plus, Amazon Kindle books stored on the cloud are available for download at any time, so if you happen to fill up your memory, just delete some off the device and download ones you want from the cloud.

The only cons are my own. Since I owned the Sony Reader, everything I have is in epub format, which is not compatible with the Paperwhite. However, I Googled for a workaround and things are fine. Even someone without extensive technical skills could figure it out, if not, you can always ask a tech-savvy friend.

Until the prices drop on the Oasis, I'll enjoy the Paperwhite for a while.

Also, check your local public library to see if they have an eBook program. You can borrow ebooks straight to the Paperwhite from a lot of different sources. I also like that you can "loan" any of your Kindle books to a friend -- Amazon made a wise decision allowing that. With a paper book it was a great way to share good books with your friends, and not being able to do that with an ebook reader was a major disappointment (although I found ways around that when I had my Sony Reader).

So, try it out and get rid of all the extra books on your shelves that just sit there collecting dust. I understand the appeal of having shelves and shelves of books in a home for the decor and style, but getting rid of stuff that you don't read will free up space and help unclutter your home and your psyche.

Here is why I cannot' give the product 5 stars.

There have been two situations where the router lost power and the firmware got corrupted and I had to reflash the router to make it work. I have NEVER had a device EVER get corrupted firmware. What a JOKE! Probably corrupted data issue as nothing will bring a system down like bad data.

Google: Router Power LED Blinks Slowly and Router No Longer Works

So rather than issue a RECALL on the defective merchandise, they do the next worst thing possible and give you some funky software called TFTP to download and fool around with to get the router re-flashed. Well, I thought the re-flash would correct the corrupted firmware. I got news for them, IT DIDN'T. I was moving my Router yesterday while the cable guy was here and then when we tried to hook everything back up, I got the blinking light of death again. I knew it was going to be a hassle to get the firmware downloaded and reflashed, so I switched back to an older working router for the time being.

In my opinion, NETGEAR should have done a 2 things amongst other things...

1) As an interim solution, Made special re-flash software that made upgrades a breeze. A one click solution to read the router's make/model MAC address and current firmware, and auto-magically download the new one and install it while PRESERVING all existing settings. It should also remember the OLD mac address and use it when you were migrating the settings to a router with a new MAC address. If their software engineering department can't do that, they need to be replaced starting with the Manager.

2) Recalled and Replaced the defective equipment for FREE, send out a new unit, and a postage paid return box for your old unit. Then use the above software to migrate the settings and old MAC address to the new unit so it works seamless with your existing cable model and service provider.

What do you call a router that does not work? An expensive paperweight? Can you say Regression Testing? Can you say Error Trapping Netgear? Words for the day for your Engineering Department. who worked on this product line.

title: VHS to Digital
text:
Finally I found a device that worked so I could plug my VHS tape player into my PC and use software to create digital files from our old tapes.

When I began this project I really didn’t think it would be near as difficult as it ended up being. I tested a couple similar devices with minimal success - I could achieve video transfer but no audio.

Even with this device I struggled and finally found the only way for audio to transfer was for me to toggle the switch on the side to 16:9 - theoretically this should have nothing to do with sound but in the 4:3 setting I have no sound transfer.

The single sheet of instructions are abysmal. Set up is relatively straightforward unless it doesn’t work. The first thing I would try is switching that toggle switch on the side.

If you are looking to transfer analog VHS tapes to digital using your PC, I recommend downloading OBS Studio (free software) via obsproject.

This device does get warm during use. Since I only used it for limited amounts of time for my specific purpose it wasn’t an issue. If this was to be used long term for connecting a game system to a TV I would question its longevity.

While this worked for my purposes it is a bit glitchy. I got it to work with time thankfully and was able to accomplish what I set out to do.

title: GREAT USB 3 card / I absolutely recommend the Inateck KT4001/KTU3FR-4P for Win10.
text:
If you need a USB 3 card with USAP, but don't need USB-C OR USB 3.1 and you use Windows 10 (or 8/7/XP) then this could be the card for you. USAP makes this card plenty fast, assuming your USB device supports it.

If you use Windows 10 all you have to do is:
- turn your PC off
- insert the card and secure it
- cable up the card to a SATA power source (15 pin power connection)
- boot your PC and wait until "the booting stops"

Windows 10 and the Inateck card should now be good to go because the driver for the Fresco Logic FL1100/FL1100EX controller is already built into Windows 10. I'm generally a cautious person so, "when the Windows 10 booting stops" I would reboot 1 more time.

If you use another Microsoft OS then you must install the drivers from the driver CD. Follow the instructions in the install booklet.

For me this card works great. Now the USB 3.0 ports are only at the rear of the case and I guess that that is a minor problem.

On further point, Inateck makes several USB 3/USB-C cards that have other port configurations/internal connecter configurations. Some of those cards use non-Fresco Logic controllers so I have no idea how well those non-Fresco Logic ports/connecters will work. YMMV. For example, with their 7 port card you might get 4 very nice ports and 3 so-so ports.

After a week of having to re-seat the cable and completely re-do the calibration i was done and sent it back.

The monitor was perfect while it was working and if you can get a panel without this issue godspeed. But for me i wont be using this and will be trying to find something else

title: Bought this too quickly...
text:
Bought this for the 750 because it didn't come with a case. A similar (smaller) case came with my 360 and I didn't think this purchase through. After using it and comparing the other cases out there, I would buy a different case.

This slipcase for the 750 fits tight. That's good. The Nuvi won't slip out. But because the 750's on/off switch is now a slider on the top left corner, if you slide it into the case naturally (unit in your right hand, case in your left) the switch rubs against the case. When you pull the unit out, it "automatically" turns on. Thus if you were to pull the unit out partially then push it back in, you could turn it on and not know it.

The solution is to invert the Nuvi so its switch will be at the open end of the case after it's in the case. That way you can see the switch's on/off position and verify it's not on.

More practical issues:

Pros:

- Nicely made: very high quality

- Very compact

- Adequate protection against rattling inside a glove compartment or briefcase

- Good basic case

Cons:

- It can accidentally turn the unit on

- It's black: can't find it easily in the dark buried at the bottom of my shoulder bag when traveling. Experienced this with the 360's case. And if it falls on the floor of a rental car at night, good luck trying to find it. Wish it came in natural leather color.

- Offers no protection while hand holding the unit while walking

The [[ASIN:B0012MI7N2 Garmin Nuvi 800 Series Carrying Case]] case is a wallet style that flips open to reveal the screen. It stays on the unit during use and offers some protection if you dropped your Nuvi on the sidewalk while walking. Downside with that unit appears to be that the cover flap does not latch, allowing the case to flip open in a briefcase and the screen to be scratched by other junk. And it's also black and can get lost on a car floor.

Another alternate is one of the many zippered semi-rigid or neoprene cases.

title: Just What I Needed
text:
My custom wooden PC case was running a bit hot (around 48* C at idle with a Pentium G3220), so I had two options. Option 1 was to buy this fan and create a recess in the lid of my case to mount it (the reason I chose this slim fan over a more powerful 25mm thick fan). Option 2 was to shell out three or four times what this fan costs for a slim CPU cooler (my case is quite small) and hope that it works better than the stock Intel cooler.

I went with the more budget friendly Option 1, took the time to create the 15mm recess, and am happy to report that my idle temp dropped 15* (33* C vs 48) and after half an hour of CPU torture with Prime95, it was holding steady at 60* C (still 12* shy of the max temp for this CPU). I have the fan mounted horizontally (not ideal for a sleeve bearing fan like this, I know) and while I understand that my use case isn't typical, I'm quite happy with my purchase.

If anything changes, I'll update my review accordingly.

Everything friction fits in this case, you just press things into place and they stay. In a couple spots I had to stop and compress the case itself because fitment was tight enough to flex a couple of my micro SD adapter cards.

The case is quite sturdy except for the latches. Hard plastic in a stiff mount are a recipe for breakage. They should have been designed better.

title: Rich Selection Of Connections & So Easy To Use
text:
With the popularity of Pico (pocket) and mini projectors in both our professional and recreational lives, this XSories X Project pocket projector with WiFi brings a lot to both. If you are looking for strictly a pocket projector to take the place of a large screen tv in your home, this would not be the correct choice, as this is tailored for someone looking for multiple uses. For myself, I have several important uses for a pocket projector- business demonstrations, family photos on the big screen using my USB Flash Drive or Memory Vaults (loved throwing out the old large projector and not having to use any more discs in the dvd player), playing movies/tv shows from either my dvd player or USB Flash Drive (especially great for large screen movie night), using the big screen with my computer or laptop, using it with my camcorder and using the big screen with any USB device or memory card.

You can also set up a wireless network, you can receive standard definition television (you need to buy the aerial/Pico station or antenna dongle), if you install the latest version of Adobe Flash Player, you can view You Tube, as this uses the Android operating system, you can connect to a smartphone or any 30 pin dock connector iPod nano (up to gen6), iPod touch (up to gen4), iPhone (up to gen4) or iPad (up to gen2) and you can use this for gaming. This X Project projector set comes with the 4 inch by 4 inch by 1 inch projector, the AC adapter with 3 different plug ends (US, UK and Europe- perfect for travel!), carrying case, remote control, standard mini-USB cable, standard mini-HDMI to HDMI cable, warranty card, Quick Start Guide and 4 User Manuals in different languages. The front of the projector has the lens with a wheel control on top for focus. Also on the top is the finger touchpad control, and you can also use the remote instead- which is easier. The top also has an LED bar which shows a blue light indicating the projector is on or in standby. I noticed I had to turn the projector OFF button very slowly sometimes to shut the blue light off, so it doesn't stay in standby mode.

On the bottom, there is a tripod socket, Pico Station connection socket and a Pico Station Port. Having a flexible leg tripod will allow you to set this on any surface as well as keep the projector well ventilated. On the rear of the projector is an Audio output for a speaker or headphones, and if you are having a large screen movie night, you will definitely want to hook up louder speakers or use headphones for gaming in this port. Also on the back is a mini HDMI port, memory card slot, mini USB port and your power supply port. One side has the standard USB port and the other side has the ON/OFF button, battery status monitor and an aerial socket. There is also a teensy emergency hole above the battery status monitor light- just in case you have a problem or freeze- just stick a dull pin into the hole and the projector will reset.

This X Project WiFi projector has a Digital video format up to 1080p and for Analogue it supports PAL, SECAM and NTSC, it has 100 lumens, it's LED can fill a space up to 120 inches and it's stereo speaker is pretty decent. It has a standard resolution of 854 x 480, a picture quality of 100 and a lamp life of 20,000- meaning your lamp is good for about 7 1/2 years. The Li-Ion battery will play a 2 hour movie- but not longer. Based on Android 2.3.1, if you don't want to use the touchpad or remote, you can use your phone for controls through the Android/iOS remote control app. Navigating on the touchpad has a lot of trackpads for everything, so using the remote or phone is easier. The trackpad is important though, as it brings up the keyboard to enter your WiFi password for your network. If you don't like the touchpad for using the keyboard, you can always use a mouse.

This projector will also give you 4 GB of memory without using an external data source- that's a huge convenience for business presentations. Set up was a breeze. Without reading directions, I plugged the unit into the wall and when the green light was ready, I touched the home on the touchpad. I scanned through the choices and then plugged in my SanDisk 64 GB Cruzer into the USB port. I chose Photos from my choices as I wanted to view my family photos on a large wall. When nothing came up, I noticed another choice was a Folder. I have all my photos in folders on my flash drives, so I hit Folder. My photos came up in huge glorious color on my wall. I focused the wheel and enjoyed the slide show. Of course, I was blown away by the simplicity of using this projector, but later learned more- and not by reading the directions, but by just scrolling through the choices.

100 Lumens is not the brightest light for a projector, but turn the lights off- the darker- the better. The picture is fantastic in the dark. Movies outside after dark are unbelievable. The colors are vivid, sharp and perfect and I found out the adjustments are plentiful in the touchpad control choices. For sound, they give you volume, bass and treble controls. For the picture they give you fit, projection, wall color correction, brightness and contrast controls. What a picture you can get from adjusting these controls to your taste. For my photo viewing, I can choose from 2 to 60 seconds to view each photo in a slide show and I can choose thumbnail or list viewing. There are 18 languages to choose from on the choices. I can even play music when photo viewing. The fan noise is pretty quiet compared to brighter Lumen projectors I have used.

You will need other items that are not included depending on your use of this projector. For viewing movies on my dvd player, I purchased an audio video adapter cable that has one end that goes into the projector and the 3 colored open ends, that the 3 male plugs go into from my dvd player. I spent under $2.00 for this cord here on Amazon. I also needed another inexpensive VGA cable for my computer. Everything you will need is pictured in the user manual. Since my main uses are my computer, movies and photos, these 2 extra cords are my first needs. Eventually, I'll be buying an aerial antenna for tv use. My happiest use for this projector was finding out that I can view my photos by just plugging in my various USB devices. More importantly, this projector reads JPEG, BMP, PNG and GIF.

I have spent years transferring family photos into the PNG format. TIFF is way too large. JPEG way too thin and pixelated. But, PNG is large and gorgeous, but can keep it's size down due to using only over 200 colors in comparison to TIFF's over 2,000 colors. For art work or graphs used in business, BMP and GIF also deliver a vivid picture that will show up beautifully on this projector. This projector is made for movies, photos, computers, gaming, camcorders, iPhones, television, everything you want to view big and in the dark. The rich selection of connections and ease of use for both home and travel make it a 5 STAR projector, even with it's 100 Lumens.

Biggest complaint is the volume control. Because this is on my desk at work, I generally don't want it overly loud. The lowest volume when controlled from my iPhone, though, is still a little too loud at times. For whatever reason, I can only go down to volume level two on the iPhone when paired with this speaker; at level one, the volume cuts out entirely. I have tried turning the speaker around and turning its face down on the desk to lower the volume but those have drawbacks too.

So, if you want a portable speaker for what most people want out of it -- volume -- it's great. If you're looking for a speaker that has good volume control on the low-end, this one may not be for you.

title: Frustrating set-up but worth the effort.
text:
Very nice features, sounds great, 2.5 balanced output! BT v5, aptXHD, top of the line DAC’s, great battery life. So why just 4 stars? The documentation leaves a lot to be desired. The included printed doc was about the size of a matchbook with writing so small it required a magnifying glass to read and for all that effort it basically said nothing. The biggest hassle was the pairing. It couldn’t be less intuitive. I have many BT devices, both receivers and transmitters and this is the first one that required a web search to figure out. Very frustrating. And to enable the BT v5 it requires a ROM flash upgrade so you have to connect it to a PC and follow a bunch of steps that are as intuitive as the pairing. I came within seconds of sending it back but stuck it out because it had some pretty stellar reviews. It turns out I’m glad I did. Once you get it sorted out it is a pretty amazing piece of kit. I use it with my HiBy r6 and BGVP DMG’S as well as my ATH M-50x headphones. I can now roam freely around the kitchen while keeping the DAP safely out of the way. I can plug-in the 2.5mm balanced cable and get outstanding sound with the added bonus of not heating up the DAP (it gets hot when plugged in directly) and the battery life of the HiBy is more than doubled. Both of these bonuses more than make up for the minor degradation in sound staging. I have listened for over 7 hours without the battery giving up, but have not used it up to it’s limit yet so I can’t say how long it will last. Is it worth the Benjamin it cost? Oh yeah.

Update: Upgraded to 5 stars after a month of use. Once the niggling little details were figured out and the unit was set up I can't say enough good things about this puppy. My main reason for getting a BT transmitter was I am going to be doing extensive bicycle touring later this year and since it will be solo touring I wanted good quality music available. I have an extensive library of 24 bit flac's as well as a couple of hundred audiobooks for the trip and while the playback of the books isn't important the music is. I invested a fair amount of cash into a HiBy R6 DAP and BGVP DMG IEM's as well as upgraded cables to connect them. The EarStudio lets me connect via 2.5" balanced with no real discernible degredation in the quality of the playback as opposed to plugging directly into the output on the DAP, and here's the kicker, instead of just getting 6 - 7 hours of playback and heating up the DAP I now get double that without any heat. I can stash the HiBy in a Pelican 1020 case and put it in my top tube bag where it's out of harms way and protected in case of misadventure. The EarStudio has a battery life of around 14 hours (I haven't run it out yet, and I have listened for over 8 hours). Added to that the App that is available for my Android based DAP is amazing. More fiddly bits than your above average geek could ever want. So I gotta give it a 5 star rating. And it's worth twicw the price but don't tell Radsone.

title: Nice Product but wont work on my boat.
text:
Not as useful as I had hoped.

I wanted some sort of mount that would keep my Nexus 5 safer that it is lying on my desk my boat and also wanted to be able to use my wireless charger with it when the phone was in the holder.

There were two problems with this mount on my boat. One is that it will not hold the phone unless it is mounted perfectly vertical or even even leaning slightly backwards. If the mount is installed so the phone is leaning forward (away from the wall) it does not hold the phone securely. The other problem is that it is not large enough to hold my phone and my wirelss charger at the same time.

So the mount is sitting in the box it came in while I decide if it has any utility.

TWO DAYS AFTER MY INITIAL REVIEW

The customer service department for this company is right on top of customer satisfaction issues. I got an email from them within hours of when my less than glowing review appeared. The person who wrote made some very good points about the fact that this product had not been misrepresented on the Amazon site. I agree that their description was accurate and not misleading. It was not detailed enough for my specialized need so I took a chance and bought the product anyway. I did post a question about whether or not my wireless charger would fit in the dockem device with my phone. I did not get an answer that was responsive to that question.

When I took the dockem device out of the box it was immediately obvious that it would not work with my wireless charger. If they had made the fit sloppy enough to allow me to do that the dockem would not have held a phone very safely without the charger taking up the extra space so it would not have worked for someone with just a phone to store in the dockem.

I did not intend my review to be a critique of the product for its intended purpose. I just thought that my experience might be valuable to someone else who looks at this product in the future. I would expect it to work fine for use on shore where the user was not interested in wireless charging. But in my application, on a boat, or probably for use in an RV this device is not appropriate. The company does not promote it for such applications.

Given the quick and thoughtful response from the customer service folks and the fact that the review looked a bit more negative than I originally intended, I changed the title and gave it a couple of more stars. I would not hesitate to try other products from this company and now have the email address of the person to go to with my questions.

title: Nifty Device and Small too
text:
(+) Great size (fits in my front pocket)
(+) Very easy to use
(+) Very portable
(+) Pretty low energy usage

(-) only on choice of connecting: USB 2.0 (but this is only a slight negative)
(-) it's just a regular HD (as opposed to being solid state)

I didn't have the opportunity to check out the instant d/l using one of the approved devices (namely, because I don't own one), but I did use this as a back up for some of the pictures I took on a recent family trip to Yellowstone National Park. As an aside, I forgot my charger for my MacBook Pro, so I was very concerned about the amount of battery power I'd be using (we brought it along to have a place to d/l our pics and videos, the HD was used as a back up jic something happened to the laptop). I was very pleased with the low amount of energy consumed by the HD when I plugged it into my Mac. The speed was what I would have expected for the amount of data I was moving from my computer to the HD, but I think that there would definitely be a great potential in affording additional types of connections. The HD itself was easy to carry along and I even kept it in my shirt pocket at times.

I think the biggest drawback for this HD is the fact that it's main component is a moving part. It was definitely hard to tell at first, but when I started transferring more files, I could tell that there was a disk in the box (all to say, it's very quiet). I haven't read anything on whether or not this thing has drop sensors, but my inclination is to doubt that it does. So while the size is generally a plus, it also worries me to think of how easy it would be to drop and how this might affect whatever I'm transferring as well as the device I'm transferring from (i.e. - might it corrupt the data, etc.?).

So, chalk it up to my threat of clumsiness to drop this from what might otherwise be a 5 star review to a four.

Altogether, this is a super portable HD that works great for folks who are (maybe) traveling and need a place to back up their files. The only wire you'll need is the USB 2.0 cable it comes with (no additional power source is required). You might want to bring something to carry it in too.

***Update***
I downgraded from a four to a two; this device has some sort of difficulty in receiving any batch of files over 10GB. Again, I know that my use may have been contrary to what was specified, but it's still an external HD and should be able to take the files fine. I ran into this issue in trying to copy HD video as well as still digitals.

In addition, the construction is pretty flimsy - I haven't been roughing it around or anything, but the external shell is not of what one might consider a superior quality.

title: Fabulous Camera
text:
I have been using this camera for several years now. I bought it when the 20D was the newest offering in the Canon line. I paid big bucks for the camera plus the lens, about $1400 at the time. It is a shock to find out that this expensive machine is now only worth about maybe $300, used.

I have gotten a lot of good use out of it, however. My photography skills have improved with the availability of the custom features that this camera offers. While it has a good selection of point-and-shoot options, I have not been using them. They work quite well, but so do the selections for manual settings, and when used correctly, these manual settings make for creative photography. I recently bought a large format printer, and I have been blowing up photos shot from this camera to 11" x 17" images. I had shot the photos from a tripod, and the details even at that extreme size are sharp and vivid.

The 17 to 85 mm IS lens that I bought with the camera has turned out to be versatile and useful. It is able to take moderate macro photos, and its wide angle feature is something that a lot of camera buyers would not specifically look for, but when you have it, it is wonderful to take wide pictures outdoors.

If I could change the camera, there are two things that bug me: one is that the viewfinder is not 100% of what comes through the lens, so that if you focus tightly on a subject, when you see the image on your computer there is extra real estate around the edges that you did not plan to put in the picture. The other problem is the LCD screen in the back. If you are shooting outdoors, it is very nearly impossible to see what you have on the LCD screen. I guess it just isn't bright enough.

Neither of these problems are bad enough for me to take a star off my rating. On the plus side, this camera takes very good pictures in low light situations. While there is, in fact, some noise at ISO 1600, it is not enough to ruin the photo the way it does on so many other cameras. It is great for taking pictures in theaters with the lights low without a flash. The flash itself is powerful, and if you like using a flash, then this is a good one.

One of the features that I most appreciate is the ability for the camera to shoot in RAW mode. When I first got the camera, I shot JPEG's. However, as I became more familiar with the RAW feature, I began to appreciate it more. Also, over the years, Adobe has greatly improved its camera RAW application. Now I would not dream of shooting anything other than RAW, because of the ability to adjust your picture before converting it to a JPEG or TIFF. In Adobe camera RAW, you can open your picture in either 8-bit mode or 16 bit mode, and you can also open it in either a small or huge size and several sizes in between. I consider this to be a great advantage.

If you are new to photography, or on a tight budget, I would highly recommend this camera. Even though it is now several models back from Canon's newest top-of-the-line, it still takes fine pictures and has many options for customizing your shooting.

title: Phenomenal sound, but not perfect
text:
My quest for the perfect set of headphones had me read endless reviews from consumers, audiophiles, gadget blogs, and anyone else who wanted to weigh in. In short I never found one set of headphones to rule them all. Since I was looking at an investment of several hundred dollars such ambiguity left me a bit unsettled. Sure there were some moments of clarity:

* multiple drivers had the potential for more accurate reproduction
* balance armature drivers are among the best for headphones
* multiple ear cushion options offer the best bet for a good fit

These factors led me to this set of headphones, and despite quite a few complaints of cord damage being too frequent (sadly it seems many competitors also suffer these issues), I took the plunge. Granted a Gold Box price of $99 made it more of an informed impulse buy.

When you first get the headphones, you'll get an immediate satisfaction that you've purchased something of supreme quality. Packaging is top notch, the included case is both attractive and functional, and there are numerous accommodations for fit. Once I tried out the headphones I was a bit underwhelmed however. First off getting the right fit was difficult, which was made a bit more awkward due to the fact I've never worn earbuds that want to wrap the cable over the ear. After multiple tries, I was able to focus on the music, which also was disappointing. Sure it sounded good, but it wasn't great. Not having fully addressed the fit, I was losing low end punch to a poor seal, and the mids and highs weren't much better than $35 headphones. Did I just blow $99? Not at all, as the mids and highs improved with use (I left my iPod running all evening at a moderate volume, and an significant improvement was evident). The lows also improved greatly due to finding a better fit, and now I'm enjoying high fidelity audio wherever I am.

Overall the sound quality is highly transparent and clean. Things just sound how they should. I can actually hear the difference between 192kps and 320kps MP3s, and I imagine I can finally appreciate lossless files enough to justify their storage demands. In short, you will hear things again for the first time. This is why I give these 5 stars despite some of my issues with fitting and numerous reports of cable failures. Sometimes greatness comes with a price that goes beyond the financial, and if you're willing to take that on, these may be the headphones for you.

Other observations:

* cable length is just about perfect for personal use
* not only do you get four types of silicone cushions and foam ones, you get a second set of foam ones
* replacement cushions seem readily available
* while I love my headphones, if someone offered me $300 for them, I'd probably go for it

title: Wireless Android Auto in a Hyundai Sonata
text:
After having experienced wireless Android Auto on a recent trip in a rental car, I knew I wanted this feature in my own car, a 2021 Hyundai Sonata.

I read an online article about this AA Wireless unit and a competing model from Motorola. The AAWireless unit had better availability at the same price, so I took the chance and ordered it. I received the unit about a 1.5 weeks later.

In 2 words: it works. I can plug in the adapter into my car's USB port and after about 20 seconds it connects to my phone, a Samsung Galaxy Note 20 Ultra 5G.

However, getting everything working was not without some initial installation woes. Here are my observations.

1. Download the app from the Google Play Store.
2. Plug the unit into your car's USB port that connects to the car stereo
3. Start the app, go through the prompts, then pair the adapter with your phone via Bluetooth. This is where I had some difficulties. Pairing took a bit of time.
4. The app will search for a firmware update. If one is available, download & install the update. Note: the AAWireless adapter forces a Wi-Fi connection to your phone and will download the firmware update using your cellular connection. Poor connection = slow download & update. This was the 2nd source of frustration.
5. Adapter will restart and attempt to reconnect with your phone. This was the 3rd source of frustration. The phone & adapter weren't pairing/connecting. I had to view the FAQ's in the app, then perform a few configuration changes in my phone. This could be a bit much for some users.
6. I ended up doing a reset of the adapter & deleting the app before reinstalling it.
7. After repeating the above steps, the unit paired via Bluetooth & established the Wi-Fi connection necessary for Android Auto. Everything worked perfectly.

Having the wireless Android Auto functionality is a huge benefit. The unit works great & sounds great. I don't notice any delays or interruptions when playing music or audio books, nor any hiccups using Google Maps.

title: Nice on a Budget but Quick Mount May Lack Long Term Toughness.
text:
NOTE: I am reviewing the BR268 which is no longer available and I believe thie BH0 is the replacement model. My concern is with the quick attachment/quick release mechanism which looks exactly the same. It's a great feature to just pop your camera into the quick mount and have it automatically lock in place and to remove, just squeeze the two levers together and turn them 90 degrees and the camera is free. Mine worked great for a while and then the spring loaded pin (which is pressed down by the base mount on the camera as you load the camera thus setting the locking levers) stopped springing back upon release of the camera. It is still usable but not at all quick or convenient.

During manufacturing the pin and spring are somehow stamped into a hole in the mount with no opportunity for future maintenence. I ended up drilling through the rear of the mount into the pin cylinder, freeing the pin from the backside, replacing the spring, and closing the hole with a stub bolt and now it works ok. I believe the pin was stuck because, as mentioned above, I frequently "popped" the camera into the quick mount and I have probably nicked the pin causing it to stick. If that is the case, the manufacture should make a baseplate and or pin that are tougher and virtually indistructable. I don't want to be mounting the camera on the tripod with the same semi-gentleness I mount my lens to the camera.

In addition to that, there is too much play in the quick mount itself unless you take extra effort and push the quick release lever firmly shut. Automatic locking alone doesn't do it. Once locked in place the base plate still has a little play in it.

Still, you pay for what you get. I only paid $38 for this ball head. I replaced it with the Manfrotto 496RC2, another "low end" ballhead but twice the cost of the BR268. The Manfrotto is very solid and the friction knob makes fine tuning of the camera position easy.

I'll end this on a good note: The Benro is very light when compared to the Manfrotto 496. If you are lugging your tripod into the outdoors you will appreciate the lighter weight of the Benro.

text:
First off, i had a little bit of a problem installing the backplate for this setup. You do not have to remove the backplate at all when you put the corsair black backplate on. My setup is consisted of a push pull system for my radiator. I have it mounted on the top of my chassis hooked up to an LGA 1155 motherboard with a 2500 cpu intel core i7. I have it setup at 3.5 Ghz so far, and i plan to push it to 4.0 ghz. I have ran Real Temp GT version 3.7 for an hour and thirty minutes. My results so far as of idle and playing some battlefield 3 on ultra consist of the following

core 1-25C min, 53C max
core 2-24C min, 53C max
core 3-25C min, 51C max
core 4-25C min, 53C max

My idle temps consist of around 30C.

Based on air to the H60, you will only see 10 degrees C difference. Of course this is also based on the pre applied thermal paste that comes on the GPU cooler. I have not tried an aftermarket thermal paste, which would result in different temps. I have an adequate chassis supported with 2 fans in the front to intake air, 1 fan on top to intake air along with the radiator setup, and 1 fan for exhaust in the back to keep the flow of the air within the chassis continuous. I currently also have the GTX 670 gpu in my computer which will soon be applied with the H60 cooler as well with my modified setup. This could potentially see a difference in temps, but nothing too major.

Overall, this is a decent way to quiet the computer and keep your cpu cool. It did take some time to setup based on how you want the GPU cooler to be setup. I would recommend this to a friend if they want all of the above. If they want to push the boundaries more, i would suggest the h100.

PERFORMANCE
Frustrations aside with the packaging, the card itself performs well. It takes video well and it also works for photos and other storage. I am going to transfer it to my outdoor camera soon which I will need it on.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This card works fine in my tablet, but the packaging makes it very easy to get lost in the box if shipped with other items.

MY RATING

title: Good but not great.
text:
Bought two Play 5's directly from Sonos and have been testing them out for over a week now.

First the good —to my knowledge —there isn't better multi-room home audio setup out there, not at this price point. But if you're reading this you probably already knew that. Setup is fast and easy, you can join / separate "rooms" on the fly and guests can add songs seamlessly (once they know how to use the controller app).

But here's what you need to know about the revamped Play 5 — the audio quality just isn't that great, not for $500 / speaker. The new Play 5 sounds airy, flat and lacks definition throughout. I'm disappointed because it's been 6 years since the Play 5 (named the ZonePlayer S5 in 2009) first launched and while the 2015 update improves audio quality it doesn't compare to wireless offerings from B&W. Are my standards high? Absolutely. But so are Sonos's.

I really wanted to like the Play 5’s, for most listeners it will be a great addition to a Sonos household (most people who buy Sonos already own at least 1 speaker). Today many people are perfectly happy with compressed audio and disposable ear buds – the Play 5 reinforces this trend. It comes down to a tradeoff do you need multi-room home audio? If so, you’ll probably be better off with Sonos if you don’t mind sacrificing audio quality. If audio quality is higher up on your list look elsewhere – B&W is a great place to start, or ditch wireless all together.

title: Chromebit for Digital Signage? - Read This!
text:
Please excuse the long review, but I personally spent WEEKS researching and testing methods of being able to "serve" content to 1 or more flat panel TVs used as "digital signage". I want to share what I've learned, in hopes I can save someone else the trouble! (Or maybe even to teach others about an AMAZING use for this device that they haven't even thought about).

Warning! This item cannot be managed through Google Device Manager (Google for work) because it does not include a license! Found out the hard way. It functions fine as a stand alone Chrome OS device, however it cannot be managed through your Google Admin Console without buying a separate license. You can buy them WITH an included license, but only through Google's authorized partner (Promevo). If you buy it anywhere else, you can buy the stand-alone license seperately, but it takes 2-5 days to provision!! Other than that, what a great piece of hardware. Just wish you could Cast to it natively.

I will be using mine (with my newly bought license) to stream content for digital signage in our lobby.

I chose those device over a Chromecast, PCstick, Android TV, etc.. because of its amazing low price point, it can be managed centrally via the web (anywhere in the world), plus it supports screen rotation! So I can mount a standard flat panel TV in portrait, and the Chromebit will display content from the web (that I serve it) in portrait mode (very hard to find a device for digital signage that supports this without spending big bucks) You just have to rotate the screen once via a keyboard, and the Chromebit will retain its rotated state even after reboot..

My requirements for a digital signage device were, it had to be cheap, it had to support portrait and landscape mode, it had to be zero maintenance (can boot up, connect, load signage stream..without any user interaction). I plan to deploy these all over the country to our different branches, so the last thing I wanted to do was have to train someone how to get it working, or have to turn it on, log in, etc each morning. Being able to manage it through Google for work device manager means it just needs to be powered, and near a working wifi internet connection to work!

To serve the content, I'm using a free, open source product called Dashkiosk (which picked up where Groupon Greenscreen left off when they gave up on it). It's a little tricky to get set up, because it must reside on a web server, and to do it yourself requires knowledge of the Linux Operating System, but if you have a serious need for bulletproof digital signage, and you don't want to pay a monthly price for cloud based digital signage software, The Chromebit + Dashkiosk is the cheapest, best way to go! If you opt to enroll the Chromebit into a managed Google for work or education environment, you can literally deploy Chromebits anywhere you need them (that has an internet connection), and program them centrally to boot up in kiosk mode, open Chrome Browser, and connect to your signage stream. I even programmed ours, at close of business each day, to automatically switch over to a simple website I created which shows the feed from nearby IP security cameras, so at night, our digital signage acts as a big, bright, "how do ya do" to anybody peaking through the windows at night, thinking about breaking in. (Nothing says, "think again" better than having a thief peak in your businesses window, and seeing a nice, close-up, live shot of their own mug with the words "Motion detected - Main entrance (door 1) - [alert notification sent!]".

I've also customized the stream with simple HTML/CSS so it overlays a "stock ticker" across the bottom of the screen - the content is fed from a simple shared Google Sheet that anyone in our company with share access can modify (even the receptionist) who has ZERO knowledge of HTML or programming, they just modify the spreadsheet to add the headlines they wish to display, and Dashkiosk refreshes the feed every 60 seconds automatically.

We use the ticker to "Welcome" important customers by name.

I can do all of this, for the cost of a Chromebit, a cheap flat panel, a spare PC (or access to a web hosting environment with a shell login) and some free software! This used to be a $10k plus job, the Chromebit makes it an $85 one!

The "feeds" can be programmed in Dashkiosk admin panel (a web interface), and they can be timed to rotate (with a nice smooth transition), and can include ANYTHING that can be normally displayed in a Chrome Browser window (video clips hosted locally or on YouTube, Google slide shows, websites..including custom pages you make that have jquery slide shows, still images hosted anywhere on the web, Facebook and Twitter feeds, or like in my case, a custom locally hosted webpage that includes my security camera feeds.

PS! (super important), Dashkiosk utilizes i-frames in such a way that the more recent versions of Chrome will not work with (natively), there's a super easy work-around, you need to download a chrome extension on each Chromebit called "Ignore X-Frame Headers" - without this, Dashkiosk will NOT work on the Chromebit!

If anyone needs more info, or a little guidance, feel free to drop me a line.. I'll do my best to try to help! (Lord knows I would have loved a little help from someone who actually has a working setup). Jumpshoutmedia at gee-male dot comm. Good Luck!

title: Too snug for my needs, but it may work for you
text:
When I first ventured into the realm of DSLR photography I started with a camera, a lens, and a hand-me down bag [[ASIN:B00004TX6V Lowepro Nova 2 Camera Bag (Black)]]. At the time and for a while thereafter, I didn't really think much about bags, as I focus my finds on acquiring more and more lenses, a flash, and misc other gear. I had outgrown my original lunch box style bag and the larger [[ASIN:B00013J8G8 Lowepro Nova 4 AW Camera Bag (Black)]] I had bought for my gear. Once on a trip my wife was surprised to see 5 lenses in a big [[ASIN:B0007W1E4W Lowepro CompuTrekker Plus AW Camera Backpack (Black)]], and asked where they all come from! Thankfully it was more of an inquisitive question than a statement of mistrust in my spending habits! Alas that backpack proved a bit bulky, but it did work as a carry on, as it consolidated my PC and my camera gear in a package that could fit in most bins and under just about any plane seat. I still lugged around one of my lunch box style bags for field use, even if they barely could fit everything in a weather induced pinch (where I couldn't count on my camera hanging around my neck).

This all changed last December, when I took the plunge on the Bigma--[[ASIN:B003A6H2Y8 Sigma 50-500mm f/4.5-6.3 APO DG OS HSM SLD Ultra Telephoto Zoom Lens for Nikon Digital DSLR Camera]] This lens eclipsed even the optimistic abilities of my shoulder bags, and even challenged the bulky CompuTrekker. It joined my upgraded camera ([[ASIN:B001ET5U92 Nikon D90 12.3MP Digital SLR Camera (Body Only)]]), [[ASIN:B002D2VSD6 Sigma 10-20mm f/3.5 EX DC HSM ELD SLD Aspherical Super Wide Angle Lens for Nikon Digital SLR Cameras]], Tokina 28-80 f/2.8, and [[ASIN:B00015GYU4 Nikon SB-800 AF Speedlight for Nikon Digital SLR Cameras - Old Version]]. I picked up a [[ASIN:B000AEEXPO Domke 700-10D F-1X Little Bit Bigger Bag (Olive Drab)]], which I affectionately refer to Domke-Kong, and it comfortably swallowed all my gear!

Alas I wanted something a bit more compact, and I tried this bag. I know the Bigma is a lot to ask of any bag, and in a pinch (literally), it fits with hood reversed (better without) mounted on my D90 & grip (better without). That's it as far as glass is concerned, and it doesn't quite wear well. I didn't try the Baby Bjorn style position, as well I don't want to be that guy. Alternatively, I did use it effectively with the Tokina 28-80 f/2.8 attached (hood reversed) in the top mount and the Sigma 10-20mm f/3.5 below (hood reversed), but not nice versa, which is an issue. I consider that scenario a more realistic expectation, and that is why I gave this 3 stars (not the limited Bigma success). Frankly this is a very limiting case for specific uses. I'd strongly suggest trying this out in the field or being prepared to return this if going via Amazon.
