title: Learning curve is well worth the effort
text:
I intended to give the [[ASIN:B00AQRUW4Q Seagate Wireless Plus 1 TB Mobile Device Storage with Built-In Wi-Fi Streaming (STCK1000100)]] a rating of four stars, but have decided that it really is a five star product. The near deduction was because of the frustration I experienced in my attempting to get the device up and running with the limited information provided in the package and on the website. Once I successfully downloaded the software to my Droid, Kindle Fire and MacBook, I still encountered more trial and error than usual until I was able to figure out how the darn thing works. Fast forward to days and weeks of loving the device!

The Wireless Plus can be used as an extra drive for storage if you're not interested in using it for streaming, but if that's your true need, I'd likely recommend purchasing something else. With it's own Wi-Fi streaming, you don't need to use your home or hot network. Using it's Wi-Fi has been quick and has been glitch free for us thus far. We have used three devices at once and found it to be problem-free, with no freezes, crashes or difficulties. We had it up and running for four hours and still had battery power, then recharged. Although it can be charged via the USB on your computer, it is much faster by plugging it into an electrical outlet if one's available. Since we haven't drained the battery yet, I can't say how long it really lasts.

Music, movies, pictures, documents, audiobook, you can use whichever you want on any networked device as long as the device has the appropriate application installed. I watched the Seagate tutorials several times and found them to be difficult to follow, however once I spent some dedicated time just feeling my way through, I discovered that I do like the applications, too. Even if I'm not accessing the Wireless Plus on my Droid, I have been using the Seagate app.

This arrives with little documentation, but it is USB 3 capable if you need it. The housing is lightly rubberized and it has a matte metal plate in a charcoal gray color on the face side. The plug appears to be proprietary, the second reason I almost deducted a star from this review. It looks like a hybrid mini plug that's attached via a thin wire, not a cable, to a USB for either a device or the two prong electrical plug. No case is included, but I have a couple that work great. The size isn't so big that it feels cumbersome, but it is heavier than it appears to be upon first glance. I don't mind the weight because this little device holds 1 TB, much more than I have loaded on it as of today. I highly recommend this device and look forward to Seagate upgrading it as time passes. It's unique and not expensive for what it offers.

title: A Nice Idea That Was Poorly Implemented
text:
Like many single guys I have various pockets of dust scattered around my place. My desk, behind the computer towers and monitors where all the cords are piled up is one of the worst. So a handheld vacuum to clean all those nooks and crannies sounded like a good idea. Sadly, this is not the portable vacuum that I am looking for.

A few design flaws were obvious as soon as I took this out of the box and started charging it. There is no stand or holder for the vacuum so it has to sit directly on the brushes you've just been cleaning with. The light indicating when the vacuum is charging/fully charged is pinhole size, barely visible from any distance. So I had to go pick it up and squint at the light to see if it was charged up. The little brush for cleaning the inside of the vacuum is one more tiny thing to keep track of and is easily lost.

Even more flaws became obvious as soon as I tried to use the vacuum. With the nozzle on I tried to clean the back of my desk where all the computer wires are. The nozzle immediately jammed up on hair and dust balls. That area is still as dusty now as it was before I tried to vacuum it. Next I tried cleaning some flat surfaces. The brushes pushed the dust back and forth while barely vacuuming any of it up. I put my hand across the bottom of the brushes and could not feel any suction at all. When I put my finger right into the center hole that the dust was supposed to be scooped up into, I could barely feel a tiny amount of suction. I still very much like the idea of a handheld vacuum but I very much do not like this one and cannot recommend it to anyone.

title: Pricey but very convenient
text:
These wireless, Bluetooth earbuds are a terrific invention. They totally eliminate the bane of earbud existence--tangling wires. The sound quality, however, is only about as good as the inexpensive earbuds I usually buy. The justification for these earbuds being four times as expensive as low-cost earbuds is spelled out in one word: convenience. Bluetooth wireless technology is convenient because it eliminates wires.

These earbuds paired easily with my iPhone 5c, and the remote controller, which is contained in the right earpiece, is user friendly and works well. You can control the volume that way or via your smart phone.

These earbuds offer three sizes of ear cushions, small, medium and large.

As is true for any Bluetooth device, these ear buds must be charged. Like my Bluetooth, this device uses a Micro-USB port which is within the controller. It takes about 4 hours to charge fully after fully drained, and the charge lasts about 90 minutes. A partial charge takes 20 minutes and lasts 60 minutes, or so the maker claims. The math doesn't add up for those two claims. So far I've been charging it several hours at a time, and switching off between other earbuds while it is charging. It's a bit frustrating that this device doesn't hold a charge very long. And I find that rather surprising since my iPhone's Bluetooth holds a charge for up to 11 hours.

These earbuds are very comfortable in the ears, but I don't like wearing them as the product information pictures them, with the hanging cords behind the neck. I find it far more comfortable and balanced when worn in the front.

These earbuds have three buttons on a controller which is located by the right ear piece. They consist of: on/off, play/pause/answer, Bluetooth pairing button, volumn control, next track button, rewind track button. They work as advertised.

A microphone is included within the controller. This means if you are listening to music or other entertainment media on your iPhone, if you get a call, you can use this device like a regular Bluetooth and take the call. I have used this device for calls, and I can hear fine, and so can the person on the other end of the call.

I had no problem pairing the device with my iPhone. The distance of reach is supposed to be up to 30 feet, but it's not that far inside a building because of the dividing walls from room to room. It's more like 15-20 feet.

Negatives include the fact that the warranty is a measly 90 days, the cost is a high price to pay mainly for convenience, it doesn't hold a charge very long, and it is made in China.

title: Grow into photography with this splendid camera
text:
If you want a camera that is reasonably compact and light that takes wonderful photos, here it is. No camera can be all things. Physical laws demand certain tradeoffs. However, this camera takes a strong position in the middle ground. It does everything well and does it with style. It fits the hand well, the controls are responsive, and the results are very satisfying. If you don't intend to print and enlarge your photos to great sizes to hang in a gallery, then consider this a worthy camera. The question is this, friends: "Do you love photography or do you love cameras?" If you love photography, you want a camera with you as much as possible. If you love cameras, you have several of them sitting around collecting dust. It may be the latest, greatest, most impressive, and most expensive but it is useless junk if it just sits around. There's an old saw about how the "best" camera in the world is useless if you don't have it with you. Well, if you want a long zoom camera that won't break your back or you wallet then here you are. The FZ300 lets beginners shoot in auto mode. For advanced type you can shoot in RAW mode or tweak dozens of settings and really get your geek on.

(On a side note, if you want a similarly capable long zoom camera that fits in your pocket, then get a Sony HX90V. I recommend it as an alternative.)

title: Why can't more cases feature this kind of sound channel?
text:
I hate how most mobile devices have speakers either on the bottom or on the back. This just make no sense to me, if you can put an ear piece on the front of the phone, why can't you put the speaker grills on the front? Anyways, this is particularly annoying with the iPad because I use it more for media consumption. I was looking around at a couple cases, I purchased a couple and decided this was the best design. Some of the cases with a sound channel were too bulky and other were a hard plastic. I like this case because the edging that goes around the iPad is malleable rubber. This makes the case easy to put on and off.

The other feature that I didn't know I liked before I bought it is the clear window on the back. The plastic for that window is harder but it is extremely clear. Not quite like glass but a lot better than some clear plastic cases. The folding stand works well when laying the iPad mostly flat on the desk. When you prop it up like in the picture though, it sits a little too vertical for my liking.

The only true issue with the case is the charging port. It fits the normal Apple cable, but I have a third party one that I didn't think was that thick, but it didn't fit in the cutout and couldn't charge the tablet. Not too big of a deal if you want to file away at the case. But this should have been considered in manufacturing.

Overall, I definitely rate this case as a 5 because it is the best at what it does. I wish more manufacturers would jump on to the sound channel routing bandwagon. If this case were even thinner, it would be perfect.

title: Great little printer easy to setup and use
text: I have always wanted a little printer like this when I was working many years ago but they were never this small.  Now that I go camping in my RV and work while I camp I may want to print something without having to drag a full size printer along for the ride.  The price of this is on the high side even higher than the average full size printer so you better have a need to make it worth it.  Don't do what I did which was to unwrap everything before I ready the manual.  I thought I would have to install the enclosed ribbon but it is already installed at the factory and the one you see is a spare.  I decided to set it up to print from my phone since I mainly use a phone or tablet when on the road.  I downloaded the suggested app and it was easy to get started and I didn't need to sign up or register to do so.  My Bluetooth found it right away.  I selected first to print a photo file and selected low quality as I didn't want to waste ink.  It came out OK.  I next selected a page in a PDF manual that had a [photo embedded in it and selected medium quality and that turned out great.  The only gripe was it only gave me the following places to look for a file to print:  iCloud, Photo, Web and my print history.  I only had a couple things in iCloud as I mainly use Google Drive so I would have to move the document to iCloud first in order to print it.  Photo didn't allow me to browse my photos so I wasn't dure where to go there.  Once I printed a photo inn iCloud then that photo showed up there to print in the future.  I thought that was what the print history was for.  So, the app could use some UI work but I can't complain as everything worked/connected so easily.  Now, the paper.  You have to use their HPRT Premium Multi-Purpose Copy Paper.  It is a bit shiny on one side and more expensive than typical print paper.  This brings me back to you have to really need a niche printer like this to make it worth it.  I cannot sweat these things because I got it to use sparingly while I travel when something just has to be in print form.  I don't even really print much anymore from my home printer so once could say I waste cartridges there.  In summary, if you need a portable printer, that costs more with proprietary paper, for those short run printing emergencies on the road then this is great.  It works great and is easy to setup.

title: As always, thoughtful design from Belkin, but could use a few improvements
text:
I have a huge Belkin surge protector in my office that meets all of my needs and also occasionally makes me lunch (it's pretty rad), but since having a baby, I've found that my definition of "rad" has changed to mean not visible, attractive, or accessible by the baby. While this isn't meant to be babyproof, I've found that the cage-like design and locking mechanism not only keep my cords tidier, but also makes them a lot less obvious and exciting to baby so that when it is placed out of reach, he isn't always clamoring to be lifted up to it, as he does with high-up cords that are not as hidden.

Two things that I don't love: One is that the sliding mechanism that opens out to allow you to put the cords in and use the diagonally-sliding plugs easily - they are a little stiff. So stiff that in fact I doubted whether I was really supposed to slide them out and was afraid I'd break the thing. I also found the locking/ opening/ closing mechanism too stiff - in fact, I gashed my finger when it opened unexpectedly after having to push it harder than I should have to open it.

The other thing is that there is no method for hanging this outlet on the wall. So I have to set it on a high shelf, which is less cool than just hanging it behind my printer or something.

Otherwise, I love that I can neaten up a decidedly un-neat portion of my office with this, and be assured of clean power to boot.

title: No more scorched thighs!
text:
The Logitech Cooling Pad N200 is a simple padded platform your laptop rests on to keep the hot underside of the laptop from roasting your legs. It connects to the laptop with a USB plug, and draws power from the laptop to run a 2-speed cooling fan (controlled by a switch located on the USB plug).

The pad works splendidly. The fan makes only minor noise in operation even at the highest speed (no more noise than the laptop's own fans make when they engage), and I am completely protected from the heat from the underside of the laptop. The bottom of the pad is nicely padded and is comfortable in use. I didn't have to adjust my position at any point, as I often have to do with the laptop alone, when I need to shift the underside's "hot spot" to another area of my legs.

I can't speak to how much this drains the laptop battery since I very rarely use my laptop without having it plugged in via an AC adapter (my laptop battery is failing and can't run for long without being plugged into the wall).

If I had one nitpick, I would suggest to Logitech that future models have some sort of attachment feature that would allow the laptop to be securely attached to the pad. At present the laptop just rests on top of pad, with the USB connector serving as the only connection between the laptop and the pad. I'd like them to be more securely attached to one another so it's less cumbersome to carry the laptop to another room. But that is a minor issue, and I am otherwise very pleased with this.

Highly recommend!

title: similar specs to Amazon Fire tablet, security updates are more than 1 year out-of-date
text:
With just 3GB of RAM and a low-end CPU, this tablet has similar specs to the Amazon Fire tablets. Build quality seems great for a 10 inch tablet that costs less than $100. The IPS screen is reasonably sharp and colorful (though slightly lower resolution than the 10" Amazon Fire tablet). It is fine for web surfing, email, and media streaming (videos, movies, music, etc). It is really too slow for playing fancier video games.

Speaker quality is mediocre (like with most phones or tablets), but there is an audio jack that you can use with headphones or external speakers (which I highly recommend for listening to music or watching movies).

32GB of storage is barely adequate if you like taking photos/videos or if you want to locally store songs and movies, but I like that there is a micro-SD card slot so you can add flash memory card.

I like that this tablet setup easily, unlike some other cheap Android tablets that I have tried. You can use your existing Google account or create a new one when you setup the tablet. The tablet runs a standard (though not the latest) Android operating system, which I think is much easier to use than the Amazon Fire operating system.

I like that they include a charging cable and charger, but I do not like that the tablet does not work with my phone's charger. My phone uses USB-C Power Delivery charging, which works with all other USB-C devices that I have tried. I have no idea why it does not work with this tablet.

I really do not like that this tablet does not get the monthly Android security patches from Google. I received this tablet in June 2022 and the latest security patch that is available from this manufacturer is from April 2021 (more than 1 year ago). Name brand Android devices should install the security patches within 1 or 2 months of when they are released, so using an Android device that is more than 1 year out-of-date is kind of risky. This device might be OK for watching movies or listening to music from name-brand streaming services, but I would not use it for any financial transactions (banking or credit card). Also beware of web surfing to any sketchy websites. Even using it for email is kind of iffy if you use the same email address for financial transactions.

2.5 stars, mostly because of the security updates issue.

one of the three fans working, and doesn't really keep the laptop cool enough.

Top points for looks - the acrylic and the blue lights are great. The price is good for what it is.
Got an expensive laptop? Get a different cooler - look for one that blows heat instead of tries to suck
heat (via the fans) away from the laptop. Try a Belkin. Forget Targus unless you don't mind going deaf while
cruising the internet.

title: Perfect USB-C Hub for MacBook and other USB-C Computers
text:
I am an Apple Consultant and have been looking for a USB-C hub to carry with me when I work on new MacBooks. I received the pluggable unit from the manufacturer in exchange for a review. Although I don’t pay for this unit I would gladly do so and will be recommending it to my clients. My requirements are pretty simple -

1. I wanted a unit that was compact.
2. It needs to be able to allow pass through so I can keep the MacBook charged.
3. I also wanted it to be connected via a cable rather than directly connected to the MacBook or any other device
4. I need to be able to boot from a connected USB Flash Drive or USB3 connected hard drive to run diagnostics.

Pros -

1. The unit is compact and is easy to store when not in use. The external cable is attached pretty securely and is of sufficient length so I could easily plug and unplug external devices.
2. It will charge a MacBook using the MacBooks charger. Couldn’t compare charge times but don’t expect them to be any different from that of a directly connected charger.
3. I could boot from both a USB Flash Drive as well as a USB3 connected SSD which I use in my daily work.
4. The status light is small but adequate.
5. The unit does not add any significant weight to my bag which is important since the whole idea of the MacBook is minimal weight to get the job done.

Cons -
None that I can find. Only time will tell how durable the unit is and whether or not there will be any heat issues as have been reported with other units.
There are three USB3 ports, nothing more. This is not a problem for my intended use and I can always add an Ethernet adaptor or a card reader if needed.

title: FANTASTIC 7 inch portable LCD TV !
text:
I am really thrilled with my purchase of this Haier HLT71 7-inch, ATSC 2009-ready portable LCD TV! I have never heard of this name brand Haier, and I had heard many nightmare stories about some of the other name brands having poor pictures on these little screens, so I thought I'd give this Haier a try.

I ordered this tv directly from Amazon and it came to me from a seller on Amazon who goes by the name ANTOnline. The seller sent this perfect and fast to start with, which is always a big plus with me. When I opened the box, the set looked very sleek and light weight, just perfect! The tv I received is exactly like the picture shows in this description, black (it is the picture that has the remote control next to the tv), with really simple control buttons on the front. I then looked at the directions, but realized, I didn't need to read them at all! Everything is really obvious! The set has a little slide switch on the side to turn on the power. The antenna screws in really easy. It comes with a plug for the inside electrical outlet, and a plug for the car lighter, and a lightweight rechargeable battery! It has a little remote control which they made very easy to read! After screwing on the antenna (or you can attach your cable cord if you are using it in the house), I basically plugged it in, slid the power switch on, pressed the button to scan for setting the channels, and it does it quickly! In about 1 minute, it was set! I then tried the small battery, and it played perfectly without the electric power!

The picture is absolutely gorgeous, as it has the new atsc digital signal receiver built in! To see the local programs in digital on this little screen was fantastic! Colors are crisp, sharp and vivid, just like a big hdtv!

I have noticed that some reviews are giving this tv a low rating because it did not pick up any channels with the single rabbit ear that comes with the set. This tv picks up EVERY signal that is being broadcast in your area. Before you buy this tv, you should first go to a website called Antenna Web. On this site, you type in your address and it will show you exactly how many channels you can receive in your area and what type of antenna you will need to pick up the signals. Antenna Web said that in my area I could receive 8 signals, and the single rabbit ear that comes with this tv picked up all 8 channels. When I used a stronger antenna, I picked up 3 more channels. When I used my cable cord, I received over 60 channels, and when I used my cable cord with my box, I picked up 250 channels.

Whatever I hooked up to the coaxial input on this tv, this tv picked up! If you live in an area that receives no broadcast signals or you need a high powered antenna to pick up anything, it is not the tv's fault, but your broadcasters. So, if you want to be certain your tv is picking up the signals correctly, go to Antenna Web and check to see what channels you can get in your area and what type of antenna you need to pick up the signals. My single rabbit ear, picked up everything including the hi-def channels, and the reception was crystal clear. (Also, don't forget to go to the tv's menu, and hit the little satellite dish picture, then hit the appropriate air or cable before you scan for your channels. This way you'll be certain your tv will receive the correct signals.)

The real plus for me on this tv, is the battery, because of so many electrical outages and bad storms, this is a must have item! UPDATE: Haier vs. Axion 7 inch portable tv's
I am posting an update for anyone who is wondering what the differences are between these two portable tv's. A friend of mine purchased the Axion, and she immediately brought it over to compare it to my Haier. Here is what I found:
RECEPTION: Antenna Web said I could receive 8 channels in my area. With the single rabbit ear antenna, Haier picked up all 8 channels. Axion picked up 7 channels, but one channel was very fuzzy. When attaching a cable cord, both sets picked up everything.
SOUND: For these small sets, the sounds were very similar, but when turning the volume louder, the Haier was louder and not as tinny sounding as the Axion.
PICTURE: Both have very nice pictures, with great color, but the Haier definitely has a more hi-def, sharper looking picture.
REMOTE CONTROL: Haier's is easier to read, larger and has volume control, where Axion's is smaller and has no volume control.
BATTERY: Haier's battery is a plug in and lasts about 2 hours before needing charging. Axion's battery is built in, cannot be removed and lasted a little less than 1 hour before needing to be charged.

Overall, the sets are very similar, my personal choice being the Haier, as I think the picture is sharper, the price is better and the battery lasts longer for my needs in bad weather. Haier also has way more picture settings and adjustments in the tv's menu, but the pictures on both these sets are so great, I've never found a need to use them. The bottom line for me is the better picture and price give the edge to Haier, since the reception on these two sets is almost identical.

UPDATE: MISSING OR NO CHANNELS AFTER DIGITAL CHANGE
This is an update for anyone who has lost channels or who has no channels after the digital change took place June 12, 2009, whether you re-scanned or not. I received this information to share with all of you from contacting the FCC, CBS, Antenna Web and Elgato Systems Technical Support.

They were all very helpful in explaining to me what exactly is going on right now, which is this: Half of the nations tv stations (which at half is 1,760 stations) are running at full power, the other half of 1,760 stations are not. Some stations are completely off the air temporarily, and are available only through cable and satellite. In most major markets some channels are still in lower frequencies which many smaller antennas will NEVER pick up except MAYBE with the highest powered amplified antenna. Digital tv was originally planned to be broadcast in UHF (digital loop antenna needed), which are the higher channels. VHF (rabbit ears), which are the lower analog channels (2-13) was supposed to be gone, but it is not. The new digital tv is being broadcast in 2 different ranges both UHF and VHF.

In other words, channels are missing, many channels are in frequencies we cannot pick up and only half of our stations are running at full power! What a mess! Antenna Web is now showing the new RF (Radio Frequency) channels in your area. Each station has 1 RF channel. If you see in your area, any low RF channels from 1-13 range, you will need a really high powered antenna to MAYBE receive your channels.

First, go to your tv to re-scan. Remove any batteries. Plug it in to the wall outlet. Find the satellite dish in your menu and set it to air (if using antenna) or cable (if cable is hooked up)and scan. You may have to do this several times and even more re-scans are needed over the next year or two!

The FCC recommends, if you are getting nothing, or very few channels, to do the following, before re-scanning:
1.) Re-orient the antenna
2.) Amplify the antenna (Not recommended by me, as these antenna's need electricity, which means it will be useless when used with the battery)
3.) Purchase a new HD antenna that will receive both VHF and UHF

When you buy an hd antenna for your set, try re-scanning it when you get home a few times to see what you get, if nothing works, return it and try another. (After re-scanning, make sure you try the tv with your battery to see what you can pick up for power outages.) Eventually one will work for your area and you'll be set for the next power outage.

With only 1/2 the stations at full power, many channels temporarily missing that went to cable and dish tv, and many running on low analog frequencies, it's amazing our antenna sets are picking up anything right now! Shop till you get a good antenna for your area, and be patient as it will be years before everything is being broadcast in higher frequency digital tv! I hope this helps everyone, as the right antenna is everything right now!

title: Here's a 4GB micro card that works with Legend CX & HCX
text:
I have the Legend CX which is great, the same as the HCX except the CX does not have the highgrade receiver (less sensitive than the HCX).

By the way the CX has slightly longer battery life than the HCX, but the HCX is very good on batts too.

Rather than just repeat the other positive reviews (which I agree with), I would like to mention a 4GB micro SD card that I have tested that works with these Gamin Legend CX and HCX: Kingston SDC4/4GB.

Amazon sells that card, right now it's under $10.

At first the Legends were released when the largest micro SD card was 512 MB, but as larger micro SD cards became available, the Legends would take almost any brand up to 2GB.

Next the micro SD format was changed to micro SDHC. Garmin made available a ROM update from their website which allowed *SOME BUT NOT ALL* 4 GB SDHC micro SD cards to work in their handheld GPS.

Garmin states that cards over 4 GB will work but only 4GB of data will load on the card, so Garmin states that there is no reason to buy micro SDHC cards over 4 GB for these handhelds. No doubt at some point newer Garmin GPS handhelds will be designed that will take larger cards.

So, while you can try various 4GB micro SDHC cards, many or most of which will work, at least some will not work. But the specific card listed above does definately work in Garmin Legend CX and Garmin Legend HCX.

It does take hours to transfer 4GB of data from Garmin MapSource or Garmin BaseCamp to the micro SD card inside the handheld, so make sure batteries are fresh enough to last many hours before starting the transfer. Otherwise the handheld might lose power and the hours up to then would be wasted. It took 12 hours for a transfer of 4GB on my Legend CX from BaseCamp. 6 hours for 2GB from MapSource.

In other words when you do the final mouseclick to start the transfer the computer will grind away for hours and hours until that one task is done.

Also, I'm told on GPS forums that downloading a mapset to the Garmin handheld will replace the old mapset you have previously downloaded with the new mapset. Which sounds like to me that you cannot download some maps and then later add more maps because the old maps will be erased when you download the new.

You can of course add new wayoints and routes and so forth without erasing any of the old data, it will be added to the old data, nothing is erased. Just can't add new mapsets to the micro SD card without erasing the mapset you previously added. (Except the original low resolution default mapset which came installed on the handheld will always remain and not be erased, I'm told).

One solution might be to trim across the bottom of those two stickers to free up the entire bump (nope, tried it on the J), or perhaps add a couple of strips of the waste material, to emphasize the difference in feel. The only other infelecity is that the lettering can be too visible. The capital keyboard "9", for example, is "(", and on an unmodified keyboard I barely notice it. The font and layout of the "9(" sticker makes the "(" more obvious than the number.

They give you two versions of the function keys -- a large version for the top of the keycap (if you have big function keys), and a small version for the front. This is for use with keyboards (like mine) that have additional function labels (Help, Undo, Redo, etc) on the top. They do not, unfortunately, provide those additional function labels, but since I never use them (I use Ctrl-Z for undo, for example), I don't miss them. So I've put the small stickers on the top of the keys.

Installation Tips: You need a sharp knife or sharp tweezers to get underneath each sticker. What worked for me was to apply them in the order they appear on the sheet, not the order on your keyboard. You will be folding the used part of the sheet under, to help peel off the stickers, so it's easier that way. Since I'm right handed, working from the upper right to lower left of the sheet was best. Also, if your keyboard isn't one of the ones directly supported, be prepared to trim the stickers - scissors are fine. For example, the SHIFT keys on my ergonomic keyboard are not as long as the stickers, and the SPACE key is thinner in the middle. The glue on the stickers is pretty strong, so once they stick, you're stuck. OK, if there's a tab hanging off, you can sometimes grab that with the tweezers and pull the sticker off for repositioning. Othewise, you risk damaging the sticker (like I did, when I put the PG UP on the PG DN key). I would recommend you start with some peripheral keys (like the arrows, or PrtScn ) for practice before applying the important ones.

Despite the issues I mentioned, I'd strongly recommend them for anyone with keyboard readability problems due to vision or key wear.

title: Excellent Results
text:
I have worked with several K&F Concept lenses and filters in the past and I have had excellent results with them. I am still very much a beginning photographer and I am still learning as I go but I have learned a lot in the process. One of the things I have especially come to appreciate is the fisheye effect. Up to this point I have only had the ability to work this out via software, so I was pleased to have the opportunity to work with this fisheye lens. So far I have had a lot of fun with it and I love how it works, though I have again learned a few things along the way.

A fisheye lens is somewhat similar to a magnifying glass with a great deal of distortion. The center comes out clear and the edges are distorted and warped, giving the effect of looking through a lens that is very thick in the middle and thins out towards the edges. Straight edge objects like sidewalks become warped and bent.

This particular lens is a chunky and hefty fellow, actually comprised of two lenses instead of just one. There is a large macro lens that can work independently of the fisheye lens and it is very good for taking very close-up shots. The fisheye lens attaches to this macro lens and relies on it.

I took several shots with the fisheye lens and I discovered something I did not realize though it is fairly obvious now. When using the minimum amount of zoom, the distortion is maximized and you get the most effect. The more you zoom in the more dampened the effect though it is still noticeable. I used the lens to take two pictures of the case in which the fisheye lens packs, one zoomed in all the way and one zoomed out all the way. For the one zoomed out, you can see the warping effect on the blinds over the windows and you even can see the entire image framed in a black circle. The image zoomed in has minimal distortion.

I should state that this particular lens is designed for 58mm threads. Make sure your camera can use it before you buy it. If you have a different thread size for your lens, buy the right sized fisheye for that lens.

This is one of the most fun lenses I have. It works great and it does a good job of giving the distortion you want with a fisheye lens, and it is not particularly expensive. I am very pleased with it and am looking forward to working with it for many years.

title: Parents MUST get this camera
text:
I bought this camera for everything it is, AND everything it isn't. First what it isn't - big and bulky, batteryhog, expensive. What it is - ideal, the size of a small cell phone (pocketable), takes superior 720p/60fps video quality (why even use 1080 when you have the smoothness of 60fps capture), and the camera, as a bonus, is shock and waterPROOF (not just resistant!).

I specifically purchased this for our first child's birth, and I try and carry it in the diaper bag everywhere we go, especially now that she is getting older. You want something like this to capture those candid moments in the grocery store, or in a restaurant, where you aren't planning to bust out your bulky camcorder bag and accessories only to find out your battery is dead anyhow.

I purchased a spare battery and standalone charger on Amazon as well (off brand), and I would highly recommend doing so. These batteries hold charge forever, so after I finally drained one battery after 6 weeks of use (captured about 30 minutes of video, watched most of those clips on the camera, and the rest is sacrificial draining due to time), I popped in the one I had charged over a month ago and it was still fairly full. I didn't miss a beat when my girl was doing tummy time!

The included software is uber-basic, which on the flip side is easy to use. The software has minor editing, like removing sound, clipping portions of video you don't want, etc. The camera captures videos in .MOV format, which can be played by Windows Media Player, even though it thinks it might be incompatible. I think it is a native quicktime format? Anyway, I found the need to download a freeware program to rename the files by the dates they were taken. The camera names them something like "Movie 100-1." 10 years from now, I want the file "2010-6-12", not some half-baked naming system of "Tummy time" (or even worse, "Movie 100-1") So when you sort by name it is sequential by date.

Now, regarding 720/1080 And 30FPS/60FPS. 1080 is good, don't get me wrong. But 30FPS is noticeably choppier if you capture movement. When kids are playing, they move. So do you want a bit more clarity on jumbled, moving pixels, or do you want perfectly fine clarity on realistic representation of what your eyes are seeing at the moment? If the latter, use 720/60 capture mode. The size of the videos are the same, byte-wise, but I have compared the modes, and when trying to capture the dogs playing or my kid doing something, the 60fps is the way to go. I have heard half-correct arguments that "well blu Ray is only 30FPS, and that is all your eyes can see." True. But nyquist theorem also states that basically to prevent anti-aliasing when sampling a waveform, you need to capture at twice the frequency to properly reproduce. You may not get it until you compare the modes. A good way to compare is sping around a room fairly fast while capturing in both modes. You'll see what I am talking about.

Oh, and low light is surprisingly good. I'll try and upload a test video of my dogs at some point which demonstrates the cameras capabilities.

Anyway, I researched the Vado, Flip, etc. and chose this one on purpose. You will not be disappointed.

title: Great cooling, very quiet, awkward for travel
text:
I've had the 19" model with 3 fans for about 4 months now. Previously I'd been using the [[ASIN:B0000BVYTV Antec USB-Powered Notebook Cooler]], but after a year or so that became so loud as to be unusable, so I had to replace it.

I hadn't realized how great the Cooler Master is at cooling my laptop until I decided not to take it with me for a 2 day trip. I discovered that without it the bottom of my laptop gets too hot for me to touch it. With it the bottom of my laptop is actually cool to the touch, and the keyboard area is just slightly warm. So I'm extremely impressed with the cooling ability. It's also very quiet, particularly compared to the Antec. It's very sturdy - my 17" laptop is quite stable on it, with about an inch extra side to side, and about a half inch extra front to back. (I got the 19" model because I wanted the 3 fans.) The nonslip pads are absolutely non-slip - I can't push hard enough to make the laptop budge.

It's really nice to be able to place the fans where needed. When I first got it, I ran my laptop without it for several minutes until the computer got hot, then I put the fans under the hottest spots. And, as I said, the laptop went from being too hot to touch to being cool to the touch. Sweet!

My only issue with it is traveling. Really, the only reasonable way to pack this is to remove the fans and slip your laptop into the curve of the stand. Like that, it will just barely fit in my [[ASIN:B0001EMM10 Targus XL Backpack Designed for 17 Inch Notebooks TXL617 (Black with Blue Accents)]]. But then I have to pack the 3 loose fans that are dangling from the USB connector. They're a little awkward to pack, and I have to detach and reattach them every time I pack / unpack the laptop. I've been traveling almost every week for the last six months, so it's gotten kind of annoying to me, which is why last week I decided to skip it for the short trip. But after discovering how hot my laptop actually gets without it, I'm now willing to deal with the inconvenience every trip.

Overall, it's a great unit, and I'd happily recommend it to anyone, especially folks who won't be traveling with it very often.

At Netgear's own page ("Security advisory for multiple vulnerabilities on some routers, mobile routers, modems, gateway, and extenders") for item WNDR3700V3, the available security fix is: "None" and "outside security support period."

Thankfully for me, I saw "The Register" published article in July 2020 which cited that detail along with 45 other Netgear products whose only available security fix was: stop using the product.

By contrast, my several-year-old Asus router still receives regular security updates.

Hope this helps you shop. Stay safe with your IT gear. Buy products that continue to receive longer-term security updates - instead.

title: Works with Androids and plugs right into Win XP boxes too
text:
I received this hub as a review sample and just had to test it on a [[ASIN:B00KCG95M6 Keedox® M8 TV Box With Remote Control]]. It was immediately recognized and worked perfectly. I also use it to extend my USB ports in my [[ASIN:B00C7SK2J2 Micro USB OTG Host Cable to USB 2.0]] with the same results. That one was connected to a Samsung Tab 3 10.1, then a Galaxy Note 3. All of those tests was using the hub unpowered.

For connecting high power devices like external hard drives and DVD ROMs, I powered this hub using a [[ASIN:B00MRGKPH8 Sabrent 5V 4A 100V-240V to DC Power Adapter]]. I only tested a single external hard drive and a DVD player with this test and then only using the USB 2.0 speed since it was connected to a ThinkPad T61 running Windows XP. The arrangement worked and I was able to get expected USB 2.0 performance - not blazing, but not molasses slow either. The only USB 3.0 device I currently own is my Note 3 phone and I could not adequately test this hub using that.

I do love the looks of the hub, but the important thing for me is I was able to use it on some legacy devices as well as three Android devices with no problems whatsoever. I also like the fact that you can transform it into a powered hub with an optional power supply, or just use it out of the box for low power devices. Just be aware that if you opt to use it as a powered hub using the Sabrent power supply make sure that the devices that you intend to plug into it do not exceed 4 Amps total. Some of the larger external hard drives can easily eat into the power budget. Also note that of you attempt to use this as a charger (which you can do standalone with the optional power supply) you are only going to get 1 Amp per port and no over charging protection. I recommend not using it for that unless you are in a pinch.

Bottom like: this is a versatile hub that has worked with every device I tested, and it looks good as well.

title: Mount Kit is 2 screws
text:
I wanted an inexpensive sound bar that wouldn't take up much room, but would still sound decent at all ranges. That's why I went with the Hisense HS214 with the built-in subwoofer.

The sound is as good as expected. It doesn't produce much bass, but enough to set it apart from those that don't have a subwoofer. This was actually a pretty big deal for me, because I didn't want much bass, but the lack of any is vastly inferior, imo.

The voice clarity is good, but I'd still say that it's average, at best. I have trouble understanding the dialogue when watching TV and I think this will help, but I've seen other inexpensive sound bars that were better here. It has surround sound and I just want to say that the NEWS mode is far more tinney than expected. I think it's worse than my TV speaker in that regard and I find it disappointing, even though I likely wouldn't have used it anyhow.

For some reason, Alexa recognized it and now shows it as an inactive device in my Alexa app. I don't think it actually works with Alexa, though, and it's not the first time I've had a device do that (i.e Alexa recognizes the device, but shows it as inactive and won't control it). I didn't expect it to work with Alexa and I'm not even sure what good it would do, so no big deal.

My only big complaint is with the "mounting kit", which consists of two screws. I wouldn't even care, except that it won't sit flat against the wall using the screws, because the cords are in the way (and I tried). As far as I'm concerned, this is a design flaw and you'll need to buy a mount for it to sit flat or just place it on a counter top. I may attempt to correct this with some spacers, but I'll have to buy some, since none were included.

Overall, I'm pleased with the Hisense HS214, but I expected a better mount from Hisense, even if it's just a couple of spacers. Advertising it with a "mount kit" is dishonest when it can't be mounted flat.

*Almost forgot to add that it worked with the nice HDMI cable with my TV remote. The volume increases in increments of 5 and seems normal around 50. It doesn't get as loud as other inexpensive sound bars I've tried, but it's loud enough for me. It won't let me just give Alexa a number for the volume, though.

title: Works very well, in-app help and documentation need work
text:
Very in-depth review below (including a Chat with LiveScribe Customer Service), but here are the basics for anyone who doesn’t want to read the whole thing. The pen performed best when used for straight handwriting to app transfer and converting text. Recording audio worked well with some caveats. All in all, I like the product and am happy with my purchase.

PROS:
• Initial set up, connecting to Bluetooth, and communicating with the app was a breeze
• Excellent delayed transfer when pen was not connected to Bluetooth as well as realtime transfer when connected
• Virtually flawless transfer of words written on the page to handwriting version on the app
• Transferring written documents out of the app was very easy
• App transcribed handwriting to text extremely well
• Pen warns you when you’re in an unrecordable area on the page
• Quick access to help via Chat on the app

CONS:
• Some menu choices lack information, online help outdated (as of 10/30/18)
• Small notebook that comes with the pen doesn’t include all the Smart Paper controls
• Difficulty quickly starting audio recording
• App needed to be active to record (did not record when phone went to sleep mode)
• Location of Ready/Record light makes it difficult to see while writing

SETUP/USER EXPERIENCE
This is my first digital pen, so this whole process was new to me. I do have a Rocketbook Everlast notebook that has some similarities.

The pen itself is very lightweight. Its texture is almost a little slippery, but I didn’t have problems with it moving in my hand. Quality pens in this price range are normally a little heavier and don’t have this kind of texture, so this was a negative for me personally. The pen felt well-balanced with the cap was off, but it was so light that it felt a little off-balance with the cap on. Another reviewer mentioned his cap didn’t click on the end of the pen securely, but mine did click on with a bit of pressure.

Steps to use the pen:
1. Download the app
2. Power on and pair the pen
3. Start writing

This was very easy and worked even when the pen was not close to the phone (iPhone X). I plugged the pen in to my computer in my home office to charge it with the cable provided, then went to the kitchen where my phone was charging to download the app. App was easy to download and came with a great little slideshow that highlighted the basics of how to use the pen. Skimmed through it quickly, thinking I could return to it later. Turned on Bluetooth, left the phone in the kitchen, went back to the office and the pen was already communicating with my phone in the other room. Couldn’t have been easier.

COMMUNICATING WITH THE APP
Since my pen was already communicating, I just started writing. However, if the pen isn’t already communicating but is on, it easily pairs by tapping the Smart Paper Device Pairing icon with the pen.

As long as you’re connected through Bluetooth, the pen will automatically sync to the app; your handwriting appears on the screen in real time, which I thought was pretty cool.

TRANSFER OF HANDWRITING/MAKING CHANGES
The pen records your writing with a tiny camera located near the tip, so the pen must be held correctly for the camera to align with your writing. I wrote five complete pages in the included mini-notebook both in print and in cursive to see how the camera and app handled things. The app transferred my handwriting flawlessly. Holding the pen correctly was intuitive.

However, you can also write with Bluetooth off as long as the pen is turned on. The pen keeps what you write in memory until the next time it pairs with the app, then it transfers everything seamlessly. I tried this and found it worked very well. I didn’t need to do anything to get the text to transfer; it just went as soon as the pen paired with the app.

The only hiccup came when I wrote out a long word, “preternatural,” pausing a few seconds in the middle of the word while Bluetooth was off. The pen transfers to the app in “snippets.” Every time you pause, even for a few seconds, a new snippet is created. Since I paused to be sure I was spelling “preternatural” correctly, it created a new snippet in the middle of the word and in the process, got the order of my text mixed up. The transfer somehow got the last half of the word first, then inserted the following line of text, then put “pre” on the next line by itself (see photo). I wrote several more pages, but this was the only time I had this problem.

I think the snippets feature would be very valuable for taking brief notes, but if you’re journaling or writing out full pages and pause every now and then, it does break things up a lot. It’s not a huge issue, however, because snippets are only visible in the Feeds tab and you can merge them easily. On the Page tab, you can see your entire page as written.

I experimented with a few things while writing and transferring, including getting close to the side and bottom edges of the paper. The pen handled the sides of the paper very well, but you cannot write all the way to the very bottom edge of the paper. If you get too close to the edge, the pen will beep and some text may be cut off. I appreciated the warning, which worked well.

A couple of times I stopped writing long enough that the pen disconnected from the app. To reconnect, you tap the Device Pairing icon on the Smart Paper. Although this didn’t work on the first try every time, it did work after a couple of tries. I’m assuming there may be a learning curve here on how exactly to hold the pen while tapping the icon so I didn’t consider this a big detraction, especially since the pen automatically transfers even if you can’t get it connected right away.

There was one time that I couldn’t get it to connect at all. I contacted Customer Support through Chat and they told me how to reset it (this didn’t take long but did involve shutting down every app on my iPhone) and re-pairing.

CUSTOMER SUPPORT/DOCUMENTATION
In addition to transferring handwritten words to the app, you can convert your handwriting to text. Unfortunately, instructions on how to do this aren’t included in the written instructions provided with the pen, and the feature wasn’t readily apparent on the app menu, either. But I knew it could be done because I’d seen it mentioned in the slideshow when the app first downloaded. I looked online for instructions on how to do this, but the only thing I could find was some outdated information about a third-party app that’s no longer used for the Livescribe 3.

Finally, I found the Help menu in the app. It’s not intuitive to find, as it’s halfway down the “Settings” page. There was an option for Chat, so I tried that.

When I first connected to Chat, I got a message that said the team would reply “as soon as possible,” “here or by email.” This was vague and not very reassuring; however, I could see that there were two reps online, so I decided to wait. After a few minutes, a rep came online. I told him I was having trouble locating the instructions to convert writing to text and asked if he could tell me where those instructions were. I also asked if there was a way to access the introduction that popped up when I first connected to the app. After a little back and forth, he told me how to transcribe.

His explanation was easy to understand and worked, although it didn’t answer either of my original questions on where to locate the instructions. I asked about that again, and the rep sent me a link to the same Quick Start Guide that was provided with the pen – the one that did NOT include instructions on how to convert handwriting. I asked again about accessing the intro, but only got a reply that the link he sent provided an introduction and a guide. Which was true, but it didn’t include any of the information I asked about.

When I pointed this out, the rep confirmed that the link didn’t include the information about transcription, then he sent me more detailed instructions. He also sent a copy of our conversation to my email, but never answered my question about how to access the slideshow again. In the process of writing this review, I went back and reviewed the Settings menu and found a Show Tutorial link. The slideshow is there, and it contains instructions on how to transcribe handwriting to text. I also found a link to Livescribe Support in the Settings menu; unfortunately, that link takes you to support for the Livescribe 3 rather than the Aegir.

I used the Chat function three more times over 2 days for other questions, and each time I got a live, helpful person within a few minutes. One of the reps did mention they don’t recommend using Chat through the mobile device, as it creates multiple cases when the web browser closes.

TRANSCRIBING HANDWRITING TO TEXT
Transcribing handwriting to text was very easy. You just go to the Feeds tab, then left swipe on the handwriting snippet you want to convert. You can select multiple snippets at once and convert all of them at the same time. I was very surprised at how well the app converted my handwritten words to text. I only saw a couple of errors in 5 pages of writing. The Livescribe app performed this task significantly better than trying to do this with the Rocketbook Everlast. You can edit the transcription, but I didn’t so it could be seen in the review.

Line breaks stay as written. Since I was writing in the small 3x5 notebook, the result was that my converted text had the look of poetry. This might be less of an issue if you’re writing in a wider notebook. Some apps handle this differently. My Rocketbook Everlast, for instance, doesn’t insert line breaks at all. I like the way the Aegir handles line breaks better even with the multiple snippets.

The app even corrected words that were not complete on the handwriting transfer. For instance, on one page, I wrote the word “ferocity” too low on the page, so the lower half of the F didn’t transfer. However, when I converted to text, the word “ferocity” was correct despite missing half the letter in the handwritten version.

In the app, your original handwriting “shows through” the converted text as if the page has been turned over (see photo). This is a cool feature because it reminds you that you can swipe back and forth between converted text and handwriting and both will still be there. However, when you send the converted text out of the app, it transfers as just text.

RECORDING AUDIO
The Aegir records audio (“Pencasts”) via the app. There is no recorder on the pen, so unlike recording your writing (which can be transferred later), you must be connected to Bluetooth to record. Your phone also needs to be within recording distance of whatever you’re listening to.

I found this was a little easier said than done. Several times I tapped the Record icon and nothing happened. This may have just been due to a learning curve of tapping with the pen in the correct position; I’m not sure. I was always able to eventually get it to record. My pen also didn’t record if my phone had gone to Sleep mode; I had to wake it back up again. This could be problematic if you’re trying to record something quickly, like if you’re in the middle of a lecture and need more explanation for later.

Theoretically you should be able to tell when you’re recording because the Ready light on the pen turns red during audio recording. In practice, however, the location of the Ready light makes this difficult to see while you’re writing since it’s located between your fingers. It would be nice if Livescribe moved the Ready light higher up so it’s easily visible while writing, both for audio and for general purposes so you can always see if you’re connected to Bluetooth or not. The app also shows a red Recording bar, which is helpful.

After being transferred to the app, Pencasts are easily located. On full page view, the text is green wherever there’s a recording. Tapping on the green text plays the recording (see photo). Individual recordings are also accessible from the main menu, the Feeds tab, and from a separate Pencasts tab. Although I’m pretty sure I saw Pencasts in my Pencast tab at first, by the time I wrote this review my Pencasts tab was greyed out so I couldn’t access them that way. However, they were still accessible from the main menu and from the Page and Feeds tabs. You can also add voice recordings directly in the app after the fact.

ADDING PHOTOS AND TEXT
You can easily add photos to your handwritten or transcribed material by tapping the paper clip in the Feeds menu. The photos are inserted at the bottom of the text. I couldn’t figure out a way to insert them anywhere else, such as between snippets, for example.

TAGS/COLLECTIONS/LIVESCRIBE PDFs
The Quick Start Guide indicates tags can be made while writing; however, the notebook supplied with the pen did not have the tags icon included on the Smart Paper. According to the Tutorial, adding tags can also be done in the Actions menu. Unfortunately, I couldn’t find the Actions menu, so I didn’t test this feature.

There are also menu options for Collections and Livescribe PDFs. I didn’t test these features because tapping on them brought up blank screens with no explanations and there was no mention of how to use them in the QuickStart Menu or the Tutorial.

TRANSFERING FILES
You can transfer files to Dropbox, Evernote, Google Drive and OneNote. These can all be pre-configured in Settings. There are also 3 “Quick Send” cloud service shortcuts that you can configure in Setup. You can also “share” individual snippets in the Files tab via email or message, and you can print snippets directly from the app. I emailed a snippet and it worked without a hitch.

My biggest complaints with the Aegir were the difficulties in initially getting the smart icons to work, which I hope resolves itself with some practice, and the lack of instructions in the app and online, which I *really* hope they fix quickly. In the first 48 hours that I had this pen, I connected with Chat 4 different times because of the lack of clarity, and I still have a few questions. This is a new product, so hopefully some changes are on the way. But overall, I thought the pen worked very well and I’m pleased with my purchase.

title: Almost five stars, but not quite - it's still a decent light and a bargain
text:
I received this is a free review sample. For the price this is a bargain, but there are two things that kept me from giving it five stars. First is this does not use a standard micro USB style cable for charging. That means that unless you can find an easy source of cables with USB A on one end and the barrel connector this one has on the other, you are stuck with a three foot limitation of cable length. I have USB micro cables that are double that, and would have made this light all the more useful. Also, since I am using this as a music stand light if I misplace it for a gig I am out of luck because I do not own a similar charging cable (although I always have spare USB micro cables in my gig bag.) If you intend to use this as a fixed table lamp the cable issue will not be the problem for you that it is for me.

Second, the gooseneck is sensitive. If I bump a music stand with this light clamped to the shelf it will move far out of place. It's not stiff enough to hold if you do plan to use it with a music stand. For tables, bed stands, etc. it should work fine, though.

Here are some of the strengths: the lowest setting of illumination is perfect for stage use or if you want to read in bed without waking your partner up. At the highest setting it is definitely bright when lose in (about 1.5 meters), and - as Goldilocks said - the medium setting is just right.

Another feature is untethered to the charger this will operate for three hours at the brightest setting and half more than double that at the lowest. That means that if you are camping, on stage (or in front of a lectern) without a power source nearby you can still use it.

Finally, the included wall wart has a 2 Amp port for phones and tablets, as well as a 500mA port for charging this light. That is handy and all the more reason why the cable style for this lamp is a frustration - it could have easily been a five star product, and especially at the going price.

title: Decent 4-port USB Hub
text:
USB hubs are one of those computer extras that don't get a lot of attention or thought until one runs out of ports. When needed, though, a hub can greatly expand the USB capabilities of a system. This particular hub is one that comes with its own power supply, which is in my opinion better for most uses.

This is an unassuming little device, about the size of a small harmonica and about as solid. Its small size allows it to take up a small amount of desk space, tucking easily behind a monitor or case (or, if being used with a laptop, behind the whole system). In my specific situation I have it plugged into a laptop with an external monitor attached to it so I have the hub just at the base of the external monitor where it is out of thew way but still easily accessible.

In use, it works as it should. My one real test for the hub was to connect up an external USB hard drive, which does not work well with my other USB hub (coincidentally, also a Belkin product). When I attached the hard drive, the system immediately saw it and assigned a drive letter to it, just as if I connected it directly. This is how a hub should handle such a drive and I was pleased when there was no issue.

The one complaint I have with this hub is that the power cord is not snug. When the hub is moved while attached it is very easy to disconnect it from the power supply. My workaround was to use a twist tie to attach the power cord to the USB cable that attaches the hub to the system, after which I can move the hub without any difficulty.

This is a decent USB hub that works as it is supposed to work. Other than the less-than-secure plug for power I have no complaints.

text:
I got these to replace my HD 280 Pro headphones, also by Sennheiser. I didn't care for the 280's as they didn't make a tight seal around my ears due to my head shape, and being closed back headphones this is essential to the way they function. So I decided on a pair of open back headphones to replace them.

Cue the HD 598. These things are incredible. I have an Asus Xonar DG soundcard, which is by no means high end, and I can hear all sorts of little details that the 280's either didn't display at all, or muffled to the extent that they weren't very noticeable. Not that the HD 280s are bad headphones, they just are made for different purposes than these are.

I had read all over the place that these headphones have lackluster bass. This is not true at all. They don't over due the bass like other headphones nowadays, which seems to be the norm. These simply make bass have the presence in music that it is supposed to, which compared to others makes them seem to have no bass.

I mainly listen to two totally different types of music: Indie Rock, and Classical. Both of these genres sound great. The violin solos in certain classical tracks give me chills at times. While the Indie tracks I can hear every little beat and feel much more immersed in the music.

Be wary that these are indeed open back headphones, meaning they leak sound out, and let sound in. You can hear everything around you, and if you listen to music loud everyone will hear your music.

I highly recommend these if you are looking for a higher end headphone, especially at the great price these have fallen to.

title: Might Be Good For Something Like Hurricane Prep, But Maybe Not Your Daily Driver
text:
This power bank will offer a little bit of everything (USB C charge/recharge, USB A x 2 @ 18W & a 110V AC voltage outlet). And with a 22500 mAh battery, this guy will (should) last across quite a few charges.

So, if you're putting together something like a hurricane kit (hurricane season starts in June), then possibly consider adding one of these guys. In the event of a power outage, you will still be able to charge multiple devices AND use the AC outlet to run a laptop all at the same time.

However, there are a couple of minor annoyances that may prevent you from wanting to use this bank day to day.

There is a handy LED readout to indicate how much juice is left. However, the power bank is designed with a small strap that is just long enough to lay across the readout. So, you kinda need to just mold it enough to stand out of the way.

Also, I had mixed results with fast-charging. Cables that I use all of the time with my Samsung tablet & Galaxy S9+ (not when using the power bank) always detect as fast charging. However, using them on the power bank would start as fast-charging, then clock down to standard charging. Interestingly, when I used the packed in cable that came with the unit (USB C to USB C) this resulted in a sustained fast-charging state.

Also, charging across the USB C cable (which is the preferred method on the Galaxy Tab & S9+) using a USB C to USB C cable yielded no better results than charging across the 18W USB A port (using a USB A to C cable).

So, your devices will all eventually get charged. It really just depends on how fast you need them charged to determine if this unit will fit your needs.

I also had an issue where AC charging (testing an iPhone SE Gen1) would just turn off in the middle of the charge cycle. Now, if there is no device connected to the AC outlet, & you turn on the power to the unit, the unit will remain on for 30 seconds (noted by built in exhaust fan) then automatically power off.

However, when connected to a device (as far as I know as the included docs are pretty weak) the unit should constantly run (at least until your device is fully charged). However, not the case here. The iPhone went from a dead state to 12%, then the bank turned off (with 63% battery life left on the power bank). So, maybe it overheat & shutdown?? Still unsure.

So with those caveats in mind, & a price tag of just under $100 at time of this review, you can decide if this unit is for you. Or, if spending a little more (and sometimes a little less) will yield a more suitable device for your needs.

title: Caveats with your KVM, sir or madam?
text:
I've been using this product for about six months now. I purchased it to allow me to switch between a Mac PPC (MDD dual 1.25 ghz) and a Dell Optiplex PC. I have several mice, but the one I use most is Logitech's MX Revolution. I left one non-cordless mouse hooked up for reasons I will explain later in the review. Let me say that if you are technically challenged, you may find setting this up a bit daunting, but if you are reasonably comfortable with basic networking and the like, you won't have trouble. I don't use the keyboard shortcuts for the switch at present (maybe I will start, now that I think of it), so I can't yet comment on those.

This unit has worked very well for me. It does take some getting used to. The rocker switches on the front of the unit represent each CPU. Press once and release, and the monitor image switches from PC to Mac or vice versa. Press and hold, and your USB devices also switch.

Which leads to caveat numero uno: The USB ports on this baby are only USB 1.1 compliant, so gamers need not apply, or will have to settle for having devices requiring USB 2.0 connections wired directly to each machine. I think this is the greatest weakness of this unit, but that said, I find it livable. I do some programming and have to switch back and forth between PC and Mac fairly frequently, and this switch lets me do that with relative ease.

When switching between computers, there is a lag time as the CPU and monitor synch up through the switch. Also, if you are using a cordless mouse, it takes a moment to activate (Like 20 to 30 seconds). I leave a wired mouse hooked up to be sure that I can wake a sleeping machine, or in the rare event that the cordless doesn't activate (usually solved by unplugging and replugging the transmitter device). Lately I haven't had to use the corded mouse at all.

I had to laugh when I read the review where the fellow states that when typing at above 60 wpm the switch has trouble keeping up with him. I only occasionally hit 60 wpm, and never when filling in passwords, so I guess I'll just have to take his word for it. I will say that I have never experienced any problem with the (Mac) keyboard connection, and I do type fairly fast when I'm replying to emails or writing lightweight material.

The second caveat for this KVM is that with a set of Altec Lansing speakers and a little boom box, the volume on the speakers must be set at less than full volume. The reason for this is that the audio picks up sounds from the computer otherwise. As you drag a window, say, you get an audible "z-z-z-zzzt!" I have found that the speakers work fine if the master volume switch is set at about half, which actually allows them to play at volumes that most non-rockers will find quite acceptable, even when they wish to soar to unusual Mozartian heights for a few minutes. Perhaps this indicates a grounding problem with my electrical supply, but I mention it here so that you are aware.

One last comment on an intermittent, but minor, phenomenon. Namely a thin line very occasionally appears on the monitor (19" LCD). This disappears spontaneously, is really negligible, and in the rare instance that it persists, seems to disappear completely on rebooting either the CPU or the switch. I mention this because it has occurred once or twice, but it is rare and easily fixed. The monitor connections on the included cables are

So why put up with these several negative points? Because reading reviews for the other switches available in this price range, I found none that dazzled without problems. KVM switches seem generally to be a dodgy proposition, and you would be better off with a Mac Pro dual-core laptop and Parallels, for sure. But you knew that didn't you? You are looking at this because you aren't ready to commit the necessary moolah for a dual OS system, and this might just do the trick.

Well, I think you are right, it will. It's been great for me. I just wish that Logitech would upgrade the USB ports on the switch (two for devices, one for keyboard, and one for mouse) to USB 2.0 compliance. That would be cream on our strawberries! It is important to mention that this switch comes with all the cables you will need to hook up to CPU's to one DVI monitor. Check out the price of cables and you will be impressed with the economy of this choice, if you weren't already.

In summary, I recommend this switch to the serious user who is reasonably technically-minded, and who has a specific need for a device like this. KVM's are not perfect, but this one is good quality and is currently providing me with reliable service, thus allowing me to easily switch between systems to carry out different tasks.

Good luck!

title: similar to the Logitech Harmony Elite except without the Harmony Hub
text:
Logitech makes the best universal remote controls and they keep introducing new models that are better and better. If you have half a dozen (or more) remote controls on your living room table and are always losing some of them or forgetting which does what, then a universal remote is for you.

The Harmony 950 appears to be mostly the same as the Harmony Elite, except without the Harmony Hub device. The Harmony Hub can be purchased separately later, though the Elite package is cheaper if you're getting it anyway. The Harmony Hub greatly expands the range and capabilities of your Harmony remote, so you should think twice before skipping it.

Logitech also sells much cheaper Harmony remotes without the touch screen. The main benefit of the touch screen is to program shortcuts to your favorite TV channels and to control more devices than the non-touch remote controls can access. If you always use your DVR or cable box's on-screen channel menu and only have a few devices, then maybe a much cheaper Harmony without the touch screen is a better value for you.

The Harmony is pretty easy to program by connecting to your PC and connecting to the Logitech website. If you have an older Harmony remote, you may be able to transfer all your device settings to this one. The buttons on the Harmony are easy to see, well spaced and give you good feedback when pressed.

Battery life is OK for a touchscreen device, but like your smartphone you will need to recharge this at least every couple of days. Most people will leave the Harmony in the recharging station most of the time, so make sure you have an electrical outlet close to where you will be using the Harmony.

If you're in the market for a universal remote, Logitech Harmony should be first on your list. The only decision you have to make is which model to buy. If you're trying to control a handful of devices (TV, cable box, DVR, stereo system, game system, DVD player), then you really have to ask yourself if the touchscreen feature is worth the big price premium. If you have a "smart home" with remote controlled lights, outlets, thermostat, etc or if your devices are spread around a large room so the IR remote has trouble connecting with them, then the Harmony Hub is a good idea.

title: Focused on looks over function
text:
The Razer Kraken BT Kitty headset is not a serious gaming headset. The lighting effects and cat ears look cool, and it’s Bluetooth so no wires like the original Kraken Kitty -- those are the big pros.

Razer Synapse does not recognize the headset, so if you want to customize it, two different phone apps are needed.

The Razer Chroma RGB app handles lighting options. The Razer Audio app handles sound settings, firmware updates, and changing the auto shutoff timer.

Do I really want to use my phone to manage my gaming headset? No. I consider having to use my phone while I’m playing a game on my computer to be a hassle!

I did find that I could customize the lighting effects with my phone, unpair the headphones from my phone and then pair them with my computer to keep the lighting effects while using with my computer. But that is also a hassle, considering Razer has a program meant to handle this!

Sound quality is just okay -- it’s not great. I’m not an audiophile so it works for me, but I have less expensive headphones that have better playback, even to my inexperienced ears. The headphones do not have ANC and I miss that a lot.

The controls are basic, a volume wheel and a power button. The power button can be used to pause and play, just hold it in for two seconds and let go, and the music will pause. Hold in for two seconds and let go to resume.

The headphones don’t have a 3.5mm audio jack, they are only Bluetooth. The charging cable is micro USB.

I have the Kraken Kitty wired headset, and I wanted a wireless version because once I started using Bluetooth headphones, I couldn’t stand being chained at my desk by a wire. But I feel like Razer wanted to appeal to women gamers -- make it pink, slap on kitty ears -- and didn’t focus as much on quality or function.

title: Versatile for users with multiple USB devices
text:
I received this as a review sample and tested the claimed specifications on a few platforms. The following are my observations that, with Debbie Lee Wesselmann's excellent review, should give you a complete picture of this hub.

First, word about using this hub for charging devices. The specs on this product page at the time of this review claim that this hub will NOT charge devices. Actually, it charged my two phones and another device while I was doing other tasks. Perhaps the specs mean it is not intended to be a standalone charger. The only thing that I do NOT like is the wall wart type power supply that is approximately 3x2x2 inches. It can (and does) block adjacent plugs in my surge protector. However, I can live that that considering the functionality I get from this hub.

My favorite feature and the reason I awarded this hub five stars is the integrated electrical safeguards that protect against over voltage, over current, leakage and short circuits. This may not be a big deal for cheap peripherals like mice, but for an expensive hard drive or my Galaxy Note 3 it's a welcome feature.

If you have a computer and peripherals that are USB 3.0 compliant this hub will boost your transfer speeds significantly. For example, my new Samsung Note 3 will transfer at the 5gbps speed, but frankly I do most of my data transfers over WiFi. However, if you wanted to attach an external 3.0 hard drive to your laptop this hum will allow it to operate to it's full potential - which is lightning fast.

Set-up is easy. You literally connect the included power supply, plug it into your system's USB port and switch it on. All of platforms with which I tested it immediately recognized the hub and the things I plugged into it (which included a flash drive, mouse, two snart phones (Galaxy Note II and Note 3), and a speaker that is powered by USB.

This hub works with Windows 98 (I have an old Sony running it and this hub plugged in and worked with it), and above. I know it works with Win XP, Vista and 7 because I also tested the hub on those platforms. I do not have access to a Windows 8 system so am taking the manufacturer's word that it works on that too. If your experience is different please leave a comment.

One final feature that makes this a five star hub in my opinion is the fact that this will simultaneously support maximum data transfer of up to four high speed devices (three of which can be USB 3.0) plugged into it. Of course the host system needs to be USB 3.0 too, but the hub will sling data as fast as the host can accept it. Not all hubs will operate in this mode, and I suspect that the external power supply has something to do with that level of performance.
