title: With a little (LOT!) of help from "Mike", we couldn't be more pleased with our new set!
text:
If you're seeking a technically fluent description of the 48" Sony we just received yesterday, this most definitely is NOT the review you need, so please just move right along to a better one! My husband and I missed the technological revolution big time, and consider ourselves very fortunate that I have a techie brother to help navigate us through all of today's terminology, gadgetry, etc. We don't know the difference between a "Bluetooth" and a tooth ache... at this stage of the game, we're just older folks with simple needs who oftentimes (ALL the times?) feel lost and rely on the expertise (and patience!) of my (much younger) brother when it comes to things like computers, cell phones, TV's, etc. When our TV went out a couple of weeks ago, we found ourselves longing for the days when all you needed to know about a TV was how to plug it into the wall socket! If that rings a familiar bell with you, then read on.

We recognize that it's because of the amazing advances in technology that we have TVs like this Sony, with its beautiful, clear picture unlike any set we've ever experienced... now that it's functioning (thanks to little bro!), we absolutely love this set! We live on a fixed income, so I did a simple google search of "5 best TVs under $500" which popped up a couple of Vizio models, an LG, a TCL, and this one. But here we go again... terms like "UHD", "LED", "HDTV", "ROKU", "Ultra HD", "Smart TV" are Greek to us! We knew the name "Sony" though, and the review talked about it being a best seller because of its clarity, high resolution images, and 48" screen size which is rare in its price range (things we understood!), going on to say you can use its USB ports to plug in your Chromecast or Fire TV and its HDMI to connect it to your other devices and gaming consoles, but that you don't need any of that because it comes with built in wifi, allowing you to stream Netflix, YouTube, etc. (we didn't understand ANY of that!) With the blessing of little brother, we forked over our $453.44 (kicking myself that I hadn't clicked that "submit order" button when the price was $427.44!)

When it was delivered, I couldn't believe how light it was! (We thought we'd died and gone to heaven back in '09 when little brother bought the "latest & greatest" and donated his old '97 Mitsubishi big screen to us... at 3'-8"W, 4'-3"H and over 1 FOOT depth, we dubbed it "The Monster" - that was the TV that finally bit the dust after serving valiantly, so - needless to say - getting the same width in a TV that was only going to take up 2'-5"H, including its 3"H stand... which I actually attached myself!, and a screen just ONE-HALF INCH thick (the base is 10-1/4" long... we weren't interested in the wall-mount feature) seemed incredible to us. I'd been a bit concerned about such a "big ticket" item being shipped to us versus picking it up at the retail level, but it was very securely packaged/protected.

BUT... if you're a dinosaur like we are, you'll panic at the brief illustrated "Setup Guide", accompanied by the 54 page Operating Instructions manual! That's when we called little brother (oh, heck - his name is Mike!), and he barely looked at the instructions as he began hooking things up (we needed our DVD player connected as well so we were ready for our shared bowl of popcorn with the grandkids while watching their favorite during the next sleepover). One thing he almost immediately realized is that we needed a... well, $20 "6 ft High-Speed HDMI Cable" is what the Radio Shack receipt says! Quick run to the store, then paging through our cable remote's instruction manual to get everything in sync. Took 2-1/2 hours (of course, that included the store trip and a lot of chit chat over a couple of cold ones!), and though I don't know HOW he did it, all I can say is we are enjoying the heck out of the results! But if you're technically disinclined, make sure you have your own "Mike" on hand lend an assist (ours is already spoken for!)

title: Stops working after little use
text:
This worked great - for a little while. I've had this monitor for about three months. I used this monitor about 2-3 times a week. It worked great for about six weeks but then became unreliable. As long as my heart rate was in the 100-120 range it gave an accurate reading but if I worked any harder than that, the heart rate displayed would actually go down - sometimes as low as 40. This '40' would be displayed on my watch at the same time I could hear my heart pounding fast in my ears.

Over the next several weeks it became less and less reliable. Now I've just given up. I can't figure out how to return it for refund. It's not worth the money if it only works for six weeks.

ETA 26-Jun-2011

I tried replacing the battery hoping that was all it was but after I put the new battery in, the device would no longer pair to my watch at all. I searched the Garmin website to see if I had some recourse and it shows they guarentee their stuff for one year and I could return the device, get an RMA number, and get a replacement. I did this a few times before with cell phones and once with a TiVo so I decided to give it a try. It turned out to be very straight forward, after a few questions from the Gramin rep clearly establishing my HRM was toast they offered to replace it and didn't even make me send in the old one. The new one came within four or five days and has sucessfully paired with my watch. I'm taking it out for its first workout later today. Hopefully it won't die within months too. I'll add another edit if it does.

So, Garmin gets an A++ for customer service and standing behind what it sells. It gets a wait-and-see on reliability.

ETA - 12-Aug-2011
It worked for awhile and then the same issue re-occurred. I know I can ask Garmin for another new one but what is the point if they stop working within months? The conditions I used it in were pretty rough - extrememly hot and humid conditions for 5 plus hours at a time. But, if a heart rate monitor isn't rugged enough to deal with some sweat and humidity, what is the point. Great idea but technology fails. Hopefully a better product will come out soon. Changing my stars back to only one star. Sorry Garmin.

ETA - 21-Nov-2011
I really needed a heart rate monitor for a trip I was taking in Sept, so I went ahead and purchased the basic garmin HRM. The cheaper HRM is larger and the plastic bites into my skin some and is less comfortable - but it works - and that's what really counts. I've been using the cheaper less comfortable model since early September. I use it around 3 times a week. Once a week for 3-5 hour hikes. No issues so far.

title: Great For Basic Photography, But Not A Pure Daylight White
text:
There are various reasons why everyone wants to have lighting for camera work. My daughter and I have had a jewelry and pottery business we wanted to start but with everything going berserk two years ago, we put a hold on it all.

In the meanwhile, my perfect light that I love which goes on my camera shorted out. That made me frustrated. This light is larger, but I figured I can set it up on a tripod.

HOW THIS COMES
This comes in a box with a foam liner. There is a Type C connector for charging , a cord, and a screw on adapter for a tripod or on top of a camera if your camera can handle it.

CHARGING
This took me a while to charge it. After I left it in overnight, this was fully charged.

BATTERY
I purposely charged this up and did not use it for a few months. This battery was still up near 10 hours at 10% lighting on 5600K when I started it up. That is a great power retention. Using it, I get a few hours out of it before I recharge and I use it at less than 50% usually.

LIGHT COLOR
For all of the colors provided by this light, they are great. What I got it for, however, was jewelry and pottery photos so I am not going to be using the RGB lights very much except for advertising photos perhaps.

WHITE LIGHT COLOR
The white light color is kind of frustrating for me. I like to have natural lighting that does not add color to the photos. That means that in my situation, anything above 50% is too bright. This light only goes to 5600K in cool tones, but when I use it under 50% it still has some green/yellow to it. Yes, I can edit it out with color adjustments in my software, but it is a bit frustrating.

Some photos work out well, but others not so much. I do like a bit of yellow in my photos, so I will pull it down a little bit toward lower K value if I want warmer tones (aka sunlight type)

CONTROLS
The controls are easy to use and I like that it is mechanical and not software driven. The battery left is shown clearly and the settings are also lit up well.

WEIGHT
This is a heavy light. It is twice the size and weight of my other light so I can not put it on my camera. I use a tripod instead.

CASE
This does not come with a hard case which disappoints me. It has a cheap velveteen bag with no padding. It is nice, but you will need a case to keep this in for protection along with your camera.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This light is not bad. It give me some settings to work with on my jewelry. I would like it better if it was just a bit cooler in capability (higher K). As it is, I use it, but sometimes I find myself adding other lights to balance out the tint of this one.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. This is nice, has nice battery capacity and retention of charge, but the light white color is not quite as nice as I was hoping for. It still is decent and I use it.

title: Good quality images from a distance
text:
The first nice thing about this system is it was easy to set up. The 4 cameras have strong bezels, and the power cords are long making it easy to find a power outlet. The base station is simple to configure once you view and understand all the pages, but it would be worth your while to download the wireless NVR pdf manual and view on your computer as it is much easier to read. There is also a C199.pdf to download about the wireless camera and in more detail using the phone app. The Base station also has a beep alarm on it for when a camera is showing movement. This works very good and even the slightest movement will signal the Beep Alarm. However, the beep in my opinion is not loud enough and should have a volume adjustment... If someone is intruding we want to know about it.

With regard to distance: The first picture I included taken with this camera system shows our mother’s home across the street from a window at our home. The base station and camera were positioned at the same level in our home at the back of our house about 100 feet away from our mother’s house. We were surprised at how clear and colorful the image was. This was a great test for showing the quality at that distance, and the video signal strength was showing at least 2 bars. The second picture was taken with one of the cameras placed in our basement which was 100% dark at the time and no lights on downstairs at all. The camera was in infrared mode as they do automatically when lighting is low. In this case the base station and camera were about 80 feet apart, with the base on the main floor of the home and the camera in the basement. This was another good test for wireless distance comparison as well as image quality in low or no light, and the video monitor of the wireless camera still had 1 to 2 bars of signal strength.

Another feature of this system is that all 4 cameras have an Ethernet plug, so if you had to mount a camera that was not in wireless range you could connect it to your internet router. As long as your base station is connected to the internet, you would be able to use this camera.

The base station can also be used with only a video monitor and the mouse without connecting to the internet or downloading the AVSS app. The AVSS application is for your computer PC, Apple, or cell phones and can easily be found at the Anlapus website. Our experience with this was the PC software works pretty good on Windows 10 but is slow at capturing video. If you do decide to use the AVSS software, after your account and software is set up you will need to point the Anlapus Base station settings to the AVSS application.

Overall, this is a good system and value. The base will connect to a video monitor by HDMI or VGA. I tested both and did not find a huge difference viewing the cameras. So with all this said and the camera's long wireless range, this Anlapus wireless system offers good security features.

title: Excellent way to get spot-on color
text:
Most times when I'm taking pictures I'm looking to express myself artistically rather than get a 100% accurate capture. So, color accuracy is not my primary concern - I'll play with color in post processing to get the picture to reflect what *I* want to depict, which may or may not be what others see when they look at what I'm shooting.

But, there are also times when you want the color to be 100% accurate. For those occasions, the Color Checker Passport is an excellent tool to have in your bag.

Using it is pretty straightforward if you're comfortable with working with color balancing charts and profiles. There are a variety of color samples and a white balance card that come in a sturdy plastic case. You unfold the case and include it in your shot (according to X-Rite, the chart needs to take up at least 10% of your image).

The case is well-designed so that it will stand up so it can be properly lit. Construction is solid - it will seems like it will easily survive the usual bumps and bruises of being carried around (unlike the more traditional paper MacBeth Color Checker).

The case alone would make this worthwhile to have in your bag, but the included software extends the functionality so you can create color profiles. It's pretty straightforward to use. First, convert the RAW file that includes the Passport in the shot to a DNG file. You can use Lightroom for the conversion or the Adobe DNG converter. You then load the DNG and the software creates the profile that you can use in Lightroom or Photoshop.

If you're a Lightroom user you can use the included Lightroom plug in which streamlines the workflow a bit. Lightroom will convert the RAW file to a DNG automatically, so you save a step.

You can create a profile from a single illumination (one DNG image) or from two different illuminations (2 DNG images). Using two DNG images allows you to create a more flexible profile that covers a broader range.

My first use was to take a shot of my kitchen counters so I could bring a photo to the store to pick out a coordinating paint color. The counter is ceramic tile with a number of subtle shades running through it (and, of course, I don't have any extra tiles to bring with me). The Passport ensured the shots I took were spot on accurate.

The shortcomings are few. The software seems a bit bloated in size, but that seems to be par for the course nowadays. I'd also like it if the case were just a wee bit bigger. Yes, the compact size is a plus, but I think X-Rite was a bit too focused on getting this to be about the size of a passport (which I'm guessing is the genesis of the name).

Excellent addition to your tool chest, especially if you do a lot of production shooting under controlled conditions.

title: Good sound - good price
text:
I'm somewhat particular about my music and my headphones and have specific things I look for. I'll try to touch on those items in this review.

Sound Quality: obviously most important. I look for solid bass (not boomy or hyped). And clear trebles (not sizzling or hyped). These headphones performed okay on both counts although it did seem the bass was a little hyped. I have some expensive headphones that these did not compare favorably to. I also look for general clarity in vocals... here, they did good... nothing nasally or buried in the mix. The exception came when turning on the noise reduction circuit. More on that later.

Comfort: okay, I have a big head (size xxl hat). So comfort is important to me. These headphones are adequate in that regard. I had to extend them fully, but at full extension they fit me properly and comfortably, sealing off around the ear. They did not completely surround my ears as some studio monitors do, but they did cover my ears. The padding is decent and I was able to listen for a reasonable amount of time before they became uncomfortable pressing on the perimeter of my ear. If your head/ears are smaller, my guess is they'd be plenty comfortable.

Noise reduction: I'm not used to using this feature and wasn't sure how to test it, so I simply sat down next to an air cleaner I have in my home and tried turning noise reduction on and off to see what happened. There was definitely a reduction in the noise... mainly in the lower frequencies. It didnt completely eliminate the sound of the blowing air, but what was left was a thinned out version of the original noise. It was definitely an improvement in the level of noise. The only thing I didnt care for was that there seemed to be an impact on the sound of the music also. Again, the noise reduction thinned the music and left it a little nasally.

Controls: straight forward controls. Theres a slider to turn noise reduction on and off and an adjacent button to activate the phone function. Since the phone button was just below the slider, I kept accidentally turning on the phone when trying to activate the noise reduction. Better button placement would have helped.

Overall, I was reasonably impressed with these headphones. Especially considering the price, they seem to do well. They come with a nice, soft sided carry case and needed cables. I expect I'll get some good use from these.

That's because it's far from little; this thing is quite big by my standards. However, considering that the function of a subwoofer is to reproduce low-pitched audio frequencies, I'll accept that fact that it's the size it needs to be do its job well.

Because I live in a multi-family building and have neighbors with which I share walls, I have not been able to crank up the volume beyond medium. That being said, I have been quite pleased with the bass sound and have not experienced any distortion with this subwoofer at the volume range that I have used. Audiophiles who do not have cost as an object will no doubt want a more expensive subwoofer than the Sub10. However, for the rest of us who are just looking for a dependable, reasonably priced subwoofer for our sound systems, the JBL Balboa Sub10 is a worthy contender.

🎧 The plastic ear tips, which are super comfortable for my tiny ear holes, eventually broke down — as aging plastic will do. I replaced them with BLLQ Replacement Ear Tips, which are nearly identical to the originals [[ASIN:B07FF9DN5K BLLQ Replacement Ear Tips]].

💵 They're $20. BT 4.1. So not the newest Bluetooth, and I'm sure Bose sounds better. But at this price point, I love these little guys.

🏆 Actually, I got them on a lightning sale for $13, so even better! So I paid $20 for the earbuds AND replacement tips.

🌚 I still want something new because I just want something new, you know. But knowing the disappointment I always feel with my attempted replacements, I'll probably keep using these sweet little babies.

🔊 I don't know what the heck they're talking about with the "noise canceling" in the product title. There is no ACTIVE noise-canceling, but the earbuds do form slight seals, which have a passive noise-canceling effect. I think I actually bought them for noise-canceling, but whatever. It's overrated as a feature unless you are willing to pay hundreds of dollars.

In sum, these are great earbuds, especially if you're prone to losing things and hate to feel heartbroken about losing something expensive.

title: I am very easily able to maintain

I own 2 of these 16 port switches housed in a wiring cabinet in a closet and another, a [[ASIN:B00MPVR50A NETGEAR 8-Port Gigabit Switch (GS108)]] at my computer desk mounted to the wall, and an, [[ASIN:B00MPVR50A NETGEAR 8-Port Gigabit Ethernet Switch (GS108)]] behind the LR TV, then another 3 separate bedroom TV's (kids and my br) have [[ASIN:B002NVOLGI Netgear GS605 5-Port Gigabit Ethernet Switch]] behind them for all the various game systems, video devices etc. I purchased them to upgrade my network from older legacy 10/100 switches a few years back. I have always trusted NETGEAR, mainly because it was used by an old employer of mine. I am very easily able to maintain, GB transfer levels, and all devices on my network are able to pull great speed tests.

I used the switches to segment my network into logical groups, the cabinet, holds the main switch's that run to things like the modem, router, alarm panel, other WiFi AP's, and they connect to my other switches.

One pro tip if you have young kids in the home, make sure and keep the network switches where they (young kids) cannot plug cords into it. At the time my 4 or 5 year old decided he would help dad by plugging the loose end of a cat5 cable into a spare port on the switch. You can guess it wreaked havoc on my system causing crashes etc.

These have held up well to years of use and show no signs of letting me down. I will certainly buy NETGEAR again.

title: Fujifilm FinePix F70EXR Digital Camera
text:
This is a high quality camera, but you must take time to read through the owner's manual to understand how to get the best pictures. You can just grab it and point and shoot using it while in the "automode" setting, but the resulting pictures may leave you a little disappointed depending upon the photographic conditions. To get the highest quality photos you must become familiar with how this little beauty works. Unfortunately, you might have to print out and tote the manual with you when you find yourself in situations where your pictures aren't what you'd like, or you can't figure out how to do certain things like know what's behind the flashing icon error message, or how to simulate different types of film, or can you choose between clarity, reduced noise and dynamic range? This is not really a simple "point and shoot" camera and all images will turn out great. You will have to study it, practice with it, and most of all have patience and you will be pleasantly rewarded for your efforts. Though the indicators vary with camera settings, there are 23 different indicators just for shooting mode, and 12 for playback mode, not to mention the date/time stamp, battery level, and indicator. It can get confusing.

Although a basic manual booklet is included with the camera, a much more detailed manual must be uploaded from the enclosed CD and then all 125 pages can be printed out or read from your computer monitor. The manual covers all the material in the booklet almost page for page but includes much more information about features the booklet leaves out and the booklet will refer you to specific pages in the manual for more information. Also, in the manual are about 50 FAQ's that are very useful. I am a manual reader, (having written many technical SOP's) and appreciate having well-written and well thought out manuals that are understandable and succinct. Though I would have preferred a manual that I don't have to upload to my computer, it is well-written and many useful pictures are included.

This camera is loaded with many different options/features but accessing and understanding many of them will require reading the manual. For people who don't want to be bothered with all the bells and whistles this camera may be more than they need. I can see very serious photographers using this camera. Reading through the manual I have compiled a list of some of the various modes, options and features available:

Digital Zoom
Movie Mode
Silent Mode
Variable ISO settings
Image size selection
Aspect Ratio selection
Intelligent Face detection
Scene Position
Shooting Modes
EXR Mode
Film simulation
Dynamic Range
White Balance
Continuous Photography
Photometry - multi, spot, average

Playback Options:
Erase
Slide Show
Red-eye Removal
Image Rotation
Protection from accidental deletion
Crop
Resize
Voice Memo
Print Order
Time Difference
Format

Pages 37, 67-68, 86-87, 97-103, and 104-107 would be good to print out and keep with your camera as they contain tables of various camera functions and a trouble shooting chart.

I have taken many pictures and movies inside and out, light and dark, with this camera set on various settings. And though I have practiced with it now for several weeks, I still need to often refer to the manual when I choose to vary from automode. Some things I have found especially desirable are:

Silent Mode - I attend classical music concerts where flash photography is prohibited. This mode will silence all beeps and flashes.

Large viewing screen on the back of the camera. It is exactly 5.5cm x 4.0 cm.

Digital Zoom - extremely good. I attended a local minor-league baseball game and sat far away on the grass well beyond the playing field. I was able to fully zoom and still get good, clear, close-up shots of the players with no blurring.

Movie Mode - Completely surpasses any other I've experienced so far. Images are clear, colorful and the sound quality is excellent. Camera noise was heard and recorded while using the "zoom" function in Movie Mode though it was not very loud.

Multi-frame play back function is very useful to quickly scan for a particular picture.

Fine Pix Viewer Program was very easy to install on my computer. I use Windows XP.

Very good photography in low-light conditions.

Also some things I did not find particularly desirable but are not major flaws:

I cannot directly burn a CD using the Fine Pix Viewer Program which comes with this camera. I have to use another camera program, import the pictures into it and then burn a CD.

Very easy to accidentally turn it on or off and easy to get misfires.

The zoom lever is too sensitive. I have learned with practice to barely move it very slowly.

The camera does not give helpful suggestions on how to get a better picture as does my HP R717.

Not HD capable.

The higher the ISO the grainier the picture though a higher ISO is desirable when shooting in dim/low light levels. I have set the ISO level to 200 and that seems to produce the best pictures so far.

Almost too many options, modes and functions to choose from. Though you can immediately begin to take pictures using Automode, it will take time to fully understand the many other aspects and features this camera has.

In Summary:

I can find no major complaint concerning this camera. It takes excellent clear and colorful photos even in situations where I least expect it - indoors with no flash. Any poor quality pictures I have taken are not the fault of the camera but due to the photographer's ignorance of how to use/understand properly the many features of the camera. The basic mechanics of such things as battery and memory card installation are very easy. Battery charging is a very simple process and battery life seems long. The manual is detailed and covers more than I would probably care to know. This is almost more camera than I need, though I will continue to use it and will update this review as necessary.

UPDATE 2.9.15 - Been using this camera all these years and now it's beginning to show it's age and giving me some problems. The viewing screen on the back has a vertical big black bar but it doesn't appear on the actual pictures. And the lens cover doesn't always completely open when the camera is turned on. I still use it but it might be time to think about a replacement. It's been good though so I really don't have any complaints.

title: Works well in Dell Optiplex 9020 SFF computer, but reconfig of rear connector brackets required.
text: My video card came with the full height rear connector metal bracket installed. The card itself fits into the PCI-e motherboard connector, but this rear connector bracket extends beyond the computer's chassis.  Use the two half-height rear connector metal brackets (included) for Small Form Factor computers instead. My card came with two half-height metal connector brackets; one for the hdmi and dvi connector, and the second for the vga connector.  I removed the default full height metal connector bracket from the video card, (this bracket uses 3 connectors; dvi, hdmi, and vga).  I installed the hdmi/dvi bracket on the video card and I rerouted the card's VGA cable and connector to the adjacent rear connector slot using the 2nd half height metal bracket.  Booted computer and loaded the Nvidia drivers, then shut-down and I disconnected the vga cable and installed a hdmi cable between the video card and monitor.  Computer then came up fine on the hdmi connection.  I'm using it now to write this review.  And this great priced video card sure beats the computers embedded video controller!  Thank-you!

title: Great stands for heavier than average monitors
text:
I purchased these stands to support my Yamaha HS80M monitors (each about 35 lbs, from Amazon). They are very stable, and I particularly like the range and quality of mounting options. I use HS80Ms with my Roland RD700GX piano, and 26" stands put the tweeters right at ear height, where they should be.

I purchased (from Amazon, where else?) some E-Z LOK Threaded Inserts For Soft Wood, and inserted them into the center-base of each speaker. That allowed me to rest the speakers on the 4 adjustable studs, while having a screw to make sure the speakers stayed in place, and were safe from being knocked off the stands. The mounting plates on the stands are already pre-drilled for this (and almost any other speaker mounting configuration) so mounting was straightforward. This method of mounting provides (I feel) the absolute greatest acoustic isolation possible for the monitor (much better than sticky tape or wood screws, both of which invite speaker cabinet coupling with the stand). I've uploaded photos to show how I mounted the speakers on these stands.

The two steel tubes that hold the monitors are very solid, yet are isolated from the top plate with cork disks, and from the floor plate with rubber. They can be filled with sand for further damping (I didn't do this, as it seemed a bit excessive and messy ... but you could).

I can't think of any 'cons' with respect to these stands. Someone mentioned that they need instructions; but simply go to the Sanus website to download instruction PDFs and you have all you need.

Appearance = A+. Yamaha's monitors are black, and the speaker stands perfectly match the speakers. I purchased these on sale for $99 for the pair, which is very reasonable for this level of quality. I can't imagine that I could ever improve on these stands for my objectives, and am very happy with my purchase.

Reasonable protection. I have the Apple Smartcover and Smartcase on my 12.9 IPad Pro. I like it. It's very light, has a stand, but does
not offer much in the way of protection. It's also very expensive, for what it is.

Cons. I was shocked that it does not have a screen protector. On the plus side, not having a screen protector maximizes enjoyment of the screen. Nothing to peel off either. If you add a screen protector, you increase the risk of leakage. If water isn't a concern, then add a screen protector. A stand feature would have been nice.

Other: The directions say to perform a water test before the first use, every 3 months, and before an expected water inflow, such as boating. A you tube video was very helpful. Otherwise, I would have thought I was missing a screen protector. There are some good amateur videos demonstrating an IPad Air installation. Same process.
